# Legacy data defects

Every defect found in the 2026-08-21 dump, with its size and what to do about it.
Reproduce with `./tools/legacy/audit.sh` — every number here comes from that script.

Severity: **BLOCKER** stops a reconciliation gate · **HIGH** loses or corrupts data
· **MEDIUM** degrades a feature · **LOW** cosmetic.

<a id="1"></a>
## 1. `v_id` is not the voucher key — **BLOCKER**

| Key | Distinct | vs 1,848 rows |
|---|---|---|
| `v_id` | 648 | ❌ merges 1,200 |
| `(v_id, v_typ)` | 1,840 | ❌ merges 8 |
| **`(v_id, v_typ, ac_yr)`** | **1,848** | ✅ |

`v_id` restarts per voucher type, so the same id exists as a PMNT and a JRNL.
Joining on it alone silently merges unrelated vouchers.

> **Correction.** `docs/migration-profile.md` first reported the key as five
> columns including `br_code` and `rt_code`. That is wrong — those two are dirty
> (defects 4 and 5) and cannot be part of a key. Grouping by them splits vouchers
> apart and reports 838 false imbalances. **Three columns, not five.**

**Do:** key on `(v_id, v_typ, ac_yr)` everywhere; carry all three into `legacy_id_map`.

<a id="2"></a>
## 2. Eight vouchers with blank scope columns — **BLOCKER**

Eight JRNL headers carry blank `ac_yr`, `comp_code = 0`, blank `rt_code`. They are
real: each has its own detail lines, each balances exactly, and their dates and
amounts differ from the well-formed JRNL 1–8 beside them. Together: **₹21,025.82**.

Any filter on `ac_yr = '2026-2027'` drops all eight and the trial balance never ties.

**Do:** derive `ac_yr` from `date1`, set `comp_code = 1`, `rt_code = 'R001'`.

<a id="3"></a>
## 3. One voucher out of balance by ₹0.01 — **BLOCKER**

```
JRNL 312, 2026-05-16 — a Paytm settlement

  credit  PAYTM PAYMENTS SERVICES LIMITED    214.14
  credit  PAYTM PAYMENTS SERVICES LIMITED    295.00
  debit   CREDIT CARD EXPENSES               431.48
  debit   INPUT IGST                          77.67
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  debits 509.15   credits 509.14   out by 0.01
```

> **Corrected.** This first named `v_id 312 PMNT, 2026-06-23, 1571.15 / 1571.14`.
> That came from grouping on `v_id` alone, which merged the payment and the
> journal sharing that number and reported the wrong one's figures — the same
> trap as defect 1. Confirmed against the migrated data: 1,847 of 1,848 vouchers
> balance, and this is the one that does not.

1,847 of 1,848 balance. This one does not. It is the float problem made visible —
exactly what `rupees.Amount` exists to prevent going forward.

**Do:** repair explicitly with accountant sign-off. Never round it away silently:
reconciliation check #4 requires every voucher to balance.

<a id="4"></a>
## 4. Detail scope columns disagree with their headers — **HIGH**

**597 `voucher_detail` rows** have `ac_yr`, `br_code` or `rt_code` differing from
their own header. 22 rows have blank `ac_yr`, 58 blank `br_code`, 22 blank `rt_code`.

**Do:** treat the header as authoritative. Never read scope from a detail line.

<a id="5"></a>
## 5. Branch encoded two different ways — **HIGH**

`voucher_detail.br_code` holds `B001` (the code), `1` (the numeric `brid`), and
blank. **495 rows carry `1`.** `voucher_main.br_code` is always `B001`.

**Do:** normalise `1` → `B001` and blank → header value during the transform.

<a id="6"></a>
## 6. Duplicate barcode — phantom stock — **HIGH**

Barcode `86065435` exists twice in `barcode_main` (ids 96399, 96409), both
`gw = 0`, both `total = 900`, and twice in `retail_all_stock` as `Opening`.

A barcode is the physical tag on an item; two rows means **₹900 of stock that does
not exist**. This is why `retail_all_stock` shows 2,820 rows against 2,816 items.

> The other two repeated barcodes in stock are **not** defects — `retail_all_stock`
> is a movement log, and those are legitimate hallmark issue/receive pairs.

**Do:** delete one copy, with sign-off. Add a unique constraint on the new table.

<a id="7"></a>
## 7. Eight stock items with no purity, item or quantity — **HIGH**

The same 8 rows fail three checks: blank `purity`, orphan `item_id`, `qty <= 0`.
They are unidentifiable stock.

**Do:** quarantine and review individually. Do not migrate silently.

<a id="8"></a>
## 8. Purity code missing from the master — **HIGH**

Five items use purity `SLVPC`, which does not exist in `gold_master`. The master
has 19 codes; stock references 20.

**Do:** add `SLVPC` with its correct fineness — **ask the business, do not guess.**
An invented fineness misprices every one of those items.

<a id="9"></a>
## 9. Zero dates — **HIGH**

`0000-00-00` appears in **20 columns**, ~180,000 values. MySQL 5.x accepted it;
MySQL 8 needs `ALLOW_INVALID_DATES` to even load it; **PostgreSQL has no such value.**

Six columns are **100% zero** and were never used: `address_book_master.rec_dt`
and `.op_bal_dt`, `ledger_master.rec_dt` and `.op_bal_dt`,
`customer_order.checked_date` and `.re_checked_date`.

**Do:** map `0000-00-00` → `NULL`. Drop the six dead columns entirely.

<a id="10"></a>
## 10. UTF-8 bytes inside latin1 columns — **HIGH**

Five party names contain non-ASCII bytes, and they are **not** latin1:

```
C2A0 20 53555348...   →  U+00A0 (UTF-8 no-break space) + " SUSHMITA BHARTI"
...4B415552 09        →  "TARVINDER KAUR" + TAB
```

`C2A0` is a UTF-8 sequence sitting in a latin1 column. **A naive latin1→UTF-8
conversion turns it into `Â ` mojibake.**

**Do:** detect valid UTF-8 sequences first and pass them through; convert only the
genuinely latin1 remainder. Strip embedded tabs and no-break spaces.

<a id="11"></a>
## 11. Voucher dated outside its own financial year — MEDIUM

One voucher is dated `2026-03-09` while labelled `ac_yr 2026-2027`. March 2026 is
FY **2025-2026**. It is one of the eight from defect 2.

**Do:** either open the prior financial year or reassign the date, with sign-off.
The `finyear` value-object tests already pin this case.

<a id="12"></a>
## 12. Voucher dated after the dump was taken — MEDIUM

One voucher is dated `2026-12-05`, nearly four months after the 2026-08-21 dump.
Almost certainly a keying error (`05-12` vs `12-05`).

**Do:** confirm the intended date with the business. Add a future-date guard.

<a id="13"></a>
## 13. Invalid mobile numbers — MEDIUM

**838 of 39,429** populated mobile numbers are not ten digits: eleven-digit
values, numbers with a trailing tab, and genuine international numbers.

> **Corrected.** This entry first said 163 of 4,414, and concluded that messaging
> could reach "about 4,250 parties, not 40,519". That was wrong, and wrong in the
> direction that would have shrunk the SMS/WhatsApp integration to nothing.
>
> The legacy table has **two** mobile columns. `mobile` holds 4,414 values;
> `mobile1` holds **39,429**, and every row with `mobile` also has `mobile1` — it
> is a strict subset. I profiled the wrong column.
>
> **Real coverage is 97.3%**, and 38,591 numbers are cleanly ten digits.

**Do:** migrate `mobile1` as the mobile number and ignore `mobile`. Strip
whitespace, keep valid international numbers, quarantine the rest.

<a id="14"></a>
## 14. Invalid email addresses — MEDIUM

57 of 7,295 populated emails contain no `@`.

**Do:** null them out rather than migrating unusable values.

<a id="15"></a>
## 15. Metal items with zero gross weight — MEDIUM

**144 items** carry a metal purity (non-zero fineness) but `gw = 0`. Inspection
shows most are flat-priced goods — 16 are `GOLD RAKHI` at `rate = 0`, `gw = 0`,
`total = 2000`.

This is **not** necessarily corruption: it is a **pricing mode the data model must
support** — priced per piece, not by weight. The billing screen needs it.

**Do:** confirm which are intentionally flat-priced and mark them explicitly, so
the distinction survives instead of looking like missing data.

<a id="16"></a>
## 16. Stock items valued at zero — MEDIUM

12 items have `total = 0`. They occupy stock but contribute nothing to valuation.

**Do:** review before migrating; they may need pricing rather than deletion.

<a id="17"></a>
## 17. Names differing only by whitespace — LOW

571 party names contain double spaces. These inflate the duplicate-name count
(3,342 names across 11,829 rows) because `"A  SHARMA"` and `"A SHARMA"` read as
different parties.

**Do:** normalise whitespace *before* the dedupe review, not after.

<a id="18"></a>
## 18. Dates of birth in the future — LOW

4 parties have a DOB after 2026-08-21. Harmless except that they will trigger the
Due Date Reminder screen.

<a id="19"></a>
## 19. Birthdays with no year — **HIGH**

Thirteen `address_book_master.d_o_b` values have a **real month and day but year
`0000`** — `0000-09-02`, `0000-08-14`, `0000-11-27`. Someone recorded a birthday
without the year.

This is dangerous rather than merely untidy: **PostgreSQL has no year zero** (it
runs 1 BC straight to 1 AD), so it does not reject these — it silently coerces
them into year 1. My first extract run did exactly that, turning 13 birthdays
into `0001-…` dates indistinguishable from defect 20. Caught by comparing staged
NULL counts against the source.

The day and month are **real information** — birthdays drive the Due Date
Reminder screen — but a `date` column cannot hold them.

**Do:** NULL them in staging (done — `isZeroDate` now catches any `0000-` prefix)
and give the domain model a partial-date concept so the day and month can be
recovered from the dump.

<a id="20"></a>
## 20. Implausible birth years — MEDIUM

317 parties have a birth year between 1 and 1899:

| Year | Parties |
|---|---|
| 1 | 247 |
| 1000 | 60 |
| 199, 200, 935, 975, 979, 996, 997, 1899 | 1 each |

These are valid PostgreSQL dates, so they load cleanly and stay wrong. Only
**7,360 of 40,519 parties (18%) have a usable date of birth.**

**Do:** carry them into staging faithfully, then quarantine at the domain
transform. Do not feed them to the Due Date Reminder.

<a id="21"></a>
## 21. Passwords stored base64-encoded, not hashed — **SECURITY**

All 24 user passwords in `legacy.users` decode cleanly from base64 into printable
text. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption — anyone holding the dump holds every
password.

Ten columns store credentials this way, including `branch_master.br_psw`
(`b001`) and `retail_master.rt_psw` (`r001`).

Two third-party integrations are worse than the passwords:

- **`api_details`** — a Maytapi WhatsApp gateway whose API token sits in plain
  text, both inside the endpoint URL and again in `key_name`. Anyone with the
  dump can send WhatsApp messages as the shop. (Its `password` column is empty;
  the token is the credential.)
- **`whatsapp_profile`** — a second WhatsApp provider at `http://223.196.94.133`,
  a bare IP over plain HTTP, with username `mcjewl` and a six-digit password.

**Do:** carry no password column into the new schema — none is. Ask anyone who
reused their ERP password elsewhere to change it, and rotate the two service
credentials. See `docs/blockers.md` B15.

<a id="22"></a>
## 22. A duplicated item — LOW

`SILVER PICHKARY` appears twice in the catalogue (item ids 1063 and 1156). The
two rows are **identical in every attribute** — same group, subgroup, type, unit,
rate and HSN — and neither carries a barcode. It is a genuine double entry.

Worth contrasting with `COIN`, which also appears twice and is **not** a defect:
those two rows differ in group, subgroup and HSN (silver coin versus pearl), and
one carries 114 barcodes. They are two products that share a name.

That distinction is why item names are not unique in the new schema. Identity is
the item id; a shop naming two products the same way is ordinary.

**Do:** confirm with the business, then delete one `SILVER PICHKARY`. Deleting a
catalogue row is their call, not a migration's.

---

## 23. Opening balances: the ledger's side is not a side — **HIGH**

`ledger_master` carries `op_bal` (the amount, stored as text) and
`op_bal_db_cr`, whose name reads as a debit/credit indicator. It is not one.
Across 785 ledgers it holds:

| Value | Ledgers |
|---|---|
| `Yes` | 389 |
| *(blank)* | 282 |
| `No` | 114 |

Never `Dr`, never `Cr`. It is a yes/no flag whose meaning is not recorded, and
it does not correlate with account type -- `No` covers 45 asset, 64 liability
and 3 expense ledgers; `Yes` covers 49 asset and 11 liability.

**This was migrated as if it were a side.** The first ledger load read the side
from it, and the counts prove the mapping survived intact: 389 `Yes` became the
389 `credit` ledgers, the remaining 396 became `debit`. The load's checksum
summed opening balances by magnitude, ignoring side, so it tied exactly and the
error passed unnoticed.

Neither reading of the flag balances the books -- debits and credits come to
₹24.55 crore against ₹8.93 crore whichever way round it is mapped.

**The real source is `ldgr_open_balance`**: one row per ledger per account year,
separate `debit` and `credit` numeric columns, no row carrying both, no
duplicates. 353 rows for 2026-2027. Ledgers absent from it opened at zero.

Cash proves which source is right, because cash is the one ledger whose
correctness is independently checkable -- a drawer cannot hold less than
nothing:

| Source | Cash opening | Negative day-end balances |
|---|---|---|
| `ledger_master.op_bal` + flag | 4,88,217.19 **credit** | 354 of 460 lines run negative |
| `ldgr_open_balance` | 2,51,071.19 **debit** | **none, across all 123 trading days** |

Repaired by `tools/legacy/repair_opening_balances.sh`, which restates every
ledger from `ldgr_open_balance` and asserts the result matches the source per
ledger rather than in total. After the repair 190 ledgers carry a non-zero
opening: 74 debit totalling ₹10,80,37,319.15 and 116 credit totalling
₹26,12,65,922.64.

Two things the repair does not fix, both needing the accountant:

- **The opening trial balance does not balance.** Credits exceed debits by
  **₹15,32,28,603.49**. The missing debit is closing stock, which this ERP does
  not carry as a ledger -- the only stock-named account, `COUNTER STOCK`, is
  filed under *Customer* with a zero balance. Stock in hand comes to
  ₹14,23,61,188.20 across 2,575 items (20,038.936 g), covering 93% of the gap.
  Barcode values are at current rates rather than opening cost, so an exact tie
  was never available. Roughly ₹1.09 crore is unaccounted for.
- **`mcj_ledgers` holds one opening balance per ledger, not one per year.** The
  legacy table is keyed by account year. This is correct while only 2026-2027 is
  live; the first year-end rollover needs a per-year table.

`ldgr_open_balance_final` holds 186 rows for **2027-2028** -- a future year that
cannot be final, and its gap is wider at ₹16.44 crore. Treated as stale rollover
output and not used.

## 24. Forty-seven voucher numbers were never recorded — MEDIUM

Found by building the Missing Bills screen (44). Voucher numbers are issued in
sequence, so an absent number is either a voucher that was deleted or one that
was never entered.

| Series | Gap runs | Numbers missing |
|---|---|---|
| JRNL 2026-2027 | 23 | 32 |
| RCPT 2026-2027 | 9 | 11 |
| PMNT 2026-2027 | 4 | 4 |
| **Total** | **36** | **47** |

**The sales bills are complete.** SALE-GST runs 1 to 224 with no gaps at all,
and the same holds for CNTR, all four purchase series and SALE-RET. That is the
finding that matters most: a missing tax invoice number is a GST exposure, and
there are none. What is missing is internal — journals, receipts and payments.

Individual gaps are mostly single numbers (JRNL 47, 82, 131 and so on) with a
few short runs (112–113). That pattern reads like ordinary deletions during data
entry rather than anything systematic, but the screen only points; it cannot know
why a number is absent and does not guess.

**Needs:** somebody who was there to say whether these were deleted deliberately.
Not urgent, and not blocking anything.

## 25. 1,537 customers are called "CUSTOMER" — MEDIUM

Found by building the Incomplete Data screen (50).

12,026 of the 40,519 address book records share a name with at least one other,
across 3,399 groups. Most of that is one entry: **1,537 records named simply
CUSTOMER**, with USER accounting for another 45.

**These are not duplicates.** They carry distinct mobile numbers — a walk-in sale
entered against a placeholder name rather than 1,537 rows for one person. The
relationship survived; the name did not. They are reachable and they are real
customers; they just cannot be greeted by name.

The rest of the address book's gaps, from the same screen:

| Missing | Records |
|---|---|
| Anniversary date | 38,594 |
| Email address | 33,224 |
| Date of birth | 32,842 |
| Any address | 11,201 |
| Mobile number | 1,090 |

Mobile coverage is the one that matters and it is strong: **39,429 of 40,519
records, 97.3%**, are reachable.

**Needs:** nothing technical. This is a counter-staff habit, and the screen now
makes the cost of it visible.

## 26. Two days where gold was bought back above its selling price — LOW

Found by building the Metal Rates screen (56) and checking the spread across all
143 days rather than the week that was on screen.

| Date | Purity | Sells at | Buys at | Spread |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 15 Jun 2026 | 995 | 15,327.00 | 16,560.00 | **−1,233.00** |
| 16 Jun 2026 | 995 | 15,327.00 | 16,560.00 | **−1,233.00** |

The shop was quoting to buy 995 gold for ₹1,233 a gram *more* than it sold it.
Two consecutive days with identical figures reads like a keying error that stood
until somebody noticed rather than a deliberate position.

These are the only two rows in 2,820 where the purchase rate exceeds the sale
rate. No stock is priced from a historical rate — a bill keeps the rate of its
own day — so the exposure is limited to whatever 995 was actually bought back on
those two days.

**Needs:** somebody to check whether any old-gold purchase was booked on 15 or
16 June against purity 995. Not blocking.

## 27. Ten per cent of sales bills carry a non-standard GST rate — MEDIUM

Found by building the sales register (59) and checking the tax on every bill
against the goods it was charged on.

| Rate charged | Bills |
|---|---|
| 3% — the standard rate on jewellery | 202 |
| **1.5%** | 20 |
| **0.25%** | 2 |

**0.25% is a real rate** — it is the GST on rough and unworked diamonds — so
those two bills are very likely correct.

The twenty at 1.5% are less obvious. They run from April to June across
different customers and amounts, so they are deliberate rather than a slip. Both
halves are present on each bill (CGST and SGST at 0.75% apiece), so it is the
rate that differs and not a missing line.

**This changed the sales bill.** It had hard-coded 3%, which would have
overcharged every one of these. The rate is now chosen on the bill, defaulting
to 3%, with 1.5% and 0.25% offered because those are what the shop actually
used.

**Needs:** somebody to say what the 1.5% bills were for, so the screen can
suggest the right rate rather than leaving it to the biller to remember.

## 28. Sixty-one live customer orders are past their delivery date — **HIGH**

Found by building the order book (65) and comparing each live line's delivery
date with today.

| | Lines | Estimate |
|---|---|---|
| Live work (Process, Urgent, On Hold) | 67 | 49,77,590.00 |
| — of those, past their due date | **61** *(as at 22 Aug 2026)* | |
| — of those, more than a year past | **12** | 17,10,000.00 |

The oldest is order `RP/2223/00194`, due **9 August 2022** and still marked
*Urgent* — **1,474 days** *(as at 22 Aug 2026)*, more than four years.

**Two of these move on their own.** Counted against 23 August the past-due figure
is **63**, not 61 — two more orders came due — and the age is **1,475 days**. The
67 live lines, the 12 over a year, ₹49,77,590.00 and ₹17,10,000.00 are stable.
Anything measured against *today* carries the date it was taken; see defect 101.

This is not a migration artifact: the dates and statuses are as the shop
recorded them. Either these pieces were delivered and never marked off, or they
are genuinely outstanding. Both matter, and they matter differently — the first
is untidy bookkeeping, the second is ₹17 lakh of work a customer may still be
waiting for.

**Needs:** somebody to walk the twelve oldest and say which they are. The order
book now shows them, oldest first, which it did not before.

Separately, **142 of the 284 orders name a customer ledger that is not in the
address book**, so the order book shows a bare code where a name should be. The
order is kept regardless: an order whose customer record has been lost is still
work the shop promised.

## 29. Barcodes are reused — a tag number is not a piece — **HIGH**

Found by building the stock history (68) and looking at a barcode with ten
movements and no tag on file.

The audit trail records a `NEW-BAR` event each time a barcode is issued. Across
its 3,021 distinct barcodes:

| | Barcodes |
|---|---|
| Issued once | 1,047 |
| **Issued more than once** | **1,974** |
| Most times one barcode was issued | **11** |
| Reused barcodes on the shelf today | **1,663** |

**A barcode does not identify a piece of jewellery across time.** Two movements
under the same number may be two different objects, and the majority of the
shop's numbers are in that position.

This is probably ordinary practice — tags get reprinted and numbers recycled —
rather than a fault. But it has a consequence that matters: **the stock history
is the history of a number, not of a piece**, and anything that traces an item
backwards through it can reach a confident wrong answer.

It also puts defect 8 in proportion. That recorded a single barcode appearing
twice in the stock table at the same moment, worth ₹900. This is the same
phenomenon across time and at a scale three orders larger.

**The screen says so.** Ask it for one barcode that was issued more than once and
it tells you how many times, at the foot of the rows.

**Needs:** nothing urgent. But if the shop ever wants per-piece traceability, the
tag number cannot be the key.

## 30. The old permission system was very nearly all-or-nothing — MEDIUM

Found by building the user rights report (70) over the legacy permission matrix.

**81.4% of the 2,755 permission entries are "full control".** The legacy system
offered six levels and the shop used one:

| Level | Entries | Share |
|---|---|---|
| **full control** | **2,242** | **81.4%** |
| entry only | 446 | 16.2% |
| read only | 31 | 1.1% |
| none | 29 | 1.1% |
| without delete | 6 | 0.2% |
| update / delete | 1 | 0.0% |

**Seven of the 24 people had full control on every screen they could reach.**
The widest was 241 screens, all of them full.

Alongside that, from the user flags:

| Able to | People |
|---|---|
| Post into a closed period | **9 of 24** |
| Change the gold rate | 6 |
| Edit a barcode | 4 |

Back-dating and rate changes are the two powers that let somebody alter what the
books say happened. Nine people held the first.

None of this is evidence that anything was done. It is the shape of the control
environment, which is what an audit asks about, and it was permissive.

**The new system starts differently** — every screen already gates read, create,
update and delete separately, and the sale, purchase and clearance screens each
refuse to a read-only user by test.

**Needs:** nothing technical. Worth an eye when deciding who gets what now.

## 31. 1,114 secondary contacts point at a party that no longer exists — MEDIUM

`address_book_sub_name` holds 1,247 additional contacts — a second name, phone
and email against a customer record, typically a spouse or a relative. **1,114
of them (89%) name a ledger code that exists nowhere**: not in the address book,
not in the chart of accounts.

| Sub-contact points at | Rows |
|---|---|
| A party in the address book | 107 |
| A ledger in the chart of accounts | 32 |
| **Nothing** | **1,114** |

399 of the 1,247 carry a mobile number, so this is not empty data — it is
detached data. Somebody's relative, reachable, with no record of whose relative
they are.

**Not migrated.** Carrying 1,114 contacts whose parent is gone into a table that
implies a relationship would assert a link that does not exist. The 139 that do
resolve are not worth a table of their own.

**Needs:** nothing. Recorded because 399 reachable people is the kind of thing
somebody might come looking for, and this says where they went.

## 32. Bank IFSC codes carry the branch name inside them — LOW

`ledger_bank_details` stores the IFSC and the branch in one column:

```
HDFC0000543 (AHURA CENTRE-ANDHERI EAST, MUMBAI-400093)
```

296 of the 389 populated values are a clean 11-character IFSC and the rest have
the branch appended, up to 54 characters.

**Fixed on the way in.** The code is extracted and the branch kept beside it,
which recovered **372 valid IFSCs where a plain copy would have kept 296** — and
a naive 20-character column, which is what the width suggested, would have cut
valid codes into invalid ones and lost every branch name.

## 33. The retail stock ledger counts metal four times on 219 tags — MEDIUM

`cla_retail_trans_bar_detail` is a per-tag stock transaction ledger — one row per
tag at creation, carrying its own `amount`. On **219 tags it records exactly four
times the metal value**, while counting the making charge once.

Barcode `89501233`, a 22 ct gold chain, is the pattern in miniature:

| | |
|---|---|
| 26.740 g at ₹9,300 | 2,48,682.00 |
| Making at 12% of metal | 29,841.84 |
| `barcode_main.total` | **2,78,523.84** |
| `cla_retail_trans_bar_detail.amount` | **10,24,569.84** |

10,24,569.84 = 2,48,682.00 **× 4** + 29,841.84. The multiplier is exactly
4.0000 on all 219, so this is a loop or a repeated accumulate in the legacy
write path, not a rounding artefact or a data-entry slip.

**The inflation is ₹1,82,88,182.61** on tags whose true value is
₹1,41,21,421.30 — those 219 are recorded at roughly 3.3× what they are worth.
Across the whole ledger it overstates stock by ₹1,83,55,013.61 against a
recorded ₹17,12,31,075.39, or **10.7%**.

`barcode_main` is the trustworthy side. Removing the inflation reconciles the
two to the rupee:

| | |
|---|---|
| `cla_retail_trans_bar_detail` total | 17,12,31,075.39 |
| less the inflation | −1,83,55,013.61 |
| | **15,28,76,061.78** |
| `barcode_main` total | 15,28,65,165.78 |
| difference | 10,896.00 — the single `SALE-RET` row |

**What to do:** never value stock from this table. Nothing in the rebuild reads
it, and nothing should start — `barcode_main` reconciles against the pricing
formula and against this ledger once corrected, which is two independent checks
that the tag master is right and this one is wrong.

Note this does **not** move B19. The 241 tags carrying `stk_status = 0` are
*sold* — 232 of them appear on a sales invoice — so they are correctly outside
closing stock, and the ₹1.09 crore that B19 cannot explain is unaffected.

## 34. The monthly payroll sheet does not carry the components — MEDIUM

> **Corrected 22 Aug 2026.** This entry first said payroll ran for 16 months
> **with no statutory deduction at all**, and advised against building PF and
> ESI on the grounds that nothing showed them in use. **That was wrong**, and
> the advice with it. The evidence was `staff_salary_sheet` and its detail
> table; the components live in a third table, `ledger_wise_payroll_detail`,
> which the first table sweep never saw because it had never been analysed.
> The original text follows, corrected.

**The shop does run statutory components.** `ledger_wise_payroll_detail` holds
them per staff member, and every one of its 46 rows carries a real amount:

| Component | Staff | Total |
|---|---|---|
| D.A | 12 | 84,200.00 |
| HRA | 12 | 33,600.00 |
| PF | 6 | 14,040.00 |
| P.TAX | 12 | 1,600.00 |
| ESI | 4 | 466.00 |
| **Total** | **12** | **1,33,906.00** |

They reach the ledgers too. `DEARNESS ALLOWANCE` carries ₹3,22,800 and
`HOUSE RENT ALLOWANCE` ₹1,26,400 over the four months the vouchers cover, which
is the right order against ₹84,200 and ₹33,600 a month.

**So PF and ESI should be built.** Not doing so would leave out something the
shop configures for every member of staff.

`staff_salary_sheet` survived intact: **246 sheets, 19 staff, 16 months** from
April 2025 to July 2026, **₹49,49,100 gross**. `staff_salary_sheet_payroll_detail`
carries a further 209 rows.

### What IS true: the monthly sheet ignores them

Every statutory and allowance field on the monthly sheet and its detail table is
**zero**, while the per-staff configuration above is not:

| Field | Rows | Non-zero |
|---|---|---|
| `pf_amount`, `esi_amount`, `overtime_amount` (header) | 246 | **0** |
| `payroll_amount` (detail) | 209 | **0** |
| `pf_amt`, `esi_amt`, `ptax_amt`, `hra_amt`, `da_amt` (detail) | 209 | **0** |

### They are in the sheets after all — as the gap

A further correction, found while building the screen. `gross_salary` minus
`paid_amount` on the monthly sheet is **the deductions**, not arrears:

| Month | Gross | Paid | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apr 2026 | 2,64,200.00 | 2,48,224.00 | 15,976.00 |
| May 2026 | 2,85,300.00 | 2,69,194.00 | 16,106.00 |
| Jun 2026 | 2,64,200.00 | 2,52,124.00 | 12,076.00 |

Against **₹16,106** of configured PF, ESI and professional tax. The gap runs
about ₹14,500 a month across the history, and falls short of the configured
figure because PF covers 6 of the 19 staff while the sheets cover 15 to 17.

Read the obvious way — as arrears — this says the shop owes its people
**₹15,71,288**. It does not. The salary screen therefore labels the column
**Deducted**, and marks the **96 sheets across 14 months that record no payment
at all** separately, because those are a different thing and adding them to the
same total produces a number that is wrong twice over.

July 2026 is one of them: ₹2,89,200 gross and nothing paid, the month the shop
went dark.

So the components are set up per person and posted to ledgers, but the **monthly
sheet does not record them line by line** — it carries a single `basic_pay` figure with
nothing computed on top, and its 209-row detail table is filled with zeroes.

A rebuilt payroll therefore has to compute each month's components from the
per-staff configuration, because the monthly history does not hold them. The
16 months of sheets give basic pay and nothing else.

**Three of the six components point at ledgers that do not exist** — P.TAX,
I.TAX and D.A, referencing codes 2677, 2657 and 3373. That is blocker B14, and
it has to be answered before the postings can be reproduced. A fourth oddity is
worth raising at the same time: PF, ESI and HRA all point at ledger **3372,
which is `DIRECTORS REMUNERATION`** — plausible for a director's own PF, odd for
twelve people's.

What *is* posted to the ledgers is the salary itself, split across component
accounts — `EMPLOYEE BASIC PAY`, `DEARNESS ALLOWANCE`, `HOUSE RENT ALLOWANCE` —
which is where the empty `hra_amt`/`da_amt` columns were evidently meant to go.

### Don't read a shortfall into this

At first look the sheets appear not to reconcile: ₹49,49,100 of gross payroll
against roughly ₹11 lakh in the component ledgers. That comparison is invalid,
and the reason matters well beyond payroll.

**The accounts cover one financial year, not two.** 1,847 of the 1,848 vouchers
fall in FY 2026-2027 and run from **1 April 2026 to 5 December 2026**. The single
earlier voucher is the misdated one from §7 above. There is no prior-year
transaction history in this capture at all, so 12 of the 16 payroll months —
April 2025 through March 2026 — have no vouchers to reconcile against.

Compare only the four months both sources cover and they agree almost exactly:

| | |
|---|---|
| Payroll sheets, Apr–Jul 2026 | 11,02,900.00 |
| Posted to BASIC PAY + DA + HRA | 11,06,800.00 |
| Difference | **3,900.00** |

So payroll **does** reconcile to the ledgers. The apparent ₹38 lakh hole is the
edge of the capture window, not money that went missing — and any figure derived
from these vouchers is a figure about April to December 2026.

Also worth knowing before building a payroll screen: **7 of the 19 staff have no
ledger in the chart of accounts**, 96 of the 246 sheets record no payment
against them, and the component configuration covers **12 staff of the 19**.

## 35. Twenty-five undelivered orders are priced at rates up to five years old — **HIGH**

`order_rate_master` was never read by any loader. It holds, per order, the rate
for **each of ten purities as at the day the order was taken** — 2,520 rows
across 284 orders.

Its `date1` is misleading: every row is stamped 2026-04-01, the year-rollover
date. The rates themselves are not. Grouping by the financial year in the order
number shows what is really stored:

| Order FY | Orders | 22 ct rate on the order |
|---|---|---|
| 2021-22 | 2 | 4,802.50 |
| 2022-23 | 5 | 5,077.60 |
| 2023-24 | 6 | 5,954.83 |
| 2024-25 | 14 | 7,371.21 |
| 2025-26 | 56 | 12,733.41 |
| 2026-27 | 201 | 14,194.90 |
| **Today's card** | | **14,239.00** |

**25 of those orders are still marked undelivered** (`delivery_status = 0`): 2
from FY 2021-22, 5 from 2022-23, 5 from 2023-24 and 13 from 2024-25. Each carries
the rate card of the year it was taken, and for the oldest that is **a third of
today's gold rate**.

Whether the shop treats that rate as binding is a business question, not a data
one — but it is worth asking before the order book is worked through, because
fulfilling a 2021 order at a 2021 rate means buying metal at ₹14,239 to sell at
₹4,802. This is the same order book as §28, cut a different way: that entry
counts repair work past its delivery date, this one counts customer orders whose
*price* has aged.

**What it costs.** The rate each order was struck at is already on the order
line, so the shortfall against today's metal is arithmetic. Across the live
order book — undelivered work marked Process, Urgent or On Hold:

| Order FY | Lines | Extra metal cost to honour |
|---|---|---|
| 2022-23 | 1 | .00 |
| 2023-24 | 2 | 6,21,530.00 |
| 2024-25 | 6 | 8,50,902.66 |
| 2025-26 | 23 | 25,85,206.15 |
| 2026-27 | 35 | 1,27,534.61 |
| **Total** | **67** | **42,85,173.42** |

Note the shape. The 35 lines taken this year cost ₹1,27,534.61 extra between
them, because gold has barely moved since April. **The 31 older lines account
for ₹40,57,638.81** — the exposure is almost entirely in work that has been
waiting, which is the same work §28 flags as overdue. An order ageing is not a
tidiness problem; it is a priced one.

The order book now carries three columns for this — the rate on the order, the
rate today, and what the difference costs on that line's weight — so the
question can be asked of a screen instead of a query.

### `amount_received` cannot be used, and was rightly not loaded

The same table's neighbour, `customer_order.amount_received`, looks like the
customer money held against each order — 273 of 284 orders carry a figure, and
they sum to **₹14,47,10,446**, of which ₹13,79,74,556 sits on undelivered orders.

It cannot be money received. The **entire order book is ₹2,68,52,217**, so the
field exceeds what was ordered by more than five times. Against each order's own
estimate the ratio is not constant either — 1.08, 1.27, 1.52, 1.71, 2.89, and on
`CO/2627/00041` exactly **10.00**, which has the shape of a decimal-place fault
rather than a payment.

`load_orders.sh` loads `advance` instead, which is zero on all 284 rows. That is
the right call — the order book shows no customer money because **none can be
recovered from this capture**, and a wrong figure there would be worse than a
blank one. If customers have paid advances, that record is not in this data.

## 36. Eighteen tags carry a placeholder metal rate, not a real one — MEDIUM

Found while checking whether stock still on the shelf was tagged at older rates
than stock that has sold. It was — but the tail turned out not to be ageing.

**Thirteen tags were created on a single day, 2025-09-16, at a round ₹3,000 a
gram** for 18 ct, when 18 ct was nowhere near that. Three more, created
2026-04-10, carry exactly ₹1,000 a gram for 9 ct against today's ₹6,199. Round
numbers entered in a batch are not prices; they are a placeholder somebody meant
to come back to.

| | |
|---|---|
| Tags | **18** |
| — of them on 2025-09-16 alone | **13** |
| Understated against today's rates | **₹6,33,930.93** |

One of them is a different fault. Barcode `16237400`, a GOLD CHAIN, carries a
rate of **3.60** and a net weight of **3.600** — the weight was typed into the
rate field. Its metal values at ₹12.96 instead of about ₹44,600.

One of the 18 is probably fine and is left in with its date showing: a 22 ct
GOLD LOCKET at ₹3,000 created in **2016**, when 22 ct really was near that.

### The near miss: 159 silver tags that look wrong and are not

The first version of the report behind this defect used "far below today's rate"
as the finding, and it was **90% noise — 159 of 177 rows**. They were silver,
tagged between November 2025 and January 2026 at ₹46 to ₹63 a gram against
today's ₹253.50, which looks indefensible until the shop's own tags are read in
order:

| Silver rate on the tag | Tags | Tagged |
|---|---|---|
| 60.00 | 141 | Nov 2025 – Jan 2026 |
| 115.00 | 37 | Nov 2025 – Jan 2026 |
| 75.00 | 36 | Nov 2025 – Jan 2026 |
| 100.00 | 22 | Oct 2024 – Jan 2026 |
| **260.00** | **11** | **May 2026** |

Silver genuinely moved roughly **four times in a few months**, and the tags trace
it. Nothing is wrong with any of them.

**The captured rate history only reaches back to 1 April 2026**, so a tag made
before that cannot be checked against the rate of its own day. Being far below
today's rate is therefore not evidence of anything at all. The report now flags
only what is wrong regardless of what the metal cost — a rate that is a whole
multiple of a hundred, or a rate equal to the item's own net weight.

### What this does and does not affect

**Selling these is safe.** The bill re-prices metal at the rate for the day of
sale, not the tag's, so a piece with a placeholder rate still bills correctly —
and the formula self-check passes it, because the check asks whether the formula
reproduces the tag's own recorded price and it does.

**Stock valuation is what suffers.** These tags are on the books ₹6,33,930.93
below what their metal is worth, and that flows into every figure derived from
book value. Screens 79 and 83 show it.

**Needs:** somebody to re-rate those 18 tags at what the metal actually cost on
the day they were tagged.

## 37. One catalogue item was merged away in 2023 and never removed — LOW

`item_merge` is an archive: when two catalogue items are merged the loser is
copied there in full, with a pointer to the winner, the date, the user and the
IP. **40 merges, the latest on 11 August 2026** — ten days before the shutdown —
so this is a feature the shop uses rather than one it forgot.

The merges were done properly. Every winner still exists, and **no stock tag,
sale line or order line anywhere points at a merged-away item.** Whoever ran
them repointed the references.

One exception: **`SILVER KOPPOR STAND`** (item 1139) was merged into
`SILVER DIPAK` (item 215) on **20 September 2023** and **left in the catalogue**.
It is inert — no tags, no sale lines, no order lines — but it is still offered in
every item list, including the tag-creation screen, where somebody could pick it
and start the duplicate again.

It is **not** B17. That is `SILVER PICHKARY`, a genuine double entry under one
name. This one has a unique name, so a duplicate-name check does not see it —
the only thing that reveals it is the merge archive.

**Needs:** delete item 1139, or confirm it is deliberately kept. Deleting a
catalogue row is the shop's call, not the migration's.

## 38. `fine_wt` on old gold is not the fine weight — LOW

`old_gold_purchase` records what came back over the counter: 25 purchases,
534.540 g, ₹50,71,370.00 — tying to the PURC-OG vouchers **exactly**.

Its `fine_wt` column does not hold the fine weight. Of the 25 rows:

| | |
|---|---|
| `fine_wt` = net × tunch, as it should be | **3** |
| `fine_wt` = net weight, with tunch below 100 | **22** |
| Rows with tunch of 100 or more | 0 |
| Fine weight if derived | **437.561 g** |
| Fine weight as recorded | 529.998 g |
| Overstatement | **92.437 g** |

**No money is affected**, and that is the useful part of the finding. On all 25
rows `total = rate × NET weight` — the purity is carried in the **rate**, not
applied to the weight. Dividing each rate by its own touch gives implied
pure-metal rates of ₹13,786 to ₹15,051, which is where the 24 ct buy-back rate
should sit. The shop's arithmetic is sound; `fine_wt` simply plays no part in it
and was filled inconsistently.

**What was done:** `mcj_old_gold_lines` carries gross, net, tunch, rate and
amount, and **deliberately has no `fine_weight` column**. Fine weight is derived
where it is wanted, from net and touch. A column that disagrees with itself on
22 of 25 rows should not be stored as though it were a fact.

Anyone reading `fine_wt` as the metal content would overstate the metal taken in
by **92.437 g**.

**Correction — that is not ₹14 lakh.** This entry originally priced the whole
92.437 g at the gold rate. **54% of it is silver**, and valuing silver as gold
overstates the overstatement by more than double:

| | Overstated | Rate today | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| OLDGOLD (22 rows) | 41.522 g | 16,482.00 | **6,84,365.60** |
| OLDSLV (2 rows) | 50.305 g | 253.50 | **12,752.32** |
| No purity stated (1 row) | 0.609 g | 16,482.00 | 10,037.54 |
| **Correct total** | **92.437 g** | | **7,07,155.46** |
| *All 92.437 g valued as gold* | | | *15,23,546.63* |

The silver line is the whole of the difference: 50.305 g of it is worth
**₹12,752.32**, not the ₹8.29 lakh the gold rate would imply. The severity is
unchanged — no money moves on `fine_wt` either way — but a figure quoted at
roughly twice the truth is the thing this record exists to prevent. Found by
[defect 163]'s sweep of columns whose values disagree with their names, which
led back here.

**How it happened:** the original figure treated a weight as though weight alone
determined value. It is the same mistake in miniature as [defect 135], where
21 carat-less rows of silver sold by weight were counted as stone.

## 39. `b2b_purchase` is an account split, not a registration flag — MEDIUM

`stock_inward` — the purchase invoices, 43 of them — carries a `b2b_purchase`
flag, and on the sales side the matching flag means *the other party is
GST-registered*. It does not mean that here.

It maps **exactly** to which purchase account the goods post to:

| Flag | Invoices | Posts to | Ledger total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7 | `PURCHASE_B2B` | 39,61,244.85 |
| 0 | 36 | `PURCHASE` | 1,94,74,168.96 |

Not one exception either way, and both tie to the ledgers.

**But 17 of the 36 unflagged invoices carry GST**, averaging 1.26%. A supplier
who charges GST is registered. So those 17 are B2B in the sense a return uses
and B2C in the sense the shop's chart of accounts uses, and the two senses are
not the same thing.

Reading the flag as a registration status would put **₹4,02,980.57 of input tax**
on the wrong part of a GSTR-2 — understating what can be set off.

**What was done:** the inward supplies report offers the filter in the shop's own
terms — *Posted to PURCHASE_B2B* and *Posted to PURCHASE* — and names the account
on every row, rather than asserting a registration status the data does not
support. Which invoices belong in which part of a filed return is a question for
whoever files it; the account split is evidence towards the answer, not the
answer.

**Needs:** the accountant to say which of the 43 are registered-supplier
invoices. The GST charged on each is in the report, which is the evidence they
would use.

## What the audit log says actually happened

`barcode_wise_all_transaction` (8,561 rows) spans **2024-04-01 to 2026-08-19** —
about 2.5 years — while every transactional table holds only FY 2026-27.

> **This corrects a claim in `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` §1**, which said there is no
> multi-year history to migrate. There is: 2.5 years of barcode audit trail
> survived, while the vouchers behind it were purged.

| Workflow | Movements in 2.5 years | First → last |
|---|---|---|
| `NEW-BAR` — tagging | 6,395 | 2024-04-03 → 2026-08-18 |
| `OP-STK` — opening stock | 1,770 | 2024-04-01 (one day) |
| `SALE-GST` — sales | 324 | 2024-05-09 → 2026-08-19 |
| `CST-ORD` — customer orders | 44 | 2024-06-12 → 2026-07-26 |
| `SALE-RET` — sale returns | 17 | 2024-08-18 → 2026-06-16 |
| **`ISS-HM` / `REC-HM` — hallmarking** | **4 / 4** | 2024-10-01 → 2025-03-01 |
| `EST` — estimates | 2 | 2025-02-02 |
| `PURC-IN` — purchase inward | 1 | 2026-07-04 |

**This bears on decision #2 (manufacturing pulled into scope).** Hallmarking did
run — 8 movements — so the empty hallmark tables reflect purged history, not an
unused feature. But across 2.5 years of complete audit trail, hallmarking appears
**8 times**, and karigar issue/receive leaves **no trace at all**.

That does not contradict the decision — the business knows its own plans, and the
subsystem may be manual today or about to start. It does mean **Tier F is building
for a workflow with no observed volume**, which is worth confirming before the
~10–14 weeks are spent.

## 40. `item_adjustment` is not a stock adjustment — and it contradicts itself — LOW

The name says stock adjustment. It is a **per-item making override keyed by rate
code** — `per_of_making`, `rt_mk_pr_gm`, `pl_minus_gold` — and it holds no
quantities at all. The seventh name in this dump that points at the wrong thing.

Of its 922 rows:

| | Rows |
|---|---|
| Total | 922 |
| Distinct items | 460 |
| Referring to an item that does not exist | **152** |
| Carrying any non-zero value | **5** |

So 917 rows are zeros, one in six points at nothing, and every row carries the
same rate code, `R001`.

The five live rows do not agree with each other. Item 1066, GOLD ORNAMENTS,
appears three times:

| Making % | Rate/gm | Plus-minus |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 250 | 10 |
| 15 | — | — |
| 8 | 250 | 10 |

The remaining two point at items 657 and 735, neither of which is in
`item_master`.

**What was done:** nothing loaded. A making-override table that disagrees with
itself on its only real item cannot be the source of a price. Making comes from
the tag, as it does everywhere else in this rebuild. Recorded so the table is not
later mistaken for the stock adjustment screen its name suggests.

## 41. The address book and the ledgers both key on `ldgr_code`, and it means different things — BLOCKER

The single worst defect found so far, because nothing about it looked wrong.

Two legacy tables hold people:

| Table | Rows | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `ledger_master` | 785 | the chart of accounts — 772 of them real parties |
| `address_book_master` | 40,519 | the marketing contact list |

Both name their key column `ldgr_code`. **The two code spaces are unrelated.**

| Code | In the ledgers | In the address book |
|---|---|---|
| 1011 | PURCHASE | ARINA INTERNATIONAL |
| 1014 | SALE_B2B | ASIAN PHOTO STUDIO |
| 1016 | SALE | ASIT BRACELETS |
| 3346 | REPAIR AND MAINTENANCE COMPUTER | BIJOY NAHA |

368 code values appear in both tables. **Not one of them names the same person.**
The same customer exists in both under different codes and is duplicated in the
address book:

| Person | Ledger code | Address-book codes |
|---|---|---|
| RASHMI SARAF | 12480 | 52025, 91666 |
| POOJA PRASAD | 12877 | 38624, 92087 |
| P. K. MUNDRA | 4781 | 41953 |

### What it broke

Every loader and the customer picker joined the two on that column.

**The picker on the sale, credit note and old gold screens** offered 368
customers and each one posted to a stranger's account. Choosing BIJOY NAHA
debited REPAIR AND MAINTENANCE COMPUTER. Choosing ASIT BRACELETS debited the
SALE control account — a bill that credits and debits the same nominal.

**547 stored rows** were attached to the wrong person:

| Table | Wrongly linked | Of |
|---|---|---|
| `mcj_bank_accounts` | 193 | 398 |
| `mcj_customer_orders` | 142 | 284 |
| `mcj_sales_invoices` | 107 | 224 |
| `mcj_scheme_enrolments` | 105 | 239 |

The order register displayed those names. `mcj_sales_invoices` also stores
`party_name` captured at the time, and it disagreed with the link on **all 107**
— which is what made this visible at all.

### Why the tests did not catch it

Every seed created a party **and** a ledger with the same code *and the same
name*, so the join worked in the test and only ever failed on real data. The due
dates test seeded a customer name that no assertion read.

### What was done

- Migration `mcj-1787384000` adds `ledger_id` to the three tables that lacked
  it, backfills from the ledger code each row already carried, and **drops
  `party_id` from all four** so the wrong join is not available to write again.
- All four loaders now join `mcj_ledgers`.
- `billableParties` reads ledgers in the Customer, Dealer and Other Debtor
  groups — 567 accounts a bill can legitimately be raised against — and
  `partyLedger` no longer joins anything.
- `taxBasisFor` takes the state from the ledger.
- Tests: `TestSale_DoesNotBillTheAddressBook` seeds a decoy contact on the SALE
  ledger's code and fails if the picker offers it;
  `TestSale_TakesTheStateFromTheLedgerNotTheAddressBook` and
  `TestDueDates_NamesTheCustomerFromTheLedger` do the same for tax and for the
  reminder list.

**Verified after reload:** 284 of 284 orders, 239 of 239 enrolments and 224 of
224 invoices name exactly what `ledger_master` names. The single remaining
difference is `DSTECHNOLOGY` against `DS TECHNOLOGY` — defect 17 whitespace, not
a wrong link.

`mcj_parties` stays as what it is: a 40,519-name contact list, used by the
customer data-quality report and nothing that posts money.

## 42. One voucher is dated three and a half months after the capture — LOW

`PMNT 576`, dated **5 December 2026**, in a dump taken on 21 August 2026.

It is a post-dated cheque and the narration says so: *Ch. No.435590,
Dt.05.12.2026 Issued Against Their Dues*. The voucher is dated to the cheque
rather than to the day it was written, which is a legitimate way to record one —
it is the only such voucher in 1,824.

| | |
|---|---|
| Amount | ₹1,35,370 |
| Credit | UNION BANK OF INDIA |
| Debit | DAYANIDHI TRADE PVT LTD (Other Loan) |

**Why it is worth writing down:** any balance computed without a date filter
already has that ₹1,35,370 out of the bank. A cash book or bank book asked for a
range ending today excludes it and disagrees with the raw ledger total by
exactly that amount. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions.

It touches no customer, so the customer-facing registers are unaffected.

**What was done:** nothing changed. The vouchers that carry date ranges already
handle it correctly. Recorded so the discrepancy is recognised rather than
investigated from scratch.

## 43. Two tags on the shelf carry metal and are priced at nothing — MEDIUM

The shelf is otherwise sound. Across **2,816 tags in stock** there is not one
negative weight, piece count or value, and not one tag whose net weight exceeds
its gross. The legacy screen for this is called *Negative Stock* and against this
data it would report nothing at all.

Two tags would bill as free:

| Tag | Item | Purity | Net wt | Priced |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 43264560 | SILVER BABY BANGLE | SLV | 14.990 g | a fixed amount — of zero |
| 46318302 | GOLD LOCKET | 22 | 1.350 g | percentage of the metal — of zero |

Roughly **₹13,000 of metal** at the rates in the capture, depending on the day.
Scanned onto a bill, each adds nothing to the total.

Two more are priced per gram of net weight and carry none, so they can only ever
come to zero — `42210478` and `96904004`, both **C GOODS**. Those are
customer-goods placeholders rather than stock the shop owns, which is why they
are named separately.

### What is deliberately NOT a defect

**359 tags on the shelf have no weight because they carry a printed price
instead** — gold rakhis at ₹2,000 among them. Flat pricing is how this shop sells
imitation, silver articles and seasonal lines, and reading those as unweighed
stock would bury the two that matter under 359 that are correct. A further 8 are
priced per piece, which also needs no weight.

**What was done:** the screen reports the faults and names the flat-priced stock
it is deliberately leaving alone. Repricing the two tags is a decision about what
the pieces are worth, which is the shop's to make.

## 44. The year-end carry-forward was run on 14 August, not at the year end — LOW

`ldgr_open_balance_final` holds 186 ledger balances stamped **2027-2028** — the
shop's own assertion about where it finished the year that was running when it
went dark. It is the only forward-looking record in the capture.

It was not produced on 31 March. Reconciling each carried figure against
`opening + movement` and sliding the cutoff date, agreement peaks sharply:

| Movement counted to | Ledgers reconciling exactly |
|---|---|
| every voucher in the dump | 164 of 186 |
| 13 Aug 2026 | 174 |
| **14 Aug 2026** | **176** |
| 15 Aug 2026 | 173 |

So it is a snapshot taken **a week before the shop closed**, and any ledger
touched after 14 August will differ from it. That is not an error in the
carry-forward; it is what the carry-forward is.

The residue at that cutoff is 10 ledgers and under ₹6,000 in total, the largest
gap being ₹4,655.56. INPUT CGST and INPUT SGST differ by the identical
₹1,096.18, which is what a consistent tax pair looks like.

One of the differences at the full-dump cutoff is **exactly defect 42**: the
post-dated cheque of ₹1,35,370 to DAYANIDHI TRADE PVT LTD, dated 5 December
2026, which the 14 August snapshot could not have known about.

### It does not balance, and that is B19 rather than a fault

| | |
|---|---|
| Carried forward — debits | 10,62,76,061.42 |
| Carried forward — credits | 27,06,82,293.35 |
| **Out by** | **16,44,06,231.93** |
| The 2026-27 openings, out by | 15,32,28,603.49 (same direction) |
| The vouchers between them, out by | **0.01** (defect 3) |

An imbalance present at both ends and absent from the movement between them is a
missing **asset** side, which is exactly what blocker B19 says: the stock was
never in the ledgers. The shelf is worth ₹14,23,61,188.20 — the same order of
magnitude as the gap, though not equal to it.

**What was done:** loaded as recorded and reconciled, not corrected. A
carry-forward is the shop's own assertion about its position, and **176 of 186
of those assertions are confirmed by its own vouchers.**

## 45. Ten of the eighteen code-list loaders reported success without loading — HIGH

Not a defect in the legacy data. A defect in the rebuild's own loader, found by
adding a nineteenth list to it.

`load_codelists.sh` reloads each reference list as `DELETE` then `INSERT` inside
a transaction, and then checks its work by comparing the source row count against
the destination row count.

Ten of the lists are referenced by other tables — colours by packets, item groups
by items, shapes by stones — so once those tables are populated the `DELETE`
violates a foreign key, **the transaction rolls back, and the old rows stay
exactly where they were**. The counts then match, because nothing changed, and
the loader printed:

```
OK   mcj_colors                        30 rows
```

having done nothing at all. The check could not fail: it compares the count
against itself.

Affected: `mcj_colors`, `mcj_cuts`, `mcj_sieves`, `mcj_stone_purities`,
`mcj_card_types`, `mcj_ledger_types`, `mcj_item_subgroups`, `mcj_item_groups`,
`mcj_shapes` and `mcj_categories` — 10 of 18.

**The loaded data is not wrong.** `load_all.sh` truncates everything first, so a
full run empties the referencing tables before the code lists are rebuilt and
every list loads correctly. What was broken is reloading a single list
afterwards, which is exactly what somebody does when a reference list needs
correcting — and it would have reported success.

**What was done:** the loader now checks the exit status of the write itself
rather than inferring it from row counts, and says so:

```
FAIL mcj_colors    not reloaded — something references it; the old rows are untouched
```

A row-count check that compares a number against itself is worth looking for
elsewhere in these scripts.

---

## 46. Reloading the masters alone would have cut 13,282 rows loose, and reported success — BLOCKER

Found by auditing the loaders after defect 45. Not triggered — the guard below
was written before anything ran.

`load_masters.sh` rebuilds `mcj_items` with `DELETE` then `INSERT`. Ten columns
across eight tables reference `mcj_items`, and every one of them is
**`ON DELETE SET NULL`**:

| Referencing table | Column |
|---|---|
| `mcj_stock_items` | `item_id` |
| `mcj_sales_invoice_lines` | `item_id` |
| `mcj_customer_order_lines` | `item_id` |
| `mcj_stock_conversion_pieces` | `item_id` |
| `mcj_customer_goods` | `item_id` |
| `mcj_designs` | `item_id` |
| `mcj_stock_stones` | `stone_item_id` |
| `mcj_design_stones` | `stone_item_id` |
| `mcj_barcode_edits` | `old_item_id`, `new_item_id` |

So the delete does not fail. It **succeeds**, silently blanking the item on
**13,282 rows** — every tag on the shelf, every invoice line, every order line,
every conversion piece and every stone. The items are then reinserted with fresh
uuids and **nothing relinks them**. The check that follows counts 322 items
against 322 and reports OK, because the item table itself is perfectly fine; it
is everything pointing at it that has been cut loose.

This is worse than defect 45. That one did nothing and said it worked; this one
destroys the links and says it worked.

`load_all.sh` is safe: it empties the referencing tables before the masters are
rebuilt, so nothing is pointing at `mcj_items` when the delete runs. The hazard
is the standalone run — which is what somebody does when one item name needs
correcting.

**What was done:** `load_masters.sh` now counts what points at `mcj_items` and
refuses:

```
REFUSED: 13282 rows currently point at mcj_items.
...
Run ./load_all.sh, which empties the referencing tables first.
Set MCJ_FORCE_MASTERS=1 only if you mean to cut those links.
```

### The rest of the loaders were checked

`mcj_ledgers` has the same six `SET NULL` references — including the four
repaired in defect 41 — but `mcj_voucher_lines` references it `RESTRICT`, so the
delete fails, `set -e` aborts, and `load_ledgers.sh` exits 3 with the data
intact. It fails loudly, which is correct.

Every other loader is a single write guarded by `set -e` and aborts the same way.
`load_codelists.sh` was the exception because its writes sat inside a loop
(defect 45); `load_stock.sh`'s loop only verifies, comparing legacy sums against
loaded sums, which is a real cross-check rather than a number against itself.

## 47. The making ladder records five different rates for the same weight band — HIGH

`item_wise_sale_rate_master` — the Item Wise Wstg and Rate master — encodes a
real and sensible ladder. A small piece costs proportionally more to make than a
heavy one:

| GOLD ORNAMENTS | Making |
|---|---|
| under 1 g | 26% |
| 1 – 2 g | 22% |
| 2 – 3 g | 20% |
| 3 – 6 g | 18% |
| over 6 g | 14% |

**It cannot price anything, because it does not say which row wins.**

95 rows describe only **3 items** and 27 distinct bands. The same band carries up
to five different rates:

| Item | Band | Rates recorded |
|---|---|---|
| GOLD ORNAMENTS | 1 – 2 g | 15 / 18 / 20 / 22 / 26 |
| GOLD ORNAMENTS | 2 – 3 g | 12 / 15 / 18 / 20 / 22 |
| GOLD ORNAMENTS | 3 – 6 g | 10 / 12 / 15 / 18 |
| EXTRA ORNAMENTS | 1 – 2 g | 18 / 20 / 22 |

There is no date, no branch and no status column to choose between them. The
table has eight columns and none of them is a discriminator.

Taking the highest legacy id — the only thing that could mean "most recently
set" — produces the ladder above. It is coherent for the light bands and **still
ambiguous over 6 g**, where three overlapping bands give three answers:

| Band | Making |
|---|---|
| 6 – 100 g | 12% |
| 6 – 250 g | 15% |
| 6 – 300 g | 14% |

**14 of the 27 bands overlap another band for the same item.**

### What is clean

Wastage. All **91 retail (`ID-SALE`) rows carry zero wastage**; all **4 trade
(`B2B-SALE`) rows carry 7–10%**. No exceptions either way. The shop charges
wastage to the trade and not at the counter.

**What was done:** every row loaded, duplicates included — collapsing them would
hide the ambiguity. The screen shows the ladder, marks superseded rows, and names
each band that carries more than one rate or crosses another. **It does not
price.** Making comes from the tag, as everywhere else in this rebuild.

**Ask:** what is the making percentage for a gold ornament over 6 g? Three
answers are recorded and nothing in the data chooses.

## 48. Ornament purchase components do not add up to the bill — MEDIUM

Two tables that had never been read hold what each purchase actually contained:
`stock_inward_main` (21 rows, the metal) and `stock_inward_detail` (39 rows, the
stones). Of the 43 purchase invoices, **11 bought metal and stones, 9 bought
metal only, and 23 bought stones only**.

The invoice's taxable value equals `stock_inward_main.value` **exactly** on every
bill that has a metal row. But the components of that value do not reproduce it:

| | |
|---|---|
| Bills with a metal row | 20 |
| Where `net × rate + stones + making` equals the bill | **5** |
| Where it does not | **15** |

Across those 20 bills the bill value is ₹1,35,68,049.00 while net weight × rate
comes to ₹58,61,360.85, the stones on those same bills to ₹28,94,996.21 and
making to ₹7,50,160.70 — leaving **₹40,61,531.24 unaccounted for**.

Something in the composition is not recorded. Candidates: the `loss` column on
the detail rows, an agreed adjustment, or a rate applied to a weight that is not
the net one. Nothing in the capture settles it.

### What is certain

**521.329 carats of loose stones worth ₹1,27,31,698.71 were bought across 34
bills**, and no screen has ever shown it. The purchase register carries one
taxable figure per bill and no breakdown at all.

**What was done:** both tables loaded, every row tied to its invoice — the loader
fails if any content row cannot reach one. The register shows the components and
the bill side by side and states that they do not agree. **Neither figure is
adjusted to fit the other**: the bill is the authority on what was paid, the
components on what arrived.

## 49. Two customers have their history split across duplicate ledgers — HIGH

Five names appear twice in the 785-ledger chart of accounts. Three are the same
name on consecutive codes — 12777/12778, 12830/12831, 12874/12875 — so somebody
created the account, failed to find it, and created it again. Two differ only by
a trailing full stop, which is why a literal name comparison finds three of the
five and not all of them.

Three are harmless. **Two are not, because both halves carry history:**

### MADHUMITA BISWAS — a savings scheme in two accounts

| Ledger | Scheme | Instalments paid | Paid |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7042 | Gold Plus | 10 of 10 | 10,000.00 |
| 8091 | Gold Plus | 10 of 10 | 10,000.00 |
| 8091 | Gold Plus | 7 of 10 | 7,000.00 |

**₹27,000 of one customer's contributions across two accounts**, one scheme
still running. Whoever serves her sees one account and not the other.

### ASHOK AGARWAL — orders under both

One order under 10990 and two under 8129.

### The other three

PARMESHWAR SINGH has two voucher lines and a bill under 12777 and nothing under
12778. SARKAR ORNAMENTS and SUNITA SHARMA have nothing on either side. All three
merge without moving anything.

**What was done:** the Duplicate Ledgers screen lists all ten accounts, spells out
what points at each — *1 bill*, *2 scheme enrolments* — and gives a verdict that
depends on the other half of the pair. **It merges nothing.** Moving a person's
financial history is a decision with their savings attached, and a test fails if
the screen ever writes.

## 50. The hallmark flag is set by hand and 739 gold pieces carry none — MEDIUM

**739 of the 1,023 gold jewellery tags on the shelf carry no hallmark record,
and they are worth ₹11,54,63,861.86.**

| Purity | On the shelf | No hallmark recorded | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18kt | 505 | 411 | 5,95,69,420.89 |
| 22kt | 319 | 217 | 4,20,34,082.23 |
| 14kt | 165 | 104 | 1,37,93,189.74 |
| 9kt | 34 | 7 | 67,169.00 |

*(The "On the shelf" column originally read 539 / 352 / 196 / 38, which summed to
1,125 against the 1,023 in the sentence above it and matched neither the tags in
stock nor all tags ever made for those purities. Corrected from the data in
defect 342; every other figure here reproduced to the paisa.)*

Bullion is excluded: 112 of the 114 pure-gold (999) tags carry no hallmark and
that is normal, so counting them would inflate the figure and weaken the real
one.

### The number needs its caveat, and there are two readings

Either the pieces were never hallmarked, or they were and the system was never
told. **The second is the more likely**, and the movement trail is why:

| | |
|---|---|
| Tags flagged as hallmarked | 432 |
| Hallmark movements in 2.5 years | **12** (6 issues, 6 receipts) |
| Hallmark charge collected across all 432 | **₹2,915.00** |

> **Correction.** This first read 8 movements, from
> `barcode_wise_all_transaction` alone. `retail_all_stock` — opened later — holds
> **4 more, none of them overlapping** (see defect 57). The real figure is 12.
> It does not change the conclusion: a flag set 432 times by a process that
> recorded six issues is still a flag being set by hand. Its absence therefore records very little, and a screen that presented
₹11.5 crore as unhallmarked stock would be asserting something the data does not
support.

**What was done:** the report shows the figure with the movement count and states
in terms that it is **about the record, not about the pieces**. Whether the shelf
is actually hallmarked is a question for somebody holding a loupe. A test fails
if the caveat is separated from the number.

## 51. ₹8.8 crore of supplier accounts sit in debit, and ₹2 crore of it never moved — HIGH

A supplier account in debit means the shop has paid ahead, or goods are owed to
it. Across the Dealer, Other Creditor and Sundry Creditors groups:

| | |
|---|---|
| Accounts the shop owes | 45, totalling 6,15,02,878.56 |
| **Accounts in debit — the shop is owed** | **17, totalling 8,80,84,874.22** |
| Of those, with **no posting at all** this year | **10, totalling 2,01,01,051.00** |

Two things about the ₹8.8 crore matter more than its size.

**One account is 77% of it.** SHREE SAROJ JEWELSS opened the year at
₹6,98,45,346.00 and closed at ₹6,79,37,571.00 across 13 postings.

**₹2,01,01,051.00 is opening balances that were carried in and never touched** —
PALSANI JEWELLERS PVT LTD at ₹99,86,295.00, VASU DEV JEWELLERS at ₹64,69,284.00,
MEHANDI DIAMONDS PVT LTD at ₹12,63,478.00 and seven more, every one with zero
voucher lines in the whole capture.

For a shop whose shelf is worth ₹14.24 crore, ₹8.8 crore owed *by* its suppliers
is a large enough position to need an explanation, and nothing in the capture
gives one.

### A method note, because I got this wrong first

Summing only the year's postings on this group reports the **opposite** — dealers
owing the shop ₹12,06,180 — because the opening balances are most of the answer
and the movement is a rounding error against them. **A balance is the opening
plus the movement.** The screen shows all three columns and a test fails if the
opening is ever dropped from the sum.

**What was done:** the Supplier Balances screen shows every account with a
balance, which way it runs, and how many postings it saw. Nothing is adjusted.
Why ₹8.8 crore is owed to the shop is a question for the shop.

## 52. The monthly sales average falls 52%; the typical bill does not — MEDIUM

Not a defect in the data. A defect in the obvious reading of it, recorded because
the obvious reading is what a monthly sales report normally shows.

Across the four full months in the capture the **average bill** falls steeply:

| Month | Bills | Average bill | **Typical (median) bill** | Bills over ₹5 lakh |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apr 2026 | 47 | 1,98,695.91 | **30,863.00** | 3 |
| May 2026 | 44 | 1,23,284.75 | **14,400.00** | 2 |
| Jun 2026 | 55 | 70,940.42 | **54,709.00** | 0 |
| Jul 2026 | 54 | 94,712.63 | **45,759.00** | 2 |

The average falls 52% from April to July and reads as customers spending less
every month. **The median does the opposite** — it rises from ₹30,863 to
₹45,759 — and the bill count barely moves at 47, 44, 55, 54.

The averages are carried by a handful of large bills: three over ₹5 lakh in
April, the largest **₹35,20,906.00**, two in May, and **none at all in June**.
Remove those and the months look alike.

**The typical customer's bill did not fall.** A report showing only the average
would have described a collapse that did not happen.

**What was done:** the Sales by Month screen shows the average, the median and
the count of large bills on every row, and its summary says to read the typical
bill rather than the average. August is marked partial — the last bill is dated
19 August 2026 — so it is not compared against full months.

## 54. The item master's coin rates are frozen about five years behind the daily list — HIGH

`coin_rate_master` — 5,966 rows, the largest table in the dump nobody had opened
— is the shop's **daily price list for coins**: 52 items across 115 trading days,
3 April to 19 August 2026, every day the shop traded.

It explains a figure that looks wrong everywhere else. **₹26,11,606.00 of coins
were billed, 17% of all sales, against ₹1,70,345.00 of tagged coin stock.** Coins
are priced and sold as products from this list, not by weight off the shelf.

### The defect

All eleven coins that carry a rate in `item_master` are priced far below their
current daily rate, and by almost exactly the same factor:

| Coin | Item master | Latest daily (19 Aug 2026) | Times |
|---|---|---|---|
| COIN-1 GM | 3,100.00 | 15,200.00 | 4.9 |
| SILVER COIN GANESH LAXMI | 520.00 | 2,500.00 | 4.8 |
| SILVER COIN-5 GM | 260.00 | 1,240.00 | 4.8 |
| SILVER COIN-20 GM | 1,040.00 | 4,940.00 | 4.8 |
| SILVER COIN-10 GM | 520.00 | 2,470.00 | 4.8 |
| SILVER COIN-100 GM | 5,200.00 | 24,680.00 | 4.7 |
| SILVER COIN-50 GM | 2,600.00 | 12,340.00 | 4.7 |
| SILVER COIN-25 GM | 1,300.00 | 6,170.00 | 4.7 |
| SILVER COIN 250 GM | 13,000.00 | 61,700.00 | 4.7 |
| SILVER COIN 500 GM | 26,000.00 | 1,23,400.00 | 4.7 |
| SILVER COIN OUNCE | 2,500.00 | 7,750.00 | 3.1 |

**A consistent 4.7–4.9× is not eleven mistakes. It is one price list that stopped
being updated.** The silver coins imply about ₹52 a gram, which is roughly where
silver sat several years ago.

**Anything pricing a coin from the item master undercharges by about 79%.** A
coin the daily list puts at ₹1,23,400.00 carries ₹26,000.00 in the master.

### Also in the table

**19 of the 52 items are never priced on any of the 115 days** — the yantras, the
Raja Rani sets, SILVER MOHOR, SILVER NOTE, OUNCE, GOLD ORNAMENTS and several
unqualified names like COIN and SILVER COIN. Those are the 2,171 zero rows: not
missing prices, but items nobody prices.

**What was done:** the list is loaded and the Coin Rates screen shows the latest
rate, the range over the period and the item master's figure beside it, flagging
every coin where the two disagree by more than half. Nothing is corrected — which
rate is right is the shop's to say, though the daily list is plainly the live one.

## 55. The design library is 5,221 pieces from 2016-17 and 69 of them were ever used — MEDIUM

`design_no_status` — 5,242 rows, the second-largest unopened table — turned out
to be a status flag over the design library, and opening it made the library
itself worth looking at.

| | |
|---|---|
| Designs on file | **5,221** |
| Total estimated value | **14,95,13,508.73** |
| Created between | **5 July 2016 and 20 January 2017** |
| Designers | 3 |
| **Designs that ever appear on a tag** | **69** |

**The whole library was entered in a six-month window nine years ago and 1.3% of
it has ever been made.** Nothing has been added since January 2017. It is a
catalogue the shop stopped using rather than one it maintains.

### The status flag

5,066 rows carry status 0 and **176 carry status 1**. The flag does not track
anything obvious — the two groups are indistinguishable on pictures (98% either
way), estimates and tagging. What separates them is their origin: **all 176 were
designed on a single day, 5 July 2016, by one of the three designers**, and they
are heavier and dearer than the rest — 13.636 g against 8.591 g, ₹49,287 against
₹28,619.

So it marks one batch entered on one day. What the mark MEANS — selected,
approved, discontinued — is not recorded anywhere in the capture.

### A smaller thing found alongside

109 tags carry a design code, referencing 93 distinct codes, and **24 of those
codes are not in the design library**. Nineteen of the 24 are placeholders —
`0`, `.` — on 34 tags. Only **5 tags** name something that looks like a real
design code and has no design on file.

**What was done:** the status flag is not loaded. It distinguishes one day's
batch from the rest and nothing in the capture says why that matters; carrying it
forward would give it an authority it has not earned. The library itself is
already loaded and reachable through the design screens.

## 56. Three quarters of the shelf is photographed only on someone else's server — BLOCKER (B24)

`barcode_image` — 3,965 rows, the third-largest unopened table — is the tag
photography, and it makes blocker B24 a much larger problem than it looked.

| | |
|---|---|
| Photograph records | 3,965 |
| Tags photographed | 1,023 |
| Of those, tags still on the shelf | **889** |
| **Shelf value of those 889 tags** | **10,73,39,445.03** |
| Shelf value in total | 14,23,61,188.20 |
| **Share of the shelf that is photographed** | **75%** |

The paths point at **two** hosts, neither of which the shop controls:

| Host | Photos | Tags |
|---|---|---|
| `http://tag09.com/mcj2/…` | **3,923** | 1,012 |
| `https://testworkz.in/mtest/…` | 42 | 11 |

```
http://tag09.com/mcj2/images/bar_pic/23635013_30683902_2.JPG
https://testworkz.in/mtest/images/bar_pic/33537049_10060840_0.JPG
```

**3,923 of the 3,965 URLs are plain HTTP.** The 42 secure ones are the
`testworkz.in` set — and that host's path segment is `mtest`, which reads like a
test deployment. Eleven tags, all still on the shelf, have their only
photographs on what appears to be somebody's staging server.

Photographs average 3.9 per tag; one tag carries 93. Nine paths are recorded
twice. 96 of the 1,023 photographed barcodes have no tag on file at all.

**The shop has no copy of any of it.** Three quarters of its stock by value is
photographed nowhere else, on a third party's server, over an unencrypted
connection, and the ERP those images belonged to has already gone offline once.

**What was done: nothing, deliberately.** `tag09.com` serves a bot check, and
working around a third party's access control is not something this rebuild will
do — retrieving the shop's own pictures is reasonable, defeating somebody else's
protection to get them is not. The ask stands and is now quantified: **open one
of these URLs in a browser today** and confirm whether the images are still
there. If they are, they need copying while that is still possible.

## 57. The stock trail is two tables, and one of them was never read — HIGH

`retail_all_stock` — 2,820 rows, the fourth-largest unopened table — is a
**second stock movement log** covering the same three accounting years as the one
already loaded. Every one of its rows resolves to a known tag.

**475 of them are events the first log does not have:**

| Rows | What | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| **278** | the FY 2025-26 opening, all dated 1 April 2025 | 358.490 g |
| **192** | tag creations, 28 Jul 2024 to 12 Aug 2026 | 963.237 g |
| 5 | hallmark and sale-return events | |

**The 192 creations are the serious ones.** 161 of those tags are still on the
shelf and worth **₹57,41,225.14**, and the log that exists to record every tag
being made does not record them being made.

The two logs are not equally rich and neither is a superset:

| | `barcode_wise_all_transaction` | `retail_all_stock` |
|---|---|---|
| Rows | 8,561 | 2,820 |
| Carries | the user and the IP | **the weight and purity at the time** |
| Records the 2025-26 opening | no | **yes** |

**It corrects an earlier finding.** Data defect 50 reported **8** hallmark
movements in two and a half years, counted from the first log alone. The second
holds **4 more, none overlapping**: the real figure is **12**. The conclusion
there is unchanged — 432 tags flagged by hand against six issues — but the number
was wrong and is now right in both the defect and the screen.

**What was done:** the movement loader now takes both, matching on barcode and
day so nothing is counted twice, and stamps each row with the table it came from.
The trail is **9,036 rows**, up from 8,561. The Hallmark Records screen reads its
count from the trail rather than carrying a literal, so it followed the data on
its own.
