## 58. 266 tags are worth less now than the creation log says, and nothing explains it — MEDIUM

`cla_retail_trans_bar_detail` — 2,816 rows, the fourth-largest unopened table —
is a **value view of the stock trail**. It carries no event the trail does not
already have: all 2,816 rows match one on barcode and day. So it is not loaded.

What it does carry is the value at the moment each tag was created, and on
**281 rows that figure disagrees with the tag's price today**. 266 of those tags
are still on the shelf.

| | |
|---|---|
| Rows where creation value ≠ current total | 281 |
| Of those, still on the shelf | **266** |
| Difference across them | **1,82,39,030.71** |
| Direction | **every one downward — not a single tag rose** |
| Ratio, creation ÷ current | 1.00 to 3.81, median **3.542** |
| **Net weight changed on** | **none of the 266** |

### What it is not

Four explanations were tested and all fail:

- **Not stones.** 214 of the 266 tags carry no stone at all, and the average gap
  (₹68,567.78) is three times the average stone value (₹21,272.59).
- **Not a weight change.** The net weight is identical on all 266.
- **Not a constant factor.** The ratio spans 1.00 to 3.81. An earlier reading of
  "about 5×" was a **ratio of averages** — the same artefact that produced the
  bogus "578% below today's rate" recorded elsewhere in this file. Per tag it
  does not cluster.
- **Not the market rate of the day.** The creation values imply about
  ₹22,000 a gram across mixed purities, which for the 222 eighteen-carat tags
  would put pure gold near ₹29,300 a gram — far above any rate in this data. The
  rate history does not cover those dates either, so it cannot be checked
  directly.

### What can be said

**Nothing in the capture explains it**, and the figure must not be read as
₹1.82 crore lost. Two records of the same tags disagree, consistently in one
direction, with the weight untouched. Which is right is a question for the shop.

A related fact that may or may not bear on it: **154 of the 266 carry a rate of
exactly ₹4,000.00 a gram at 18kt**, and others sit on round numbers — ₹3,300,
₹3,000, ₹7,500. Round rates on that many tags look like placeholders, which is
what data defect 36 found on a smaller set.

**What was done:** the table is not loaded, since it adds no events. Recorded as
an open question with the tests that were run against it, so the next person does
not repeat them.

## 59. The order book locks a rate per order, and honouring it costs ₹60,14,200.75 — HIGH

`order_rate_master` — 2,520 rows, the last of the large unopened tables — answers
the question data defect 35 asks.

**Every one of the 284 customer orders has a rate locked against it, per purity.**
2,520 rows is 284 orders across nine or ten metal grades. The system was built to
honour the rate an order was taken at, and it recorded one every time.

### What honouring the live book costs

152 live order lines carry a weight; **150 of them match a locked rate** and a
current one.

| Purity | Lines | Net weight | Locked rate (avg) | Rate on 21 Aug | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 22kt | 53 | 933.040 g | 12,814 | 15,153 | **38,50,685.32** |
| 18kt | 44 | 458.520 g | 10,894 | 12,398 | 8,38,805.52 |
| Silver | 31 | 13,024.210 g | 227 | 254 | 8,40,163.48 |
| 995 | 10 | 209.000 g | 13,139 | 15,482 | 4,23,099.00 |
| 14kt | 10 | 28.570 g | 8,280 | 9,643 | 59,493.43 |
| 9kt | 2 | 6.000 g | 5,916 | 6,199 | 1,954.00 |
| | **150** | | | | **60,14,200.75** |

| | |
|---|---|
| Metal at the locked rates | 2,06,58,955.08 |
| Metal at the rates of 21 August 2026 | 2,66,73,155.83 |
| **Cost of honouring the book** | **60,14,200.75** |

**22kt alone is ₹38.5 lakh of it, on 933 grams.** Silver looks large by weight —
13,024 g, 88% of the live book — and contributes ₹8.4 lakh, because silver is
₹254 a gram against gold's ₹15,153.

> **Note on an earlier figure.** The asks list carried **₹42.85 lakh** for this.
> That was computed before `order_rate_master` was opened and without the locked
> rates. **₹60,14,200.75** is the figure computed from the rates the orders
> actually carry, per purity, against the last rates in the capture.

**What was done:** recorded, not loaded — the rates belong to a decision the shop
has not made. Whether to honour them is defect 35 and remains an ask, but it is
now an ask with the right number on it.

## 60. 1,445 vouchers were transferred in one year, 82% of them by one person — MEDIUM

`voucher_transfer_check` (1,445 rows) is an audit log of vouchers being moved or
renumbered: the old `(v_typ, v_id)`, a new id, a timestamp and a user.

It covers only the four money voucher types, and not all of them:

| Type | In the log | Vouchers on file |
|---|---|---|
| PMNT | 631 | 626 |
| JRNL | 541 | 624 |
| RCPT | 242 | 269 |
| CNTR | 31 | 31 |

### Who did them

| User | Transfers | Voucher types |
|---|---|---|
| **BAPI** | **1,186** | all four |
| KESHAV | 153 | 3 |
| ADMIN | 69 | 3 |
| RAJENDRA KICHER | 10 | 2 |
| *(no user recorded)* | **9** | 2 |
| PRIYA, MAHESH, ASHOK, SHIBANANDA, SUBHAM | 18 between them | |

**One person made 82% of every voucher transfer in the year**, and **9 transfers
record no user at all**. Neither is wrong on its face — BAPI is in the CASH
department and this may simply be the job — but a movement log where one account
does four fifths of the work and some entries are anonymous is worth the shop
knowing about.

### The new id cannot be used

`new_vid` looked like the global voucher key that data defect 1 says is missing.
It is not one. 1,445 rows carry only **949 distinct values**, and the collisions

- **`new_vid = 1` appears 23 times** across CNTR, JRNL, PMNT *and* RCPT, which no

**What was done:** not loaded. It is an audit trail of an operation the rebuild
does not perform, and its target id is unusable. Recorded for the concentration
finding and so `new_vid` is not mistaken later for the key defect 1 is looking
for.

## 61. The diamond price grids record what a stone sells for and never what it cost — MEDIUM

`diamond_rate_master` (774 rows) and `dealer_wise_diamond_rate` (642) were both
unread. For a shop holding **₹6,04,28,535.00 of stones — 42% of its shelf** —
they are how those stones are priced, and nothing in the rebuild could see them.

### The retail grid

774 rows: one item, 4 shapes, 17 colours, 7 qualities, 9 carat bands.

| | |
|---|---|
| Rows carrying a **retail** rate | **774** |
| Rows carrying a **wholesale** rate | **3** |
| Rows carrying a **cost** | **3** |

**The shop records what it sells a diamond for and not what it paid.** That is
the same gap the marked-against-sold screen hits from the other side: there is no
cost recorded against a piece anywhere in this capture, which is why no screen in
the rebuild can report a margin, and why gross profit needs B19 answering rather
than a better query.

### The dealer grid

642 rows across **two ledgers, and they are one grid**: 321 of the 323 comparable
rows carry an identical rate, differing on two. Rates run ₹35,500 to ₹60,500 a
carat across five bands.

One of the two ledgers is **MANIK CHAND JEWELLERS** — the shop's own name, which
also stands as a Dealer in the chart of accounts carrying a credit balance of
₹64,38,009.10 (see the supplier balances screen). The other, ledger 4986, is not
in the chart at all.

**What was done:** both grids loaded into `mcj_diamond_rates` with the grid they
came from, and a Diamond Rates screen built under Diamond Setup — where the old
menu has seven screens for shape, colour, purity, sieve, cut, mm and packet, and
none for the rates those attributes combine into. An unrecorded wholesale rate or
cost shows as **empty rather than zero**, and a test fails if that changes: 771
rows reading "0" would say the shop buys diamonds for nothing.

## 63. Fourteen order rows carry stones against an order with no lines — MEDIUM

`customer_order_detail` (115 rows) was unread and holds the stone a customer has
asked for. With it the stone picture is whole:

| | Value | Carats |
|---|---|---|
| Bought | 1,27,31,698.71 | 521.329 |
| Held on the shelf | 6,04,28,535.00 | 2,645.661 |
| Sold | 36,44,121.33 | 131.946 | *(corrected — see defect 135)* |
| **On order** | **24,69,792.15** | **402.997** |

All 115 rows tie to an order on file. Split by what became of that order:

| Rows | Carats | Value | The order |
|---|---|---|---|
| 58 | 162.358 | **16,36,662.00** | still live |
| 43 | 197.600 | 4,05,236.00 | every line cancelled |
| **14** | **43.039** | **4,27,894.15** | **has no lines at all** |

**Those fourteen are the defect.** An order header carrying 43 carats of stone
and no items — nothing on the order says what to make, so it cannot be fulfilled
and cannot be quoted. ₹4,27,894.15 of somebody's expectation with no work
attached to it.

### A trap in the grain

**The stones attach to the ORDER, not to a line.** Joining them to lines fans
them out: doing so reports **545 carats against a true 403**, because an order
with three lines multiplies its one stone row three times. That was caught by the
totals not tying, and both the loader and the screen keep the order-level grain
the legacy uses. A test seeds an order with three lines and fails if its stone is
counted more than once.

**What was done:** loaded into `mcj_ordered_stones`, and a Stones on Order screen
built under Customer Report. The order's condition is computed once per order and
joined, never derived by joining stones to lines.

## 64. The payroll configuration is a copy of the last month, not a check on it — MEDIUM

`staff_salary_sheet_payroll_detail` (209 rows) was unread and holds sixteen
months of statutory payroll — what was actually deducted and allowed, per person
per month.

| | |
|---|---|
| PF | 2,01,600.00 |
| ESI | 8,728.00 |
| P.TAX | 27,720.00 |
| HRA | 5,29,100.00 |
| D.A | 14,02,300.00 |
| **Total** | **21,69,448.00** across 16 staff and 16 months |

Data defect 34 said PF and ESI should be built and pointed at
`ledger_wise_payroll_detail`, the **configuration**. This is the **history** that
configuration describes, and it had never been loaded.

### The trap

The configuration holds a monthly entitlement of **₹1,33,906.00**. The last month
in this history — July 2026 — comes to **₹1,33,906.00**.

They are the same number because **the configuration is a snapshot of the final
month**, not an independent record of it. Reading the two as corroborating each
other would be reading one number twice. The screen says so and a test fails if
that warning is removed.

### What the history does say on its own

**Headcount fell from 15 to 11** between April 2025 and July 2026, and the
monthly statutory cost fell with it:

| | Staff | Monthly statutory |
|---|---|---|
| April 2025 | 15 | 1,54,392.00 |
| December 2025 | 13 | 1,37,332.00 |
| March 2026 | 11 | 98,402.00 |
| July 2026 | 12 | 1,33,906.00 |

`payroll_amount` is zero on all 209 rows and is not carried.

**What was done:** loaded into `mcj_payroll_history` with a loader check that
compares the last month against the configured entitlement and prints both, so a
future divergence is visible rather than silent. A Payroll History screen shows
each month with its headcount, and a component nobody pays reads **empty rather
than zero** — sixteen rows of "0.00" would look like a charge levied and come to
nothing.

## 65. 104 customer identity documents were held on the ERP server, and the files are gone — HIGH

`ledger_wise_document_upload` (104 rows) records documents uploaded against
customer ledgers between **4 June 2019 and 20 January 2026**.

| | |
|---|---|
| Documents | 104 |
| Customers | 81 |
| Types | 95 images, 4 PDFs |
| **Paths that are relative** | **104 of 104** |

Every path is of the form `../ledger_doc/<hash><name>.jpeg`. They are **relative
to the ERP's own web root**, not URLs to a host — so the files lived on the
server that went offline on 21 August 2026, and **the dump contains the names and
paths but none of the files**.

### What they are

Named explicitly in the filename:

| Kind | Documents | Customers |
|---|---|---|
| PAN | 6 | 4 |
| Visa | 4 | 1 |
| Aadhaar | 2 | 1 |
| Named only after the person | 92 | 79 |

The 92 carry a customer's name and nothing else, so what they are cannot be told
from the capture. For a jeweller collecting KYC on high-value transactions, most
will be identity documents of some kind.

### Two separate problems

**The files are unrecoverable.** 104 documents for 81 customers, held for up to
seven years, on a server that is gone. If the shop needs to prove a KYC check was
performed, this dump cannot help it.

**The capture still names them.** It does not hold the images, but it does pair
**customer names with document types** — that a named individual's visa or
Aadhaar was on file is itself information about that person, and it is sitting in
the same dump as blocker B18 covers.

**What was done:** not loaded — there are no files to load and the paths point
nowhere. Recorded, and added to the asks: **if the old server or its backups
still exist, these 104 files are on it**, and whoever holds that hardware is
holding customers' identity documents.

## 66. The same bill number identifies two different sales — BLOCKER

`sale_bill_link` (135 rows) maps a bill number in the shop's own system to a bill
number in a second one. It was unread, and what it says is serious.

| | |
|---|---|
| Links | 135 |
| Distinct MCJ bills linked | **132 of the 224 on file** |
| Links where the two numbers are the same | **2** |
| Links where they differ | **133** |
| **Links whose "other" number is also a real MCJ bill** | **85** |
| **…for a genuinely different sale** | **83** |

The numbering drifts apart and then overlaps:

| MCJ bill | Other system | The sale that MCJ number actually belongs to |
|---|---|---|
| GST/2627/00004 | GST/2627/00007 | 4 Apr 2026, ₹32,886.00 |
| GST/2627/00005 | GST/2627/00008 | 5 Apr 2026, ₹7,500.00 |
| GST/2627/00006 | GST/2627/00009 | 5 Apr 2026, ₹2,46,000.00 |

**A customer holding invoice GST/2627/00007 from the second system is holding a
number that, in the shop's own records, belongs to somebody else's sale.**

Two MCJ bills map to two different numbers each, so the mapping is not even
one-to-one in that direction.

### Why it is a blocker rather than a curiosity

**Any reconciliation that joins on a bill number across the two systems matches
the wrong sale 83 times in 135.** That includes matching a customer's copy of an
invoice against the ledger, chasing a payment, or answering a tax query. The
number on the paper is not sufficient to identify the sale.

The second system is not hypothetical: 42 of the tag photographs (defect 56) are
hosted on `testworkz.in` under a path segment `mtest`, and this table names its
bills.

**What was done:** not loaded — a mapping this ambiguous should not be given the
authority of a table in the new system until somebody says which numbering is
authoritative. **Ask: which of the two numberings does the shop consider its own,
and do customers hold invoices carrying the other one?**

## 67. The reorder levels contradict themselves and cannot be checked against the shelf — MEDIUM

`item_wise_tagging` (158 rows) holds a minimum stock quantity per item and
category — how few of something the shop is willing to have before making more.
It cannot be used, for two independent reasons.

**It disagrees with itself.** 158 rules cover only 115 distinct (item, category)
pairs. **43 pairs carry more than one rule and 41 of those contradict:**

| Item | Category | Minimums recorded |
|---|---|---|
| DIAMOND BANGLE | 2 | **30 / 6** |
| DIAMOND BANGLE | 5 | **30 / 6** |
| DIAMOND LOCKET | 12 | **45 / 5** |
| DIAMOND BANGLE | 1 | **14 / 6** |
| DIAMOND BANGLE | 49 | 2 / 4 |

There is no date, status or branch on the table to choose between them — the
same shape as the making ladder in data defect 47 and `item_adjustment` in
defect 40.

**And the shelf cannot answer it anyway.** The rules are stated per item AND
category, but **only 1,461 of the 2,575 tags on the shelf carry a category at
all** — 43% do not. A reorder report would compare a rule against 57% of the
stock and call the rest missing.

The one thing that can be said without the rules is that the levels are of a
plausible size: GOLD RING at 60 against 38 on the shelf, DIAMOND LOCKET at 45
against 43. If the rules were trustworthy the shop would be short on several
lines.

**What was done:** not loaded and no screen built. A reorder report that is wrong
about which rule applies and blind to 43% of the shelf would be worse than none.
Recorded so the table is not mistaken for a working reorder policy.

## 69. ₹2.6 crore of stone has passed through the stock journal, and nothing can say which way — HIGH

`stock_conversion_details` (816 rows) was unread. It is the stone content of the
stock journal — the stones inside the pieces that were melted down or remade.

| | |
|---|---|
| Rows | 816 |
| Conversion vouchers | 393 |
| Tags | 411 |
| Carats | **2,554.341** |
| Value | **2,60,68,682.20** |
| Rows tying to a voucher on file | **816 of 816** |

**That is more stone value than the shop bought or sold in the whole capture:**

| | Value | Carats |
|---|---|---|
| Bought | 1,27,31,698.71 | 521.329 |
| Sold | 36,44,121.33 | 131.946 | *(corrected — see defect 135)* |
| **Through the stock journal** | **2,60,68,682.20** | **2,554.341** |
| Sitting on the shelf | 6,04,28,535.00 | 2,645.661 |

2,554 carats through conversions against 2,731 on the shelf. Whatever a
conversion is in this shop, a great deal of stone goes through it.

### Why no screen was built

The stock journal's direction is the legacy `add` column, and **which value means

Until that is answered a report cannot say whether these 2,554 carats came *out*
of pieces or went *into* them, and the two readings mean opposite things: stones

one would be asserting the very thing in question.**

**What was done:** loaded into `mcj_conversion_stones`, with the loader failing if
any row cannot reach its voucher. No screen. When the `add = 1` question is
answered, the data is already in place to build on.

## 70. The chart of accounts was missing its third level, leaving 84% of ledgers unrooted — HIGH (now fixed)

`sub_subgroup_master` (36 rows) is the third level of the ledger group hierarchy
and had never been loaded. The rebuild carried two levels — 15 groups and 47
subgroups — and that was not enough to place most of the chart.

**54 distinct group names appear on the 785 ledgers.** 36 are groups or
subgroups. **18 exist only at the third level, and they carry 662 of the 785
ledgers:**

| Group name | Ledgers |
|---|---|
| Customer | **485** |
| Dealer | 76 |
| Sundry Creditors Expenses | 53 |
| Liabilities For Statutary Dues | 6 |
| Other Loan | 6 |
| Other Debtor | 6 |
| …and twelve more | |

So **84% of the chart of accounts had a group name with nothing above it**. No
profit and loss or balance sheet can roll up a ledger whose group has no parent,
which made this a structural obstacle independent of blocker B19.

### The id is not a key

The obvious load fails. **36 rows carry 30 distinct ids, and six ids each name two
unrelated groups:**

| id | Names it carries | Their parents |
|---|---|---|
| 60 | Security Deposit · Interest On Bhagalpur | 7 · 13 |
| 64 | Other Creditor · Short Term Provision | 14 · 14 |
| 65 | Liabilities For Statutary Dues · Shareholders Fund | 17 · 18 |
| 61 | Legal,professional & Consultancy Charges · Bhagalpur Loan | 28 · 13 |
| 63 | Interest & Penalty Charges Statutary · Goods And Services Tax | 28 · 17 |
| 66 | Advances · Utilities | 7 · 28 |

The same shape as data defect 1, where `v_id` is not the voucher key. Carrying it
collides on the unique index; picking one of each pair would silently drop six
groups. **No legacy id is carried at this level**, and the loader says why.

### After loading

**34 groups added, and ledgers with no parent went from 662 to 0.** The chains
resolve as an accountant would expect:

```
Customer    → Sundry Debtors    → Current Assets
Dealer      → Sundry Creditors  → Current Liabilities
Other Loan  → Unsecured Loans   → Loans (Liability)
```

96 groups over three levels under 15 roots. **This does not answer B19** — the
stock is still outside the ledgers — but the hierarchy is no longer a second
reason the statements cannot be produced.

away into just four targets:**

| Merged into | Items absorbed |
|---|---|
| **GOLD ORNAMENTS** | **25** |
| SILVER ORNAMENT | 12 |
| SILVER DIPAK | 2 |
| PLATINUM MIX ORNAMENTS | 1 |

- data defect 40 — `item_adjustment` names GOLD ORNAMENTS three times with
  contradictory making values (8% + ₹250/gm, then 15%, then 8% again)
- data defect 47 — the making ladder records GOLD ORNAMENTS at five different
  rates for the same weight band

Twenty-five different products merged into one code will do that. The
contradictions are not corruption; they are the settings of twenty-five items
collapsed onto one.

### One id was reused

The single surviving merged-away item is **id 1139**, recorded in the merge as
`SILVER KOPPOR STAND`. The item on file at that id today is **`Rudraksha`** — the
id was released by the merge and later handed to something else.

The same shape as barcode reuse in data defect 29 and the duplicate ids in defect
70: **an id in this system identifies a row, not a thing.**

**What was done:** not loaded. The merges are already reflected in the item master
and nothing references what they removed. Recorded because it explains two
existing defects rather than adding a new one.

---

## 72. The load pipeline had not been run end to end, and three faults were waiting in it — HIGH (now fixed)

Eleven loaders were added over the course of the rebuild and each was tested on
its own — against a database that already held everything it depended on.
**`load_all.sh` had never been run from a truncated database since.** It failed
three times before it passed.

### 1. A stale assertion

`load_masters.sh` checked `mcj_ledger_groups` for **62** rows. The third level
added in data defect 70 makes it **96**. The loader's own check caught it and
stopped the run — which is the check working, but it should have been updated
with the change rather than by the pipeline.

### 2. Backticks inside an unquoted heredoc

`load_stock.sh` writes its SQL through `psql_do <<SQL` — **unquoted**, because it
interpolates the tenant id. Bash therefore expands everything else in the body
too. A comment added for the tag-size fix mentioned a table name in backticks,
and bash tried to **run it as a command**:

```
./load_stock.sh: line 41: barcode_size: command not found
```

The loader aborted before writing a single tag. A second instance was found in
`load_masters.sh`, where a comment carried `` `code` `` — and `code` is a command
that exists on many machines, so that one would have launched an editor rather
than failing loudly.

Both comments are now plain text, and the heredoc carries a note saying why prose
inside it must avoid backticks and bare `$`.

### 3. Two loaders running before their dependencies

`load_purchase_contents.sh` ran **eighteen steps before** the purchase invoices it
joins to, and `load_sold_stones.sh` before the sales invoices. On a populated
database both worked, because the invoices were already there from an earlier
run. From empty, every row reached no invoice.

Both loaders assert that every row reaches its bill, so the pipeline stopped
rather than loading 263 orphaned rows. **The guards were the only reason this did
not pass silently.** Both are now ordered after their dependencies, with a comment
saying what they need.

### After

`=== all loads complete ===`, **85 OK lines, no errors**, and the figures rebuild
exactly: 2,575 tags on the shelf worth ₹14,23,61,188.20, 1,848 vouchers, 96 ledger
groups with **0 ledgers unrooted**, 9,036 stock movements, 203 sold stones and 60
purchase content rows.

**The lesson is the ordering one.** A loader tested against a database that
already contains its dependencies is not tested. The only defence that worked was
that each loader asserts its own joins resolved.

---

## 73. 559 of the shop's 593 payment references were never migrated, and the bank could not be reconciled — HIGH (now fixed)

`mcj_vouchers` carries `cheque_number` and `cheque_date`, filled from
`legacy.voucher_main`. That table holds **34** of them. The real data is on
`legacy.voucher_detail`: **593 references across 435 vouchers, carrying
₹4,86,12,771.04**. None of it was migrated, and `mcj_voucher_lines` had no
column to put it in.

The consequence is not cosmetic. The bank reconciliation screen reads the
reference off the voucher header, so **for 1,814 of 1,848 vouchers it showed a
blank cheque column** — and a bank statement cannot be reconciled against the
books without the instrument reference. The screen was built, tested and passing
the whole time.

### How it surfaced

Not by looking for it. A voucher dated **2026-12-05**, four months into the
future, turned up while checking a report's default date range. It was worth
₹1,353.70 — trivial — but a future date can mean a **day/month swap in my own
loader**, which would be systematic. It was not: the narration itself reads
`Ch. No.435590, Dt.05.12.2026 Issued Against Their Dues`, DD.MM.YYYY, and the
loader had stored it correctly. A genuine post-dated cheque.

That narration suggested a check I had not thought of — **198 narrations embed
the cheque date as text**, an independent second source for the parsed dates.
Comparing them found no parsing error (and **112 of the 198 have a first field
above 12**, which settles DD.MM.YYYY conclusively). What it did find was that
`cheque_date` was **NULL for all 198**.

### Why it goes on the line

The header cannot hold it. **109 of the 435 vouchers carry two or three
different references** — 96 with two, 13 with three — one payment settling
several bills, each with its own instrument.

The field is also not always a cheque number. Real values include `Gpay` and
`NEFT AXNGG1663185928` beside numbers like `416331`, so it is stored as text and
never parsed. It sits on the bank or wallet line, which is the line the
reconciliation screen already reads: **UNION BANK OF INDIA 446, Google Pay 81,
Paytm 30**.

### Done

Migration `mcj-1787404000` adds `cheque_number` and `cheque_date` to
`mcj_voucher_lines`; the loader fills them and now **asserts 593 and 680**, so
this cannot silently regress. The screen reads the line first and falls back to
the header for the 34 that have it there, joining multiple references with a
comma rather than picking one.

Three tests cover it, and **two of them fail against the old query** — verified
by reverting it, not assumed.

---

## 74. A systematic search for the kind of gap defect 73 was — MEDIUM

Defect 73 — 559 missing payment references — was found by accident, following a
future-dated voucher. That is not a method. The same class of fault is
findable directly: **a legacy column that holds real data and no loader reads.**

Every column of the 70 legacy tables the loaders touch was measured for how many
rows carry a value — **1,438 columns** — and cross-referenced against the text of
all 40 loader scripts. **126 well-filled columns are named in no loader.**

### Most of the 126 are not data

The largest looked alarming: `address_book_master.rate_tds`,
`rate_of_interest`, `credit_amt`, `calc_tds` and `brokage_percentage`, each
**100% filled across 40,519 rows**. Writing that up as "202,595 dropped values"
would have been wrong. Every one of them holds **a single distinct value** — a
column with a default, never used. The same is true of 13 columns on
`ledger_master` (TDS, brokerage, making and certificate rates) and of
`item_master.percentage`, `min_sale_rate` and `min_purc_rate`.

**Fill rate is not evidence. Distinct count is.** The check that separates them
costs one query and belongs in front of every claim of this shape.

### What was genuinely missing

Only one thing needed fixing, and it is small: **`ac_name` is capped at 50
characters** and one ledger is cut mid-word — `SONANI JEWELS UNIT OF SONANI
INDUSTRIES PRIVATE LI`, a supplier whose full legal name is wanted on GST
paperwork. `ledger_display_name` holds the full 55.

It is taken **only** where `ac_name` sits at the cap and the display name
extends it. The two names differ on 9 ledgers and the other 8 are unrelated
variants — `URVASHI TALWAR` is recorded there as `MAMTA TALWAR`, `AVA
CHATTERJEE` as `SHYAMALI CHaTTERJEE` — which must not be adopted. Whether those
8 are corrections or errors is a question for the shop, not the loader.

### Still open from the audit

`sales_vou_main.actual_gw` and `actual_nw` (251 and 236 distinct over 328 rows),
`voucher_detail.subgrp` (27 distinct over 4,931) and `dept_code` on four tables
(7 distinct) are real values no loader reads. None is money and none blocks a
screen, so they are recorded rather than acted on.

`design_transaction_main.picture_sketch` was already known — and checking it
corrected a figure. See below.

### A number corrected while checking

`docs/screens.md` said **5,104** designs name an image file. The true count of
rows carrying a path is **5,105**, pointing at **5,045 distinct files**, 60 of
them shared by two designs each. **Four references are malformed in the source**
and would not have resolved even while the server was up: `../image/467903` and
`../image/561676` have no extension, `../image/84348720jpg` and
`../image/83792824jpg` are missing the dot before `jpg`. Corrected in place.

## 75. The coverage figure was wrong in both the numerator and the denominator — MEDIUM (now fixed)

The status doc read **112 of 188 screens, 60%**. The true figure is **111 of
187, 59%**. Both halves were wrong, in opposite directions, which is why the
percentage looked stable.

**The denominator counted the CSV's header row.** `legacy_menu.csv` opens with
`Top Menu,Sub-Group,Item,Link` — column names. Counting distinct values in the
fourth column picks up `Link` as though it were a screen. The application does
not make this mistake: `navigation.go` reads `records[1:]`. The fault was in the
counting, not the product.

**The numerator counted test files.** Scanning `modules/mcj/**/*.go` for
`LegacyFile:` matches the navigation tests as well as the registry —
`colur_master.php` appears **seven** times, six of them in
`navigation_test.go`. Excluding `_test.go` gives 117 distinct claims, of which
**111 name a menu row**.

### The six that name no menu row

`day_book.php`, `label_print.php`, `add_gold_rate_fix.php`,
`set_rate_gold_opening.php`, `add_sales_voucher_combined.php` and
`print_sales_vocher_register_gst.php` are all real legacy pages — four have
their own captured page and `day_book.php` is linked from **255** of them. They
are reached from other screens rather than the menu, so they are legitimately
built and legitimately add nothing to coverage.

### Whether the menu is the whole inventory — it is

Worth testing, because if real screens existed outside the menu the denominator
would be meaningless. **270 pages were captured; only 178 are menu entries**, so
**92 captured pages sit outside it**, several of them substantial:
`add_sample_issue_to_karigar.php` at 829 KB, `add_cust_order.php` at 676 KB,
`add_party_scheme.php` at 500 KB.

**All 92 are linked from a menu page.** Every one is an add form, a drill-down
or a print view belonging to a screen already counted; none is standalone.
Writing them up as ~85 more screens to build would have been a large error in
the other direction.

The ten menu entries with no captured page are `?type=`, `?bill_type=` and
`?rec_type=` variants whose base page **is** captured — not missing references.

### Guarded

`TestNavigation_EveryLegacyFileNamesAPageThatExisted` now enforces the rule the
navigation tests already state — that an invented `.php` name "reads as evidence
about the old system, and would be a fiction". A claim must name a menu row, a
captured page, or a page a captured page links to.

The first version was too strict and failed two screens: `/mcj/invoice` and
`/mcj/sales/new` rest on **link evidence alone** —
`add_sales_voucher_combined.php` is referenced by 254 captured pages and was
never captured itself. Those names are real; the test was wrong, and was
widened rather than the claims being changed. It also asserts that a fabricated
name is still rejected, so the widening did not empty it out.

## 76. 90% of the shelf names a maker who exists nowhere in the database — HIGH (needs the shop)

`barcode_main.karigar_code` is filled on **1,743 of 2,816 tags**, carrying **110
distinct codes** — `D599` on 470 tags, `D142` on 113, `DL236` on 104, `d76` on
99, and so on. On the shelf specifically it is **1,625 tags worth
₹12,77,72,008.04 — 90% of the ₹14,23,61,188.20 stock**.

**Not one of the 110 resolves to anything.**

Tested and rejected, in order:

- `mcj_ledgers.code` — **0 of 110**
- `legacy.ledger_master.ldgr_code` — 0
- `legacy.ledger_master.ac_code` — 0
- the same match case-insensitively (the codes are mixed case: `D599` beside
  `d76`) — 0
- `legacy.address_book_master.ldgr_code` — 0
- the `design_code` on the same tag — 0

Then every text column in the legacy schema was searched for the literal value
`D599`. It occurs in **exactly one place: `barcode_main.karigar_code`**. There
is no karigar master table in the dump — the only karigar-named tables are
`karigar_gold_stock` (2 rows) and `karigar_wip_bal` (1 row) — and the chart of
accounts holds **76 Dealer ledgers and exactly one Karigar ledger**.

So the field is free text against no master. It is the same shape as defect 41,
where `mcj_parties.ledger_code` was joined to `mcj_ledgers.code` and 368 codes
collided without naming a single same person — except that here there is nothing
to collide with.

### What this settles

The 31 unclaimed MANUFACTURING and Karigar Report screens are not waiting on
effort. `receive_amount` (141 rows, a payments table) aside, every issue and
receive table is empty — **except `karigar_gold_stock`, whose 2 rows issue
869.850 g of fine gold to MA TARA JEWELLERS and are the subject of
[defect 164]**: `karigar_gold_stock` 2, `karigar_wip_bal` 1,
`dealer_wise_making` 7, `customer_own_goods_receive` 6, `estimate_main` 2. There
are **no karigar transactions, no work orders, no stone issues and no
hallmarking movements to report on**, and no master to name the maker even
where a tag remembers one.

**Two exceptions were found later and both are recorded:** `karigar_gold_stock`'s
two rows issue 869.850 g of fine gold to a named goldsmith ([defect 164]), and
`retail_all_stock` carries 4 hallmarking rows covering 2.230 g, issued and
received back ([defect 166]). The first materially contradicts this paragraph;
the second only makes it absolute where it should read "almost none".

A Karigar Ledger built on this would render 110 headings, each an unexplained
code, with no opening balance, no issues and no receipts under any of them.

### The question for the shop

**What is `D599`?** If it is a workshop shorthand kept on paper or in someone's
head, a two-column list — code against name — turns 90% of the shelf from
anonymous into attributed, and is the whole of what these screens need to become
buildable. If the makers were tracked in a system outside this ERP, that system
holds the other half of the manufacturing record.

## 77. The retail voucher variants have no data, and one table's name is a trap — MEDIUM

Fourteen unclaimed RETAIL screens were checked against what the shop actually
recorded. Most cannot be built, and the reasons are worth stating so they are
not re-examined.

### Approval sales were never configured, let alone used

Across the **entire** legacy schema the word "approval" appears in exactly two
columns: `sales_vou_main.appr_sale` and `default_settings.def_sale_on_appr_ldgr`.

`appr_sale` is **0 on all 328 sale lines**. `def_sale_on_appr_ldgr` — the ledger
an approval sale would post to — is **empty** on the single settings row. There
is no purchase approval table at all.

That settles seven screens: Sales Approval Voucher, Sales Approval Return
Voucher, Purchase Approval Voucher, Purchase Approval Return Voucher, Sales
Approval Register, Purchase Approval Register and Approval Pending Report.

### There is only one kind of sale

All **224** bills are `SALE-GST`; `bill_type` is `local` on 221 and `central` on
3. Nothing distinguishes an exhibition, an export or a repair sale, so
Exhibition Sale, Export Sale and Repair Sale have no rows to show — three more.

Of the line flags, `ret_status` is set on **3** lines (the three sale returns,
which reconcile with `sale_return`) and `mrp_status` on **38**, which the MRP
sales register already reports.

### `sales_quotes` is not quotations

The table is named as though it holds customer quotations, and an Estimate
screen built on it would have looked right. It holds **motivational quotes for
the dashboard**:

> "Customer Satisfaction is worthless .. Customer Loyalty is priceless"
> "The purpose of a Business is to create a customer who creates Customers."

Ten rows of them. The real estimates are in `estimate` and `estimate_main` —
**two** of them, `EST/2526/00001` and `EST/2526/00002`, with full line detail:
barcode, item, gross and net weight, purity, rate and making, totalling
₹12,294.00 and ₹5,01,000.00.

**A table's name is not evidence of what it holds.** This is the same lesson as
`COUNTER STOCK` being filed under *Customer* with a zero balance.

## 78. 12.30 kg of gold is recorded as raw stock, unvalued and never migrated — HIGH (needs the shop)

`barcode_main_rawstone` holds **10 rows** the loaders have never read. It is not
scrap notes. The metal is broken down by purity the way a jeweller records it:

| Item | Purity | Net weight |
|---|---|---|
| GOLD ORNAMENTS | 9 | 82.156 g |
| GOLD ORNAMENTS | 14 | 1,073.049 g |
| GOLD ORNAMENTS | 18 | 5,566.291 g |
| GOLD ORNAMENTS | 22 | 4,973.818 g |
| COIN | 22 | 84.490 g |
| COIN | 995 | 524.720 g |
| SILVER ORNAMENT | SLV | 9,971.290 g + 2,998.751 g |
| SILVER COIN | SLV | 2,052.044 g |
| SILVER ARTICLE | ARTIC(PCS) | 0.000 g |

**12,304.524 g at gold purities and 15,022.085 g of silver**. Every item id
resolves in `item_master`. Not one row carries a barcode, a rate or a value.

**Correction — this entry said 11,779.804 g of gold and 15,546.805 g of silver.**
Both were wrong by the same row: the **524.720 g COIN at purity 995**, listed in
the table above, was left out of the gold total and added to the silver one. 995
is **99.5% fine gold**. Valued as silver it is worth ₹1,33,016.52; valued as what
it is, **₹81,23,715.04** — an ₹80 lakh difference on one line. The title's
"11.78 kg" should read **12.30 kg**.

`barcode_detail_rawstone` holds 9 stone rows totalling 475.433 carats, and they
are **not part of this holding**: **8 of the 9 carry `main_id = 0`**, which
matches no raw stock row at all. Only **0.380 ct** attaches to a parent. Those
8 orphans describe 28,603.429 g of stone gross weight — more than the entire
raw metal above — hanging off nothing. Counting them as part of the raw stock,
as an earlier draft of this entry did, overstates it.

For scale, the entire tagged shelf is **20,038.936 g**. This is more than half as
much metal again, held outside it.

### It cannot be current stock, on the accounts' own evidence

The tagged shelf blends to **₹7,104.23 per gram**, and this entry used to value
the raw gold at that rate — **₹8,36,86,423.98**.

**That rate cannot be applied to gold.** It is the whole shelf divided by the
whole shelf's weight, and **48% of that weight is silver**: 9,600.508 g of silver
against 10,238.962 g of gold. Split by metal the shelf blends to

| | Net weight | Value | Per gram |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gold | 10,238.962 g | 13,77,71,338.90 | **13,455.60** |
| Silver | 9,600.508 g | 30,57,474.70 | **318.47** |
| Purity 95 | 199.466 g | 15,32,374.60 | 7,682.38 |

At **today's metal rates**, purity by purity, the raw holding comes to:

| | Net weight | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Raw gold (9, 14, 18, 22, 995) | 12,304.524 g | **16,46,39,828.53** |
| Raw silver | 15,022.085 g | 38,08,098.55 |
| **Total** | 27,326.609 g | **16,84,47,927.08** |

So the raw metal is worth **around ₹16.5 crore of gold**, not the ₹8.37 crore
this entry carried — a figure produced by pricing gold at a rate half of it is
silver. It **exceeds the entire tagged shelf**, which sharpens rather than
softens the question this defect asks.

The trial balance is short by ₹15,32,28,603.49 and the tagged shelf explains
₹14,23,61,188.20 of it, leaving **₹1.09 crore** unexplained. If this metal were
also held and unrecorded, the books would have to be short by roughly **₹8.4
crore more than they are**.

The shelf rate carries making and certification, so it overstates raw metal —
but even at half of it the figure is several times the residual. **The
arithmetic says this is a historical opening that was since tagged or consumed,
not metal sitting in the shop today.** It does not say so conclusively, and this
is not a question to answer by inference.

### Why it was invisible

`barcode_main_rawstone` has **10 rows**, and the tables around it are of a size
that reads as noise. It was skipped for the same reason `old_gold_purchase` was
— a small table is not an unimportant one. This one describes more metal than
the shelf.

### What this settles

Of the seven SETUP Opening Stock screens, six cannot be built: **no
`studded_opening_stock` table exists at all** (Own Studded Stock, Party Sample
Stock, Karigar/Dealer Studded Stock), and raw stock exists only as `type='sh'` —
there are **no `co` or `kr` rows**, so Party Raw Stock and Karigar/Dealer Raw
Stock have nothing. Own Tag Stock is already built.

### The question for the shop

**Is this metal still in the shop?** If it is, the accounts are short by around
₹8 crore more than anyone has counted and the balance sheet's difference line is
badly understated. If it was tagged into the shelf years ago, it is a historical
opening and can be loaded as one — but it should not be loaded as current stock
on a guess either way.

### ANSWERED, and the accounting inference above was wrong — see defect 133

The shop's own raw-stock movement report survived in a scratch table excluded
from staging. It shows this metal **opening, being received and being issued
through to 17 June 2026**, and closing at **11,998.005 g at gold purities** —
more than it opened with. The inference that the books "have no room" for it was
sound arithmetic about the ledgers and wrong about the world: **the metal is
real, it is moving, and it sits outside the accounts exactly as the tagged shelf
does.**

## 79. There is no cost basis anywhere in the data, so gross profit cannot be reported — HIGH

The Gross Profit Report (`gross_profit_report.php`) and Ratio Analysis
(`ratio_analysis.php`) both need to know what the goods cost. Nothing in this
database records it. Three independent routes were tried and all three close.

### 1. The tag's value is a selling price, not a cost

232 of the 328 sale lines match a tag by barcode. Those tags are valued at
**₹1,05,03,577.58** and the pieces sold for **₹1,05,56,997.00** — a difference of
**0.5%**. The tag carries the price the piece is billed at, which is what a
price tag is for. Subtracting one from the other gives a half-percent "margin"
that is really just rounding, and no jeweller's margin looks like that.

*(The average of the per-line ratios is 1.110 while the ratio of the totals is
1.005. Both are arithmetically correct and they answer different questions —
the per-line average is pulled about by small lines. The ratio of totals is the
one that describes the trade. This is the same ratio-of-averages trap that once
produced a "constant factor of 5×" here.)*

### 2. Purchases cannot be traced to tags

`barcode_create_from_purchase_detail` links a purchase to the tag it created.
It holds **21 rows**. There are **2,816 tags**. That is **0.75%** — enough to
cost less than one piece in a hundred.

### 3. The one place that separates cost from price never used it

`barcode_details` — the stone detail behind each tag — carries **both**
`rate_stock` and `rate_sales`, which is exactly the cost-versus-selling
distinction a gross profit needs. **727 rows have both populated, and the two
values are identical on every one of them.** Not close: equal, on all 727. The
field was there and was filled with the same number twice.

### What this means

A gross profit screen could be made to render. It would subtract a selling
price from a selling price and call the remainder margin. That number would be
quoted in a meeting.

It also explains the shape of the profit and loss account: with no cost of
goods sold, the P&L nets income against purchases and shows a **₹1,10,87,494.08
shortfall the shop did not make**. The missing figure is the same one in both
places.

**Both screens are recorded as unbuildable rather than built.** If the shop
prices from a cost sheet kept outside this ERP, that sheet is the missing input
and both become possible.

---

## 80. A stone figure was labelled "on the shelf" in seven places and was not — MEDIUM (now fixed)

Every figure repeated across the four documents was re-checked against the
database. Most verify to the paisa. One did not, and it was repeated seven
times.

**`₹6,21,95,953.60` is every stone record in `mcj_stock_stones`** — 819 lines
over 692 tags, 2,731.821 carats. It was written as "Held on the shelf",
"Sitting on the shelf" and "**44% of its shelf**".

The stones actually on the shelf are **₹6,04,28,535.00**: 672 lines, 562 tags,
2,645.661 carats, **42.4% of the ₹14,23,61,188.20 shelf**. The difference —
**₹17,67,418.60 and 86.160 carats** — sits on tags that have already been sold.

### How it happened

Not a bad query. A scope slip inside one sentence:

> `819 stone lines over 692 barcodes`, and covers **every one of the 486
> in-stock tags that carries stone value**. 2,731.821 carats, ₹6,21,95,953.60.

The first clause counts the whole table, the middle clause counts in-stock tags,
and the total belongs to the first. Read quickly it says the shelf holds ₹6.22
crore of stones. It was then quoted onward into a blocker, a defect and two
status entries, and the "44% of the shelf" was derived from the wrong numerator.

**Every count in a claim has to answer the same question the money in it does.**
Where a sentence needs both scopes, both get named.

### Verified alongside it

The shelf value ₹14,23,61,188.20 and 20,038.936 g, the opening imbalance
₹15,32,28,603.49, the raw stock 27,326.609 g and its silver 15,546.805 g, and
the one-paisa difference across all voucher lines — **all exact**.

## 81. The status doc misstated a blocker by 3.4× and mislabelled who it affects — MEDIUM (now fixed)

Continuing the figure audit into the "Waiting on you" table — the numbers most
likely to be acted on.

**B9 is 165 items whose stored price cannot be reproduced.** `docs/STATUS.md`
described it twice as **566 certified pieces**:

> Bill the 566 certified pieces
> B9 — Were the certified pieces priced by hand? *566 pieces cannot be billed*

Both halves are wrong. The count is **165**, not 566 — 3.4× overstated — and
they are **not the certified goods**. `blockers.md` and `pricing-formula.md` both
say so plainly: the 165 *cluster* by certification type (`by_val` 98, `per_ct`
35, so 133 of 165) which is why certification was suspected, but the shop holds
**549 certified pieces in stock** and 678 across all tags. Neither is 566, and
none of those counts is what B9 blocks.

Read as written, the table says a fifth of the shelf cannot be billed. What is
actually true is that **9% of computed-price items** carry a pricing component
this rebuild cannot see, off by −₹66,585 to +₹10,731.

Corrected in both places, with the cluster stated so the certification link is
not lost.

### The rest of the table verified

- **40,519** customer records — exact
- **1,023** photographed tags over **3,965** image rows — exact
- **889 tags worth ₹10,73,39,445.03, 75.4% of the shelf** — exact
- **1,625 tags worth ₹12,77,72,008.04** naming an unidentifiable maker — exact
- **135** bill links, **284** orders, **2,520** order rate rows — exact
- All **25** documented legacy table row counts — exact

*(One near miss while checking B24: `sum(DISTINCT total)` reports
₹10,63,93,293.99 because it sums distinct **values** and drops tags that happen
to be worth the same. The figure is ₹10,73,39,445.03. `DISTINCT` inside an
aggregate answers a different question than `DISTINCT` on the rows.)*

## 82. My own tenant fix scoped the list and left the detail page open — HIGH (now fixed)

Defect-in-progress, found by re-reading `tenant_scoped_repository.go` an hour
after writing it.

The wrapper built for B11 scoped `List`, `Count` and `GetAll`. It passed `Get`,
`Exists`, `Update` and `Delete` **straight through to the unscoped repository**.

All four take a key, and **a key from another tenant is exactly as valid as one
of ours unless it is checked**. So anyone holding another tenant's row id could
read that row through the ordinary detail page, and `Update` and `Delete` accept
the same id — editing and removing it.

That is worse than the leak it replaced. The original defect exposed rows in a
list; this exposed rows to modification. And the clean list makes it **harder to
notice, not less true**: the row never appears anywhere the user can see, so
nothing suggests the id would work.

### The fix

`ownsKey` counts rows matching the key **with the tenant filter applied**, and
`Get`, `Exists`, `Update` and `Delete` all consult it first. A counting query
rather than fetch-and-compare, because the entity is generic here — there is no
`TenantID()` to read off it — and a count cannot accidentally return the row it
is checking.

`Exists` returns **false** rather than an error for another tenant's row.
Answering "it exists but is not yours" leaks the thing being withheld. For the
same reason the error is `ErrNotOurs = errors.New("no such record")`, worded as
absence rather than refusal.

Two tests cover it: one that `Get` cannot reach another tenant's row, one that
`Update` and `Delete` cannot touch it — and the second re-reads the row
afterwards to confirm it is still there and unchanged.

### And the write side, checked rather than assumed

`Create` and `Update` were left passing values through. The repository **honours
a supplied `tenant_id`** — measured: creating a row with another tenant's id in
the values lands it in that tenant.

**This is not reachable from the web.** The crud controller skips readonly
fields when parsing a form (`crud_controller.go:432`) and `tenant_id` is declared
readonly, so a crafted POST cannot aim a write. Reported as the defence-in-depth
gap it is, not as a live hole.

Closed anyway: `forceTenant` replaces any supplied `tenant_id` with the caller's
own, on both `Create` and `Update`. Replaced rather than rejected — a caller
passing the right tenant is doing nothing wrong, and one passing the wrong tenant
should not learn whether that tenant exists.

Five tests now cover the wrapper: reads, the unwrapped leak, `Get`, `Update` and
`Delete`, and this.

### The lesson

**A partial fix to an isolation bug is not a partial fix.** Scoping the front
door and leaving the side door open reads, in a diff, exactly like closing both.
Nothing failed; every test still passed; the list was demonstrably clean.

---

## 83. `legacy_id` is not an identity, and ten tables prove it — MEDIUM

Reviewing the Own Raw Stock screen written earlier today: it looks an item up by
`legacy_id` to copy the name, which silently assumes one match. That assumption
turned out to be worth checking generally.

**58 of the 63 tables carrying `legacy_id` have no unique constraint on it**, and
**10 already hold duplicates**:

| Table | Duplicated values |
|---|---|
| `mcj_voucher_lines` | 984 |
| `mcj_design_stones` | 690 |
| `mcj_purchase_contents` | 21 |
| `mcj_ordered_stones` | 20 |
| `mcj_purchase_invoices` | 19 |
| `mcj_salary_sheets` | 17 |
| `mcj_ledger_groups` | 13 |
| `mcj_customer_order_lines` | 10 |
| `mcj_bank_accounts` | 7 |
| `mcj_scheme_payments` | 4 |

### None of them is a bad load

The first look suggested rows had been inserted twice. They had not.
`mcj_voucher_lines` holds **5,229** rows against a source of **5,229** — exact.
What the source holds is **1,186 distinct `id` values across those 5,229 rows**.
`legacy.voucher_detail` reuses its own id, and the loader copies it faithfully.

`mcj_ledger_groups` is the clearer illustration. `legacy_id` **1** is both
*Capital* — a group, from `main_group` — and *Credit Card*, a subgroup from
`subgroup_master`. Two source tables, each numbering from 1, merged into one
table. Its third level carries **NULL**, having no source row at all.

**`legacy_id` is only unique within a source table.** Several of these tables
merge more than one, so it was never going to be an identity, and any
reconciliation keyed on it alone will mismatch.

### What was done

One constraint, on `mcj_items` only, where the source genuinely is single and
genuinely is unique: `item_master` 322 rows, 322 distinct `item_id`, 322 loaded.
That is the table the raw stock lookup reads, so the assumption it makes is now
enforced rather than merely true.

**Deliberately not generalised.** Applied as a rule this constraint would reject
a correct load of nine other tables. The full pipeline was re-run after adding
it: exit 0, 87 OK lines.

---

## 84. A screen I wrote today let "may add" mean "may delete" — MEDIUM (now fixed)

The Own Raw Stock screen puts adding a line and removing one on the **same POST
route**. A route gate can therefore only ask for one permission, and it asked for
`ItemCreate`.

So a user trusted to record metal could **delete** records of it. Not through a
crafted request — through the Remove button, which the screen renders for
everyone who can reach it.

Fixed by checking `ItemDelete` inside the handler when a `remove` is submitted,
which is the only place the two actions are distinguishable. A test asserts a
user holding `ItemRead` and `ItemCreate` can add a line, is refused **403** on
removal, and that the line is still there afterwards. Verified to fail with the
check taken out.

### Checked whether it was a pattern

Four other controllers branch on a submitted action — credit note, tag, sale and
old gold, all on `action != "save"`. They are safe, and for a reason worth
stating: their two actions are *price* and *save*, and both sit behind
`VoucherCreate`. Gating a preview behind the create right is **stricter** than it
needs to be.

The dangerous direction is the opposite one — the **more** privileged action
sharing the **less** privileged gate — and this was the only instance. It was in
code written today.

---

## 85. The load pipeline said "safe to re-run at any time", and it is about to stop being true — HIGH (now guarded)

`load_all.sh` opened with:

> Idempotent: safe to re-run at any time.

That was true while the database held only migrated data. **It stops being true
the moment the shop enters anything.** Every loader clears its tables and
rewrites them from the legacy dump, so a sale, a voucher or a raw stock line
entered through the application is deleted — and the capture cannot put it back,
because it never contained it.

The sentence is the dangerous part. "Safe to re-run at any time" is exactly what
somebody reads before running it on a live database, and this project has
already lost 40,519 parties, 1,848 vouchers and 785 ledgers once to a
`migrate down` that looked equally harmless.

The Own Raw Stock screen built today is the first screen whose whole purpose is
to write rows the dump does not contain. It made the wording actively wrong
rather than merely fragile.

### The guard

Every migrated row carries the id it had in the legacy system. **A row with none
was created in the application** — so it is precisely what the script would
destroy and could never restore.

`load_all.sh` now counts those rows across `mcj_vouchers`,
`mcj_sales_invoices`, `mcj_stock_items`, `mcj_raw_stock`, `mcj_estimates` and
`mcj_customer_goods` before clearing anything, and refuses if it finds any,
naming the tables and counts. `MCJ_FORCE_RELOAD=1` overrides it for the case
where rebuilding from the dump really is the intent.

Verified all three ways: a clean run still completes (exit 0, 87 OK lines); a
single hand-inserted raw stock line makes it refuse with **exit code 1**, which
matters because a caller reads the status rather than the message; and the
override completes and restores the migrated figures exactly — 10 raw stock
rows, 2,575 tags.

The header now says what is actually true: idempotent against the capture, and
**not safe on a database the shop is using**.

### The same guard one level down

Protecting only `load_all.sh` protects the careful path. Somebody debugging runs
a single loader — `./load_rawstock.sh` — and that is exactly where losing a few
rows is least likely to be noticed. The five loaders whose tables the
application writes to (`load_rawstock`, `load_vouchers`, `load_invoices`,
`load_customer_goods`, `load_estimates`) now carry the same check through a
shared `guard_app_data.sh`.

**The first version of that was broken and only the full pipeline showed it.**
The loaders `cd` to the repository root before the guard is sourced, so
`$(dirname "$0")` no longer points at the script: standalone runs worked, and
`load_all.sh` died with `./guard_app_data.sh: No such file or directory` after 38
successful steps. Resolved from the repository root instead, and verified from
all three invocation paths — `bash tools/legacy/load_rawstock.sh`, `cd
tools/legacy && ./load_rawstock.sh`, and through `load_all.sh` — each refusing
with **exit 1** and each completing under `MCJ_FORCE_RELOAD=1`.

## 86. A test failed about one run in three, and had done since before today — MEDIUM (now fixed)

`TestCategorise_FiltersToUntaggedOnly` failed in a full-package run, then passed
on its own, then passed three times in a row. Running the whole package twice
more reproduced it: **run 1 FAIL, run 2 ok.**

The assertion was:

```go
if strings.Contains(body, "T3") { … "a tag that already has a category appeared" }
```

`T3` is the seeded barcode of the one categorised tag, and the test asserts it is
**absent** from the rendered page. `T3` is also **two characters**, and the page
carries a session token and other generated values — any of which can contain
`T3` by chance. When one did, the test failed and the screen was innocent.

An absence assertion on a short string is the fragile direction. `Contains` on a
present string only fails when the page is wrong; `!Contains` fails whenever
anything else on the page happens to spell it.

Fixed by seeding barcodes that cannot occur by accident —
`TAGUNCATEGORISED1`, `TAGUNCATEGORISED2`, `TAGCATEGORISED3`. Three full-package
runs clean afterwards.

### Two things it caught on the way

Renaming the barcodes broke two other tests, which is how the seed turned out to
be read in three places: the insert, a `WHERE barcode IN ('T1','T2')` that
collects the ids to post, and the assertions. The id query still named the old
barcodes, so nothing was submitted and the tags came back uncategorised —
**a passing test would have been possible only because both halves used the same
wrong list.**

The failure messages also still read `T1 is "", want RINGS` after the rename, so
they now describe the tag rather than quote a barcode that no longer exists.

**This flakiness predates today.** It is recorded rather than quietly fixed
because an intermittent failure that nobody writes down is indistinguishable
from an environment problem, and gets re-run instead of investigated.

---

## 87. Some of my own "suite green" checks never ran — MEDIUM (now fixed)

`just test-e2e` ran `go test -tags=integration ./...` with no `-count=1`.

Go's test cache keys on the source tree. **It cannot see the database.** So
applying a migration, reloading the legacy data, or adding a constraint — none
of which touches a `.go` file — leaves the cache valid, and the next run reports
`ok (cached)` for tests that never executed against the new state.

Demonstrated directly: two consecutive integration runs with no source change,
both `ok (cached)`, neither having run.

This happened repeatedly during the rebuild. Several times today a migration was
applied and the suite immediately reported `ok ... (cached)` for
`presentation/controllers` — an integration package. **Those confirmations were
weaker than they were reported to be**, and any of them could have been hiding a
schema change that broke a screen.

Nothing appears to have been missed: the final runs were uncached and clean,
five consecutive full passes. But that is luck rather than method.

`just test-e2e` now passes `-count=1`, as `just test-smoke` already does after
the same trap caught a deliberately broken report "passing". The plain `just
test` recipe keeps the cache, correctly — those tests read only the source tree.

**A test whose inputs live outside the source tree must never be cached.** This
is the second instance of that rule today, in a different recipe.

## 88. `migrate down` says it rolls back one migration and rolls back all of them — HIGH (SDK defect)

This project has lost its entire database twice to `migrate down`, and both
times it was recorded as carelessness. It is not. **The command's own
documentation is wrong**, and here is the line.

`pkg/commands/cli_migrate.go`:

```go
Short: "Rollback the last migration",
Long:  `Rolls back the most recently applied database migration.`,
```

`pkg/application/migrations.go:153`:

```go
plannedMigrations, dbMap, err := ms.PlanMigration(db, "postgres", migrationSource, migrate.Down, 0)
```

The final argument is `max`. In `sql-migrate@v1.7.0`, `migrate.go:75`:

```go
} else if max > 0 && max < toApplyCount {
    toApplyCount = max
}
```

**The cap applies only when `max > 0`.** Passing `0` leaves `toApplyCount` at
every applied migration — so `migrate down` rolls back **all 119**, dropping
every table and everything in them.

`just migrate down` reaches the same command through the `direction` parameter.

### Why this matters more than a wrong help string

Someone reaching for `migrate down` is usually trying to undo one bad migration.
The help confirms that is what will happen. What they get is an empty database,
and on 21 August that meant 40,519 parties, 1,848 vouchers and 785 ledgers that
existed nowhere else, because the original migration had been run as ad-hoc SQL
and never version-controlled.

The load pipeline exists because of that day. It can now rebuild everything from
the capture — but only what the capture contains, which is nothing the shop has
entered since.

### Recorded, not worked around

`redo` has the same shape: it calls `Rollback()` and then `Run()`, so it is
"roll everything back and reapply everything", not "redo the last one". It
happens to end in the same schema, but every table is dropped in between.

**Nothing here is patched.** The Justfile now warns at the point of use, and
`docs/blockers.md` B25 carries it for upstream. Rolling back one migration is
`psql` and the `Down` block from the file, by hand.

---

## 89. The balance sheet's difference line was absorbing ₹13,197 that is not stock — MEDIUM (now fixed)

The difference line is the one figure on that screen whose **size is the
evidence** — it is what justifies saying the missing asset is stock, because it
is the same order of magnitude as the shelf. Anything else quietly added to it
weakens exactly the argument it exists to make.

Chasing a gap left open earlier: the opening trial balance is out by
**₹15,32,28,603.49**, but the balance sheet's difference line read
**₹15,32,16,805.48**. **₹11,798.01** apart, and nothing named it.

It reconciles exactly:

| | |
|---|---|
| Opening imbalance | 15,32,28,603.49 |
| less expense opening balances the sheet excluded | −13,197.00 |
| plus pre-year trading counted on one side only | +1,398.99 |
| **= the difference line** | **15,32,16,805.48** |

**Three expense ledgers carry an opening balance** — ₹13,197.00 credit. That is
an earlier year's trading, which a balance sheet would have closed into retained
earnings. This ERP has no retained earnings account, so the sheet had nowhere to
put it and left it out, whereupon it reappeared inside the difference and read as
missing stock.

The second component is the single pre-1-April voucher line found while making
the profit and loss agree with the balance sheet: its asset side is inside the
closing balances, its income side is outside the year's result.

### Done

The openings now appear as their own row — *"Opening balances on income and
expense ledgers"*, filed under *"An earlier year's result, with no account to
hold it"*. The sheet still ties, and the difference line is now
**₹15,32,30,002.48**, which is the opening imbalance plus that ₹1,398.99 and
nothing else.

A test seeds an expense ledger with a credit opening, asserts the row carries it,
and asserts the sheet still ties with it in.

*(The reconciliation closes to within one paisa: the pre-year component is
₹1,399.00 by direct sum and ₹1,398.99 by subtraction, a rounding artefact of the
paisa conversion. Stated rather than smoothed over.)*

---

## 90. The trial balance and the balance sheet disagreed about what does not tie — MEDIUM (now fixed)

Both screens describe the same books, so **the amount that fails to tie must be
the same figure on each**. It was not:

| | |
|---|---|
| Trial balance suspense | 15,32,28,603.48 |
| Balance sheet difference | 15,32,30,002.48 |
| | **₹1,399.00 apart** |

The same ₹1,399 as before — one voucher line dated before 1 April. This is its
third appearance: it split the profit and loss from the balance sheet, then it
sat inside the difference line unnamed, and now it splits the balance sheet from
the trial balance.

The cause is structural. The balance sheet's result for the year is **bounded at
1 April**; the trial balance has no such split and carries the line inside the
ledger's closing balance. So a pre-year income or expense line is counted on the
asset side by both and on the other side by only one.

Defect 89 added a row for income and expense **opening balances**. That was half
the category. The other half is income and expense **movement dated before the
year** — the same thing arriving by a different route.

### Done

The row now carries both, and is named for what it holds: *"Income and expense
from before this year"*, ₹11,798.00 on the real books — ₹13,197.00 of openings
less the ₹1,399.00 line. **Both screens now report ₹15,32,28,603.48**, and a test
asserts they agree, treating an absent difference and a zero one as the same
claim.

### What the fix did to the tests

Three failed, and all three were the tests being wrong rather than the code:

- The seeded books now tie **with no difference line at all** — the ₹400 pre-year
  sale is properly placed rather than unexplained. The test had asserted the
  ₹400 gap, so it now asserts there is none.
- The openings row shows **900**, not 500: the 500 brought forward plus the 400
  dated 31 March. Both are last year's.
- The agreement test had to accept "neither screen reports a gap" as agreement.

A fix that makes a seeded ledger balance completely will break a test written
against the imbalance. That is the test doing its job.

---

## 91. A post-dated cheque is booked on its future date, so the debt it settles still shows as owed — LOW (recorded, for the shop to decide)

Cross-checking one bank account across four screens turned this up. The screens
themselves are sound; what they revealed is a modelling question.

**Every figure agreed.** For `UNION BANK OF INDIA` (code 3137) as on today:

| Screen | Closing |
|---|---|
| Trial balance | 4,91,62,109.87 Cr |
| Ledger book | 4,91,62,109.87 Cr |
| Bank reconciliation, per the books | 4,91,62,109.87 Cr |
| Direct SQL | 4,91,62,109.87 Cr |

The bank book shows **4,91,12,150.78 Cr**, which is not a disagreement: it
carries all four bank accounts together, and −4,91,62,109.87 + 0.11 + 11,460.00
+ 38,498.98 is exactly −4,91,12,150.78.

### What it exposed

The reconciliation showed the statement balance **equal** to the book balance,
which would make the screen useless if it were always so. It is not. Of the
vouchers touching that account, **497 are cleared and exactly one is not** — and
that one is `PMNT 576`, the post-dated cheque from defect 73, dated **5 December
2026**. It sits outside a reconciliation run to today, so the two balances
correctly coincide.

Following it through: the cheque pays **DAYANIDHI TRADE PVT LTD**, an *Other
Loan* account.

| | |
|---|---|
| Balance as on today | 25,00,000.00 Cr |
| Balance including the December voucher | 23,64,630.00 Cr |

The shop has **issued a cheque for ₹1,35,370.00** and its books will not
recognise it until December. The debt still reads as ₹25 lakh, and the cheque
appears as an outstanding item on no reconciliation run before then.

### Not changed

Booking a post-dated cheque on its own date is defensible — it is not a payment
until it clears — and it is what the shop did. The alternative, recording it on
issue with `cheque_date` carrying the future date, is what the `cheque_date`
column exists for and what makes the cheque visible as outstanding.

**One voucher and ₹1.35 lakh today.** It is written down because the *practice*
matters more than the amount: every post-dated cheque the shop writes from now on
lands the same way, and only they can say which treatment they intend.

## 92. The invoice columns are not additive, and I nearly reported ₹8.96 lakh of nonsense — MEDIUM (a trap, not a fault)

Cross-checking sales across three sources. The three totals differ, and they are
supposed to:

| Source | Amount | Rows |
|---|---|---|
| `mcj_sales_invoices.bill_total` | 2,47,65,386.00 | 224 |
| `mcj_sales_invoice_lines.amount` | 1,51,40,109.00 | 328 |
| Income ledgers, net credit | 2,20,03,143.00 | 227 |

**`goods_amount` sums to ₹2,40,66,454.00, which is the income ledgers' credits
to the rupee** — 2,20,03,143.00 net, plus the 20,63,311.00 of sale returns the
ledgers net off. That is the tie that matters, and it is exact.

### The trap

`mcj_sales_invoices` carries `goods_amount`, `making_charge`, `other_making`,
`certification`, `discount` and `round_off` beside `bill_total`. They read as
components of the total. Adding them up gives ₹2,56,61,020.13 against a
`bill_total` of ₹2,47,65,386.00 — **₹8,95,634.13 apart**, which looks exactly
like a real defect and was almost written up as one.

**They are not components. Making, other making and certification are already
inside `goods_amount`.** The relationship is simply:

```
bill_total = goods_amount + GST
```

Checked on the five largest bills first — 1,02,551/34,18,355, 95,890/31,96,335,
28,064/9,35,462 and the rest all come to **3.000%** — then across all 224.

### And the rate spread is legitimate

| Rate | Bills | Goods |
|---|---|---|
| 3.00% | 196 | — |
| 1.50% | 19 | 12,05,520.00 |
| 0.25% | 2 | 1,80,451.00 |
| other | 6 | ₹246 to ₹1,033 each |

The three rates are the real GST slabs. The six stragglers are **rounding on
bills under about ₹1,000**, not errors. Total tax ₹6,98,932.00, an overall
2.904%.

**Nothing is wrong here.** It is recorded because the column names invite the
mistake, and the ₹8.96 lakh it produces is large enough to be believed.

## 93. 14% of the stock movement trail refers to tags the tag master does not contain — MEDIUM (source property, not a migration fault)

Cross-checking the stock screens. `mcj_stock_items` holds **2,816** tags;
`mcj_stock_movements` references **3,314 distinct barcodes**. **499 of them exist
on no tag**, carrying **1,298 movements — 14% of the 9,036.**

### It is not the migration

Checked before writing it up as a gap:

- `legacy.barcode_main` holds **2,816** rows and **2,816** were loaded. Complete.
- `legacy.barcode_wise_all_transaction` references **3,314** distinct barcodes of
  its own accord.

**The legacy tag master already held 498 fewer barcodes than its own movement
trail.** Both were copied faithfully. Formatting was ruled out too: of the 499,
only **2** match when trimmed and case-folded, and only **3** are suffix variants
(`94751337R1`) of a barcode that exists.

### What the orphaned movements are

| Movement | Count |
|---|---|
| NEW-BAR | 1,099 |
| OP-STK | 134 |
| SALE-GST | 42 |
| CST-ORD | 15 |
| SALE-RET | 5 |
| PURC-IN | 1 |

Dated **1 April 2024 to 14 August 2026** — up to nine days before the capture, so
not an ancient tail. The bulk is tag creation for tags the master no longer
carries, which reads as the legacy system removing a tag row at some point in its
life while keeping the trail.

### The sales are traceable, but not through the tag

**31 distinct barcodes were sold** with no tag behind them. **24 appear on a
sales invoice line**, so the sale is fully recorded. The remaining 7 name a bill
in the movement's own reference — and those bills exist and carry lines, except
**`GST/2526/00308`, which is in no invoice table at all**. One bill from the
2025-26 year, referenced by a movement, with no invoice behind it.

### Why it is recorded rather than fixed

Nothing can reconstruct a tag the source never kept. What this changes is what
may be *claimed*: any statement of the form "every movement belongs to a tag" is
false by 14%, and a stock report that inner-joins movements to tags silently
drops 1,298 rows. The registers already outer-join, which is why none of them is
wrong today.

## 94. The books are one financial year deep; the stock trail is three — HIGH

Following `GST/2526/00308` — a bill named by a stock movement and present in no
invoice table. It is not a missing row. **The source contains no 2025-26 sales at
all.**

Every financial table in the dump holds one year:

| Table | Coverage |
|---|---|
| `sales_vou` | **224 bills, all 2026-2027** |
| `voucher_main` | **1,840 in 2026-2027**, plus the 8 orphans of blocker B4 |
| `old_gold_purchase` | 25, all 2026-2027 |
| `customer_order` | 284, all 2026-2027 |

The stock movement trail does not:

| `barcode_wise_all_transaction` | Rows |
|---|---|
| 2024-2025 | 2,138 |
| 2025-2026 | 4,317 |
| 2026-2027 | 794 |
| blank | 1,312 |

**6,455 of its 8,561 rows — 75% — predate the only year the books cover.**

*(That 8,561 plus 475 rows drawn from `retail_all_stock` is the 9,036 in
`mcj_stock_movements`. Checked, because a count that nearly matches is worth
less than one that does.)*

### What it means concretely

**38 tags were sold between 9 May 2024 and 21 October 2025, and not one has a
bill on file** — the movement is the only evidence the sale happened. The
remaining 286 SALE-GST movements are in 2026-27 and reconcile to invoices.

The legacy system evidently purged or archived transactional tables at year end
and left the stock trail alone. What survived is a shop with a detailed
three-year stock history and a single year of accounts.

### What may not be claimed

- **No year-on-year comparison is possible.** There is one year of revenue.
  Any "last year" figure would have to be invented.
- **The opening balances are the only trace of everything before April 2026** —
  which is why blocker B19's ₹15.32 crore imbalance cannot be investigated by
  looking at prior transactions. There are none to look at.
- A stock report joining movements to sales will find nothing for 75% of the
  trail, correctly.

Recorded, not fixed. Nothing can recover a year the dump does not contain.

## 95. Purchases reconcile exactly, and the ₹2.98 I first saw was my own arithmetic — LOW (a trap, not a fault)

Cross-checking purchases the way sales were checked.

| Source | Amount |
|---|---|
| `mcj_purchase_invoices.total` | 2,39,56,798.00 |
| Credited to suppliers on the vouchers | 2,39,56,798.00 |
| | **gap 0.00, on all 43 bills** |

### The false start

The first comparison put invoice `total` against **total voucher debits** and
found ₹2.98 across the 43 — small enough to look like accumulated rounding, and
the per-bill pattern reinforced it: `GDP/2627/00004` showed 7,98,202.00 against
7,98,202.36, with a `round_off` of −0.36 sitting right there.

The voucher tells a different story:

| Ledger | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|
| ZM LIFESTYLE PVT. LTD. | | 7,98,202.00 |
| ROUNDED OFF | | 0.36 |
| INPUT IGST | 23,248.61 | |
| PURCHASE_B2B | 7,74,953.75 | |

The supplier is credited the **rounded** total, and the rounding sits as its own
credit line. Debits exceed the bill total by exactly the round-off **because the
round-off is on the other side**. Comparing a bill total to one side of a
double-entry voucher counts it twice.

This is the second instance today of the same shape — after treating
`making_charge` and `certification` as additions to a sales `bill_total` when
they were already inside `goods_amount` (defect 92). Both produced a plausible
figure from a wrong comparison rather than from wrong data.

**Nothing is wrong with the purchases.** Recorded because the wrong comparison
is the natural one to reach for.

### Noted while there

`PURCHASE%` ledgers carry a net debit of **₹2,76,65,794.29** against the
₹2,39,56,798.00 of purchase invoices. That is not a discrepancy either: those
ledgers also carry old gold (`PURC-OG`, 25 vouchers) and purchase returns
(`PURC-RET`, 3), which have no purchase invoice. Not decomposed to the rupee
here — flagged so the next person does not read it as one.

## 96. `amount_received` on an order is not money received — HIGH (trap; the loader is correct)

Cross-checking orders. They migrate cleanly: **284 orders and 366 lines against
284 and 366 in the source, no orphaned lines.** But `advance` is **₹0.00 on all
284**, which is worth a second look on an order book worth lakhs.

The source has another column beside it: **`amount_received`**, populated on
**273 of 284 orders and totalling ₹14,47,10,446.00.**

**That is ₹14.47 crore of apparent customer money, on a shelf worth ₹14.24 crore
and an order book worth ₹60,14,200.75.** Loaded as an advance — which its name
invites — every order screen would show money the shop has not got.

### What it actually is

The largest single value is **₹7,38,00,000.00**, on order `CO/2526/00402`:

| pcs | net weight | rate | estimate | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 3,000.000 g | 24,600.00 | 0.00 | **Cancelled** |

3,000 × 24,600 = **73,800,000** exactly. It is a computed goods valuation, on a
cancelled order carrying three kilograms of gold.

Tested across all 267 orders where both sides exist:

| Formula | Orders matching |
|---|---|
| net weight × rate **+ making** | **178** |
| net weight × rate | 157 |
| gross weight × rate | 157 |
| the line `estimate` | 16 |

Two thirds land on goods-plus-making. **Nothing about it is a receipt.**

### The loader is right, and was right by reading rather than by luck

`load_orders.sh` takes `o.advance` and ignores `amount_received`. `advance` is
genuinely zero on every row, so **the order book correctly shows no advances**.

### The real question underneath

**284 orders and not one advance recorded.** Either the shop takes no money up
front — unusual against ₹60,14,200.75 of live orders — or advances are receipted
as ordinary `RCPT` vouchers with no link back to the order. If it is the second,
the order screen cannot show what a customer has already paid, and the shop would
have to find it in the ledger by name.

Recorded for the shop. Not guessed at.
