## 99. The voucher renumbering log cannot be used as a map, and 1,411 vouchers were renumbered — MEDIUM (candidate closed, context for B4)

`voucher_transfer_check` — **1,445 rows, read by no loader** — maps a voucher's
old id to a new one per type and year, with a timestamp and a user. It looked
like the authoritative answer to blocker B4's eight orphaned vouchers, which the
loader currently handles by matching on `legacy_v_id` and hoping.

**1,411 of the 1,445 rows record an actual renumbering** (`v_id` ≠ `new_vid`).
Voucher renumbering was not an eight-row exception in this system; it was
routine.

### But it does not resolve to a map

| | |
|---|---|
| Rows | 1,445 |
| With a blank financial year | 5 |
| Old ids pointing at several different targets | 2 |
| **Target numbers claimed by more than one source voucher** | **123** |

`JRNL` alone shows `v_id` 3 → 6 and `v_id` 4 → 6, and `v_id` 4 → 6 *and* → 1.

The table carries a `datetime`, so the obvious reading is append-only with the
latest entry winning. **Tested: taking the latest row per type, year and old id
gives 1,442 mappings and leaves all 123 collisions standing.** It is a log of
transfer events, not a reconciliation, and nothing in it says which entry
prevailed.

### The load does not need it

`load_vouchers.sh` ignores it and matches on `legacy_v_id`. That produces 1,848
vouchers and 5,229 lines exactly, **0 lines with an unresolved ledger**, and
1,847 of 1,848 balancing — the one exception being the known `JRNL 312`. Adding
a map with 123 ambiguous targets could only make that worse.

### What it does explain

B4's eight orphans are not a curiosity. Legacy `JRNL` ids 1–8 became 649–655 and
1, and the same reassignment happened 1,411 times across the system. It is also
the backdrop to defect 66, where **83 of 135 bill links point at a number that is
also a real bill for a different sale** — a shop that renumbers vouchers this
freely will produce exactly that.

Candidate closed. Recorded so B4 is not re-investigated through this table.

## 100. Row count is not information: three more tables that are full and empty — LOW (candidates closed)

Working through the legacy tables no loader reads — **54 of them, 25,674 rows
between them**. The large ones have each been examined and written up already
(`design_no_status`, `barcode_image`, `cla_retail_trans_bar_detail`,
`order_rate_master`, `voucher_transfer_check`, `barcode_history`,
`address_book_sub_name`, `item_wise_tagging`, `sale_bill_link`). These three
were the remaining ones big enough to be worth opening:

| Table | Rows | Populated |
|---|---|---|
| `ledger_ref_details` | 1,071 | **2** have a reference name, **1** a mobile |
| `item_adjustment` | 922 | **5**, and those contradict each other (defect 97) |
| `voucher_hsn` | 756 | **0** — `hsn_no` is `0` on every row |

`voucher_hsn` is the cleanest case: 756 rows, one distinct value, no HSN recorded
anywhere. A feature switched on, written to on every voucher, and never given
anything to record.

### The pattern, now seen five times

Counting the earlier ones — `address_book_master`'s TDS and brokerage columns
(**100% filled across 40,519 rows, one distinct value each**, defect 74) and
`sales_quotes` (**a table named like customer quotations holding motivational
sayings**, defect 77) — this is the fifth instance today of a table that is full
of rows and empty of data.

**Row count is not information.** The checks that separate them are cheap and
should come before any claim about a table's contents:

- **distinct count**, not fill rate — 40,519 filled rows with one distinct value
  is a default, not data
- **look at the values**, not the column name — `sales_quotes`,
  `amount_received` and `item_merge` are all named for something they do not
  contain

Each of these was opened because a name or a row count suggested it mattered.
None did. Recorded so the next sweep does not open them again.

## 101. A figure that drifts on its own, in a document that does not — LOW (now dated)

Cross-checking blocker B23. Every figure reproduces from the database exactly:

| | Documented | Recomputed |
|---|---|---|
| Enrolments, all active | 239 | 239 |
| Instalments paid | 2,144, ₹87,90,900.00 | same |
| Gold promised at maturity | ₹1,03,10,400.00 | same |
| Enrolments already matured | 235 | 235 |
| Gold due on those matured | **₹99,74,900.00** | **same** |
| Oldest maturity | 25 July 2017 | same |

One did not: **"matured more than a year ago — 215"** recomputes as **216**.

It is not an error. It was 215 when written on 22 August and 216 today, because
one enrolment — party 10262, maturing 23 August 2025 — crossed the one-year line
overnight. Verified by asking the database for both dates: 215 as at 22 August,
216 as at 23 August.

### Why it is worth writing down

A static document holding a figure defined *relative to today* is wrong from the
day after it is written, and the person who notices has no way to tell drift from
a mistake. They will either correct a correct document or — worse — start
distrusting the figures around it, which here include a ₹99.7 lakh liability that
is exactly right.

The row now carries **"(as at 22 Aug 2026)"** and a note that it moves. The other
B23 figures are stable until a scheme matures or is settled, and are left alone.

Worth a sweep of the other documents for the same shape: anything counted "so
far", "to date" or "more than a year ago" needs the date it was taken.

## 102. The sweep for drifting figures found two more, in the same defect — LOW (now dated)

Following defect 101 through the other documents. **41 statements combine a
number with a time-relative phrase**; most are "at today's rates" or narration
and are fine. Three are counts defined against *now*, and they had already
drifted:

| Figure | Written 22 Aug | Recomputed 23 Aug |
|---|---|---|
| Scheme enrolments matured over a year ago (B23) | 215 | **216** |
| Live orders past their due date (defect 28) | 61 | **63** |
| Age of the oldest overdue order | 1,474 days | **1,475** |

Everything stable in those entries reproduces exactly: 67 live order lines,
12 over a year past, ₹49,77,590.00 of live work, ₹17,10,000.00 of it over a
year old, oldest due 9 August 2022 — and B23's 239 enrolments, 2,144
instalments, ₹87,90,900.00 paid and **₹99,74,900.00 due**.

So in one day, one defect entry gained two wrong numbers without anybody
touching it. The order one is worse than the scheme one because **the count is in
the title** — *"Sixty-one live customer orders are past their delivery date"* —
where it will be quoted from.

All three now carry *(as at 22 Aug 2026)* and a note of what they read today, in
`blockers.md`, `data-defects.md` and `screens.md`.

**The rule this leaves:** a number measured against *today* belongs with the date
it was taken, or it belongs in a screen rather than a document. The screens
recompute; the documents do not.

## 103. The status table is now taken rather than typed, and taking it found another 28-screen drift — MEDIUM (now automated)

Every figure in `docs/STATUS.md`'s summary table was hand-maintained, and every
one of them has been wrong:

- **"20 of 188 screens"** stood while the true figure reached 117 — and the
  denominator counted the CSV's header row as a screen (defect 75)
- **"11 open blockers"** while 18 were open
- **migrations and loaders wrong twice in one day**, the second time within
  hours of correcting the first — `guard_app_data.sh`, a helper, counted as a
  loader

`tools/status_figures.py` now prints the table from the filesystem, the
navigation registry and the database. `--check` compares it against what is
written and exits 1 on a difference.

### It immediately found one more

**"Screens written up in `screens.md`: 41"** — the true figure is **69**. The
headings cover ranges (`## Screens 34–35` is two screens, `## Reference lists
(screens 1–10)` is ten), so counting headings gives 36 and counting them by hand
gave 41. Distinct screen numbers: 69, spanning 1 to 82.

### And the first version of the check passed when it should not have

It searched the whole document for each value. `docs/STATUS.md` said 41, the
script computed 69, and **the check reported agreement** — because "69" appeared
somewhere else on the page.

Now it locates the row by its label and compares that row's value, allowing a
trailing note (`**91 of 149** — 2 more examined and deliberately not loaded`) to
count as agreement rather than drift.

**Third vacuous check written today**, after a field-label test that covered only
schemas with no UUID selects and a smoke test that reported `ok (cached)` against
a deliberately broken server. The pattern is the same each time: a check that
cannot fail is indistinguishable from one that passes, and only trying to make it
fail tells them apart.

## 104. Three tests would have passed while checking nothing — MEDIUM (now guarded)

Defect 103 ended on the observation that a check which cannot fail is
indistinguishable from one that passes. Applying that to the test suite.

**84 test files.** Of the tests whose every assertion sits inside a `range` loop,
most iterate a hard-coded table of cases and cannot be empty — `TestWords`,
`TestAcceptsEveryRealLegacyCode`, and so on. Those are fine. The ones that matter
loop over something **fetched**: a registry, a query, a spec.

Checked individually rather than by the heuristic, because the heuristic
over-flagged badly — 80 candidates, then 24, and most of those turned out to
assert on accumulated state *after* the loop, which fails correctly on an empty
result. `TestHolidays_ShowsWhichYearsAreRecorded` is the pattern: it collects
into a map, then asserts 2016 and 2017 are present.

Three were genuinely vacuous-on-empty:

| Test | Loops over | Passes empty because |
|---|---|---|
| `TestAuth_EveryBusinessRouteRefusesAnonymous` | routes built from `mcj.CodeLists` | an empty registry means no route is checked |
| `TestReconcile_TickingRecordsTheStatementDate` | voucher ids **from the database** | a seed that produces nothing clears nothing |
| `TestRawStock_CarriesNoValuation` | the report's declared columns | a spec with no columns has no money column |

The first is the one that matters. **It asserts that no business route serves an
anonymous visitor** — and it would have reported success having tested zero
routes.

Each now fails with a message saying what it failed to prove. Verified on the
security one by emptying the registry: it fails with *"no routes to check, so
this proves nothing about anonymous access"*, and passes again when restored.

The other two were guarded without a live failure being staged, because their
emptiness would require a code change that would fail other tests first.

## 105. The pipeline audit found nothing, and my checking was wrong twice in the finding of it — LOW (clean result, method noted)

Applying the vacuity question to the loaders: does every one verify what it
actually wrote, or do some just check that a tenant exists?

**All 37 do. There are 95 guard statements across the pipeline**, and every
loader compares what it loaded against the source — `load_vouchers.sh` asserts
1,848 and 5,229, `load_codelists.sh` compares source to destination for each of
its lists, `load_masters.sh` runs every count through a `check` function that
exits on a mismatch.

Nothing to fix.

### The part worth keeping is how badly the checking went

Two crude patterns, two false alarms:

- Grepping for `FAIL` reported **17 loaders with no assertion**. They use
  `ERROR:` and `exit 1` instead. `load_coin_rates.sh` compares source rows to
  loaded rows and exits — it simply does not contain the word.
- The corrected pattern still flagged three, all artefacts: `load_all.sh`'s guard
  is an `exit 1` inside an `if` rather than after a `||`, and the other two
  compute their counts into shell variables that no longer look like `mcj_`
  table references.

**Fourth time today the check was wrong rather than the thing checked** — after
querying `status='Cancel'` where the data says `Cancelled`, joining on
`category_id` where the column is `category`, and comparing a bill total against
one side of a double-entry voucher.

Each produced a confident, wrong result that looked like a finding: *17 loaders
have no assertion* would have been a serious claim about this pipeline. The only
thing that caught it was opening one of the seventeen and reading it.

**A negative result from a pattern is a claim about the pattern until one case is
read by hand.**

## 106. Any user could delete the shop's own particulars — HIGH (now fixed)

Auditing permissions across every write route. Two crud screens declare fewer
permissions than they expose operations:

| Screen | Declared | Omitted |
|---|---|---|
| `company.go` | Read, Create, Update | **Delete** |
| `tagprint.go` | Read, Update | Create, Delete |

An omitted permission is not a closed door. `CrudController.accessDenied`:

```go
if perm == nil { return false }
```

**A permission that was never set denies nothing**, and the route is registered
on a separate flag — `enableDelete`, which **defaults to true**.

`tagprint.go` is safe, but not for the reason its permissions suggest: it also
calls `WithoutCreate` and `WithoutDelete`, so those routes never exist. Remove
either line and the screen opens to anybody.

**`company.go` did not.** A user holding only `CompanyRead` issued
`DELETE /mcj/company/{id}` and received **303 with the row deleted** — verified,
not inferred. That row is the shop's **name, GSTIN and address**: the particulars
printed on every invoice it issues.

### Fixed

`WithoutDelete` on the company screen. The shop's own particulars should not be
deletable through the interface at all — there is exactly one such row and every
bill depends on it. The DELETE route is now unregistered rather than merely
guarded, so no future permission slip can reopen it.

Two tests hold it: the read-only user now gets **405** where they got 303 and a
deletion, and a second records that `tagprint`'s safety comes from
`WithoutCreate` rather than from its permission list.

### The general shape

**A missing permission reads like a restriction and behaves like an open door.**
The other 16 crud screens declare all four and are unaffected; the nine non-crud
write routes were checked too, and the two POSTs gated on a read permission —
tag label and stock take — write nothing, so a read right is correct there.

---

## 107. Every report was served to any logged-in user, whatever their role — HIGH (now fixed)

Following defect 106 into the report screens. `navigation.Screen.Permissions`
carries a declaration for each of the 70 reports, and its own comment says what
it does:

> Permissions gate visibility. A menu entry nobody can open should not show.

**Visibility.** `ReportController.Register` mounted every report behind
authentication middleware and **no permission gate at all**. So the declarations
hid menu entries from users who were still served the page at its URL.

Measured, with a user holding one unrelated permission (`ColorRead`):

| Report | Response |
|---|---|
| `/mcj/reports/salary-sheet` | **200** |
| `/mcj/reports/trial-balance` | **200** |
| `/mcj/reports/user-rights` | **200** |

The salary sheet carries **basic pay, gross, paid and deducted, per person**,
defaulting to everyone — 246 rows across 19 people. The trial balance is the
whole of the books. The user-rights report is who may do what.

### How it was nearly missed

The first thing found was an inconsistency: the salary sheet declared
`ReportRead` while the sibling payroll master declared `PayrollRead`. Changing
the declaration was a one-line fix and it would have achieved **nothing** —
because the declaration only hides a menu entry. The real question was whether
the route was gated at all, and it was not.

**Tightening a declaration that turns out to be decorative is worse than leaving
it: it looks like the hole was closed.**

### Fixed

Each report route is now gated on the permissions its navigation entry declares,
with `ReportRead` as the floor for anything that declares none — so a report
added without a menu entry is closed rather than open. `gateAll` requires every
listed permission rather than any, because a screen declaring two is declaring
both are needed. The salary sheet's declaration is now `PayrollRead` and, being
enforced, means something.

Nobody loses access today: there is one role, Administrator, holding all 171
permissions — which is exactly why it is worth fixing before a second exists.
Full suite green, and the admin still reaches all 136 pages.

---

## 108. The rest of the route surface is gated, checked rather than assumed — LOW (clean result)

Completing the sweep that found defects 106 and 107. Every `Register` in the
module was read for routes mounted without a gate.

**One is ungated, and correctly so:** `home.go` serves `/` to any authenticated
user. It is 81 lines with no SQL, no money and no party data — it reports rebuild
progress against the legacy menu. Checked rather than assumed, because a landing
page that had grown a shelf figure would have been exactly the same shape of
leak as the reports.

The generic crud handlers were read in the SDK rather than trusted:

| Handler | Checks |
|---|---|
| `List` | `readPerm` |
| `Details` | `readPerm` |
| `GetEdit` | `updatePerm` |

All three consult the right permission — which is why defect 106 mattered so
much and defect 107 so much more. The crud screens were **correctly gated on
permissions that were mostly declared**; the reports were **not gated at all**,
so their declarations never ran.

### Where that leaves the route surface

- **70 report routes** and their `/export.xlsx` twins: gated on the navigation
  entry's declared permissions, floor of `ReportRead` (defect 107)
- **18 crud screens**: gated by the SDK on declared permissions, all four now
  declared or the operation disabled outright (defect 106)
- **20 hand-registered routes**: gated, and the two write routes behind a read
  permission write nothing
- **1 landing page**: open to any authenticated user, by design

Nothing further outstanding on this surface. What is *not* covered by any of
this is authorisation **within** a screen — a user who may read the ledger book
may read every ledger in it. That is how the legacy system worked and is not a
regression, but it is worth stating that no screen filters rows by who is asking.

## 109. SQL is built by concatenation in 29 files, and none of it takes user input — LOW (clean result, verified twice)

Report parameters reach SQL. Searching for query strings built by concatenation
rather than binding found **33 sites across 29 files**, which is the sort of
number that looks like a finding.

Every one is safe, and for four distinct reasons:

- **Package constants.** `openingSQL` in `trialbalance.go` and `balancesheet.go`
  is a `const` in this repository.
- **Fixed literals chosen by a branch.** `returns.go` sets
  `goodsSide, taxSide := "l.debit", "l.debit"` and swaps both to `"l.credit"` in
  one place. The value can only ever be one of two strings written here.
- **Slice iteration.** `negativestock.go` ranges over `stockFaults`;
  `dataquality.go` selects from `dataChecks` by index with a nil guard.
- **An explicit whitelist.** `movements.go` interpolates a column name and
  guards it with `switch column`, defaulting to
  `%q is not a filterable column` — with a comment saying the name comes from
  the file and never from a request.

The `where` clauses in `estimates.go`, `customergoods.go`, `categorise.go` and
`voucherprint.go` append a fixed fragment when a select parameter is not its
default. The parameter chooses **which literal**, never the text.

### Verified against the running server, not only by reading

Four payloads through report parameters:

| Parameter | Result |
|---|---|
| `ledger=' OR 1=1--` | 200, no rows, nothing executed |
| `as_on=2026-08-23';DROP TABLE mcj_ledgers;--` | **refused by the date parser** |
| `show=all' UNION SELECT null--` | 200, value ignored |
| `from=' OR 'a'='a` | 200, no rows |

**785 ledgers still here.** The one that reached a message was rejected at
parameter validation rather than at the database, which is the right place.

Recorded because "SQL built by string concatenation in 29 files" is true, alarming
and wrong as a conclusion — the next person to grep for it deserves the answer
rather than the count.

---

## 110. The template layer escapes, and nothing bypasses it — LOW (clean result, verified live)

templ escapes interpolated values by default, so the question is only what
bypasses it.

**`templ.Raw` appears nowhere in the module.** There is no hand-written HTML path
at all.

**`templ.SafeURL` appears 18 times**, and it does bypass URL sanitisation — a
`javascript:` URL passed through it would render as written. So every assignment
to the props it wraps was traced: **24 assignments to `Action`, `CancelURL`,
`NewURL` and `Href`, and none comes from a request.** They are path constants
(`RawStockPath`, `CategorisePath`), constants joined to a compiled slug
(`TradePath + "/" + kind.Slug`), or navigation entries built at start-up.

### Checked live as well

Reading tells you what the code does today. The Own Raw Stock screen has a
free-text `purity` field — added this morning — so it was posted with
`<script>alert(1)</script>` and the page read back:

| | |
|---|---|
| Raw `<script>alert(1)</script>` in the response | **0** |
| Escaped `&lt;script&gt;` | 1 |

Escaped, as templ promises. The test row was deleted afterwards; the table holds
its 10 migrated rows and **0 app-entered rows**.

Nothing to fix. Recorded so the next audit knows the `SafeURL` count was looked
at rather than counted, and that the escaping was confirmed against a running
page rather than assumed from the framework's documentation.

## 111. The admin password is published in the repository, and nothing said so — MEDIUM (now warned)

Scanning the 706 tracked files for credentials. `.env` is gitignored and
untracked, and there is exactly one hit:

```
Justfile:19:  seed-admin email="admin@mcj.local" password="wingold123":
```

`README.md` repeats it — *"creates admin@mcj.local / wingold123"* — and so does
the `just start` banner. That is three places, all of them the first things a
person reads.

On a laptop it is a convenience. On a server reachable by anyone else it is a
**published credential on an ERP holding 40,519 customer records**, and nothing
in the tooling or the documentation said so. `just start` runs `seed-admin` with
no arguments, so the default path creates it.

### Now

`seed-admin` compares the password it was given against the documented one and
prints to **stderr** when they match:

> WARNING: "wingold123" is the documented development password. It appears in the
> Justfile and the README, so anyone who can read this repository knows it.
> Before this server is reachable by anyone else, re-run with -password.

The constant is declared once, next to the check, so the warning cannot drift
away from the recipe that uses it. Verified both ways: the default triggers it,
`-password smoketest123` does not.

The README now carries the same warning at the point where it tells you to sign
in.

**Not removed.** A default that lets someone start the system in one command is
worth keeping; a default nobody is told about is not. This is a deployment
question, and it belongs beside blocker **B1** — which is still open on whether
this ever faces the internet at all.

## 112. Database errors are shown to the user, verbatim — MEDIUM (recorded as a trade-off, not fixed)

**62 places across 14 files** put `err.Error()` in front of the person using the
screen. Where the error came from the database, that is the database's own text.

Seen during the injection testing, when a report query was deliberately broken:

> This report could not be run: estimates: ERROR: relation
> "mcj_estimates_typo" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42P01)

A jeweller reads that and learns nothing. Anyone else reads a table name, a
schema convention and a SQLSTATE code.

### Why it has not been changed

It is a real trade-off rather than an oversight, and both sides are worth
stating:

- **For keeping it.** The shop can quote the message when reporting a problem,
  which is worth a great deal for a system with one administrator and no support
  desk. It is also what made the pipeline's failures diagnosable all day.
- **Against.** It describes the schema to whoever is looking, and the
  `TestEveryMenuPageAnswers` smoke test greps for `could not be run:` — so the
  test currently depends on the leak.

The standard remedy is to log the detail server-side and show the user a short
message with a reference to quote. That is a **62-site change** touching every
error path in the module, and it would break the smoke test's detection until it
is rewritten alongside.

### The condition that decides it

**While this runs on the shop's own machine, the exposure is to the shop.** If
blocker **B1** resolves toward a cloud VPS reachable from the internet, this
becomes information disclosure to strangers and should be changed before that
happens rather than after.

Recorded rather than done, because it is a decision about deployment and support
rather than a fault in the code — and because a 62-site refactor made without
that decision would be the wrong kind of thorough.

---

## 113. Every money value exported to Excel was text, so nothing could be summed — MEDIUM (now fixed)

The `/export.xlsx` routes had never been exercised. All four tested produce valid
`Microsoft Excel 2007+` files with the right contents — the estimates export
carries both bill numbers and both customers, matching the screen.

**But every money cell was a shared string.** The trial balance exported **1,205
cells, 964 of them text and not one numeric money cell**. Its Debit column read
`4262.51` as *text*.

An accountant exports a trial balance to add it up. Selecting that column in
Excel gave no total, and every cell carried the "number stored as text" warning.

### The mechanism

`rowSource.GetRows` did `out[j] = row[c.Field]`, handing the raw value to the
writer. A `rupees.Amount` is a struct with no case in that writer, so it arrived
as its string form. Columns already holding a Go `int64` — like the raw stock
`Lines` count — came out as real numbers, which is why the behaviour looked
inconsistent between reports.

`Money: true` and `Numeric: true` affect the **screen**. They never reached the
export.

### Fixed

`exportValue` converts a `rupees.Amount` to `float64(a.Paisa()) / 100`. Paisa are
`int64` and a `float64` holds every integer to 2^53, so no real amount loses
anything. Divided rather than formatted — a formatted string is what caused this.

Numeric cells in the trial balance went from **241 to 481**, and the exported
file now totals **₹29,58,46,599.44 on both sides, difference 0.00** — the same
figures as the screen, including the suspense line.

### Noted, not fixed

Weights are still text. They arrive as strings from `to_char(...)` in the query
rather than as numbers, so the same conversion cannot reach them. Money was the
column with a reason to be summed; weights are worth revisiting if anyone
totals them.

*(Two of my own counts were wrong on the way here: "241 numeric cells" in the
trial balance were style and index cells, not money, and a first regex reported
zero numeric cells at all. Fifth time today the check was wrong rather than the
thing checked.)*

---

## 114. The exports are correct, and my counting was wrong for the sixth time — LOW (clean result)

Following defect 113: does an export honour the filters applied on screen, or
dump the whole report? An accountant who filters to one supplier and exports
everything would not necessarily notice.

**It honours them, and matches the screen row for row:**

| View | Screen data rows | Export rows |
|---|---|---|
| Designs, default | 500 | 500 + header |
| Designs, `?show=all` | 500 | 500 + header |
| Designs, filtered to one item | *No designs match.* | the same message |

The export URL carries the request's query string, so the filtered export runs
the filtered query. Even the empty state travels: the sheet contains the row
reading *"No designs match."* rather than a bare header.

### The sixth wrong check

The first comparison used `grep -oE '<tr'` **across the whole page** and reported
502 screen rows against 501 exported — a consistent off-by-one that looked
exactly like the export dropping a totals row. It was counting `<tr>` in the
parameter form and the page furniture along with the report table.

Counting only the rows inside `<tbody>` that contain a `<td>`: **500 and 500.**

That is the sixth time today the check was wrong rather than the thing checked,
and the second time this exact mistake was made — the categorise flakiness
(defect 86) was also `grep -c` counting lines rather than rows.

**The pattern is specific enough to name: counting markup with a text pattern
over a whole document.** Every instance produced a plausible discrepancy in a
place where a real one would have mattered.

## 115. The 40,519-row lists are paginated, searchable and fast — but never say how many matched — LOW

`mcj_parties` holds **40,519 rows**. A screen that renders them all would be
unusable, so the list screens were checked.

They are fine:

| Screen | Rows served | Response |
|---|---|---|
| `/mcj/address-book` | 25 | 0.06 s |
| `/mcj/ledgers` | 25 | 0.05 s |
| `/mcj/items` | 25 | 0.05 s |

Paging is **infinite scroll**, not links: the last row carries
`hx-get="…?limit=25&page=2"` with `hx-trigger="intersect once"` and
`hx-swap="afterend"`, so the next 25 append as you reach the bottom.

Search works. The parameter is `Search`, capitalised — `?Search=TRISHANA`
returns one row, `?Search=SHAW` twenty-seven. That matters more than paging here:
reaching row 40,000 by scrolling would take about **1,600 fetches**, so search is
the only practical way to find a customer, and it is there.

### What is missing

**No total is displayed.** Searching "SHAW" fills a screen and gives no
indication whether that is 27 matches or 2,700 — and with infinite scroll there
is no last page to arrive at either. A shop looking up a customer cannot tell
whether to refine the search or keep scrolling.

The list is rendered by the SDK's crud table, so this is not a line in this
repository. Recorded rather than attempted: it is a small usability gap in a
component we do not own, and it sits behind a real question — whether the shop
searches by name often enough for the count to matter.

## 116. A sale made in the new system appears in neither the sales register nor the GST return — HIGH

The billing screen had only ever been smoke-tested for a 200. A real sale was
put through it: customer `KIRAN ASWANI`, one tag, `64091403` — a silver locket.

**The pricing is right.** 0.250 g net at today's rate is 63.38, making 25.00,
goods **88.38**; CGST 1.33 and SGST 1.32 (3% split in half, uneven by a paisa
because rounding is honest), rounded off −0.03, **91.00 to the customer**. It
prices at today's metal rate rather than the tag's stored 43.75, which is
correct for metal.

**The accounting is right.** A balanced `SALE-GST` voucher:

| Ledger | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|
| KIRAN ASWANI | 91.00 | |
| SALE | | 88.38 |
| CGST | | 1.33 |
| SGST | | 1.32 |
| ROUNDED OFF | 0.03 | |

It reaches the day book, the ledgers and the trial balance. The tag leaves the
shelf.

### What it does not do

| | |
|---|---|
| Row in `mcj_sales_invoices` | **none** |
| Row in `mcj_stock_movements` | **none** |
| Appears in the sales register | **no — 0 rows for the day** |
| Appears in the GST return (`gstr-sales`) | **no** |

The registers and the returns read `mcj_sales_invoices`, which only the migration
fills. So a bill raised in this system collects GST from a customer and **does
not appear in the return that reports it**, and the day's takings cannot be
reviewed on the screen built for that.

The stock trail is the second half: `in_stock` flips, but no movement is written,
so the tag's history ends at the day it was created. That is the same shape as
defect 93 — a trail that does not account for every disposal — except this one
we are creating ourselves.

### Not fixed here

This is the Tier 0 billing path and the fix is a design decision, not a patch:
either the sale writes an invoice row alongside the voucher, or the registers and
returns are rebuilt to read vouchers. The first is smaller and keeps the legacy
shape; the second is truer to double entry. **It should be decided before the
shop bills anything real**, because every bill raised before it lands is a bill
missing from a GST return.

*(The test sale was reversed: voucher and its five lines deleted, `in_stock`
restored. Verified afterwards — 1,848 vouchers, **0 app-created**, 2,575 tags,
₹14,23,61,188.20.)*

## 117. Nothing the application does writes a detail row, so the registers freeze at migration — HIGH

Defect 116 found the sale screen posting a voucher and no invoice. That is not
one screen's omission. **The entire module has four insert paths:**

| File | Writes |
|---|---|
| `infrastructure/persistence/voucher_repository.go` | `mcj_vouchers`, `mcj_voucher_lines` |
| `presentation/controllers/partysample.go` | `mcj_customer_goods` |
| `presentation/controllers/rawstock.go` | `mcj_raw_stock` |
| `presentation/controllers/tag.go` | `mcj_stock_items` |

Nothing writes `mcj_sales_invoices`, `mcj_sales_invoice_lines`,
`mcj_purchase_invoices`, `mcj_purchase_contents`, `mcj_old_gold_lines` or
**`mcj_stock_movements`**. Confirmed against the data — every one of those tables
is entirely migrated:

| Table | Rows | Written by the app |
|---|---|---|
| `mcj_sales_invoices` | 224 | **0** |
| `mcj_purchase_invoices` | 43 | **0** |
| `mcj_old_gold_lines` | 25 | **0** |
| `mcj_stock_movements` | 9,036 | **0** |

*(475 movements carry no `legacy_id`, which looked like app-written rows until
checked: they come from `retail_all_stock`, a migration source with no id of its
own.)*

### What that means after go-live

- **GST returns** report the 224 migrated bills forever; every new sale is missing
  (defect 116). *(The sales register is NOT affected — it reads vouchers. That
  half of defect 116 was a 404, corrected in defect 137.)*
- **Purchase register** the same for the 43.
- **Old gold** posts the money and never records the metal — the gross, net,
  touch and rate that defect 40's loader existed to recover.
- **The stock trail stops.** Its last entry is 19 August 2026. Tags will keep
  leaving the shelf, because `in_stock` flips, but nothing records that they did.
  Within a month the movement history and the shelf disagree, with no way to
  reconstruct the difference.

The accounting is unaffected throughout: vouchers and lines are written properly,
so the day book, the ledgers, the trial balance and the balance sheet stay
correct. **The books will be right and the registers will be empty.**

### Not fixed

Same decision as defect 116, one level up: either each posting screen writes its
detail rows alongside the voucher, or the registers are rebuilt to read vouchers
and the movement trail is written from the same place stock is flipped.

This is the largest open item in the rebuild and it is a design choice, not a
bug to patch quietly. **It belongs in front of the shop before the first real
bill.**

## 119. The same tag cannot be sold twice, and the refusal says why — LOW (clean result)

A jeweller's worst billing error is selling one piece to two customers. The sale
screen was tested for it: the same tag, `64091403`, billed twice in succession.

**Two attempts, one voucher.** The second was refused.

It is refused at **pricing**, before the save guard is reached, and the message
names the piece in plain language:

> These tags are not on the bill and must be priced by hand: 64091403 SILVER
> LOCKET — **not on the shelf — already sold or issued**

There is a second guard behind that one, which matters because pricing and saving
are separate requests and a tag can be sold in between:

```sql
UPDATE mcj_stock_items SET in_stock = false
WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = ANY($2) AND in_stock
```

It then compares `RowsAffected()` to the number of tags on the bill and refuses
the whole sale if they differ —

> N of M tags were no longer on the shelf — someone else may have sold them

The `AND in_stock` is what makes it safe: the update cannot clear a tag twice, so
two tills racing on the same piece produce one sale and one refusal rather than
two bills. The code says so in its own comment: *"better than billing a piece
twice."*

Nothing to fix. Recorded because it is the failure a jeweller would care about
most, and because it holds under the race rather than only in sequence.

Both test sales were reversed — **1,848 vouchers, 0 app-created, 2,575 tags,
₹14,23,61,188.20.**

---

## 120. The one duplicate barcode is benign, and the schema does not stop the next one — MEDIUM

Blocker **B8** records a duplicate barcode. It is still live, and it is the only
one: **2,575 tags on the shelf carry 2,574 distinct barcodes**, and across all
2,816 tags there are 2,815.

`86065435` is on two in-stock tags. The sale resolves a barcode with:

```sql
WHERE s.tenant_id = $1 AND s.barcode = $2
ORDER BY s.in_stock DESC LIMIT 1
```

— which picks one of the two arbitrarily. That would matter a great deal if the
pair differed. **It does not.** Every priced field is identical:

| gross | net | rate | amount | making | total | item | purity | pieces |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.000 | 0.000 | .00 | .00 | .00 | **900.00** | same | same | 1 |
| 0.000 | 0.000 | .00 | .00 | .00 | **900.00** | same | same | 1 |

Two identical `MALA` pieces at ₹900.00, created the same day. Scanning the
barcode sells one; the second stays on the shelf and can be sold on its own
merits. **Nobody is billed the wrong amount and no piece is sold twice** — the
arbitrary choice costs nothing because there is nothing to choose between.

### What is not protected

The tag screen refuses a barcode *"already on a tag that is still on the shelf"*,
which is the right rule — a barcode belonging to a sold tag may legitimately be
reused, and this shop reuses them.

But **there is no database constraint**. `mcj_stock_items` carries a primary key
on `id` and nothing on `barcode`, so the rule lives only in one controller. A
loader, a script, or a second screen written later can create a duplicate without
meeting it — and the next pair may not be two identical ₹900 malas.

A partial unique index on `(tenant_id, barcode) WHERE in_stock` would express it
in the schema. **Not added here**: it would reject the existing pair, so it needs
that pair resolved first, which is a question for the shop — are there two malas
on the shelf, or one counted twice? That is B8, and it is still the right
question.

## 121. The credit note posts a correct reversal — LOW (clean result)

The refund path, untested until now. A wrong credit note gives money away, and
the direction is the whole of it.

Priced: goods 1,000.00, CGST 15.00, SGST 15.00, **payable 1,030.00** — 3% split
in half, as on a sale.

Posted as `SALE-RET 4`, continuing from the three migrated sale returns:

| Ledger | Classification | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| KIRAN ASWANI | asset | | **1,030.00** |
| SALE_RETURN | income | **1,000.00** | |
| CGST | liability | 15.00 | |
| SGST | liability | 15.00 | |

Every direction is the mirror of a sale. The customer is **credited**, so what
they owe falls. `SALE_RETURN` is an income account **debited** — contra-revenue,
which is why the profit and loss nets returns off rather than adding them. The
tax ledgers are **debited** to give back the liability the sale created. It
balances at 1,030.00 both ways.

Worth stating because the opposite would look almost identical on screen and
would quietly inflate revenue while crediting the customer twice.

**Defect 117 applies here too**: no row is written to any register table, so the
return will not appear in the sales register or the GST return either. The
accounting is right and the register is silent, as with the sale.

Test voucher reversed — **1,848 vouchers, 0 app-created, 3 SALE-RET**, as
migrated.

The shop buying gold back over the counter. Priced: 10.000 g at 22kt, today's

Posted as `PURC-OG 26`:

| KIRAN ASWANI | asset | | **1,42,530.00** |

That loader was written to fix exactly this gap in the migrated data — **and the

## 123. The purchase screen behaves exactly as predicted, which is worth having checked — LOW (clean result, prediction confirmed)

The insert audit said the purchase screen would post a voucher and no invoice
row. Predictions have been wrong eight times today, so it was tested rather than
assumed.

Posted as `PURC-GSC 25`, continuing from the 24 migrated:

| Ledger | Classification | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|---|
| JAI KRISHNA JEWELLERS CO.PVT.LTD. | liability | | **5,150.00** |
| PURCHASE | expense | **5,000.00** | |
| INPUT CGST | liability | 75.00 | |
| INPUT SGST | liability | 75.00 | |

Balanced, and correct in a detail worth naming: the tax posts to **INPUT** CGST
and SGST, not the output accounts a sale uses. Input tax is recoverable and
output tax is owed; a screen that confused them would file a GST return claiming
credit it is not entitled to, and the voucher would still balance.

**`mcj_purchase_invoices` stayed at 43** — defect 117 confirmed here too, so the
purchase register will not show it.

### Why record a confirmed prediction

Because the prediction being right is a fact about this codebase, not a
foregone conclusion. Of the eight wrong checks today, several began as
confident readings of code that the data then contradicted. **Reading the insert
paths told me what should happen; posting a purchase told me what does.**

Five of the six B26 screens have now been exercised end to end. Only the debit
note and purchase-against-an-order remain, and they share the credit note's and
the purchase's controller respectively.

Test voucher reversed — 1,848 vouchers, 0 app-created, 24 PURC-GSC, 43 purchase
invoices.

## 124. The debit note and purchase order are correct, and the ninth wrong check was one I had warned myself about — LOW (clean result)

The last two B26 screens, completing the set of six.

**Debit note — `PURC-RET 4`**, the exact mirror of the purchase:

| Ledger | Dr | Cr |
|---|---|---|
| JAI KRISHNA JEWELLERS | **2,060.00** | |
| PURCHASE_RETURN | | **2,000.00** |
| INPUT CGST | | 30.00 |
| INPUT SGST | | 30.00 |

The supplier is **debited**, so what the shop owes falls. `PURCHASE_RETURN` is
credited as contra-expense, and the input tax is **given back** rather than
claimed — which is the half a wrong implementation would get wrong while still
balancing.

**Purchase against an order — `PURC-GCO 20`:** supplier credited 2,000.00,
PURCHASE debited 2,000.00, and **no tax lines at all.**

That looked like an omission. It is not:

| Legacy voucher type | Vouchers | Carrying input GST |
|---|---|---|
| PURC-GCO | 19 | **0** |
| PURC-GSC | 24 | **24** |

The screen reproduces the shop's own pattern exactly.

### The ninth wrong check, and this one I had warned myself about

The first query said **all 19** PURC-GCO vouchers carry input GST — the opposite
answer. It joined `voucher_detail` to `voucher_main` on `v_id` alone:

```sql
WHERE d.v_id = m.v_id   -- and nothing about the type
```

**`v_id` is not unique across voucher types.** Defect 83 measured that:
`legacy.voucher_detail` holds 5,229 rows with **1,186 distinct ids**, reused
freely. Defect 99 found 1,411 renumberings on top. I wrote both entries today and
then joined on the key they describe as ambiguous.

Adding `d.v_typ` to the grouping gives 0 and 24. **A key documented as unsafe is
not safe because the person joining on it wrote the documentation.**

All six B26 screens are now exercised end to end. Every test voucher reversed —
**1,848 vouchers, 0 app-created, 5,229 lines, 3 PURC-RET, 19 PURC-GCO, 2,575
tags.**

## 125. Every way the checking went wrong today, in one place — REFERENCE

Nine investigations produced a confident wrong answer because of how the question
was asked, not because of the data. They are scattered through the entries above;
gathered here because the next person will reach for the same shortcuts.

| # | What was asked | What it returned | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `status = 'Cancel'` on order lines | **0 of 366** | the value is `Cancelled` |
| 2 | join `address_book_sub_name` on `category_id` | error, then 0 | the column is `category` |
| 3 | invoice `total` against **voucher debits** | a ₹2.98 gap on 43 bills | the round-off sits on the credit side; comparing a document total to one side of a double entry counts it twice (defect 95) |
| 4 | `grep FAIL` in the loaders | **17 with no assertion** | they use `ERROR:` and `exit 1` (defect 105) |
| 5 | `grep -c '<tr'` for report rows | every report looked empty | templ minifies a table onto one line, so it counted **lines**, not rows (defect 86) |
| 6 | `grep '<tr'` across a whole page | screen 502 against export 501 | it counted the parameter form and page furniture too (defect 114) |
| 7 | `sum(DISTINCT total)` for B24 | ₹10,63,93,299 instead of ₹10,73,39,445 | it sums distinct **values**, dropping tags worth the same (defect 81) |
| 8 | `name LIKE 'CASH%'` for the cash ledger | a payment missing from the cash book | it matched **CASHFREE PAYMENTS PVT.LTD** (defect 118) |
| 9 | join `voucher_detail` on `v_id` alone | all 19 PURC-GCO carry GST — the opposite of the truth | `v_id` is reused across types: 5,229 rows, **1,186 distinct ids** (defects 83, 124) |

Three more of the same family, caught before they became claims:

- **Fill rate read as evidence.** `rate_tds` is 100% filled across 40,519 rows and
  holds **one distinct value**. Reporting "202,595 dropped values" would have been
  badly wrong (defect 74).
- **A whole-document search in a `--check`.** `status_figures.py --check` reported
  agreement while `STATUS.md` said 41 and the truth was 69, because "69" appeared
  elsewhere on the page (defect 103).
- **A regex counting style cells as money.** "241 numeric cells" in the trial
  balance were nothing of the kind (defect 113).

### What they have in common

Every one produced a **plausible** figure, in the place where a real defect would
have mattered, and several were large enough to be believed: ₹8.96 lakh
unexplained, 17 unguarded loaders, an export dropping a totals row.

Three defences worked, and only these three:

1. **Read one case by hand.** Opening a single "unguarded" loader ended #4.
2. **Reconcile against a second source.** The narration text settled the cheque
   dates; the weight settled the shelf column; the voucher lines settled #3.
3. **Try to make the check fail.** Emptying the registry exposed a vacuous
   security test; breaking a report exposed a cached smoke run.

**A pattern that returns a number has not answered the question. It has answered
a different question that may happen to have the same shape.**

## 127. Stock take is correct, and it matters more because of defect 117 — LOW (clean result)

Defect 117 leaves the movement trail frozen at 19 August 2026: tags will keep
leaving the shelf and nothing will record that they did. **Physical verification
then becomes the only way to know what is actually there**, which raises this
screen from a periodic chore to the fallback.

It was given four barcodes — two real tags on the shelf, one belonging to a tag
already sold, and one invented:

| | |
|---|---|
| Scanned | 4 |
| On the books | 2,575 |
| **Not found** | **2,573** — ₹14,23,34,155.40 |
| **Not on the books** | **2** — the sold tag and the invented one |

The arithmetic ties to the paisa: the shelf is ₹14,23,61,188.20, the two tags
actually scanned are worth ₹27,032.80, and the remainder is **₹14,23,34,155.40**
exactly.

A sold tag and a barcode that never existed are both reported as *not on the
books*, which is the honest classification — the screen cannot tell a
mis-scan from a piece that came back.

### What it refuses to do

> 2,573 tag(s) on the books but not on the shelf — ₹14,23,34,155.40. Each is
> either mislaid, out with a karigar or on approval, or gone. **Nothing here is
> written off; somebody has to walk this list.**

It adjusts nothing. A stock take that silently wrote off ₹14.23 crore of
unscanned tags would balance the books and lose the shop its stock record — and
that is exactly what a partial count looks like on the first pass.

Nothing to fix.

## 128. The tax invoice omits the tax rate and the reverse-charge statement — MEDIUM (for the shop's accountant)

The invoice is what the customer physically receives, so it was rendered and read
rather than pattern-matched. Two bills: one without item detail, one with.

**It is comprehensive.** Supplier name, address, **GSTIN `19AADCM7443D1ZH`** and
PAN; the customer with mobile, state and GSTIN field; invoice number and **date in
full** ("18 April 2026"); **place of supply**; the goods value, the tax, the
rounding and the total; **amount in words** — *"Rupees Thirty Five Lakh Twenty
Thousand Nine Hundred Six Only"* — a declaration, CIN, terms, bank details and a
signatory block. On a bill with lines, the item table carries **`# · Description ·
HSN · Purity · Pcs · Gross · Net · Rate · Making · Amount`**.

Two things are not there:

| Missing | Where it is required |
|---|---|
| **The rate of tax** — the bill shows `IGST 1,02,550.65` and never `@ 3%` | CGST Rules, rule 46(i) |
| **Whether tax is payable on reverse charge** | rule 46(m) |

No percentage appears anywhere on either bill.

The legacy print screen (`sales_bill_print.php`) was **never captured** — the app
generated it in JavaScript — so there is nothing to compare against and no way to
tell whether the shop's own bills carried these.

**Recorded rather than added.** Both are one line of template each, but an
invoice is a legal document and the wording is not mine to invent: "3%" against
IGST is easy, and a reverse-charge line has to say the right thing. This is a
question for the shop's accountant, alongside blocker **B3**, which already asks
for a real printed bill to compare the layout against.

*(Reaching this took four failed attempts to read the page — patterns that
reported the GSTIN missing when it was 222 characters from the heading. Eleventh
and twelfth false positives; the answer only came from printing the lines and
reading them.)*

## 129. The voucher print is correct, and it guards the trap that caught me three times — LOW (clean result)

The receipt a customer gets for money paid. Rendered `RCPT 1` of 2026-2027 and
read it:

```
MANIK CHAND JEWELLERS & SONS PVT.LTD.
25A,CAMAC STREET, KOLKATA-700016
GSTIN: 19AADCM7443D1ZH

Receipt Voucher
No:              RCPT 1
Financial year:  2026-2027
Date:            01 April 2026
With:            TRISHANA SHAW

Account          Debit      Credit
TRISHANA SHAW               6,150.00
CASH             6,150.00
Total            6,150.00
```

Matches the database exactly: the customer credited 6,150.00, cash debited
6,150.00.

### The detail worth noticing

It prints the **financial year**, and the controller says why:

> A voucher number repeats across types and years, which is the same key trap
> that broke the migration's voucher load and the bank clearing dates. Without
> the year, "RCPT 3" is several different vouchers.

That is the same trap as defect 83 — `legacy.voucher_detail` holding 5,229 rows
with **1,186 distinct ids** — and defect 99's 1,411 renumberings. **It is also
the trap I fell into myself**, joining `voucher_detail` on `v_id` without the
type and getting the opposite answer about input GST (defect 124).

So a receipt handed to a customer identifies the voucher unambiguously, while
the person auditing the system wrote a query that could not. The product is
more careful here than its author was.

Nothing to fix.

## 131. The shop's own system also computed a loss, and the working survived — HIGH (corroborates B19)

Both migration reconciliations pass — **154 tables against the ERP's own backup
manifest, 0 mismatches; 149 staged tables against MySQL, 0 mismatches** — so the
chain from backup to staging is verified row for row.

Five manifest tables are not staged, all `temp_*` scratch. Correctly excluded,
but one of them is worth reading. **`temp_pl` is the legacy system's own profit
and loss working, six rows, left where it last ran:**

| Group | Type | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Sales Account | income | 2,11,39,143.00 |
| Direct Income | income | 0 |
| Indirect Income | income | 0 |
| Purchase Account | expense | 2,62,33,491.29 |
| Indirect Expenses | expense | 42,66,733.51 |
| Direct Expenses | expense | 11,458.75 |

Income **₹2,11,39,143.00** against expenses **₹3,05,11,683.55** — the shop's own
ERP computed a **loss of ₹93,72,540.55**.

### Why this matters

The profit and loss screen built here reports a shortfall of **₹1,10,87,494.08**
and refuses to call it a profit or a loss, because a jeweller's cost of sales
needs closing stock and this ERP carries none as a ledger (defect 79, blocker
B19). That reasoning was inference from the data.

**It is no longer only inference.** The legacy system, given the same ledgers,
produced the same shape of answer: a nine-figure sales line, a larger purchase
line, and a net that reads as a substantial loss. The shop was not running at a
₹93 lakh loss; its own P&L said so because stock sits outside the accounts there
too.

The two figures differ by **₹17,14,953.53**, which is expected and not
reconcilable: `temp_pl` is a scratch table with no date stamp, written whenever
the screen was last opened, while the figure here is bounded to 1 April–23
August 2026. What matches is the **shape**, and the shape is the argument.

**For B19 this is the strongest evidence yet** that closing stock was always held
outside the ledgers rather than lost in migration — the previous system had the
same hole and printed the same misleading total.

**TCS — tax collected at source — which appears nowhere in this rebuild.**

It was never used. Checked at every level:

|---|---|

| Sales bills with a TCS rate | **0 of 224** |
| Total TCS collected | **₹0.00** |

| Ledgers named TCS | **0** |

`legacy.sales_vou` and `legacy.stock_inward` both have `tcs_per` and `tcs_amt`

The provision exists in the old system because a jeweller can need it. The

## 133. The raw metal is real, still moving, and my accounting inference about it was wrong — HIGH (corrects defect 78)

`temp_tag_untag_report_new` — 171 rows, one of the five scratch tables excluded
from staging — is the shop's own **raw stock movement report**. Its opening rows
are exactly the `barcode_main_rawstone` figures of defect 78: 82.156 g at 9,
1,073.05 at 14, 5,566.29 at 18.

It covers **1 April to 17 June 2026** and carries three document types:

| Purity | Opening | Receive | Issue | Balance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9 | 82.156 | 86.498 | 19.402 | **149.252** |
| 14 | 1,073.050 | 448.003 | 129.687 | **1,391.366** |
| 18 | 5,566.290 | 82.377 | 148.830 | **5,499.837** |
| 22 | 5,058.310 | 1.900 | 102.660 | **4,957.550** |
| 0 / blank | 95.010 | 16.630 | 1.396 | 110.244 |
| **Total** | **11,874.816** | **635.408** | **401.975** | **12,108.249** |

**11,998.005 g at gold purities, after 146 issues and 14 receipts** — worth
**₹15,76,50,889.76** at today's metal rates, purity by purity:

| Purity | Balance | Rate today | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9 | 149.252 g | 6,199.00 | 9,25,213.15 |
| 14 | 1,391.366 g | 9,643.00 | 1,34,16,942.34 |
| 18 | 5,499.837 g | 12,398.00 | 6,81,86,979.13 |
| 22 | 4,957.550 g | 15,153.00 | 7,51,21,755.15 |
| **Total** | **11,998.005 g** | | **15,76,50,889.76** |

The metal was not a historical remnant. It was being worked with — issued out and taken
back in — eleven weeks before the system died.

### What I got wrong

Defect 78 argued this could not be current stock, from the accounts:

> At the shelf's blended ₹7,104.23 per gram the raw gold alone is
> ₹8,36,86,423.98… the trial balance's unexplained residual after tagged stock is
> ₹1.09 crore. If this metal were also held and unrecorded the books would be
> short by roughly ₹8.4 crore more than they are.

The conclusion does not follow — and **the ₹8,36,86,423.98 was itself wrong**,
which was not known when this entry was written. ₹7,104.23 is the whole shelf
divided by the whole shelf's weight, and **48% of that weight is silver**; it
cannot be applied to gold. Priced purity by purity at today's metal rates the
11,998.005 g comes to **₹15,76,50,889.76**, not ₹8.37 crore. See the correction
in [defect 78].

The reasoning fault stands on its own regardless of the figure. It assumed the
books would show the metal if the shop had it. **They do not, and that is the
whole of B19**: this ERP holds no stock in its ledgers, tagged or raw. Reasoning
from an absence in accounts that are known not to record stock was circular, and
I did not notice because the arithmetic was clean.

The honest reading is simpler and worse: **the shop holds roughly 12 kg of gold
in raw stock that appears in no ledger, on top of ₹14.24 crore of tagged stock
that appears in no ledger.** B19's hole is larger than the shelf, not smaller.

### What follows

- Defect 78's inference is retracted; its measurements stand.
- The raw stock screen shows the **opening** figures, which is what
  `barcode_main_rawstone` holds. The 146 issues and 14 receipts are in a scratch
  table, not a real one, so there is nothing to load them from — the movement
  history exists only as a report someone happened to run.
- **The question for the shop is unchanged but sharper.** Not *"is this metal
  still there?"* — the report says it was in June — but **"where is it now, and
  who has it?"**

## 134. The migration's scope is provably complete, and the check that proved it only looked one way — MEDIUM (now fixed)

`verify_rowcounts.sh` compares every manifest entry against MySQL and reported
**154 tables, 0 mismatches**. That is a real check and it was passing honestly.

It says nothing about a table that is **in MySQL and not in the manifest**. Such
a table is never looked at, and the check passes.

The database holds **451 base tables** against **154 manifest entries** — so
**297 are unlisted.** Every one was counted:

| | |
|---|---|
| Unlisted tables | **297** |
| Of those, non-empty | **0** |
| Rows between them | **0** |

So the manifest is exactly the set of tables that hold data, and nothing was
missed. That is worth knowing precisely, because it closes the question that has
been open all day in the background — *is there anything we have not looked at?*

**The whole chain, verified:**

| Stage | Count |
|---|---|
| Base tables in the legacy MySQL | 451 |
| — holding any data | **154** |
| Row counts matching the ERP's own backup manifest | **154, 0 mismatches** |
| Staged into Postgres | 149 (the 5 omitted are `temp_*` scratch) |
| Staging matching MySQL row for row | **149, 0 mismatches** |
| Read by a loader | 91 |
| Examined and deliberately not loaded | the remainder, each written up |

### Fixed

The script now walks the other direction too: every base table absent from the
manifest is counted, and a populated one fails the run with its name and row
count. Today that finds nothing, which is the point — **it is a guarantee about
the next dump, not a discovery about this one.**

*(The five `temp_*` tables excluded from staging turned out to carry the shop's
own P&L working and its raw-stock movement report — defects 131 and 133, the two
most consequential findings of the day. "Excluded as scratch" was right for
loading and wrong for reading.)*

## 135. A third of "stones sold" is silver sold by weight — HIGH (figure corrected)

Following the excluded scratch tables into `temp_sale_register`, which listed 55
June bills. **17 of them show no item detail on the invoice** — the screen says
so: *"This bill carries no item detail in the migrated data."*

The detail exists. `sales_vou_main` — the line table the loader reads — has **0
rows** for those 17 bills, while `sales_vou_detail` has 17. Reading one:

| bill | barcode | item | gw | purity | fine wt | metal | rate | amount |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GST/2627/00092 | *(none)* | 660 | 200.000 | 92.50 | 185.000 | **SLV** | 262.14 | 52,427.00 |

**200 grams of silver sold by weight, untagged.** `sales_vou_main` covers tagged
pieces only, so bulk metal sales appear nowhere as invoice lines.

### The consequence is worse than a missing line

`load_sold_stones.sh` loads **all 203 rows** of `sales_vou_detail` into
`mcj_sold_stones` with no filter. So those metal rows are counted as stones:

| | Rows | Carats | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Genuine stones | 182 | 131.946 | **36,44,121.33** |
| **No carats — metal sold by weight** | **21** | **0.000** | **75,39,341.00** |
| Total as loaded | 203 | 131.946 | 1,11,83,462.33 |

By metal purity the metal rows are unmistakable: `SLV` 14 rows, `995` 2 rows,
`SLV999` 1 row — **17 rows with a metal purity and not one carat between them**,
₹75,39,341.00.

**The figure published as "stones sold — ₹1,11,83,462.33" is three times the
truth.** Stones sold is **₹36,44,121.33**. The carat figure, 131.946, was always
right: metal rows carry no carats, so they inflated the money and left the
weight alone — which is exactly why it survived being written down four times.

### Corrected, not yet fixed in the loader

Every occurrence in the record now reads ₹36,44,121.33 with the correction
noted. The loader is left alone deliberately: whether those 21 rows belong in
`mcj_sold_stones` at all, or as invoice lines for the 39 bills worth
**₹89,26,345.00** that currently show no detail, is the same question as blocker
**B26** — what a posting writes and what a register reads. Splitting the table on
a guess would move the error rather than remove it.

## 136. The purchase side already makes the distinction the sale side missed — LOW (the fix has a pattern to follow)

Defect 135 found metal sold by weight counted as stones. The symmetric question:
does the purchase side make the same mistake?

**It does not, and it never did.** `mcj_purchase_contents` is fed from
`stock_inward_main` and `stock_inward_detail`, and **28 of its 60 rows carry no
carats** — the same shape that went wrong on sales. The report handles it:

- a **`kind` parameter** offering *Everything · Stones · Metal*
- a **`kind` column** on every row
- a footer that counts them apart — *"6 stone row(s), 1 metal row(s)"*
- a test, `TestPurchaseContents_KeepsCaratsAndGramsApart`, asserting stone rows
  are measured in `ct` and metal rows in `g`

Live, filtered three ways: **6 stone rows and 1 metal row**, and the unfiltered
view shows exactly those 7.

### Why this matters for fixing 135

The distinction between metal and stones is not something this codebase failed to
understand. It is implemented, tested and surfaced on the purchase side, and
absent on the sale side. **That makes defect 135 an oversight with a pattern to
copy rather than a design question to settle** — whoever splits
`mcj_sold_stones` has a working example twenty files away, including how to word
the filter and how to measure each kind.

*(The three filtered views first counted 9, 8 and 3 rows, which do not add up.
Each count included the two footer rows. Fifteenth counting artefact of the day,
same family as the rest: a row count taken from markup rather than from the
data.)*

## 137. Defect 116 was half wrong: the sales register does show new sales — HIGH (correction)

Defect 116 reported that a sale made in this system *"appears in neither the
sales register nor the GST return"*, and blocker **B26** was raised partly on it.

**The sales register half is wrong, and the cause was a 404.**

The report key is `sales-register`. I queried `sale-register`:

| URL | Response | Rows |
|---|---|---|
| `/mcj/reports/sale-register` | **404** | 0 |
| `/mcj/reports/sales-register` | 200 | **224** |

An empty page from a wrong URL reads exactly like an empty register. Re-tested
with a real sale posted:

| Report | Rows for the day | The new sale |
|---|---|---|
| `sales-register` | 1 | **present** |
| `gstr-sales` | 1 | **absent** |

**`salesregister.go` reads `mcj_vouchers` and `mcj_voucher_lines`**, so it sees
anything the shop posts. The GST return reads `mcj_sales_invoices`, so it does
not.

### What is actually affected

Thirteen reports read one of the three migration-only tables
(`mcj_sales_invoices`, `mcj_purchase_invoices`, `mcj_old_gold_lines`):

`gstr-sales` · `mrp-sales` · `mrp-purchases` · `sale-cost` ·
`sales-comparison` · `sales-targets` · `sold-stones` · `statistics` ·
`customer-metal` · `old-goods-register` · `order-to-barcode` ·
`purchase-contents` · `ledger-merge`

**The GST return is the one that matters** — a bill raised in this system still
does not reach it, which is a compliance exposure and B26 stands on that alone.
The day book, cash book, ledger book, trial balance, balance sheet, P&L **and the
sales register** all read vouchers and are unaffected.

### What I should have done

The claim rested on a single empty page. Two things would have caught it
immediately: **checking the HTTP status** — a 404 was right there in the response
— and **listing the report keys** rather than guessing one from the screen's
name. Sixteenth wrong check of the day, and the most consequential: it escalated
into a blocker and a caveat on the coverage figure.

## 138. Every other report path in the record is real — REFERENCE (audit after defect 137)

Defect 137 turned on a URL that did not exist. The obvious question is whether
anything else in the record rests on one.

**69 report keys are defined.** Nineteen distinct report paths are cited across
`STATUS.md`, `data-defects.md`, `blockers.md` and `screens.md`. **Eighteen of the
nineteen are real keys.** The exception is `sale-register`, and it now appears in
exactly three places — all of them describing the mistake:

- the defect 137 entry, as the 404 it was
- the B26 correction note
- the status log entry

Nothing else cites it as a working path.

That the rest hold up is partly luck and partly method: **most of the day's
sweeps harvested their URLs from the rendered menu rather than typing them.** The
136-page smoke sweep, the 140-run parameter sweep and the export checks all took
their paths from `href` attributes, so a wrong key was impossible by
construction. The two hand-typed ones went wrong — `sale-register` (404, defect
137) and `gstr1` (404, caught at the time and corrected to `gstr-sales`).

**Both hand-typed URLs were wrong. Neither harvested one was.** That is the
argument for `TestEveryMenuPageAnswers` harvesting its list rather than carrying
one, and it applies to investigation as much as to tests: **ask the system what
its paths are, do not tell it.**

## 139. All 69 reports run and none is silently empty — REFERENCE (clean result, harvested)

## 140. The quote report reprices correctly, and shows how stale a tag's stored value is — LOW (clean result)

The last of the 69 reports never seen with data. Quoted `31595399`, a diamond
set:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| Metal | 147.242 g net at **₹12,398.00** per g | 18,25,506.32 |
| Stones | carried from the tag | 24,76,760.00 |
| Making | ₹1,500.00 per gram of net weight | 2,20,863.00 |
| **Price before tax** | | **45,23,129.32** |

Every line checks: 147.242 × 12,398 = 1,825,506.32; 147.242 × 1,500 = 220,863.00;
the three sum to 4,523,129.32 exactly.

### What it shows about the shelf

The same tag stores `total` **₹32,86,591.00** at a stored rate of **₹4,000.00**
per gram. Today's quote is **₹45,23,129.32** — **₹12,36,538.32 more**, because the
18kt rate has gone from ₹4,000 to ₹12,398 since the tag was priced.

That is a **3.1× move in the metal rate**, and it is the clearest illustration of
why several figures in this record carry the phrase *"at today's rate"*:

- the shelf's **₹14,23,61,188.20** is the tags' stored values, priced when each
  tag was made
- a quote, a sale and the stock-at-today's-rates screen all reprice the metal
- so the shelf's book value and what the stock would fetch are **different
  numbers**, and neither is wrong

Nothing to fix. Recorded because a reader comparing ₹32,86,591.00 on the tag
against ₹45,23,129.32 on the quote would reasonably suspect one of them — and
both are right.

## 141. Most of the "shelf is worth half as much again" comes from an opening-book rate, not a price rise — MEDIUM

Ran **Stock at Today's Rates** for the first time with the totals reconciled:

| | Book value | Value today | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rate-bearing tags (1,607) | 13,74,96,960.20 | 20,67,35,594.36 | **+6,92,38,634.16** |
| Fixed price (968) | 48,64,228.00 | 48,64,228.00 | 0.00 |
| **Shelf** | **14,23,61,188.20** | **21,15,99,822.36** | **+6,92,38,634.16** |

The book column totals **₹14,23,61,188.20**, matching the shelf figure this record
has carried all along — an independent confirmation of it.

### The report's arithmetic is sound

Worth stating, because I doubted it and was wrong. The tag's metal value is
`rate x net_weight` and the report reprices exactly that, leaving stones and
making alone. On stone-set tags `amount` already contains the stone value, so
the identity is `amount - stones = rate x net_weight` — which holds for
**478 of 478** such tags, to the paisa. No tag is mispriced by this report.

### But the baseline is not what the screen implies

**358 of the 360 tags** carrying a stored rate of exactly **₹4,000.00** are
flagged `is_opening`. That is an opening-stock valuation — a round number the
shop's books opened at — and it sits across **five different purities**
(18, 22, 14, 9, 95) over **19 months** (2024-04-01 to 2025-11-21). One rate
cannot be the market price of 18kt and 22kt on the same day, let alone for a
year and a half. It was never meant to be a market rate.

Those tags are **34%** of the rate-bearing book value but produce **57% of the
entire uplift**:

| | Tags | Book value | Uplift produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stored rate = ₹4,000.00 | 360 | 4,69,44,332.28 | **3,94,01,031.93** |
| Every other tag | 1,247 | 9,05,52,627.92 | 2,98,37,602.23 |

So the larger half of "the shelf is worth half as much again" is **the distance
between an opening book entry and today's gold price**, not the gain on those
pieces since they were bought. The remaining ₹2,98,37,602.23 is the part that
reflects an actual price movement against a real tagging rate.

Nothing here can be repaired from the data: **`mcj_metal_rates` begins
2026-04-01**, and every one of these tags was created in 2024 or 2025. There is
no rate history reaching back to when they were tagged, so what gold actually
cost on those dates cannot be recovered from this database.

### A visible symptom

107 tags carry a stored rate **above** today's rate for their purity, so the
report marks them **down by ₹7,28,869.28**. 91 of them are 14kt and 9kt, and
**every one of those 91 is stone-set**, with implied fine-gold rates reaching
₹26,333/g (14kt) and ₹38,755/g (9kt) against today's ₹16,531/g. A historic
*market* rate cannot sit 1.6x-2.3x above today's when gold has risen throughout.
Those are loaded in-house rates for stone-set mounts, and repricing them to a
market rate is not meaningful. It is why the **9kt line reads as a loss of
₹1,55,823.65** on screen — an artefact, not a fall in value.

### What to do

The figure is not wrong, but "the shelf is worth half as much again" should not
be quoted without the split above. Ask Rahul what the 2024 opening rate was
meant to represent before this screen is shown to anyone valuing the business.
Relates to [defect 140] and [defect 79] — the tag's stored value is a stale
price, and this is the same fact at portfolio scale.

## 142. There is no accounting history behind 87% of the stock, and it is not recoverable — HIGH

Chasing [defect 141] into the ledgers produced the reason B19 has never tied out.

### The books begin in March 2026

The legacy `voucher_main` holds **1,848 vouchers in total**. Every one is filed
under `ac_yr` **2026-2027** (eight carry a blank year), and the **earliest voucher
of any kind is dated 2026-03-09**.

That is the whole accounting history the shop possesses. It is not a migration
gap — our `mcj_vouchers` holds **1,848** rows, matching the legacy table exactly,
so nothing was dropped on the way in. The source system simply does not retain
vouchers beyond the current financial year.

### The shelf begins in 2016

| Shelf stock | Tags | Book value | Net weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| Created **before** the first voucher (2026-03-09) | **2,305** | **12,43,38,210.80** | 18,777.098 g |
| Created after it | 270 | 1,80,22,977.40 | 1,261.838 g |
| **Total** | **2,575** | **14,23,61,188.20** | 20,038.936 g |

**87.3% of the shelf by value predates the first voucher in the books.** Those
2,305 tags cannot have a purchase document behind them, because no document from
that period exists anywhere in the system.

The tags themselves say so. Their `voucher_no` values reference financial years
**1617, 1920, 2021, 2122, 2223, 2324, 2425** and **2526** — years for which both
databases hold **zero** vouchers. And **83% of shelf value** (2,207 tags,
**₹11,84,27,092.95**) entered through `created_from='stk'`, a direct stock entry
citing an `STK/NNNNN` number that carries **no financial year at all** and matches
nothing in the ledger set.

### Why this matters

- **B19 is explained.** Stock is not merely held outside the ledgers; for 87% of
  it the accounting record that would place it inside them **no longer exists**.
  The opening trial balance cannot be reconstructed from documents.
- **It is unrecoverable.** Not a load to re-run. The rows are absent from the
  shop's own MySQL, and `newgst.in/mcj` went to 404 on 2026-08-21, so there is no
  second copy to go back to.
- **Provenance stops at the tag.** For ₹12.43 crore of goods, what the shop paid
  and who it bought from cannot be established from this data. Only the tag's own
  stored value survives — and [defect 141] shows that value is an opening-book
  figure for 360 of those tags.

### What to do

Ask Rahul whether purchase history exists **outside** this ERP — paper invoices,
a previous system, an accountant's books. If it does, that is the only route to
provenance for ₹12.43 crore of stock. If it does not, the opening stock figure
has to be asserted rather than derived, and B19 closes as *by design* rather than
as a defect to fix.

## 143. Eight reports print a footer that counts their own summary row a second time — HIGH

The `report.Spec` comment warns about exactly this: *"a report containing both
groups and their totals would count each figure twice and print a footer nobody
can reconcile."* That is `NoTotals`, and eight reports that emit their own
summary row never set it. The shell treats the summary row as data and adds it
to the detail rows it already summarised.

Every one of these was read off the running screen:

| Report | Its own summary says | Footer prints | |
|---|---|---|---|
| stone-ledger | 6,04,28,535.00 | **12,08,57,070.00** | 2x |
| hallmarking | 11,54,63,861.86 | **23,09,27,723.72** | 2x |
| opening-stock | 8,51,58,772.85 | **17,03,17,545.70** | 2x |
| customer-metal | 50,71,370.00 | **1,01,42,740.00** | 2x (4 columns) |
| ordered-stones | 16,36,662.00 | **32,73,324.00** | 2x |
| sold-stones | 4,17,856.40 | **8,35,712.80** | 2x |
| mrp-sales | 1,800.00 | **3,600.00** | 2x (3 columns) |
| purchase-contents | 14,38,899.00 | **42,76,377.00** | **2.97x** |

`purchase-contents` is the worst because it carries **two** trailing summary rows
(*"6 bill(s)"* and *"Billed for these purchases"*), so its value column is counted
three times: 14,38,899.00 + 14,38,899.00 + 13,98,579.00 = 42,76,377.00.

`opening-stock` is the useful cross-check. Its summary row, **₹8,51,58,772.85**,
is exactly the opening-stock book value computed independently against the
database in [defect 142]. The summary row is right; the footer is wrong.

**`order-to-barcode` is NOT affected** and was checked: it also emits a summary
row, but leaves the money cell blank, so its footer (₹66,11,878.00) equals the
sum of its 35 detail rows. Correct as it stands.

**Fix:** `NoTotals: true` on the eight. Applied — see below.

**Incomplete — see [defect 160].** Two further reports, `sale-cost` and
`mrp-purchases`, had the same fault and were missed here, because the sweep read
only the *last* body row and `sale-cost` carries two summary rows.

## 144. Three reports total a per-unit rate — MEDIUM

Distinct cause, same footer. `Column.Money` makes a column both money-formatted
and *summable*, and three reports mark a per-unit rate as money:

| Report | Column | Footer prints |
|---|---|---|
| stone-ledger | Rate a carat | **2,67,79,476.58** |
| sold-stones | Rate a carat | 5,73,301.92 |
| purchase-contents | Rate | 1,63,234.11 |

₹2,67,79,476.58 is 673 per-carat rates added together. It is not a quantity of
anything — no stone costs it, no total contains it — and it sits in the footer in
the same style as the genuine value total beside it.

Rates are averaged, not added, and an average of rates weighted by nothing is
also misleading. The right answer is to print nothing.

**Fix:** a `NoTotal` flag on `report.Column` that keeps money formatting but
excludes the column from the footer. Applied — see below.

### 143 / 144 — fixed and verified

- `NoTotals: true` on the eight reports that carry their own summary row.
- A new `report.Column.NoTotal` keeps a money column out of the footer while
  leaving its money formatting intact; set on the three per-carat rate columns.
- Re-fetched all 69 reports from the running app: the eight wrong footers are
  gone, **no doubled footer remains anywhere**, and the 32 reports with a
  legitimate footer still have one — including `order-to-barcode`, which was
  correct before and is untouched.
- Three unit tests in `report_totals_test.go`. They were checked by removing the
  `NoTotal` guard and confirming the rate test fails with the summed
  `"50,000.00"` — they catch the regression rather than passing vacuously.
- The Excel export writes no totals row, so it never had either defect.
- Full suite green, integration included.
