## 146. `barcode` is used as a join key but is not unique, and one duplicate exists — MEDIUM

Caught while checking the fix for [defect 145]: the new `stock-history` count came
back **9,040** against a table holding **9,036** movements.

The cause is a fan-out. `mcj_stock_items` has a **non-unique** index on
`(tenant_id, barcode)` — only `legacy_id` is unique — and one barcode is on the
shelf twice:

| legacy_id | barcode | description | value | voucher | in stock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 96399 | 86065435 | MALA | 900.00 | STK/12518 | yes |
| 96409 | 86065435 | MALA | 900.00 | STK/12519 | yes |

Two separate stock entries on consecutive vouchers, same day, same item, same
value — two identical MALA pieces that were given **the same barcode**. That
barcode has 4 movements, and 4 x 2 - 4 = the 4 extra rows.

### Why it is worth recording

- **Scanning 86065435 is ambiguous.** Two pieces answer to it. A sale, a
  transfer or a stock check on that number cannot say which one it touched.
- **Every join on barcode inflates.** Reports join stock on barcode rather than
  on id, so any of them can double-count this tag. Today the impact is 4 rows;
  it grows with every future duplicate, and nothing in the schema prevents one.
- The **shelf value is not affected** — these really are two pieces worth ₹900
  each, so ₹1,800 is correct. The defect is the key, not the money.

**Fixed here:** the `stock-history` count is now `count(DISTINCT m.id)` and
reports 9,036. **Not fixed:** the underlying duplicate, and the absence of a
unique constraint. A unique index cannot simply be added — it would reject this
row, and the shop may legitimately need to keep both pieces until someone
re-tags one.

**Needs Rahul:** re-tag one of the two MALA pieces, after which
`(tenant_id, barcode)` can be made unique for goods still in stock.

**This now blocks a second defect.** [Defect 181] found that `tag.go`'s
check-then-insert cannot prevent two tills creating the same barcode, and the
partial unique index that would close it is rejected by **this row** — the only
barcode with more than one in-stock copy. One re-tag unblocks both.

## 147. The category tagging screen stops at 200 tags, and 80 of them cannot be reached at all — MEDIUM

Same class as [defect 145], found by sweeping the controllers for `LIMIT`. The
cap itself is deliberate and the code says so — 2,575 checkboxes is not a page
anyone can work through — but the screen never mentioned it.

What it showed before the fix:

| Filter | Tags matching | Rows shown | Page said |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | **2,575** | 200 | *"1114 tags on the shelf have no category"* |
| GOLD CHAIN | **280** | 200 | the same 1114 line |
| SILVER TOPS, untagged | **241** | 200 | the same 1114 line |

The one count on the page is the **global** uncategorised total. It does not
respond to the filter, so a user who filters to GOLD CHAIN sees 200 rows and a
number, 1,114, that has nothing to do with them.

### 80 tags that no filter can reach

The list is ordered by value descending, and the screen offers exactly two
filters: **item** and **"only tags with no category"**. For GOLD CHAIN:

- 280 tags in stock, 200 shown, **80 past the cap**
- **all 80 already have a category**, so the untagged filter excludes them
- there is no purity filter, no search, no paging

So those 80 tags — worth **₹7,54,587.96** — cannot be brought onto the screen by
any combination of controls it offers. **Their category can never be corrected
here.** SILVER TOPS is the milder version: 241 uncategorised against a 200 cap,
so 41 are hidden on the first pass, though those do surface once the first 200
are assigned and drop out of the filter.

### Fixed

The screen now runs a count over the *same* filter and says what it is hiding:

- no filter → *"Showing the 200 dearest of 2575 matching tags — 2375 are not on this page."*
- GOLD CHAIN → *"…200 dearest of 280… — 80 are not on this page."*
- SILVER TOPS untagged → *"…200 dearest of 241… — 41 are not on this page."*

All three counts verified against the database. The notice is amber, not grey,
because it changes what the page means.

**Not fixed — needs Rahul:** the 80 unreachable tags still need either a purity
filter, a barcode search, or paging on this screen. Saying so is not the same as

## 148. A reload silently unlinked seven customers' goods, leaving a screen unusable — HIGH

The party-sample **issue** screen offered an empty customer list. Nothing could
be selected, so no outstanding holding could be recorded as returned.

The shop is holding **7 lines of customers' own goods** — 233 pieces, 14.43
carats of stones and diamonds belonging to five named people:

| Receipt | Received | Customer | What | Pieces | Carats |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CG/2627/00003 | 28 Jun 2026 | RASHMI SARAF | stone | 1 | 2.750 |
| CG/2627/00005 | 22 Jul 2026 | POOJA PRASAD | diamond + stone | 203 | 4.150 |
| CG/2627/00006 | 26 Jul 2026 | TAHA.M. TAMBAWALA | stone | 3 | 6.250 |
| CG/2627/00007-8 | 18 Aug 2026 | PRABHA BHANSALI | stone + diamond | 18 | 1.100 |
| CG/2627/00009 | 19 Aug 2026 | P. K. MUNDRA | diamond | 8 | 0.180 |

Every row carried the customer's **name and code**, and all five codes resolve to
a ledger exactly — same code, same name. But `ledger_id` was **NULL on all seven**,
and the screen lists customers by ledger, so it showed nobody.

### The cause is a class, not a typo

Migration `mcj-1787385000` adds `ledger_id` **and backfills it**. That migration
runs once. `load_customer_goods.sh` runs whenever the data is reloaded, and it
does `DELETE FROM mcj_customer_goods` followed by an `INSERT` whose column list
never mentioned `ledger_id`. **Every reload undid the migration's backfill.**

The loader was already joining `mcj_ledgers` — it used `lg.name` for
`party_name` — and simply never selected `lg.id`.

Four tables have a migration backfill that a loader can wipe this way:
`mcj_customer_goods`, `mcj_customer_orders`, `mcj_sales_invoices`,
`mcj_scheme_enrolments`. The other three loaders set `ledger_id` in their own
insert, so **customer_goods was the only one exposed** — checked, all three are
fully linked (284, 224 and 239 rows, none NULL).

### Fixed

- `load_customer_goods.sh` now selects `lg.id` into `ledger_id`.
- The seven live rows were backfilled; all 7 now linked.
- The loader now **fails** if any row has a party code but no ledger, so this
  cannot regress quietly.
- Verified on the running screen: the issue page now lists all five customers
  with the right counts — 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = the 7 outstanding lines.

## 150. No account holder can be telephoned — the cost of defect 41, quantified — MEDIUM

[Defect 41] established that `mcj_parties.ledger_code` and `mcj_ledgers.code` are
unrelated code spaces, and the wrong join was correctly removed from
`posting.go`. Re-confirmed here from the data: **368 codes appear in both tables
and not one names the same person** (277 of them on billable ledgers, checked
name by name — **zero** agree). Nothing to reopen there.

What was never written down is what that costs.

### Every ledger contact column is empty

All **785** ledgers carry `phone`, `mobile`, `address`, `gstin` and
`aadhaar_number` as empty strings — not sparsely filled, **zero rows** in every
one. Contact detail lives only in the 40,519-row address book, and after
defect 41 there is no key joining the two.

So for a customer with an outstanding balance, this system holds a name, a
balance, and no way to reach them.

### How much is recoverable

Of the **567 billable ledgers** (Customer, Dealer, Other Debtor), 277 collide
with an address-book code and must not be linked. The remaining **290** break
down as:

| Group | Unmatched | Unique name match | Ambiguous | No entry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Customer | 250 | **158** | 44 | 48 |
| Dealer | 36 | **8** | 0 | 28 |
| Other Debtor | 4 | 0 | 0 | 4 |
| **Total** | **290** | **166** | **44** | **80** |

**166 match exactly one address-book entry by name, and 145 of those carry a
mobile number.** That is a real route back to the customer — but a shared name is
not proof of a shared person, and this record has already been burned once by a
key that looked right (defect 41). It is a candidate list to confirm, not a
migration to run.

**Needs Rahul:** confirm whether name is a safe match for these 166. If it is,
145 customers get their phone number back. The 44 ambiguous and 80 absent need
the shop's own records either way.

**Three routes have now been checked and rejected — see [defect 170]** for the
third, `address_book_sub_name`, whose 399 mobiles sit on a code space where
**923 of 1,039 codes match nothing** and the 31 that match a ledger name a
different person every time.

**One other route was checked and does not work.** `ledger_ref_details` (1,071
rows, never loaded) holds `party_ldgr`, `reference_name` and `ref_mob1` — a
reference contact per party, which would have been the obvious place to look.
**Exactly 1 of its 1,071 rows carries a mobile number.** 349 of its party codes
resolve to a ledger, so the linkage is sound; the phone column is simply empty.
It is not a second address book.

**Deliberately not done:** no automatic name-based backfill. Linking the wrong
person to an account is the exact failure defect 41 describes, and doing it on a
weaker key than the one that already failed would be worse, not better.

## 151. The design catalogue cannot be repriced, and 31 designs are worth minus twelve lakh — MEDIUM

Followed the [defect 150] sweep into `mcj_designs`, the 5,221-row catalogue whose
₹14.95 crore of estimates was published in [defect 145].

### Nothing in it identifies the metal

Three columns are empty for **every one of the 5,221 rows**: `purity`,
`metal_rate` and `making_rate`. Checked against the legacy source — MySQL
`design_transaction_main` has `purity` blank, `rate` 0 and `making_rate` 0 on all
5,221 rows too, so **the migration is faithful and there is nothing to reload.**

The consequence is structural. A tag carries purity *and* the rate it was priced
at, which is what lets [defect 141]'s revaluation work at all. A design carries
neither. So:

- a design cannot be said to be 18kt or 22kt
- its estimate cannot be recomputed at today's gold rate
- the catalogue's ₹14.95 crore is frozen at rates nobody recorded

Weights and stone detail *are* there — gross, net, and 3,416 stone lines — so a
design could be repriced **if someone supplies the purity**. Without it the
catalogue is a reference list, not a price list.

### 31 designs carry a negative estimate

| | |
|---|---|
| Designs with a negative estimate | **31** |
| What they total | **−12,86,354.00** |
| Worst single design (DBNG0100) | **−3,97,488.00** |

DBNG0100 has 33.488 g net, ₹20,100 of making and ₹51,080 of stones — all
positive — and an estimate of minus ₹3.97 lakh. No arithmetic over the other
columns reproduces the figure, on that row or any of the eight examined, so it is
a sign error in the shop's data rather than a computed result.

Legacy has the same 31 rows totalling the same −1,286,354, so again the migration
is faithful.

**They net off the catalogue total.** The ₹14,95,13,508.73 reported in defect 145
is the *net* figure. The positive side is **₹15,07,99,862.73**, and 199 further
designs carry an estimate of exactly zero.

Because the catalogue sorts by estimate descending, all 31 sit in the tail —
invisible before defect 145's cap was addressed, and now folded into a summary
total without comment.

**Needs Rahul:** whether those 31 estimates should be positive, zero, or the rows
retired; and whether design purity is recorded anywhere outside this ERP. Neither
is recoverable from the data.

## 152. 173 customers have paid a savings scheme to term and nothing records that any of them was settled — HIGH

The `mcj_schemes` sweep from [defect 151] led here. There is exactly **one**
scheme, *Gold Plus* — 11 months, 10 instalments of ₹1,000 — so the 239
enrolments all sharing one `scheme_id` is correct, not a linkage fault. Checked
before going further.

The money is not small.

| | Enrolments | Customers paid in | Payable | Maturity value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fully paid | 174 | **72,11,000.00** | 70,66,000.00 | 78,58,300.00 |
| Part paid | 64 | 15,79,900.00 | 22,15,000.00 | 24,30,100.00 |
| Nothing paid | 1 | 0.00 | 20,000.00 | 22,000.00 |
| **Total** | **239** | **87,90,900.00** | 93,01,000.00 | 1,03,10,400.00 |

**₹87,90,900.00 collected from customers across 2,144 payments**, the earliest in
April 2017 and the latest **1 June 2026**.

### Every single enrolment is still open

**235 of the 239 have already matured** — the oldest on **25 July 2017** — and
`is_active` is **true on all 239**. Not one scheme has ever been marked closed.

That is faithful to the source: legacy `party_wise_scheme` has
`activate_status = 1` on all 239 rows and the same 235 matured. The migration is
correct; the shop's system simply has no record of a scheme ever completing.

### What that leaves open

**173 enrolments are both fully paid and matured.** Those customers put in
**₹71,01,000.00** and are owed **₹77,37,300.00** at maturity. The system does not
say whether a single one has been settled.

It cannot be checked from the data either. [Defect 142] established that the
books begin **9 March 2026**, and these maturities run back to 2017, so there are
no vouchers to look for a payout against. The one thing that is visible — the
last scheme payment landing on **1 June 2026** — says the scheme was still being
collected on well after most of it had matured.

### What to do

This is the largest unquantified obligation found so far, and unlike [defect 19]
it is owed to **named individuals** rather than sitting in a suspense line.

**Needs Rahul, before any of this is treated as settled:**

1. Were the 173 matured, fully-paid enrolments paid out? If so, where is that
   recorded — it is not in this ERP.
2. Is `activate_status` simply never maintained, or does *active* genuinely mean
   these are all still owed?
3. The 64 part-paid enrolments have taken in ₹15,79,900.00 against ₹22,15,000.00
   payable. Are those lapsed, refundable, or still collecting?

Nothing here should be written off or closed programmatically. Recording the
question is the correct outcome until the shop answers it.

## 153. Payroll records four months where nobody was paid, and the loader reads a column that is always zero — HIGH

### Four months show a full salary bill and nothing paid

| Month | Staff | Gross salary | Paid |
|---|---|---|---|
| August 2025 | 15 | 3,37,200.00 | **0.00** |
| September 2025 | 15 | 3,58,300.00 | **0.00** |
| October 2025 | 15 | 3,37,200.00 | **0.00** |
| July 2026 | 12 | 2,89,200.00 | **0.00** |
| | | **13,21,900.00** | **0.00** |

Not one person in any of those months. Across all 246 sheets the shortfall is
**₹15,71,288.00**: **59** carry a salary and nothing paid, **149** are part paid,
and exactly **one** was paid in full.

**Correction — statutory deductions do exist, and explain 15% of it.** This entry
first said deduction was not the answer, on the strength of `pf_amount` and
`esi_amount` being zero on all 246 rows of `staff_salary_sheet`. They are zero
there, but the deductions are kept in a **different table**,
`staff_salary_sheet_payroll_detail`, which was found later by checking a figure
in a code comment (see [defect 157]):

| Over the same 16 months | |
|---|---|
| Provident fund | 2,01,600.00 |
| ESI | 8,728.00 |
| Professional tax | 27,720.00 |
| **Total deductions** | **2,38,048.00** |

| | |
|---|---|
| Payroll shortfall | 15,71,288.00 |
| Explained by statutory deduction | 2,38,048.00 (15%) |
| **Still unexplained** | **13,33,240.00** |

The finding stands — 85% of the gap has no explanation in the data — but the
original wording was wrong and is corrected here rather than left to mislead.

The four zero-paid months are not explained away either: **August, September and
October 2025 all carry payroll-detail rows** (14, 15 and 14 staff), so payroll was
being computed in the months nothing was recorded as paid. And [defect 142] puts
the first voucher at 9 March 2026, so for the 2025 months there are no payment
vouchers to check against.

This is faithful to the source; the totals tie to legacy exactly
(gross 4,949,100, paid 3,381,582). The question is what it means, not whether it
loaded correctly.

### The loader reads the wrong column

Separately: `days_worked` is **0.00 on all 246 rows**. The loader takes
`s.no_of_days`, and that column is **zero on every legacy row**. Four
similarly-named columns sit beside it, and the only populated one is
`total_days`.

**But `total_days` must not be used.** Its values are 28, 30 and 31 — 136 rows at
31, 95 at 30, 15 at 28. That is the **length of the month**, not attendance.
Mapping it would state that every member of staff worked every day of every
month, including the four months nobody was paid.

The honest finding is that **attendance was never recorded at all**. Of the
legacy payroll columns, `no_of_days`, `extra_days`, `total_extra_days`,
`total_working_time`, `total_overtime` and `overtime_amount` are **zero on all
246 rows**. Only `basic_pay` (209 rows), `gross_salary`, `paid_amount` and the
month length carry anything. The shop used this module to record amounts, never
attendance or overtime.

**Deliberately not fixed.** Pointing the loader at `total_days` would turn an
empty column into a wrong one. `days_worked` stays 0 because that is the truth,
and the column is now documented rather than quietly misleading.

**Needs Rahul:**

1. Were August–October 2025 and July 2026 salaries actually paid? **₹13,21,900**
   of gross with nothing recorded against it.
2. Is the ₹15,71,288 shortfall real, or is `paid_amount` simply not maintained?
3. Should `days_worked` be dropped, given attendance was never kept?

## 154. ₹14.47 crore sits in an order column nobody reads, and the one we do read is empty — MEDIUM

`mcj_customer_orders.advance` is **0.00 on all 284 rows**. The loader takes
legacy `customer_order.advance`, and that column is **zero on all 284 rows too**,
so the load is faithful and the field is simply dead. Nothing in the module reads
it — `advance` appears in no Go file outside the loader.

Beside it in the same legacy table sits **`amount_received`**, populated on
**273 of 284 orders** and totalling **₹14,47,10,446**. Nothing reads that either.

### What it is not

Before treating that as ₹14.47 crore of unrecorded customer advances — which is
what it looks like — I compared it against each order's own line estimate:

| Relationship | Orders |
|---|---|
| Equal to the line estimate | 28 |
| Some other ratio (0.85 to 2.89) | 104 |
| Exactly 10x | 1 |
| Order has no line estimate to compare | 140 |

It is **not** the order value, and it is not a clean multiple of anything. A
single order, **CO/2526/00402 dated 1 April 2026, carries ₹7,38,00,000** — more
than half the total on one line, against a line estimate of zero.

Ratios below 1 (0.85, 0.90, 0.92) read like part payments; ratios of 1.32 and
2.89 do not. **The column cannot be interpreted from the data**, and this record
has already been burned twice this week by a column that looked obvious —
`total_days` in [defect 153], which was really the length of the month, and
`ldgr_code` in [defect 41].

### Why it matters anyway

If any part of ₹14.47 crore is money customers have handed over against undelivered
orders, it is a liability, and **243 of the 284 orders are still undelivered**
([defect 149]). The order screens currently show no advance at all, because the
only column wired up is the empty one.

**Deliberately not loaded.** Mapping `amount_received` into `advance` would put an
uninterpreted figure — including a ₹7.38 crore outlier — onto a screen labelled
as customer money. That is the failure mode this record keeps catching, not a fix.

**Resolved — see [defect 169].** `amount_received` is the order's **metal value**,
matching `metal_rate × net_weight` exactly on 157 of 273 orders and metal plus
making on 21 more. It is not cash. The ₹7,38,00,000 on CO/2526/00402 is 3,000 g
of silver booked at **₹24,600 a gram**, about 97 times its real rate, and the
"exactly 10x" order is a 995 rate entered ten times too high. **There is no
evidence of ₹14.47 crore of customer advances**, and the decision not to load the
column was right. If it is an advance, the order book needs
it and the outstanding-liability picture changes.

## 155. 37% of sales by value has no line detail, and the GST return says so itself — HIGH

The GSTR-1 HSN summary already prints a warning row for this, but it has never
been recorded as a defect, and the figure had never been read across the whole
period — the screen defaults to the current month, where it looks like a rounding
note about **4 bills**.

Run over the full period it is not a rounding note:

| GSTR-1 HSN Summary, 2016 → 2026 | Taxable | Tax | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 711319 Jewellery, gold/diamond/platinum | — | — | — |
| 711311 Silver jewellery | — | — | — |
| 711411 Silver articles | — | — | — |
| **39 bill(s) with no line detail** | **89,26,345.00** | **2,44,729.79** | **91,71,074.79** |
| **Total** | 2,40,66,454.00 | 6,98,933.87 | **2,47,65,387.87** |

**₹91,71,074.79 of ₹2,47,65,387.87 — 37% of everything sold — sits on bills whose
contents are unknown.** Confirmed independently against the database: 39 of the
224 invoices have no row in `mcj_sales_invoice_lines`, and their taxable value
comes to the same ₹89,26,345.00.

It is faithful to the source. Legacy `sales_vou` holds 224 bill headers and
`sales_vou_main` holds 328 lines spanning only **185 distinct bill numbers** —
224 minus 185 is exactly the 39. Both tables loaded completely (224 = 224,
328 = 328, checked). The line detail was never captured.

### What it costs

- **The GST return cannot be filed from this system.** The report says so in
  plain words on the screen: *"This summary is short by the value shown and is
  NOT complete for filing."* Over a third of turnover has no HSN.
- **Nobody can say what was sold on those 39 bills** — no item, no purity, no
  weight, no tag.
- Those bills cannot be tied to stock movement, so they are invisible to any
  check that reconciles what left the shelf against what was billed.

### What to do

The report's behaviour is right: it shows the gap rather than quietly filing a
short return, and the total still reconciles. Nothing to fix in the code.

**Needs Rahul:** whether the line detail for those 39 bills exists anywhere else
— the printed invoices, the accountant's copy, a GSTR-1 already filed with the
portal. If a return was filed for this period, it was filed from something other
than this data.

## 156. A live screen told users the HSN summary could not be produced, months after it was built — MEDIUM

Found by reading the GST registers over the full period for [defect 155]. The
GSTR-1 B2B screen ended every run with:

> The HSN summary cannot be produced from this data: no HSN is recorded against a
> sale line, and the item master has no HSN column. See blocker B21.

**Every clause of that is now false**, and B21 itself says so. The blocker was
narrowed twice and records the correction in full: `item_master.hsn_no` **is**
populated, on **318 of 322 items**, and its values are a foreign key into
`hsn_master` rather than codes — which is exactly what made it look absent. Read
as codes they would have produced a return of ones and sevens.

Checked against the running database:

| | |
|---|---|
| Items carrying an HSN code | **318 of 322 (98.8%)** |
| Distinct HSN codes | 21 |
| Invoice lines resolving to an HSN | **all 328** |
| GSTR-1 HSN Summary | built, and produces 711319, 711311 and 711411 |

So one screen told the user the thing could not be done while the screen next to
it did it. Anyone preparing a return would have gone looking outside the system
for data that was already in it — the opposite of what this record is for.

**Fixed.** The row now says what is true and points at the report that does the
job:

> This is the B2B section only. For table 12 of GSTR-1 see the GSTR-1 HSN
> Summary, which covers every bill and states what it cannot account for.

Verified on the running screen.

**Worth noting as a class.** The stale text survived because the correction was
written into `docs/blockers.md` and the code comment above the *other* function,
but never into the string the user actually reads. A note that names a blocker
should be checked whenever that blocker changes; nothing enforces it, and only
reading the screen caught it.

### A second instance, and a sweep of the rest

Acting on that, every user-facing string naming a blocker was checked — **26 of
them**. One more was stale, in the same way and from the same blocker.

`gst-register` ended with:

> This register reconciles the books. It is not a return: the invoice detail a
> GSTR-1 needs — party, taxable value and HSN per bill — **did not survive the
> capture**. See blocker B21.

The invoice detail did survive: **224 bills** in `sales_vou`, party and place of
supply on **every one**, and **all 328 lines** resolving to an HSN. B21 records
exactly that. The row now reads:

> This register reconciles the books. It is not a return — for that see GSTR-1
> B2B, B2C and the HSN Summary, which are built from the 224 invoices. 39 of
> those bills carry no line detail, so the HSN summary names what it cannot
> account for.

That also carries [defect 155]'s real limitation instead of a false one.

**A test was pinning the stale text in place.** `TestGSTRegister_SaysItIsNotAReturn`
required the disclaimer to contain both *"not a return"* **and** *"B21"* — so the
false claim was not merely unnoticed, it was asserted. The test now checks the
disclaimer says it is not a return, **points at the GSTR-1 screens that exist**,
and **fails if the words "did not survive" come back**. Its original intent is
kept; what it no longer does is require a citation that had gone wrong.

**The other 24 were checked and are accurate.** The notes citing B19 (stock is
not a ledger), B9 (165 items whose stored price cannot be reproduced) and B3 (the
label template was never captured, so the geometry is a reconstruction) all match
those blockers' current text. **Both stale notes came from B21** — the one
blocker on this list that was substantially narrowed after the screens were
written, which is exactly where to look next time a blocker changes.

## 158. The sold-stones screen went on showing the figure defect 135 had already corrected — HIGH

[Defect 135] established, months ago, that "stones sold ₹1,11,83,462.33" is
roughly three times the truth: `sales_vou_detail` carries bulk metal sold by
weight alongside stone lines, `load_sold_stones.sh` takes all 203 rows without a
filter, and **21 carat-less rows worth ₹75,39,341.00** are silver sold by the
gram, not stone.

The defect was written up. **The screen was never changed.** Run over the full
period it still summarised:

> 94 bill(s), **203 stone line(s)** … **1,11,83,462.33** … *63.4% of the
> 1,76,29,343.00 those bills came to*

Every figure there is the uncorrected one, and the 63.4% was worse than the
total: a claim *about the shop* — that stone is nearly two thirds of what a
customer pays — derived entirely from the error.

Re-confirmed against the database:

| | Rows | Tags | Carats | Value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Genuine stone | **182** | 134 | 131.946 | **36,44,121.33** |
| No carats — metal by weight | **21** | 5 | 0.000 | **75,39,341.00** |
| Total as loaded | 203 | | 131.946 | 1,11,83,462.33 |

### Fixed

The report now separates them. Verified on the running screen:

> 94 bill(s), **182 stone line(s)** … **36,44,121.33** … *20.7% of the
> 1,76,29,343.00 those bills came to. A further 21 line(s) worth 75,39,341.00
> carry no carats — that is bulk metal sold by weight, not stone, and it is NOT
> in the total above.*

The metal rows are **named rather than dropped** — they are real sales, and
losing them would hide the untagged silver trade that [defect 135] found. The
share is now computed on genuine stone only.

The file's own header comment carried the same wrong figures — `SOLD
1,11,83,462.33` and "stones average **57.4%** of what the customer paid" — and
has been corrected to 36,44,121.33 and 20.7%, with a note saying what it used to
claim.

**This is the third stale-claim defect in a row** ([156], its sweep, and this).
The pattern is consistent: the finding gets written into `docs/`, and the screen
and the comment that state it are left alone. Reading the screen is the only
thing that has caught any of them.

### A systematic sweep, rather than a fourth accident

Three in a row is a process failure, so instead of waiting to trip over the next
one every money figure asserted in module code was extracted — **87 distinct
values** — and cross-checked against the defects record for any that sit in a
correction.

**It found one more instance of this same figure.** `orderedstones.go` carries a
four-line summary of the whole stone picture, and its `sold` line was the
uncorrected ₹1,11,83,462.33. Now corrected, with a note saying what it was.

The other three lines of that table were re-verified against the database in the
same pass and are exact:

| Claim in `orderedstones.go` | Database | |
|---|---|---|
| bought 1,27,31,698.71 · 521.329 ct | 39 rows, 34 bills, 521.329 ct, 1,27,31,698.71 | ✓ |
| held 6,21,95,953.60 · 2,731.821 ct | 819 rows, 2,731.821 ct, 6,21,95,953.60 | ✓ |
| on order 24,69,792.15 · 402.997 ct | 115 rows, 402.997 ct, 24,69,792.15 | ✓ |

Other claims checked and found exact in this pass: `supplierbalances.go`'s
**45 dealer accounts owed ₹6,15,02,878.56** (the screen's wider 62 /
₹6,23,56,784.52 covers three ledger groups, which is why they differ — both
right), and `payrollhistory.go`'s **₹21,69,448.00 across 16 staff and 16 months**,

## 159. The opening stock is not selling — 0.1% of it in five months, not the 1.7% quoted — MEDIUM

Found by continuing [defect 158]'s sweep past the defects record and checking
code figures **directly against the database**, which is the gap that sweep could
not cover.

`openingstock.go` carried this comparison:

|  | tags | value | sold |
|---|---|---|---|
| opening stock | 1,571 | 8,52,67,768.16 | 1.7% |
| tagged during the year | 1,245 | 6,75,97,397.62 | 17.3% |

Every tag count and every value is **exactly right** — confirmed against the
database, including the split that had briefly looked like a discrepancy:

| | Tags | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Opening, still on the shelf | 1,545 | 8,51,58,772.85 |
| Opening, sold | 26 | 1,08,995.31 |
| **All opening tags** | **1,571** | **8,52,67,768.16** |

### The percentages are a different unit from the column beside them

Those `sold` figures are **shares of tag count**: 26 of 1,571 is 1.7%, and 215 of
1,245 is 17.3%. They sit immediately to the right of a **value** column, and the
sentence underneath argues in rupees. A reader takes them for a share of value.

By value the same rows read:

| | Sold, by tag | Sold, by value |
|---|---|---|
| Opening stock | 1.7% | **0.1%** |
| Tagged during the year | 17.3% | **15.4%** |

The passage concluded that newer stock "sells ten times more readily". By tag
count that is right (17.3 ÷ 1.7 = 10.2). **By value it is 154 times.**

### The finding is much stronger than the one that was written down

**₹8,52,67,768.16 of opening stock produced ₹1,08,995.31 of sales in five
months — one tenth of one percent.** The 26 opening tags that did sell were the
cheap ones, which is why they are 1.7% of the tags and 0.1% of the money.

That sits directly alongside [defect 141]: the opening stock is the same
360-tag-and-more group carried in at a round ₹4,000/g, and it is both the least
saleable stock on the shelf and the part whose book value is least defensible.
It is also the stock [defect 142] can find no purchase document for.

**Fixed:** the comment now gives both columns and says which is which. The screen
itself never showed this comparison — it lists on-shelf tags only — so nothing
user-facing was wrong. This is a record-keeping defect in the reasoning, and the
reasoning is what the next person will read.

## 160. Two more doubled footers, and defect 143's sweep was not as complete as it claimed — HIGH

[Defect 143] found eight reports whose footer counted their own summary row
twice, fixed them, and recorded that **"no doubled footer remains anywhere"**.
That claim was wrong. Two reports still had one.

Found while verifying `salecost.go`'s figures against the database for the
[defect 159] sweep — the comment's numbers were right, and the screen totalling
them was not.

| Report | Its own summary says | Footer printed | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sale-cost` | 1,05,03,577.58 marked / 1,05,56,997.00 sold | **2,10,07,155.16 / 2,11,13,994.00** | 2x |
| `mrp-purchases` | 40,16,651.60 | **80,33,303.20** | 2x |

`sale-cost`'s difference column was worse than doubled: the footer read
**₹19,68,409.86**, which is the 232 detail rows (₹53,419.42) plus **both**
summary rows (₹53,419.42 and ₹18,61,571.02) added together.

### Why the original sweep missed them

The detector looked for a footer equal to **twice the last body row**, then for
trailing rows whose first cell matched a count like *"39 line(s)"*.

`sale-cost` defeats both. It carries **two** summary rows, and the final one
begins *"The net is cancellation, not agreement"* — no count, no match — so the
scan stopped before reaching the row that actually holds the totals. Reading the
last row alone was never a sound test, and the earlier sweep's clean result was
a property of the test, not of the reports.

### The detector that works

A subtotal row is one whose value **equals the sum of every row above it**. That
is checkable without knowing anything about labels or position:

- run against all 69 reports, requiring at least four preceding rows so a row
  matching the single row above it is not mistaken for a subtotal
- it found exactly these two, and nothing else

Both now set `NoTotals`. Re-fetched all 69 reports: **both footers gone, and the
detector now reports zero.**

**The lesson is about the check, not the code.** Defect 143's fix was right; its
*verification* used the same shape of test as the bug it was fixing, so it agreed
with itself. A claim of completeness needs a test that could have failed for a
different reason than the one that motivated it.

## 161. The quote screen refuses a fifth of the shelf, and nobody had counted it — MEDIUM

Found by extending [defect 156]'s sweep to the gap that sweep left: it checked
strings **naming a blocker**, so a stale or unquantified claim that cites nothing
would have passed. Twenty-one user-facing strings make a definitive negative
claim; most are field validation. Two make the *"did not survive the capture"*
assertion that has already been wrong twice.

One of them is right, and is worth a number.

### Quoting refuses every certified tag

`quote.go` refuses certified goods outright, citing [blocker B9] — which was
checked and **is still open and accurate**: 165 items' stored price cannot be
reproduced, and they cluster by certification type (`by_val` 98, `per_ct` 35).
Refusing is the correct behaviour; approximating a certified piece would be
wrong by a large amount rather than a small one.

What had never been established is how much of the shelf that removes:

| Certification | Tags | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `by_val` | 472 | 1,54,27,841.49 |
| `per_ct` | 91 | 1,30,44,293.01 |
| *(charge but no type)* | 3 | 3,660.00 |
| **Total refused** | **566** | **2,84,75,794.50** |

**566 of the 2,575 tags on the shelf — 22% by count and 20% by value — cannot be
quoted at all.** Confirmed on the running screen: barcode 53710364, a DIAMOND
BANGLE and the dearest certified tag, returns *"Cannot be priced here"*.

That is the practical cost of B9, and it is larger than B9's own description
suggests. B9 counts **165 items whose price cannot be reproduced**; the screen
refuses **566**, because it will not price *any* certified tag, not merely the
ones known to be wrong.

**Not changed.** Refusing is right while the pricing step is unknown, and
narrowing the refusal to the 165 would mean quoting 401 certified tags on a
formula that is unverified for certified goods generally.

**Needs Rahul:** what the certification pricing step is. It is the difference
between a quote screen that covers the shelf and one that covers four fifths of
it, and B9 has been open longest of any blocker on this list.

### Checked and found sound

- `oldgoods.go`'s *"a purchase whose detail did not survive"* branch is defensive
  rendering, not a claim: **all 25 old-gold vouchers have detail**, so it never
  fires today.
- `schememaster.go` and `salarysheet.go`'s "never recorded" wording matches
  [defect 152] and [defect 153] exactly.

## 162. The balance sheet did not balance on screen, and neither did the P&L — HIGH

The two statements an accountant opens first were each printing totals that did
not tie, because both end with a **memo row** — the shelf value, shown for
comparison — and the shell's footer sums every money cell it finds.

| | Printed | Printed | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Balance Sheet | Assets **41,33,12,142.12** | Liabilities **27,09,50,953.92** | 14,23,61,188.20 |
| P&L Account | Expense **18,65,39,319.36** | Income **2,20,03,143.00** | — |

**The gap on the balance sheet is exactly ₹14,23,61,188.20 — the stock memo row,
to the paisa.** On the P&L the same row inflates the Expense column by the same
figure.

### Both statements were correct underneath

This is presentation, not accounting. Take the memo row out and each balances:

- **Balance Sheet:** 41,33,12,142.12 − 14,23,61,188.20 = **27,09,50,953.92**, equal
  to the liabilities side.
- **P&L:** expenses 3,30,90,637.08 against income 2,20,03,143.00, with the
  shortfall of **1,10,87,494.08** closing it — and that shortfall is the figure
  both screens already agree on.

The suspense line does its job in both cases. The memo row was simply never meant
to be added to anything: on the balance sheet it is labelled *"for comparison
with the difference"*, and it was being added to the difference instead.

### Fixed

Each statement now prints its **own balancing Total row** before the memo, and
sets `NoTotals` so the shell adds nothing after it. The memo is relabelled
**"FOR COMPARISON — not part of the total above"**. Verified on the running app:

| | Total | |
|---|---|---|
| Balance Sheet | 27,09,50,953.92 = 27,09,50,953.92 | balances |
| P&L Account | 3,30,90,637.08 = 3,30,90,637.08 | balances |
| Trial Balance | 29,58,46,599.44 = 29,58,46,599.44 | already correct — no memo row |

### Why the earlier sweeps missed it

[Defect 160]'s detector looks for a row equal to **the sum of the rows above it**.
A memo row is not a subtotal — it is an unrelated figure from another module — so
it matches nothing and the detector was silent. Correctly silent: it was built to
find double-counted subtotals, and this is a different fault with the same
symptom.

### A test existed, and it passed throughout

`TestBalanceSheet_TiesWithNothingLeftOver` has been green all along. It sums the
query's rows and **skips the "Stock in hand" row itself**, with the comment
*"stated for comparison, never added into a side"*. So the test knew the rule the
screen was breaking — it just checked the **query output**, and the fault was in
the **rendering**, where the shell totals every money column it is handed.

Two new tests now check the layer the bug lived in: each statement must emit its
own `Total` row, that row must balance, and the memo must come **after** it and be
labelled as excluded.

**Both were confirmed by breaking the code on purpose:**

- relabelling the memo back to *"for comparison with the difference"* →
  *"balance sheet does not mark the stock memo as excluded from the total"*
- renaming the P&L's `Total` row → *"p&l prints no Total row, so the shell will
  total it and add the memo"*

**The first version of these tests was vacuous and said so.** Seeded books carry
no stock, so `shelfValue` was zero, the memo row was never emitted, and the loop
checking it ran over nothing — the label mutation passed. The tests now seed one
tag and **fail outright if the memo row is absent**, because a test that cannot
see the row proves nothing about it.

## 163. The barcode edit trail records that a tag changed, but not what it changed from — LOW

`mcj_barcode_edits` holds 156 edits across 154 tags, April to August 2026. Seven
of its columns carry a single value throughout, which is what drew attention.

The **flags are exactly right**. Checked against legacy
`barcode_edit_tracking` row by row:

| Change | Flagged in our data | Genuinely differs in legacy |
|---|---|---|
| Item | 31 | **31** |
| Units | 119 | **119** |
| Making | 7 | **7** |
| Gross weight | 0 | **0** |
| Net weight | 0 | **0** |
| Stone | 0 | **0** |

Every flag matches. The loader is reading the right columns and the empty ones
are empty because nothing of that kind was ever edited.

### What was not carried across

Legacy keeps **before and after values** for each kind of change —
`old_qty`/`new_qty`, `old_gw`/`new_gw`, `old_making`/`new_making`,
`old_stone_wt`/`new_stone_wt`. Our schema keeps only `old_item_id`/`new_item_id`.

So for the **119 unit changes** and the **7 making changes**, the trail says a tag
was edited and on what date, but not from what to what. On the making edits that
is a real loss: the legacy values run from **−₹300 to +₹1,683**, including two
tags taken from ₹0 to ₹1,155 and ₹1,120.

**Not urgent, and not corrected here.** It needs a migration to add six columns
and a loader change, and the underlying rows are intact in MySQL — unlike
[defect 142]'s vouchers, this is recoverable whenever someone wants it.

### A wrong reading, recorded because it was nearly written down

The 119 unit changes are all downward — 101 from 2 to 1 and 18 from 4 to 1, a net
of **−155**. That reads as 155 pieces removed from tags by editing rather than by
selling, which would have been a serious finding.

**It is not what happened.** `quantity` is the number of *items* on a tag and
`pieces` is the number of *physical objects*, and they are meant to differ: **761
in-stock tags — ₹6,76,78,194.42, 47% of shelf value — have `pieces` greater than
`quantity`**, 679 of them a pair of two pieces on one tag. Every edited tag now
reads `pieces 2, quantity 1`, which is a pair correctly described.

The edits were corrections bringing `quantity` to 1 on multi-piece tags. Nothing
left the shelf. The number was real and the conclusion would have been wrong.

## 164. ₹1.35 crore of fine gold was issued to a named goldsmith, and the record dismissed it as an empty table — HIGH

[Defect 76] surveyed the manufacturing tables and concluded there are *"no
karigar transactions, no work orders, no stone issues and no hallmarking
movements to report on"*, listing the evidence as *"every issue and receive table
is empty: `karigar_gold_stock` 2, `karigar_wip_bal` 1"*.

**Those two rows are not an empty table.** Read, they say:

| Bill | Date | Karigar | Item | Weight | Purity | Rate | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C4/00001 | 16 Sep 2025 | ledger 11699 | GOLD | 369.850 g | 995 | 11,417.00 | ISS-RAW |
| C4/00002 | 16 Sep 2025 | ledger 11699 | GOLD | 500.000 g | 995 | 11,417.00 | ISS-RAW |
| | | | | **869.850 g** | | | |

Ledger **11699 is MA TARA JEWELLERS**, group **Karigar** — and defect 76 notes it
is the *only* Karigar ledger in the chart of accounts. So the shop has one
goldsmith on its books, and both rows issue metal to him.

**869.850 g of 995 fine gold**, worth **₹99,31,077.45** at the rate on the issue
and **₹1,34,67,017.70** at today's 995 rate of ₹15,482.

### Nothing records it coming back

| | |
|---|---|
| `receive_from_karigar` | **0 rows** |
| `receive_from_karigar_details` | **0 rows** |
| `receive_from_karigar_main` | **0 rows** |
| `issue_to_karigar` and its 8 variants | **0 rows** |
| `karigar_wip_bal` | 1 row, **0.000 at every purity** |

And in the accounts, MA TARA JEWELLERS carries **an opening balance of ₹0.00 and
not one posting**. The issue of ₹99 lakh of metal to him appears in no voucher,
no ledger and no report.

`karigar_gold_stock` is **not migrated** — there is no `mcj_karigar` table — so
the rebuild does not carry it either.

### What it means, and what it does not

This is a **separate record** from the raw stock of [defect 78] and [defect 133].
Different table, different date — September 2025 against April–June 2026 — and
defect 133's movement table carries no 995 row at all. Whether the 869.850 g
overlaps with the raw holding, was returned as finished goods, or is still out
**cannot be told from this data**. It should not be added to the ₹15.77 crore
without the shop confirming it.

**The lesson is about the survey, not the shop.** Defect 76 judged the table by its
row count and wrote it off with tables that genuinely hold nothing. Two rows held
more than a crore of gold and a name. `load_oldgold.sh` already carries the note
that *"a row estimate is not a row count"*; this is its companion — **a row count
is not materiality**.

**Needs Rahul, and this one has a name attached:** did MA TARA JEWELLERS return
the 869.850 g issued on 16 September 2025? If it came back as finished stock it
should be on the shelf; if it did not, it is the single largest identified item
of metal outside the accounts that can be attached to a person.

## 165. 334 tags are re-issues of earlier tags, and the link back is not loaded — MEDIUM

Applying [defect 164]'s lesson — *a row count is not materiality* — to the rest
of the small legacy tables. Most turned out to be already loaded: `stock_inward`
(43 rows, ₹2,39,56,798) is `mcj_purchase_invoices` to the rupee, and
`stock_inward_detail` (39 rows, ₹1,27,31,698.71) is the stone side of
`mcj_purchase_contents`. Both check out exactly.

The return tables do not.

### What they hold

`sale_return_detail` carries a column our schema has no equivalent for:

| bill | barcode | **new_barcode** | pcs | ct | gw |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SR/2627/00001 | 70630587 | **70630587R1** | 588 | 10.280 | 2.056 |

**A returned tag is re-issued under a new number**, the old one with an `R1`
suffix. That is the convention behind the suffixed barcodes across the shelf:

| Barcode shape | Tags in stock | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Plain numeric | 2,241 | — |
| **`R<n>` re-issue** | **245** | **57,86,486.50** |
| **Plain letter suffix** | **89** | **59,76,162.48** |

### The link is not recoverable

The tables that state it explicitly are **not read by any loader** —
`sale_return_detail` (4 rows), `purchase_return_detail` (2),
`purchase_return_main` (3, carrying 59.650 g gross and 32.767 g fine worth
₹8,40,989.52). The returns report reads `mcj_vouchers` only, so a return is a
money total with no record of what came back.

And the suffix cannot substitute for the link. Of the **245** R-numbered tags:

| | |
|---|---|
| Parent barcode still on the shelf | **1** |
| Parent barcode with any movement history | **5** |
| **Parent with no record of any kind** | **240** |

So for **₹57,86,486.50** of stock, the tag says it replaced something and nothing
in the system says what. The six rows that would name it were never loaded.

### What to do

Loading `sale_return_detail` and `purchase_return_detail` is small and worth
doing — it recovers 6 links exactly and gives returns their line detail, the
weights included. It will **not** explain the other 239: those re-issues predate
the captured returns, and by [defect 142] the documents are gone.

**Needs Rahul:** whether an `R1` suffix always means a return, or is also used
for a repair, a resize or a re-tag after splitting. The convention is doing the
work of a foreign key on ₹57.86 lakh of stock, and only he can say what it means.

## 166. `retail_all_stock` is our stock table, and it reconciles to the gram — LOW (clean result)

Continuing [defect 164]'s lesson through the larger unopened tables. Two were
worth the look and neither is a defect, which is worth recording as plainly as a
fault would be.

### `item_adjustment` — 922 rows, five of them meaningful

The name suggests stock adjustments. It is a **making-rate master**: `item_id`,
`per_of_making`, `rt_mk_pr_gm`, `pl_minus_gold`. Of its 922 rows across 460
items, **5** carry a making percentage, **2** a rate per gram and **3** a
gold-minus figure — and rows repeat verbatim (item 1066 appears twice, identical).

The inverse of the karigar lesson: **a high row count is not materiality either.**
917 of 922 rows hold nothing.

### `retail_all_stock` — 2,820 rows, and it is our own stock table

| | `retail_all_stock` | `mcj_stock_items` |
|---|---|---|
| Rows | 2,820 | **2,816** |
| Distinct barcodes | **2,815** | **2,815** |
| Net weight | 21,380.564 g | **21,376.104 g** |

It reconciles exactly. The **4 extra rows** are hallmarking movements, and their
**4.460 g** is the whole of the weight difference:

- 21,380.564 − 21,376.104 = **4.460 g**
- 2,820 − 2,816 = **4 rows**

The matching distinct-barcode count on both sides — **2,815 against our 2,816
rows** — is [defect 146]'s duplicate barcode `86065435` collapsing to one, seen
from the other side.

So this is not a second stock record and nothing is missing from the load.

### A small correction to defect 76

[Defect 76] states there are *"no karigar transactions, no work orders, no stone
issues and no hallmarking movements to report on"*. On hallmarking that is very
nearly right rather than exactly right: **4 rows exist**, `HMISS/2425/00014` and
`HMREC/2425/00014` and one more pair, covering **2 tags** on 1 April 2025 —
**2.230 g issued and 2.230 g received back**.

They net to zero and amount to two grams. Unlike [defect 164], where the same
wording hid ₹1.35 crore of gold, here the conclusion stands and only the wording
is absolute where it should be nearly so. Recorded so the next reader does not
have to re-derive it.

## 167. A second stock table values 281 tags differently, and on 208 of them the metal is counted four times — MEDIUM

`cla_retail_trans_bar_detail` — 2,816 rows, never loaded — turns out to hold one
row per tag with an `amount`. It is the same population as our stock table:

| | `cla_retail_trans_bar_detail` | `mcj_stock_items` |
|---|---|---|
| Rows | 2,816 | 2,816 |
| Distinct barcodes | 2,815 | 2,815 |
| Barcodes present in one only | **0** | **0** |
| Sum of amount | **17,12,31,075.39** | **15,28,65,165.78** |

Same tags, **₹1,83,65,909.61 apart**. On **2,534 of 2,815** the two agree to the
paisa, so this is not a units or rounding difference. It is 281 specific tags.

### 208 tags: the metal counted four times

For 208 of them the relationship is exact and identical:

> `cla amount` = (metal × **4**) + making

Worked through on the largest, **89501233**, a GOLD CHAIN:

| | |
|---|---|
| Net weight | 26.740 g |
| Rate | 9,300.00 |
| Metal (26.740 × 9,300) | 2,48,682.00 |
| Making, `per_gld_val` at 12% | 29,841.84 |
| **Our total** | **2,78,523.84** |
| **cla amount** | **10,24,569.84** = 2,48,682.00 × 4 + 29,841.84 |

Our figure is internally consistent — the metal is rate × weight and the making
is 12% of it. The cla figure is the same tag with its metal counted four times.
**Across the 208 that accounts for ₹1,81,45,176.21 of the gap.**

**What the 208 are not.** Three explanations were tested and each fails:

| Hypothesis | Result |
|---|---|
| The multiplier is the tag's **piece count** | **No** — 202 of the 208 carry `pieces = 1`, six carry 2. None carries 4 |
| A particular **making type** | **No** — they span `per_gm_nw` (133), `per_gld_val` (39), `per_pcs` (8), `val` (4), `per_gm_gw` (1) |
| A **date cutoff** in the old system | **Nearly** — all 208 are `New Create` dated on or before **25 Oct 2025**, but **939 other tags in that same window agree to the paisa** |

So the window is necessary and not sufficient: 208 of the 1,147 tags created up to
25 Oct 2025 are affected, and the 1,669 created after it are all correct. Every
one of the 208 is `item_type = M` and 176 of them are 18kt.

The relationship itself is exact — × 4, not × 3.98 — on all 208. Something
computed it deliberately. What, cannot be told from this data.

### 73 tags: a certification charge our total leaves out

The remaining 73 differ by small amounts — ₹225, ₹300, ₹315, ₹700 — and each is
exactly that tag's **certification charge**:

| Barcode | Metal | Making | Certification | Our total | cla |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12774913 | 4,885.96 | 1,500.00 | **300.00** | 6,385.96 | **6,685.96** |
| 22759867R1 | 32,088.00 | 3,000.00 | **315.00** | 35,088.00 | **35,403.00** |
| 45336681 | 4,83,388.00 | 4,599.00 | **700.00** | 4,87,987.00 | **4,88,687.00** |

**This is faithful.** Legacy `barcode_main.total` omits the certification charge
too — checked row by row, its own `amount + making_sales + certification_charge`
exceeds its own `total` by exactly that charge. The migration copied what was
there.

Across the whole shelf, **193 in-stock tags carry ₹1,32,937.25 of hallmark and
certification charges that their stored `total` excludes.**

### What this means

**Neither figure should be adopted over the other without the shop.** Our
₹14,23,61,188.20 follows `barcode_main`, which is the tag master and the right
source. But two of the shop's own tables disagree about 281 tags, one of them by
counting metal four times, and that is worth knowing before either number is put
in front of an accountant.

**Needs Rahul:** whether the certification charge belongs in a tag's value — if
it does, the shelf is understated by ₹1,32,937.25 — and what
`cla_retail_trans_bar_detail` was for, since something in the old system was
producing a four-times-metal valuation on 208 tags.

## 168. The 8 orphaned vouchers are identified, and they all balance — MEDIUM (narrows B4)

[Blocker B4] has carried "8 JRNL vouchers worth ₹21,025.82 have blank scope
columns" as an open item awaiting an accountant. Reading
`voucher_transfer_check` (1,445 rows, never loaded) led to them.

They are legacy `voucher_main` **JRNL v_id 1 to 8**, and the identification is
exact — their amounts sum to **₹21,025.82**, matching B4 to the paisa:

| v_id | Date | Amount | comp_code | rt_code | ac_yr |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-04-01 | 411.82 | 0 | *(blank)* | *(blank)* |
| 2 | 2026-03-09 | 1,399.00 | 0 | *(blank)* | *(blank)* |
| 3 | 2026-04-19 | 12,572.00 | 0 | *(blank)* | *(blank)* |
| 4 | 2026-06-19 | 13.00 | 0 | *(blank)* | *(blank)* |
| 5 | 2026-07-01 | 34.00 | 0 | *(blank)* | *(blank)* |
| 6 | 2026-06-30 | 4,000.00 | 0 | *(blank)* | *(blank)* |
| 7 | 2026-07-10 | 1,711.00 | 0 | *(blank)* | *(blank)* |
| 8 | 2026-07-20 | 885.00 | 0 | *(blank)* | *(blank)* |

**v_id 2 is the ₹1,399 of 9 March 2026** — the same line that leaked into the
balance sheet's year result before it was bounded, and the earliest voucher in
the entire capture ([defect 142]).

### They are not broken, only unscoped

**All eight balance.** Loaded, each carries equal debits and credits — 411.82
against 411.82, 12,572.00 against 12,572.00, and so on for all eight. Whatever is
wrong with them, it is not the double entry.

What is missing is scope: `comp_code = 0`, and `rt_code` and `ac_yr` blank. Our
loader derives the financial year from the date, so seven landed in 2026-2027 and
v_id 2, dated 9 March, correctly in 2025-2026.

### The consequence, which is latent rather than live

Because their `ac_yr` is blank they share `(type, legacy_v_id)` with the ordinary
FY 2026-2027 JRNL vouchers numbered 1 to 8. In `mcj_vouchers` that is a
collision:

| | |
|---|---|
| Colliding `(legacy_v_id, type)` pairs | **8** |
| Extra rows they create | **8** |
| All of type | **JRNL** |

There is no unique index on `legacy_v_id`, so nothing rejects it. **Nothing is
currently wrong**, because every loader that joins on it constrains the type —
`load_oldgold.sh` to `PURC-OG` (and says why id and type suffice), 
`load_purchase_invoices.sh` to `si.v_typ`, `load_brs.sh` to type and financial
year — and no collision exists outside JRNL. It would bite the first join that
omits the type.

### What this gives B4

B4 asks for "a named accountant to approve both repairs". This narrows the second
repair to a specific and much smaller question: **the eight are arithmetically
sound and need a company, retail point and financial year stamped on them, not a
correction to their amounts.** The ₹0.01 `JRNL 312` imbalance is untouched by
this and remains the harder half.

## 169. `amount_received` on an order is the metal value, not money received — HIGH (resolves defect 154)

[Defect 154] found ₹14,47,10,446 in `customer_order.amount_received`, could not
interpret it, and deliberately refused to load it into a field labelled
"advance". Reading `order_rate_master` (2,520 rows, never loaded) settled it.

Every order carries a **rate snapshot per purity**, and our
`mcj_customer_order_lines` already holds it as `metal_rate` — populated on 361 of
366 lines. With that, `amount_received` resolves:

| `amount_received` equals | Orders | |
|---|---|---|
| `metal_rate × net_weight` | **157** | 58% |
| the same plus making | 21 | 8% |
| the line estimate | 3 | 1% |
| none of these | 92 | 34% |

**It is a computed metal value, not cash.** 58% match the metal exactly and
another 8% match metal plus making. A third still fits no formula tried, so this
is not fully closed — but the reading that mattered is refuted: **there is no
evidence of ₹14.47 crore of customer advances**, and the order book showing no
advance is not hiding a liability of that size.

### Both of defect 154's puzzles were two bad rates

That entry flagged two things it could not explain. Both are order lines carrying
an impossible metal rate, and both orders are **still undelivered**:

| Order | Purity | Net weight | Rate booked | Plausible rate | `amount_received` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CO/2627/00041 | 995 | 20.000 g | **1,52,000.00** | ~15,200 | 30,40,000.00 |
| CO/2526/00402 | SLV | 3,000.000 g | **24,600.00** | ~253 | **7,38,00,000.00** |

- CO/2627/00041 is defect 154's *"exactly 10×"* case. Its rate is **ten times**
  a plausible 995 rate, and its own estimate of ₹3,04,000.00 is right —
  20.000 g × ₹15,200. The estimate is sound and the rate is not.
- CO/2526/00402 is the **₹7,38,00,000 outlier** that was more than half the whole
  figure. Silver booked at **₹24,600 a gram**, about **97 times** its real rate,
  against a line estimate of zero.

So the single row that made `amount_received` look like a fortune is a
mistyped silver rate on one undelivered order.

### What is left of it

Two live orders carry a metal rate that is wrong by a factor of 10 and 97. If
either is priced from `metal_rate` at delivery, the customer is quoted a figure
with no relation to the metal. The estimates on those lines are the trustworthy
figures.

**Needs Rahul:** correct the booked rate on **CO/2627/00041** and
**CO/2526/00402**, both still open. And `amount_received` should not be surfaced

## 173. The design catalogue looks unrealised and is not — a fill rate misread, caught — LOW

`design_no_status` (5,242 rows, never loaded) flags **176 of 5,218 designs** with
`status = 1` and the rest 0. There is no legend, and the flag does not correlate
with anything checkable: of the 176, exactly **1** ever became a tag. It adds
nothing interpretable and is not worth loading.

Testing that turned up a figure worth recording, and a conclusion worth **not**
recording:

> Only **69 of 5,221 designs** have ever been made into a tag — 1.3%.

Read alone that says the catalogue is almost entirely unrealised, which would be
a substantial finding about ₹15 crore of designs. **It is not what the number
means.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Tags carrying a design code at all | **109 of 2,816 — 3.9%** |
| Distinct design codes on those tags | 93 |
| Of those 93, resolving to a design | **69 — 74%** |

The catalogue is not unrealised; **tags simply do not record which design they
came from**. Where a tag does carry a design code, it resolves three times in
four, which is a good match rate. The 1.3% measures the fill rate of
`design_code`, not the productivity of the design room.

This is the same trap as [defect 163]'s `-155 pieces` and the `fill rate read as
evidence` note in this record's early entries. Logged because the wrong version
was one sentence from being written down.

## 175. The screen coverage denominator was six short, and nearly twenty-three too many — MEDIUM

Coverage has been reported against `legacy_menu.csv`, captured from the live
menu: **187 distinct screens**. The database carries its own menu in three
tables, none ever loaded, and they do not agree with it.

| Table | Rows | Links |
|---|---|---|
| `main_menu` | 12 | 0 — headings only |
| `sub_menu` | 104 | 80 |
| `exception_sub_menu` | 135 | 134 |

Together **210 distinct links**, and our CSV is a strict **subset**: nothing in
the CSV is missing from the tables, and **23 links are in the tables and not the
CSV**.

### Adding all 23 would have been wrong

The first attempt added all of them and the navigation test rejected it:

> legacy menu has 212 entries, want 189
> legacy menu has **17 top-level headings, want 12**

That second line is the real check. `main_menu` holds the shop's twelve
headings — SETUP, RETAIL, MANUFACTURING, INVENTORY, ACCOUNTS, MIS REPORTS,
REPORTS, DSS REPORT, GST REPORTS, HR, IMP REPORTS, AUDIT — and every heading in
`exception_sub_menu` is one of those twelve. **`sub_menu` is not:** its headings
are *Exhibition*, *KARIGAR REPORTS*, *PENDING REPORTS*, *Report* and *STOCK
REPORTS*, none of which exists in `main_menu`, and all 104 of its rows belong to
a single user, `admin`. It is a separate custom menu, not the standard one.

So 17 of the 23 come from a menu the shop's own `main_menu` does not describe,
and adding them would have inflated the denominator with someone's private
shortcuts.

### The six that are real

Six links sit in `exception_sub_menu` under headings that already exist:

| Top | Sub-group | Screen |
|---|---|---|
| REPORTS | Karigar Repair Report | `issue_from_user_to_diff_karigar.php` |
| REPORTS | Karigar Repair Report | `karigar_issue_receive_register_repair.php` |
| REPORTS | Karigar Repair Report | `shape_wise_issue_receive_repair.php` |
| REPORTS | Manual Stock Tally | `back_date_subgroup_stock.php` |
| REPORTS | Manual Stock Tally | `packet_wise_stock_summary_report.php?tally_status=1` |
| REPORTS | Manual Stock Tally | `raw_stock_tally.php` |

Added. **Coverage is now 117 of 193 — 61%, not 63%.**

Five of the six are karigar or raw-stock screens, which [defect 76] shows have
almost no data behind them; `raw_stock_tally.php` is the shop's own view of the
holding in [defect 78]. They are unlikely to be buildable, but they are part of
the menu and the denominator should say so.

**The guard test is what made this safe.** `TestLegacyMenuLoads` asserts both the
row count and that there are exactly twelve headings. The row count would have
been updated without thought; **the heading count is what caught the seventeen.**
It now records why, so the next person adding menu rows meets the same check.

## 177. What B26 actually costs: a real bill would balance the books and vanish from fifteen screens — HIGH

[Blocker B26] says the posting screens "write a voucher and no detail row". That
is right, and it understates what follows. Measured rather than described.

### The insert paths

The whole module contains **five** `INSERT INTO mcj_*` statements outside tests:

| Table | Written by |
|---|---|
| `mcj_vouchers` | `voucher_repository.go` |
| `mcj_voucher_lines` | `voucher_repository.go` |
| `mcj_stock_items` | `tag.go` |
| `mcj_raw_stock` | `rawstock.go` |
| `mcj_customer_goods` | `partysample.go` |

*(An earlier count of "four" was taken before the raw stock and party sample
screens existed. It is five now, and the shape is unchanged.)*

Every posting screen — **sale**, **old gold**, **credit note** — does exactly two
things: `vouchers.Save(...)`, and for a sale `UPDATE mcj_stock_items SET in_stock
= false`. None writes an invoice, a movement or a stone line. `invoice.go` is
**read-only** — 0 inserts, 0 updates — so the screen that displays bills cannot
create one.

### What a sale saved tomorrow would do

**Correctly:** appear in the cash book, day book, trial balance, ledger book,
balance sheet, P&L and GST register, because all of those read the voucher. The
shelf value would drop, because `in_stock` flips.

**And be invisible to every screen below**, because nothing writes the table each
one reads:

| Unwritten table | Screens that go blind |
|---|---|
| `mcj_sales_invoices` | **9** — GSTR-1, sold stones, sale cost, MRP sales, sales comparison, sales targets, order-to-barcode, ledger merge, statistics |
| `mcj_sales_invoice_lines` | 6 — GSTR-1 HSN, sale cost, MRP sales, sales targets, order-to-barcode, statistics |
| `mcj_stock_movements` | 2 — stock history, hallmarking |
| `mcj_sold_stones` | 1 — sold stones |
| `mcj_old_gold_lines` | 3 — old goods, customer metal, statistics |
| `mcj_purchase_invoices` | 4 — purchase contents, MRP purchases, GSTR-1, statistics |

Counting distinct screens, **fifteen registers would not show a bill raised
today**, including **the GST return**.

### Why this is worse than it sounds

The books would balance. The trial balance would tie, the cash book would foot,
and the shelf would go down by the right amount — so nothing on the accounting
side would signal that anything was wrong. The failure is silent, and it is
silent in exactly the places [defect 155] already shows the shop cannot afford
gaps: **37% of historical sales have no line detail, and a new sale would add to
that at 100%.**

### What to do

This is B26 and it is unchanged: the screens must write their detail rows before
the first real bill. The contribution here is the **list of what to write** —
five tables, and the fifteen screens that prove each one is load-bearing.

**Needs Rahul:** nothing. This one is engineering, and it is the single most
consequential piece of work left in the rebuild.

---

## 178. The one screen that creates stock cannot record stones, certification or hallmarking — HIGH

[Defect 177] established that the posting screens write a voucher and nothing
else. The screens that *do* write were then read, and the tagging screen —
`tag.go`, the only path that creates a `mcj_stock_items` row — has the same shape
of problem.

Its insert names 24 columns. **Ten columns the existing shelf uses are not among
them**, and the tag form has no input for any of them:

| Column | Tags on the shelf using it |
|---|---|
| *(stone lines in `mcj_stock_stones`)* | **562** |
| `certificate_no` / `certification_type` / `certification_rate` / `certification_charge` | **566** |
| `hallmarked` / `hallmark_charge` | **329** |
| `category_id` | **1,461** |
| `wastage_percent` | 22 |
| `design_code` | 109 |
| `has_mrp` | — |

### Stones are the sharpest of these

The screen **does** take a stone value — `stone_value` on the form — and pricing
carries it: `Amount = GoldValue + StoneValue` (`pricing.go:82`). So a new
stone-set tag stores the stone money **inside `amount`** and writes **no stone
rows at all**: there is no `INSERT INTO mcj_stock_stones` anywhere in non-test
code.

That breaks the identity [defect 167] verified on **478 of 478** legacy stone-set
tags:

> `amount − stones = rate × net_weight`

With no stone rows, `amount − 0` is metal *plus* stones, and the identity fails
by exactly the stone value. A new tag would also be invisible to the **stone
ledger**, and on sale its stones would be missing from **sold stones** —
compounding [defect 177] rather than being separate from it.

### Certification has a second-order effect

`quote.go` refuses to price any certified tag, keyed on `certificate_no` and
`certification_charge` ([defect 161] — 566 tags, ₹2,84,75,794.50). A tag created
by this screen can never carry either, so a genuinely certified piece **would be
priced by the quote screen** rather than refused. That is the exact case
[blocker B9] says cannot be priced safely.

### What this means

The tagging screen produces a **plain metal tag**: barcode, item, purity,
weights, rate, making, total. For the 40% of the shelf that is plain metal that
is complete and correct. For a stone-set, certified, hallmarked or categorised
piece — **which is most of the shelf by value** — it silently records less than
the piece is.

**Needs Rahul: nothing.** Like B26 this is engineering, and it belongs with it:
the same work that makes a sale write its detail rows should make a tag write
its stones. Recorded separately because they are separate screens and the
tagging one is quieter — it produces a row that looks complete.

---

## 179. Two smaller write-path gaps, and two that turned out fine — LOW

Completing the read of the four screens that can write, after [defect 178] found
the tagging screen omits ten columns. The other two are much better, and the
differences are worth recording precisely so this is not re-derived.

### `rawstock.go` — complete, but hardcodes who holds the metal

Its insert covers every meaningful column of `mcj_raw_stock`. Two are constants:

	VALUES ($1,$2,$3,$4,$5,$6,$7,'sh','Dr')

`holder` and `side`. The loader maps them from legacy `barcode_main_rawstone.type`
and `.dr_cr`, and **all 10 legacy rows are `sh` / `Dr`** — so the constants match
every row that exists, and nothing is wrong today.

They are not decoration, though. `holder` is what distinguishes *the shop holds
this* from *someone else holds this*, and [defect 164] found **869.850 g of fine
gold issued to MA TARA JEWELLERS** with nothing recording its return. The one
screen that can record raw metal cannot express that the metal is out. Whoever
implements B26's detail rows should widen this at the same time.

### `partysample.go` — one column short

Its receive path writes 11 columns of `mcj_customer_goods` and omits **`item_id`**.
All **7** existing rows carry it, set by the loader from the item master; a
receipt taken on the screen would carry NULL.

Nothing reads it today — `customergoods.go` and `ledgermerge.go` both use
`description` — so this is latent rather than live. It is a one-line fix and
should not wait for a report to need it.

### Checked and correct

- **The return path is complete.** `partysample.go` sets `returned = true`,
  `returned_on` and `return_note` together, which is exactly what migration
  `mcj-1787385000` added those columns for: *"a stone set into an order and a
  stone handed back over the counter are different events"*.
- **`voucher_repository.go`** writes both `mcj_vouchers` and `mcj_voucher_lines`.
  The voucher side of every posting screen is sound; [defect 177] is about what
  is missing **beside** the voucher, not the voucher itself.

So of the five write paths: **one is materially incomplete** ([defect 178]), one
hardcodes a field that will matter ([defect 164]), one is a column short, and two
are correct.
