## 180. No permission says "may create stock", so the tagging screen borrows one named for printing — MEDIUM

Following the write-path audit ([defect 177] to [defect 179]) into the gates on
those same paths. **Nothing is ungated** — every POST requires a permission, which
is the fix [defect 107] put in. The problem is which permission.

| Screen | What it writes | Gated on |
|---|---|---|
| sale | voucher + lines | `VoucherCreate` |
| old gold | voucher + lines | `VoucherCreate` |
| credit note | voucher + lines | `VoucherCreate` |
| **tag** | **a stock item — value onto the shelf** | **`TagPrintUpdate`** |
| **categorise** | **the category on up to 2,575 tags** | **`VoucherUpdate`** |
| **raw stock** | **a raw metal holding** | **`ItemCreate`** |
| **party sample** | customers' goods held | `VoucherCreate` *(no voucher written)* |

The three voucher screens are right. The other four are gated on a permission
from a different domain, because **the permission vocabulary has no word for
stock**. Of **144** permissions in the module, **not one** is named
`StockCreate`, `BarcodeCreate` or `TagCreate` — the set runs `ItemCreate`
(the item *master*), `TagPrintRead` / `TagPrintUpdate` (tag *printing*) and
`VoucherCreate` / `VoucherUpdate` / `VoucherRead`.

So:

- **Whoever may print tags may create stock.** `TagPrintUpdate` reads as a
  printing right and grants the act that puts a priced item on the shelf.
- **Whoever may amend a voucher may re-categorise the shelf.** `categorise.go`
  can rewrite the category on any of the 2,575 tags, gated on `VoucherUpdate`.
- **Party sample writes no voucher** yet requires `VoucherCreate`, so the gate is
  both wrong in name and stricter than needed.

### This is least-privilege, not an open door

Nothing here is reachable by an unauthenticated user, and nothing is
unprotected. The risk is that a grant made for one reason silently confers
another — and the shop's legacy access matrix shows this is not hypothetical:
**24 roles across 2,755 grants**, with tag and barcode screens granted to at
least six of them (Ashok 21 grants, ankush 19, GKS 19, rps 18, Bapi 17, anand 15).
Whoever maps those roles onto these permissions will be choosing, without knowing
it, who can create stock.

**Not changed.** Adding `StockCreate` and `StockUpdate` means renaming gates that
[defect 107] has only just made correct, and the mapping from legacy roles is not
yet built — doing it now would be guessing at an allocation the shop has not
made. It belongs with that work.

**Needs Rahul, when roles are set up:** who may create a tag, and who may
re-categorise stock. Those are two separate answers today given by one grant each
for the wrong thing.

---

## 181. Two tills tagging the same barcode would both succeed — MEDIUM

`tag.go` guards barcode uniqueness carefully, and says why:

> The uniqueness check is repeated here rather than trusted from the preview.
> Between pricing and saving somebody else may have used the number, and two
> pieces sharing a barcode is exactly the defect this rebuild inherited.

The intent is right and the implementation cannot deliver it. `barcodeInUse` runs

	SELECT count(*) FROM mcj_stock_items
	WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND btrim(barcode) = btrim($2) AND in_stock

— a plain read, no `FOR UPDATE`, nothing to lock because the row does not exist
yet. No isolation level is set anywhere in the module, so PostgreSQL's default
**READ COMMITTED** applies: two concurrent saves of the same barcode each see
zero, each insert, and both commit.

**Nothing in the database stops them.** The only barcode index is not unique:

	CREATE INDEX idx_mcj_stock_items_barcode ON mcj_stock_items (tenant_id, barcode)

So the check-then-insert is the whole of the protection, and it is exactly the
pattern that does not hold under concurrency.

### The fix is blocked by the defect it was written to prevent

The right guard is a partial unique index matching the check's own semantics —
unique among tags **in stock**, which leaves the shop's deliberate practice of
reusing a sold tag's barcode alone (1,974 of 3,021 barcodes have been reused
this way):

	CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON mcj_stock_items (tenant_id, btrim(barcode)) WHERE in_stock

**It cannot be created today.** [Defect 146]'s duplicate is barcode
**86065435** — two MALA pieces at ₹900 each, **both `in_stock`** — and it is the
only one. Confirmed: exactly one barcode has more than one in-stock copy.

So the chain is: **defect 146 must be resolved before this race can be closed**,
and defect 146 needs Rahul to re-tag one of the two pieces. Until then the index
would be rejected by the very row that proves it is needed.

**Interim, if the shop starts tagging from two terminals before that:** a
transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed on the barcode would serialise the
check and insert without needing an index. Not applied — it is a workaround for
a race that a single till cannot hit, and the real fix is one re-tag away.

**Severity is bounded by how the shop works.** One person tagging at one screen
can never trigger it. Two people tagging simultaneously, or any future import
running beside the screen, can.

---

## 182. Requests are not transactional, and a rejected save can leave half its rows behind — HIGH (proven)

Chasing transaction boundaries through the write paths found that **there are
none**, and it was confirmed against the running application rather than
inferred.

### The proof

A party-sample receipt was posted with two lines: the first valid, the second
carrying a carat value too large for `numeric(14,3)`.

	http 422
	receipt_no  | description       | pieces | carats
	TXTEST/001  | TX PROBE LINE ONE |      1 |  1.000

**The request was rejected and the first line was written anyway.** The probe row
was deleted immediately; `mcj_customer_goods` is back to its 7 rows, verified.

### Why

`composables.UseTx(ctx)` returns the transaction from the context **if one is
there**, and otherwise falls back to `UsePool(ctx)`:

	func UseTx(ctx context.Context) (repo.Tx, error) {
	    tx := ctx.Value(constants.TxKey)
	    if tx == nil {
	        return UsePool(ctx)      // <- a pool, not a transaction
	    }
	    ...

Nothing puts one there. **No middleware in the SDK sets `TxKey`** — checked every
file in `pkg/middleware`, none references `TxKey` or `pool.Begin` — and **no
controller in this module calls `composables.InTx`**. So every `tx.Exec` in a
hand-written controller runs on the pool and commits on its own.

### What that costs, screen by screen

| Screen | Statements per save | Partial outcome |
|---|---|---|
| **sale** | voucher, then N line inserts, then the stock UPDATE | a committed voucher whose tags are still on the shelf |
| **old gold / credit note** | voucher, then N line inserts | a voucher with some of its lines — **an unbalanced voucher** |
| **party sample** | one insert per line | proven above |
| tag, raw stock | one insert | safe by having nothing to divide |

The sale case is the sharpest. Its stock update is written to refuse the sale if
a tag was sold in the meantime:

	"%d of %d tags were no longer on the shelf — someone else may have sold them"

That refusal is correct and now cannot help: **the voucher is already
committed** when it fires. The books would carry a sale the shop declined, with
the goods still on the shelf.

### The tests cannot catch this

`itf` wraps every request in a real transaction — `suite.go:195` does
`ctx = composables.WithTx(ctx, s.env.Tx)` — and rolls it back between tests. So
in tests `UseTx` returns a transaction and everything is atomic; in production it
returns a pool and nothing is. **The suite is green precisely because it does not
reproduce the condition.** That is why 86 test files and a full integration run
have never shown it.

### What to do

Wrap the mutating handlers in `composables.InTx`. The SDK's generic CRUD service
already does exactly this (`crud/service.go:157` and `:218`), which is why the
18 CRUD screens are safe and the seven hand-written ones are not.

### Fixed and proven

An `atomic` wrapper now runs each mutating handler inside one
`composables.InTx`, rolling the transaction back when the handler answers 4xx or
5xx. The response is already written by then, which is the wanted outcome: **the
client is told no and the database agrees.** Applied to all seven hand-written
mutating routes — sale, old gold, credit note, tag, raw stock, party sample,
categorise.

Verified against the running app with the same probe that proved the defect, and
with its counter-test:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Two-line receipt, second line invalid | 422 — **line one persisted** | 422 — **0 rows left**, table unchanged at 7 |
| Valid single-line receipt | *(not tested)* | 200 — **row written and present** |

The counter-test matters as much as the fix: a wrapper that rolled back
everything would also return 200 and lose the sale. Both probe rows were deleted;
`mcj_customer_goods` is back to 7, verified.

Integration suite green.

**Needs Rahul: nothing.** It was engineering, it was small, and it belonged
**before** [B26]'s detail rows — writing more rows per save without a transaction
would have widened the failure rather than narrowing it.

---

## 183. My own fix for defect 182 covered seven routes of ten — MEDIUM

[Defect 182]'s fix was applied to "all seven hand-written mutating routes". That
list came from [defect 177]'s write-path audit, which counted **`INSERT INTO`
statements** — and so counted the voucher repository once, as one path, without
asking how many screens reach it.

Checking the fix by a different measure — **every non-GET route in the module**,
which is the question the fix is actually answering — found three more:

| Route | Writes | Was wrapped |
|---|---|---|
| `voucher.go` → create | `repo.Save` — voucher + N lines | **no** |
| `voucher.go` → update | `repo.Save` — UPDATE, **DELETE all lines**, re-insert | **no** |
| `reconcile.go` → update | `UPDATE mcj_vouchers` in a loop | **no** |

**The voucher update path was the worst one left.** `voucher_repository.go`
handles an edit by deleting every line of the voucher and inserting the new set.
Without a transaction, a failure between the delete and the inserts leaves a
voucher with **no lines at all** — not merely unbalanced, empty. That is the
general journal, payment and receipt entry screen.

`reconcile.go` marks cheques cleared one `UPDATE` at a time, so a failure
part-way through leaves some cheques reconciled and some not, with the screen
reporting an error over a partly-applied change.

All three are now wrapped. **Ten of the module's twelve POST routes are atomic**;
the two that are not — `stocktake.go` and `taglabel.go` — were checked and write
nothing, being a report filter and a label preview.

### The lesson is the same one as defect 160

That entry recorded a sweep whose clean result was "a property of the test, not
of the reports". This is the same shape: the fix was verified against the list
that produced it. **Counting inserts answers "what writes?"; counting routes
answers "what can a user submit?" — and the second is the question a transaction
boundary belongs to.**

Full integration suite green after the change.

---

## 184. Voucher numbers are race-safe; almost nothing else is — MEDIUM

Following [defect 181]'s barcode race to its parallel: does the same
check-then-write pattern threaten voucher numbers?

**It does not, and the reason is instructive.** `nextNumber` is exactly the
vulnerable shape —

	SELECT COALESCE(MAX(number), 0) + 1 FROM mcj_vouchers
	WHERE tenant_id=$1 AND type=$2 AND financial_year=$3

— two concurrent saves would read the same maximum and choose the same number.
But the database refuses the second:

	CREATE UNIQUE INDEX mcj_vouchers_tenant_id_number_type_financial_year_key
	    ON mcj_vouchers (tenant_id, number, type, financial_year)

The race exists and cannot produce a duplicate. **The constraint is doing the
work the query cannot**, which is the whole argument of defect 181 stated the
other way round.

### A unique index is not the same as a protected table

The schema carries **133 unique indexes**, which reads as thorough until they are
read for what they cover. The two that matter most are keyed on the **migration**
id, not on anything a user enters:

| Table | Unique index | Constrains a new row? |
|---|---|---|
| `mcj_stock_items` | `(tenant_id, legacy_id) WHERE legacy_id IS NOT NULL` | **No** — an app-created tag has `legacy_id` NULL, so the index does not apply to it at all |
| `mcj_sales_invoices` | `(tenant_id, legacy_id)` | **No** — same |

So the tag table looks constrained and is not, which is precisely how
[defect 146]'s duplicate barcode survived and why [defect 181] can happen.

### Tables with no business key at all

Of the transactional tables, **eight** have no unique index beyond the primary
key: `mcj_voucher_lines`, `mcj_stock_movements`, `mcj_stock_stones`,
`mcj_sold_stones`, `mcj_old_gold_lines`, `mcj_purchase_invoices`,
`mcj_customer_goods`, `mcj_raw_stock`.

Most are line tables where duplication is legitimate — a voucher may debit the
same ledger twice, a tag may hold two identical stones — and [defect 168] records
that the legacy line table had no key either, one id being shared by 51 rows. So
this is mostly correct.

`mcj_purchase_invoices` is the odd one: it is a **header** table with a bill
number, and nothing stops the same bill being recorded twice. Its sales
counterpart is only protected on `legacy_id`, which no new row will have.

### What to do

Nothing here is a live fault — no screen writes purchase invoices at all today
([defect 177]). It becomes one the moment [B26] makes them writable, and the
cheapest time to add `(tenant_id, bill_no)` is before there is data to conflict
with it.

**Recorded rather than fixed**, because adding constraints to tables nothing
writes yet is guessing at the shape B26 will give them.

---

## 185. The transaction wrapper would have committed a panicking handler — MEDIUM

Auditing [defect 182]'s own fix. Two things were checked and one was wrong.

### Checked and safe: the response is rendered inside the transaction

`atomic` writes the response before the transaction closes, so a handler whose
error page reads the database could show a row that the rollback is about to
remove. Every error path was read: they render from **props already in memory**,
and the only database read on a failure path is `billableParties` — the ledger
list, which no save touches. Nothing displays a doomed write.

### Wrong: a panic committed

`composables.InTx` has **no deferred cleanup**:

	if err := fn(WithTx(ctx, tx)); err != nil {
	    ... tx.Rollback(ctx) ...
	}
	return tx.Commit(ctx)

If `fn` panics, neither branch runs — the transaction is abandoned mid-flight,
holding its pooled connection, with whatever it had written neither committed nor
rolled back. The SDK recovers panics further up the stack (`middleware/auth.go`,
`middleware/logging.go`), so the request answers 500 and the data is left in
limbo.

**Fixed.** The wrapper now catches the panic, sets the named return so `InTx`
rolls back, and raises it again **after** the transaction is closed — leaving the
SDK's recovery middleware to answer the request exactly as before:

	var panicked any
	_ = composables.InTx(r.Context(), func(ctx context.Context) (err error) {
	    defer func() {
	        if p := recover(); p != nil { panicked = p; err = errRolledBack }
	    }()
	    ...
	})
	if panicked != nil { panic(panicked) }

Recovering without re-raising would have been worse than the bug — a panicking
save would answer 200 with an empty page.

### And a test for the rule itself

The wrapper's whole behaviour is one comparison: `status >= 400` unwinds,
anything else commits. **A redirect is how every successful save answers** — the
sale screen ends with `http.StatusSeeOther` — so a wrapper that treated 3xx as
failure would roll back every completed sale and report success. That is now
asserted directly, along with implicit 200, 422 and 500.

Three unit tests, no database needed.

---

## 186. The report gate was tested on three reports of sixty-nine, and never on the export — MEDIUM

[Defect 107] found every report served to any authenticated user and gated them.
The test written alongside it, `TestReports_RequireAPermissionAndNotJustALogin`,
checks **three** reports — `salary-sheet`, `trial-balance`, `user-rights` — and
only the screen, never `export.xlsx`.

The gate itself is right. `report.go` registers both routes through the same
call:

	router.HandleFunc("/"+key,                gateAll(required, c.show))
	router.HandleFunc("/"+key+"/export.xlsx", gateAll(required, c.export))

So nothing was exposed. But the export is **the same data in a more portable
form** — a spreadsheet a user can keep — and it was protected by a line nobody
had ever exercised.

### Widened

The test now sweeps **every key in the registry**, both routes, and refuses to
run at all if the registry holds fewer than 60 reports — so trimming the registry
cannot quietly shrink the sweep:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Reports covered | 3 | **69** |
| Routes per report | screen only | **screen and export** |
| Assertions | 3 | **138** |

**Confirmed non-vacuous.** Removing `gateAll` from the export route produces
**67 failures**, each naming the report it served. Restored, green.

### Why three was not enough

The three chosen are the obviously sensitive ones — salaries, the trial balance,
user rights. That is the instinct that picks a sample, and it is the wrong
instinct for a gate: defect 107 was not "three screens were exposed", it was
**every screen in a class**, found only because the whole class was checked. A
sample proves the three; a sweep proves the rule.

## 187. Nothing asserted that the CRUD screens use the tenant guard — MEDIUM

[Blocker B11] found that `crud.DefaultRepository` does not scope reads to the
tenant, and `persistence.TenantScoped` was written to fix it. Four isolation
tests prove **the wrapper works**: it filters List and Count, refuses Get and
Exists on another tenant's row, and cannot be told which tenant to write to.

**Nothing proved the screens use it.** A new CRUD controller written without the
wrapper would leave all four isolation tests green and serve every tenant's rows.
That is B11 reintroduced one file at a time, and it would look like a normal
controller.

The 18 call sites were checked by hand while investigating [defect 180]. A count
taken by hand is true on the day it is taken.

**Now a test.** `TestEveryCrudRepositoryIsTenantScoped` reads every controller
source and fails if any `crud.DefaultRepository[` is not immediately preceded by
`TenantScoped(`. It also refuses to pass if fewer than 15 generic repositories
are found, so removing the CRUD screens cannot make the guard vacuously true.

**Proven non-vacuous, and not by mutation.** Unwrapping a real controller orphans
the `persistence` import and fails the build — which proves nothing about the
assertion, only that Go noticed an unused import. The rule is therefore split
into `unwrappedRepositories(src string)` and exercised directly against three
synthetic sources: a wrapped call (0 flagged), a bare call (1 flagged), and both
together (exactly 1). That is the check testing itself rather than testing the
compiler.

### A note on the attempt

The first mutation attempt restored from a backup path, `/tmp/color.bak`, that
already existed from unrelated work. It wrote a 137-line `package color` file
into the controllers directory and broke the build with *"found packages
controllers and color"*. Removed, build verified clean, and the retry used a
session-scoped scratch path. Recorded because a backup filename that is not
unique is a trap, not a mishap.

---

## 188. The transaction fix was held in place by a grep, not a test — MEDIUM

[Defect 182] made the mutating routes transactional; [defect 183] found the first
attempt had covered seven of ten. Both were verified by reading the source at the
time. Neither left anything behind that would notice a POST route added tomorrow
without `atomic`.

That matters more than the tenant guard of [defect 187], because the failure is
silent in both directions: an unwrapped route looks identical, behaves
identically until something fails part-way, and then leaves half its rows
committed — which is exactly what defect 182 demonstrated against the running
app.

**Now a test.** `TestEveryPostRouteRunsInATransaction` walks the controller
sources and requires every `Methods(http.MethodPost)` registration to be wrapped:

	12 POST routes, 10 wrapped, 2 exempt by name

The two exemptions are named individually with the reason — `stocktake.go` is a
report filter and `taglabel.go` a label preview, neither writing anything — so
adding a third is a deliberate act rather than an oversight. The test also fails
if fewer than 10 POST routes are found, so deleting the posting screens cannot
make it pass by having nothing to check.

**Proven non-vacuous:** unwrapping the raw-stock route makes it fail by name —

	1 POST route(s) are not wrapped in atomic() and are not exempt:
	  rawstock.go: router.HandleFunc("", gate(permissions.ItemCreate, c.post)).

Restored and green.

### The first version of the guard was wrong, and said so

Reading one line at a time, it reported `creditnote.go` as unguarded. That file
registers across four lines and closes with a bare `}))).Methods(http.MethodPost)`
— the `atomic(` sits three lines above. The check now takes the whole statement,
from its `router.HandleFunc` back to the `Methods` call.

Worth recording because the failure was a **false positive on correct code**, and
the tempting response is to add an exemption. The right response was to fix the
check: an exemption would have hidden creditnote.go from the guard permanently,
so the day someone unwrapped it nothing would have said so.

---

## 189. The doubled-footer rule cannot be a unit test, so it is a script — LOW

[Defect 186] to [defect 188] replaced hand checks with tests. The same was
attempted for [defect 160]'s rule — that no report's footer may count a summary
row the query already produced — and it does not fit in a test.

**A source-level rule does not hold.** The obvious one, *"a report that appends
its own `report.Row` must set `NoTotals`"*, is wrong: many reports correctly
append a note row carrying no money at all — `audit.go`, `daybook.go`,
`dataquality.go`, `gst.go` among them. Requiring `NoTotals` of those would be
requiring them to suppress a footer they should have.

**A seeded test would pass over nothing.** The property only appears when a
report has enough rows to produce a subtotal. Against `itf`'s fixtures most
reports return two or three rows, so the detector would examine nothing and go
green — the same vacuity caught in [defect 162] and [defect 187].

So it stays a sweep, and the sweep is now a **script that can be re-run** rather
than something reconstructed by hand each time:

	python3 tools/check_report_footers.py --port 3250

It fetches every report from a running instance, applies defect 160's detector —
a subtotal is a row equal to the sum of every row above it, with at least four
rows above so a coincidence is not mistaken for one — and exits non-zero on a
find.

| | |
|---|---|
| Clean tree | `69 reports checked, 0 doubled footer(s)`, exit **0** |
| `NoTotals` removed from `sale-cost` | **3** doubled columns named, exit **1** |

**Two things this cost, both mine.** The first check of the exit code piped the
script into `tail`, so the shell reported `tail`'s status and not the script's.
The second read exit 1 on what should have been a clean tree — because restoring
the source and running `go build ./...` does not rebuild the binary the server
runs from; the scratch build still held the mutation. Both are the same mistake:
**verifying a thing through something that is not the thing.**

---

## 190. ₹69 lakh of customer debt has not moved, and the shop holds ₹21 lakh of customers' money — MEDIUM

The customer ledger position, which no entry in this record had yet stated. Of
**485 customer accounts**, 457 are square and 28 are not:

| | Accounts | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Owe the shop | 10 | **73,96,553.00** |
| Shop owes them | 18 | **21,41,852.00** |

### The debt is dormant, not current

Splitting by whether the account saw any posting in the captured period:

| | Accounts | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Owes — **no posting at all** | **6** | **69,28,065.00** |
| Owes — active | 4 | 4,68,488.00 |
| Shop owes — **no posting at all** | 4 | 11,52,636.00 |
| Shop owes — active | 14 | 9,89,216.00 |

**94% of the receivable is an opening balance that has not moved.** The three
largest are entirely inherited:

| Customer | Opening | Movement | Balance | Postings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HARSIT ANAND SULTANIA | 32,30,681.00 | 0.00 | **32,30,681.00** | **0** |
| AMIT SINGH YADAV | 25,55,000.00 | 0.00 | **25,55,000.00** | **0** |
| SHEJAN TAJ | 7,81,837.00 | 0.00 | **7,81,837.00** | **0** |

Two customers account for **₹57,85,681.00** — 78% of everything owed to the shop —
and neither has a single transaction in the period the books cover.

**It cannot be aged.** [Defect 142] puts the first voucher at 9 March 2026, so
there is nothing to say whether these balances are three months old or ten years
old. An opening balance with no history is a number, not a debt with a date.

### The other side is customers' money

**₹21,41,852.00 sits on 18 customer accounts in credit**, the largest being
**SHARON WINES at ₹10,50,000.00 with no postings at all**. A credit balance on a
customer is money taken and not yet turned into goods — the same shape as
[defect 152]'s matured schemes and, unlike [defect 169]'s order figures, this one
**is** money: it is in the ledgers.

### What to do

**Needs Rahul, and this is a collections question rather than a data one:**

1. Are **HARSIT ANAND SULTANIA (₹32,30,681)** and **AMIT SINGH YADAV
   (₹25,55,000)** live debts, or written-off balances carried forward? Together
   they are 78% of the shop's receivables.
2. What is **SHARON WINES' ₹10,50,000 credit** — an advance against goods, or a
   deposit to return?

Nothing here is a fault in the data or the rebuild. It is a position the shop
should see stated, and no screen states it: the supplier side has one
([defect 145]'s supplier balances) and the customer side does not.

## 191. Twelve cheque payments cannot be reconciled, and the first count of them was wrong — LOW

The bank reconciliation screen matches on a cheque number. Counting where those
numbers live:

| | |
|---|---|
| Vouchers naming a cheque **in the narration text** | **163** |
| Of those, carrying the number on a voucher **line** | **151** |
| **Invisible to reconciliation** — narration only | **12** |

The reconcile query reads the line-level number first, then the voucher-level
one, so 151 of the 163 are perfectly reconcilable. **Twelve are not:** their
cheque number exists only inside a sentence such as
*"Ch. No.435590, Dt.05.12.2026 Issued Against Their Dues"*, and no query can
match on that.

**The first reading of this was wrong and is recorded as such.** Counting only
`mcj_vouchers.cheque_number` gave *"34 structured, 163 narration-only"* and
implied 83% of cheque payments were unreconcilable. That ignored
`mcj_voucher_lines.cheque_number`, which holds **593** numbers. The real figure is
12 — a twelfth of what the first count suggested, and the difference was one
table.

**Also checked and correct:** the one voucher dated in the future — PMNT 576,
**5 December 2026**, ₹1,35,370.00 to DAYANIDHI TRADE PVT LTD — is a **post-dated
cheque**, exactly as its narration says. It is properly balanced and correctly
excluded from an as-on-today balance sheet, which is why the sheet reads
₹4,91,62,109.87 against ₹4,92,97,479.87 counted across all dates.

**Not fixed.** Extracting a cheque number from prose is guesswork, and twelve
vouchers is a smaller job by hand than a parser is to trust.

## 192. A sale now records what was sold — B26's sales half, done and proven — HIGH (fixed)

[Defect 177] measured what [blocker B26] costs: every posting screen wrote a
voucher and nothing else, so a bill balanced the books and was invisible to
fifteen registers including the GST return. The sales half is now written.

`writeSaleDetail` runs inside the same transaction as the voucher and the stock
update, and writes four things in the order a bill is read:

| Table | What it records |
|---|---|
| `mcj_sales_invoices` | the bill — number, customer, place of supply, goods, making, rounding, total |
| `mcj_sales_invoice_lines` | one row per line, with **`item_id`**, purity, weight, rate and making |
| `mcj_stock_movements` | the piece leaving the shelf, referencing the bill |
| `mcj_sold_stones` | the stones, copied from the tag so the sold record matches the shelf |

The bill number follows the shop's own format, taken from its 224 captured
bills: `GST/2627/00225`.

### Proven against the running app

A real sale was posted for a stone-set 18kt nose pin and every count moved by
exactly one:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Vouchers | 1,848 | 1,849 |
| Invoices | 224 | **225** |
| Invoice lines | 328 | **329** |
| Stock movements | 9,036 | **9,037** |
| Sold stones | 203 | **204** |
| Tags in stock | 2,575 | 2,574 |

And it appears in the registers that were blind. The GSTR-1 HSN summary moved by
exactly the sale:

| HSN 711319 | Before | After | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quantity | 34.956 g | 35.206 g | **0.250 g** — the tag |
| Taxable | 5,64,137.00 | 5,67,836.50 | **3,699.50** — the goods |
| Tax | 16,924.16 | 17,035.15 | **110.99** — CGST + SGST |

Stock history, sold stones and sale cost all show the bill by name. `gstr-sales`
and `mrp-sales` correctly do **not**: the first is the B2B section and this is a
counter sale, the second is MRP goods only.

**The test sale was reversed in full** — all six counts and the shelf value
₹14,23,61,188.20 verified back to where they started.

### Two mistakes worth keeping

**Four columns that do not exist.** The first version inserted `taxable`, `cgst`,
`sgst` and `igst` onto the invoice header. Go compiles SQL as a string, so the
build passed; the first real sale would have failed. The table deliberately has
no tax columns — the GST is read from the voucher's own tax lines, which is how
the GSTR screens already compute it for the captured bills, and storing it twice
would let the two drift.

**A line with no item.** The second version wrote the line but not its `item_id`,
and the HSN summary joins line → item → HSN code. The sale recorded perfectly and
was still absent from the GST return. That is [defect 148] and [defect 179]'s
lesson a third time: **a detail row without its foreign key is a row that reports
cannot see.**

**And one wrong test.** The check "is the bill number in the report?" reported the
HSN summary as blind when it was not — that report groups by HSN code and never
prints a bill number. The figures had to be compared before and after instead.

### What is left of B26

Old gold and credit note still write a voucher only. Their detail tables —
`mcj_old_gold_lines` and the return side — are next.

## 193. Old gold now records the metal, not just the payment — HIGH (fixed)

The second of [blocker B26]'s three posting screens. Before this, buying back a
customer's chain wrote a `PURC-OG` voucher and nothing else: the money was in the
books and **the metal was in no record at all**. `mcj_old_gold_lines` is read by
the Old Goods Register, Customer Metal and Statistics, and nothing wrote it
([defect 177]).

The screen already computed each lot — purity, net weight, buy-back rate,
amount — and then threw the detail away, passing `save` only a total and a
**count**. It now passes the lots.

`writeOldGoldLines` runs inside the same transaction as the voucher and writes
one row per lot, numbered in the shop's own format: `OGP/2627/00026`.

### Proven against the running app

A 5.000 g lot of 22kt was bought back at the buy-back rate:

	OGP/2627/00026 | party 12843 | 22 | 5.000 g | rate 14,253.00 | 71,265.00 | PURC-OG 26

5.000 × 14,253.00 = **71,265.00**, exactly. It appears in both registers that
read the table:

- **Old Goods Register** — `23 Aug 2026 | PURC-OG 26 | ABDUL RAHMAN | 22 | 5.000 | 14,253.00 | 71,265.00 | Set against their account`
- **Customer Metal** — the same lot, closing *"the shop owes this customer"*

Reversed in full: 25 old gold lines, 1,848 vouchers, 5,229 voucher lines and the
shelf at ₹14,23,61,188.20, all verified back.

### Tunch is written as zero, deliberately

The screen does not ask for touch and none is invented. [Defect 38] established
that this shop prices old gold as **rate x NET weight with the purity carried in
the rate** — tunch plays no part in the money — and that its legacy `fine_wt`
column was so unreliable it was left unloaded. A fabricated touch figure would be
a guess printed as a fact, which is the failure this record exists to prevent.

### Two wrong turns, both mine, both the same shape

**A purity that has no buy-back rate.** The first attempt used `OLDGOLD`, which
is what the 22 captured lots carry — and the screen correctly refused: *"there is
no buy-back rate for OLDGOLD on or before 23 Aug 2026."* Buy-back rates exist for
the numeric grades (9, 14, 18, 22, 95, 995, SLV), not for the legacy bucket name.
The screen was right and the test was wrong.

**A report key that does not exist.** Checking visibility, `old-goods` returned
zero rows and looked like a failure. The key is **`old-goods-register`**. The
report was working the whole time.

Both are the error of [defect 189]: **verifying a thing through something that is
not the thing.** Three times now in one session.

### And a third: `go build` passed on a broken format string

Changing `save` to take the lots rather than a count left the narration reading
`fmt.Sprintf("... %d lot(s)", lots)` — a slice formatted as a number. **`go build
./...` reported success.** It is a `go vet` finding, not a compile error, and vet
runs as part of `go test` — so the integration suite caught it and the build did
not.

Worth keeping beside [defect 192]'s four non-existent columns: that was SQL the
compiler cannot see, this is a format string it will not check. **Two different
ways a green build meant nothing, on consecutive screens.**

### B26 remaining

Credit note — the sale-return side — still writes a voucher only.

The credit note was the last of the three. Returning a customer's goods wrote a
voucher and set `in_stock = true` — the tag reappeared on the shelf with nothing
saying when or why, which is [defect 192]'s silence seen from the other side.

It now writes a `SALE-RET` movement in the same transaction, taking the weight
and purity from the tag rather than re-entering them. The same code serves all
four trade kinds, so a purchase return records `PURC-RET` without further work.

**Proven against the running app.** A ₹5,000 credit note against a 76.264 g 18kt
diamond bracelet, and the tag's own history now reads in order:

	23 Aug 2026 | 70630587 | DIAMOND BRACELET | returned by customer | SALE-RET 4
	15 Apr 2026 | 70630587 | DIAMOND BRACELET | returned by customer | SR/2627/00001
	02 Apr 2026 | 70630587 | DIAMOND BRACELET | sold                 | GST/2627/00004

The new return sits beside the shop's own captured one from April, in the same
form. Reversed in full — 1,848 vouchers, 5,229 lines, 9,036 movements, 2,575 tags
and the shelf at ₹14,23,61,188.20, all verified back.

### Where B26 now stands

| Screen | Writes |
|---|---|
| Sale | voucher, invoice, invoice lines, stock movement, sold stones ([defect 192]) |
| Old gold | voucher, old gold lines ([defect 193]) |
| Credit note / trade returns | voucher, stock movement |

A bill raised today is no longer invisible. The fifteen registers [defect 177]
listed now see a sale, and the GST return moves by exactly the sale's own
figures.

**What B26 does not yet cover:** there is still no screen that records a
**purchase invoice**. `mcj_purchase_invoices` and `mcj_purchase_contents` hold
the shop's 43 captured bills and nothing writes them, so buying stock from a
supplier remains voucher-only. That is the next piece, and it is the one
[defect 184] warned to add a `(tenant_id, bill_no)` constraint to **before** it
becomes writable.

## 195. Buying from a supplier now records the bill — the trade path is complete — HIGH (fixed)

The last gap in [blocker B26]. `mcj_purchase_invoices` held the shop's 43
captured bills and nothing created a forty-fourth, so every purchase was
voucher-only and the purchase-side registers were frozen at migration
([defect 177]).

Purchases run through the same trade controller as returns — the kinds
`purchase` (PURC-GSC) and `purchase against an order` (PURC-GCO). Both now write
a header in the same transaction, numbered in the shop's own format
`GDP/2627/00025`. The other two kinds are deliberately excluded: a **sale return
is not a purchase**, and a **debit note reverses one** rather than making one —
which matches the data, where 43 bills sit against 25 PURC-OG and 3 PURC-RET
vouchers carrying none.

Unlike the sales header, this one **does** carry the tax split — the table has
`taxable`, `cgst`, `sgst` and `igst` and the captured bills fill them. That is
the opposite of [defect 192]'s mistake, and it is opposite for a reason: the two
tables genuinely differ.

**Proven.** A ₹1,00,000 purchase from A 1 SILVER:

	GDP/2627/00025 | 12835 | A 1 SILVER | interstate | taxable 1,00,000.00 | total 1,03,000.00 | PURC-GSC 25

Reversed in full — 43 invoices, 1,848 vouchers, 5,229 lines, shelf
₹14,23,61,188.20, all verified back.

### The constraint went in first

[Defect 184] warned that `mcj_purchase_invoices` is a header table with a bill
number and no uniqueness, and that the cheapest moment to fix it is before
anything writes to it. Migration `mcj-1787408000` adds

	CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON mcj_purchase_invoices (tenant_id, btrim(bill_no))
	    WHERE btrim(bill_no) <> ''

applied before the first write, with all 43 existing bills verified distinct
beforehand. Unlike [defect 181]'s barcode index — which cannot be created because
a duplicate already exists — this one went in unopposed because it was done at
the right time.

### A wrong expectation, checked before it became a defect

The test purchase recorded **interstate** with the tax in IGST, while the form
said `interstate=0`. That looked like the flag being ignored. It is not: the
screen overrides a stale form value when the party has changed, and **A 1 SILVER
is in Maharashtra against the shop's West Bengal**. IGST is correct.

The check also settled something the record had left vague: **562 of 785 ledgers
carry a state**, including 433 of 485 customers. [Defect 150] found the contact
columns empty and it would have been easy to assume `state` was among them. It is
not, which is why the sale writer takes the party's own state and falls back to
the shop's only for the 52 customers without one.

### B26 is closed

| Screen | Records |
|---|---|
| Sale | invoice, lines, movement, sold stones |
| Purchase / purchase against order | purchase invoice |
| Old gold | old gold lines |
| Credit note / debit note | stock movement |

A day's trade — buy, tag, sell, take goods back, buy old gold — now leaves a
record on every screen built to read one.

## 196. Two screens built, and each one found something in the data — LOW

Starting the 42 screens that have data behind them. Both of these came with a
finding, which is the usual pattern: building a screen is how the data gets read
properly.

### Subgroup Stock Tally — `tag_untag_subgroup.php`

The shelf grouped the way it is counted, leading with tags and weight rather
than value, because a tally is a sheet somebody carries around with a pen. Ten
subgroups, **2,575 tags, ₹14,23,61,188.20** — tying to the shelf exactly.

**369 tags carry no weight at all** and the screen says so on the row rather than
showing a blank: 218 imitation pieces are counted by the piece and never weighed,
and 16 22kt and 5 silver tags have no weight recorded when their neighbours do.
The first is correct; the second is worth someone's eye.

### User Master — `user_master.php`

Who could sign in to the old system and what each was trusted with. **24 logins,
11 of whom could change something after the fact** — back-date a voucher, change
a rate, edit a barcode, move a due date. Those four were worth a column each in
the legacy master because every one alters something already recorded.

Read-only and deliberately so: these are the shop's OLD logins as the dump found
them, not accounts in this rebuild. **No password or security-code column is
read** — they are in the dump and [blocker B15] keeps them shut.

### `role_code` is not a role code

The first version joined `mcj_legacy_access.role_code` to
`mcj_legacy_users.role_code` and every user rendered *"no screens granted"*.
The two columns share a name and hold different things:

| Table | `role_code` holds |
|---|---|
| `mcj_legacy_users` | a **number** — 2, 5, 6, 8, 12 |
| `mcj_legacy_access` | a **login name** — ankush, Ashok, dipak, GKS, Priyanka |

Grants in this ERP are per **person**, not per role. Joined on the login instead,
the screen reads properly: ANKUSH 231 screens, ANAND 175, ANURADHA 22, ARVIND 11.

This is [defect 41]'s shape for the fourth time — a column named for one thing
holding another — and it is worth stating that **the wrong join produced a
plausible screen**: every row said "no screens granted", which for a shop with
one admin would have looked entirely believable.

### And a self-inflicted one

The comment explaining that join was written with **backticks around a column
name** — inside a Go backtick raw string, which it silently terminated. Eleven
compile errors from one pair of quotes. Fixed by writing the name plainly.

Coverage **119 of 193**. Integration suite green.

### Quarterly Report — `quarterly_report.php`

Trading by quarter, read from the vouchers rather than any quarterly table — the
dump has none, and a quarter is an arrangement of dates rather than a thing to
store.

| Quarter | Vouchers | Income | Expense | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 Q1 | 1 | 0.00 | 1,399.00 | −1,399.00 |
| 2026 Q2 | 1,196 | 1,61,16,345.00 | 2,22,63,668.57 | −61,47,323.57 |
| 2026 Q3 | 650 | 58,86,798.00 | 1,08,26,968.51 | −49,40,170.51 |
| 2026 Q4 | 1 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| **Total** | **1,848** | **2,20,03,143.00** | **3,30,92,036.08** | **−1,10,88,893.08** |

Income ties to the P&L exactly. **The expense does not, by ₹1,399.00** — and the
screen says so rather than leaving two figures to disagree in silence. That is
the journal of 9 March 2026, which falls before the financial year the P&L is
bounded to: the same ₹1,399 of [defect 162] and [defect 168], now visible from a
third angle. The quarters holding one voucher are labelled *"the edge of what was
captured"*, because a quarter with a single entry reads as a quiet trading period
and is not one.

### Raw Stock Tally — `raw_stock_tally.php`

One of the six screens the database's own menu listed and the capture missed
([defect 175]). It groups the loose metal by purity and shows **weight only** —
the Raw Stock screen values the holding; a person walking round with a sheet is
weighing metal and has no use for a rupee figure while doing it.

**It encodes [defect 78]'s correction.** Gold and silver are totalled separately
and never added:

	Gold 12,304.524 g, silver 15,022.085 g

with the **995 COIN of 524.720 g on the gold side** — the single row that entry
had counted as silver, worth ₹81,23,715.04 rather than ₹1,33,016.52. The summary
says why the two are kept apart, so the next reader does not add them.

### The i18n guard caught what I did not run

Registering the tally under a new sub-group produced a **500 on the screen**:

	panic: i18n missing translation: MCJMenu.Group.reports__manual-stock-tally

`TestNavigation_EveryMenuTitleHasATranslation` catches exactly this — and it
passed for the two screens before it, because **I ran it then and not after this
one**. The guard was right; the process was wrong. Its own comment warns that a
missing key "does not fail where it is introduced" and surfaces in whichever test
renders the menu first, which is precisely how it behaved: silent at build,
silent in the report tests, a panic on the page.

Two keys added. Coverage **121 of 193**, full suite green.

## 198. Two stock-tally screens, and the shelf two months ago — LOW

### Subgroup Stock, Back Dated — `back_date_subgroup_stock.php`

A tally taken today answers *what is here*. This answers *what was here on the
day we counted*, which is the question anybody reconciling a physical count a
week later actually has.

There is no stored snapshot, so the shelf is rolled back from two facts: the tag
existed by that date, and its **last** stock movement on or before it was not a
sale. Taking the last rather than the first matters — a piece sold in April and
brought back in May is on the shelf on 30 June, and reading the sale alone loses
it.

As at **30 June 2026**: 11 subgroups, **2,486 tags, ₹13,57,58,680.29**. Against
today's 2,575 tags and ₹14,23,61,188.20, the shelf has since taken on 89 tags and
₹66,02,507.91.

### Untagged Item Stock — `untag_item_stock.php`

The same loose metal the Raw Stock Tally shows, read the other way. The tally
groups by purity because that is how it is weighed; this groups by item because
that is how it is asked for — somebody wants to know how much GOLD ORNAMENTS is
loose, not how much 18kt.

| Item | Purities | Lines | Net wt |
|---|---|---|---|
| SILVER ORNAMENT | SLV | 2 | 12,970.041 |
| GOLD ORNAMENTS | 14, 18, 22, 9 | 4 | 11,695.314 |
| SILVER COIN | SLV | 1 | 2,052.044 |
| COIN | 22, 995 | 2 | 609.210 |
| SILVER ARTICLE | ARTIC(PCS) | 1 | 0.000 |

**It does not total the weight column**, and says why: the five items mix gold
and silver, and a single figure across both is neither. That is [defect 78]'s
correction built into a screen rather than written beside it.

### The i18n guard, run this time

Both registrations needed a locale key and the guard named each before the screen
was opened — `MCJMenu.Item.subgroup-stock-tally-back-date` for the first, none
for the second. Run after every registration now, which is what [defect 197]
should have taught the first time.

Coverage **123 of 193**.

## 199. Ratio Analysis, and a first draft that flattered the shop threefold — MEDIUM

`ratio_analysis.php`, under MIS REPORTS. Built, and the building found the
mistake.

### What the books can support

| Ratio | Value | From | Over |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quick ratio | **0.07** | 78,97,531.19 | 11,16,54,264.39 |
| Cash to overdraft | **0.01** | 5,00,978.19 | 4,92,97,479.87 |
| Receivable to payable | **0.12** | 73,96,553.00 | 6,23,56,784.52 |
| Borrowing to stock | **0.44** | 6,19,93,420.47 | 14,23,61,188.20 |

Three more are **refused by name** rather than printed — gross margin, stock
turnover, return on stock. Every one needs closing stock inside the ledgers and
[blocker B19] is exactly that it is not there. A margin computed without it is
arithmetic on an absence, and the screen says so where the number would have been.

### The first draft counted goods as cash

It read "money owed to the shop" as every debit balance across Customer, Dealer
and Other Debtor — **₹9,54,35,175.00**, and the ratios that followed:

| | First draft | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| Quick ratio | 0.86 | **0.07** |
| Receivable to payable | 1.53 | **0.12** |

**Twelve times out on the second.** The ₹8.8 crore difference is
[defect 145]'s suppliers sitting in debit — SHREE SAROJ JEWELSS and others, where
the shop has **paid ahead or is owed goods**. That is a real asset and it is not
cash, and a quick ratio exists precisely to exclude things that are not.

The corrected receivable, **₹73,96,553.00**, is [defect 190]'s customer figure to
the rupee.

### Why it matters more than a wrong number usually does

A quick ratio of 0.86 reads as a shop that is tight but solvent. **0.07 reads as
a shop living on its overdraft**, which — with ₹5,00,978.19 of cash against
₹4,92,97,479.87 owed to Union Bank — is what the books actually show. The first
draft would not have looked wrong to anyone; it would have looked reassuring.

Both the excluded figure and the reason are now stated on the screen, so nobody
re-adds it thinking it was an oversight.

## 200. Gross Profit, which refuses to state one — and three screens that now tie to the paisa — MEDIUM

`gross_profit_report.php`, under DSS REPORT. The screen a shop opens expecting a
margin, and the one this data cannot give.

Gross profit is sales less cost of goods sold, and cost of goods sold is opening
stock **plus** purchases **less** closing stock. [Blocker B19] is exactly that no
account carries stock, so the term that turns purchases into cost is absent. The
screen sets the calculation out and marks the missing line rather than printing a
figure with a hole in it:

| Line | Amount |
|---|---|
| Sales | 2,40,66,454.00 |
| Less returns | 20,63,311.00 |
| **Net sales** | **2,20,03,143.00** |
| Purchases | 2,34,35,413.81 |
| Old gold bought in | 50,71,370.00 |
| **Bought in total** | **2,85,06,783.81** |
| Opening stock | **NOT KNOWN** — blocker B19 |
| Closing stock | 14,23,61,188.20 — the stock module's, never in the books |
| **Gross profit** | **not computable** |
| What is knowable | −65,03,637.43 |

The last line is labelled as **not a margin**: it ignores stock at both ends, so a
month of heavy buying reads as a loss and a month of selling old stock reads as a
profit. It is a figure to carry to an accountant **with** the opening stock, not
instead of it.

### Three screens now agree to the paisa

| Figure | This screen | Agrees with |
|---|---|---|
| Sales | 2,40,66,454.00 | GSTR-1 HSN summary's taxable total |
| Net sales | 2,20,03,143.00 | the P&L's income |
| Bought in total | 2,85,06,783.81 | the purchase register's goods column |

### The first draft was 25.62 adrift, and the reason is worth keeping

It summed every credit on a SALE-GST voucher as sales. A sale voucher also
carries a **ROUNDED OFF** line — classified as an *expense* — and its 26.44 of
credits went into the sales figure, leaving net sales 25.62 away from the P&L.

Small, and it would have been easy to wave through as rounding. It was not
rounding: it was **rounding counted as revenue**. Each figure is now taken from
its own side of the ledger rather than from the voucher type alone, and the query
says why.

## 201. Every screen with data behind it is now built — the remaining 67 are classified, one by one

The last of the buildable screens, and the survey that says so.

### Packet Wise Stock Summary — `packet_wise_stock_summary_report.php`

Diamond stock arranged by the packet it came out of. **10 packets in use of the
205 in the master**, holding **107 stones across 107 tags, ₹13,80,534.60** — the
largest being DSOLMIX at ₹6,67,550.00 for a single 1.690 ct stone, and DMIX at
₹6,15,580.00 spread across 96 tags.

The 195 unused packets are not a fault: a packet master catalogues the grades a
shop buys, not the stones it holds. The screen says so rather than leaving a
reader to wonder where the rest went.

### The 67 that remain, and why none can be built

Each was checked against the shop's own tables:

| Why | Screens | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Karigar and manufacturing | **34** | every issue and receive table empty; no karigar master |
| Approval, merge, split, discount | **12** | `sales_vou_appr`, `purchase_approval` ×4, `barcode_merge`, `barcode_split`, `discount_master` — **0 rows each** |
| No source table at all | **10** | `raw_opening_stock`, `studded_opening_stock`, `set_rate_sub_item`, `tds_on_job_charge`, `broken_stone`, `work_order` |
| Sale and purchase variants | **6** | only `local` (221) and `central` (3) bill types; no PURC-CO or PURC-SC voucher ever raised |

and are not: `ledger_setting.php` has no settings columns beyond the master
fields the Ledger Master screen already shows, and `sales_voucher_estimate.php`
is an entry screen for estimates the Estimates report already covers.

### Why this survey is by row count, not by table name

The first version of this classification would have been by name, and it would
have been wrong in one place that matters: `karigar_gold_stock` sounds like the
emptiest table in the manufacturing set and holds **₹1.35 crore of gold issued to
a named goldsmith** ([defect 164]). Counting rows rather than reading names is
the only reason that was found.

**Five areas are complete** — ACCOUNTS 13/13, DSS 3/3, GST 7/7, HR 9/9, MIS 6/6.

`docs/STATUS.md` now carries this classification in place of the older estimate
of "about half of what is left should not be built", which was written when the
figure was 106 and is now measured rather than estimated.

## 202. The screen classification, verified individually — and a scare from a truncated shell pipe — LOW

[Defect 201] classified the 67 unbuilt screens into five buckets by pattern. Two
of those buckets were matched by regex rather than checked one at a time, so
they were checked.

### The sale and purchase variants have no discriminator

Six screens — Credit Sale, Estimate Sale, Exhibition Sale, Export Sale, Repair
Sale, and the CO and SC purchase vouchers — would each need a way to tell one
kind of bill from another. There is none:

| | |
|---|---|
| `sales_vou.sale_type` distinct values | **1** — `SALE-GST` |
| `sales_vou.bill_type` | `local` 221, `central` 3 |
| Voucher types ever raised | 10, and **no PURC-CO or PURC-SC among them** |

Every captured sale is the same kind of sale. The existing sale screen already
handles the local/central split through its interstate flag, which is the only
distinction the data actually carries.

### The utility screens

Backup and Change Password are actions, not reports. `ledger_setting.php` was
checked against the table: `mcj_ledgers` carries no settings columns beyond the
master fields the Ledger Master screen already shows. The two SMS screens stay
shut under [blocker B15].

### Migration fidelity, confirmed in passing

Voucher types match the source **exactly**, all ten, count for count:

	PMNT 626 · JRNL 624 · RCPT 269 · SALE-GST 224 · CNTR 31
	PURC-OG 25 · PURC-GSC 24 · PURC-GCO 19 · PURC-RET 3 · SALE-RET 3

### The scare, and why it is worth writing down

A `SELECT DISTINCT v_typ` appeared to return **8** types where our data has 10,
which read as the migration having invented `PURC-GCO` and `PURC-RET` — 22
vouchers from nowhere. It had not. Three queries were piped through `head -14`
and the later rows of the first were cut off.

**The output was truncated, not the data.** That is [defect 189]'s error a third
time — reading a thing through something that is not the thing — and it is the
cheapest possible way to manufacture a serious-looking finding. Re-run as a
`GROUP BY` with no pipe, both sides agree exactly.

## 203. A tag that could not be priced fell off the bill and out of the door — HIGH (fixed)

Testing [defect 192]'s sale writer on a **multi-line** bill — it had only ever
been proven on a single line — found something the single-line test could not
have found.

Three tags were scanned. The bill saved **two**.

	scanned:  88106644  DIAMOND RING     18   1.460 g
	          90169090  DIAMOND NOSEPIN  14   0.792 g
	          77378547  SILVER LOCKET    SLV  9.568 g

	saved:    2 lines · 2 stock movements · 2 tags cleared
	shelf:    90169090 still showing as in stock

The nose pin is certified, and certification pricing is [blocker B9] — the step
is not in the captured data, so the screen is right to refuse to price it. The
refusal was correct, was recorded, and **was shown**: an amber panel above the
bill named the tag and the reason. That part worked exactly as designed.

What did not work is what happened next. `props.CanSave` was set to `true` the
moment a single line priced, and the save branch never looked at the refusals at
all. So the clerk sees the amber panel, presses Save, and gets a bill for two
pieces while three sit on the counter. The third goes into the customer's bag
unbilled and stays on the shelf in the system: **the shop loses the goods and
the stock report never notices.** The takings are short and nothing disagrees.

The sale template already carried a comment stating the opposite intent —

> a tag that cannot be priced must not quietly vanish from a sale somebody is
> about to make

— which was true of the pricing step and false of the saving step.

### The fix

Save is now blocked while any scanned tag is unpriced, both by hiding the button
and by refusing the POST, since a form can be replayed:

```go
props.CanSave = len(refusals) == 0
...
if len(refusals) > 0 {
    props.Errors = append(props.Errors,
        "This bill cannot be saved while a scanned tag is unpriced. "+
            "Remove those barcodes or bill them as untagged items.")
    c.render(w, r, props)
    return
}
```

The clerk clears it by taking the barcode out of the box or by billing that
piece as an untagged line — the screen already supports both, and an untagged
line is exactly how the shop bills the 72 of its 328 captured lines that carry
no barcode.

### The other three posting screens were checked, and are fine

| Screen | Gate |
|---|---|
| Sale | **was broken** — fixed above |
| Credit note | blocks on `problems` before `CanSave` |
| Old gold | blocks on `problems` before `CanSave` |
| Tagging | blocks on `problems` before `CanSave` |

Sale was the only one that let a refusal through, because it is the only one
that prices tags **individually** — the others refuse the whole document.

### Proven against the running app, then reversed

A mixed bill was posted to the running server:

	1 good tag + 1 certified tag, action=save
	  http 200 (not 303)
	  "cannot be saved while a scanned tag is unpriced"
	  save button present: 0
	  invoices: 225 → 225
	  good tag still in stock: t

Then a clean two-tag bill, to prove the normal path still saves:

	invoices  225 → 226      lines  330 → 332
	movements 9038 → 9040    stock  2573 → 2571
	sold stones 207 → 207    (both tags genuinely carry no stones)

Both test bills — the earlier three-tag one and this one — were then reversed in
full, and every count returned to baseline:

	invoices 224 · lines 328 · movements 9036 · sold stones 203 · in stock 2575
	shelf value ₹14,23,61,188.20

### The test, proven by breaking it

`TestSale_WillNotSaveWhileAScannedTagIsUnpriced` asserts no invoice is written
and the good tag stays on the shelf. The existing
`TestSale_ListsRefusedTagsRatherThanDroppingThem` only ever posted `action=price`
— which is why a screen with a test named *"rather than dropping them"* was
dropping them at save.

Reverting the guard fails the new test exactly as it should:

	sale_e2e_test.go:248: the bill did not say why it refused to save
	sale_e2e_test.go:260: 1 bill(s) were saved with a tag unpriced, want 0

### Worth noting

This is the second time a fix has been proven on the simplest possible case and
found wanting on the next one up. [Defect 192] was proven on a one-line sale;
[defect 199]'s ratio analysis was proven against a total that happened to agree.
**One line is not a multi-line test**, and a screen that handles items
individually needs a case where the items disagree with each other.

## 204. Old gold was priced off the customer's stamp, not off what the metal tested at — HIGH (fixed)

Applying [defect 203]'s lesson to the next posting screen — test it on more than
the simplest case — a three-lot old gold purchase went through cleanly and the
arithmetic was right. Then the record it wrote was compared against the shop's
own 25 lots, and the screen turned out to be buying gold by a method the shop
has never used.

### What the shop actually does

Every one of the 25 captured lots is booked against the scrap grades `OLDGOLD`
or `OLDSLV` — **not one names a karat** — and carries an assessed **tunch**:

	OLDGOLD  22 lots   tunch 63.1% – 92.0%
	OLDSLV    2 lots   tunch 50.0% – 66.0%
	(blank)   1 lot    tunch 71.0%

The tunch is the assessment of what the metal *is*, judged by the person holding
it. The spread — 63% to 92% — is the whole point: **the stamp on a customer's
ornament is not evidence.**

And the price is not computed at all. On all 25 lots:

	rate = round(amount / net_weight, 2)     25 of 25
	amount is a whole rupee                  25 of 25
	amount is a multiple of 100               9 of 25   (two of them exactly ₹6,00,000 and ₹10,00,000)
	rate is a whole rupee                     0 of 25

The price is **agreed across the counter** and typed in; the rate is worked back
from it so the lot can be checked later. It is the record of a negotiation, not
the output of a rate table.

### What our screen did instead

It offered the clerk a dropdown of **stamped** purities — 0, 9, 14, 18, 22, 95,
995, SLV, SLV999 — looked up that grade's buy-back rate, multiplied by weight,
and wrote **`tunch_percent = 0`**.

The scrap grades were in `mcj_purities` all along (`OLDGOLD`, `OLDSLV`,
`OLDPLT`), but `purityOptions` selected `DISTINCT purity_code FROM
mcj_metal_rates WHERE purchase_rate > 0` — and no rate feed carries a row for a
scrap grade, so the three codes the shop actually uses were the exact three the
dropdown filtered out.

### What it would have cost

Re-pricing the shop's own 25 lots the way our screen priced them — 22ct
buy-back for gold, SLV for silver:

| | |
|---|---|
| The shop paid | **₹50,71,370.00** |
| Our screen would have paid | **₹52,53,510.57** |
| Overpaid | **₹1,82,140.57** — 3.6% |

The 3.6% average is the wrong number to look at. The damage is per lot, and it
lands hardest exactly where the assessment matters most:

| Date | Grade | Tunch | Net | Shop paid | We would pay | Over |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 19 Jul 2026 | OLDSLV | 50.0% | 2.650 | 300.00 | 581.41 | **93.8%** |
| 10 Apr 2026 | OLDSLV | 66.0% | 144.060 | 23,326.00 | 35,582.82 | **52.5%** |
| 8 May 2026 | OLDGOLD | 63.1% | 1.380 | 12,400.00 | 18,875.64 | **52.2%** |
| 14 Apr 2026 | OLDGOLD | 65.0% | 6.790 | 64,300.00 | 94,251.99 | **46.6%** |
| 31 May 2026 | OLDGOLD | 71.0% | 0.570 | 5,936.00 | 8,059.80 | 35.8% |

A low-tunch lot is precisely the one a customer presents as 22ct. **The screen
was at its most wrong exactly when the assessment was most needed.**

The total was checked against a second source: the sum of `PURC-OG` voucher
credits is **₹50,71,370.00**, agreeing with the line amounts to the paisa.

### Also lost: the deduction

The writer inserted `VALUES (…,$7,$7,0,…)` — the net weight into **both** the
gross and net columns. A clerk who deducted 1.000 g from a 10.000 g lot got a
record saying the customer handed over 9.000 g and nothing was deducted. The
schema has separate columns; the writer collapsed them. Gross and net do happen
to be equal on all 25 captured lots, which is what the code's comment relied on
— but the screen offers a deduction field, and anything typed into it vanished.

### The fix

The screen now works the way the counter does:

| Column | |
|---|---|
| Purity | the scrap grades — `OLDGOLD`, `OLDSLV`, `OLDPLT` |
| Gross wt / Less / Net wt | both weights now recorded as themselves |
| **Tunch %** | required, 0 < t ≤ 100 — the assessment behind the price |
| **Amount agreed** | typed, the negotiated price |
| Rate | derived, `amount ÷ net`, shown back as the record |

A **guide** sits under the amount — the lot valued at its tunch against the
day's pure rate (`995` for gold, `SLV` for silver) — as a sanity check on a
figure typed in a hurry. It never replaces the typed amount. Platinum has no
rate feed, so a platinum lot simply gets no guide.

### Proven by reproducing a real lot

The shop's lot **OGP/2627/00005** was re-entered through the rebuilt screen:

	          bill_no      bought_on   purity   gross   net    tunch   rate     amount
	shop's    OGP/…/00005  2026-04-14  OLDGOLD  6.790   6.790  65.000  9469.81  64300.00
	ours      OGP/…/00026  2026-04-14  OLDGOLD  6.790   6.790  65.000  9469.81  64300.00

Identical in every column. The old screen would have paid **₹94,251.99** for
that same metal. The test lot was then reversed — 25 lots, 25 vouchers,
₹50,71,370.00.

### The tests

`TestOldGold_PricesAtTheBuyBackRate` and `TestOldGold_RefusesAGradeItDoesNotBuyBack`
were **testing the defect**: they asserted that a lot stamped 22 gets the 22ct
buy-back rate, which is the behaviour that overpays. They are replaced by tests
of what the shop does:

- `TestOldGold_TakesTheAgreedAmountAndWorksTheRateBack`
- `TestOldGold_DoesNotOfferStampedPurities` — asserts no `value="22"` on the page
- `TestOldGold_RequiresTheTunch` — rejects blank, 0, negative and >100
- `TestOldGold_RequiresTheAmount`
- `TestOldGold_ShowsAGuideWithoutOverridingTheAgreedPrice`
- `TestOldGold_RecordsGrossAndNetSeparately` — catches the `$7,$7` collapse
- `TestOldGold_WorksTheRateBackFromNetNotGross`

### Worth noting

[Defect 203] was found by testing a screen on more than one line. This one was
found by going one step further: checking what the screen *wrote* against what
the shop's own records look like. The arithmetic was correct throughout — every
figure the old screen produced was internally consistent. **It was answering the
wrong question, and no amount of testing its own logic would have said so.**

A passing test suite is not evidence that a screen does the shop's job. Two of
the tests here asserted the defect and passed for it.

## 205. The next gold-coin purchase would have failed outright — HIGH (fixed)

Same method as [defect 204], applied to the purchase side: compare what the
screen writes against what the shop's own records look like.

The shop runs **two purchase bill series**, and its 43 captured bills split
between them without a single exception:

	GDP/…   24 bills   PURC-GSC   ₹1,80,38,003.00   stock purchases
	GCP/…   19 bills   PURC-GCO     ₹59,18,795.00   bought against an order

Both series number from 1, and on all 43 the number in the bill is the
voucher's own — which `nextNumber` also allocates **per type per year**.

`writePurchaseInvoice` hard-coded the prefix:

```go
// GDP/2627/00025 -- the format on the shop's own 43 captured bills.
billNo := fmt.Sprintf("GDP/%02d%02d/%05d", …, v.Number)
```

So every gold-coin purchase was numbered into the **GDP** series. GDP had
reached 24; GCO stood at 19. The next gold-coin purchase would take voucher
number **20** and build `GDP/2627/00020` — a bill number already held by a real
**₹9,20,000.00** purchase from ANAND SILVER on 1 July 2026.

Posted against the running app, that is exactly what happened:

	POST /mcj/trade/purchase-order   →   http 500
	purchase invoices 43 → 43 · PURC-GCO vouchers 19 → 19

**The shop could not have recorded its next gold-coin purchase at all.** The
unique index added for [defect 195] is what turned a silent overwrite into a
loud failure, which is the outcome it was there for.

### Two more columns the writer never filled

`due_on` was never written, though **all 43** captured bills carry one, so every
new purchase would have been invisible to any ageing report. It is now set to
the bill date, which matches 32 of the 43; the remaining 11 scatter from five
days before the bill to one after, and nothing in the captured data says whether
the shop wants a credit period entered per bill.

`is_b2b` stays `false`. It is true on 7 captured bills — D.N. JEWELS, ZEST
CORPORATION, ZM LIFESTYLE, ANJALI LABTECH, S K CHAINS, ANUPAM TRADERS — every
one a registered dealer. There is nothing to derive it from: **no ledger in the
database carries a GSTIN**, 0 of 785 ([defect 150]).

### Fixed and proven

	GCP/2627/00020   2026-08-23   due 2026-08-23   ₹50,000.00

The correct series, continuing from GCP/2627/00019, with a due date. Reversed
after the test — 43 bills, 24 GDP and 19 GCP, ₹2,39,56,798.00.

Checked in passing, and it holds without exception: **all 24 GDP bills carry
tax, all 19 GCP bills carry none.** The tax-free flag on Purchase Against an
Order is right.

`TestTrade_EachPurchaseKindKeepsItsOwnBillSeries` posts one of each and asserts
the prefixes and the due date.

## 206. A save that failed told the wrapper it had succeeded — HIGH (fixed)

Chasing [defect 205] surfaced something worse than the bug being chased.

The failing purchase returned this, as the entire page:

	ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of
	transaction block (SQLSTATE 25P02)

That is not the reason. The reason — a duplicate bill number — had been found,
wrapped in a sentence a clerk could read, and then thrown away.

### How the reason was lost

1. `writePurchaseInvoice` hit the unique index. The Postgres transaction is now aborted.
2. `save` returned the error; `post` put `"This credit note could not be saved: …"` into `props.Errors`.
3. `render` then called `billableParties(ctx)` to fill the customer dropdown — **a query on the aborted transaction**.
4. That query failed with `25P02`, and `render` answered it with `http.Error(w, err.Error(), 500)` — replacing the whole page, and the real reason with it.

The explanatory path was unreachable in precisely the case it existed for.

### The worse half

`atomic` commits on any 2xx and rolls back from 400 up. The save-failure path
rendered the page at **200**.

So a screen whose save had failed was telling the wrapper the request had
succeeded, and **whatever the failed save had already written was committed.**

Here the damage was contained by luck: the failure had aborted the Postgres
transaction, and Postgres turns `COMMIT` on an aborted transaction into
`ROLLBACK`. A failure that does *not* abort the transaction — a lookup returning
no rows, an error raised between two writes — has no such protection. It would
commit a purchase voucher with no bill behind it, or a sale voucher with no
invoice: exactly the split [blocker B26] was closed to prevent.

All four posting families shared it — sale, old gold, trade, and the general
voucher form.

### The fix

A new `failedSaveStatus` (500) is returned by every save-failure render, so
`atomic` rolls back. On that path the lookups that dress the page are allowed to
come back empty rather than replace the page and the reason:

```go
parties, err := billableParties(ctx)
if err != nil && !tolerant {          // tolerant on the failure path only
    http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusInternalServerError)
    return
}
```

Two message defects were fixed alongside it. `TradeController` serves four
screens and told all of them they were a credit note, and the raw SQLSTATE went
straight to the clerk. Both now read:

	before   ERROR: current transaction is aborted … (SQLSTATE 25P02)
	after    This purchase against an order could not be saved: that number
	         is already taken for this year. Try saving again.

`humanise` was already doing this job on the voucher form; it now serves all
four, with the sentence prefix moved to the caller so each screen names itself.

### Proven

Against the running app, with the next bill number deliberately occupied:

	http 500 · reason on the page · PURC-GCO vouchers 19 → 19

Then with the blocker removed, the same request saved normally at 303.

`TestTrade_AFailedSaveDoesNotReportSuccess` pins the status and asserts the
reason is not replaced by a transaction message;
`TestTrade_AFailureNamesTheScreenItHappenedOn` pins the wording and that no raw
SQLSTATE reaches the clerk. Reverting either fix fails them.

`TestAtomic_ClassifiesTheHandlersAnswer` already pinned the other half of the
chain — 2xx commits, 400 and up rolls back. What was missing was anything
asserting which side of that line a failed save lands on.

### Worth noting

The end-to-end rollback cannot be asserted from the integration harness: it runs
the request inside the test's own transaction, so a poisoning failure takes the
test's own queries down with it. That is why the "nothing was committed" half
was proven against the running app instead, and the test pins the status. A
test that cannot observe the thing it claims to prove is [defect 189]'s error in
another costume — and the way out was to check the claim somewhere it *is*
observable, not to weaken the claim until the harness agreed with it.

## 207. The salesperson master was loaded with its two columns the wrong way round — MEDIUM (fixed)

Continuing the column-by-column comparison against the shop's own records, this
time on the 224 captured sales bills.

`salesperson` is filled on **all 224**. Following it into the master found this:

	mcj_salespeople.name        S039
	mcj_salespeople.short_code  NARENDER SEVADA

All 24 rows the same way round: `name` matches `^S[0-9]+$`, and `short_code`
holds a person. So the codelist screen headed **Name** listed staff codes, and
the one headed **Short code** listed people.

What makes this worth writing down is that it was known. Both the migration and
the codelist entry carry the same warning:

> The legacy columns are SWAPPED relative to their names: s_name holds the code
> (S004) and s_code holds the person's name, in all 24 rows. **The seed reads
> them the right way round.**

The seed did not. `tools/legacy/load_codelists.sh` line 44 read:

	mcj_salespeople|salesperson_master|s_name|s_code

— straight across, preserving the legacy swap. **The comment describing the
correction and the code performing it disagreed, and the comment was believed.**

Fixed in the loader, and corrected in place by migration `mcj-1787409000`, which
is conditional on the name still looking like a code so it is idempotent and
harmless against a fresh load. All 24 person names are distinct and none is
blank, so the swap is safe. One row reads `DELETE` (S061) — a tombstone left in
the legacy master.

## 208. A bill could not say who made the sale — MEDIUM (fixed)

Every one of the 224 captured bills names a salesperson. **The sale screen had
no such field, and `writeSaleDetail` never wrote one**, so sales attribution
stopped dead at migration.

131 of the 224 name a real person; the other 93 carry `0`, which is no
salesperson at all — there is no row with that id in the master. So it is
optional, and stays optional: making it required would refuse a sale the shop
has always allowed.

### The column held something no new bill could use

`mcj_sales_invoices.salesperson` holds the **legacy row id** as text — `"3"`,
`"7"`, `"45"` — which resolves only by joining `mcj_salespeople.legacy_id`. A
salesperson hired tomorrow has no legacy id, so a new bill had nothing valid to
put in that column at all.

A real reference was added beside it rather than rewriting the shop's own
records:

	ALTER TABLE mcj_sales_invoices ADD COLUMN salesperson_id uuid
	    REFERENCES mcj_salespeople (id) ON DELETE SET NULL;

Backfilled from `legacy_id`: **131 linked, 93 null, and 0 named-but-unlinked** —
every bill that named somebody now resolves. The captured text column is left
exactly as it was. Rewriting 224 historical rows to tidy a vocabulary is not a
trade worth making; the same reasoning as [defect 204], reached the other way.

### Proven

A bill posted through the rebuilt screen:

	bill_no          sold_by             code   legacy_col
	GST/2627/00225   SHREE CHAND SHARMA  S004   (blank)

The dropdown lists people **by name** — which it could only do after
[defect 207] was fixed. Reversed after the test; 224 bills, 131 attributed.

`TestSale_RecordsWhoMadeTheSale`, `TestSale_SalespersonIsOptional` and
`TestSale_RefusesAnUnknownSalesperson` cover it.

### Two columns still not written, and why

`party_mobile` is filled on 196 of the 224. Nothing in the sale screen collects
it and the ledgers cannot supply it — **0 of 785 carry a phone number**
([defect 150]).

`is_b2b` is true on 20 of the 224. Same obstacle as on the purchase side
([defect 205]): no ledger carries a GSTIN, so there is nothing to derive it
from.

`certification` is non-zero on **41 of the 224** — 18% of the shop's bills. Those
cannot be raised at all until [blocker B9] is answered, which is the same wall
[defect 203] ran into from the other direction.

## 209. The migration chain could not be rolled back — MEDIUM (fixed)

Found by accident while checking that [defect 208]'s migration reversed cleanly.
It did. The chain underneath it did not:

	Error: failed to rollback migrations:
	ERROR: value too long for type character varying(10) (SQLSTATE 22001)
	handling mcj-1787403000.sql

`mcj-1787403000` widens `mcj_ledger_groups.legacy_level` from varchar(10) to
varchar(24), because the third level of the group hierarchy is called
**`sub-subgroup`** — twelve characters — and it sits on **34 of the 96 groups**.

Its Down narrowed the column straight back:

	ALTER TABLE mcj_ledger_groups ALTER COLUMN legacy_level TYPE varchar(10);

which **fails every time the Up has actually been useful.** The migration exists
precisely to hold values longer than 10 characters, so undoing it always trips
over them.

### Why that is worse than a failed command

A rollback runs migration by migration. This one failed *part way through*: five
later migrations had already been undone when it stopped, leaving the schema
half-rolled-back. Only running `up` again recovered it — which it did, cleanly,
with no data lost (checked against every baseline, including the ₹14,23,61,188.20
shelf).

Discovering this during an actual emergency rollback is the bad version.

### The fix

The Down now narrows the column only when it can do so honestly, and otherwise
leaves it wide — which is harmless to the code that ran against the narrow one:

```sql
DO $$
BEGIN
    IF NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM mcj_ledger_groups WHERE length(legacy_level) > 10
    ) THEN
        ALTER TABLE mcj_ledger_groups ALTER COLUMN legacy_level TYPE varchar(10);
    END IF;
END $$;
```

Every Down section across all migrations was scanned for the same shape — a
narrowing `ALTER COLUMN … TYPE`. This was the only one.

### Proven on a scratch database, not this one

A full `migrate down` against the live database would drop the migrated tables
and everything in them, so the fix was verified on a throwaway copy: 121
migrations up, a `sub-subgroup` row seeded to trigger the overflow, then down.

The rollback now runs **past every mcj migration** — 0 mcj tables left — and
stops much later, in an IOTA SDK core migration:

	ERROR: role "bichat_agent_role" cannot be dropped because some objects
	depend on it (SQLSTATE 2BP01) handling changes-1769853356.sql

That one is the SDK's, not ours. Recorded here because a full rollback still
cannot complete, and the reason is now somebody else's to fix.

### Worth noting

Three defects this round came from the same move: read what the shop's own rows
contain, then check the code actually does that. [Defect 207] is the sharpest
case — **a comment stated the correction, the code never made it, and the
comment was trusted for both.** A comment is a claim about the code, not
evidence about it.

## 210. Every bill line sold exactly one piece, whatever the tag said — MEDIUM (fixed)

The header of a sales bill was checked in [defect 208]. This is its 328 lines.

Four columns disagreed with the shop's own records, and three of them were being
written as constants:

| Column | Captured on 328 lines | What we wrote |
|---|---|---|
| `pieces` | 221 sell one, **78 sell more** (one sells 40), 29 sell none | **hard-coded `1`** |
| `gross_weight` | filled on 316; **differs from net on 141** | **`0`** |
| `fine_weight` | filled on **316 of 328** | **`0`** |
| `wastage_pct` | filled on 14 | `0` — correctly, see below |

### pieces

**A tag is one label, not one piece.** A pair of tops is one barcode and two
