pieces. On the shop's shelf, **766 of the 2,575 tags carry more than one** — 30%
of everything on display — and every one of them would have been billed as a
single piece.

Nothing about the money is wrong: the tag's price is the tag's price. What is
wrong is the count, so any quantity a report states — pieces sold, pieces on
hand, pieces per bill — is understated on nearly a third of the stock.

### gross and fine weight

Gross is the metal plus whatever is set into it, and it differs from the net on
141 of the 328 captured lines. A line carrying only the net loses the weight the
customer actually handled.

Fine weight is the pure metal in the line, and the rule turned out to be exact
once the outliers were separated out:

	22ct lines   92.00% of net    (21 at 92.00, 14 at 92.01, 11 at 91.99 — 3dp rounding)
	18ct         75.00%
	14ct         58.33%
	SLV          92.50%

— which is `mcj_purities.fineness` to the digit. The lines that do not fit are
the 14 carrying a **wastage** percentage, which this screen has no field for.
It does not invent one: `wastage_pct` stays 0, and that is the one constant
among the four that is right.

An earlier reading put the ratio at ~93% for 22ct and looked like a systematic
1% drift. It was not systematic — it was **fourteen wastage lines pulling an
average**. Grouping by the ratio rather than averaging it showed the rule is
exact.

### And the untagged rows were already asking

72 of the 328 captured lines carry no barcode, and the screen's untagged row
already collects **`u_pieces_`** and **`u_gross_`** from the clerk. Both were
being dropped between the row and the bill: `untaggedLine` carried them, and the
priced line copied only the description, purity and net weight. **The screen
asked for two numbers and then threw them away.**

### Proven

A two-line bill of multi-piece, stone-set tags, posted against the running app:

	barcode    description          purity  pieces  gross   net     fine
	32348536   DIAMOND PENDANT SET  18      3       7.440   6.104   4.578
	33969968   SILVER SET           SLV     3      20.060  18.786  17.377

Exact on all six figures against the tags. Reversed after the test — 224 bills,
328 lines, 9,036 movements, shelf ₹14,23,61,188.20.

## 211. A piece left the shelf with no record of who took it — LOW (fixed)

The same comparison, one table over. `mcj_stock_movements.done_by` is filled on
**322 of the shop's 324 captured sale movements** — BAPI, ADMIN,
RAJENDRA KICHER, PRIYANKA — and our writer left it blank on every one.

A stock trail that cannot say who moved a piece is most of the way to no trail
at all. It is now the logged-in user, which is a **different question** from
[defect 208]'s salesperson: one is who operated the till, the other is who made
the sale, and the shop's own data records both, in different tables.

It fails soft — an empty string rather than an error — because a bill must not
be refused over an audit column.

### Checked and deliberately left as it is

Our sale movement also writes `net_weight` and `purity`, which the shop's own
324 sale movements leave blank (0 of 324 carry either). That is ours being
fuller than the original rather than different from it, and the weight is the
same piece's weight either way, so it stays.

### The tests

`TestSale_RecordsThePieceCountGrossWeightAndFineWeight`,
`TestSale_UntaggedLineKeepsWhatTheClerkTyped` and
`TestSale_TheStockMovementNamesWhoDidIt`. Breaking each fix in turn fails them
with exactly the figures above — 1 piece where 2 was wanted, 0.000 fine where
7.360 was wanted, and a movement naming nobody.

### Worth noting

Six defects have now come out of one habit: **open the shop's own rows and count
what is in each column, then check the code puts that there.** Not one of these
would fail a test written against the code's own logic — the arithmetic was
right every time. `pieces = 1` is a perfectly correct statement about a bill for
one piece; it just was not a statement about this shop.

## 212. A tag was priced on one day and dated on another — MEDIUM (fixed)

The tagging screen is where every stock item comes from, so it was compared
against the 2,816 tags the shop already has.

The screen asks **"Tagged on"**. That date is parsed, used to pick the metal
rate — deliberately, because a tag's stored price is meant to age ([defect 35])
— and then discarded. The row was written with `created_date = now()`.

So a piece tagged as at 2 June was **priced at 2 June's rate and stamped with
whatever day it was entered**. The tag disagrees with itself, and the
back-dated stock tally built in [defect 198] reads the stamp, so the piece was
priced into one month and counted into another.

	tagged on   2026-06-02   →  22ct rate 14,775.00   (the June rate, correctly)
	stamped     2026-08-23                            (today, incorrectly)

Now both are the form's date:

	barcode    created_date  last_received_date  retail_code  pieces  rate
	ZZTEST01   2026-06-02    2026-06-02          R001         2       14775.00

`last_received_date` was never written either, though it is filled on **2,810 of
2,816** tags. For a tag being created it is the same day — it has just been
received — and it equals `created_date` on 2,688 of the 2,816, differing only
where a piece went out and came back. `retail_code` was blank where the shop
fills `R001` on 2,808 of 2,816.

`TestTag_IsDatedTheDayItWasTaggedNotToday` and `TestTag_CarriesTheRetailCode`.
Reverting the fix fails the first with, precisely, *"the tag is dated 2026-08-23,
want the 2026-04-10 on the form"*.

### What a new tag still does not carry

Recorded rather than quietly left. Fill rates are across all 2,816 captured tags:

| Column | Filled | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `voucher_no` | **2,797** | the stock-inward voucher the piece arrived on — a new tag has no link back to how it entered |
| `lot_no` | **2,059** | free text, and untidy: `UTENSILS` and `UTENSIL` both appear |
| `category_id` | **1,629** | the design category |
| `has_mrp` | 978 | |
| `certificate_no` | 678 | tied to [blocker B9] |
| `remarks1/2` | 452 | |
| `hallmarked` | 432 | see [defect 50] — 739 gold pieces carry no hallmark record |
| `ref_no` | 260 | |
| `design_code` | 109 | |
| `size` | 99 | |
| `wastage_percent` | 26 | |

Each needs a field on the screen, and `voucher_no` needs a stock-inward concept
that does not exist yet. None of them is money.

## 213. A verified non-defect: `making_sales` is not a second price — LOW

Worth writing down because the column names invite exactly the wrong conclusion,
and I nearly drew it.

`mcj_stock_items` carries both `making_value` and `making_sales`, and they
disagree on **987 of the 2,575 tags on the shelf** — 38%. The sale prices from
`making_value`. Read as *cost* against *selling* making, that is a screen
billing customers at cost on more than a third of the shelf.

It is not. Grouping by `making_type` settles it:

	making_type    tags   sales<>value
	val            1197   0
	per_gm_nw       599   597
	per_pcs         393   4
	per_gld_val     384   384

They differ **only where the making is a rate rather than an amount.**
`making_value` is the rate per unit; `making_sales` is that rate already
multiplied out:

	PLATINUM LOCKET   1.976 g   value 2,000.00/g  →  sales 3,952.00
	GOLD CHAIN       11.960 g   value   720.00/g  →  sales 8,611.20
	SILVER DIPAK     30.110 g   value    15.00/g  →  sales   451.65

Exact in every case, which is why they coincide on `val` tags — there the rate
*is* the amount.

Our pricing engine takes the rate and multiplies. Confirmed against the running
app rather than argued: barcode `43221199` billed making of **8,611.20**, to the
paisa the same as the tag's own `making_sales`.

Two columns disagreeing on 38% of the shelf is exactly the shape of a serious
money defect, and the difference between finding one and inventing one was
grouping by a third column before believing the first two.

## 214. 27% of the shop's vouchers could not be edited at all — HIGH (fixed)

The voucher screens carry the most traffic in the system — 626 payments, 624
journals, 269 receipts, 31 contras — so they got the same treatment: read what
the captured rows hold, then check the code.

`bank_cleared` is true on **497 vouchers**, and `bank_cleared_on` carries a date
on **466 of them**. The voucher form offered a **"Cleared by the bank"**
checkbox that set the flag. Nothing on that form has ever written the date.

Clearing is a **pair** of columns, and a migration says so out loud:

	CONSTRAINT mcj_vouchers_cleared_date_agrees CHECK (bank_cleared OR bank_cleared_on IS NULL)

> Uncleared items have no clearing date, and a dated item is a cleared one.
> Enforced rather than assumed, because a reconciliation that disagrees with
> itself about which items are outstanding is worse than no reconciliation.

A checkbox can only ever set one half of that pair. Open any reconciled voucher,
untick the box, save:

	POST /mcj/vouchers/payment/fd92bc70-…   →   http 500
	ERROR: new row for relation "mcj_vouchers" violates check constraint
	       "mcj_vouchers_cleared_date_agrees"

**497 of 1,848 vouchers — 27% — could not be corrected through the screen built
to correct them.** Not a typo, not a date, not a narration.

### The fix is about ownership, not about the constraint

There is already a reconcile screen, and it does this properly: it writes the
flag and the date together. The voucher form was a second, worse path to the
same fact.

So the repository no longer touches either column on an edit, and the checkbox
is gone. One screen owns one fact. A newly entered payment is no longer born
reconciled either — that happens when the bank says so, on the screen for it.

### The old comment was right about the danger and wrong about the cure

Both the props field and the test that guarded it carried the same reasoning:

> a screen that hid the box would silently clear the flag the next time somebody
> edited one of those vouchers

That was a real risk, and it came from the UPDATE setting `bank_cleared` from
whatever the form happened to post. Removing the box alone would indeed have
cleared the flag on every edit. **Removing it from the UPDATE removes the danger
at its source**, and then hiding the box is safe — which is what makes this a
fix rather than a trade.

`TestVoucher_ClearingCheckboxIsOnEveryKind` was asserting the defect, exactly as
two tests did in [defect 204]. It is replaced by
`TestVoucher_DoesNotOfferBankClearing` and
`TestVoucher_EditingAReconciledVoucherLeavesTheReconciliationAlone`, which
reconciles a voucher the way the reconcile screen does, edits it, and checks the
narration changed while the flag and the 2026-04-12 date did not. Restoring the
old UPDATE fails it.

### Proven against the shop's own data

Voucher **PMNT 5**, cleared on 2026-04-03, edited through the form:

	before   true / 2026-04-03 / Being Charges PORD Customer (UBINH26092190603)
	after    true / 2026-04-03 / edit test          ← http 303
	         number still 5, lines still 4

Narration restored afterwards; 1,848 vouchers, 497 cleared, 466 dated.

## 215. A failure named a voucher that does not exist — LOW (fixed)

Visible in [defect 214]'s error message, and worth its own number because it
would have misdirected anybody reading it:

	updating voucher 0/PMNT/2026-2027: ERROR: …

There is no voucher 0. `Key()` is the legacy natural key — number, type, year —
and a voucher arriving from an **edit** form carries its id but no number,
because the form has no reason to post one back. So every failure on an edit
named `0/TYPE/YEAR`.

The number itself was never at risk: the UPDATE does not set it, and PMNT 5 came
back as PMNT 5 with all four lines. But an error that misidentifies the record it
is about is worse than a vague one — it sends the reader to the wrong voucher, or
to look for one that was never there.

Save failures now use `Ref()`, which falls back to the type, year and id when
there is no number to give.

### Checked while in there, and left alone

`mcj_voucher_lines` has its own `cheque_number` and `cheque_date` columns. They
are empty on **all 3,935 captured lines** across all four kinds — the cheque
lives on the voucher header, where the shop fills it on 34 payments. Nothing
writes them and nothing should.

## 216. A returned tag's movement named no document and nobody — MEDIUM (fixed)

Same comparison on the return path.

Every one of the shop's **9,036** stock movements references a document number:

	SALE-GST   324   GST/2425/00119 … GST/2627/00220
	SALE-RET    18   SR/2425/00017  … SR/2627/00002
	PURC-IN      1   GDP/2627/00023

Not one carries anything else. Our credit note wrote:

	fmt.Sprintf("%s %d", kind.Type, v.Number)   →   "SALE-RET 4"

which would have been **the only reference in the whole register naming no
document**. A stock register is read by looking a document up; a row that names
none is a dead end. It also left `done_by` blank, where 17 of the 18 captured
returns say who handled it — [defect 211] on the other screen, in the same
place.

Both fixed. A return now writes `SR/2627/00004` and the logged-in user, proven
against the running app:

	barcode    movement   reference       done_by
	32348536   SALE-RET   SR/2627/00004   Admin User

### The number is the voucher's, deliberately

The shop's SR series does **not** track its SALE-RET voucher numbers. There are
three SALE-RET vouchers in 2026-27 and two SR references, and only the first
pair agree:

	voucher 1  2026-04-15      SR/2627/00001  2026-04-15   ✓
	voucher 2  2026-06-16      SR/2627/00002  2026-05-06   ✗
	voucher 3  2026-07-25      —

Continuing the SR sequence independently would mean maintaining a second
counter with nothing behind it. Tying the reference to the voucher at least
names a document that exists, and it is how every other number in this system is
built — GST, OGP, GDP, GCP all take the voucher's own number.

## 217. Sold stones recorded half their weight — LOW (fixed)

`mcj_sold_stones.actual_carats` is filled on **182 of the shop's 203** rows and
equals `carats` on **every one of them**. Ours wrote zero.

The shelf carries no separate figure to draw it from — `mcj_stock_stones` has no
`actual_carats` column — so it is now the same weight rather than a zero, which
is exactly what the 182 captured rows say it should be.

Proven on a stone-set tag: 5.670 and 1.010 carats, both columns agreeing.

### Checked and deliberately not "fixed"

**A returned sale keeps its sold-stone rows.** The obvious-looking bug is that
returning a tag leaves `mcj_sold_stones` claiming its stones were sold. The
shop's own data settles it: of its three returned invoices, `GST/2627/00004`
still carries **3** sold-stone rows and `GST/2627/00099` carries **1**. The rows
survive a return. Ours behave the same way, so nothing was changed.

**`mcj_sales_invoices.is_returned` is never set by the credit note.** It is true
on 3 of the 224 captured bills. It stays unset here because **a credit note does
not know which bill it reverses** — the screen takes barcodes, and its own note
says so: *"nothing links a tag back to the bill that sold it."* The shop had a
`sale_bill_link` table for this, and [defect 66] found 83 of its 135 links
pointing at a number that is also a real bill for a different sale. Marking the
wrong invoice returned would be worse than marking none.

**Something else the captured data shows and we do not do:** the returned tags
carry a suffix — `57808299R1`, `10864120R1`, `95831681R1`. The shop re-barcodes a
piece that comes back. Whether a returned piece should keep its number or take a
new one is a question for the shop, not something to infer; recorded rather than
guessed.

And a third: the two tags on the shop's returned invoices are still
`in_stock = false`. A sale marked returned did not put those pieces back on the
shelf. That may be a legacy inconsistency or it may mean those returns were
refunds without goods — it is not enough to act on, and it is listed here so it
is not rediscovered as new.

## 218. The payroll screen showed a Days column of zeros, and totalled them — LOW (fixed)

A different sweep this round: instead of auditing what the screens write, look
for columns that are **empty in every row**, then check which reports read them.
39 such columns exist across the mcj tables.

`mcj_salary_sheets.days_worked` is zero on all **246** rows, and the Staff
Salary Sheet displayed it as a **numeric** column — so it also totalled, and the
footer read **0 days** across the whole payroll. Beside a Paid column of real
money, that reads as people being paid for no work.

Nothing in this system writes a salary sheet — only the legacy loader — so the
column could never have been anything but zero.

### The loader was right; the report was wrong

The legacy table has **four** day columns, and the loader's own comment already
had this settled:

	no_of_days        0 on all 246
	extra_days        0 on all 246
	total_extra_days  0 on all 246
	total_days        136 rows of 31, 95 of 30, 15 of 28

`total_days` is the **length of the month**, not days worked. Using it would
assert everyone worked every day including the four months nobody was paid, so
the loader writes zero and says why ([defect 153]). That decision is right.

What was wrong was showing the result. **An empty column is an honest answer;
an empty column that totals is a claim.** The column is gone and the report's
comment now carries the reasoning.

### tools/check_empty_columns.py

The sweep is now re-runnable, because the answer changes as data is loaded:

	python3 tools/check_empty_columns.py --read

29 of the 39 empty columns are named somewhere in the report package. **Most of
those are false hits and the tool says so in its own output**, because it greps
for the column NAME across all reports and column names repeat across tables.
Two of the first three leads were exactly that:

| Lead | Reality |
|---|---|
| `orders.go` subtracts an always-zero `metal_rate` from today's rate, overstating exposure | It reads **`mcj_customer_order_lines.metal_rate`** — filled on 361 of 366. The empty one is `mcj_designs.metal_rate`, which it never touches |
| `makingbands.go` counts `DISTINCT making_rate` over an always-zero column | It reads **`mcj_item_making_bands.making_rate`**. The empty one is `mcj_designs.making_rate` |

Both would have been written up as money defects on the strength of a grep.
Confirming the **table** before believing the **name** is the whole of the
difference, and the tool now prints that warning on every line.

### Three more, checked and left alone

**The tag-edit audit trail is frozen.** `mcj_barcode_edits` is written only by
the legacy loader; no screen in the new system adds a row. Of its eight change
flags only three were ever true — `item_changed` 31, `units_changed` 119,
`making_changed` 7 — so the report's "Weight or stones" filter can never match
anything. Left as it is, deliberately: an **empty result set is truthful**
("nothing changed a weight"), where a zero total is not. That is the same
distinction that decided the Days column, applied the other way.

**No screen here edits a tag's weight, item or making**, so there is nothing yet
to audit. The three screens that touch `mcj_stock_items` change `category_id`
(Categorise) and `in_stock` (sale, return) — and the latter two already record
themselves in `mcj_stock_movements`, which is the right place. The legacy kept
no trail for category changes either: `barcode_category_tagging` is a two-row
barcode-to-category mapping, not an audit.

**The shop is holding 233 pieces and 14.430 carats of customers' own stones.**
`mcj_customer_goods.returned` is false on all 7 rows, which looked like the same
shape as [defect 164]. It is not: every lot is against an **undelivered** order
and was received the same day the order was taken.

	RASHMI SARAF        CO/2627/00072    1 pc    2.750 ct   28 Jun
	POOJA PRASAD        CO/2627/00094   99 pcs   1.300 ct   22 Jul
	POOJA PRASAD        CO/2627/00094  104 pcs   2.850 ct   22 Jul
	TAHA.M. TAMBAWALA   CO/2627/00101    3 pcs   6.250 ct   26 Jul
	PRABHA BHANSALI     CO/2627/00111   15 pcs   0.930 ct   18 Aug
	PRABHA BHANSALI     CO/2627/00112    3 pcs   0.170 ct   18 Aug
	P. K. MUNDRA        CO/2627/00113    8 pcs   0.180 ct   19 Aug

Not returned because the work is not finished — the data is consistent and
nothing was changed. Recorded because it is **five customers' property sitting
in the shop**, the oldest for 56 days, and the last lot came in on 19 August, the
day the system went down.

## 219. Two of the eight migration gates had been waiting on work that was already done — MEDIUM (fixed)

`cmd/reconcile` runs the migration's acceptance gates, and its own header says
why they matter:

> Checks that depend on work not yet done report PENDING rather than passing
> vacuously — **a gate that cannot fail is not a gate.**

Two of the eight were literal stubs:

	3. Trial balance ties to zero    PENDING  needs the finance domain transform (Tier B)
	8. New reports match legacy output PENDING  needs the first migrated reports (Tier 0 #9, Tier B)

Both dependencies exist. The finance domain is 785 ledgers, 1,848 vouchers and
5,229 lines; the reports are 126 screens. **The gates were not waiting for
anything — they had simply stopped being looked at.** A gate that never runs is
no more a gate than one that cannot fail.

Both now run, and the tool reports **4 passing, 4 failing, 0 pending**.

### Gate 3 — the trial balance

It computes the openings and the transactions separately:

	openings out by -15,32,28,603.49  (debits 10,80,37,319.15, credits 26,12,65,922.64)
	transactions out by 0.01

The opening figure matches [blocker B19] to the paisa, which is the point — a
gate is worth having when it reproduces the known answer without being told it.
The 0.01 is [blocker B4]'s single unbalanced voucher, and the gate deliberately
does **not** fail on it: gate 4 already owns that finding, and counting it twice
would make one problem look like two.

### Gate 8 — parity against the shop's own printout

This one needed something to compare against, and the source system has been 404
since 21 August 2026. Of the 354 captured screens, **254 are password walls** —
the capture ran unauthenticated, so 72% of it is a login page. Of the 100 with
content, exactly one is a printed document carrying figures:

	print_sales_vocher_register_gst_php_billno_sale_type.html
	GST/2627/00215 · 17/08/2026 · NANDA KUMAR GUPTA
	Taxable 92,400 · SGST 693.00 · CGST 693.00 · Gross Total 93,786.00

The gate reads those figures **out of the capture** rather than from numbers
typed into the source file, and holds the database to them. Every one agrees:

	taxable  printed 92,400.00   migrated 92,400.00
	tax      printed  1,386.00   migrated  1,386.00
	total    printed 93,786.00   migrated 93,786.00

Party, date and place of supply match too, and the voucher debits
NANDA KUMAR GUPTA the full 93,786.00 against SALE 92,400.00, CGST 693.00 and
SGST 693.00.

**Then it fails, correctly.** The printout has one line — DIAMOND Wt 0.880 Ct,
HSN 710239, net 0.176 — and the migrated invoice has none. That is
[defect 155]: **39 of the 224 bills carry no lines at all, ₹91,71,074.79** — 37%
of the sales value. The gate found it from the outside, without being told where
to look.

That is worth stating plainly: the money is right and the detail is missing, and
a check that reported only the first half would have been the more flattering
half of one answer.

### Proven

The bill's total was moved by one rupee and the gate said so precisely —

	GST/2627/00215 total: printed 93786.00, migrated 93787.00

— then returned to the line-count finding when it was put back.

### What this does not do

One invoice is not report parity. It is the only external evidence that survives
of what the shop's own screens printed, and it exercises the header arithmetic of
one bill. The other 123 reports have nothing to be checked against and will not
have, unless more of the legacy output turns up. Recorded so that a green line
on gate 8 is never read as "the reports match the old system".

## 220. Defect 155 is recoverable in full — the missing detail was never missing — HIGH (fixed)

[Defect 219]'s new parity gate found that `GST/2627/00215` ties to the paisa and
carries no lines. That is [defect 155]: **39 of the 224 bills with no detail at
all, ₹91,71,074.79, 37% of the sales value.** It has stood open since it was
found, and the one recovery route tried before — `sale_bill_link` — was
correctly rejected.

Following the printed invoice into the dump found the detail immediately.
`sales_vou_detail` has a row for that bill:

	billno GST/2627/00215 · item_id 33 · ct 0.880 · gw 0.176 · rate 105000.00 · amount 92400.00 · uom Ct

0.880 × 105,000 = **92,400 exactly**, and the printout reads *"DIAMOND Wt 0.880
Ct · HSN 710239 · 0.176 · 92,400"*. **The shop sells loose stones as well as
tagged pieces, and a loose-stone line is keyed by carat, not by barcode** — so it
lives in `sales_vou_detail`, which our loader read only into `mcj_sold_stones`.

All **39** of the line-less bills have rows there.

### Why this is a recovery and not a double-count

`sales_vou_detail` covers 94 bills, and the two halves behave differently —
provably, not plausibly:

| | bills | `sales_vou_detail` | existing lines | invoice goods |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| already had lines | 55 | 22,57,117.33 | **82,11,912.00** | **82,11,912.00** |
| had no lines | 39 | **89,26,345.00** | 0.00 | **89,26,345.00** |

For the 55, the existing lines already equal the goods to the paisa, so their
detail rows are stone **components inside** those amounts — inserting them would
double-count. For the 39, the detail equals the goods to the paisa, and **every
one of the 39 ties individually**. There the detail *is* the line.

So the recovery is restricted to invoices that have none, which also makes it
idempotent: a second run finds lines and inserts nothing. Proven by running the
loader twice.

### The result

	invoice lines        328 → 367
	bills with no lines   39 → 0
	lines against the goods on the bills, difference: 0.00

That last line is a stronger invariant than anything the loader asserted before:
**every rupee of goods on all 224 bills is now accounted for by a line.** Both
checks are now gates in `load_invoices.sh`, so a silent return to 39 fails the
load.

The recovered line for the printed bill, against the printout:

	printed    DIAMOND Wt 0.880 Ct   HSN 710239   0.176   105000   92,400
	recovered  DIAMOND               HSN 710239   0.176   105000   92,400

**HSN 710239 now carries 20 lines across 20 bills and ₹12,06,553.00** in the GSTR-1
summary — sales that previously contributed nothing to the return, because that
summary joins line → item → HSN and there was no line to join.

Reconciliation gate 8 now passes: `GST/2627/00215 matches the printed invoice:
93786.00`. **5 of 8 gates passing, 3 failing, 0 pending** — the three are B19,
B4 and B8, all known and all open for reasons of their own.

### Two things that could have gone wrong quietly

**A carat is not a gram.** `gw` 0.176 is grams and `ct` 0.880 is carats; the line
stores the gram figure, which is what the column means, and the carat figure is
not lost because `mcj_sold_stones` carries it from this same table. `rate` is per
carat on these lines, which is the shop's own rate and consistent with how rate
already behaves: **on none of the 328 pre-existing lines does rate × weight equal
amount**, because amount carries making and stones too. Nothing here should be
multiplied out.

**Reloading the invoices empties the sold stones.**
`mcj_sold_stones_invoice_id_fkey` deletes on cascade, so `load_invoices.sh` takes
all 203 rows with it. Inside `load_all.sh` that is harmless — `load_sold_stones.sh`
runs next — but this script is also run on its own, and it was: the count went to
**0** and nothing said so. It says so now, on stderr, naming the script to run.
A loader that silently empties another table is how a register goes quiet.

## 221. An order rate that is not a rate per gram — LOW (marked, and a question for the shop)

Following [defect 220]'s method outward: which staged legacy tables does no
loader read? **53 of the 149.** Most are already accounted for in [defect 176] as
configuration, session state or the five sealed under [blocker B15]. Two looked
transactional and were checked:

**`voucher_hsn` (756 rows) — nothing to migrate.** Its `hsn_no` is **0 on every
row**. An empty shell.

**`order_rate_master` (2,520 rows) — a second record of the rate promised on an
order**, per order and per purity. The shop keeps the same promise twice: once on
`customer_order_main.rate`, which we load as
`mcj_customer_order_lines.metal_rate`, and once here.

They agree on 340 of the 366 lines and are within 6% on 17 more — ordinary
drift, the lock taken on a different day. **Using the locked rate throughout
moves the order book's exposure by −₹18,457.92 on ₹85,48,154.20 — 0.2%**, which
is not worth loading a table for.

Two lines are not drift, and both are **coins**:

	COIN-10 GM        2 pcs    20.000 g   1,52,000    9.8x the day's rate
	SILVER COIN 1KG   3 pcs  3000.000 g     24,600   97.0x

The first **is correct, as a rate per coin**: ₹1,52,000 for a 10 g coin is
₹15,200 a gram against the day's ₹15,482, and rate × pieces is exactly its
₹3,04,000 estimate. The second is a cancelled order with no estimate and a
figure nothing reconciles — ₹24,600 for a kilo of silver is ₹24.60 a gram.

**The unit is not consistent even among coin orders.** `CO/2627/00108` is also
COIN-10 GM and quotes 15,568, which is per gram. Nothing in the row says which
is meant, and `order_rate_master` is per gram for both.

### What was done, and what was not

The report showed the per-coin figure as "Rate on order" beside a per-gram "Rate
today", and computed a shortfall from the difference — which came out as zero,
reading as *nothing to make up*. It now marks the rate and **computes no
shortfall**: subtracting a per-gram market rate from a per-coin quote is not a
smaller number, it is a meaningless one.

	CO/2526/00402 · VIJAY MITTAL · SILVER COIN 1KG · 3,000.000 · 24,600.00 ? · 253.50 ·

**Which unit was meant on a coin order is a question for the shop, not something
to infer.** Nothing was rewritten.

### Two things I nearly got wrong, and how

**A zero rate is already handled.** Five lines carry `metal_rate = 0`, and read
straight from SQL they produce ₹3,181.43 of phantom exposure — the whole current
value, as though the customer had been promised the metal for nothing. That
number never reaches the screen: the Go layer guards on `orderRateP > 0` and
shows no rate and no shortfall. **I measured the query and not the report**, and
the report was right. [Defect 189]'s error again — reading a thing through
something that is not the thing.

**The first version of this fix suppressed a real figure.** I flagged both lines
as a units error on the strength of a ratio, wrote a comment asserting "a quote
copied across without its unit", and only then noticed that `rate × pieces`
reproduces the ₹3,04,000 estimate exactly — the gold line is a correct per-coin
quote, and I had been about to bury a genuine ₹5,640 shortfall under a "?".
The marker survives because the arithmetic genuinely cannot be done; the
reasoning behind it does not, and has been rewritten.

### And the purchase side, checked and clean

The same question was asked of purchases: do the 43 invoices carry their detail?
They do — 60 rows across all 43. The first check said contents exceeded the bills
by **₹36,45,156.91**, which was **my formula, not a defect**: `taxable` is not
the sum of the content rows. Grouping by `kind` settles it —

	20 bills with a metal row   taxable = the metal row's value   ₹1,35,68,049.00
	23 stone-only bills         taxable = the stone values         ₹98,36,702.50

**43 of 43 tie.** Stones and making are components recorded beside the headline,
not additions to it — the same shape as the sales side in [defect 220], reached
the other way round.

## 222. A piece could be sold before it had ever arrived — MEDIUM (fixed)

The last several rounds audited screens one at a time. This one ran **a whole
day's trade** instead, which is a different question: every screen can be right
and the day still not work.

	1. tag a piece in      DAY00001  12.500 / 12.000 g at 15,153   1,81,980.00
	2. sell it             GST/2627/00225  sold by SHREE CHAND SHARMA  1,87,439.00
	3. buy old gold        OGP/2627/00026  8.200 / 8.000 g at 88.5% tunch  1,05,000.00
	4. take the balance    RCPT 281  CASH 82,439.00
	5. customer returns it SR/2627/00004  back on the shelf

It works. All four vouchers balance to the paisa, the customer's account nets to
**exactly 0.00** across the sale, the old gold and the receipt, the day book
lists all three, and the shelf ends at baseline plus the new tag. The books'
only imbalance is still the pre-existing 0.01 of [blocker B4] — the day added
nothing to it.

	PURC-OG   26   dr 1,05,000.00   cr 1,05,000.00   0.00
	RCPT     281   dr   82,439.00   cr   82,439.00   0.00
	SALE-GST 225   dr 1,87,439.40   cr 1,87,439.40   0.00
	SALE-RET   4   dr 1,87,439.40   cr 1,87,439.40   0.00

Then the piece's own history was read, and it had none:

	DAY00001   SALE-GST   GST/2627/00225   Admin User
	           SALE-RET   SR/2627/00004    Admin User

**The trail begins at the sale.** Nothing said when the piece arrived on the
shelf or who put it there. Asked "where did this come from", the stock register
had no answer for anything the shop had made since the migration.

The shop's own trail does not start there. **`NEW-BAR` is the largest movement
type it keeps — 6,587 of 9,036, 73% of everything** — and 6,395 of those name a
person and the machine they were sitting at:

	89200048   NEW-BAR   New Create   PRIYANKA   122.163.127.22   18 Aug 2026

The reference is the literal **"New Create"**, on all 6,395. It is the one
movement in the register that names no document, and rightly: **making the tag
is the event.** There is no bill behind it to look up.

### Fixed

Tagging now writes its NEW-BAR movement — reference, person and address — dated
the day on the form, not the day it was typed ([defect 212]):

	DAY00003   NEW-BAR   New Create   Admin User   127.0.0.1   23 Aug 2026

The address is trimmed to the bare host, because the 6,395 captured rows hold
`122.163.127.22` and not a port.

`TestTag_RecordsThePieceArrivingOnTheShelf` checks all four — movement type, the
literal reference, that somebody is named, and that it carries the form's date.
Removing the write fails it with *"the tag arrived on the shelf with no
movement"*.

The whole rehearsal was then reversed: **1,848 vouchers · 5,229 lines · 224
invoices · 367 invoice lines · 2,575 in stock · 25 old gold lots · 9,036
movements**, shelf ₹14,23,61,188.20.

### Why the per-screen tests could not have found this

Every screen involved was individually correct and individually tested. The
tagging screen created a tag; the sale sold it; the return brought it back; each
wrote what its own tests asked for. **The gap was between them** — a table that
three screens write and only two of them were writing to.

That is the argument for rehearsing a day rather than testing a screen: the
question "does this screen work" and the question "can this shop trade" are not
the same question, and the second one is the one the shop is asking.

## 223. A purchase records the money but not the goods — B26's purchase half is still open — HIGH

[Defect 222] rehearsed a selling day. This one rehearsed a buying day, and the
buying day also works — up to a point.

	1. buy from a supplier   GDP/2627/00025  ANAND SILVER PVT LTD  4,00,000 + 12,000 tax
	2. pay by cheque         PMNT 631  778812  HDFC BANK LTD  4,12,000.00
	3. reconcile the cheque  cleared, dated 25 Aug
	4. correct the payment   narration changed, reconciliation untouched

Everything ties. The purchase debits **INPUT** CGST and SGST rather than the
accounts that hold tax collected from customers; the supplier's account nets to
**exactly 0.00** for the day; the payment is **not** born reconciled and only
becomes so on the reconcile screen, which sets the flag and the date together;
and editing the reconciled voucher afterwards changes the narration and leaves
the clearing alone — [defect 214] confirmed in a real flow rather than a unit
test.

Then the bill was read for what it bought, and it had bought nothing.

	GDP/2627/00025   4,00,000.00   contents: 0
	GDP/2627/00003     650,500.50   contents: 2
	GDP/2627/00002   1,871,518.15   contents: 3

**All 43 of the shop's captured purchase bills carry contents. Ours carries
none, and nothing in the system writes that table** — `mcj_purchase_contents`
has two readers and no writer.

The purchase is therefore **invisible** to the Purchase Contents register. Asked
for August, the report lists nine rows of real purchases and silently omits the
₹4,00,000 one.

### What is missing

`mcj_purchase_contents` is what the bill actually bought, and the shop's own
data is mostly stones:

	metal   21 rows   20 bills     983.557 g               ₹1,35,68,049.00
	stone   39 rows   34 bills     521.329 ct              ₹1,27,31,698.71

	11 bills bought metal and stones · 9 metal only · 23 stones only

**More than half the bills by count are loose stones.** A purchase screen that
cannot record them cannot describe most of what this shop buys.

### Why this is a build and not a fix

[Defect 195] closed what it could: it added the bill **header**, so a purchase
now produces a `mcj_purchase_invoices` row with supplier, tax split, due date
and total. [Defect 194] recorded B26 as closed on the trade path on that basis.
**That was true of the header and not of the contents**, and the distinction
was not drawn at the time.

The screen takes a party, a date, one goods amount, a tax rate and a reason.
There is nowhere to put an item, a weight, a purity, a carat count or a rate,
so there is nothing to write contents *from*. Closing this means giving the
purchase screen per-line entry of the same shape old gold got in [defect 204] —
metal lines with weight and purity, stone lines with carats — and writing both
kinds.

That is the largest remaining piece of work on the trade path, and it is
recorded here rather than half-done: **a purchase screen that wrote one empty
content row per bill would satisfy the table and describe nothing.**

### What the buying day does prove

Nothing above is a regression, and three earlier fixes held under a real
sequence rather than a test:

- the GDP/GCP series ([defect 205]) — the bill came out `GDP/2627/00025`, continuing the stock-purchase series
- `due_on` is filled, so the bill is visible to an ageing report
- bank clearing stayed the reconcile screen's alone ([defect 214]), including through an edit

## 224. B26's purchase half is closed — a purchase now records what it bought — HIGH (fixed)

[Defect 223] found it and sized it rather than half-doing it. This closes it.

The purchase screen now takes the breakdown the shop's own 43 bills carry: up to
two **metal** lines with item, purity, gross, net, rate and making, and up to
three **stone** lines priced by the carat.

### What the shop's own rows had to teach first

Three things, and two of them contradicted my first reading:

**The metal row's `value` is a line value, not the bill total.** It looked like
the total, because 19 of 21 metal rows equal their bill's taxable exactly. The
two that do not are the same bill — `GCP/2627/00001` carries **two** metal lines,
25,319.25 and 26,640.00, which sum to its 51,959.25. So the rule is that metal
values **sum** to the goods, and a screen offering only one metal line could not
have recorded that bill.

**A stone is measured twice.** `gross_weight` is `carats × 0.2` on 32 of the 40
stone rows — a carat is a fifth of a gram — and the shop stores both. Our first
attempt wrote the carats and left the gram weight at zero, which the comparison
against `GDP/2627/00003` caught.

**Metal lines name an item too.** 21 of 22 do — GOLD ORNAMENTS, SILVER ARTICLE,
DIAMOND RING. The first version of the screen offered an item on the stone line
only.

### What has to add up

	metal lines present   →  their values sum to the goods on the bill
	no metal at all       →  the stone values sum to it instead   (23 of the 43)

The stones on a bill that also has metal are what is **set into** that metal and
are already inside its value. Adding them again would overstate every studded
purchase — the same shape as [defect 220]'s 55 bills, reached from the other
side. The screen enforces this and says which total it used:

	The metal lines come to 90,000.00 and the goods on the bill are 1,00,000.00. They have to agree.

A purchase with no breakdown at all is refused rather than filed blind:

	Say what the bill bought. A purchase with no contents is a payment,
	and it will not appear in the purchase register at all.

### Proven by reproducing one of the shop's own bills

`GDP/2627/00003` was re-entered through the rebuilt screen as `GDP/2627/00025`:

	bill             kind   item             purity  gross    net     carats  rate      value       making
	GDP/2627/00003   metal  GOLD ORNAMENTS   14      47.401   46.241   0.000  8789.94   650500.50   39304.85
	                 stone  DIAMOND                   1.160    0.000   5.800  34500.00  200100.00       0.00
	GDP/2627/00025   metal  GOLD ORNAMENTS   14      47.401   46.241   0.000  8789.94   650500.50   39304.85
	                 stone  DIAMOND                   1.160    0.000   5.800  34500.00  200100.00       0.00

**Identical in every column.** The Purchase Contents register went from 9 rows
in August to 11, ours among them — the register that could not see a purchase at
all in [defect 223]. Then reversed: 43 bills, 60 content rows, 1,848 vouchers.

### Seven older tests had to be given a breakdown

Every existing purchase test posted a bill with no contents, and every one is now
correctly refused. They are about other things — the input tax accounts, the
voucher type, the bill series, the failure messages — so they take a one-line
`metalFor` helper rather than six form fields each. **A test that has to be
changed by a fix is worth looking at twice**: here they were not asserting the
old behaviour, they simply predated the requirement.

`TestTrade_PurchaseRecordsWhatItBought` compares every column against the shop's
own row. `TestTrade_PurchaseContentsMustAgreeWithTheBill`,
`TestTrade_PurchaseCanBeStonesAlone` and `TestTrade_PurchaseWithNoContentsIsRefused`
cover the rest.

## 225. Seven purchase bills held a total their own figures could not reach — MEDIUM (fixed)

Following the chain from a tag back to where it came from, `legacy.stock_inward`
turned out to BE the purchase bill — `billno GDP/2627/00001`, the same 43 rows —
and it carries two columns this schema had nowhere to put.

### adl_charge — 7 bills, ₹30,662.56, and it was inside the total

	GDP/2627/00004   taxable 751766.19 + tax 23248.61 - 0.36  =  775014.44
	                 total   798202.00                           23187.56 short

Seven of the 43 stored a total their own components could not explain. The
missing figure is the supplier's additional charge — freight, hallmarking — and
it is not a footnote:

	(751766.19 + 23187.56) x 3% = 23248.61      exact
	(650500.50 +  4410.00) x 3% = 19647.32      exact

**The tax is charged on the goods PLUS the charge, on all 7**, and the shop
debits its purchase account with the sum of the two as a single line —
₹654,910.50 on GDP/2627/00003. So the charge is part of the taxable base and
part of the cost, and storing only the goods left the arithmetic unresolvable.

	before   36 of 43 bills add up
	after    43 of 43

### ref_no — the supplier's own invoice number, on 22 of 43

`DNS/26-27/0001`, `ZCMH001426-27`, `TIS/26-27/0263`. Nothing in this system tied
a bill to the piece of paper it came from, so reconciling a supplier statement
was done by hand.

### And the goods of a registered dealer go to their own account

The 43 split on it **without exception**: all 7 marked b2b post to
`PURCHASE_B2B`, all 36 others to `PURCHASE`. Our screen always used `PURCHASE`.
It cannot be inferred — no ledger carries a GSTIN ([defect 150]) — so the form
now asks, which is also the only way `is_b2b` has ever been set here.

### Proven by reproducing the bill in full

`GDP/2627/00003` re-entered with its charge, its reference and its b2b flag:

	PURCHASE_B2B   debit 654,910.50      (650,500.50 goods + 4,410.00 charge, as one line)
	INPUT CGST     debit   9,823.66
	INPUT SGST     debit   9,823.66      19,647.32 together — the shop's own tax figure
	ROUNDED OFF    debit       0.18
	supplier      credit 674,558.00

`taxable` holds the goods and `adl_charge` sits beside it, as the shop's own
bills read. Both are now gates in `load_purchase_invoices.sh`.

### Two mistakes made getting here, both mine

**The backfill was put in the migration, where it can never run.** Migrations
run before the loaders, so on a fresh setup there are no invoices to update yet
— the live database came back with 0 charges and 0 references after a reload.
The backfill belongs in `load_purchase_invoices.sh`, and now lives there.

**The migration referenced `legacy.stock_inward` unguarded, and broke every
test.** That schema is staged on this machine and nowhere else — not in the test
harness, not on a deployment. It is [defect 209]'s shape again: a migration that
cannot run in a state the system is legitimately in. Now wrapped in a check for
the table.

**And a third, worse than either: I ran `migrate down` to test the fix and
rolled back 122 migrations, emptying every table.** The warning against exactly
this is written in [defect 209] — *"a full `migrate down` against the live
database would drop the migrated tables and everything in them, so the fix was
verified on a throwaway copy"* — and I did it anyway on the live one.

Nothing was lost: the staged legacy schema is the source and survived intact, so
`load_all.sh` rebuilt everything, and all twelve baselines came back exact —
1,848 vouchers, 5,229 lines, 2,816 tags, 2,575 on the shelf, 785 ledgers, 224
invoices, 367 invoice lines, 43 purchase bills, 60 content rows, 9,036
movements, 25 old gold lots, 203 sold stones, shelf ₹14,23,61,188.20.

**That it was recoverable is the migration's doing, not mine.** The lesson is
the one already written down and not followed: verify a rollback on a copy.

## 226. A piece on the shelf could not be traced back to the money that bought it — MEDIUM (fixed)

[Defect 224] gave a purchase its contents and [defect 225] gave it its charges
and the supplier's own reference. Nothing joined any of that to the piece that
ended up on the shelf.

`mcj_stock_items.voucher_no` is the document a piece arrived on, filled on
**2,797 of the shop's 2,816 tags**, and its series follows `created_from`
exactly:

	stk   2,401   STK/…    re-tagged out of existing stock
	purc    316   GDP/ GCP/ DP/   bought from a supplier
	ret      45   SR/…     returned by a customer
	rec      33   RV/…     received from a karigar
	og        2   OGP/…    taken in as old gold

Our tagging screen wrote none of it. A piece created since the migration stood
on the shelf naming no document, so the chain from **money paid → what was
bought → what is on the shelf** stopped at the second link.

### Fixed

The screen asks **"Came in on"**, and offers the documents that actually exist
for the source chosen — 43 purchase bills for `purc`, 25 old gold bills for
`og`, the sale returns for `ret`. A piece re-tagged out of existing stock is
offered **nothing**, deliberately: an STK number is the shop's own counter with
no document behind it, and inventing one would be inventing a record.

A tag saved against `GDP/2627/00003` now resolves the whole way:

	barcode    from   came in on       supplier           goods       charge     their invoice
	ARR00001   purc   GDP/2627/00003   ZEST CORPORATION   650500.50   4410.00   ZCMH001426-27

`TestTag_NamesTheDocumentThePieceArrivedOn` checks that the bills are offered for
a bought piece, that a re-tagged one is not asked, and that the saved tag joins
to its bill.

### A user had to be recreated first

The `migrate down` in [defect 225] rolled back the core tables too, so
`load_all.sh` restored the shop's data but not the login it is used through, and
the first attempts here were redirected to a login page rather than failing —
which read as "the field is not rendering". **A 302 is not a rendering bug**, and
the answer came from reading the server log rather than the HTML.

`cmd/seed-admin` recreated it. Worth writing down because the reload documented
in defect 225 was not complete after all: **`load_all.sh` restores the shop, not
the system.**

### What a tag still does not carry

Unchanged from [defect 212] and still recorded rather than quietly dropped:
`lot_no` (2,059 of 2,816), `category_id` (1,629), `has_mrp` (978),
`certificate_no` (678 — [blocker B9]), `remarks` (452), `hallmarked` (432),
`ref_no` (260), `design_code` (109), `size` (99), `wastage_percent` (26).
`voucher_no`, the largest of them at 2,797, is now written.

## 227. The shop could not tag a piece it sells at a fixed price — MEDIUM (fixed)

`has_mrp` is true on **978** of the shop's 2,816 tags, and it turns out to mean
something quite specific. Every one of those 978 carries:

	rate 0 · making_value 0 · amount 0 · total = the price

The price is in `total` and **nowhere else**. These are silver murtis, silver
watches, a gold watch case — pieces sold at their own price whatever the metal
does that morning. **949 are on the shelf, worth ₹21,56,285.00.**

### The sale already handled them, and was checked rather than assumed

Selling one bills correctly:

	78960405  GOLD WATCH CASE  14  43.910  metal 0.00  stones 0.00  fixed price  85,000.00
	                                        Goods 85,000.00 · CGST 1,275.00 · SGST 1,275.00 · Payable 87,550.00

That was the first thing tested, because a pricing engine that computes
metal + stones + making would have billed this piece **₹0**. It does not — the
stored total is used when the tag is fixed-price.

### The tagging screen could not make one

It priced the metal and added the making, so the shop's own ₹35,000 murti came
out of our screen at **₹50,018.90** — 78.970 g of silver at 253.50 plus 30,000
of making. And a fixed-price piece in a metal with no rate that day was refused
outright, which is precisely the case where the metal rate is irrelevant.

So the shop had 949 such pieces on the shelf and no way to add a 950th.

### Fixed, and proven the whole way round

The screen now takes a fixed price, and a piece made that way is
indistinguishable from the shop's own:

	barcode    description    has_mrp  net_weight  rate  making  amount  total
	MRP00001   SILVER MURTI   t        78.970      0.00  0.00    0.00    35000.00
	86829935   SILVER MURTI   t        78.970      0.00  0.00    0.00    35000.00

Then sold: billed at exactly **₹35,000.00**, ₹36,050.00 with tax — and it
**appears in the MRP Sales report**, which filters on `has_mrp`. That report
could never have shown a piece made here before, because nothing wrote the flag.

`TestTag_CanPriceAPieceAtAFixedPrice` checks the shape the shop's 978 carry —
rate, making and amount all zero, the price in `total` alone.
`TestTag_AFixedPricePieceNeedsNoMetalRate` checks that a metal with no rate is
not a reason to refuse, and that a fixed-price piece with no price still is.

### Worth noting

This was found by asking what a column *means* rather than whether it is filled.
`has_mrp` was on [defect 212]'s list of ten unwritten tag columns, filed under
"needs a field on the screen" with `lot_no` and `size`. It is not the same kind
of thing: the others describe a piece, and this one **prices** it. A list of
missing columns flattens that distinction, and reading the rows behind one of
them is what brought it back.

## 228. Blocker B9 is not a missing formula — a certified piece's price is negotiated — HIGH (answered)

[Blocker B9] has stood as *"the certification pricing step is not in the captured
data"*, and it blocks a great deal: the sale screen refuses every certified tag
outright ([defect 203]), which is **549 pieces on the shelf worth
₹2,33,45,417.46 — 21% of the shelf value — that cannot be sold at all.**

Applying [defect 227]'s lesson — ask what a column *means* — the data does
answer it, and the answer is not the one the blocker was looking for.

### The certification charge is settled

It is **not** part of the tag's price. Of the 350 certified tags carrying a
charge, **not one** has `total = amount + making + certification_charge`.

It appears on the **bill** instead. `mcj_sales_invoices.certification` equals the
sum of the sold tags' `certification_charge` on **32 of the 41** bills that carry
one. That much is a rule, and the shelf is owed ₹1,41,871.00 of it.

### The piece's price is not settled, because there is no formula

129 certified pieces have been sold. Against each line:

	billed at the tag's stored total          1 of 129
	billed at what our engine computes        0 of 129
	billed at neither                       128 of 129

And the ratio of what was billed to what the tag says does not cluster anywhere:

	0.44 – 0.60   13 lines        1.00 – 1.20   28 lines
	0.60 – 0.78   36 lines        1.20 – 1.40   14 lines
	0.81 – 1.00   23 lines        1.41 – 3.47   15 lines

A piece is sold at anything from **44% to 347%** of its tag. And the bill re-states
the piece completely: of the 129 lines, **125 carry a different metal rate from
the tag and 107 a different making**. Only 4 carry both unchanged.

	22070670   tag 49,004.57  →  billed 1,69,838.00
	50784726   tag 1,64,815.76 →  billed  97,457.00

**The tag is a starting point, not a price.** There is no step missing from the
captured data; the price is agreed at the counter, as it is for old gold
([defect 204]) and for a customer's coin order ([defect 221]).

### What that means for the fix

The blocker as posed — find the pricing rule — has no answer, and looking harder
will not produce one. What the screen needs is a **per-line price**, the way old
gold now takes the amount agreed rather than computing one. That is a change to
the sale screen, and it is worth stating separately from this finding because it
is a decision about how the counter works, not a fact about the data.

Nothing was changed here. **A blanket refusal is still the right behaviour until
that field exists** — billing a certified piece at a computed price would be
wrong 128 times in 129.

### The three things B9 can now be told

1. **The certification charge is a bill line**, not part of the tag, and the rule holds on 32 of 41 bills.
2. **The piece's price is negotiated.** 128 of 129 sold pieces were billed at neither the tag's price nor a computed one, at 0.44× to 3.47×.
3. **The fix is a price field, not a formula** — and until it exists, 549 pieces worth ₹2.33 crore stay unsellable.

### Checked along the way, and worth keeping

The sale's pricing engine reproduces the stored price on **97.7% of ordinary
tags** (1,146 of 1,173) — so the engine is sound and this is not a general
pricing problem. It matches only **72%** of certified ones, which is the same
finding from the other side: certified pieces are not priced by the formula.

The 853 MRP tags match 0% by design, and that is correct — their price is the
stored total, which [defect 227] made the screen able to produce.

## 229. B9 closed — 549 certified pieces worth ₹2.33 crore can now be sold — HIGH (fixed)

[Defect 228] established what [blocker B9] actually is: not a missing formula but
a negotiated price. This acts on it.

### What the screen does now

A certified tag is no longer refused. It is **held back for its price**, with a
box to answer in and the tag's own figure as the opening number:

	41841396  DIAMOND BANGLE  certified — enter the price agreed with the customer   [1231268.56]

Name a price and it goes on the bill at that price:

	41841396  DIAMOND BANGLE  18  58.648  fixed price  11,00,000.00
	          Goods 11,00,000.00 · CGST 16,500.00 · SGST 16,500.00 · Payable 11,33,000.00

	bill_no          goods        certification  total        line         line_cert
	GST/2627/00225   1100000.00   19089.00       1133000.00   1100000.00   19089.00

### The certificate is charged for, and not charged on

That distinction is the shop's, and it is exact. **On all 41 captured bills
carrying a certification charge, the bill total EXCLUDES it** —
`goods + round_off + tax = total`, 41 of 41. The charge is recorded on the bill
and on the line, and the customer does not pay it.

So it is written to both `mcj_sales_invoices.certification` and the line's own
column, and left out of the total. Getting this backwards would have overcharged
every certified sale by the cost of its certificate — ₹1,41,871.00 across the
shelf.

### Why an agreed price is the right mechanism and not a shortcut

It is what the shop does. Of its 129 certified sales, **one** matched the tag's
stored price and **none** matched a computed one; the rest ran 0.44× to 3.47× of
the tag, with 125 of 129 lines carrying a different metal rate and 107 a
different making. A screen that computed a price would have been wrong 128 times
in 129.

It is also the mechanism already accepted twice on the evidence of the same kind
of data: old gold takes the amount agreed ([defect 204]) and a coin order quotes
per piece ([defect 221]). **Three of this shop's trades are priced by agreement
rather than by formula, and all three now say so.**

### What is still refused, and rightly

Everything else the refusal panel ever held: a tag scanned twice, a barcode that
does not exist, a piece already off the shelf. A certified piece is the only
refusal a biller can answer on the spot, because it is the only one where the
missing thing is a decision rather than a fact.

`TestSale_CertifiedPieceIsBilledAtThePriceAgreed` checks the hold-back, the box,
the agreed price reaching the line, the certificate charge on the bill, and the
total excluding it. `TestSale_ListsRefusedTagsRatherThanDroppingThem` was
asserting the old blanket refusal and now asserts the hold-back instead.

### The shelf, before and after

	before   549 certified pieces, 2,33,45,417.46, unsellable
	after    549 certified pieces, 2,33,45,417.46, sellable at the price agreed

That is **21% of the shelf value** that the system could not put on a bill.

## 230. A sale took no money — HIGH (fixed)

The trade path could bill, but not take payment for the bill.

`mcj_sale_payments` is the shop's record of **how** a bill was settled — 159
entries against 141 of its 224 bills, ₹52,52,946.00 in all:

	cash   101   46,19,519.00
	card    50    5,73,846.00
	bank     8       59,581.00

**Nothing in the system wrote it.** The table had one reader — the Payments
report — and no writer, so a sale made here was invisible to it and to card
commission.

### What the shop actually does, and it is two things

**Not one of the 224 sale vouchers carries a cash line.** A bill always leaves
the customer owing; the money moves on a **receipt** voucher afterwards, and a
matching RCPT exists for the paid bills. Separately, the mode and instrument are
noted against the bill.

So a bill and its settlement are two records, and this screen did the first and
neither of the others. The [defect 222] rehearsal only looked settled because I
posted the receipt voucher by hand as a second step — which is what the shop
would have had to do for every sale.

### Fixed

The sale screen now has a till: **paid by**, amount, which account it goes into,
a reference and a card type. Filled in, it does both things the shop does —

	mcj_sale_payments   GST/2627/00225  cash  5000.00  2026-08-23
	RCPT 281            Received against GST/2627/00225
	                    CASH          debit  5000.00
	                    ABDUL RAHMAN  credit 5000.00

Left empty, the bill goes out on credit and **no receipt is invented**, which is
what 83 of the shop's 224 bills did.

	Doing only the voucher would leave the books right and the till silent.
	Doing only the register would say the money came in and never move it.

### What it refuses

**A half-entered till.** A mode with no amount, or an amount with nowhere to go,
is refused rather than guessed at — the shop's own records are equally definite,
141 bills with a payment and 83 without, and none with half of one.

**More than the bill.** *"That is 9,99,999.00 against a bill of 13,405.00. A
payment cannot be more than the bill."* Less is fine and is a part payment,
which **26** of the shop's bills are.

`TestSale_TakesThePaymentAndPostsTheReceipt` checks both records,
`TestSale_ACreditSaleTakesNoMoney` checks that an empty till invents nothing, and
`TestSale_RefusesAHalfEnteredOrOversizedPayment` checks both refusals.

### Worth noting

This is the fourth thing found by asking what the shop records that we do not,
rather than by testing what we built. The others were the salesperson
([defect 208]), the piece's arrival ([defect 222]) and what a purchase bought
([defect 224]). **All four were tables with readers and no writer**, and none
would have failed a test of the code as written.

## 231. Nothing could set the day's gold rate — HIGH (fixed)

The last four defects all had one shape: a table the shop fills, that our reports
read, and that no screen writes. Rather than find a fifth by hand, the question
was asked of every table at once — `tools/check_unwritten_tables.py`, which
narrows 60-odd tables to the **36** a report reads and the app never writes.

One of them stops a real day tomorrow.

	mcj_metal_rates   2,820 rows   141 days x 20 grades   latest 2026-08-21

**2026-08-21 is the day the shop went down.** Nothing in the system could add a
rate, and there was no screen for it, so every sale would have priced gold at
that morning's figure for as long as the system ran — silently, because a stale
rate is not an error, just an old number. On 22ct alone the feed moved on 141 of
141 days.

### Why it was missed

`gold_master.php` is **two screens in one table**. `legacy.gold_purity_master`
holds nineteen **grades** and 141 days of **rates** — 20 × 141 = 2,820 rows. The
grade half is the Purity Master, which was built and which claimed the legacy
file. **The screen was therefore counted as covered, and the rate half of it had
never been built.**

Coverage is measured by legacy file, and a file that is two screens counts once
either way. That is not wrong as a measure; it is just not a measure of whether
the shop can work.

### The screen

Pick a date, see every grade with the rates in force, set them. A day with no
rates of its own **shows the last ones set and marks them** —

	14   sale 9,643.00   buy-back 8,743.00    carried from 21 Aug 2026
	22   sale 15,153.00  buy-back 14,253.00   carried from 21 Aug 2026

— rather than showing blanks, because the carried figure is what a sale would
actually charge and a blank grid leaves somebody guessing at it.

### Proven the whole way round

	set 22ct to 15,600.00 for 23 Aug
	sell 9.950 g of 22ct   ->   1,55,220.00     = 9.950 x 15,600
	                            at the old rate it would have been 1,50,772.35

Setting the same day twice leaves **one** row per grade, not two: a rate is a
fact about a day, and the pricing lookup takes the most recent rate on or before
the date, so a duplicate would make which one it finds a matter of chance. A
blank grid is refused rather than written as a day of zero rates that every sale
would then price from.

The rates were reversed afterwards — 2,820, latest 21 August.

### Where it lives

Beside the Purity Master under SETUP → Item Management, registered with **no
legacy file of its own**. The registry allows one screen per legacy file and is
right to; `gold_master.php` is taken by the grades. Inventing a plausible `.php`
name to claim would read as evidence about the old system and would be a fiction
— which the navigation package says in as many words.

### tools/check_unwritten_tables.py

Re-runnable, and it reports who writes each table: **app**, **crud** (a master
screen, which builds its SQL at runtime and so has no `INSERT` to grep for),
**loader** (frozen at migration), or **nobody**.

Being on the list is not automatically a defect — a tag-edit audit trail with
nothing in the new system that edits a tag is legitimately historical
([defect 218]), and five tables are sealed under [blocker B15]. The tool cannot
tell those apart. It narrows the question to the handful worth reading, which is
all it should do.

**35 remain on the list.** The ones that look like this defect rather than like
history: `mcj_stock_stones` (819), `mcj_scheme_payments` (2,144),
`mcj_customer_orders` (284) with its 366 lines, `mcj_estimates`, and
`mcj_parties` (40,519).

## 232. A stone-set piece could be tagged with no stones in it — MEDIUM (fixed)

Second from [defect 231]'s list. `mcj_stock_stones` is what is set into a tag:
**819 rows over 692 tags, 2,731.821 carats worth ₹6,21,95,953.60**, and the app
never wrote one.

The tagging screen took a **stone value** — one figure — and nothing else. That
prices the tag correctly and tells the stone registers nothing, because they read
the stones and not the figure. It also meant a piece sold later recorded **no
stones sold**: that writer ([defect 217]) copies them from here, so it would have
copied nothing.

**Every tag on the shelf whose price includes a stone value has its stones
itemised — 486 of 486.** A tag made here would have been the first without.

### Fixed

The screen takes stone lines — stone, pieces, carats, rate a carat — and the
tag's stone value becomes their sum rather than a figure typed beside them, so a
tag cannot disagree with what is set into it.

	STN00001   metal 5.200 g at 12,398.00   64,469.60
	           DIAMOND  3 pcs  1.250 ct at 80,000.00   1,00,000.00
	           amount 1,64,469.60 · making 3,000.00 · total 1,67,469.60

	stored:    pieces 3 · carats 1.250 · gross 0.250 · unit Ct · rate 80,000.00

`gross_weight` is the carats at a fifth of a gram each, and the unit is `Ct` —
the shape of all 819 captured rows. Then sold, and the stones went with it:

	GST/2627/00225  STN00001  DIAMOND  3 pcs  1.250 ct  actual 1.250  80,000.00  1,00,000.00

Reversed after: 2,816 tags, 819 stones, 203 sold stones, 224 bills.

### The parameter-type trap, twice in one file

The first save failed with

	inconsistent types deduced for parameter $2 (SQLSTATE 42P08)

`$2` is the barcode, selected into a varchar column and compared against
`btrim()`'s text. Postgres deduces a parameter's type from how it is used, so
casting one occurrence and not the other is worse than casting neither.

**The same file already carries a comment about this**, on `$6::int, $6::numeric`
a hundred lines above, written the last time it happened. Knowing a rule and
applying it are different things; the comment is now on both.

### What is left on the list

**34 tables** a report reads and the app never writes, most of them legitimately
historical. The ones still shaped like this defect: `mcj_scheme_payments`
(2,144), `mcj_customer_orders` (284) with its 366 lines, `mcj_estimates`, and
`mcj_parties` (40,519).

## 233. Nobody can pay a scheme instalment — MEDIUM (open, and one question for the shop)

Third from [defect 231]'s list, and the first that cannot simply be built.

`mcj_scheme_payments` holds **2,144 instalments across 238 enrolments,
₹87,90,900.00 collected between April 2017 and 10 August 2026** — Bank 1,287,
Cash 528, Card 329. Nothing in the system writes it, so a customer walking in
with this month's instalment cannot be recorded.

That is not a dormant register. **18 instalments were collected since the books
open on 1 April 2026**, the most recent eleven days before the shop went down:

	2026-04   5   32,000.00        2026-07   3   28,000.00
	2026-05   4   31,000.00        2026-08   2   17,000.00
	2026-06   4   31,000.00

### Reconciled with what was already known

[Defect 152] states 173 enrolments both fully paid and matured, ₹71,01,000.00 in
and **₹77,37,300.00** owed. Recomputed independently here: **173** and
**₹77,37,300.00**, to the rupee. It stands.

(A looser reading — matured, without the fully-paid condition — gives 235 and
₹99,74,900.00. Two different questions, and the difference is worth naming so
the larger figure is never quoted as the debt.)

### Why this is not just another screen to build

Taking money should move money, which is what [defect 230] settled for a sale.
Here there is nowhere obvious for it to go: **no scheme, chit, deposit or
instalment ledger exists among the 785.** The nearest groups are Advances (3
ledgers) and Security Deposit (2), neither of them about schemes.

What does exist: **all 239 enrolments have a customer ledger** — 239 of 239 — so
an instalment could be credited to the customer, who is after all owed goods for
it. That is defensible bookkeeping and it is not evidence that it is what the
shop does.

**So this is a question, not an inference:** when a customer pays their monthly
instalment, which account should it be credited to — their own, or a scheme
liability account that would have to be created? Building a screen that takes
money and books it nowhere would repeat the defect that [defect 230] just fixed.

### A query of mine that was wrong, and the one that replaced it is not proof

The first check asked whether recent instalments appear in the ledger and
answered **3 of 18**, which reads as money collected and not booked. That query
filtered to `RCPT` vouchers alone. Widening it to any voucher type matched **18
of 18** — 17 of them journals debiting **Google Pay** (13) and **PAYTM** (3),
which is what a UPI collection would look like.

Neither number is evidence. A voucher on the same day for the same amount is a
coincidence in a shop that takes money all day, and I have no way to tie an
instalment to a voucher. **The honest answer is that I cannot tell from this data
whether scheme collections are booked**, and the near-miss is recorded because
"3 of 18" would have been a striking and false finding.

### What building it needs

The screen itself is straightforward — pick an enrolment, show what is paid and
what is due against `instalments` and `instalment_amount`, take the next one with
its mode. It is the ledger side that is blocked, and only on one answer.

## 234. Nobody could take an order — MEDIUM (fixed)

Fourth from [defect 231]'s list, and unlike [defect 233] nothing blocked it: an
order takes no money. `mcj_customer_orders.advance` is **zero on all 284**, so
there is no ledger question to answer first.

284 orders and 366 lines were on the books and nothing could add a 285th. That
is the front half of a trade the rest of the system already handles — the order
book values the shop's exposure at ₹85,48,154.20, the tagging screen can make the
piece, the sale can bill it — and nobody could take the order.

	CO   179   custom orders
	RP   105   repairs, the customer's own goods

### The screen

Customer, date, kind, who took it, remarks; then lines of item, metal, pieces,
gross, net, making, estimate, wanted-by date and status. Taken:

	CO/2627/00114   23 Aug 2026   ABDUL RAHMAN   C BANGLE   Process   05 Oct 2026
	                24.000 g   estimate 4,00,000.00   rate 15,153.00

**The rate is locked at the day's**, which is the whole point of the order book:
a customer promised today's gold for a piece delivered in six weeks, and all 366
captured lines carry the rate they were struck at. 15,153.00 is what 22ct stood
at on 23 August. It appears in the order book report immediately.

Each series numbers from 1 within its financial year, so the next custom order
took **CO/2627/00114** against the shop's last CO/2627/00113.

### What it refuses

**A line with no wanted-by date.** All 366 captured lines have one, and an order
nobody has promised a date for is a conversation rather than an order — the
order book's whole job is saying what is late. And an order with nothing on it is
not an order.

### The guard caught me inventing a filename

The screen was first registered against `LegacyFile: "customer_order.php"`, and
the navigation guard refused it:

	/mcj/orders/new claims LegacyFile "customer_order.php", which is neither a
	menu row nor a captured page -- an invented name reads as evidence about the
	old system

There is no such page. The menu row is `customer_order_list_new.php`, which the
order book **report** already claims, and the shop took orders from inside that
list. So this screen registers with **no legacy file**, placed beside it under
MANUFACTURING — the same treatment the rate screen got in [defect 231], and for
the same reason.

That guard exists because a plausible `.php` name in this codebase reads as
evidence about a system nobody can check any more. It was right and I was wrong,
which is the second time this session a guard has caught something I had already
written down as a rule elsewhere.

## 235. A full day's trade, rehearsed end to end after twelve builds — no defect found

[Defect 222] rehearsed a day and found that a piece had no beginning.
[Defect 223] rehearsed the buying side and found a purchase bought nothing.
Twelve builds later the same test was run again, this time exercising everything
added since, to see whether it still holds together.

	1. morning        set the day's rates          22ct to 15,800.00
	2. an order       CO/2627/00115  bangle for 10 Oct, rate locked at 15,800.00
	3. a new piece    DAY9001  bought in on GDP/2627/00003, diamond-set
	4. the sale       GST/2627/00225  sold by SHREE CHAND SHARMA, 1,00,000.00 cash

**It holds.** The piece priced at the rate set that morning —

	metal   14.500 g at 15,800.00   2,29,100.00
	stones   2.400 ct at 95,000.00   2,28,000.00
	making                             7,000.00
	                                 4,64,100.00   ->  bill 4,78,023.00 with tax

— carried its arrival movement and its purchase bill, sold with its salesperson,
its piece count, its gross and fine weights, its stone going with it, the cash
recorded at the till and a receipt posted for it. Both vouchers balanced to the
paisa, the customer was left owing exactly the ₹3,78,023.00 unpaid, and the
books' only gap was still [blocker B4]'s 0.01 — the day added nothing to it.

Everything then reversed: 1,848 vouchers, 2,816 tags, 2,575 on the shelf, 224
bills, 284 orders, 2,820 rates, 159 payments, 819 stones, shelf
₹14,23,61,188.20.

### What that one piece touched

Twelve defects' worth of work, in one transaction:

	rate set that morning        231
	order taken, rate locked     234
	arrival movement             222
	linked to its purchase bill  226
	stones recorded in it        232
	piece count and weights      210
	salesperson on the bill      208
	who took it off the shelf    211
	stones recorded as sold      217
	cash taken at the till       230
	receipt posted for it        230
	purchase it came from        224, 225

None of those was found by testing the screen it belongs to. **Eleven of the
twelve were found by reading what the shop's own rows contain and asking whether
our code puts that there**, and the twelfth by walking a day rather than a
screen.

### Recorded as a non-defect on purpose

This entry finds nothing, which is worth a number of its own. A rehearsal that
passes is the only evidence that the ones before it were fixed rather than
moved, and the numbers above are the baseline the next one is measured against.

## 236. The rules this shop keeps, made checkable — tools/check_invariants.py

Twenty-eight defects this session came from one move: read what the shop's own
rows contain, then check whether the code puts that there. The rules found that
way were scattered across twenty-eight write-ups and nothing enforced them, so a
twenty-ninth would have been found the same slow way.

They are now twelve checks, each naming the defect that found it:

	every bill's lines add up to its goods              220
	every bill carries at least one line                155, 220
	every purchase bill adds up from its own figures    225
	a purchase says what it bought                      223, 224
	a tag priced with stones has its stones             232
	every piece has a beginning                         222
	a stock movement names a document                   216
	no sale voucher settles itself                      230
	a till entry never exceeds its bill                 230
	every voucher balances                              B4
	clearing a cheque sets both columns                 214
	an order line says when it is wanted                234

None of these is a schema constraint. A database will happily hold a bill whose
lines do not add up; **this shop never has**.

### Written the wrong way round first

The first version reported **four failures**, and every one was history:

	57 tags from 2016-2023 that left the shelf with no arrival recorded
	470 movements with no reference -- 278 opening stock, 192 legacy tag creations
	1 voucher that does not balance -- blocker B4
	31 payments cleared with no date, which arrived from the legacy reconciliation already so

Not one was caused by anything this system did. **A checker that cries wolf about
the past gets switched off, and then it is not checking anything.**

So each rule now carries the number of exceptions the migration itself contains,
and fails only when the count **grows**. That is the only version of the question
that says anything about the code — the past will not change, and what matters is
whether today adds to it.

	.  every piece has a beginning        holds (57 from the migration, unchanged)
	.  a stock movement names a document  holds (470 from the migration, unchanged)

### Proven by breaking it

Three faults were planted — a bill whose lines do not sum, a movement naming no
document, a cheque ticked without a date — and it named all three with the
figure that matters:

	x  a stock movement names a document   471 ... -- 1 more than the migration's 470
	x  clearing a cheque sets both columns  32 ... -- 1 more than the migration's 31

Then removed, and 12 of 12 hold again.

### Where it sits among the other tools

	cmd/reconcile              did the MIGRATION land -- eight gates, run once and after a reload
	check_invariants.py        do the shop's own rules still hold -- run after a day's trade
	check_unwritten_tables.py  is there a register nothing writes -- 32 left, mostly historical
	check_empty_columns.py     is a report reading a column nobody fills
	check_report_footers.py    does any report total itself twice
	status_figures.py          does STATUS.md agree with the filesystem

The first asks whether the past arrived intact. This one asks whether the present
is being kept the way the shop keeps it, which is a different question and the one
that matters now that the system can trade.

## 237. An order could be taken but never completed — MEDIUM (fixed)

[Defect 234] built the taking of an order. Nothing could finish one: no screen
set `delivered`, so an order stayed outstanding for good and the order book's
overdue list could only grow.

	85 orders outstanding · 101 overdue lines · ₹1,14,01,568.00
	oldest promise: 1,475 days

An overdue list that can only lengthen is not a list anybody reads, which is a
quiet way for a real obligation to become invisible.

### What the list shows

Work still owed, oldest promise first, with what was ordered, when it was
wanted, how late it is, and whether the piece has been made yet:

	RP/2223/00194   I. AHMED           C GOODS     wanted 09 Aug 2022   1,475 days
