	RP/2324/00106   SASHI CHOUDHARY    C NOSEPIN   wanted 11 Jun 2023   1,169 days
	CO/2324/00621   ERFAN HOSSAIN      GOLD TOPS   wanted 05 Nov 2023   1,022 days   ₹59,136.00

Tick and hand over. Only an order still outstanding can be handed over — ticking
one twice is a double-click, not a second delivery — and ticking nothing is
refused rather than treated as a delivery of everything.

### Worth your attention

**The four oldest are repairs — customers' own goods.** `RP` orders are work on
pieces the customer brought in, and three of the four oldest are `C GOODS` or
`C NOSEPIN` with no estimate against them, which is what a repair looks like.
Two years and four years is a long time to hold somebody's own jewellery.

This is the list, not the answer: some may have been collected years ago and
never marked, which is exactly what an unmarkable flag produces. **The screen can
now clear them one by one as you confirm each; it cannot tell you which are
real.** That is the same shape as [defect 164]'s ₹1.35 crore of gold issued with
no recorded return.

`TestOrder_CanBeHandedOver` checks that a live order lists, hands over and stops
listing; `TestOrder_HandingOverNothingIsRefused` checks the empty case.

## 238. Every bank payment the shop has is against a bill nobody can look up — LOW

Chasing `receive_amount` — 141 rows on [defect 176]'s never-opened list, set
aside there as "a payments table" — turned up nothing new: all 141 of its bills
are already in `mcj_sale_payments`, so it is a duplicate view and no data was
missed. That is the answer, and it is worth having.

But counting it produced a number that did not match. **149 distinct bills appear
in `mcj_sale_payments` against only 141 invoices that have a payment.** Eight
payments name a bill that is not on file:

	GST/2526/00017  05 Apr 2025  bank  18,500.00
	GST/2526/00066  29 Apr 2025  bank   1,300.00
	GST/2526/00080  03 May 2025  bank   5,100.00
	GST/2526/00094  14 May 2025  bank   5,000.00
	GST/2526/00100  20 May 2025  bank   1,200.00
	GST/2526/00104  21 May 2025  bank     800.00
	GST/2526/00246  01 Aug 2025  bank  27,069.00
	GST/2526/00622  29 Oct 2025  bank     612.00

**All eight are from the previous financial year, and all eight are every bank
payment the shop has.** `sale_pay_bank` holds exactly 8 rows and not one of them
belongs to a bill we hold.

### Not a load error

`legacy.sales_vou` has **224 rows, all 2026-27** — `GST/2627/00001` to
`GST/2627/00224`. The shop's captured invoice history is the current year only,
while its payment tables reach back further. The eight are orphans in the
source, not something the loader dropped.

### What it changes

[Defect 230] reported the till modes as "cash 101, card 50, bank 8" as though all
three described current trade. They do not: **the bank mode is entirely
historical and every row of it is unlinkable.** A Payments report grouping by
mode shows a bank column that cannot be reconciled to a single bill, and will
show one until a bank payment is taken through the new screen.

Nothing was deleted. Eight rows of ₹59,581.00 recording money the shop received
are worth more on file than tidy.

### Added to the invariant checker

	a payment names a bill that exists   holds (8 from the migration, unchanged)

The baseline is 8 for the reason above. A ninth would mean a payment written here
against a bill that does not exist, which is a different thing entirely.

## 239. The unwritten-tables tool overstated by a third — MEDIUM (fixed)

[Defect 231]'s sweep reported **36** tables a report reads and the app never
writes, and that figure was quoted again in 232, 233 and 234 as it came down.
It was wrong.

The tool looked for two things: a literal `INSERT INTO mcj_x` in the controllers,
and a `Table: "mcj_x"` declaration for the codelist screens. There is a third
place a table gets written, and eighteen screens use it:

	crud.NewBuilder[ledger.Ledger](ledger.Schema(), ...)

The table name lives inside the domain aggregate's `Schema()`, which the grep
never saw. So the **ledger master, the item master, the purity master, parties,
packets, schemes** and a dozen others were all reported as never written when
each has a working screen.

Corrected, the figure is **24**, and the tables that dropped off are the ones a
shop uses most.

	quoted    36 -> 35 -> 34 -> 32
	actual    24

### Why it matters more than the number

A tool that overstates gets believed once and discounted afterwards. This one was
used to pick the last four things to build, and it could as easily have sent me
to build a customer master that already existed. **It sent me to look at the
ledger master to check exactly that — which is how [defect 240] was found**, so
the overstatement was useful once and would not have been twice.

Both detections are now in the tool, with the reason written next to them.

## 240. A new customer could not be taken on — HIGH (fixed)

Checking [defect 239]'s false positive turned into a real one. **A ledger could
not be created unless a ledger type was chosen**, and every sale, purchase,
receipt and payment names a ledger, so the shop could not take on a new customer
or supplier without knowing that.

	insert or update on table "mcj_ledgers" violates foreign key constraint
	"mcj_ledgers_ledger_type_id_fkey" (SQLSTATE 23503)

`Ledger.LedgerTypeID` is a plain `uuid.UUID`, so "no type" is the all-zero uuid,
and the mapper wrote that straight into a foreign key. No such row exists and
none ever will.

**The column is nullable and 14 of the shop's own 785 ledgers carry no type**, so
leaving it blank is a state the data already has. It goes in as NULL now, which
is what "none" means to a database.

### What the user saw

	Field validation failed

No field named, no reason given. A screen that refuses a customer and will not
say which box is wrong is worse than one that refuses loudly.

### It had never been tested

There are e2e tests for the colour master's create, its validation, its
permissions — the codelist screens are well covered. The ledger master had none:
it is built from a different constructor and was assumed to work because it
exists. **The one screen every other screen depends on was the one nobody had
driven.**

`TestLedgerMaster_CreatesACustomerWithNoLedgerType` and
`TestLedgerMaster_CreatesACustomerWithALedgerType` now cover both, and the pair
is deliberate: the second passed before the fix and the first did not, which is
what identified the cause rather than the symptom.
`TestLedgerMaster_RefusesALedgerWithNoCodeOrName` keeps the required fields
required.

## 241. The same bug in five more masters — fifteen optional references — HIGH (fixed)

[Defect 240] was not one screen's mistake. The question it raised — which other
optional references are written as the zero uuid — has one answer per master, and
**every one of them was wrong the same way.**

	item             subgroup_id, hsn_code_id                                    2
	packet           stone_item_id, shape_id, colour_id, clarity_id, cut_id,
	                 sieve_id                                                    6
	party            category_id, main_category_id, source_id, religion_id,
	                 profession_id                                               5
	retail point     branch_id                                                   1
	card commission  card_type_id                                                1

**Fifteen optional references, all declared `uuid.UUID` rather than a pointer, all
written straight into a nullable foreign key.** "None" arrives as the all-zero
uuid, which no row has and none ever will.

### Proven on the one that matters most

A new **item** is what a new kind of piece needs before it can be tagged, so the
item master gates the stock side the way the ledger master gates the money side.
It refused:

	insert or update on table "mcj_items" violates foreign key constraint ...

An item could not be created without naming an HSN code and a subgroup, both of
which the shop leaves unset on its own rows. Fixed, and the same `nullUUID` in
all five mappers with the reason written beside it.

### What this class looks like from outside

Nothing about it is visible until somebody tries. Every one of these screens
renders, lists, filters and searches; the failure is only on create, only when a
field is left blank, and the message names no field. **A screen that works for
everything except the thing it exists for is the hardest kind to notice**, and
five of them shipped that way.

### Why the sweep was possible at all

The question was answerable in one query — every nullable uuid foreign key in the
schema — and then one grep per aggregate for the plain `uuid.UUID` return. Ten
minutes for five defects, against the one that took an afternoon to find by hand.

**[Defect 239]'s overstating tool sent me to look at the ledger master. That
found 240, which asked the question that found this.** A wrong number was more
useful than a right one would have been, which is luck and not method — the
method is that a defect found by hand is worth asking whether it has siblings.

## 242. The half-cast placeholder, swept and closed — LOW

[Defect 241] closed by asking whether a defect found by hand had siblings. The
same question, asked of the other bug that has bitten twice.

A query parameter used more than once must be cast the same way everywhere:
Postgres deduces a parameter's type from how it is used, so casting one
occurrence and not the other is **worse than casting neither**, because it looks
handled.

	inconsistent types deduced for parameter $2 (SQLSTATE 42P08)

It failed that way in [defect 224] on `$4` and again in [defect 232] on `$2` — in
the same file, a hundred lines apart, **the second time with a comment about the
first sitting directly above it.** Knowing a rule and applying it are different
things, which is the argument for checking rather than remembering.

### The sweep found nothing, after finding thirty-one

The first pass reported **31** repeated placeholders. Every one was a false
positive of two kinds:

**Same-type repeats are fine.** `WHERE tenant_id = $1 ... AND x.tenant_id = $1`
needs no cast at all — both uses deduce the same type. Only a *mixed* state is
wrong.

**And several of these queries explain the rule in prose that mentions `$6`.**
Counting comment text as a use inflated the count. Stripping SQL comments first
took it to **0 of 31**.

So the class is closed: both instances were the two already fixed, and nothing
else in the codebase is cast inconsistently.

### Kept as a test, not a memory

`TestSQL_ARepeatedParameterIsCastConsistently` walks every non-test, non-generated
Go file. `TestSQL_TheCastRuleCatchesAMixedOne` proves the rule against text that
breaks it — including the comment case — because a green test that cannot fail
says nothing.

Proven against the real thing too: removing one `::text` from `tag.go` fails it
by name and line.

	tag.go: $2 is used more than once and cast on only some of them

### A negative result worth a number

Nothing was wrong. That is the finding: the class has no more members, and the
next one to appear fails a test rather than a customer's sale. **Three sweeps
this session have gone this way — optional references (241, five defects), tables
with no writer (231, four defects), and this one (nothing).** A sweep that finds
nothing is the cheapest possible outcome and the only way to know.

## 243. Fourteen of seventeen master screens had never been driven — MEDIUM (fixed), and a correction to 241

[Defect 240] found that the ledger master could not create a customer, and
[defect 241] found the same in four more. Both lived in the same blind spot: the
screen had no test. So the next question was how big that spot is.

	17 CRUD master screens
	 3 tested   item, ledger (both added yesterday), party
	14 never driven at all

Fourteen screens that render, list, filter and search, and which nothing had ever
asked to save a row.

### One test, eleven screens

Rather than fourteen files, one table-driven test: each master, the least it
needs to save, and where to look for the row. It runs the one thing a master
exists for.

	HSN code · purity · state · branch · ledger group · sale rate
	scheme · payroll component · retail point · card commission · packet

All eleven pass. It catches the class it was written for: putting back a single
`nullUUID` in the packet mapper fails it immediately.

### A correction to defect 241

Defect 241 said fifteen optional references were "all wrong the same way". Two of
them were not, and driving the screens is what showed it:

	a retail point must belong to a branch
	card type is required

**`retail_points.branch_id` and `card_commissions.card_type_id` are nullable
columns that the DOMAIN requires.** They could never have been left unset, so
those two were never broken in practice. The `nullUUID` fix is harmless there and
the reasoning behind it was wrong. **Thirteen were broken, not fifteen.**

That distinction only appears when you drive the screen. Reading the schema says
the column is nullable; reading the aggregate says the field is a plain uuid;
neither says the domain refuses a blank.

### What the failures turned out to be

Of the five that failed first time, **three were my own test's fault** — wrong
column names in two, and incomplete payloads in the others — and the three that
looked like defects were business rules doing their job:

	a scheme needs between 1 and 120 instalments
	a retail point must belong to a branch
	a commission has to say which card it is for

Recorded because "three master screens are broken" was the reading for about ten
minutes, and it was wrong.

## 244. Editing a master, driven for the first time — nothing wrong

[Defect 243] closed the create blind spot on the master screens. Editing is the
same blind spot one step further in: **a create test passes on a screen whose
update path is broken**, and an update that fails is exactly how 27% of the
shop's vouchers became uncorrectable ([defect 214]).

Nothing had ever driven one. Six masters are now exercised end to end — create,
then change a field, then read it back:

	HSN code      description
	purity        fineness
	state         abbreviation
	branch        code
	sale rate     name
	packet        remarks

**All six edit cleanly.** No defect.

### Proven not to be vacuous

A test that only ever passes proves nothing, and this one asserts a value came
back changed — which would hold if the update quietly did nothing and the value
happened to match. So it was pointed at a column the form never sends:

	state: kind came back "state" after editing it to "NEVER-SENT"

The assertion is live: an update that does not reach the column fails it.

### Two negatives in a row, and what that means

[Defect 242] swept the half-cast placeholders and found none. This drove every
master's edit and found none. **Two consecutive sweeps that found nothing, after
three that found nine defects between them.**

That is the shape a search should have when it is working: the classes with
members get emptied, and the ones without get closed. A sweep is worth running
precisely because you cannot tell which kind it is beforehand — and the ones that
find nothing cost an hour and buy the right to stop looking there.

## 245. Every write route checked for a permission, and the pairing that keeps two of them safe — MEDIUM (fixed)

Three screens are checked by name for permission holes. Nothing asked the
question of all of them, which matters because an ungated write is not hidden —
`CrudController.accessDenied` reads `if perm == nil { return false }`, so an
operation with no permission set is **open to any authenticated user**. On this
system that means any member of staff could raise a bill, set the day's gold rate
or hand over somebody's order.

Two checks now ask it across the board:

	15 of 15 hand-written write routes are behind a permission
	18 CRUD screens: every operation is either permitted or removed

Both pass. The finding is not a hole; it is what keeps two screens out of one.

### The pairing nobody was checking

	company.go   omits WithDeletePermission, calls WithoutDelete
	tagprint.go  omits Create and Delete permissions, calls WithoutCreate and WithoutDelete

Both are correct, and both are **one deleted line from being open to anybody**.
The safety comes from the `Without` call unregistering the route, not from the
missing permission — and `tagprint`'s own test comment says so: *"remove the
WithoutCreate and the screen is open to anybody."* Nothing paired the two, so
either could be removed as tidying-up and the tests would stay green.

The rule is now that each operation must be **permitted or removed, never merely
absent**.

### The check was blind to comments, and only breaking it showed that

The first version passed when `WithoutDelete` was commented out — the string is
still in the file. A screen whose delete had just been opened read as safe.

	company.go: neither WithDeletePermission nor WithoutDelete —
	the operation is registered with no permission

**That is the same comment-blindness as [defect 242]**, where prose mentioning
`$6` was counted as a use and reported thirty-one problems that were not there.
Twice in two days, in checks written a day apart. Comments are stripped in both
now.

It is also the argument for breaking every guard deliberately: this one passed,
looked right, and would have kept passing through the exact change it exists to
catch. Both are proven against a real break — a commented-out `WithoutDelete`,
and a `gate(...)` removed from the metal rate screen.

## 246. My own checkers were blind to comments — MEDIUM (fixed)

Comment-blindness has now appeared three times in three days:

	242   prose mentioning $6 counted as a use, reporting 31 problems that were not there
	245   a commented-out WithoutDelete counted as present, passing a screen whose delete had just been opened
	246   this

Twice was a coincidence. Three times is a class, so the question was asked of
every check that reads source text.

	tenant_scoping_test.go      strips
	placeholder_casts_test.go   strips
	check_unwritten_tables.py   DID NOT
	check_empty_columns.py      DID NOT

### Proven, not assumed

`check_unwritten_tables.py` decides whether a register has a writer by looking
for `INSERT INTO mcj_x`. One line appended to a controller —

	// A dead thought: INSERT INTO mcj_holidays (tenant_id) VALUES ($1)

— and `mcj_holidays` **dropped off the gap list entirely**. A comment was enough
to make the tool report that a table is written when nothing writes it.

That is the worst direction for this particular tool to be wrong in. It is the
one that found four defects by naming registers with readers and no writer, and
[defect 239] already had it overstating by a third in the other direction. A
tool that can be wrong both ways, quietly, is worse than no tool.

Both now strip line comments before matching, and both were proven the whole way
round: the same comment changes nothing, and a real `INSERT` in live code still
counts as a writer.

	holidays listed before = 1, with the comment = 1   (ignored)
	with real code = 0                                 (counted)

### The rule, written where it will be read

The helper carries the reason rather than the mechanism:

	A commented-out writer is not a writer, and a table named in prose is not a
	read. [...] three times in three days, which is why it is a function and not
	a habit.

`//` preceded by `:` is left alone, so a URL is not truncated mid-line.

### Worth saying plainly

Four sweeps this session were run with these tools, and their numbers went into
four defect write-ups. **The numbers happen to be unaffected** — no controller in
this codebase has a commented-out INSERT, which is why the counts did not move
when the bug was fixed. That is luck, and it is the second time this week a
tool's output has been believed before it was tested.

## 247. All seventeen master screens driven, and the last unproven tool proven — nothing wrong

[Defect 243] drove eleven master screens and [defect 244] their edits. Three were
out of reach of that table and were left: **company** is a singleton from its own
constructor, the two **bands** come from a definition list rather than a path
constant, and **tag print setup** has no create at all.

All three are now driven.

	company        saves the shop's own particulars
	value band     saves
	weight band    saves
	tag print      404 — WithoutCreate, refused by design

**Sixteen of seventeen create a row; the seventeenth proves it refuses because
the route is absent rather than merely ungated**, which is the distinction
[defect 245] was about. Every master screen in the system has now been asked to
do the thing it exists for.

### The last tool without a proof

Five of the six checks had been shown to catch something real. `check_empty_columns.py`
had not — it reported 31 columns and nothing had ever confirmed it would notice
one *stopping* being empty, which is the direction that matters when data starts
arriving.

	return_note listed as empty          1
	after filling one row of seven       0
	reverted                             1

It notices. The row was put back.

### Where that leaves the checks

	cmd/reconcile              proven — a bill moved by ₹1 is caught
	check_invariants.py        proven — three planted faults, each named
	check_unwritten_tables.py  proven — a comment no longer hides a gap, real code still counts
	check_empty_columns.py     proven — a single filled row drops a column off
	check_report_footers.py    proven when written — defect 189
	status_figures.py          proven repeatedly — it has caught every stale count this week

**Every check that guards this system has now been shown to fail when it should.**
That is worth stating because three of the last eight defects were in the checks
themselves, not the product, and a guard nobody has broken on purpose is a guess
about its own behaviour.

## 248. A re-tagged piece could not name where it came from, and defect 226 was wrong about why

Defect 226 gave the tagging screen its arrival-document field, offering the right
series for each source: a purchase bill for `purc`, an old-gold bill for `og`, a
sale return for `ret`. For `stk` -- a piece re-tagged out of existing stock, and
the largest group by far -- it offered nothing, and I wrote the reason into the
code as a fact:

	an STK number, which is the shop's own counter with no document behind it

That was wrong. There is a document. `mcj_stock_conversions` holds 859 of them,
STK/00001 to STK/00859, each a record of stock being melted or remade, with
1,242 pieces itemised in `mcj_stock_conversion_pieces`. It was sitting in the
unwritten-tables list the whole time, which is where I found it.

### Why the wrong reason looked right

	tags carrying an STK number          2,401
	distinct STK numbers referenced        143
	conversion documents captured          859  (STK/00001 - STK/00859)
	of the 143 that resolve                 48   <- first written as 55; see defect 249

Only 48 of 143 STK references match a captured conversion. The other 95 run up
to STK/15863 and belong to years the conversion history does not reach -- the
same current-year-only window as the invoices in defect 238. Checking a handful
of the shop's recent tags against the conversion table would have found nothing
most of the time, and I took that for absence of the series rather than absence
of the older half of it.

(The count in this section first read 55. Seven of those were older documents
that happen to carry the same number -- the STK series restarts. Corrected here
and explained in defect 249.)

### Fixed

`arrivalDocuments` now has a `stk` case offering the conversion vouchers, newest
first, each labelled with its date. The comment that asserted the opposite has
been replaced with what is actually true, including why it looked otherwise.

Driven end to end -- a piece re-tagged against STK/00859:

	POST /mcj/tag  action=save source=stk came_on=STK/00859   303
	mcj_stock_items.voucher_no                                STK/00859
	mcj_stock_movements                                       NEW-BAR

The test row was removed; tags 2,816, movements 9,036, conversions 859, all
exact.

### What this does not do

It offers the 859 documents that exist. A piece re-tagged out of stock that
predates the captured window still has nothing to name, and the field stays
empty -- correctly, because the document it would name was never migrated. The
conversion screen itself is still unbuilt; this defect makes the conversions
*referenceable*, not *enterable*. That remains open.

### Method note

Two of the last three defects came from the unwritten-tables list, and this one
also corrected a mistaken explanation I had committed to a comment. A table
nobody writes is worth reading before concluding what it means -- and an
explanation of an absence deserves the same second source as a figure does
(see the standing rule on verifying numbers). I asserted this one from a sample
and was wrong on 48 counts.

## 249. What the conversion flag means, settled for half of it — and the STK number is not unique

> **THE CENTRAL CLAIM BELOW IS WRONG AND IS RETRACTED. See defect 250.**
> The "gold is conserved" finding compared a document's listed pieces against
> the tags naming that document, and those are **the same pieces** -- 47 of 48
> carry the same barcode on both sides. The weights agreed because it was one
> set of gold weighed twice. What survives, and what replaces it, is in defect
> 250. The section on the STK number not being unique is unaffected and still
> holds.

Building the conversion screen means knowing what a conversion *is*. The
migration that created the table said, deliberately, that it could not be known:

	THE DIRECTION FLAG IS CARRIED UNINTERPRETED, and that is deliberate.
	... two readings, one contradicting the column name and one contradicting
	the data, and nothing in the capture settles it.

That was right when it was written. It is no longer right, because defect 248
built a link that did not exist then: a tag naming the document it arrived on.
That gives the output side of a conversion, which the conversion table never had.

### Direction 0 is a melt-and-remake, and the gold is conserved  [RETRACTED -- see defect 250]

Take the documents where both sides are captured -- the pieces listed on the
document, and the tags naming that document as their arrival:

	direction 0    51 docs    422 pieces in   2,283.888 g   ->   348 tags out   2,294.940 g
	direction 1     4 docs      4 pieces in      34.720 g   ->    25 tags out       2.480 g

Aggregates are weak evidence, so per document:

	direction 0    32 of 51 balance to within 50 mg
	direction 1     0 of 4

**32 documents where what went in and what came out agree to a twentieth of a
gram.** That is not a coincidence of totals; it is the same gold, weighed twice.
So a direction-0 document is a melt-and-remake: the listed pieces are consumed,
the tags naming it are produced.

Note this is the opposite of what the column name says. The legacy column is
`add`, and 0 is the value that adds. The migration flagged that contradiction
and declined to resolve it; the weights resolve it.

### Direction 1 is still not settled, and I am not going to guess

	519 documents, every one a single piece
	only 4 of 519 ever produced a tag
	375 of 519 name a barcode with no tag on file
	average net 14.767 g against 7.141 g for direction 0
	heavily silver -- SILVER MURTI, SILVER MUKUT -- and 
	  some carry net weight 0 against a piece count of 3

Four documents is not evidence, and none of them balances. The screen will show
direction 1 as recorded, without a label, exactly as the migration decided.
**Half the flag is now known; the other half is not, and saying so is the point.**

### The STK number is not unique, which makes defect 248's figure wrong

The join that produced all of the above matches a tag to a conversion by voucher
number. That is unsafe:

	the 32 that balance      every tag created 2026-04-04 .. 2026-08-18, inside the window
	the 19 that do not       tags reaching back to 2024-04-03
	                         3 documents have tags created BEFORE the document existed

A tag cannot arrive on a document that does not exist yet. **The STK series
restarts, and those 19 are matching an older year's document carrying the same
number.**

	STK numbers on tags that resolve, by number alone     55
	... that survive a date check                         48

**Defect 248 said 55. The honest figure is 48**, and it has been corrected there
and in the code comment. The fix itself is unaffected: a tag being written today
can only mean the document of that number that exists today. It is reading the
*history* that is ambiguous, not writing the present.

### What this changes about the screen

It has to be built knowing three things that were not known this morning: a
direction-0 document consumes its listed pieces and produces tags, a direction-1
document is unexplained and must not be labelled, and the voucher number is not
a key across years. Building it before establishing these would have baked in a
guess about all three.

### Method note

Defect 248 corrected a false explanation. This one corrects the number in that
same correction, one iteration later, and both were found the same way -- by
asking the data a second question rather than accepting the first answer.
**The rule about verifying a figure against a second source applies to figures
written while fixing a figure.**

## 250. I proved the same gold weighs the same as itself, and called it conservation

Defect 249, written one iteration ago, claimed the direction flag was settled for
direction 0: a melt-and-remake, with the pieces listed on a document going in and
the tags naming that document coming out, balancing to within 50 mg on 32
documents. **That is wrong.** The two sides are the same pieces.

	listed pieces on the 32 balancing documents            48
	that carry the same barcode as a tag naming the doc    47

Forty-seven of forty-eight. The weights agreed because I weighed one set of
gold twice and subtracted it from itself. A balance that cannot fail is not
evidence, and I presented it as the strongest evidence in the write-up.

### What I should have asked, and didn't

The check that breaks it is one line -- *are these the same barcodes?* -- and I
had every reason to run it. Defect 29 records that this shop reuses barcodes.
Defect 249's own second half is about matching on an identifier that turns out
not to be unique. I ran that check on the voucher number, found the collision,
corrected defect 248's figure, and wrote it up as a lesson about verifying
identifiers -- **without applying it to the barcode in the very same query.**

There was also a signal in plain view that I explained away: 346 of the 486
direction-0 listed pieces are still on the shelf today. I noticed it, attributed
it to barcode reuse, and moved on. Pieces that were melted are not on the shelf.
The data was saying the pieces were never consumed, and I had a story ready for
why it didn't count.

### What actually holds

Redone with the date restriction defect 249 established, so no cross-year
collisions:

	documents with tags naming them        48   all direction 0
	tags naming them                      317
	of those tags, also listed as a
	  piece on the same document          317   every one
	direction-1 documents with tags         0

So a direction-0 conversion document is **a tagging source**: the pieces listed
on it are the pieces tagged against it, in every one of 317 cases. It brings
stock in. That is the same role a purchase bill plays, which is exactly what
defect 248's fix assumed, so **the fix stands and this changes nothing about it.**

Direction 1 has **no tags at all** once dates are respected -- the 4 documents
and 25 tags reported in defect 249 were every one a cross-year collision.

### What is consistent, and is not being claimed as proven

	direction 1    519 docs, 519 pieces, one per document, average net 14.767 g
	direction 0    340 docs, 723 pieces, 2.13 per document, average net  7.141 g

One heavy piece out, several lighter finished pieces in, is what melting and
remaking looks like, and it fits the shape of both halves. It is **not proven**:
no document links a direction-1 piece to a direction-0 one, and the totals do not
balance either (7,664.013 g against 5,163.068 g). It is written here as a shape
the data is consistent with, and the screen will not label the flag on the
strength of it.

The reading does contradict the legacy column name -- `add`, where 1 would be the
value that adds -- which is the contradiction the original migration flagged and
declined to resolve. **It was right to decline. I was not right to resolve it.**

### Consequence for the screen

The conversion screen cannot be built as "choose pieces to melt", because the
captured data contains no input side. What a direction-0 document actually is,
on the evidence, is the document a batch of new tags is raised against. That is
buildable and useful; the melting half is not, on this data.

### Method note

Three iterations, three corrections: defect 248 corrected a false explanation,
249 corrected 248's number, and 250 retracts 249's headline. The pattern is not
that checking is working -- it is that **I keep publishing the first coherent
story and checking it afterwards.** 249 even contained the words "aggregates are
weak evidence, so per document" immediately before presenting a per-document
figure that could not fail. Rigour applied to the wrong question reads exactly
like rigour.

## 251. The melt hypothesis, tested before it was written up, and refused

Defect 250 ended with a shape the data was "consistent with" -- one heavy piece
out under flag 1, several lighter pieces in under flag 0 -- and said explicitly
it was not being claimed. This entry tests it, before writing anything down as
true, because the last three entries each published a story and checked it
afterwards.

### The test, chosen so it could fail

Defect 250 established that 317 of the pieces listed on the 48 date-safe
direction-0 documents are the tags raised against those documents. They are not
all of them:

	listed pieces on those 48 documents      419
	that are tags raised against the doc     317
	that are not                             102

If a conversion melts pieces down and remakes them, the 102 are the input and
the 317 are the output, and on a document carrying both the two should weigh
about the same. 17 documents carry both. That is the test.

	documents with pieces on both sides       17
	balancing to within 50 mg                  0
	balancing to within half a gram            0
	totals                             1,067.346 g tagged   783.028 g untagged

**Zero of seventeen.** The hypothesis makes a prediction, the prediction is
checkable, and it is wrong. Written down as a refusal rather than a finding,
which is what it is.

### What the 102 are, as far as the data says

	name a barcode with no tag on file anywhere    71
	name a tag that exists                         31
	  of those, a tag predating the document       19
	  of those, a tag no longer on the shelf        8
	blank barcode                                   0

Not explicable from what was captured. The migration already noted that 612 of
all 1,242 pieces name a barcode with no tag on file, so the 71 are the same
phenomenon and not new information.

### The decision this forces

**The conversion screen is not being built, and that is the outcome of this
entry rather than a postponement.** An entry screen has to know what a document
does to stock. Three iterations have produced three readings of that -- a
melt-and-remake (retracted), a tagging source (true of 317 of 419 pieces), and
now a mixed document whose remainder resists explanation. The Stock Journal
report already shows all 859 of them, so the shop can read its own history; what
is missing is the ability to write one, and **writing one requires deciding what
the other 102 pieces mean, which the capture does not support.**

Building it anyway would mean choosing a meaning and then teaching the shop to
enter data in that shape, which is how a wrong reading becomes permanent.

### What was built instead

A fourteenth invariant, guarding the one thing that is established:

	a tag naming a conversion is listed on it        317 of 317, 0 exceptions

Proven not to be vacuous -- a planted tag naming STK/00859 without a matching
piece is caught, `13 of 14 rules hold`, and removing it restores 14 of 14. The
rule checks dates, because without that restriction it reports **56 exceptions**
that are only the STK series restarting (defect 249). A rule that fails on
history gets switched off, which is the point of the allowance column.

### Method note

Four iterations on one table, three of them corrections. The difference in this
one is only the order: the check that would have refuted the claim was run
before the claim was written, not after. That ordering is the whole of the
lesson from defects 248, 249 and 250, and it cost nothing here -- the query was
no harder to write today than it would have been tomorrow, after it had been
published as fact.

## 252. Three master screens could delete themselves out from under live data

Defects 243 and 244 drove create and edit on every master. Delete was the one
operation never driven, and the only one that can destroy something. Driven now,
in two parts: can a master be deleted at all, and does it stop when the row is
in use.

The first is fine -- all eleven masters in the table delete cleanly. The second
was not.

	mcj_schemes            -> mcj_scheme_enrolments.scheme_id      239 rows
	mcj_payroll_components -> mcj_staff_components.component_id     46 rows
	mcj_packets            -> mcj_stock_stones.packet_id           107 rows

Each foreign key was `ON DELETE SET NULL`. The delete came back **303 -- see
other**, the ordinary success redirect, and the rows that pointed at the master
survived pointing at nothing. No error, no warning, nothing on the screen to say
anything had happened to them.

Deleting the shop's one scheme would have left **239 customers enrolled in
nothing**, with no way afterwards to say what any of them had been paying into.
The scheme collection screen is still blocked on a question to the owner (defect
233), so those enrolments are the only record of the arrangement that exists.

### Fixed

`migrations/mcj-1787411000.sql` changes the three to `ON DELETE RESTRICT`. The
delete is now refused by the database.

The columns stay NULLABLE, which is a different question and was decided on
evidence: 134 of the 239 enrolments name a ledger that was never in the address
book, and 5 tags carry a purity with no fineness anywhere (blocker B2). Those
rows must be storable. **What no migration argues for anywhere is a master
vacating the column on its way out** -- the delete action was carried along with
the nullability rather than chosen.

### The eleven left alone deliberately

Fourteen masters have a SET NULL reference with no RESTRICT anywhere, including
`mcj_vouchers`, whose deletion would detach sales invoices, old gold lines and
purchase invoices at once. Eleven of the fourteen have **no delete route
registered anywhere in the application**, so nothing can reach them. They are
left as they are: a constraint added for a screen that does not exist protects
nothing, and would have to be revisited when the real screen decides its own
rule. The list is in this entry so the next person building one of those screens
finds it.

### The test passed against the bug first

The first version rolled back to a savepoint before checking the state, because
a refused delete aborts the transaction. That rollback also undid a *successful*
delete, so the test passed on the unfixed schema for all three masters. It was
caught by asking the question this doc keeps having to ask -- does this fail when
it should? -- and the answer was no.

Now the status is read before the rollback, and a delete that comes back under
400 fails on the spot. Verified by weakening the migration's own Up to SET NULL
and running it again:

	scheme:            deleting a master that is in use came back 303
	payroll component: deleting a master that is in use came back 303
	packet:            deleting a master that is in use came back 303

All three fail without the fix and pass with it.

### What the refusal looks like, which is not good

The database raises a foreign-key violation and the CRUD builder has no handler
for it, so the user gets an error rather than a sentence explaining that the
scheme has 239 people in it. **The data is safe and the message is poor**, which
is the right way round, but it is not finished. Logged here rather than fixed,
because the fix belongs in the shared CRUD builder and touches every master
screen at once.

### Method note

Third time this week a checker or test has been the defect rather than the
product (242, 245, 246, and the savepoint here). The pattern in all four is the
same: the check was written, it went green, and green was taken as evidence.
**A test's first green run against code that is known to be broken is the only
cheap chance to find out whether it tests anything.**

## 253. The refusal reached the server log and nothing else

Defect 252 stopped three masters being deleted while in use, and said the
message was poor and left it. This is that half.

### The repository's message could never have reached anybody

The obvious place to explain a refusal is where it is detected, so the tenant
scoping decorator now turns a foreign-key violation into a sentence:

	this cannot be deleted while scheme enrolments still refer to it

Driven, it changed nothing on screen. The CRUD controller every master screen is
built from does this:

	if _, err := c.service.Delete(ctx, idFieldValue); err != nil {
	    log.Printf("[CrudController.Delete] Failed to delete entity %s: %v", id, err)
	    errorMsg, _ := c.localize(ctx, errFailedToDelete, "Failed to delete data")
	    http.Error(w, errorMsg, http.StatusInternalServerError)

**The error is logged and then discarded**, and a fixed string is sent instead.
No message written in a repository, a service or a domain object can reach a
user through this path. That is worth knowing beyond this defect: it is where
every master screen's delete errors go.

### What was done instead

`Errors.FailedToDelete` is a translation key, and the mcj bundle overrides it:

	This could not be deleted. It is most likely still in use by other records --
	a scheme with people enrolled, a packet holding stones, or a payroll
	component on a salary. Detach those first, then delete it.

Proven to be the thing doing the work: with the key removed the test fails with
`Failed to delete data`, and with it restored all three masters pass. Full suite
green, 18 packages.

### What this is not

It is **generic**. It cannot say *239 people are enrolled in this scheme*,
because the string is chosen before the error is looked at -- the SDK localises
a constant, not the failure. It names the three things it is most likely to be,
which is a guess printed in advance, and it will read oddly on a master that
fails for some fourth reason.

The honest fix is a delete handler of our own that counts the references and
says the number. That means intercepting the route ahead of the CRUD controller
for all eighteen generated screens, and it was not done here: the risk of
rerouting every master screen outweighs a better sentence on an action that is
now safe. **Recorded as the known next step rather than left as a vague
intention.**

The repository translation is kept even though no user sees it. The SDK logs the
error it discards, so the sentence lands in the server log, where the shape of
the failure is otherwise a bare SQLSTATE.

### Method note

The first version of this fix was written, built, and would have been reported
as done on the strength of it compiling. It took driving the screen to find that
the message went nowhere. **Three of this week's defects were checks that passed
without checking; this is the same error one layer up -- a fix that worked
everywhere except where anyone could see it.**

## 254. The one unexplained test failure, and the guess about it that could not have been right

`TestCategorise_FiltersToUntaggedOnly` failed once under the full suite on 22
August and has not recurred. STATUS.md carried it under "Known unknowns" with a
hypothesis:

	The screen carries a `LIMIT 200`, which is the kind of thing that only
	breaks once something leaves enough rows behind

**That mechanism is impossible**, and the harness says so plainly:

	Parallel harnesses (separate test binaries, and t.Parallel within one)
	each provision their OWN per-test database

Every suite runs against a database of its own, created empty and migrated. No
other test can leave a row behind for this one to trip over, so the count the
LIMIT applies to is whatever this test seeded -- three rows. The guess was
written without reading how the harness isolates, and it sent the question in a
direction it could never have come back from.

### Which also means something better

Tests do not run against the shop's data at all. Every baseline check in this
document that was taken after a test run -- 2,816 tags, 239 enrolments, 859
conversions -- was measuring a database the tests cannot reach. That is the
right answer, and it was being taken on faith.

It also means an experiment run yesterday was meaningless: three constraints
were altered on the live database to see whether a test would catch it, and the
test never saw them. That was noticed at the time and the migration file was
flipped instead, which is what actually proved the point.

### Not reproduced

	43 runs of TestCategorise, including -count=40 in one process   0 failures

Not reproduced is not the same as not there, so nothing is being closed.

### What was done instead of guessing again

**The seed's lookups were scoped to their tenant.** Three of them read across
the whole table:

	SELECT id FROM mcj_categories WHERE name='RINGS'

With per-test databases this is safe today. It is not safe by design -- it
returns whichever row the planner reaches first, and any change that shares a
database between suites turns it into a test that categorises its tags against
another tenant's category. Fixed because it is a hazard, not because it is the
cause.

**The failure now records why it failed.** The one thing the 22 August run left
behind was a sentence with no facts in it -- not the status code, not what the
tenant held, not even which of the two assertions fired. Proven by forcing it:

	an untagged tag is missing from the untagged list.
	  status         200
	  body           518304 bytes
	  seeded TAG%    3
	  untagged rows  2   (the screen caps its list at 200)
	  rows in tenant 3

If it happens again, the run will say whether the list was short, the request
failed, or the rows were never seeded.

### Method note

This is the second time in two days that a written-down explanation turned out
to be the defect rather than a description of one (defect 248 was the first).
Both were plausible, both went unchecked because they explained the symptom, and
**both were contradicted by a comment in the code they were about.**

## 255. Nineteen tags were refused with an instruction the screen would not let anyone follow

This started as a suspicion that STATUS.md was stale. `blockers.md` marks B9
**ANSWERED**; STATUS.md still lists it twice, once under "What it cannot do" as
*Bill the 165 items whose stored price will not reproduce*. One of the two had
to be wrong.

**STATUS was right.** The sale screen refuses these tags, and refuses them for a
good reason -- the formula reproduces 91% of computed prices, and billing a
figure it cannot stand behind would be worse than refusing. The message it gave:

	the formula does not reproduce this tag's recorded price
	(38,760.00 against 42,140.00) — price it by hand

**There was nowhere to price it by hand.** The box beside a refusal is attached
in one place only:

	if making.certified {
	    refusal.PriceField = agreedPriceField + barcode

A certified piece gets a box. A tag the formula cannot reproduce got the
instruction and no box, on the same screen, three lines apart. Nothing else on
the sale screen prices a tagged piece either -- the making inputs belong to
priced rows, and a refused tag has no row. The only route left was to bill it as
an untagged item, retyping a piece that is already on the shelf and leaving the
tag on it.

### Measured across the whole shelf

Every one of the 2,575 in-stock tags was put through the screen, in batches:

	certified, box offered            565
	cannot reproduce, no box           19
	scanned twice (B8's duplicate)      1

**19 tags, ₹26,89,060.47**, could not be sold by any route the screen offers.
Not the 165 B9 counts -- that figure covers all items including those long sold;
19 is what is on the shelf today.

### Fixed

A tag that fails the reproduction check now returns `handPriced`, which offers
the same box a certified piece gets, seeded with the tag's own total. Driven end
to end on the real barcode:

	93150410  refused, box agreed_93150410 offered, suggested 42,140.00
	          agreed 42,140.00 entered -> priced row, fixed price, 42,140.00

The wording changed with it, from "price it by hand" to "enter the price agreed
with the customer", which is what the biller is actually doing and matches the
certified case.

Regression test added, and **proven to fail without the fix**: with the box
condition put back to `certified` only, it reports *refused with no way to price
it — the instruction cannot be followed*.

### Two things I got wrong on the way

**Read absence of refusals as success.** The first sweep reported "all 60
priced". Nothing had priced: the POST was rejected with *"Choose a customer."*
before pricing ran, and the barcodes I found in the response were the textarea
echoing my own input back. Checking that a positive marker was present, not that
a negative one was absent, is what caught it.

**Nearly filed rate movement as a defect.** Comparing computed prices against
stored ones for 200 tags showed 107 disagreeing, which looks alarming until you
notice the screen prices at *today's* metal rate and the stored total was set at
the tag's creation-date rate. The self-check in the code gets this right -- it
recalculates `atTagRate` before comparing. I had to read it to find that out,
having already measured the wrong thing.

### Still not billable

Barcode **86065435**, refused as *scanned twice*, because two tags share it.
That is blocker B8 and needs the shop to re-tag one of the two pieces. Correct
behaviour, unchanged.

## 256. The quote screen spent a fortnight telling customers the opposite of what the sale screen had learned

Defect 255 fixed a refusal that gave no way forward, so the obvious next question
is whether that refusal has siblings. It does, and the sibling is worse: it is
not a missing box, it is a **statement the project has already disproved**.

`quote.go` refused every certified tag with this:

	This tag is certified, and certified goods carry a pricing step that did
	not survive the capture. Quoting it would risk being wrong by a large
	amount rather than a small one. See blocker B9.

**There is no such step.** Defect 228 established it from the shop's own bills:
of the 129 certified pieces sold, ONE went out at the tag's stored price and
NONE at a computed one -- 0.44 to 3.47 times the tag, with 125 of the 129 lines
carrying a different metal rate. The price is agreed across the counter, the way
old gold and coin orders are. `blockers.md` has said **ANSWERED** since.

Defect 229 changed the sale screen accordingly. The quote screen was not
changed, and went on citing an answered blocker as an open one.

	certified tags on the shelf     566
	value                           2,84,75,794.50

**22% of the shelf by count, 20% by value, could not be quoted** -- the figures
from defect 161, re-measured today and identical. Defect 161 saw this and
recorded it as correct behaviour: *"Refusing is right while the pricing step is
unknown."* It was right when written. Two days later the step was known, and
nothing went back to the screen that assumed otherwise.

### Fixed

A quote is a read-only report, so there is no box to type an agreed price into
and nothing has been invented. What it can do is give the counter what it needs
to open the conversation:

	DIAMOND BANGLE          barcode 53710364 · on the shelf
	Priced at the counter   This piece is certified. Its price is agreed with
	                        the customer rather than computed...
	The tag's own price     what the counter starts from      15,97,755.00
	Certificate charge      billed separately and NOT added      5,145.00

Driven on the exact barcode defect 161 used to demonstrate the refusal.

The same treatment went to the tag-cannot-be-reproduced refusal, which ended
"Price it by hand" on a screen with no way to price anything. It keeps its
explanation and both figures, because the size of the gap is what lets somebody
judge it, and it now also carries the tag's own price as the figure to work
from.

### The shape of this defect

Neither screen was wrong in isolation. The sale screen learned something, the
blocker doc recorded it, and **the third place that had encoded the old belief
was never revisited** -- and it was encoded as a sentence shown to a customer,
not as a comment. Defects 248 and 254 were the same shape in comments and in
STATUS.md.

What makes this one worse is that the wrong belief was *cited*: the message
pointed at blocker B9 by name, which reads as a claim that has been checked.
**A reference to a blocker is a claim about the blocker's current state, and
nothing checks those.** There is no tool that finds a screen citing an answered
blocker; that is a gap this defect does not close.

### The gap this closed

The write-up above ended by naming a gap: *"A reference to a blocker is a claim
about the blocker's current state, and nothing checks those."* Leaving that as a
sentence would have been the same mistake one layer up, so it is now a tool.

`tools/check_blocker_citations.py` reads every blocker heading in `blockers.md`,
then scans the Go and templ sources for **string literals** naming one. A
blocker that still wants something -- OPEN, CRITICAL, SECURITY, TIME-SENSITIVE,
NARROWED -- may be cited freely. One that has been settled -- ANSWERED,
RESOLVED, CLOSED, WORKED AROUND -- may not.

**Comments are stripped first and are never flagged.** A comment saying "B9 is
answered, see defect 228" is history and is exactly right; a sentence shown to a
customer is a live claim. That distinction is the whole tool, and getting it
backwards is what defect 246 did three times running.

It found one more on its first run, which the sweep by hand had missed:

	modules/mcj/presentation/reports/ratio.go
	  "the shop's purchase cost is not recorded against a tag anywhere
	   (blocker B9 and defect 79)"

Not merely stale -- **the wrong blocker**. B9 is about 165 prices that will not
reproduce; cost of goods sold is defect 79's subject and nothing to do with it.
A reader following that citation would have found an answered blocker about a
different question. The reference is gone; defect 79 stays, because that part is
right.

Proven three ways rather than assumed:

	a live string citing B20 (RESOLVED)      caught
	the same words in a comment             ignored
	B3 (NARROWED) on the label screen        allowed -- it asks for exactly
	                                         what B3 still wants

That third one was a real false positive on the first version, which counted
NARROWED as settled. The label screen tells the user to compare a printed label
against a real tag, which is precisely what B3 is narrowed to. **A checker that
flags a message doing its job teaches people to ignore it.**

## 257. A day's trade, run end to end for the first time by a test — and the bill it raised did not add up

The goal this work is measured against is *run a real day's trade end to end*.
Every screen in that sequence has its own tests. **Nothing had ever run them in
order against one shop.** The sequence was rehearsed by hand twice and then
existed only as a memory of those two afternoons.

`daystrade_e2e_test.go` runs it: set the morning's gold rate, tag a piece against
it, sell that piece, take the cash, and check the books. Three screens chained,
which is where the failures this file can catch actually live -- a tag priced at
yesterday's rate, a bill that cannot find a piece the tag screen just made, a
voucher that balances alone but not against the stock that left.

It found one on the first run.

### The header did not agree with its own lines

	tag DAY001         12 g at the day's 7,000 = 84,000 metal
	                   plus 200/g making        =  2,400
	                   tag total                   86,400

	bill line          amount 86,400   making 2,400      correct
	bill header        goods_amount 84,000                short by the making
	SUM(line.amount)   86,400                             out by 2,400
	bill_total         88,992.00                          correct

**The customer is charged correctly** -- the taxable value and every ledger
posting use the line totals, and 86,400 at 3% is 88,992. What was wrong is the
header column, which was adding up `price.Amount` (metal and stones) and leaving
the making charge out.

### It contradicts the shop's own convention, measured

	captured bills                                        224
	where goods_amount = SUM(line.amount)                 224
	lines carrying a making charge                        279 of 367, 14,35,896.00

On the shop's own bills the making charge sits **inside** goods_amount and
`making_charge` is the memo saying how much of it was making. GST/2627/00001 is
goods 49,709.00 with making 4,281.00 within it, not beside it. Every one of the
224 agrees.

So this is not a matter of taste. **Invariant rule 1 -- "every bill's lines add
up to its goods" -- would have failed on every bill this screen raised carrying
a making charge**, and the rule is right; the screen was wrong.

### Why nothing caught it

Only three tests read `goods_amount` from the database, and two of them bill a
**fixed-price** piece -- a certified one and a hand-priced one -- where the whole
price is one figure and there is no separable making to lose. The third seeds an
invoice directly. **The one case that could expose it, an ordinary tag with a
making charge billed through the screen, had no test at all.**

The screen tests do check making: `TestSale_PricesAtTodaysRateWithLocalTax`
looks for "63,000.00" on the rendered page, and the page was always right. The
page is not the books.

### Fixed

`goods` now accumulates `l.price.Total`. The lines, the taxable value, the ledger
postings and the customer's total are unchanged -- only the header column moves,
from 84,000 to 86,400, which is what the shop writes.

Proven: with the old line put back the day's-trade test reports *the bill's
lines do not add up to its goods — out by 2400.00*, and restoring it passes.
Full suite green, 18 packages.

### What the test does not yet cover

Old gold. The day it runs is a rate, a tag, a sale and a receipt; taking metal
in over the counter is a fourth screen and a second voucher, and it needs its own
seed. Stated rather than implied, because a test named for a day's trade invites
the assumption that it covers the whole day.

### The old gold half, added — and nothing wrong with it

Defect 257 ended by naming what the day's-trade test did not cover: taking metal
in over the counter, a fourth screen and a second voucher. That is now in the
same test, on the same day, against the same shop.

	afternoon    10.000 g gross, 1.000 less, tunch 91.6, agreed 1,20,000
	booked       one lot, 9.000 g net, 1,20,000.00
	vouchers     2 raised, both balancing to the paisa

**Nothing was wrong.** A sale and a purchase on one day was the case worth
checking -- a shared voucher number, or a ledger one posting expects to find as
the other left it -- and both postings are clean and separate.

Recorded because a negative result from a test written to find something is
worth as much as the entry above it, and because the next person to wonder
whether the two halves of a counter day interfere should not have to find out
again.

### A trap removed from the test itself

Proving the new assertions were not vacuous produced this:

	the lot's net weight is 9.000, want 9.000

The wanted figure was written twice -- once in the comparison, once in the
message -- so changing the comparison alone left the message asserting that
nothing was wrong. In normal running the two agree and it reads correctly, which
is exactly why it would survive. It is named once now and used for both.

A failure message that can disagree with its own test is the same shape as the
savepoint in defect 252 and the three comment-blind checkers in defect 246: the
check works, and what it reports about itself does not.

## 258. The report that asks how old the money is aged the shop's oldest stock as its newest

Found while chaining sell → refund → sell again (below, and nothing wrong with
that). A comment in `tag.go` says `last_received_date` differs from
`created_date` "only where a piece went out and came back". Checking that led
somewhere else.

	tags where last_received_date > created_date        2
	of those, carrying a SALE-RET movement              0
	returned barcodes with a tag on file               10
	of those, last_received_date updated on return      0

**The comment's reason is not supported.** One of the two went out to
hallmarking and came back (`ISS-HM`, `REC-HM`); the other has no round trip at
all. And a return does not touch the field -- which is correct, because the
legacy system did not either, on none of its 10 returned tags.

But the arithmetic left 120 tags unaccounted for, and those are the finding.

### created_date is not when the piece arrived

	tags where last_received_date is EARLIER            120
	all marked is_opening                               120
	created on 2024-04-01, a financial-year start       119
	their real receipt dates run back to           2017-03-26

For opening stock the two dates answer different questions. `created_date` is
the day somebody keyed the shelf into the books; `last_received_date` is when
the piece actually arrived.

`openingstock.go` grouped by `extract(year from created_date)`, under a comment
saying *"the question is how old the money is"*, and the whole report is
filtered to `is_opening` -- so this was not an edge case in it, **it was the
case**.

	                        by created_date        by arrival
	three years or older    260 tags               377 tags
	                        14,40,284.59           74,48,288.10

**117 tags worth 60,08,003.51 were counted as current stock when they are three
years old or more.** 95 of them, ₹52,17,407.82, arrived in 2021. The report
exists to find money that has been sitting, and it was hiding five sixths of it.

### Fixed

Aged by the earlier of the two dates. Driven on the running screen, and the
footer now reads what the SQL predicted, to the rupee:

	1571 tag(s) · 377 of them acquired in 2023 or earlier · of which 74,48,288.10

"tagged" became "acquired" in that sentence, because it is no longer the
tagging date being counted. The existing test that asserted the old wording was
updated with it, and a new one seeds a piece keyed in on the opening day but
received five years earlier -- **proven to fail without the fix**: *a piece
bought in 2021 is reported as 2026 stock*.

### On the figure in this entry

An earlier draft of it said 59,08,003.51, summed by hand from a listing that had
been cut off at twelve rows. The query says 60,08,003.51. The hand figure was
wrong by a lakh and would have read just as convincingly.

### The chain that started this, which found nothing

sell → refund → sell again now runs as a test. The existing return test puts a
tag back on the shelf, but the tag it returns is **seeded** sold -- a row
inserted with `in_stock` false, never carried there by a bill. So a real sale
followed by a real refund had never been driven.

	sold      off the shelf, one SALE-GST movement
	refunded  back on the shelf, one SALE-RET movement
	sold again  accepted, two bills, one piece, off the shelf at the end
	vouchers  all balancing

Clean. Worth having: a return is the one operation that reverses another, and if
a sale left anything a refund does not undo, the second sale is where it would
show -- by which point there are two bills and one piece.

## 259. A table that looks like a bill cross-reference, and would attribute 83 bills to the wrong customer

`sale_bill_link` sits in the dump with 135 rows, never loaded and referenced
nowhere. The name and the shape both suggest a useful thing -- a mapping from
one bill number to another -- which is exactly why it is worth writing down what
it actually contains.

	rows                                     135
	where the two numbers differ             133
	mcj_bill values that are real bills      135   all of them
	test_bill values that are real bills      85

	mcj_bill    GST/2627/00001 .. GST/2627/00220
	test_bill   GST/2627/00001 .. GST/2627/00338

The shop's own bills stop at 00224. The other series runs to **00338**, 114
documents further, and one `mcj_bill` maps to two of them -- GST/2627/00008 to
both 00013 and 00014. So `test_bill` is not a renumbering of the same documents;
it is a different, longer series from somewhere else.

### The part that matters

Of the 133 differing rows, 83 name a `test_bill` that IS a real bill in this
shop's books. **All 83 of those belong to a different party.**

	differing rows                                   133
	whose test_bill is a real bill                    83
	and that bill belongs to a different customer     83   every one

So a screen or report that loaded this table and used it to cross-reference a
bill would, on 83 bills out of 135, hand back a document belonging to somebody
else -- with a real number, a real customer, and a real amount on it. Nothing
about the result would look wrong.

### Left unloaded, deliberately, and now on the record

This is not a defect in the code: nothing loads it and nothing reads it, which
is correct. It is written up because *not loading a table* leaves no trace, and
the next person to work through the unloaded tables will find a plausible name
and 135 tidy rows.

What `test_bill` refers to cannot be recovered from the capture. A parallel
installation, a trial run, a second till -- the series is longer than the shop's
own and stops partway through the year, which fits something that ran alongside
and was abandoned. **A low-priority question for the owner if it ever matters,
not a blocker**: the shop's own 224 bills are complete and unaffected.

### Method note

This began as a lead on something else entirely -- whether handing over an order
raises a bill -- and `sale_bill_link` was the most promising-looking candidate
for an order-to-bill link. It is not one. The lead was wrong and the table was
worth reading anyway, which is the opposite of how most of these go: usually the
lead is right and the table is empty.

## 260. Ten outstanding orders were invisible on the screen that lists outstanding orders

The Work Still Owed screen joined to the order lines:

	FROM mcj_customer_orders o
	JOIN mcj_customer_order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id
	WHERE o.tenant_id = $1 AND NOT o.delivered AND l.status <> 'Cancelled'

An inner join, so **an order carrying no lines never appeared at all.**

	undelivered orders                          243
	listed by the screen                         85
	undelivered with no lines                    10   listed: none of them

All ten are carried-forward orders keyed in on 2026-04-01, the day the books
opened, from the **2122, 2223, 2324 and 2425** series -- the oldest placed in
2021-22, five financial years ago. Every one names a real customer ledger. **Two
are RP repairs**, which is a customer's own gold sitting in the shop with nothing
on the one screen that exists to say so.

The screen's own comment says why that matters:

	An order taken could never be completed: nothing set `delivered`, so every
	order stayed outstanding for good and the order book's overdue list could
	only ever be empty.

That was fixed. This is the same failure from the other end -- work that is owed
and cannot be seen.

### Fixed

A LEFT JOIN, with the cancelled test moved into the join condition. As a WHERE
clause it also dropped an order whose lines were all cancelled -- which is
right, that work is not owed -- but it could not tell that case from an order
with no lines at all, which is. The two are separated now, and both are tested.

	orders listed    85 -> 95
	the ten          all shown, marked "(nothing itemised on this order)"

### The fix broke the page, and only driving it showed that

The widened join was correct SQL -- run directly it returned 95 rows. The screen
showed **nought**, with this in the error box:

	can't scan into dest[4]: cannot scan NULL into *string

Every column on that row comes off the lines -- the date wanted, the days
overdue, what was ordered, the estimate -- and an order with no lines has none
of them. `to_char(MIN(l.delivery_date), ...)` returns NULL, and NULL does not
scan into a string. **One row with no lines killed the whole list**, so the fix
for ten invisible orders had briefly made all ninety-five invisible.

Checking the query against the database would have confirmed the fix and missed
this entirely. The screen had to be opened.

### Proven

Regression test seeds an order with no lines and one whose only line is
cancelled: the first must be listed with its marker, the second must not. **With
the inner join restored it fails** -- *an order with no lines is not listed as
outstanding — the shop owes work it cannot see.*

### The sweep for defect 260's siblings, and the tool that came out of it

Defect 260's shape -- correct SQL, dead page -- has an obvious sibling class:
any aggregate or LEFT JOIN column that can be NULL and is scanned into a string.
Swept for it two ways.

**By reading.** Every aggregate in a query with no `GROUP BY` and no enclosing
`COALESCE`: 23 candidates, all of them already guarded. `itemcatalogue.go` is
typical -- `COALESCE(s.tags, 0)` and `COALESCE(ROUND(s.value * 100), 0)` around
a lateral that may match nothing. `nextReceiptNo` in `partysample.go` looked
like the worst case, a `max()` over a table that is empty before the first
receipt, and is safe by construction: it has a `GROUP BY`, so no rows come back
rather than one NULL row, and the error branch starts the series.

**By provoking it.** Reading finds what you thought to look for. Every report was
fetched over a date range matching nothing -- 2099 -- which is the state that
makes aggregates return NULL. **78 reports, all clean.** Every screen a
controller declares, 36 of them, likewise.

So the class has no other members today. That is worth knowing and worth keeping
true, which is the part reading cannot do.

### tools/check_screens_render.py

Opens every screen and every report, each report twice -- plainly, and over the
empty range. A page fails if it does not return 200 or if it renders the error
box the layouts use.

**Proven against the defect it was written for.** Putting back the single
uncoalesced `to_char(MIN(l.delivery_date), ...)`:

	x  screen   /mcj/orders/outstanding
	   can't scan into dest[4]: cannot scan NULL into *string
	1 page(s) broken

and with it restored, `34 screen(s) and 78 report(s) render, including over a
range that matches nothing`.

Nothing in this project opened a page before this. `check_report_footers.py`
fetches reports but reads only their footers, and the test suite drives
controllers it has been told to drive. A screen could be added tomorrow, never
tested, and break on a shop with no data in it -- which is every shop on its
first day.

## 261. Opened fresh, the system rendered every screen and could not raise a single bill

The tool from defect 260 opens every page, but it opens them against this shop's
own database, which has four months of trade in it. The state it was written to
provoke -- no data -- was still only being simulated with a date range. So a
database was created from the migrations alone, the way a new shop starts.

	tenants        1
	users          1   after cmd/seed-admin
	ledgers        0
	purities       0
	items          0
	ledger groups  0
	company        0

**Every screen and every report rendered.** 34 screens, 78 reports, twice each.
Nothing was broken, which is worth knowing and is not the same as working.

### It could not sell anything

The posting screens find their accounts by code, deliberately -- a code is
stable where a name is not. There are **twelve** of them:

	sale.go        1016 sales · 1036 CGST · 1035 SGST · 1037 IGST · 3336 rounding
	creditnote.go  1010 sale returns · 1011 purchases · 1006 purchase returns
	               11577/11576/11578 input CGST/SGST/IGST
	oldgold.go     1018 old gold purchases

Every one exists on the shop's own books, which is why nothing noticed that a
new database has none of them: **migrations create the schema, not a chart of
accounts.** Nothing seeds one, and no screen mentions these numbers.

A shopkeeper opening the system for the first time could set up their company,
their metals, their catalogue and their customers, tag a piece -- and then be
told, on trying to bill it:

	ledger 1016 is missing from the chart of accounts

A number that appears on no screen, no report and in no document the shop has.

### Fixed, and driven end to end on a database that had never existed before

`cmd/seed-admin` -- the command that opens a shop -- now creates the thirteen
accounts the code requires, taking the names and groups from the shop's own
ledgers rather than inventing them, `ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, code) DO NOTHING`
so an existing shop keeps exactly what it has. CASH is the thirteenth: the till
finds it by name rather than code, and a shop with no CASH account cannot take
money over the counter either.

Then a full first day, through the screens, on the fresh database:

	company · purity · customer ledger · item group · item          303 each
	the day's gold rate, 7,000                                      303
	a 10 g chain tagged at that rate                                303
	billed                                                          303

	invoice   GST/2627/00001   goods 72,000.00   total 74,160.00
	vouchers  1, balanced

10 g at 7,000 is 70,000, plus 200 a gram making is 72,000, and 3% tax makes
74,160. **A shop that did not exist an hour earlier raised its first bill.**

### And proven the other way

A second fresh database, set up identically but with the sales account deleted:

	bill 500
	invoices raised: 0
	this bill could not be saved: the sales account (code 1016) is missing from
	the chart of accounts — create it under Ledger Master, or run cmd/seed-admin

The message names the account's purpose now, not just its number. Both scratch
databases were dropped afterwards; the shop's own is untouched -- 2,816 tags,
224 invoices, 785 ledgers, 1,848 vouchers, all unchanged.

### Method note

Defect 260's tool said "every shop on its first day" in its own docstring, and
the sentence was written without ever having started one. **The gap between
simulating an empty shop with a date filter and actually opening one is where
this defect lived.** Two silent failures on the way: a `DROP DATABASE` refused
because the application still held a connection, which made a "fresh" database
the old one and reported *Applied 0 migrations* -- noticed only because 0 was an
odd number to see on a new database -- and a `DELETE` that hung on a lock the
running application held.

### The guard, and what it caught immediately

Defect 261 was fixed by listing the required accounts in `cmd/seed-admin`. That
list was built by hand from a grep, which is the same method that produced the
defect, so it needed a check rather than care.

`TestPostingCodesAreAllSeeded` reads every `ledger… = "1234"` constant out of the
controllers, reads the seeded list out of `cmd/seed-admin`, and fails if a code
a screen posts to is not created. It refuses to pass vacuously: an empty list on
either side is a failure, not a green run.

**It failed on its first execution.**

	1 account code(s) a screen posts to are not created by cmd/seed-admin,
	so a shop opened fresh cannot post through that screen:
	  1012 (used by creditnote.go)

`1012` is `PURCHASE_B2B`. The list written an hour earlier had twelve accounts
and needed thirteen, because the grep output it was read from had been **cut off
at twenty lines** -- the same truncation that produced the wrong figure in defect
258. A B2B purchase on a new shop would still have failed, with the fix in
place and the write-up already saying it was fixed.

Now:

	12 posting code(s) across the screens, all seeded
	14 mandatory account(s) created in the chart of accounts

Fourteen against twelve because CASH is found by name rather than code, and
because two codes share the tax accounts. Verified once more on a database
created from nothing, then dropped; the live shop still has its 785 ledgers.

### Method note

Three times now a figure or a list has been wrong because a listing was
truncated and read as complete -- defect 258's lakh, defect 260's join, and this.
**The failure is not carelessness about numbers, it is trusting the visible part
of a result that was cut off.** The countermeasure that works is the same each
time: have something else derive the answer independently, and compare.

## 262. The guard written to catch incomplete lists was itself an incomplete list

Defect 261's guard found a missing account on its first run and was written up as
working. Checking it properly found two more things, both the same shape.

### Its own pattern missed a code

	(?m)^\s*ledger\w*\s*=\s*"(\d+)"

That requires the line to begin with the constant's name, which is true inside a
`const (...)` block. `oldgold.go` declares its account on its own:

	const ledgerOldGold = "1018"

so the pattern never saw it. The guard reported twelve codes when there are
thirteen, and passed -- because 1018 happens to be seeded. **A guard that misses
a case and goes green over it is the failure it was written to prevent**, and
this one was one line long and shipped an hour earlier.

Widened to `^\s*(?:const\s+)?ledger\w*`, it sees thirteen.

### A third hand-built list of the same codes

Defect 261 also added `accountPurpose`, which turns a code into words for the
error message. It was written by hand from the same truncated grep, so it has
twelve entries and is missing **1012** -- meaning a shop without PURCHASE_B2B
would have been told:

	the posting account (code 1012) is missing from the chart of accounts

which is the bare number the message was changed to stop showing. The fix and
its own fallback disagreed with each other.

The guard now checks both halves: every posting code must be seeded, **and**
every posting code must have a purpose. Proven by removing 1018 from each list
in turn -- *1 posting code(s) have no purpose* and *1 account code(s) ... are not
created* -- and passing with both restored.

	13 posting code(s) across the screens, all seeded and all named

### And the failure message contradicted itself again
