The purpose check was a `t.Errorf`, which does not stop the test, so a failing
run still logged *"all seeded and all named"* one line later. That is the third
time in this document: defect 252's savepoint, defect 258's hardcoded want, and
now this. It is a `t.Fatalf`.

### Method note

Three lists of the same thirteen codes now exist -- the constants, the seed, and
the purposes -- and two of the three were wrong within an hour of being written.
The lesson is not to write more carefully. It is that **a list derived by hand
from another list should be checked by a machine on the day it is written**,
because the moment to catch it is before the write-up says it is done.

## 263. The financial-year rollover, proven rather than assumed — and nothing wrong with it

A bill number carries the year it belongs to: GST/**2627**/00224 is the 224th
bill of 2026-27, and the count restarts each April. That is a thing which can
only go wrong once a year, on a day the shop is open, and this shop reaches it
on **1 April 2027**.

The repository scopes numbering to `(type, financial_year)`, and its comment says
so. Nothing had ever run a shop across the boundary.

	31 March 2027   GST/2627/00001
	 1 April 2027   GST/2728/00001
	vouchers        two, one in each financial year

**It is correct.** The count restarts, the year code advances, and the two
vouchers land in separate years -- which matters beyond the number, because a
trial balance for either year would otherwise pick up the other's trade.

### Proven to fail when it should, at the second attempt

The first attempt at breaking it replaced the year filter with `$3 IS NOT NULL`.
The test failed -- and for the wrong reason. Postgres could no longer infer the
parameter's type, so the save itself errored and the failure landed on the
status assertion rather than the bill number. **A test that fails for the wrong
reason proves nothing**, and it looked exactly like proof: a red run, the right
test name, immediately after the change.

That is defect 232's parameter-typing problem showing up in a deliberately
broken query, which is a fair reminder that a break has to be as carefully made
as a fix.

Broken properly -- `(financial_year=$3 OR true)`, which keeps the parameter
typed and only stops it narrowing:

	the first bill of 2027-28 is "GST/2728/00002", want GST/2728/00001 —
	the count did not restart with the year

### Also checked, also fine

	customers' own goods    7 lots held, 4 to 56 days, every one against a
	                        live order, none delivered, none returned
	receive / list / return every step has a screen, and the return path
	                        guards with AND NOT returned
	the report's comment    "233 pieces, 14.43 carats, five customers, none of
	                        it returned" -- matches the data exactly today

Customer property is the one thing in the shop that is not the shop's, and the
flow around it is complete and consistent. Recorded because the alternative is
finding out later that nobody looked.

## 264. The GST return reconciles to the rupee, and told the reader it was the wrong section

The outward-supplies return is the one report in this system that gets filed with
a government, and **nothing drove it**. Reconciled it against the books by hand
first, because a report that does not agree with the ledgers is worse than one
that does not exist.

	                 the books                    the report
	B2B    20 bills   95,15,937.00  98,01,417.00   95,15,937.00  98,01,417.00
	B2C   204 bills 1,45,50,517.00 1,49,63,969.00 1,45,50,517.00 1,49,63,969.00
	both  224 bills 2,40,66,454.00 2,47,65,386.00 2,40,66,454.00 2,47,65,386.00

Tax on the whole year is 6,98,933.87 -- CGST 2,27,893.80, SGST 2,27,893.80,
IGST 2,43,146.27 -- and the two halves add to the whole. **Exact, in every
figure.** The report reads the taxable value from the VOUCHER rather than the
invoice header, deliberately, and the vouchers are what the books are.

### What was wrong

The closing note said, whichever section was chosen:

	This is the B2B section only.

So a B2C listing -- 204 bills and 1,45,50,517.00 of taxable value -- described
itself as B2B, and so did Both, which is not a GSTR-1 section at all. On a
document that gets filed, a label naming the wrong section is worse than no
label: it is an assertion, and it is false on two of the three settings.

Fixed. The note now names what is shown, and says of Both that it is every bill
rather than a section as filed.

### Tested, at the second attempt

Two tests: each section reconciles, and the note names the section.

The first version read `rows[len(rows)-2]` as a totals row. **The report does not
return one** -- the shell adds totals, and the report returns its bills and the
note. So that read the LAST BILL, which is the same figure whenever a section
holds one bill. It passed on B2B and on B2C and failed only on Both:

	all taxable = 40,000.00, want 1,40,000.00

Two of three green for the wrong reason. It sums the rows itself now.

Both tests proven against the defects they describe: filtering B2C as B2B gives
*b2c taxable = 1,00,000.00 over 1 bill(s), want 40,000.00*, and putting the note
back gives *with kind=b2c the note reads "This is the B2B section only."*

### Method note

A test that passes on two cases out of three, for a reason unrelated to what it
claims to check, is the same failure as defect 262's guard and defect 252's
savepoint. What caught it here was **having three cases where two would have
done** -- Both was included because it exists, not because it was suspected, and
it is the only one that could expose the mistake.

## 265. The purchase return knew something dangerous and kept it in a comment

Defect 264 tested the sales return, so the inward one was the obvious sibling.
It reconciles exactly:

	                          the books                    the report
	PURCHASE_B2B   7 bills    39,33,602.29  40,79,648.00   39,33,602.29  40,79,648.00
	PURCHASE      36 bills  1,94,71,149.21 1,98,77,150.00 1,94,71,149.21 1,98,77,150.00
	both          43 bills  2,34,04,751.50 2,39,56,798.00 2,34,04,751.50 2,39,56,798.00

The screen also avoids the trap its sibling fell into: its filter is labelled
in the shop's own terms -- *Posted to PURCHASE_B2B*, *Posted to PURCHASE* --
rather than B2B and B2C, and there is a "Posted to" column. Whoever wrote it
understood the risk.

### And then wrote the reason down where nobody would read it

Above the function:

	It is NOT "the supplier is registered" ... 17 of the 36 unflagged invoices
	carry GST, so those suppliers are plainly registered ... Labelling them B2C
	in the sense a return uses would understate recoverable input tax by
	4,02,980.57.

Verified today and still exact: **17 of 36**. That is the single most important
sentence about this screen, it names a figure of over four lakh, and it was
visible only in the source. A person filing a GSTR-2 sees a split that looks
like the registered/unregistered one and nothing telling them it is not.

The sales return carries a closing note; this one had none at all.

### Fixed

The return now ends with what the comment knew:

	This is the shop's own split between its two purchase accounts, not the
	registered-supplier split a GSTR-2 asks for: 17 of the 36 invoices posted
	to PURCHASE carry GST, so those suppliers are registered. Which invoices
	belong in which part of a filed return is for whoever files it; this is
	evidence towards that, not the answer.

Tested on all three sections, and proven by removing the note -- *with kind=b2b
the return does not say what its split is: "REGISTERED SUPPLIER"*, which is the
last supplier row standing in for a note that is no longer there.

### Method note

This is the fourth time this week a correct piece of reasoning existed only as a
comment: defect 248 (an explanation that had gone stale), 254 (a hypothesis
contradicted by the harness's own docstring), 256 (a screen citing an answered
blocker), and now one that was right the whole time and simply never reached
the person it was written for. **A comment is a note to whoever edits the code.
When the reader who needs it is the shopkeeper, it has to be on the screen.**

## 266. A comment told the next reader that table 12 could not be filed. It has been filable for a fortnight

Sweeping for the pattern defect 265 named -- reasoning that lives only in a
comment -- turned up thirty reports whose doc comments carry a warning or a
figure. Most are ordinary documentation. One is the HSN summary, which is table
12 of GSTR-1, and its comment said:

	WHAT IS STILL MISSING is line detail for 39 of the 224 bills ... That is
	89,26,345.00 of taxable value ... A return filed from a 63% summary would
	be wrong.

**Every one of the 224 bills carries line detail today.** Defect 155 recovered
those 39 from the capture -- the lines went from 328 to 367 -- and invariant
rule 2 has checked it on every run since. The screen agrees: the summary totals
2,40,66,454.00 of taxable value and 6,98,933.87 of tax, matching the books
exactly, across twelve HSN rows.

So the report was filable and its own documentation said it was not, on the one
screen in this system whose output goes to a government.

### What I got wrong while fixing it

The first correction said the paragraph was stale and replaced the lot. It was
stale in its figures and **right in its design**, which I only found by trying to
break the test I had just written.

A bill whose lines cannot be resolved to an HSN is not dropped. It comes back as
a row coded **"—"** carrying its taxable value, so the table always adds to the
books and any gap is visible IN the return rather than missing from it. That is
what "states it on the face of the table" meant, and it still works:

	with one bill's line removed:
	  row 0  hsn 711319  1,00,000.00
	  row 1  hsn —         40,000.00
	  total            1,40,000.00 = the books

The corrected comment keeps that and fixes only the figures.

### The test I wrote could not fail

It asserted the summary's total equals the books'. **That is true by
construction** -- the "—" row exists to make it true -- so the assertion passes
whether coverage is complete or nothing is attributed at all. Removing a bill's
line left it green.

It took three attempts to see. The first break did not apply, because shell
quoting mangled it; the second applied and still passed, which I could not
explain; instrumenting it showed why. **A test whose green run I cannot account
for is worth no more than one that is red.**

Now it asserts what matters -- that the "—" row is empty -- and refuses to run
against empty books. Proven: leaving a bill without lines gives *40000.00 of
taxable value has no HSN behind it — it appears in the return under "—", and a
return filed with that row is incomplete.*

### Method note

The sweep that found this looked for warnings in comments and had to be read by
hand, because its own "does the screen say it?" test was unreliable -- it missed
the note added in defect 265 an hour earlier, since that note is built by
concatenating two short strings. **The heuristic was wrong and the list it
produced was still useful**, which is the argument for looking at thirty
candidates by eye rather than trusting a filter over them.

### The rest of the sweep: 92 claims in report comments, and they hold

Defect 266 came out of a sweep that listed thirty reports whose doc comments
carry a figure or a warning. Only the warnings had been read. The figures --
**92 claims** across those comments -- were checked next, because a document
that quotes a number is asserting it.

The most-repeated and most consequential, against the database today:

	shelf value, in stock          14,23,61,188.20   used by 5 reports   exact
	opening stock                   8,52,67,768.16                       exact
	sales goods                     2,40,66,454.00                       exact
	bill totals                     2,47,65,386.00                       exact
	stock stones                    6,21,95,953.60   used by 3 reports   exact
	sold stones                     1,11,83,462.33                       exact
	old gold taken in                 50,71,370.00                       exact
	purchase register        71 vouchers, 2,85,06,783.81                 exact
	pricing pending           4 tags; 952 / 951 / 968                    exact
	negative stock                    0, 0, and 0                        exact

**Every one holds.** The one claim that had gone stale is defect 266's, and it
went stale because the PRODUCT changed underneath it -- 39 bills were recovered
-- not because a number was mis-transcribed.

That is the useful distinction. A comment quoting a total stays true while the
data does; a comment describing a GAP is a claim about what the software cannot
do, and every fix is a chance to falsify it. Swept for that shape specifically:
eight lines, six of them historical narrative or genuine properties of the data
("a stone is bought by the carat and has no ticket price"), and the two live
ones both verified above.

### Three of the "mismatches" were my own measurements

Every apparent discrepancy in this pass turned out to be me comparing a
different quantity from the one stated:

	purchase register     compared 43 purchase INVOICES (2,39,56,798.00)
	                      against a comment about 71 purchase VOUCHERS
	                      (2,85,06,783.81) -- driving the register gave 71 rows
	                      and the exact figure
	pricing pending       counted every shelf tag with no rate (968) against a
	                      comment about those with making_type 'val' (952) --
	                      and the comment's own 968 was sitting in the next
	                      sentence
	order detail          joined the legacy table on the wrong key, getting
	                      "212 of 273 orders have no lines" where our own data
	                      says 13 of 284 (defect 260)

Two of the three were within a sentence of being written up as defects.

**The pattern is not carelessness with numbers, it is answering a question
adjacent to the one asked.** The countermeasure that worked every time was
reading the claim again before believing the disagreement -- and, where the
claim is about what a screen shows, driving the screen instead of querying the
table behind it.

## 267. Three of the four voucher screens had never been driven

The voucher controller mounts four kinds -- receipt, payment, contra, journal --
from one constructor. Ten tests exercise it, and every one of them posts to the
**journal** path.

	journal    624 of the shop's vouchers      driven
	payment    626                             never
	receipt    269                             never
	contra      31                             never

**926 vouchers' worth of screen against the journal's 624**, and the payment
kind carries a cheque block the journal has not got, so that field's whole path
was code no test had executed.

Same blind spot as defects 243 and 244 on the master screens: one of a set is
exercised and the rest are assumed to follow because they share a constructor.
Here they do follow -- all four save, land under their own type and balance --
but that was not known.

Driven now, including a payment with cheque 004521 dated 2026-04-10, which is
read back off the voucher.

### Two mistakes in the test, both mine, both caught by driving it

**It asserted the wrong table.** The first version read the cheque back from
`mcj_voucher_lines`, and failed:

	payment: the cheque details were not written: no rows in result set

Both tables carry `cheque_number` and `cheque_date`. The screen writes the
voucher's; the shop's own data has 34 on vouchers and **593 on lines**, which is
what made the line the obvious place to look. It is not where this screen puts
them, and the reconciliation screen already handles both -- it reads the line
first and falls back to the header, with a comment explaining the same 34.

**It asserted a figure I made up.** The test comment said 419 of the shop's 626
payments carry a cheque number. The number is **34**. Nothing had been measured;
it was written while looking at 593 lines and reasoning about vouchers.

### And the type check could not fail

It compared the saved type against the kind's own declared type -- so retyping
contra as a journal moved both sides together and the test stayed green. Proven
by doing exactly that.

The kinds are now collected and compared to each other, which is the property
that matters: a receipt that posts as a journal is not a receipt, and the day
book, the cash book and the voucher list would all file the shop's money under
the wrong heading. Retyping contra now gives:

	contra and journal both post as "JRNL" — they are one kind wearing two names
	4 kind(s) produced only 3 distinct type(s)

### Method note

Three tests written this week have compared a value against the same source that
produced it -- defect 262's guard, defect 266's total, and this. **A test is only
worth what its two sides are independent of each other**, and the quickest way to
tell is to break the thing it claims to check and watch what happens. All three
were caught that way, and none of them by reading.

## 268. The fourth trade kind was missing from the test that reads as full coverage

Defect 267 found three of four voucher screens undriven, so the sibling was the
trade controller, which mounts four kinds from one constructor the same way.

`TestTrade_EachKindPostsItsOwnType` looks like the answer to exactly this
question. It drives three:

	credit-note      SALE-RET    driven
	purchase         PURC-GSC    driven
	debit-note       PURC-RET    driven
	purchase-order   PURC-GCO    never

**Purchase against a customer's order** -- 19 of the shop's purchases, and the
only trade kind that is tax-free by design -- was absent from the one test whose
name promises every kind. A test called *EachKind* that covers three of four is
worse than no test, because it answers the question wrongly.

Driven now, and it posts PURC-GCO correctly.

### The list is checked against the source

Writing the expected types out by hand is deliberate -- reading them from
`TradeKinds()` would compare the code against itself, which is what made defect
267's type check green while contra was retyped as a journal. So the values stay
written down, and the SET of slugs is checked against `TradeKinds()` instead:

	trade kind(s) [purchase-order] are not exercised here

That is the failure with purchase-order removed from the expected map. A kind
added tomorrow fails here rather than being silently uncovered.

### What actually stops a new kind slipping through

Planting a fifth kind to test the guard did not reach the guard. It panicked
first:

	navigation: screen "/mcj/trade/planted-kind" has no LegacyFile,
	so it must give Top and Item

The navigation registry refuses a screen that names neither a legacy file nor a
menu position, so a trade kind cannot be added without being placed somewhere a
person can find it. **That is a stronger guard than the one I was writing**, it
was already there, and it caught the plant in under a second.

Worth recording because it is the opposite of this week's usual finding: a
protection that existed, worked, and was better than what was being added beside
it.

### Method note

Three sets of screens built from one constructor have now been checked --
masters (243, 244), vouchers (267), trade (268) -- and every one had members
nobody had driven. **The shape to look for is a constructor taking a list**, and
the question is not whether the code handles each member but whether anything
has ever asked it to.

## 269. Seventeen reports were named by no test at all

The list-shaped blind spot of defects 267 and 268 has a bigger instance: 79
reports registered from one list, and no count of how many had ever been
asserted about. **17 of the 79 are named by no test.**

	BackDatedSubgroupStock   ItemCatalogue        SalesRegister    SubgroupStockTally
	DesignCatalogue          PacketStockSummary   SchemeBook       SuspectRates
	GrossProfit              Quarterly            StockHistory     UntaggedItemStock
	RawStockTally            RatioAnalysis        StockJournal     UserMaster
	                                              StockValuation

They are not unexercised: `check_screens_render.py` opens every one of them,
twice, and they render. What none of them has is an assertion about what the
figures ARE.

### Reconciled by hand, and they are right

	sales register     224 bills   2,40,66,454.00  6,98,933.87  2,47,65,386.00
	the books          224 bills   2,40,66,454.00  6,98,933.87  2,47,65,386.00

	stock valuation    shelf 14,23,61,188.20, matching the tags exactly

Both agree. The sales register reads from the VOUCHER, like the purchase
register and the GST return, so this is the fourth report checked this week that
ties to the books to the rupee.

### The sales register now has a test, and it took three corrections

**The seed made vouchers with no debit side.** Two credits and nothing else --
which is not a voucher, and the register lists the customer's name off the debit
line, so it returned nothing at all. Adding the customer's leg fixed it and made
the seeded vouchers balanced, which they should have been from the start.

**The test read the wrong key.** The register calls its column `goods`; the test
asked for `taxable`, got nothing from every row, and summed zero.

That would have passed as a green run against an empty sum, except for the one
line that saved it:

	if bills == 0 {
	    t.Fatal("the register listed no bills, so this test proves nothing")
	}

**That guard is the only reason this was caught rather than shipped.** It is the
same guard defect 266 needed and did not have.

Proven by zeroing the register's goods subquery: *the register totals 0.00
taxable against the books' 140000.00*.

### Method note

Five times this session a query or a test has asked for something adjacent to
what it meant: purchase invoices for purchase vouchers, rate-zero tags for
val-priced ones, a legacy join on the wrong key, `mcj_voucher_lines` for
`mcj_vouchers`, and now `taxable` for `goods`. Every one produced a plausible
answer -- usually zero, sometimes a real number belonging to a different
question.

**A test that can return zero and pass needs a line saying zero is not an
answer.** That is cheap, and it is the difference between the two outcomes here.

## 270. Nine tests asserted that a report does not list something, and would have passed if it listed nothing

Defect 269's saving line -- *"the register listed no bills, so this test proves
nothing"* -- is the only reason a test that summed the wrong key was caught. So:
how many tests are missing it?

Swept for assertions made inside a loop over a report's rows, with no check that
there were any. **38 candidates**, most of them fine -- they look up a specific
row through a helper and fail on nil. The class that is not fine is the negative
assertion:

	for _, r := range rows {
	    if got, _ := r["status"].(string); got == "Cancelled" {
	        t.Fatal("a cancelled order line was listed")
	    }
	}

Nine of these. *LeavesCancelledLinesOut*, *DoesNotMixDocumentsUp*,
*StaysInsideThePeriod*, *IgnoresACancelledBill*, *CountsOnlyGoldJewellery* and
four more -- every one of them satisfied by a report that returns nothing at
all. They were testing that a filter excludes what it should, and a report that
excludes everything passes.

### The first guard I wrote was decoration

`if len(rows) == 0` -- which is never true. **This codebase's reports return one
placeholder row when they have nothing to show**: "No live order line matches
that choice.", "Nothing was bought between those dates.", and so on. That is
good behaviour and it is the house style, and it means row count is not evidence
of anything having been listed.

I found that out by neutering a report and watching the guards not fire. Two
unrelated tests failed and the two I had just "protected" passed.

The guards now count the rows carrying the field each test actually reads, so a
placeholder does not count:

	listed := 0
	for _, r := range rows {
	    if _, ok := r["status"]; ok {
	        listed++
	    }
	}
	if listed == 0 {
	    t.Fatal("the report listed nothing, so the check below proves nothing")
	}

Proven by suppressing the report's rows entirely:

	TestOrderToBarcode_DoesNotTreatUnmadeWorkAsAProblem
	    the report listed nothing, so the check below proves nothing
	TestOrderToBarcode_LeavesCancelledLinesOut
	    the report listed nothing, so the check below proves nothing

### Method note

Two guards in two days have been written, shipped green, and turned out to check
nothing -- defect 262's regex and this one. Both were caught the same way, by
breaking the thing they claimed to guard rather than by reading them.

**The rule that keeps holding: a check is not a check until it has been seen to
fail.** It costs a minute. Neither of these would have been found by any amount
of care at the time of writing, because both looked exactly right.

### A report that has gone silently empty, and the check that now catches it

Defect 270 is a trap inside the tests; the same trap exists outside them. Every
report here answers an empty result with **one placeholder row** -- good
behaviour, and it means a 200 and a rendered table prove nothing about whether
anything was listed. A report whose query stops matching looks exactly like a
report with nothing to say.

Measured across the shop's whole history, 2024-04-01 to 2027-03-31:

	reports showing real data          76 of 78
	showing none                        2 — ledger-book and quote

Both of those take a **subject** rather than a period: the ledger book needs a
ledger and the quote needs a barcode, and an empty page without one is the right
answer. So nothing is silently empty today.

`check_screens_render.py` now asserts that, with those two named as exceptions
in the source and the reason written beside them. Proven by silencing one
report's row loop:

	x  report (no data)  /mcj/reports/hallmarking
	   renders, but shows no data over the whole of the shop's history —
	   a report that has stopped matching looks like one with nothing to say

	1 page(s) broken

and restoring it gives *34 screen(s) and 78 report(s) render, including over a
range that matches nothing, and 76 of them show real data*.

This is the check that was missing when the tool was written yesterday: it
opened every page and confirmed none of them broke, which is a different
question from whether any of them still work.

## 271. The shop sells 17% of its billing from a price list nothing could set

`mcj_coin_rates` sat in the unwritten-tables list with **5,966 rows** -- read by
a report, written by nobody. It is not history.

	52 coin items, priced across 115 trading days
	3 April to 19 August 2026, the day before the system went down
	26,11,606.00 of coins sold — 17% of all billing
	against 1,70,345.00 of tagged coin stock

**A coin is a product with a published price, not metal weighed off the shelf.**
The shop set that list every trading day and the system had no screen to set it.

### The screen that looked like it did

Daily Metal Rates has a coin column. It writes `mcj_metal_rates.coin_rate` --
and that column is populated on **none** of the shop's 2,820 rate rows. It is a
different figure, one per metal grade, that the shop never used. The list it
actually sells from is one price per coin per day, and nothing wrote it.

So the gap was invisible twice over: a table with a reader and no writer, beside
a screen that appeared to cover it.

### Built

`/mcj/coin-rates`, Daily Coin Prices, modelled on the metal rate screen because
it answers the same shape of question. Driven against the shop's own data:

	52 coins listed
	prices carried from 19 Aug 2026 and labelled as carried
	a price set for 24 Aug 2026 wrote SILVER COIN 1/2 TOLA at 7,42,500.00

The test row was removed and the table is back to 5,966.

**The item master's own rate is shown beside each coin and never used as one.**
Every one of the eleven items carrying a rate there is 4.7 to 4.9 times below
its latest daily price -- pricing a coin from the master undercharges by about
79%, a coin the list puts at 1,23,400.00 carrying 26,000.00 there (data defect
54). It is displayed because it is what somebody would otherwise reach for, and
it is never filled into the price box.

Seven tests: the list holds coins and not other items, a carried price is
labelled, the frozen master rate is shown but not offered, a price saves,
setting twice leaves one row, a blank row is not an error -- 19 of the 52 are
never priced on any day -- and something that is not a price is refused rather
than stored as nought.

### One correction

The first test compared the stored value as text and failed:

	the price came back 126900.00000, want 126900.00

The column is `numeric(18,5)`. The price was right; the comparison was against
Postgres's rendering of it rather than against money. Formatted before
comparing.

	tables read but never written    24 -> 23

## 272. Which of the unwritten tables are still alive, and the one the shop uses daily that cannot be done

Defect 271 built the coin price list because it turned out to be operational. The
obvious question is which of the remaining 23 are. **Asked by last activity
rather than by name**, because a table called "holiday calendar" sounds annual
and this shop's is not.

	stock_conversions    859    18 Aug 2026   live — screen refused, defect 251
	barcode_edits        156    15 Aug 2026   live — NOTHING CAN DO THIS
	ordered_stones       115    10 Aug 2026   live — customers' stones on orders
	scheme_payments    2,144    10 Aug 2026   live — blocked on defect 233
	scheme_enrolments    239    11 Feb 2026   blocked on defect 233
	estimates              2    23 May 2025   two rows, a year old
	holidays             109    26 Dec 2024   abandoned
	designs            5,221    20 Jan 2017   nine years old

**The holiday calendar is not the annual thing it looks like.** 52 Thursdays in
2016, 53 in 2017, then four days in December 2024 and nothing since -- the
shop's weekly closing day recorded for two years and given up. Building an entry
screen for it would be building for a practice that stopped in 2017. That is
exactly the assumption defect 271's method exists to avoid.

**The design catalogue's 5,221 rows are from 2017.** The largest table on the
list by far, and the most obviously dead.

### The one that matters: a tag cannot be corrected

`mcj_barcode_edits` is the trail of corrections to a tag. It is live -- 156 of
them between 12 April and 15 August 2026, about one a working day -- and every
one of the 156 is on a tag **still on the shelf today**.

What the shop corrects:

	the unit count    119 of 156   <- said "piece count" first; see defect 273
	what the item is   31
	the making charge   7
	gross weight        0
	net weight          0
	stones              0

So a tag is corrected for what it IS and how many, and never for what it weighs.

The rebuild cannot do any of it. Every `UPDATE mcj_stock_items` in the codebase
sets one of three things: `category_id` from the categorise screen, and
`in_stock` from a sale and a refund. **There is no screen that changes a tag's
item, piece count or making** -- which is why nothing writes the audit trail, and
why the trail's absence looked like an ordinary unwritten table rather than a
missing operation.

A piece tagged as one ring when it is two cannot be put right. It can be sold
wrongly, or left.

### Not built here, and why

The screen is well defined by the measurements above -- three fields, plus a row
in `mcj_barcode_edits` recording old and new, who and from where, which the
table already has columns for. It is the next build.

It is not this one because the coin price list was built in this same pass and
a second screen begun now would be a screen half-driven. **The measurements are
the useful part and they are recorded**, so the build starts from evidence rather
than from a guess about what a tag edit changes.

### Method note

Three tables were assessed by name this session and two of the three were wrong:
holidays reads as operational and is dead, `barcode_edits` reads as an audit
artefact and is a missing operation. **The one question that separated them was
"when was the last row written", and it takes one query.**

## 273. A pair of bangles was tagged as two units, and defect 272 named the wrong field

Setting out to build the tag-correction screen defect 272 called for, the first
question was what the shop's 156 corrections actually change. That answer turned
out to be wrong in the write-up, and following it produced a real defect
somewhere else.

### The correction to defect 272

It said 119 of the 156 edits "fix the piece count". They do not. They fix the
**unit** count, and the report's own comment says so:

	Units, not pieces. old_units/new_units come from barcode_main.qty, which is
	not what a bill counts -- that is nag.

Compared against `nag` first, and got a contradiction that looked like a serious
data defect: the tag's count matched `old_qty` on all 119, while item and making
matched their `new_` side. Against `qty` -- the column the trail is actually
about -- **119 of 119 match `new_qty`**, consistent with everything else. There
is no defect in the trail, and the one I nearly wrote up would have been the
sixth thing this session measured one field away from the question.

### The real defect, found by following it

pieces and quantity are different numbers, and this tag screen wrote the piece
count into both:

	VALUES (..., $6::int, $6::numeric, ...)

The shelf says otherwise:

	tags that are ONE unit               2,787 of 2,816
	holding more than one piece            803 — 719 pairs, 56 sets of 3, 21 of 4
	tags where quantity equals pieces       21

A pair of bangles is **2 pieces and 1 unit**. The screen made it 2 units of 2
pieces, which matches the 21 exceptions and contradicts the 2,787.

Fixed: a tag is one unit. Proven by restoring the old line -- *the tag is 2.000
unit(s), want 1.000 — a pair is one unit*.

### What this is and is not

**Nothing reads `quantity` today.** It is written by this screen and consumed by
no report, which is why 803 tags could disagree with a new one and nothing
showed it. So no bill is wrong and no figure moves.

It matters because it is the field the shop corrects most -- 119 of its 156 tag
edits -- so it is plainly the one they care about, and because a column written
wrongly and read by nobody is a column that will be read eventually.

### And a self-inflicted one

The comment explaining all this went into the SQL string, and contained
backticks around the column names. The SQL is a Go raw string, which backticks
terminate:

	syntax error: unexpected name pieces in argument list

Caught by the compiler in a second, and worth a line because the fix was to
write the names plainly -- the quoting that reads well in prose is the quoting
that breaks the string it is inside.

## 274. A tag on the shelf can be corrected, and the correction is on the record

Defect 272 measured what the shop corrects and left the screen unbuilt; defect
273 corrected the measurement. This is the screen.

	the unit count   119 of 156 edits
	what the item is  31
	the making         7
	gross weight       0
	net weight         0
	stones             0

**Weights are not offered.** The shop has never corrected one in 156 edits, and
a weight is what a scale settles rather than a screen.

### Changing the making reprices the tag

Checked before building, on the shop's own seven making corrections: `total`
equals `amount + making + other making` exactly on all seven afterwards. So the
legacy repriced, and so does this.

Leaving the total alone would have been the quiet kind of wrong. A tag whose
price no longer follows from its own figures is one the sale screen holds back
for a hand price (defect 255) -- correcting a making charge would have made the
piece harder to sell, and nothing on the screen would have said so.

### Driven on the shop's own data

Barcode 10060840, a real pair, 2 pieces and 1 unit:

	units 1 -> 2
	making and total unchanged, which is right — units are not a price
	mcj_barcode_edits: units_changed t, old 1, new 2, item_changed f,
	                   named a person and an address

That matches the shop's own convention, where `new_units` is what the tag ends
up holding -- 119 of 119 (defect 273). The tag was put back and the trail
returned to its 156 rows.

### Seven tests, two of them proven by breaking the screen

Units change without repricing; making changes and reprices to 51,500.00 from
50,000 of metal and 10 g at 150; the item changes; a sold tag is refused *by
name* -- "a piece already sold cannot be corrected" rather than pretending it
does not exist; an empty correction is refused rather than written to the trail,
because an audit entry that changed nothing is a lie about the shelf; and no
weight field is offered.

Proven: writing the audit row against the wrong barcode gives *the correction
was not recorded*, and dropping the reprice gives *total came back 51000.00,
want 51500.00 — the tag was not repriced*.

### One that did not prove anything

The first attempt to break the audit write deleted the INSERT and left `time`
imported, so the package did not compile and the test never ran. **A break that
does not build is not a break**, and the run that "passed" against it proved
nothing -- it was caught only because the compiler said so out loud.

	tables read but never written    23 -> 22
	screens                          35 -> 36

## 275. An order for a diamond ring was recorded as an order for a ring

`mcj_ordered_stones` is what a customer has asked to be set into the piece they
have ordered. It is live -- 115 rows to 10 August 2026 -- and the order screen
could not write one.

	orders carrying stones            68 of 284
	stones asked for                 115 rows, 24,69,792.15
	of that, on orders still live               16,36,662.00

So a customer ordering a diamond ring was recorded as ordering a ring. The
karigar is not told what to set, and the estimate carries the metal and nothing
else.

### Only the fields the shop fills

Counted before the form was drawn, from its own 115 rows:

	the stone itself   115 of 115
	weight             113
	carats             107
	pieces             101
	rate and value      86
	shape               64
	colour              37
	cut                  4
	sieve                0

**Cut and sieve are not offered.** Four rows and none, against seven Diamond
Setup masters in the old menu -- the shop keeps the masters and does not use
them on an order. Offering every column the table has would have been drawing
the schema rather than the shop.

### Order level, not line level

The stones attach to the ORDER. That is how the shop's own rows sit, and joining
them to lines fans out: the stone report measured 545 carats that way against a
true 403. A part-cancelled order cannot split its stones between what was
cancelled and what was not, which is why the report states the order's condition
rather than a line's -- and why this screen writes them the same way.

### Driven on the shop's own data

	CO/2627/00114   4 pc · 1.250 ct · 0.250 g · RUBY at 45,000.00 = 56,250.00

The order and its stone were removed afterwards; 284 orders, 366 lines and 115
stones, all back where they were.

Three tests: a stone is recorded against the order, stones are optional -- 216
of 284 orders carry none and the ordinary case must not be made harder -- and a
carat weight that cannot be read is refused rather than stored as nought.
Proven by stopping the write: *the stone was not recorded against the order*.

	tables read but never written    22 -> 21

## 276. Twelve people read as unpaid on a screen, and the ledgers say they were paid

Defect 153 asked the shop a question worth ₹13,21,900: were August, September and
October 2025 and July 2026 salaries actually paid? Each month shows a full salary
bill and nought against it. **One of those four months can now be answered from
the books, and the answer is yes.**

	July 2026 sheets        12 people, 2,89,200.00 gross, 0.00 paid
	staff ledgers, 5 Aug    12 people, 2,73,094.00 paid
	the month's deductions             16,106.00

2,89,200 less 16,106 is 2,73,094, to the rupee, and every one of the twelve
matches a staff ledger by name. **They were paid.** The payment is in the
ledgers and was never written back to the sheet.

Wages for a month are paid in the next one -- every month the shop paid, the
voucher falls in the month after the sheet -- so the July sheet was still
reading nought when the dump was taken on 21 August, sixteen days after the
money went out.

### The screen said the wrong thing about it

	July 2026 | ANKUSH KHANDELWAL | 23,000.00 | 40,000.00 | 0.00 | no payment recorded

"No payment recorded" is true of the sheet and false of the shop, on the one
screen somebody would use to decide whether staff are owed money.

The report was already careful here -- it distinguishes deductions from arrears
by name, and says so at length, because the naive reading would have it announce
that the shop owes 15,71,288. It just had no way to know the payment existed,
because it never looked outside the sheet.

### Fixed

The sheet now consults the ledgers for the month after it, and says which case
each row is:

	12 rows   paid 2,73,094.00 per the ledgers; the sheet was never updated
	37 rows   nothing due                      (gross is nought too)
	47 rows   no payment recorded, and none in the ledgers either

96 zero-paid sheets, all three cases named. The 47 are the ones that are actually
open.

### What that does to the question for the owner

	was              4 months, 13,21,900.00
	is               3 months, 11,11,800.00

July 2026 is answered and comes out. What remains is August, September and
October 2025 -- 10,53,800.00 -- plus 58,000.00 across three sheets in February
2026 and 21,100.00 in April 2025.

The 2025 months still cannot be settled from the books: the voucher history does
not reach back that far (defect 142), which is why defect 153 could not check
them. **That has not changed. What has changed is that the question is a quarter
smaller and no longer includes a month where the money demonstrably moved.**

### Method note

This came out of asking which unwritten tables are still alive. Payroll is --
sheets run to July 2026, 12 to 17 people a month -- and the intention was to
build the screen that writes one. Reading the data first found that a screen
already built was saying something untrue, which is worth more than the screen
that is missing.

## 277. One person was paid more than their salary, and the screen had no branch for it

Following defect 276 into the next column: the salary sheet DERIVED its deducted
figure as gross minus paid, while `mcj_payroll_history` records the real one --
PF, ESI and professional tax, 209 rows against 246 sheets.

Compared like for like, per person per month:

	paid sheets                150
	where the two agree        149
	where they differ            1

**RAJENDRA PRASAD JAT, June 2026: 21,100.00 gross, 24,870.00 paid.** Paid
3,770.00 MORE than the month's salary, while payroll history records a 130.00
deduction.

### The screen said nothing about it

The switch had a case for nothing paid, and a case for gross exceeding paid, and
**no case for paid exceeding gross**. That row fell through both: blank deduction
column, no note, indistinguishable from an ordinary line.

It is the one row on that screen anybody would want pointed out -- somebody paid
above their salary is either arrears, an advance settled with the wages, or an
error, and all three are worth a sentence.

Fixed: *paid 3,770.00 more than the month's gross — arrears or an advance
settled with it.* The screen names it and leaves the reading to whoever knows.

The deducted column now shows what payroll history RECORDS, falling back to the
derived figure only for the 37 sheets that have no history row. It changes
almost nothing -- 149 of 150 agree -- which is the point: the number was right
by luck rather than by source.

### Three wrong measurements on the way to one right one

	"3 of 12 months differ by 11,608"    compared paid sheets against ALL
	                                     history rows, including staff whose
	                                     sheet was unpaid — filtered on one
	                                     side only
	"the disagreement is per-row"        the note never fired, which said the
	                                     hypothesis was wrong before any of it
	                                     was written down
	"then it must be unmatched rows"     zero unmatched in those months

Only the fourth attempt -- joining sheet to history per person per month --
gave the real answer, which is one row, not three months.

**Seventh time this session a query has answered a question next to the one
asked.** The pattern each time is a filter applied to one side of a comparison
and not the other. What caught it here was the screen: the note I had written
for the disagreement never appeared, and a fix whose evidence does not show up
where you expect it has not been proven.

## 278. The check that finds a silent report called an empty shop broken 55 times

Defect 274 and 275 added screens; the obvious question is whether they work on a
shop that has just opened, so a database was built from the migrations alone
again (defect 261's method) and every page opened against it.

**Every screen and every report rendered, including the three built today.** No
scan errors, no non-200s, nothing broken.

What did happen is that the tool said 55 pages were broken.

	55 page(s) broken

All 55 were the emptiness check added one iteration earlier: *renders, but shows
no data over the whole of the shop's history*. On a shop that has not traded,
showing no data is the correct answer, and the check had no way to know the
difference.

### It was written against one kind of shop

The check exists because a report whose query stops matching looks exactly like
a report with nothing to say. That is true -- and the same sentence, read the
other way, says the check cannot tell an empty shop from a broken one either. It
was written and proven against the shop's own populated database and never run
against an empty one, which is precisely the gap defect 261 opened and this tool
was built to close.

### Fixed by counting

One quiet report among many that speak is a fault. Nearly all of them quiet at
once is an empty shop.

	against the fresh shop
	  55 of 76 reports show no data, so this looks like a shop that has not
	  traded yet — the emptiness check does not apply and was skipped.
	  36 screen(s) and 78 report(s) render ... and 21 of them show real data

	against the shop's own data
	  36 screen(s) and 78 report(s) render ... and 76 of them show real data

	with one report silenced on the populated shop
	  x  report (no data)  /mcj/reports/hallmarking
	  1 page(s) broken

So it still catches the thing it was built for, and no longer accuses a new
shop of being broken on its first morning.

### Method note

Three tools have now been written this week and two of them were wrong on their
first serious use -- defect 262's guard missed a case, defect 270's guard checked
nothing, and this one failed the first time it met a database it had not been
developed against. **A tool proven against one dataset has been proven against
one dataset.** The fix each time was cheap; finding it required running the thing
somewhere new, which is not something reading can substitute for.

## 279. Two more checks that passed against a shop with nothing in it

Defect 278 ended with the observation that a tool proven against one dataset has
been proven against one dataset. So the rest of them were run against the empty
shop as well.

**Two more had the same trap.**

	check_invariants.py       14 of 14 rules hold
	check_report_footers.py   78 reports checked, 0 doubled footer(s)

Both true. Both examined nothing.

Every invariant counts exceptions and compares against what the migration
already contained, so on a database with no bills, no vouchers and no tags the
count is nought and nought never exceeds an allowance. A doubled footer can only
appear under rows, so a report with no rows cannot have one.

The database was genuinely empty and the tools genuinely ran against it -- the
first reading of the invariants output looked like it had ignored `DB_NAME`,
because a rule's allowance is printed as prose ("8 from the migration") and reads
like a live count. It had not; the figures were checked against both databases
side by side before anything was changed.

### Both now say what they looked at

	check_invariants, empty shop
	  This shop has no bills, no vouchers and no tags. Every rule below counts
	  exceptions, so all of them hold trivially and none of them says anything.
	  Nothing was checked.

	check_report_footers, empty shop
	  78 reports checked, 5 of them with numbers in, 0 doubled footer(s)

	check_report_footers, the shop's own data
	  78 reports checked, 76 of them with numbers in, 0 doubled footer(s)

76 matches the render checker's count of reports showing real data, from a
different tool reading different markup, which is the first time two of these
have agreed on anything independently.

### The two that were fine

`status_figures.py` and `check_blocker_citations.py` read the filesystem and
never touch the database, so an empty shop cannot fool them.
`check_unwritten_tables.py` reports row counts as -1 when it cannot get them and
still lists the tables correctly, because its real subject is the source.

### Method note

Three of the six checks guarding this system reported success against a database
they had examined nothing in. None of them was wrong; all three were useless in
a way their output did not admit. **The question that found all three is the same
one: what did you actually look at?** -- and it is worth asking of any check that
reports a count of problems rather than a count of things examined.

## 280. The four unnamed staff stop a month before the payroll does, and how a salary is worked out

Payroll is the largest live gap left: the shop's sheets run to July 2026, twelve
to seventeen people a month, and nothing in this system can produce one. Before
building that screen, the arithmetic behind a salary had to come from the shop's
own records rather than from an assumption about payroll.

### Both formulas, verified

	gross = basic + HRA + dearness allowance          209 of 209 rows
	paid  = gross − (PF + ESI + professional tax)     149 of 150 paid rows

The single exception is RAJENDRA PRASAD JAT, June 2026, which defect 277 already
found and named on the screen -- paid 3,770.00 above his gross.

`mcj_staff_components` carries exactly those five components, 46 rows over 12
people, and nothing else. So a salary sheet is fully determined by a basic pay
and that setup.

**Basic pay is not fixed.** It changes for 12 of the 19 staff across the sixteen
months, so a screen must carry the last one forward and let it be changed rather
than read it from a master. That is the same shape as the metal rates and the
coin list.

### The correction

Defect 157 records four staff codes that name nobody -- 4023, 8827, 8828 and
8855 -- taking 10,66,400.00 gross and 7,14,430.00 paid. Both figures are exact.
The period was written as **Apr 2025 – Jul 2026** and is **Apr 2025 – Jun 2026**:

	each of the four   15 sheets, last period 2026-06
	July 2026          12 sheets, none of them these four

**They stop one month before the payroll does.** Twelve other people have a July
sheet; these four do not. That is not proof of anything, but it is a fact about
them that was not known, and it narrows what they might be: four people who left
the payroll together in June 2026, or four rows that stopped being written.

It matters because this is a figure the owner is being asked to explain, and the
question is better asked about the right sixteen months.

### The screen this was for

Not built here. What it needs is now settled and written down: pick a month,
list the staff, carry each basic pay forward from the last sheet, take the five
components from the per-person setup, compute gross and net by the two formulas
above, and write `mcj_salary_sheets` and `mcj_payroll_history` together -- the
second is where the deductions live, and defect 277 showed what happens when a
screen derives them instead.

## 281. The month's payroll can be prepared, and the guard against a known bug did not see it

Defect 280 settled the arithmetic; this is the screen. `/mcj/salary-sheets`,
Monthly Payroll.

	gross = basic + HRA + dearness allowance
	pay   = gross − (PF + ESI + professional tax)

**Only the basic is typed.** The allowances and deductions come from each
person's own setup in `mcj_staff_components` and are shown beside the row so the
arithmetic is visible rather than asserted. The basic is carried from that
person's last sheet and labelled as carried, because it moved for 12 of the 19
staff over sixteen months and a figure repeated silently is a figure nobody
checks.

**Both tables are written.** `mcj_salary_sheets` carries the pay and
`mcj_payroll_history` the deductions. Writing only the first would leave every
future month in the position defect 277 found: a report deriving the deduction
from gross minus paid, which is right on 149 of 150 rows and wrong on the one
that matters.

Driven on the shop's own people, August 2026:

	ANKUSH KHANDELWAL   23,000 basic  40,000 gross  39,850 to pay
	ANURADHA MALHOTRA   20,000        35,000        34,850
	MADHURIMA DAS       11,000        19,300        19,170

Each gross matches what the shop itself recorded for July. The sheets were
removed afterwards; 246 and 209 rows, back as they were.

Six tests: the basic carries forward and says so, both formulas hold, the
deductions are recorded separately, preparing a month twice leaves one sheet,
somebody with no basic is left out rather than paid nothing -- the shop's sheets
run 12 to 17 people against 19 codes -- and a basic that cannot be read is
refused.

### The guard that did not catch the bug it exists for

The first save failed:

	inconsistent types deduced for parameter $2 (SQLSTATE 42P08)

That is defect 232's failure exactly, and there is a test for it --
`TestSQL_ARepeatedParameterIsCastConsistently` -- which passed over this query.

Its rule is that a repeated parameter must be cast everywhere or nowhere, and
its comment explains why nowhere is safe: *both uses then deduce the same type*.
**That is not always true.** Here `$2` was uncast in all three places and
deduced two different types anyway -- once as a value being inserted into a
varchar column, once inside `btrim(col) = $2`.

Widening the rule to flag every repeated parameter would flag the tenant id in
nearly every query in this codebase, so the rule stays and the gap is written
into it instead. **What caught this was saving a payroll, not reading the SQL**,
and the honest thing is for the test to say so rather than to imply a coverage
it does not have.

	tables read but never written   21 -> 19
	screens                         36 -> 37

## 282. Payroll reconciles completely, and the four unnamed staff are documented month by month

Having built the payroll screen, the question was whether anyone can be paid by
it. Twelve of the nineteen staff codes have a components setup; seven do not,
and **those seven are exactly defect 157's unnamed codes** -- 4023, 8827, 8828,
8855 and three others.

That looked like a finding and it is not. Payroll reconciles, completely:

	sheets with a payroll-history row     209    gross = basic + HRA + D.A on all 209
	sheets without one                     37    gross = basic on all 37, no allowance
	                                             to explain
	                                      246    every sheet accounted for

There is no allowance anywhere in sixteen months that lacks a record. The four
unnamed codes carry 4,34,200.00 of allowances above basic and every rupee of it
is in `mcj_payroll_history`, month by month -- 1,98,000.00 for 4023,
1,02,000.00 for 8827, 59,500.00 for 8828 and 74,700.00 for 8855.

### The near-miss

That 4,34,200.00 was measured first against `mcj_staff_components` and written
down, in a draft, as *allowances with no setup to explain them*. It would have
told the owner that four people no one can identify were paid four and a third
lakh of unexplained allowances.

`mcj_staff_components` is a **current** setup, one row per person per component.
`mcj_payroll_history` is the **per-month** record. Sixteen months of changing
allowances cannot match a single current setup, and the proof was already in
front of me: only 61 of 172 sheets belonging to people who DO have a setup match
it either. The setup explains almost nobody, which should have said at once that
it was the wrong source rather than that these four were unusual.

**Eighth time this session a measurement has been taken against a source next to
the right one.** It is the first that was caught before it reached the document,
and what caught it was checking the contrast -- if the four are anomalous, the
twelve should be clean, and they were not.

### What is actually true of the four

	no name on any sheet
	no ledger, in our copy or the legacy one (defect 157)
	no components setup, alone among the nineteen
	last sheet June 2026, a month before the payroll stops (defect 280)
	pay fully recorded month by month, 10,66,400.00 gross, 7,14,430.00 paid

A person who has left would have no current setup, which is consistent. What
remains unexplained is only the name -- and that is the question already put to
the owner, unchanged. **The money is documented; it is the people who are not.**

## 283. Payroll could run the months the shop already had and could not take on anybody new

Defect 281 built the screen that prepares a month. It reads each person's
allowances and deductions from `mcj_staff_components`, and nothing could write
that table -- the component MASTER had a screen (six components, PF through
D.A) and the per-person amounts did not.

So a shop could re-run August for the people already on file and could not hire
anybody. `/mcj/staff-pay`, What a Person Is Paid, is the other half.

	the master's six components, every one offered
	which way each goes — PF, ESI, P.TAX and I.TAX come off the pay,
	HRA and D.A go on it
	a blank is not a component: 8 of the shop's 12 people pay no ESI,
	6 pay no PF

Driven on a real person first -- ANKUSH KHANDELWAL comes back D.A 11,500.00,
HRA 5,500.00, P.TAX 150.00 and nothing else, which is exactly his setup -- and
then on somebody new, whose four amounts were written, linked to the master, and
removed again. 46 rows before and after.

**Saving replaces rather than merges.** A component taken off the form is one the
person no longer gets, and an old row left behind would go on paying it every
month. Proven by removing the clearing step: *3 row(s), HRA at 9000.00 — HRA
should be gone and D.A raised.*

The setup screen writes what the payroll screen reads, so a test drives both:
set up a new hire with D.A 8,000, HRA 3,000 and P.TAX 130, then run August on a
basic of 20,000.

	gross  31,000.00   = 20,000 + 8,000 + 3,000
	to pay 30,870.00   = less 130 professional tax

Payroll now works end to end for somebody who did not exist when the shop's data
was captured, which is the only version of it that is any use to a shop that is
still trading.

## 285. Two crore of stone data that no screen, report or test can reach

Defect 284 ended by naming what its own measurement could not see: *a table
nothing reads and nothing writes is invisible to it*. Measured, and it was not
hypothetical.

	tables in the schema                              79
	named nowhere in any non-test Go source            2

	mcj_conversion_stones   816 rows, 393 conversions,
	                        2,554.341 carats, 2,60,68,682.20
	mcj_financial_years     0 rows

**816 rows of stones, worth 2.6 crore, loaded by a script and reachable from no
screen, no report and no test.** It could never have appeared in the
unwritten-tables list, because that list's entry condition is that something
reads the table.

### What they are, as far as can be said

	barcode is a tag on file    450 rows   1,075.760 ct   1,38,77,247.10
	no tag with that barcode    366 rows   1,478.581 ct   1,21,91,435.10

More than half share a barcode with a tag that exists, so those may be the same
stones the stone ledger already values -- and **may not**, because this shop
reuses barcodes (defect 29) and a shared barcode is not a shared stone. That is
the trap defect 250 fell into, comparing the same gold to itself and calling it
conservation, so no total is claimed here.

What can be said is that the stone ledger describes 819 rows on the shelf and
these 816 are not those, and that nothing in the application shows them.

**They are not built into a screen for the same reason defect 251 refused the
conversion screen**: a conversion's meaning is not settled by the capture, and
showing its stones would mean choosing one. The finding is that the data exists
and is unreachable, which was not known.

`mcj_financial_years` is the other kind: empty, unread, unwritten. The finyear
package computes years in code, so the table serves nothing.

### The check now looks for both

`check_unwritten_tables.py` reports them, and the distinction is the useful part
-- loaded-and-unread is data the shop has and cannot see; never-touched is a
table that should not exist.

**The first version missed the case it was written for.** It required the table
to have no loader either, so `mcj_conversion_stones` -- which a loader does fill
-- did not appear. It printed only `mcj_financial_years`, and the tell was that
the 816-row table I had just measured was not in the output. **A fix whose
evidence does not show up where you expect it has not been proven**, which is the
third time that sentence has been earned this week.

## 286. A screen could name a real legacy file, be placed nowhere, and appear in no menu

Checking STATUS.md's headline -- **126 of 193 legacy menu screens rebuilt** --
against the source. It is right, and the check found something next to it.

	distinct LegacyFile values in the source   132
	the captured menu lists                    193
	matched                                    126   <- the headline, correct
	claimed but NOT in the menu                  6

The six are real legacy screens that were never menu entries: `day_book.php`,

`print_sales_vocher_register_gst.php`, `add_gold_rate_fix.php` and
`set_rate_gold_opening.php` -- print actions and "add" forms reached from inside
another screen. The navigation code already knows about this case and says so:

	screens were never menu entries.

**Nothing required it.** The guard fires only when `LegacyFile` is empty, so a

appear in no menu at all.

All six declare a position today, so nothing is lost. Nothing kept them right.

called 126 times at start-up. Proven by taking the position off `day_book.php`:

	panic: navigation: screen "/mcj/reports/day-book" names day_book.php, which
	the captured menu does not list, so it must give Top and Item to say where
	it belongs

The first count of this was taken from `links.go` alone: 126 registrations, 104

counterpart and a headline overstated by that much.

`LegacyFile` is declared in five files, not one: 104 in `links.go`, 18 in

132 in all, and `status_figures.py` reads every one of them, which is why its

**Ninth time this session a measurement has come from a narrower source than the

disagreed with a tool that had been right for a fortnight, and the tool was

rather than checking the method.**

Defect 287 left two legacy tables nobody had read. One of them is an audit trail
the rebuild was missing.

	BAPI              1,186
	KESHAV              153

	six others

of the shop's 324 captured sale movements do, and the sale screen writes it. So

The other table, `ledger_ref_details`, is 1,071 rows of party references with
**2 names and 1 mobile number filled in**. Nothing to load.

### Done

	migration      entered_by on mcj_vouchers, '' meaning not recorded
	loader         load_voucher_authors.sh, joined on (type, legacy_v_id),
	               earliest row per voucher — 10 vouchers name two people and
	               the first is who created it
	result         1,416 of 1,848 vouchers now say who raised them
	going forward  all five places that raise a voucher name the current user:
	               a sale, its receipt, a credit note, old gold, and the

### Two of my own mistakes, both cheap

**The context was wrong in one of the five.** Four voucher literals had `ctx` in
scope and the fifth did not, so the build failed on `undefined: ctx` -- caught by
the compiler in a second.

**The list test looked at the wrong month.** The register defaults to the current
month and the seeded voucher is dated April, so the table had no rows and no
headers, and the test reported "the voucher list has no column for who raised
it" when the column was there. The tell was that the page contained *Narration*
and *Voucher* -- the other headers -- which cannot happen if the header row is
missing. **A failing assertion is worth reading twice when the thing it says is
absent has a neighbour that is present.**

## 289. A year-end snapshot was merged as if it were an event log, so four hallmark events happened twice

The stock trail is built from two legacy logs. The first,
`barcode_wise_all_transaction` (8,561 rows), is an event log. The second,
`retail_all_stock`, was treated as one too, and it is not: it is partly a
**year-end snapshot**.

The tell is in its own dates. Eight of its rows carry a voucher number, and
every one of those vouchers belongs to financial year 2024-25 -- yet five of the
eight are stamped **1 April 2025**, the first day of the next year:

	barcode    movement  log 1 (the event)  log 2 (the snapshot)  voucher
	94132093   ISS-HM    2024-10-01         2025-04-01            HMISS/2425/00014
	94132093   REC-HM    2024-10-01         2025-04-01            HMREC/2425/00014
	45148896   ISS-HM    2025-03-01         2025-04-01            HMISS/2425/00023
	45148896   REC-HM    2025-03-01         2025-04-01            HMREC/2425/00022
	10864120R1 SALE-RET  2025-03-28         2025-04-01            SR/2425/00058

The voucher number is what proves these are one event and not two: a hallmark
issue voucher cannot issue the same tag twice, and `HMISS/2425/00014` names
barcode 94132093 once.

The loader skipped a second-log row when the first log already had **the same
barcode on the same day**. That rule catches the three rows whose dates happen
to agree and lets these five through. So the trail said tag 94132093 was sent
for hallmarking and came back in October 2024 *and again* eighteen months later
-- and because the phantom copy is the later one, "issued for hallmarking,
1 April 2025" was the **last thing the trail said about a tag sitting on the
shelf today**.

It reached the owner. The hallmarking report fetches this count rather than
asserting it:

	"The trail holds 12 hallmark movement(s) in two and a half years, so the
	 flag is set by hand rather than by the process."

There are **8**. The sentence is an argument about how little the shop hallmarks,
built on a number 50% too big.

### Done

`tools/legacy/load_movements.sh` now skips a second-log row on either of two
tests: the first log has the same barcode on the same day, **or** it has the same
barcode, movement and voucher number. The second test applies only to rows that
carry a voucher number -- opening and "New Create" rows do not, and stay on the
day rule, which is right, because the 2024 and 2025 openings are two real events
over the same tags.

Trail 9,036 -> **9,031**. `retail_all_stock` no longer contributes any hallmark
row; the report now says 8. `SALE-RET` 18 -> 17, and where 17 of 18 named a
person, all 17 now do -- the row that named nobody was the phantom.

Invariant rule 15, "one voucher moves a tag once", counts events recorded twice
under a single voucher number. It is allowed **18**, which is the legacy's own:
those sit twice in the *first* log with two row ids each, because re-saving a
bill re-logged its tags -- the eight tags on GST/2627/00150 appear on both 3 and
4 July 2026. That is the shop's history. The rule guards the merge, which is
ours. Checked by inserting one duplicate: 19 against an allowance of 18, fails.

Six code comments quoted the old total and two quoted "18 sale returns"; all
corrected. One said "every one of the 9,036 movements references a document
number", which was never true -- 396 carry a document number, 6,395 say
"New Create", 1,770 "Opening" and 470 nothing. Corrected to what the trail
actually holds rather than to a smaller wrong number.

## 290. The same event was spelled two ways, so asking for opening stock missed a year of it

The same two logs disagree about how to spell one movement. The first says
`OP-STK`; the second says `OPN-STK`, and its own wording column for those rows
reads, in words, "Opening". Every other code -- `NEW-BAR`, `SALE-RET`, `ISS-HM`,
`REC-HM` -- is spelled identically in both, so this is the only pair.

Both openings are real: 1,770 tags on 1 April 2024 and 278 on 1 April 2025, a
financial year apart. The defect is not the events, it is that the rebuild
carried both spellings through and then treated them as different kinds of thing.

`movementLabel` in the stock history screen names nine codes in plain English and
`OP-STK` is one of them. `OPN-STK` is not, so it fell to the default, which
returns the code. Two consequences, both on the screen an audit uses:

- 278 rows read `OPN-STK` sitting among "sold", "returned by customer",
  "opening stock".
- The Movement filter is built from the distinct codes in the data, so it offered
  **both** "opening stock" and a raw "OPN-STK" as separate choices. Asking for
  opening stock returned the 2024 opening and silently dropped the whole of the
  2025 one.

### Done

The loader spells it `OP-STK` on the way in, with the reason on the line. Nothing
is lost: the `source` column already records which log a row came from, so
provenance survives normalisation. This follows the loader's own precedent --
it already upper-cases the user column "so a person appears once in a report
rather than twice".

`OP-STK` is now 2,048 rows spanning both openings, and the filter offers one
"opening stock" that returns both years.

Invariant rule 16, "the trail speaks words, not codes", counts movements the
stock history screen cannot name. Rather than pin this one code, it **reads the
`case` labels out of `movements.go`** and checks the data against them, so a new
code from the legacy or a renamed label in the screen cannot drift apart
silently. Checked by inserting an `OPN-STK` row: 1 against 0, fails.

The runner described every allowance as "the migration's", which was already
untrue of the allowances that come from legacy history rather than from a
migration; reworded to "allowed".

## 291. The audit screen showed every event twice for the one tag an auditor was told to look at

Found by checking the fix for defect 290 against the database instead of
accepting the page. Asking the stock history screen for the April 2025 opening
returned **280 rows**; the database holds **278** movements matching. Two rows
came from nowhere.

The join is the reason. The screen joins the stock table only to name the item:

	FROM mcj_stock_movements m
	LEFT JOIN mcj_stock_items s ON s.barcode = m.barcode AND ...
	LEFT JOIN mcj_items i       ON i.id = s.item_id

`barcode` is not unique in `mcj_stock_items`, so a movement is printed **once per
stock row that shares its barcode**. Exactly one barcode in the shop has two:
**86065435** — which is blocker **B8**, the duplicate barcode. Its four movements
were drawn as eight rows.

So the one tag an auditor has been told to look at was the one tag whose history
was doubled, on the screen whose entire purpose is answering where a piece went.

This is defect 146 in the same file, half fixed. That defect found the same join
inflating the count under the list, and the count was changed to
`count(DISTINCT m.id)` with a comment explaining why. **The query that draws the
rows was left alone.** The guard was put on the summary and not on the thing the
summary summarises.

### Done

The rows now join `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (... ORDER BY s.id LIMIT 1)`, so exactly one
stock row can ever name a movement, and the `ORDER BY m.moved_on DESC` the screen
needs is untouched. Which of the two pieces names the item is arbitrary but
stable; for a barcode held by two pieces there is no right answer, which is what
the caveat row already on this screen says.

The summary count lost its joins altogether. It only ever joined so that
`count(DISTINCT m.id)` could undo the duplication the join itself caused, and
nothing in the filters touches the stock table — so the join was a hazard being
corrected for, and removing it is the correction.

Live: the April 2025 opening now returns 278 rows against the database's 278, and
barcode 86065435 returns 4 against its 4 movements. Those four are genuine — two
pieces share the barcode and each was counted in both the 2024 and 2025 openings.

`TestStockHistory_ListsAMovementOncePerMovement` seeds two stock rows on one
barcode and a single movement, and asserts it is listed once. Checked against the
bug by restoring the plain join: *"one movement against a barcode held by two
tags was listed 2 times"*.

A second test was written and deleted rather than kept. It asserted the
truncation footer did not appear — but with one movement the footer is absent
whether the rows are doubled or not, so it could not have failed against the bug.
That is the same decoration as defects 266 and 270.

### Then the same join was looked for everywhere else

Seven queries join the stock table. One joins on `id` and is safe
(`stoneledger.go`). The other six all join on `barcode`, so each would print a
row twice for a duplicated barcode:

	conversions.go (twice)   mcj_stock_conversion_pieces
	salecost.go              mcj_sales_invoice_lines
	mrpsales.go              mcj_sales_invoice_lines
	barcodeedits.go          mcj_barcode_edits
	ordertobarcode.go        mcj_customer_order_lines
	stocktake.go             the barcodes a person has just scanned

**None of them is affected today.** 86065435 appears in no table but the movement
trail — 0 rows in conversion pieces, 0 in invoice lines, 0 in barcode edits. They
are latent, not live, and no change was made to them.

`stocktake.go` was worth checking by hand because a person can put that barcode
in by scanning it. Its filter is `WHERE t.id IS NULL OR NOT t.in_stock`, and both
of 86065435's rows are `in_stock` and identical (MALA, 1 piece, ₹900.00, no
weight), so a scan of it produces no exception row at all.

What makes six latent joins worth a guard is that a **second** duplicate would
make all of them live at once, silently. New invariant rule, "a barcode names one
tag", allowed **1** — B8 itself, which is a blocker and not news. Checked by
copying a stock row: 2 against an allowance of 1, fails.

The first attempt at that check inserted nothing — the copy collided with a
unique index on `(tenant_id, legacy_id)` — and the rules reported "17 of 17 hold"
over a database that had not changed. Recorded because a self-check that silently
verifies nothing is the failure mode of defects 278 and 279, and it happened again
here, in the act of guarding against it.

## 292. The two biggest unread legacy tables, read and dismissed — and B24 turns out to be about three quarters of the shelf

Continuing down defect 287's list of tables nothing loads or reads. These were
the two largest left.

**`design_no_status` — 5,242 rows. Nothing to load.**

Three columns: a design code, a status of 0 or 1, and one retail point. 5,218
distinct codes, of which 176 carry status 1.

	all 5,218 codes already exist in mcj_designs
	status 0   5,042 designs, 68 of them ever became a tag
	status 1     176 designs,  1 of them ever became a tag

The flag does not mark designs that were used — 1.3% of the unflagged became
tags against 0.6% of the flagged, so whatever it means, it is not that. No legacy
screen reads the table; the only file in the capture that names it is
`back_up_php.html`, which lists every table in the database.

And the catalogue underneath it is nine years dormant: all 5,221 designs are
dated **5 July 2016 to 20 January 2017**, and **none** since the trail begins in
April 2024. Loading an unexplained flag over a dead catalogue would add a column
nobody could interpret. The 24 codes that appear more than once are all status 0,
so there is no conflict to resolve either.

**`barcode_image` — 3,965 rows. Nothing to load, and it made blocker B24 worse.**

Three columns: a barcode and a URL. Every URL points at
`http://tag09.com/mcj2/images/bar_pic/…` — the third-party host of B24, which
answers with a bot-challenge page rather than the images, and which I have
deliberately not worked around. So there is nothing here to load: the rows are
pointers, and what they point at is not retrievable from a script.

But nobody had measured what the pointers are worth. B24 said "1,023 tags'
photographs" and stopped there:

	tags with a photograph                        1,023
	of those, on the shelf today                    889
	their value                       ₹10,73,39,445.03
	the shelf                         ₹14,23,61,188.20
	                                            = 75.4%

**Three quarters of the shelf by value has its only photograph on a domain the
shop does not appear to control.** That is not a photo archive of things long
sold. B24 and its summary line now carry the figure.

The shelf total was checked against the established baseline rather than taken
from one query. `SUM(amount)` over the same rows is ₹12,97,04,187.18 — that is
the goods before making and tax, not the shelf, and quoting it would have
understated the total by ₹1.27 crore. The figure above is `SUM(total)`, which is
the number every other shelf figure in these documents uses.

### Done

Nothing loaded, by decision, for both tables. B24 gained the measured stake and
its summary row now says 889 tags and 75.4%.

## 293. The shop could say what its departments were, and nothing could say what any of them did

`barcode_history` was the last of defect 287's unread tables. As an event log it
is dead: all **3,083** of its rows match a movement the trail already holds on
barcode, movement and day — not one event is missing. Nothing to load.

But it has a column the trail does not, and following that column found something
much bigger than the table.

**`dept_code` sits on twenty-eight legacy tables.** Every sale, order, estimate,
sale return, purchase return, stock inward, old gold purchase, karigar stock row
and conversion records the department that raised it. The department master was
loaded — `mcj_legacy_departments`, 12 rows, and there is a Departments screen
reading it — but **not one transaction carried a department**. The only columns
matching `%dept%` on our side were `mcj_packets.depth_mm` and `depth_percent`,
which are a physical depth.

So the shop could say what its departments *were* and nothing could say what any
of them *did*.

It is not a formality with one dominant value. On the three header tables:

	224 bills        CASH 185, ORDER 19, DATAENTRY 11, SUB ADMIN 5, WORKSHOP 4
