	284 orders       WORKSHOP 117, SALES 103, DATAENTRY 58, RECEPTION 3, CASH 2, Back Office 1
	859 conversions  WORKSHOP 427, CASH 347, ORDER 60, ADMIN 21, +3

### Done

Migration `mcj-1787413000.sql` adds `department varchar(8)` to
`mcj_sales_invoices`, `mcj_customer_orders` and `mcj_stock_conversions`. The
**code** is stored and joined to `mcj_legacy_departments.code`, so a department
renamed in the master is renamed everywhere. `''` means the legacy row named none
— the same choice as `entered_by` in defect 288, and for the same reason a NULL
would confuse "not recorded" with "name missing".

The three loaders fill it. **All 224 bills, 284 orders and 859 conversions are
attributed; none is blank, and every code resolves to a named department.** That
is unusual in this data and worth stating.

New screen, **What Each Department Did** (`/mcj/reports/department-work`). It
walks the master so a department that raised nothing says "raised nothing" rather
than being left off — three of the twelve are in that state, including
Retail (Sales), which defect-era notes already flagged as the retail face nobody
was assigned to.

	WORKSHOP       4 bills      3,42,669.00  117 orders  83,87,663.00  427 conv  8,856.236 g
	CASH         185 bills  1,77,91,355.00    2 orders      8,494.00  347 conv  3,130.227 g
	SALES          -                         103 orders  78,01,322.00    -
	ORDER         19 bills     61,06,653.00    -                        60 conv    707.776 g
	DATAENTRY     11 bills      3,52,209.00   58 orders 1,05,79,231.00    2 conv      9.508 g
	             224        2,47,65,386.00  284       2,68,52,217.00  859      12,827.081 g

**What the screen refuses to be:** a league table. A bill is attributed to the
department that RAISED it, and CASH raises most of them because CASH is where
bills are made. The reading worth having is the other one — ORDER raises 19 bills
averaging over three lakh while CASH's 185 average under one, and WORKSHOP takes
117 of the 284 orders. That is how work flows, not who sells well. The screen says
so on its face.

### The figures were checked against gates that already existed

Three of the four footer totals are numbers something else already asserts, so
they are cross-checks rather than restatements:

	224 bills           the invoice loader's own count
	284 orders          the order loader's own count
	859 conversions     the conversion loader's own count
	2,68,52,217.00      the order loader's gate: "estimates tie at 26852217.00"
	12,827.081 g        the conversion loader's gate: "net weight ties at 12827.081 g"

The weight total was missing on the first render — the per-department weights were
right and the footer showed nothing, because I had not accumulated it. Adding it
produced 12,827.081 g, which is what made it a cross-check rather than a fourth
unverified number.

### Two mistakes of mine, recorded

**I measured the wrong tables first.** The department splits I originally wrote
into the migration comment — "sales CASH 198, ORDER 109", "orders WORKSHOP 230,
SALES 83" — came from `sales_vou_main` and `customer_order_main`, which are the
**line** tables. The columns I was adding sit on the **header** tables
`sales_vou` and `customer_order`, whose splits are 185/19 and 117/103. Caught by
noticing that the header counts must add to 224 and 284, which the line figures do
not. The migration comment now carries the header figures and says that the counts
adding up is how the join key was checked. This is the eleventh time in this
project that reading a table adjacent to the right one has produced a plausible
wrong number.

**A second test I wrote was worth keeping only because I broke the code to check
it.** `TestDepartmentWork_CountsDoNotMultiplyEachOther` seeds CASH with 2 bills
and 3 conversions. Swapping the scalar subqueries for a naive three-way join makes
it fail, which is the only reason to trust it — three one-to-many tables hanging
off one department is exactly the shape that produced defect 291, and a report
that multiplied 2 by 3 would have looked entirely plausible at 6.

### The bigger half: which department HOLDS the stock

Carrying the department onto bills, orders and conversions says who RAISED a
transaction. The same sweep found the other half, and it covers the whole shelf.

`cla_retail_trans_bar_detail` carries a `dept_code` on **every one of the 2,816
tags**. `barcode_main`, which the stock loader reads, does not — which is why the
column was missed. Deduplicated by barcode and joined to the shelf it accounts
for all 2,575 tags in stock and every rupee of the ₹14,23,61,188.20:

	WORKSHOP       862 tags   ₹3,64,42,394.60
	ORDER          799        ₹3,67,55,414.59
	SUB ADMIN      604        ₹4,62,20,787.74
	CASH           239        ₹1,19,44,679.89
	Back Office     66        ₹1,07,02,187.42
	ADMIN            5           ₹2,95,723.96

**The most tags and the most value are in different departments.** WORKSHOP holds
862 tags worth ₹3.64 crore; SUB ADMIN holds 604 worth ₹4.62 crore; Back Office
holds 66 worth ₹1.07 crore, which is ₹1.62 lakh a tag against WORKSHOP's ₹42,000.
Nobody could ask that before.

Migration `mcj-1787414000.sql` adds `department` to `mcj_stock_items`; the stock
loader fills it from the transfer detail, deduplicated by barcode. **All 2,816
tags are attributed, none blank.** The screen gained "Tags held" and "On the
shelf", and is now ordered by what a department holds.

Only one barcode has more than one row in that table — 86065435 again — and its
two rows agree on the department, so which one the dedup takes does not matter.
That was checked rather than assumed: earliest against latest disagreed on 0 of
2,815 barcodes.

**I hit defect 291's own mechanism while measuring this.** The first version of
the query joined the detail table to the shelf without deduplicating, and
reported 2,577 tags worth ₹1,800 too much — the duplicate barcode counted twice,
in an ad-hoc query, minutes after fixing the same fault in the code. It was
caught by the totals failing to equal 2,575 and ₹14,23,61,188.20, which is the
only reason the figures above can be trusted.

### What is deliberately still uncarried

`dept_code` is on twenty-eight legacy tables and the department is now on four of
the things they describe. The rest are small: estimate 2 rows, purchase_return 3,
sale_return 3, customer_own_goods_receive_detail 7, karigar_gold_stock 2,
old_gold_purchase 25, stock_inward 43 — about 85 rows between them. They are left
alone rather than done quietly, and this is the note saying so.

Invariant rule 18, "a transaction's department exists", counts transactions whose
code names no department in the master. This matters because the screen walks the
master and asks each department what it did — so a bad code produces no error and
no row, it simply vanishes. Checked by setting one bill's department to '99':
1 against 0, fails; the bill was then restored by re-running the loader rather
than by writing a value back by hand.

## 294. A loader reported OK while emptying a register another loader owned

Found by a guard rather than by looking: `check_screens_render.py` reported
`/mcj/reports/stone-ledger` rendering with no data over the whole of the shop's
history, and `check_unwritten_tables.py` reported `mcj_conversion_stones` at
**0 rows** where it holds 816. I had done it, ten minutes earlier, by re-running
one loader.

Three child tables reference their parent **ON DELETE CASCADE**:

	mcj_conversion_stones  ->  mcj_stock_conversions   CASCADE
	mcj_ordered_stones     ->  mcj_customer_orders     CASCADE
	mcj_sold_stones        ->  mcj_sales_invoices      CASCADE

Each parent loader begins by deleting its own rows, so it silently takes the
child's with it. Inside `load_all.sh` that is harmless, because the child loader
runs next. Run on its own — which is exactly what I did, three times, to fill in
the new department column — it leaves a register empty.

**And every gate still passed.** The loaders' gates count their own rows:
`load_conversions.sh` confirmed 859 conversions and 1,242 pieces and printed OK,
while 816 stone rows it had just destroyed went unmentioned. A checker that only
audits its own output cannot see what it broke next door.

Damage as found: `mcj_conversion_stones` 816 -> 0, `mcj_sold_stones` 203 -> 0,
`mcj_ordered_stones` 115 -> 0. All three restored by running `load_all.sh`, which
orders them correctly.

### The guard was already there for one of the three, and was too quiet

`load_invoices.sh` already knew. A prior defect had put a check in it:

	NOTE: reloading the invoices cascaded mcj_sold_stones to empty.
	      Run ./load_sold_stones.sh to put its 203 rows back.

It printed to stderr and **exited 0**. So it did not stop anything, and I lost it
anyway — I ran the loader, filtered the output for `OK` and `FAIL`, and the word
NOTE was not in either. A warning that a caller can filter out is not a guard.
The other two parents had nothing at all.

### Done

All three parents now **put the rows back** rather than report them missing. Each
ends by checking the cascaded child and, if it is empty, running that child's
loader and confirming it worked:

	echo "-- mcj_conversion_stones was cascaded away; reloading it --"
	"${HERE}/load_conversion_stones.sh"
	CH=$(...); [ "$CH" != "0" ] || { echo "FAIL: still empty"; exit 1; }

Repairing rather than complaining was the second attempt. The first version
failed with the remedy named — which read well and **broke `load_all.sh`**, since
the parent now exited 1 before the child it was complaining about could run. That
is worth recording: a guard that turns a silent data loss into a hard stop of the
whole load is not obviously an improvement. Both are idempotent, so load_all
running the child again straight afterwards costs nothing.

Verified three ways: each loader run standalone now exits 0 with its child intact
(203, 115, 816 rows); `load_all.sh` still completes with `=== all loads
complete ===`; and the stone ledger has its data back.

## 295. The screen I had just built would have lost the first bill raised in the new system

Asked of my own work an hour after finishing it: the What Each Department Did
screen walks the department master and asks each department what it did — so
what happens to a record no department claims?

It disappears. Not from one column: from the table, because there is no row for
it, and from the footer, because the footer sums the rows. The screen would have
gone on reconciling to the rupee — 224 bills, ₹2,47,65,386.00, 2,575 tags,
₹14,23,61,188.20 — while quietly leaving trade out.

**And it is not hypothetical, because nothing in the app writes a department.**
A grep across every controller and repository finds no writer: the four INSERTs
that create a bill (`sale.go:1513`), an order (`order.go:496`), a tag
(`tag.go:427`) and a conversion do not mention the column. Every legacy record is
attributed, so the totals are whole *today* — and the first bill made through the
new screens would have been invisible on a screen that looked exact.

This is the same shape as defect 288, where the shop recorded who raised a
voucher and the app recorded nobody. The difference is that here I built the
reader and the gap in the same afternoon.

### Done

The screen now ends with a **(no department recorded)** row counting everything
the master cannot claim — blank department or a code the master does not have —
and adds it to the footer, so the totals are the whole shop rather than the
attributable part of it. Today that row is absent, because there is nothing
unattributed; it appears the moment there is.

`TestDepartmentWork_DoesNotLoseWhatNoDepartmentClaims` inserts a bill exactly as
the sale screen writes one — `department = ''` — and asserts it is listed, that
the footer counts 3 bills and ₹7,444.00 rather than 2 and ₹3,000.00, and that the
summary still says "2 active, 1 raised nothing" rather than counting the
unattributed row as a thirteenth department. That last assertion caught a real
mistake: the summary read `len(out)-idle`, and appending the new row to `out`
made it call the row a department. Departments are now counted as they are read.

### What is NOT done, and why it is a question rather than a task

Which department should a bill raised in the new system be attributed to?

There is no way to answer it from the data. The legacy user table carries the
department on `role_code`, keyed by `login_id`; the app's users are SDK users
keyed by email, and nothing links the two. `entered_by` stores the app user's
display name, and matching that against legacy names — BAPI, KESHAV, ADMIN —
would be a guess dressed as a lookup.

So the options are the shop's to pick, not mine: attach a department to each app
user, put a department picker on the billing screen, or decide the new system does
not track it and let the column describe history only. **This goes on the list of
things needing an answer.** Until then the screen says "does not yet record a
department" on the face of the row rather than implying the shop has one.

## 296. A report about a flag, and nothing in the system can set the flag

> **Corrected by defect 297.** The count below is too low. I decided "written by"
> with a filename grep, and a file that mentions a column is not a file that
> writes it — `certificate_no` (678 tags) and `certification_charge` (371) are
> READ by the sale screen when billing, not written, so they belong in the first
> table here and are missing from it. The real total is 17 columns, not 11. The
> hallmark finding itself stands.

Defects 288 and 295 are the same shape — a column the shop fills that the app
never writes — so the family was swept for rather than waited for. For every
column on `mcj_stock_items`, how many tags carry a value, which screens write it,
and which screens read it.

**The tag creation screen writes 28 of the table's 51 columns.** Most of the rest
are keys or timestamps. Three are not.

	column              tags with a value   written by   read by
	hallmarked                        432       NOTHING   Hallmark Records
	hallmark_charge                    76       NOTHING   Hallmark Records, Quotation
	wastage_percent                    26       NOTHING   Quotation

`hallmarked` appears in exactly one non-test file in the whole codebase —
`reports/hallmarking.go` — and every appearance reads it. There is no INSERT, no
UPDATE, no form field. The column is `NOT NULL DEFAULT false`, so **every tag
created through this system is permanently recorded as not hallmarked, and there
is no screen on which anyone can say otherwise.**

### The report was saying so, and saying it wrongly

Hallmark Records carries a caveat, and the caveat is the honest part of a ₹11.5
crore headline. It read:

	"...so the flag is set by hand rather than by the process."

That was true of the old system. In this one the flag is not set by hand either,
because no hand can reach it. The sentence invited the owner to think a clerk
could fix the record, and nothing could.

`wastage_percent` and `hallmark_charge` have a quieter version of the same
problem: the Quotation report reads both off the tag, so a quote for any tag
created here silently omits a wastage percentage and a hallmark charge, and looks
complete.

### Done

Both notes on Hallmark Records now say no screen can set the flag, and the doc
comment says the same. The `missing > 0` note reads:

	"...and NO SCREEN HERE CAN SET THE FLAG — so this is a report about a
	 record that has stopped being kept, not about the pieces."

`TestHallmarking_CarriesTheCaveatWithTheNumber` asserted the note contained
"set by hand" and **failed when the wording was corrected — which is the test
working.** The assertion was moved to the new claim rather than deleted: what it
exists to prevent is the headline travelling without a caveat, and that is still
what it checks.

### Not fixed, because it needs a decision rather than a screen

A hallmarking screen is buildable — the document series pattern
(`HMISS/2425/00014`) is the same one four other screens already use. What stops me
choosing is that **the shop has recorded 8 hallmark movements in two and a half
years, over 4 tags.** Against 432 flagged tags, that says the flag was set
somewhere other than the movement trail, and probably not as part of any workflow.
Building a send-and-receive screen on that evidence would be inventing a process
rather than restoring one.

So the question is the shop's: is hallmarking recorded in the ERP at all, or on
paper and in the BIS portal? **This goes on the list of things needing an answer.**
Until it is answered, the report says plainly that the record has stopped rather
than implying somebody is keeping it.

### The other half of the sweep: columns loaded and read by nobody

The same measurement found eight columns carrying legacy data that **no screen
writes and no screen reads** — invisible in a different way from defect 285's
unreachable tables, because these sit on a table five screens do use:

	certification_type   2,801 tags   by_val 2,683, per_ct 118
	lot_no               2,059 tags   59 distinct lots
	making_sales         1,825 tags
	remarks1               451 tags
	certification_rate     371 tags
	design_code             96 tags
	order_sl                10 tags
	remarks2                 2 tags

`certification_type` is on 2,801 of 2,816 tags and says whether stone
certification was charged by value or per carat — the companion to
`certification_rate` and `certification_charge`, the second of which the sale
screen does write. So the shop's tags record how certification was priced and
nothing in the rebuild reads it.

None of these is fixed here. They are recorded so the next screen built on this
table knows what is already sitting in it, which is the same reason defect 285
exists. `legacy_user_id` (2,808 tags) is deliberately excluded from that list: it
is a legacy key, not shop data.

## 297. The receipt in the customer's hand said how the money moved; the one this system prints did not

Defect 296 swept one table by hand and got part of it wrong. This is the tool
that does it properly, what it found, and the correction it forced.

### The correction to defect 296 first

296 said three columns on `mcj_stock_items` were read by reports and written by
nothing, and eight more were touched by nobody at all — eleven in total. The real
number is **seventeen**, because I decided "written by" with a filename grep, and
a file that mentions a column is not a file that writes it.

	certificate_no        678 tags   I credited sale.go. sale.go READS it (line 1246).
	certification_charge  371 tags   likewise.
	ref_no                260 tags   I credited creditnote.go. Its INSERT at line 805
	                                 names ref_no on a DIFFERENT TABLE.
	order_no               11 tags   likewise, order.go and partysample.go.
	size                   99 tags   the readers I found were the word "size" elsewhere.

**`certificate_no` and `certification_charge` matter more than the three 296 did
report.** The sale screen reads both off the tag when billing, so a certified
piece created in this system carries no certificate number and no certification
charge onto its bill, and looks complete. That belonged in 296's first table and
was not there.

### The tool

`tools/check_unwritten_columns.py` asks the question 288, 295 and 296 each
answered by hand: which columns did the shop fill that no screen here can fill
again. It does not grep for the column name. It parses the SQL in non-test Go —
the parenthesised list after `INSERT INTO <table>`, and the assignments in an
`UPDATE <table> ... SET` — so a column counts as written only if a statement
against **that** table names it. Its own docstring lists what it cannot see:
runtime-built SQL, and whether a read exists (the "read" column is a grep, and
says so).

### The tool's first output was wrong, in the way its own note predicted

It reported 44 columns on 12 tables, and seven of them were `mcj_ledgers` —
`account_code` and `display_name` on all 785 rows, `country` on 598, `pan` on
177. I wrote that down as "a party created here can be given neither".

**A clerk can type into every one of them.** `mcj_ledgers` has a full
create-and-edit screen built on `pkg/crud`, which builds its SQL at runtime, so
there is no INSERT in the source for the parser to find. The docstring warned
about exactly this and I believed the output anyway.

The fix was two attempts. Matching `crud.New*Field("col")` was not enough,
because each aggregate wraps those in helpers of its own naming — `text("size")`,
`pctField("making")` — so `mcj_sale_rates` was still reported as unwritable when
every rate on it is editable. **The authority is the aggregate's `mapper.go`**,
whose write map names exactly the columns the generic repository sends to the
database. That is now what the tool reads.

And the first version silently skipped any table it found no INSERT for, on the
reasoning that a loader-only table is another tool's question. That hid whole
tables: `mcj_packets` has an editing screen whose mapper writes 6 columns and a
loader that fills 27, and none of the difference was reported.

**Corrected: 58 columns on 13 tables.** (Defect 298 then wrote two of them — a stone's shape and colour — so the tool now reports **56**.) The largest:

	mcj_stock_items    department 2816, certification_type 2801, lot_no 2059,
	                   making_sales 1825, certificate_no 678, remarks1 451,
	                   hallmarked 432, certification_rate 371 ...
	mcj_voucher_lines  cheque_date 680, cheque_number 593
	mcj_stock_stones   shape_id 555, colour_id 416, packet_id 107, cut_id 28
	mcj_packets        21 columns — the whole solitaire grading detail: depth %,
	                   table %, crown and pavilion angles, girdle, polish,
	                   symmetry, fluorescence, Rapaport price
	mcj_sales_invoices department 224, party_mobile 196, salesperson 131

### What the cheque turned out to be

The tool pointed at `mcj_voucher_lines.cheque_number` and the first reading of
that was wrong too — `voucher.go` does take a cheque number from its form. It
writes it to the **header**, `mcj_vouchers`, and the shop keeps it on the lines:

	vouchers recording how the money moved        554
	  ...on the lines only                        520
	  ...on both                                   34
	  ...on the header only                         0

`reconcile.go` already reads the lines and falls back to the header. **The printed
voucher read the header only**, so on 520 of 554 — 94% — it printed no reference
at all, while the counterfoil the customer kept had one. A receipt is signed by
the person handing over money; this is the field that lets them check it later.

And the column is not really a cheque number. Of its 593 values:

	looks like a cheque number   215      five to eight digits
	bank transfer                112      RTGS, NEFT, IMPS
	UPI                           85      GPAY, PAYTM
	something else               181      "Direct", "IMPSAB", ...

### Done

`voucherprint.go` now falls back to the lines for both the reference and the date,
as the reconciliation screen already did.

The wording is decided in the controller, not the template, because **"Cheque
GPAY" is not a sentence**. `paymentInstrument` prints "Cheque 416710" for a run of
five to eight digits and otherwise prints what the shop wrote, on the grounds that
the shop's own word for it beats a guess at a category. The template's field is
named `Instrument` rather than `ChequeNumber` so the next person reading it knows
the column's name is not its meaning.

Proven on the running app against real vouchers: PMNT 6 and PMNT 8, whose lines
carry 416710 and 416709, print "Cheque 416710" and "Cheque 416709"; JRNL 1, whose
line says Gpay, prints "Gpay" and not "Cheque Gpay".

Two tests, both checked against the old behaviour by reverting the query to
header-only: *"the receipt does not show the cheque its own line records"* and
*"the receipt does not show how the money moved"*.

### Still open from this sweep

Nothing else here is fixed. The 58 columns are now listed by a tool that can be
re-run rather than by a paragraph that goes stale, and the two biggest untouched
groups are the stone attributes — shape on 555 rows, colour on 416, so a
stone-set tag made here cannot record what its stones are — and the packet
grading detail, 21 columns describing solitaires that the packet screen cannot
enter.

`mcj_stock_items.department` heads the list at 2,816 and is defect 295's open
question, not a new one. Two columns are worth nothing and are named so nobody
spends time on them: `mcj_ledgers.display_name` is a 50-character truncation of
`name` (784 of 785 identical, the exception being SONANI JEWELS UNIT OF SONANI
INDUSTRIES PRIVATE LIMITED cut short), and `account_code` equals `code` on 784 of
785 — the exception is `1034 SALES GST`, whose nominal account number is 34.
Those two were the ones I had called the next thing to look at.

## 298. Pricing a tag threw its stones away, and the price kept their value

Taken from defect 297's named-not-fixed list: the stone attributes. Fixing them
uncovered something worse sitting underneath.

### What was asked for

`tag.go` writes twelve columns into `mcj_stock_stones` and omits five. A stone
added through the tagging screen recorded pieces, carats, weight and rates — and
nothing about **what the stone is**. The Sold Stones register joins shape and
colour to name them, so a stone added here would sit in that register with two
blank columns.

The shop's own rows decide the scope:

	shape      555 of 819 stone rows
	colour     416
	cut         28
	sieve        0

Shape and colour are ordinary; cut is on 3% and sieve on none. **Only shape and
colour were added.** A form field nobody fills is a field everybody has to skip,
and the honest place to record that judgement is beside the code — which is what
the comment above `stoneShapeOptions` now says, including that cut belongs there
next if it starts being recorded.

Both are optional and never refuse a tag: the shop leaves them off a third of its
own rows, so demanding them would stop work the old system allowed.

### What was found on the way

The tag screen **prices before it saves**. A post without `action=save` re-renders
the form with the price on it, and the clerk then presses Save — which posts
whatever the form holds at that moment.

`Props.Stones []StoneRow` was declared, read by the template on every row, and
**never assigned anywhere in the controller.** So the grid came back empty, and
the second post carried no stones at all.

The comment above `readStones` is what makes that serious, and it was already in
the file:

	"Every one of the 486 tags on the shelf whose price includes a stone value
	 has its stones itemised -- 486 of 486 -- and the stone registers read the
	 stones, not the figure. A tag with a stone value and no stones would be the
	 first in the shop's history."

Pricing a stone-set tag and then saving it made exactly that tag: a stone value in
the price, and no stones behind it. The invariant was written down, the screen
broke it, and nothing checked.

### Done

`stoneRowsFromForm` hands the grid back on every render. It returns the **raw**
strings rather than the parsed ones, so a carat weight that could not be read
comes back as typed for correction instead of vanishing — the same principle as
the rest of the form.

`stone_shape` and `stone_colour` are parsed, carried on `tagStone`, and written
to `shape_id` and `colour_id`. `check_unwritten_columns.py` now reports only
`packet_id` (107) and `cut_id` (28) for that table, which are the two the evidence
said to leave.

Three tests. `TestTag_KeepsTheStonesWhenItPricesTheTag` was checked against the
bug by removing the one line that fixes it: *"the priced form has lost the stone
that was chosen / its carats / its rate"*, all three.

### Two mistakes of mine in one test

**The test passed by skipping.** The first version looked up an item named
DIAMOND and called `t.Skipf` when it found none — and nothing seeds one, so
`go test` printed `ok` and I had proved nothing. Caught only by re-running with
`-v`. That is defects 270 and 278 again — a check that cannot fail — in the one
new place I had not looked, and the skip made it invisible rather than merely
vacuous. The helper now seeds the item, and a stone row referencing it, because
the screen offers only items some stone or purchase already used.

**One of the three assertions passed for the wrong reason.** Checking that the
response contained the stone's id proved nothing: the id appears in the options
list whether or not the row remembers which was chosen. It now asserts
`value="<id>" selected`, and only then did it fail against the bug.

## 299. A guard that had never once run, found by asking whether defect 298's mistake had siblings

Defect 298 ended with a test of mine that passed by skipping. The obvious next
question is whether anything else in the suite does that, and one thing does —
and it is not a test I wrote.

	$ grep -rn "t.Skip" modules/ --include="*_test.go"
	navigation_links_test.go:136   the captured legacy pages are not on disk
	navigation_test.go:137         no screens registered in this test binary

The first is honest: it skips only if the capture is missing. The second **skips
every single time.**

`TestEveryRegisteredFileExistsInTheLegacyMenu` lived in the navigation package and
read the screen registry directly. Screens register themselves from
`modules/mcj`, so that package's own test binary has an empty registry — the test
hit its guard, printed `no screens registered in this test binary`, and reported
PASS on every run since it was written.

Its comment records that it caught a real fault once: screen 17 registered
against `category_master.php`, which is not in the menu at all — the address
category screen is `category_list.php`. It has caught nothing since, silently,
and its own comment even says *"An earlier version of this test hardcoded a
single filename and so proved nothing"* — the second version proved nothing in a
new way.

### Done

`InLegacyMenu` is exported, and the assertion now lives in
`modules/mcj/navigation_links_test.go`, which imports `mcj` so `links.go` runs and
the registry is real. It **fails** where the old one skipped:

	if len(registered) == 0 {
	    t.Fatal("no screens are registered, so this test proves nothing")
	}

The old location keeps a comment saying what was there, why it could not work,
and not to move it back.

It reports its own coverage rather than passing quietly: **126 registered screens
are in the legacy menu; 6 name a real legacy file that was never a menu entry and
are placed by hand.**

### My first revival asserted the wrong rule and "found" six faults

Revived as written, it failed immediately on six screens — the day book, the GST
sales voucher register print, two rate screens and two add forms.

They are all deliberate, and the code says so where I had not read it:

	// A screen WITH one may still need placing, because plenty of real legacy
	// screens were never menu entries -- print actions and "add" forms reached
	// from inside another screen. Both declare Top and Item.

The rule is **in the menu, OR placed by hand with Top and Item** — which is what
`Register` enforces at start-up. Had I trusted the revived test I would have
logged six defects that are not defects. The assertion now mirrors the real rule,
and the count of each kind is printed so the split stays visible.

The failure path is not guesswork: it was exercised, by that wrong first version,
which is how I know the loop reports rather than passing over.

**No test in the suite skips any more.** Running the whole of it with `-v` and
counting `--- SKIP` gives **0**, which is the figure that says this defect is
closed rather than moved: the only unconditional skip is gone, and the one
conditional skip left — the legacy capture being absent from disk — did not fire,
because the capture is there.

## 300. Nothing tagged in this system could ever be a certified piece

Next from defect 297's list: the certification columns on `mcj_stock_items`.
Following them found that the missing fields are not descriptive — they choose
how a piece is billed.

### Certified is a route, not a label

`sale.go` decides it in one line:

	if certificateNo != "" || certChargeP > 0 {

A certified piece is **not priced by the formula at all.** The screen refuses to
compute and asks the biller for the price agreed across the counter, and defect
228 is why: of the 129 certified pieces the shop has sold, exactly ONE went out at
the tag's stored price and NONE at a computed one — they went at 0.44 to 3.47
times the tag, with 125 of the 129 lines carrying a different metal rate and 107 a
different making.

	certified for billing            699 of 2,816 tags
	  ...of those, on the shelf      566, worth 2,84,75,794.50
	carrying a certificate number    678
	carrying a certification charge  371, 2,12,569.15 in total

**The tag screen wrote neither column.** So a diamond piece with a certificate,
tagged in this system, would have been quietly priced by a formula the shop does
not use for it — and the biller would never have been asked. The refusal that
protects a quarter of the shelf was unreachable for anything new.

This is the sharpest example yet of the defect-297 family. `hallmarked` (296) made
a report untrue; this one changes what a customer pays.

### Done

`certificate_no` and `certification_charge` are on the tag screen, written by the
tag INSERT, and carried on `tagDraft`.

Either field alone makes a piece certified, exactly as the sale screen reads it,
so neither is inferred from the other and both are optional. A charge that cannot
be read **is** reported as a problem — unlike a stone's shape in defect 298,
which is dropped silently, because this one changes the price.

`certification_rate` (371 tags) and `certification_type` are deliberately left
out. The type is on 2,801 of 2,816 tags including plain gold — `by_val` on 2,683,
`per_ct` on 118 — so it is a default rather than a property of certified goods,
and the rate only explains how the charge was reached. The bill uses the charge.

The test is cross-screen, because a one-screen test could not have found this:
`TestDaysTrade_ACertifiedPieceIsBilledAtAnAgreedPrice` sets the day's rate, tags a
piece with a certificate through the tag screen, and then puts it on a bill —
asserting the sale screen asks for the agreed price. Checked against the bug by
making the INSERT write an empty certificate: *"the certificate number was not
recorded"*.

### The assertion I nearly got wrong again

The first version asserted the response contained the word `"certified"`. It
appears in the screen's own explanatory text whether or not this line took that
route, so it would have passed against the bug — the same mistake as defect 298's
options-list assertion, two defects later. It now asserts the whole phrase the
refusal actually prints: *"enter the price agreed with the customer"*.

## 301. The biller chose a salesperson and the invoice showed none

Continuing the defect-297 sweep into `mcj_sales_invoices`. This one is not an
unwritten column — it is two columns for one fact, with the writer using one and
the reader the other.

	all 224 captured bills   name a salesperson in the TEXT column
	                         and carry NO salesperson_id
	every bill raised here   carries a salesperson_id
	                         and leaves the text EMPTY

`sale.go` offers a list from `mcj_salespeople` and writes `salesperson_id`. The
tax invoice reads `i.salesperson`, the text. So the invoice printed **no
salesperson at all** on any bill raised in this system — the template's
`if inv.Salesperson != ""` simply never fired — while the biller's choice sat in
the next column along.

The bill a customer is handed is where this shows. "Served by: …" is on the
invoice because the shop puts it there on all 224 of its own.

### Done

The invoice resolves the name from whichever column holds it, falling back from
the text to a lookup on `mcj_salespeople`:

	COALESCE(NULLIF(btrim(i.salesperson),''),
	         (SELECT sp.name FROM mcj_salespeople sp WHERE sp.id = i.salesperson_id), '')

The reader was changed, not the writer: the id is the better record — it
references a real table rather than repeating a name — and rewriting history into
the text column would lose that. This is the same shape as defect 297's cheque,
where the print learned to read where the shop actually keeps the fact.

Nothing else reads that column: a grep across every report and controller finds
only this one, now fixed.

Two tests, one for each shape, and both were checked against the old code — which
**fails the new-bill test and passes the captured-bill test**, exactly as it
should, showing the fix restored one without breaking the other.

### The test failed for the wrong reason first

Both tests failed on the first run, including the captured-bill one that the old
code should have passed. `invoiceSuite` builds the harness and does **not** seed;
seeding is a separate `seedInvoice` call every other test in the file makes, and
I had not. So the UPDATE matched no rows and the assertion failed against an
empty page.

Had only the new-bill test failed I would have believed it and moved on with a
fix that happened to work. The tell was the test that should have passed failing
too — a fix's evidence appearing where it should not is the same signal as defect
285's, where evidence failing to appear where it should was the tell.

The setup now checks itself before asserting: it counts the bills wired the way
the sale screen writes them and fails with *"no bill is set up the way the sale
screen writes one"* if there are none.

## 302. The GST return's two halves disagreed about whether to say which tax applied

Swept for defect 301's shape — one fact in two columns — and found only one other
pair, `mcj_staff_components.component`/`component_id`, which is fine: all 46 rows
carry both and `staffpay.go` writes both. So I went looking at the tax basis
instead, and the first thing I found was not there.

### What I claimed, and why it was wrong

The sale screen lets the biller override the tax basis. The override reaches the
voucher — an overridden bill posts to IGST — and the sale writes
`place_of_supply` as the party's state, so the bill keeps no record of the
decision. The invoice computes an `Interstate` flag from `place_of_supply` against
the shop's own state.

From that I concluded the printed invoice would show CGST and SGST while the
ledger held IGST, wrote a test asserting the two disagreed, and it failed exactly
as predicted:

	the books charged IGST but the bill records place_of_supply="West Bengal"
	against the shop's "West Bengal", so the invoice will print CGST/SGST

**The invoice prints neither.** `readInvoiceTax` takes the tax from the VOUCHER,
by ledger, so the invoice already agrees with the books — that is what
`TestInvoice_TakesTheTaxFromTheBooks` has been asserting all along. My test proved
that a derived boolean was false; it never checked what the invoice prints, so it
could not have found a contradiction that does not exist.

The `Interstate` field it derived was assigned to the invoice's props and **used
by nothing** — a non-trivial SQL expression with a comment explaining why it
mattered, feeding a field no template reads. It looked load-bearing and was not,
which is how I came to believe it.

### What is actually true

	GSTR-2, purchases   prints a "Tax basis" column -- CGST and SGST, or IGST --
	                    reading mcj_purchase_invoices.interstate, a stored column
	GSTR-1, sales       printed no basis at all, because the sales side stored
	                    nothing to print

The two halves of one return disagreed about whether to say which tax applied.
And the sales side could not have said it: the biller's decision was recorded
nowhere, so even deriving it would have been wrong for any bill that was
overridden.

### Done

`mcj_sales_invoices.interstate`, **nullable on purpose**: the 224 captured bills
have no such flag and must keep deriving it, which they do correctly — 18 are
Bihar against a West Bengal shop. NULL means "not recorded, work it out"; true or
false means somebody decided.

The sale records it. GSTR-1 now prints a Tax basis column exactly as GSTR-2 does,
preferring the stored flag and falling back to place-of-supply against the shop's
state. On the shop's own data: **206 CGST and SGST, 18 IGST**, which is the Bihar
count exactly.

The unused `Interstate` field is gone from the invoice, along with the SQL that
fed it and the now-pointless join to the company table. A field that looks like it
decides something and decides nothing is worse than no field.

`TestSale_RecordsTheTaxBasisItWasBilledOn` asserts the bill records the basis it
was billed on, checked against the bug by reverting the write: *"the bill does not
record which basis it was raised on"*.

### Two things this cost, both worth recording

**I built the fix before I checked the claim.** The migration and both code
changes were written against the invoice-contradicts-ledger story, and only when
I went to prove the invoice printed the wrong tax did I find it prints the right
one. The column survived because the real finding needed it too; the invoice
changes were reverted. Writing the test first would not have helped here — I wrote
one, and it passed against a premise I had not checked.

**The test skipped, and the skip hid a broken form.** Its first version called
`t.Skip` when the override had not reached the books, and it took that branch —
not because the override failed, but because my form was missing nothing at all
and instead had too much: `pay_mode` and `pay_amount` with no `pay_account`, which
made the save fail. The skip turned a broken test into a quiet one, three defects
after 299 was logged for exactly that. It is now a `t.Fatal`.

## 303. Five fields computed for screens that never showed them, and a comment that said the opposite of the code

Defect 302 turned on a props field that was computed, assigned, documented, and
read by nothing. Go does not warn about that — an unused struct field compiles
cleanly — so it was worth asking how many others there are.

Every field on every page struct, checked against whether the package renders it:

	taglabel      Label.Total          a price, formatted and never printed
	taglabel      Geometry.FoldAt      where the tag folds, parsed and unused
	stocktake     Result.MatchedCount  computed and never shown
	voucherprint  Voucher.ShopState    read from the company record, unprinted
	partysample   ReceiveProps.CanSave declared, never set, never read

### The one that mattered was a comment

Chasing `FoldAt` led to the tag label's header, which said of the shop's stored
print setup:

	"That is the shop's own setup and is used as it stands."

It is not. **Only the type size is applied** — six point, through `labelStyle`.
The margins, panel positions, fold centres and printer type are printed on screen
as a sentence describing the setup, and nothing is laid out by them.

That matters because of how blocker B3 closes: somebody holds a printed label
against a real tag. Doing that against this claim, they would measure margins the
screen never applied and conclude the reconstruction was wrong.

The neighbouring helper has always said it correctly — *"The rest of the geometry
is shown to the user rather than applied blindly, because the unit those numbers
are in is exactly what blocker B3 is still missing"* — so the two comments in one
feature disagreed, and the wrong one was in the header, where a reader arrives
first. The header now says what the code does and why.

`FoldAt` is deleted rather than applied, with `centreX` that fed it. Not applying
it is the same deliberate decision the helper documents; a parsed value sitting
unused only suggests somebody forgot.

### The rest

**`Label.Total` is deleted, and the query no longer reads the price.** A price on
the tag would be wrong here rather than merely absent: this shop bills at the
day's metal rate, not the tag's stored figure, and of 129 certified pieces sold
exactly one went out at the stored price (defect 228). A number on the tag is one
the customer can reasonably expect to pay. Whether a real tag carries one belongs
to B3, and the struct now says so instead of implying an answer.

**`MatchedCount` is now shown** — a fifth figure on the stock take, "Found: on the
books and scanned". It is derivable from two of the others, which is presumably
why nobody noticed, but making a stock-taker subtract is not the same as telling
them.

**`ShopState` is now printed.** The address stops at the city — "25A, CAMAC
STREET, KOLKATA-700016" — so the receipt named no state at all, while the value
sat fetched and unused.

**`CanSave` is deleted.** No controller ever set it and no template read it.

### The sweep was wrong the first time, in the same way twice

Its first run reported eight fields. Two — `Line.Pieces` and `Line.Number` on the
invoice — are used through methods, `PiecesText()` and `NumberText()`, which a
search for `.Pieces` does not see.

Worse, I read the templates for the tag label's geometry, found every field
appearing only inside one descriptive sentence, and concluded that **none** of the
shop's print setup was applied. That was about to become the finding. The font
size is applied — by `labelStyle(g)`, a helper in a plain `.go` file in the
templates package, which my search of `.templ` files never opened.

Both misses have the same shape as defect 302's: a value reached through
something other than a direct field reference. The sweep now reads the package's
`.go` helpers alongside its templates, and treats a method of the field's name as
a use. Re-run, it reports one field — `Voucher.Kind`, which the controller uses to
choose the voucher's label and is legitimately never rendered.

### And the verification was wrong before the code was

Checking the receipt afterwards, the shop's state was still missing. The change
looked to have failed.

The server I was reading had not been started by me. A new one had been launched
in the background and had died immediately —

	bind: address already in use

— leaving an older process serving the port and answering with code from before
the edit. Nothing said so: the launch was backgrounded, so its exit was silent,
and the page came back 200 with the old markup. **A false negative from talking
to the wrong process**, and had I trusted it I would have "fixed" a change that
was already correct. Restarted properly, the receipt reads MANIK CHAND JEWELLERS
/ 25A, CAMAC STREET, KOLKATA-700016 / West Bengal / GSTIN.

Clearing it out cost something too: `pkill -f wingold` matches the compiled test
binaries as well as the server, so it killed the full suite that was running in
the background, which exited 144 and had to be started again.

## 304. "Set Aside" could only ever mean nothing was set aside

Following the unwritten columns into the order book. `mcj_customer_order_lines`
carries a `barcode` on 59 of its 366 rows — the piece put by for the customer who
ordered it — and the order screen writes 12 columns, not that one.

Worse than unwritten: **no UPDATE of an order line exists anywhere in the
codebase.** A line is inserted with a status and stays that way for ever.

	Cancelled   214 lines     0 name a tag
	Set Aside    82           58 name a tag
	Process      33            0
	Urgent       29            0
	On Hold       5            0

`Set Aside` is the status that means a piece is reserved. The Order to Barcode
screen already flags the gap in the captured data — *"24 are Set Aside with
nothing set aside"* — and this system could produce **nothing but** those: it can
write the status, because status comes off the form, and it can never write the
barcode that gives the status its meaning.

The outstanding-work screen made it plainer still. It **shows** the reserved tag
in a column of its own, so it displayed a fact that nothing in the system could
put there.

### Done

A tag can now be set aside from the outstanding list — a box on each row, which
writes the line's `barcode` and moves it to `Set Aside`.

Only where it is unambiguous. A piece is reserved against a LINE and that screen
is per ORDER, so an order with one live line takes an input and an order with
several shows its line count instead. **74 of the 95 orders the screen lists have
exactly one live line, 11 have several, 10 have none.** The refusal is on the
screen rather than in a message after the fact.

The tag must be on the shelf. Reserving a piece already sold would put by
something that cannot be handed over, and the screen says which of the two is
wrong: *"There is no tag X"* against *"Tag X has already left the shelf"*.

Four tests, and the first was checked against the bug by reverting the SET clause:
*"the line names "", want RESERVE1"*.

### The screen refused its own new feature

Setting a piece aside without handing anything over failed, and the tests said so
before I noticed anything else. The handler opened with a guard — no ticks, no
work — and returned before reaching the reservation. That was right when the
screen did one thing and wrong the moment it did two.

Handing over and setting aside are now both whole actions, and either alone is
accepted. The existing `TestOrder_HandingOverNothingIsRefused` asserted the old
wording *"Tick the orders"*; its assertion moved to the new refusal rather than
being deleted, because what it exists to prevent — an empty submission taken for
work — has not changed.

### Two figures and one server, all wrong

**The figure I put in the code was counted from the wrong population.** I wrote
"190 of the 243 outstanding orders have exactly one line", from every undelivered
order. This screen deliberately leaves off orders whose lines are ALL cancelled,
so the number describing it is **74 of 95** — which the page then confirmed
exactly, 59 rows offering an input plus 15 already reserved. Counting the wrong
population is how a comment comes to describe a screen nobody is looking at.

**And I read a stale server again, one defect after logging that lesson.** The
page showed no input boxes at all. The launch had died on `bind: address already
in use`, because `pkill -f cmd/wingold` does not match the temporary binary
`go run` builds. Killing by port — `lsof -ti tcp:3210` — is what actually works,
and the fresh server showed all 59. Twice now the same false negative, and both
times the tell was in a log I had not read before trusting the page.

## 305. An order could be taken and handed over, and never cancelled

The other half of defect 304. Having found that no UPDATE of an order line
existed, the question is what else that made impossible.

**Cancelled is the commonest status the shop records** — 214 of its 366 lines,
more than the other four together — and nothing in this system could set it after
an order was taken. The order screen offers it in the status list, which only
makes it stranger: a status you can choose when taking an order and never
afterwards, for the one thing that always happens afterwards.

The consequence is on the outstanding list, the screen that says what the shop
owes. An abandoned order stays there for ever: it is not delivered, its lines are
not cancelled, and there is no third thing to do. **The only way to clear it was
to tick Delivered — recording a hand-over that never happened**, in the register
a customer's claim would be checked against.

### Done

A Cancelled tick beside the Delivered one. It sets every live line on the order to
Cancelled, and the outstanding list drops an order once no live line remains — so
the order leaves the screen without anybody claiming it was collected. The test
asserts exactly that: lines cancelled, order gone from the list, and
`delivered` still false.

Order level, unlike setting a piece aside in defect 304: cancelling an order
cancels everything on it, so there is no line to choose between and no need to
refuse the multi-line case.

Two refusals rather than silent nothings:

- **An order cannot be handed over and cancelled in one submission.** Both boxes
  are on the same row and both are ticked by hand.
- **An order with nothing itemised cannot be cancelled at all.** The status lives
  on the line and there is none, so it says so instead of reporting success
  having changed nothing. Ten of the 95 orders on this screen are in that state,
  and that is a limit of the data model rather than of the screen: there is
  nowhere to record the cancellation of an order that itemises nothing.

### What this does not settle

Whether a 58.5% cancellation rate is normal, or whether the status is used for
tidying up, is still a question for the shop — it is in *Waiting on you* and this
does not answer it. What changed is that the rate can now be a record of what
happened rather than an artefact of the only status anybody could reach.

The order line's `making` column was examined on the way and left alone: 122 rows
carry it, the same 122 that carry `making_amount`, and **nothing reads either
one**. It is not a rate the amount is derived from — `making * net_weight` matches
the amount on 8 of the 122 — and the order screen takes both making and estimate
as figures the biller types, which is consistent with a shop that agrees prices
rather than computing them (defect 228). No formula was reconstructed, because
the data does not support one.

## 306. A bill returned in full still printed as a clean sale

Generalising defect 304's discovery. If no UPDATE of an order line existed, what
else can this system create and never change? Every table it writes:

	19 of the 24 tables the app writes to are create-only.

Most are right. `mcj_barcode_edits` and `mcj_stock_movements` are audit trails and
must be append-only; the rate tables are deleted and rewritten. `mcj_ledgers`
appears only because its screen is `pkg/crud` and builds its SQL at runtime — the
same blind spot defect 297's tool has, met again in a different tool.

`mcj_sales_invoices` is the one that matters. It carries two flags:

	is_cancelled   0 of 224 bills
	is_returned    3 of 224 bills

**Nothing in this system writes either.** The tax invoice prints a banner from
each — `CANCELLED`, `GOODS RETURNED` — across the top of the sheet the customer
is handed, and six reports filter on `is_cancelled`. A bill returned against
through the credit note screen printed as an ordinary sale.

The credit note does everything else: puts the tag back on the shelf, writes the
SALE-RET movement, raises the purchase-side documents. It never touches the bill.

### The shop's own flag does not settle how to set it

	everything came back    4 bills   2 flagged
	part came back          1 bill    0 flagged
	nothing came back     219 bills   1 flagged

Of the four bills where every piece came back, **two are flagged and two are
not.** The single partial return is not flagged. And one flagged bill has **no
return movement at all**. Like the hallmark flag in defect 296, this is set by
hand and is not a reliable record of what happened.

So the rule implemented is the one that cannot be wrong: **the bill is marked
returned when everything on it has come back.** A banner reading GOODS RETURNED
across a bill of three pieces where one came back would overstate what happened,
and the shop's own data gives no warrant for it — its one partial return is
unflagged.

`is_cancelled` is left alone. The shop has never cancelled a bill in 224, and a
credit note is what it does instead; inventing a cancel action would be inventing
a workflow, as in defect 296.

### Done

The credit note marks the bill, in the same transaction as the return. Two tests:
one asserting a fully-returned bill says so, one asserting a partly-returned bill
does not. The first was checked against the bug by neutering the SET clause —
*"everything on the bill came back and the bill does not say so"*.

### The test harness hid a broken save

The first version of the UPDATE named `updated_at`, which `mcj_sales_invoices`
does not have. The statement failed, the whole transaction aborted, and **the
test did not notice**: `credit()` posts and reads the body without asserting a
status, so a 500 came back as a string and the test carried on. The first sign
was a later read failing with *"current transaction is aborted, commands ignored
until end of transaction block"* — an error about the test's own query, pointing
nowhere near the cause.

A save that fails should fail the test that made it, where it happens. There is
now a `creditSaved` helper that insists on the redirect, and the new tests use it.
The nine existing `credit()` calls are left alone: several of them post a save
that is *meant* to be refused, so a blanket assertion would be wrong.

## 307. The shop could see what its suppliers owed it and not what its customers did

Following defect 306's create-only sweep into `mcj_sale_payments`, which nothing
can correct once written. That turned out to be sound — the payments reconcile:

	149 bills carry a payment
	115 paid in full
	 26 part paid, 13,55,888.00 short
	  0 paid MORE than the bill

Part payment is ordinary in a jeweller and no bill is overpaid, so there is
nothing wrong with the record. But asking who is short led somewhere else.

**Supplier Balances exists. There is no customer equivalent.** Its own note makes
the argument: *"the old system had purchase registers, which show what was
bought, and a ledger book, which shows one account at a time. Neither puts the
supplier side together, and what it shows is worth a screen of its own."* Every
word applies to customers, and there are **491 customer accounts against 76
dealer ones** — the side without a screen was the larger one.

	10 accounts owe the shop            73,96,553.00
	20 accounts the shop owes           27,17,486.77
	10 balances saw no posting this year

The second line is the one nobody could see. A customer account in CREDIT means
the shop is **holding that person's money** — an advance against an order, a
part-payment on something not yet delivered — and ₹27.17 lakh of it is a
liability that appeared on no screen.

### Done

**Customer Balances**, mirroring the supplier screen: opening, movement, postings
and balance per account, with the same four views — who owes the shop, everyone
with a balance, money the shop is holding, and balances that never moved.

Verified against the database rather than against itself: the screen returns 10
rows totalling **₹73,96,553.00** under "owe the shop", 20 under "holding" and 10
under "never moved", which are the three figures an independent query gives. The
largest single debtor is HARSIT ANAND SULTANIA at ₹32,30,681.00.

The screen says on its face what it is not: **an account balance is not a list of
unpaid bills.** A customer who paid one bill and left another outstanding nets to
one figure here.

Three tests. The one that matters is the sign: debit positive, so a customer who
owes reads positive and an advance reads negative. Checked against the bug by
making the balance the year's postings alone — the mistake the supplier screen's
own notes record its author making — which drops the 50,000 brought forward and
reports it as nil: *"an account that owes 50,000 from last year is missing — the
year's postings alone are not a balance"*.

### Not a defect, checked and left

`mcj_sale_payments` cannot be corrected once written, and that is defensible: a
payment is part of a posted sale, and the accounting answer to a wrong posting is
a correcting entry, which the voucher screen can make. The payments report reads
only its own table, so a correcting journal would not reach it — that is worth
knowing before anybody relies on it as a cash-reconciliation tool, and it is why
the reconciliation above was run against the bills rather than assumed.

## 308. Nothing checked that the bill in the customer's hand equals what the books say

Defect 307 left a thread: the payments report reads its own table rather than the
ledger, so a correcting journal would never reach it. That raised the general
question — which money on a screen comes from a subsidiary table rather than from
the books, and does it still agree?

The tax invoice and the GST return already answer it well: both take the tax from
the VOUCHER, deliberately, and say why. But **no rule held the bill and its
voucher together.** A bill could drift from its own posting and every screen would
go on agreeing with itself, because each reads one side.

### Checked, and they agree

	224 bills, 224 agree, difference 0.00

Exactly. Every bill has a voucher, and every bill total equals the debit side of
that voucher, to the paisa — 204 debiting a Customer account and 20 a Dealer, the
shop's B2B sales.

That is worth stating plainly because the shop's accounting has three open
blockers against it (B19, B4, B8), and this is one large thing that is not wrong:
**₹2,47,65,386.00 of sales, and the bills and the books do not disagree by a
rupee.**

### The rule now guards it

Invariant 19, "a bill agrees with its own voucher". Checked by adding one rupee to
GST/2627/00206: *1 bill(s) that disagree with the voucher behind them*.

### It looked like a 28-rupee hole first

The first comparison summed **every** debit on the voucher, and reported 115 of
224 bills disagreeing by ₹28.31 in total. That is not a discrepancy, it is the
rounding, and one voucher shows it:

	THE SATURDAY CLUB   Customer                4000.00
	ROUNDED OFF         Miscellaneous Expenses     0.52
	SALE                Sales Account                      3884.00
	SGST                Duties & Taxes                       58.26
	CGST                Duties & Taxes                       58.26

The customer is debited 4,000.00 — exactly the bill — and the 52 paise the shop
rounded away are an expense. Debits and credits both come to 4,000.52 and the
voucher is right. **The bill total was never meant to equal the total debits; it
equals the party's debit.**

Reading one voucher settled it in a minute, where the aggregate had suggested a
systematic fault across half the bills. The rule therefore excludes the round-off
account by name and says why, so the next person to run this comparison does not
rediscover the same ₹28.31.

This is the twelfth measurement in this project where the number was right and the
question was wrong.

## 309. The first thing on the list of decisions I was waiting for had already been decided

Defect 308 reconciled the sales side. The purchase side is the same question
mirrored — a purchase credits the supplier where a sale debits the customer — so
it was asked the same way.

	43 purchases, 43 agree, difference 0.00, on 2,39,56,798.00
	25 old gold lots, 25 agree, on 50,71,370.00 for 534.540 g

Both clean. Invariant 20, "a purchase agrees with its own voucher", now holds it.

Old gold also carries a weight and a rate on **every one of its 25 lines**, which
is what sent this somewhere else.

### Blocker B26 said the opposite, and was the first thing on your list

B26 — *"Posting screens write a voucher and no detail row"* — was the top row of
**Waiting on you**, asking for a decision before the first real bill. It says:

- *"nothing writes `mcj_sales_invoices`, `_lines`, `mcj_stock_movements`,
  `mcj_sold_stones`, `mcj_old_gold_lines` or `mcj_purchase_invoices`"* —
  **all six are written.**
- *"Old gold ... the metal itself — weight, purity and rate all unrecorded"* —
  **`oldgold.go:365` writes purity, gross, net, tunch, rate and amount.**
- *"Two ways to close it"* — **the first was taken.** Each screen writes its
  detail rows beside the voucher.

So the first decision I was waiting for had been made and built, and the document
kept asking for it. That costs the one thing this project cannot make more of,
which is your attention.

### Closed on its own criterion, by test

B26 names what would prove it: *"A bill raised today would balance the books and
be invisible to fifteen screens, including the GST return."* So the closing
evidence is a bill raised today, looked for on the return.

`TestDaysTrade_ASaleReachesTheGSTReturn` sets the morning's rate, tags a piece,
sells it at the counter through the sale screen, and then asserts the bill appears
in `gstr-sales` carrying a taxable value — and that the tag has exactly one
SALE-GST movement, which is the other half B26 says is lost.

**A grep showing six INSERT statements is not that.** It shows the statements
exist; it does not show a bill reaching a return, and this blocker has twice been
closed on evidence of that weaker kind.

### It has been declared closed twice before, and reopened

That history is the reason for the test rather than the grep:

- **Defect 194** closed B26 on the trade path, when the credit note began writing
  a SALE-RET movement.
- **Defect 195** closed it again for purchases, on the bill header. **Defect 224
  found that was true of the header and not of the contents** — 23 of the shop's
  43 purchase bills are stones only, and none of the contents was written.

Each closure was true of what it measured and wrong about the whole. This one is
closed on the blocker's own stated criterion, exercised end to end, which is the
narrowest claim that actually settles it.

The blocker is marked RESOLVED with everything it said while open kept below a
line, because the measurements in it are the record of what was wrong. Its row is
gone from Waiting on you.

## 310. A second answered question was still on the decision list, and now a check says so

Defect 309 found B26 asking for a decision that had been made. The obvious
question is whether it was the only one, and the obvious way to answer it is not
by reading.

`check_blocker_citations.py` already reads every blocker heading to catch a
SCREEN citing a settled blocker. It now checks the other direction as well: a
blocker still sitting on **Waiting on you** in STATUS.md when its own heading says
it is settled.

**It found one immediately.** B9 — *"Were these priced by hand?"* — has been
**ANSWERED** since defect 228:

	There is no formula to find. Of the 129 certified pieces the shop has sold,
	one went out at the tag's stored price and none at a computed one.

The answer is in the blocker, the sale screen was rebuilt around it — that is
what returned 549 pieces worth ₹2,33,45,417.46 to being sellable — and the
question was still on the list. Removed.

### Why this is worth a check rather than a habit

That table is the shopkeeper's decision list. A row on it is a request for their
attention, which is the scarcest thing this project spends, and a stale row
spends it on nothing. Both stale rows had been stale for a while and neither was
noticed by reading, including by me reading that table several times this week to
write the closing summary of a turn.

The check cannot produce a false alarm: it compares an id on the list against
that id's own heading, both of which are written by hand in the same repository.
Verified by putting B20 (RESOLVED) back on the list — *"asks about B20, whose
status is: The data loads were never version-controlled — RESOLVED"* — and
removing it again.

### The rest of the list was checked by measurement, and holds

The other rows assert figures. Those that can be re-derived unambiguously were:

	1,625 tags naming a maker who exists nowhere      1,625, worth 12,77,72,008.04
	  and none of the 103 codes matches a ledger      0 of 103
	214 of 366 order lines cancelled                  214 of 366
	14.43 carats of customers' own stones held        14.430 ct on 7 rows

Two others — defect 50's hallmark count and defect 78/133's raw stock weight —
were NOT confirmed, because my query is not their query: I picked the purity codes
that count as gold jewellery and summed a weight column across every raw-stock
row, and got 732 pieces against their 739 and 27,326.609 g against their
11,998.005. **That is a difference in method, not evidence of drift**, and saying
otherwise would be the adjacent-measurement error this project has made twelve
times. Left alone rather than reported as stale.

**What it cannot do** carried this:

	Anything manufacturing | Deliberate. 2.5 years of audit log show karigar
	issue/receive leaving **no trace at all**

Defensible about the audit log, which is what it was measured from: the stock

	11699   2025-09-16   500.000   C4/00002   ISS-RAW   1

**869.850 g of gold issued to a named maker on a dated bill.** Ledger 11699 is
MA TARA JEWELLERS, and it sits in a ledger group called **Karigar** — the shop
has that concept in its chart of accounts. `karigar_wip_bal` is a single row of
zeros, which agrees with both rows being marked finished: it went out and came

That is a small trace and it is not nothing. The row now says what the trail

	Karigar ledgers in the chart of accounts            1

	codes matching that ledger                          0

**The shop can do this today** had not kept up with the week. Six capabilities

	a tag recording what its stones ARE -- shape and colour              defect 298
	setting a piece aside against an order                              defect 304
	cancelling an order                                                  defect 305
	what each customer owes and what the shop holds for them             defect 307

## 312. Two of the eighty reports were exempt from the check that they show anything

Chasing what today's schema changes might have broken, the rebuild was run from
scratch — `load_all.sh` clean, every baseline back to the rupee, 20 of 20 rules
holding — and then the render sweep, which said:

	38 screens and 80 reports render ... and 78 of them show real data

Two short. Not because two were silent: because two were **excluded**, and the
line did not say so.

`NEEDS_A_SUBJECT = {"ledger-book", "quote"}`. Both answer a question about one
thing — an account, a barcode — and show nothing until told which, so the
emptiness check skipped them. **2 of 80 reports had never been verified to
produce anything at all**, and the summary read as though 78 was the total.

That is the shape of defect 278, where a tool could not tell an empty shop from a
broken one, and of defect 299, where a guard skipped every run and reported PASS.
This one is milder — it under-reports rather than lies — but its own file says a
checker that hides its blind spots is worse than none, and this blind spot was
hidden in a subtraction.

### Both reports are fine

Given a real subject by hand:

	quote        a 147.242 g DIAMOND SET — 17,15,369.30 of metal, 24,76,760.00 of stones
	ledger-book  CASH, 462 rows from the opening balance on

### Done

The checker now finds its own subjects, over HTTP, from pages it already fetches:
the ledger book's own select for an account, and the stock history register for a
barcode. **80 of 80 reports are checked**, and the two are named in the output
with the subject used, so a reader can see they were checked rather than exempted.

Failing to find a subject is reported as a broken page, not skipped — the whole
point being that a skip is what hid this.

Checked by pointing the barcode finder at a tag that does not exist:
*"given a real subject (a barcode that does not exist) it still shows nothing"*.

### The rest of the sweep found nothing wrong

Recorded because a negative result is worth the same as a positive one when the
question was real:

- **The rebuild is sound after three migrations and four changed loaders.**
  2,816 tags, 2,575 on the shelf, ₹14,23,61,188.20, 1,848 vouchers, 9,031
  movements, 224 bills. Every column added today survived: 2,816 of 2,816 tags
  carry a department, 224 of 224 bills, 1,416 of 1,848 vouchers name who raised
  them. `interstate` is recorded on none, which is correct — it is nullable so
  the captured bills keep deriving it.
- **The three capped reports still say they are capped.** Defect 145's fix is
  intact on all of them: `conversions` and `designs` each run a second query over
  the whole selection so the page cannot present 500 rows as the total, and
  `movements` says how much is not on the page.
- **Schemes are already covered.** 235 of 239 have matured, the oldest in July
  2017, and none is closed — which the due-date reminder already reports, in
  those words.

## 313. Every legacy screen that has data behind it is built; the 67 that are not have none

The goal says to build every screen that has data behind it. **126 of 193 legacy
menu screens are rebuilt** and nobody had asked what is in the other 67 — the
figure was a percentage, not an answer. Asked properly, by taking the 67 and
looking for their data.

	~30  manufacturing and karigar   two rows, 869.850 g -- defect 311
	  5  sales voucher variants      none: all 224 bills are SALE-GST
	  1  estimate entry              2 estimates in two and a half years
	  4  barcode merge and split     no such table in the capture
	  5  purchase approval           no such table in the capture
	  7  setup and opening stock     setup tasks for data already loaded
	  2  SMS and WhatsApp            blocker B15's tables, deliberately unopened
	 13  the rest                    backup, password, discount master, TDS ...

**Nothing unbuilt has data behind it**, and the one exception is named: the
manufacturing screens, whose whole evidence is the two rows defect 311 found, and
which STATUS records as a deliberate exclusion.

Three of these are worth stating because the answer was not obvious:

- **The five sales-voucher variants** — credit sale, estimate sale, exhibition,
  export, repair — sound like real trade. Every one of the shop's 224 bills is
  `SALE-GST`, 221 local and 3 central. There is no credit sale, no export sale
  and no repair sale in two and a half years.
- **Estimates** have a register (`estimate_list.php`, built) and no entry screen
  (`sales_voucher_estimate.php`, not). That asymmetry is right at this size: the
  shop made **2 estimates** in the whole capture. Building an entry screen for a
  workflow used twice would be inventing one, which is the argument defect 296
  made about hallmarking.
- **Barcode merge and split** have four menu entries between them and **no table
  in the capture at all**. The screens existed; the shop never used them.

### The one table this turned up: `item_merge`, 40 rows, never read

Not barcode merges — the CATALOGUE's own history. Forty items folded into four,
between 20 September 2023 and **11 August 2026**, which is recent.

**39 of the 40 merged-away items are correctly absent from our catalogue. One is
not, and it is the interesting one:**

	legacy item 1139 was SILVER KOPPOR STAND, merged into 215 SILVER DIPAK
	                    on 20 September 2023
	legacy item 1139 in our catalogue today is called Rudraksha

The id was reused. **`legacy_id` is therefore not a stable identity for an item**
— 1139 means one thing before September 2023 and another after — which is the
same trap the stock history screen carries on its face about barcodes, found for
a second kind of key.

**Nothing is wrong today.** Nought tags, nought bill lines and nought order lines
point at that item, and nought tags anywhere name any of the 40 merged-away
items. The finding is that a join on `legacy_id` across a date could mislabel
history, and that nobody had opened the table that says so.

Both sides of the book reconcile (defects 308, 309), so the question moved to the
stock side: does the shelf agree with the movement trail? Grouping every tag by
its LAST movement:

	last movement   tags   still on the shelf   gone
	NEW-BAR         2332            2299          33
	OP-STK           270             261           9
	SALE-GST         205               9         196
	SALE-RET           6               3           3
	CST-ORD            3               3           0

**Nine tags have a sale as their last movement and are still marked in stock**,
worth **₹99,492.23** — counted in the shelf's ₹14,23,61,188.20.

	53541166   DIAMOND RING   52,445.17   sold 09 Aug 2026   GST/2627/00207
	81846212   GOLD BANGLE    25,668.00   sold 21 Oct 2025   GST/2526/00590
	67675269   SILVER RING     9,512.97   sold 26 Jul 2026   GST/2627/00193
	41075931   GOLD RAKHI      2,000.00   sold 23 Aug 2025   GST/2526/00308
	83267807   GOLD RAKHI      2,000.00   ...same bill
	30043849   GOLD RAKHI      2,000.00
	14880124   GOLD RAKHI      2,000.00
	27099313   GOLD RAKHI      2,000.00
	15551589   SILVER RING     1,866.09   sold 18 Aug 2026   GST/2627/00219

### It is not barcode reuse, which is the obvious explanation and was checked first

This shop reuses barcodes — 1,974 of 3,021 have been "created" more than once,
and the stock history screen carries that caveat on its face. If the tag on the
shelf were a NEW piece wearing an old number, there would be no defect.

	none of the nine was tagged AFTER its own sale
	none of the nine barcodes was created more than once
	all three bills still on file are live -- not cancelled, not returned

So the piece the trail sold is the piece the shelf is counting.

### The clearest one, which explains the shape

Bill GST/2627/00207, 09 August 2026, ₹98,300. The trail shows **two** diamond
