	69343561R1   68,424.00   in_stock = false   ← cleared
	53541166     52,445.17   in_stock = true    ← still on the shelf

The bill carries **one** line, for ₹95,437, naming 69343561R1. So two pieces left
against a bill that itemises one, and the one the line does not name is the one
still on the shelf. **Nine bills show more tags leaving in the trail than they
have lines.**

This is the shop's own record, faithfully loaded — not something this system did.
It sits beside B8's duplicate barcode as a fact about the data.

### The other direction, for completeness

**42 tags are off the shelf with no movement saying they left** — their last
movement is a creation or an opening — worth ₹29,90,169.63. That is the safer
direction: the shelf is understated rather than overstated, and a piece that left
without a movement is what defect 192 fixed for sales made here.

### Done

Invariant 21, "a tag the trail sold is off the shelf", allowed **9** — the
legacy's own. What it guards is a tenth, which would mean a sale made HERE left
its piece on the shelf. Checked by planting a SALE-GST movement against the most
valuable tag in stock: *10 tag(s) ... 1 more than the 9 allowed*.

## 315. The GST return could see every rupee, and a blocker still said it could see 63%

Defect 314 compared the shelf against the trail. The same question, asked of the
two records of a SALE, turned up something else.

	tagged bill lines                          256
	  ...with a matching sale movement         256
	sale movements naming a bill               324
	  ...with a matching bill line             271
	  ...bill not in the capture at all         38   (8 bills, pre-2026-27)
	  ...bill here, no line for that tag        15   (10 bills — defect 314)

The bill never claims a sale the trail missed. **All 256 tagged lines have their
movement.** The disagreement runs one way only, which is what defect 314 measured.

But counting bills without line detail to explain the 38 gave a figure that
should not have been possible.

### B21 said 39 bills have no line detail. There are none

**0 of 224.** B21's remaining scope was HSN completeness, and it recorded:

	sales_vou_main carries lines for 185 of the 224 bills and no rows at all for
	the other 39 ... the HSN summary sees ₹1,51,40,109.00 of taxable value and
	cannot see ₹89,26,345.00

True of `sales_vou_main`. **The loader also reads `sales_vou_detail`, which
carries the other 94 bills** — the two sources together cover all 224, and the
loader's own gate has been asserting "bills with no lines: 0" the whole time.

	sales_vou_main      lines for 185 bills
	sales_vou_detail    lines for  94 bills
	loaded              367 lines, 224 of 224 bills, 0 lines without an HSN code

**Checked against the books rather than the bills**, because the books are what a
return must agree with:

	invoice lines                      2,40,66,454.00
	Sales Account credit on SALE-GST   2,40,66,454.00

Exactly equal. And B21's own two figures — 1,51,40,109.00 seen, 89,26,345.00
unseen — sum to 2,40,66,454.00, which is the arithmetic proving the gap it
described is precisely the part now loaded. The HSN summary reports that total
with ₹6,98,933.87 of tax and carries no shortfall note, because there is none.

**B21 is RESOLVED.** That is the third blocker closed this week by measuring what
it asserted rather than by arguing about it — after B26 in defect 309 and B9 in
defect 310, both of which were also asking for something that had already been
done.

### The guard

Invariant 22, "the line detail sees every taxable rupee", compares the two totals
directly. Checked by taking ₹100 off one line: it reports the gap, and so does
rule 1, which catches the same edit from the bill's side.

A unit test for this already existed and was not enough:
`TestHSNSummary_AccountsForEveryRupee` seeds its own bills and proves the report's
arithmetic. It cannot say anything about whether the SHOP's line detail is
complete, which is the whole of what B21 was about. Arithmetic and coverage are
different questions and needed different checks.

## 316. Two open blockers re-measured, and one of them is ten thousand rupees rather than unbounded

Three blockers closed this week by measuring what they asserted — B26, B9, B21.
The same treatment applied to the ones still open does not close any, which is
itself the answer: they are open because they need a decision or an action, not
because nobody has looked. Two were worth re-measuring anyway.

### B2 — `SLVPC` purity — accurate, and it was reading as bigger than it is

	5 stock items use purity code SLVPC, which does not exist in gold_master
	Blocks: correct valuation of those 5 items; ANY STOCK TOTAL THAT INCLUDES THEM

The first line is exactly right. **All five carry `SLVPC`, no purity master has
that code, and all five are on the shelf.** They are worth **₹10,000.00 between
them** — 0.007% of ₹14,23,61,188.20.

The second line is what needed sizing. "Any stock total that includes them" reads
as though the shelf figure were suspect. It is ten thousand rupees, and knowing
that is the difference between a blocker somebody drops everything for and one
answered next time the owner is passing.

**A separation worth having:** 13 tags have no purity, not 5. The other **8 carry
a BLANK purity** and resolve to none either — but **all eight are off the shelf**,
so they affect no valuation at all. Anyone measuring "tags with no purity" gets 13
and concludes the blocker is nearly three times its size.

### B17 — `SILVER PICHKARY` — accurate in every particular

	item 1063  SILVER PICHKARY  metal  gm  0 tags
	item 1156  SILVER PICHKARY  metal  gm  0 tags

Two identical rows, neither carrying a single tag, exactly as recorded. Still the
shop's call to delete one, and still costing nothing while it waits.

### B4 and B8, checked in passing

	B4  vouchers that do not balance   1, out by ₹0.01
	B8  duplicated barcodes            1

Both exactly as stated. B8's is the barcode defect 291 found doubling rows on the
audit screen and defect 314 found among the nine sold-but-shelved tags, so it has
now been met three times from three directions and is the same single tag each
time.

### What this says about the open list

Of the 17 open blockers, the ones carrying a measurable claim have now been
measured and every one holds. The list is not stale — B26, B9 and B21 were, and
they are closed. What remains genuinely waits on somebody: a fineness from the
business, a duplicate confirmed for deletion, an accountant's two repairs, a
photograph opened in a browser.

## 317. The 29.9 lakh that left with no movement is accounted for; 400 rupees of it is not

Defect 314 recorded the other direction of the shelf-against-trail comparison and
left it there: **42 tags are off the shelf whose last movement is a creation or an
opening — nothing says they left — worth ₹29,90,169.63.** That figure deserved
chasing rather than filing.

	on a bill AND in a conversion    33 tags   29,89,769.63
	neither                           9 tags          400.00

**Thirty-three of the forty-two are accounted for twice over**: they appear on a
bill line and among the pieces of a stock conversion. They did leave, and the
trail simply carries no exit movement for them — which is the silence defect 192
fixed for sales made in this system.

So the ₹29.9 lakh is not missing. **What is unexplained is ₹400.00.**

	49242293               MALA     400.00   tagged 16 Mar 2021
	67141215               (blank)    0.00
	45174064               (blank)    0.00
	30223979/SR            (blank)    0.00
	30683902               (blank)    0.00
	19684380/SR            (blank)    0.00
	65910625/SR/SR/SR/SR   (blank)    0.00
	55380544               (blank)    0.00   tagged 22 Jan 2019
	69375796               (blank)    0.00   tagged 18 Apr 2023

One real piece and eight empty shells — no description, no value, six with no
creation date — all last seen in the opening stock of 1 April 2025.

### Two conventions for "this piece came back"

`65910625/SR/SR/SR/SR` is not a typo. The shop marks a returned piece by changing
its barcode, and it does so **two different ways**:

	suffixed R<n>              263 tags   245 on the shelf   57,86,486.50
	suffixed /SR once            7 tags     4 on the shelf    1,27,936.85
	suffixed /SR more than once  1 tag      0 on the shelf
	plain                     2,545 tags 2,326 on the shelf 13,64,46,764.85

	                                     2,575 on the shelf 14,23,61,188.20

The `R<n>` form INCREMENTS — R1, R2 — so a piece returned twice is one barcode.
The `/SR` form APPENDS, so the same history becomes `X/SR/SR`, and four returns
become the barcode above. **263 tags carry the first convention against 8 the
second**, so the incrementing form is the shop's practice and the other is a
handful of survivals.

Anything matching a returned piece to its original has to know both. Only **one**
R-suffixed tag has its plain original still on file, so the two rarely coexist —
which is why nothing has tripped over this yet.

Nothing here is broken. It is recorded because the next person to match barcodes
across a return will meet it, and because the ₹29.9 lakh in defect 314 should not
be left looking like a hole when it is ₹400.

## 318. Nobody could check this repository without being told how

Three hundred and seventeen defects, eight checkers, a Go suite and a reconciler,
and **no way to run them.** Every verification in this project has been a sequence
assembled from memory, in a terminal, by whoever ran it last.

That is a real fault and not a tidiness one. The knowledge that mattered was
nowhere written:

- Two of the eight checkers need the application answering on a port, and one of
  them reports `connection refused` as a **failure** if it is not — indexed under
  the same exit code as a genuine fault.
- Three of the checkers are informational: the reconciler fails three of its
  eight gates on purpose, because they are blockers B19, B4 and B8 and need an
  accountant rather than a patch. Anybody running it cold would read red and
  conclude the migration was broken.
- The Go suite takes twelve minutes and the rest take two, so there is a fast
  answer and a slow one, and no way to ask for either.

Somebody handed this repository could not tell whether it was sound.

### Done

`tools/check_all.sh`, with `--quick` for everything but the Go suite. It starts
the application if it is not already up, stops it on the way out, and ends with a
list rather than a scroll:

	  ok   it builds
	  ok   it vets
	  ok   the shop's own rules
	  ok   STATUS.md matches reality
	  ok   blockers and the ask list
	  ok   every screen renders
	  ok   no report doubles a total
	  --   the migration against the backup (informational)
	  --   tables nothing reads (informational)
	  --   columns nothing writes (informational)

	7 check(s) passed. Nothing is wrong that this repository can detect.

**Must-pass and informational are separated by design.** Making the run red for
three blockers that need a person is how everybody learns to ignore red.

It stops the application by PORT, not by name, and says why in a comment:
`pkill -f cmd/wingold` does not match the temporary binary `go run` builds, which
is how defects 303 and 304 both came to read a stale page and believe a working
change had failed.

STATUS.md now opens with how to run it, because a document that says what is done
should say how to check it.

### Verified, and my own check was wrong first

Planted a false figure in STATUS.md: the run reports `FAIL STATUS.md matches
reality`, lists the seven that passed, and **exits 1**. Clean, it exits 0. The
application is not left running either way — `lsof -ti tcp:3210` is empty
afterwards.

**The first attempt to read that exit code piped the script into `tail` and
printed `exit was 0`.** `$?` after a pipeline is the LAST command's status, so I
had measured `tail`. This project has recorded that exact mistake before, in the
same words, and the fix is to run the thing and read `$?` before piping anything.

## 319. Defects 304 and 305 walked back into defect 206, and the screen said the save had failed while it committed

Asked of my own work, because 206 is the kind of fault that comes back: does the
outstanding-orders screen return a failing status when a save fails?

**It did not.** `renderOutstanding` ended with

	templ.Handler(orderpage.Deliver(props)).ServeHTTP(w, r)

— no status, so 200. And both of this week's new save paths, setting a tag aside
(defect 304) and cancelling an order (defect 305), reported their refusals
through it.

`atomic` commits the request's transaction on any 2xx and rolls back from 400 up.
So a submission that reserved one tag and then met a tag already sold **told the
wrapper it had succeeded** — and the first reservation was committed while the
screen said the whole thing had failed.

The comment above `failedSaveStatus` warns about exactly this, and adds that a
failure which ABORTS the Postgres transaction is survivable by luck, since
Postgres turns COMMIT on an aborted transaction into ROLLBACK. **That luck does
not apply here.** These refusals are logical — a tag not on the shelf, an order
with no lines — so the transaction is perfectly healthy and commits.

### Proved against the running app, because the harness cannot show it

	with the 200   status 200   reserved lines 59 → 60
	                            tag 10016845 reserved on CO/2627/00113
	                            and the screen said "has already left the shelf"
	with the 500   status 500   reserved lines 59 → 59

The itf harness runs the request inside the test's own transaction, so it cannot
demonstrate a rollback either way — `TestTrade_AFailedSaveDoesNotReportSuccess`
records that for the credit note, and the same applies here. **My first version
of this test asserted the row count and failed for that reason**, reporting "1
reservation(s) were written" against a harness that never rolls anything back.
It now asserts the STATUS, which is what the screen controls, and the rollback
was confirmed on the running app as above.

The reservation the proof wrote into the shop's data was undone by re-running
`load_orders.sh`: 60 back to 59.

### Done

`renderOutstanding` takes a status, and every caller says which. The two that
mean "nothing was asked for" stay 200; the four that mean a save failed —
including the malformed-id path, which can run after a reservation has already
gone in — return `failedSaveStatus`.

Two tests, one per new save path, asserting the status and the message.

### Why this matters more than the money

Nothing was lost: a tag was reserved that should not have been. The failure is
that **the screen and the database disagreed about whether anything happened**,
and the screen was the one telling the truth as far as the user could see. A
clerk told "that tag has already left the shelf" has no reason to check whether
the other one went through.

## 320. Four more screens told the wrapper a failed save had succeeded

Defect 319 found the orders screen rendering a failed save on a 200. The question
that matters is not whether that one is fixed but whether it is the only one, and
it is not.

Every controller, every branch where a save can fail:

	coinrate.go:114     if err := c.save(...)    -> c.render(...)   200
	metalrate.go:111    if err := c.save(...)    -> c.render(...)   200
	salarysheet.go:158  if err := c.save(...)    -> c.render(...)   200
	staffpay.go:138     if err := c.save(...)    -> c.render(...)   200
	tagcorrect.go:193   if err := c.apply(...)   -> c.render(...)   200

**None of the ten controllers that write was status-aware.** Every one of these
five saves writes more than once — coin rates two statements, metal rates two,
the salary sheet four, staff pay two, the tag correction two — so a failure
partway leaves the earlier writes standing, and `atomic` commits them because the
screen answered 2xx.

**`tagcorrect` is the one that matters most.** `apply()` corrects the tag and then
writes the row saying what changed. If the second fails, the tag is corrected with
nothing in the edit trail — on the one screen that exists *because* the legacy
kept `barcode_edit_tracking`. Its own header says so: *"recorded what changed in
barcode_edit_tracking — which this system loaded, read with an audit report, and
could not add to."*

### Done

All five renders take a status; every caller says which. Pre-write validation
failures stay 200 and now say so out loud rather than by omission, which is the
difference between a decision and an oversight.

`TestTagCorrect_AFailedSaveDoesNotReportSuccess` arms the audit write to fail with
a CHECK constraint and asserts the screen answers 500. Checked against the bug by
setting it back to 200: *expected: 500*.

### Three occurrences is a class, so it has a check now

	defect 206   four posting families, found by reading
	defect 319   the orders screen, reintroduced by my own defects 304 and 305
	defect 320   four more, found by the sweep after 319

`tools/check_failed_saves.py` looks for a save-shaped call whose failure branch
renders without naming a status of 400 or more, and it is wired into
`check_all.sh` as **"no failed save says ok"**. Checked by putting the tagcorrect
fault back: it names the file, the line, the save and the render.

Its docstring says what it cannot see — a save spelled some other way, and
whether the write really happened before the failure — and that it errs towards
reporting, so a screen rendering a pre-write refusal must pass `http.StatusOK`
explicitly to say that is deliberate.

### Two mistakes making the change, both from editing Go with regular expressions

**The first attempt spliced a duplicate function** and left a stray `{`, which
compiled — Go allows a bare block — so `go build` said nothing was wrong while the
file was nonsense. Reverted and redone as a parameter on the existing function.

**The second broke three files**: `c\.render\((w, r, [^)\n]*)\)` stops at the
first `)`, so `c.render(w, r, props, time.Now())` became
`c.render(w, r, props, time.Now(, http.StatusOK))`. That one the compiler did
catch. Redone with a paren-matching pass rather than a pattern.

## 321. The check I built to make verification easy ran the test suite twice

Defect 318 gave this repository one command. Read back with the same eye used on
everything else, that command had two faults of its own.

### It ran the whole Go suite twice

	go test ... | grep -E "^(ok|FAIL|---|panic)" ; ! go test ... | grep -q "^FAIL"

Once to show the output, once to decide whether it passed. Go caches test
results, so this would normally be nearly free — except both runs pass
`-count=1`, which exists precisely to defeat that cache. **Six minutes of work
took twelve.**

That matters beyond tidiness. The whole point of defect 318 was that nobody could
check this repository; a check that takes twelve minutes when it could take six is
one people skip, and then it checks nothing at all.

One run now, filtered into a temporary file, read twice from there.

	before   about 12 minutes
	after    6 minutes 33 seconds, measured

### It could not see a skipped test

`go test` prints nothing for a skipped test unless asked. So the one command that
claims to say whether this repository is sound was **blind to the failure mode
that has hidden more broken tests here than any other**:

	defect 299   a guard that skipped every run for months and reported PASS
	defect 312   two reports exempted from a check, the exemption hidden in a sum
	defect 298   my own test, skipped because nothing seeded what it looked for
	defect 302   my own test, skipped because my form was wrong

Four times, and the last two were mine, in this week's work. It runs `-v` now and
filters to the four line shapes that matter, so a skip is **reported by name and
fails the run**:

	tests SKIPPED -- a skip is how a broken test hides:
	--- SKIP: TestZZSkipProbe (0.00s)

Verified by adding a test that does nothing but skip, watching the step report it,
and removing it again.

There is one legitimate skip in the suite — a test that stands down when the
captured legacy pages are not on disk. It does not fire while the capture is
there, and if it ever does, the run failing with that test's name is the right
answer: you cannot verify what you cannot read.

### Both faults were in the tool, not the shop

Recorded because the tooling deserves the same treatment as the code, and because
a verification tool that is slow and partly blind is worse than an honest absence
of one — it produces a green tick that nobody has any reason to believe.

	the April-2026 sheets' gross             2,64,200.00

To the rupee, on 11 named staff.

## 323. The stock journal's flag, asked again from the other side, and still not answerable

One of the questions waiting on the shop is whether `add = 1` on a stock
conversion means tagged or untagged. It has been open since the conversions were
loaded, and it is worth more than it looks: it decides what 859 documents did,
and whether **₹2,60,68,682.20 of stone across 2,554.341 carats** went into the
shop or out of it. Both figures verify exactly as the list states them.

The screen had reasoned about it from the DOCUMENTS' side and stopped, carefully,
at what that could support. This asked from the TAGS' side.

	                                            flagged 0      flagged 1
	pieces whose tag names that document        317 of 486     0 of 144
	tags created the SAME DAY as the document   328 of 486     3 of 144
	pieces with no tag on file at all           237 of 723   375 of 519

Every line points the same way: **0 raises tags, 1 consumes them** — which makes
`add = 1` mean UNTAGGED, against what the column's name suggests.

### And it is still not proof, so the label stays off

The whole case for 1 is an **absence**: no tag names it. That is consistent with
consuming tags and also with any number of other things, and this shop reuses
barcodes — a barcode pre-dating a document does not prove that piece went into
it, because it may have been reused before as easily as after.

The weights make it worse rather than better:

	flag 1   7,664.013 g
	flag 0   5,163.068 g

Read as 1-in and 0-out, a third of the metal is lost, which is too much for gold.
Read as 0-in and 1-out, gold is created from nothing — unless the conversion also
draws on raw metal, which the shop certainly does and this capture cannot show.
**Two impossible readings and one unmeasurable escape is not an answer.**

The stones do not break the tie either: flag 1 carries more carats (1,364.071
against 1,190.270) and less value (₹1,19,87,286.30 against ₹1,40,81,395.90), which
is what sorting looks like and also what nothing in particular looks like.

### What changed

Nothing on the screen, deliberately. The flag is still shown as the shop recorded
it, because labelling it "In" and "Out" would make the journal readable and
possibly backwards, and for a stock journal that is worse than making the reader
ask.

What changed is that the three measurements are now written beside the code, so
the next person to have this idea can see it has been had, and how far it got.
The question on the list now carries its own evidence rather than being a bare
ask — **the answer is one sentence from somebody who worked there**, and this is
the second time this week that has turned out to be the whole of what is missing.

## 324. Fourteen coin prices are out by a digit, and one stood for five days

The coin rate list is 5,966 quotes over 115 days — the largest table nobody had
examined. Grouping each coin's quotes by how far they sit from that coin's own
median:

	COIN-30 GM        01 Jul 2026   40,00,110.00   usually  4,30,350.00
	SILVER COIN 1KG   25 May 2026   29,33,000.00   usually  2,56,000.00
	COIN-8 GM         26 May 2026   15,00,400.00   usually  1,14,860.00
	COIN-8 GM         27 May 2026   14,94,800.00
	COIN-8 GM         29 May 2026   14,93,900.00
	COIN-8 GM         30 May 2026   14,86,500.00
	COIN-8 GM         31 May 2026   14,86,500.00
	COIN-4 GM         15 Jul 2026    5,40,400.00   usually    57,580.00

and the same fault the other way:

	COIN-100 GM           17 Apr 2026   1,46,310.00   usually 14,32,000.00
	COIN-20 GM            30 May 2026      46,270.00   usually  2,86,700.00
	COIN-20 GM            31 May 2026      46,270.00
	SILVER COIN 1/2 TOLA  01 Jul 2026         156.00   usually     1,640.00
	COIN-50 GM            21 Jul 2026      68,150.00   usually  7,16,750.00

**Fourteen quotes, every one with the signature of an extra or a missing zero.**
Gold's largest real move in this data is a few per cent; these are factors of six
to fourteen.

**A hundred-gram gold coin was listed at ₹1,46,310 against a usual ₹14,32,000.**
Anybody selling one at the listed price hands over ₹12.86 lakh of gold for the
price of one gram short of ten.

**And COIN-8 GM stood at thirteen times its price for five consecutive days** —
26, 27, 29, 30 and 31 May. It was not a slip that somebody noticed and corrected;
it was typed again each morning for a working week.

### Why nothing caught it

The list is a fact about a day and nothing validates it. The screen accepted any
number. And the list is ADVISORY — no sale prices from it, which is why the shop
survived this — so a wrong quote does nothing at all until somebody reads it to a
customer, which is precisely what the list is for.

### Done

**The screen refuses a price more than three times, or less than a third of, the
last one set for that coin**, naming both figures: *"COIN-8 GM at 15,00,400.00 is
a long way from its last price of 1,14,860.00. Check the figure — a coin price
out by a digit is the commonest mistake on this list."*

Three times either way is wide enough for any real move and narrow enough for
every one of the fourteen. It compares against the last price rather than the
median so it works from the first day onwards, and a coin priced for the first
time has nothing to compare and passes.

It refuses rather than warns, because a coin price is read off this screen by
somebody about to quote a customer, and a warning on a figure already saved is
one nobody sees the second time.

Two tests: a price ten times yesterday's is refused, shows what the price was
before, and **writes nothing**; a real eight per cent move goes through. Checked
against the bug by removing the call — *"a price ten times yesterday's was
accepted without a word"* and *"1 price(s) were written for a day that was
refused"*.

Invariant 23 holds the fourteen already in the list at fourteen, so a fifteenth
means the refusal has been removed or got around.

### What this does not settle

Defect 54 asks which coin price is right, the daily list or the item master.
Still open, and this does not touch it: these fourteen are wrong against the
list's OWN other days, which needs no view on that question. Worth saying because
the two look alike and are not — one is a typing slip, the other is a question
about which of two records the shop trusts.

## 325. A bill dated before the shop set any rate charged nothing for the gold

Defect 324 found bad prices in the coin list, so the metal rates got the same
test. **They are clean** — nought quotes more than three times or less than a
third of their purity's median, across 1,410 priced rows. The rates the shop
sells from are sound.

The other half of that table is where this went. Of 20 purities, **10 have never
had a sale rate** — 141 days each of zero. Nine of them hold no stock: scrap
grades, stone and article categories that need no rate. The tenth, `IMT`, holds
**220 tags**.

### The chase, and the wrong turn in the middle of it

210 of the 220 are fixed-price and unaffected. Ten are not, and reading the code I
concluded all ten were unsellable — `rateForPurity` fails, the caller returns
"no rate available", and that refusal carries neither `certified` nor
`handPriced`, so it is not offered the price box defect 255 added.

**That was wrong, and the test I wrote to prove the second half of it failed.**
`rateForPurity` does not fail:

	err = tx.QueryRow(...).Scan(&paise, &when)
	if err != nil {
		return rupees.Zero, on, nil     // <- no error
	}

On finding no row it returns a **zero rate and no error**. So `if err != nil`
never fires for a metal nobody has priced, nothing was ever refused, and the
eight per-piece tags were being billed correctly at their making all along.

I had built a fix on that premise. It was a dead branch and was reverted.

### What is actually wrong, which is worse

A zero rate is a missing rate, and the tagged path did not say so. The untagged
path eighty lines above gets it right:

	if err != nil || rate.IsZero() {        // untagged lines
	if err != nil {                         // tagged lines

Two halves of one screen disagreeing about the same question. The tagged half
prices metal at nought whenever no rate is found — and **the rates begin on
1 April 2026**, so any bill dated before that finds no row for any purity at all.
The making is charged, the gold is given away, and the bill looks entirely
ordinary.

Proved: a bill dated 1 January 2020 for a 22kt tag prices without complaint.

### Done

	if err != nil || (rate.IsZero() && makingType != per_pcs)

The exception is narrow and earned. Eight tags on the shelf are priced per PIECE
with amount 0.00 and the total equal to the making to the rupee — a photo frame
and seven malas — and refusing those would make **₹13,620.00** of stock
unsellable to close a hole they are not part of. Per-piece is the one basis whose
arithmetic cannot involve a rate.

Three tests: the back-dated bill is refused, the metal-free piece still sells at
its making, and a per-gram piece with no rate is refused because it would price to
nothing. The first was checked against the bug.

### The lesson, which is the third time this week

I read a code path, concluded what it did, measured the data to size the
consequence, and started fixing — and the premise was false because the function
three lines away swallowed the case I was reasoning about. **The test that failed
was the one I wrote to confirm the part I was already sure of.** Defects 302 and
319 were the same shape: the check written to confirm the obvious half is the one
that catches the reasoning.

## 326. The bill and the quote no longer answer the missing-rate question the same way

Defect 325 came from two halves of one screen disagreeing. The same shape has a
second instance, and this one is written down in the code as an invariant:

	// The refusals mirror the quote screen exactly, because a bill that prices
	// a tag the quote screen refuses would be the more dangerous of the two.

That claim was true when written and 325 made it false. Where a grade has no
rate:

	the quote   falls back to the rate stored on the tag, and says so on its face:
	            "the rate on the tag -- this grade has no rate feed"
	the bill    refuses

### Which is right depends on the document, so the divergence stays

A quote is a conversation. It can price something at a stale rate as long as it
admits to it, and the quote screen does, in the row the customer is looking at.

A bill is what the customer takes away. **A bill that quietly charges a
three-year-old rate is worse than one that will not print until somebody sets
today's**, and there is no way to make a bill "admit" to a stale rate that
survives being folded into a wallet.

So they diverge on purpose, and the comment now says which way and why instead of
claiming a mirror that is not there.

**The direction is the safe one.** The bill refuses what the quote will price,
never the reverse — which is exactly the case the original comment was written to
prevent. If it ever runs the other way, that is the dangerous one.

### The rest of the mirror was checked and holds

The quote's other refusal is the tag whose own recorded price the formula cannot
reproduce — *"Cannot be priced here … a computed quote would be a guess"* — and
the bill has the matching route, the hand-priced box defect 255 added, across
1,626 non-fixed-price tags on the shelf. Certified pieces mirror likewise
(defect 228 on one side, defect 300 on the other). Weight and making-value
failures refuse on both.

One point of difference, deliberate, documented, and in the safe direction. The
others hold.

### Also checked, and clean

The untagged half of the bill fills a missing weight from the other side
(`net = gross` and back), which the tagged half does not. **No tag needs it**:
nought tags on the shelf have one weight and not the other. 369 have neither, and
they are accounted for — 359 fixed-price, 8 priced per piece with the total equal
to the making, and 2 that defect 325's change now refuses because they are priced
per gram with no rate. Nothing there to fix.

## 327. The stock journal shows the metal a conversion yielded and hides the stones

`reports/conversions.go` reads `mcj_stock_conversion_pieces` and stops there. So
when the shop melts a piece down, the screen lists the gold that came out of it
and says nothing about the stones prised out first.

	stone lines loaded                                816
	conversions carrying stones             393 of  859
	pieces                                     24,478
	carats                                  2,554.341
	value                              2,60,68,682.20
	anything under modules/ that reads them      NONE

**2.6 crore of stone detail, loaded faithfully and reachable from no screen, no
report and no test.** This was already *found* -- `check_unwritten_tables.py`
has been printing `mcj_conversion_stones` as loaded-and-unread since defect 285
-- and then left there. A finding that sits in a tool's output for six defects
is not being tracked, it is being tolerated, and the goal says build every
screen that has data behind it.

### The number is right

Checked three ways before it was written down. Against the legacy source, on
all four figures at once:

	legacy.stock_conversion_details   816   24,478   2,554.341   2,60,68,682.20
	mcj_conversion_stones             816   24,478   2,554.341   2,60,68,682.20

and again by summing the fourteen stone kinds separately -- DIAMOND 430 lines at
1,45,05,443.00 down to YELLOW SAPPHIRE 2 at 2,59,000.00 -- which adds to the same
2,60,68,682.20 across the same 816 lines.

### A separate report, not more columns

The two halves of a conversion do not share a grain or a unit. A document has
both pieces and stones; one table would invite a reader to add a gram to a carat,
and the value column would total the same document twice -- which is the thing
`check_no_double_totals.py` exists to catch. The new report joins only
single-row lookups, and the count comes back 816 in and 816 out, so nothing
fans out.

### Two absences belong to the capture, not the screen

Sieve is null on all 816 rows and cut on all but 22. That looked like a LEFT JOIN
silently dropping matches -- a lookup table that never matches loses data without
saying so -- so it was measured on the legacy side rather than assumed:

	                    legacy carries      loaded
	seives_id                        0           0
	cut_id                          22          22
	color_id                       482         482
	shape_id                       636         636

The loader dropped nothing. Sieve therefore gets no column at all: a column
empty for every row the shop will ever see reads as a fault in the screen.

### A zero that means two different things

88 lines carry no value. 24 of them are CUSTOMER DIAMOND and CUSTOMER STONE --
the customer's own stones, worth nothing *to the shop* and correctly zero. The
other 64 are the shop's own stones recorded without a price, which is a gap in
the capture. Same figure, two different facts, so the row says which rather than
showing a bare zero.

**Fixed:** `reports/conversionstones.go`, registered as `conversion-stones`.
81 reports now render and all 81 show real data.

## 328. A tag raised in this system belongs to no department, and every one of the shop's own does

`department` is absent from the tag INSERT. The shop's 2,816 tags all carry one
-- seven of the twelve departments hold stock -- and a tag raised here carries
the empty string.

	1014  6  WORKSHOP          71  4  Back Office
	 837  5  ORDER              6 10  ADMIN
	 614  9  SUB ADMIN          1  2  DATAENTRY
	 273  8  CASH
	                        2,816 tags, none blank

**Nothing goes missing, which is why this took until now to notice.** The
department report has carried a `(no department recorded)` row since defect 295,
built for exactly this: an unattributed piece is visible rather than lost, and
the totals still reconcile. So the failure is not a wrong number, it is a
breakdown that gets less useful with every tag the shop adds -- the catch-all
row grows and the department it belongs to never learns of it.

**Fixed:** a Department select on the tag screen, written through to the column.
Checked on the running app rather than in the markup: the select renders with all
twelve departments and the blank.

### Blank stays allowed, deliberately

`selectField` offers an empty first option and the save accepts it. A required
box the counter cannot answer does not produce a correct department, it produces
a wrong one -- and a wrong department is worse than none, because none is
already visible in a row built to show it.

### Two tests, and the first was made to fail

`TestTag_RecordsTheDepartment` and `TestTag_SavesWithoutADepartment`. The first
was run against the un-fixed INSERT before being kept:

	--- FAIL: TestTag_RecordsTheDepartment
	    tag_e2e_test.go:752: the tag records department "", want 6

which is the check defects 298 and 302 earned -- a test that passes on both
sides of the change is not evidence.

### The same sweep, a column that is a trap rather than a bug

`making_sales` is filled on 1,825 tags, named by no INSERT or UPDATE, and read
by no non-test Go at all. That looks like a second making rate the bill is
ignoring, which would be serious, so it was measured instead of assumed:

	tags where making = making_sales        2,816 of 2,816

They are the same number on every row, so nothing is being ignored and no bill
is wrong. **But the tag INSERT writes `making` and not `making_sales`**, so the
first tag raised here breaks an equality that has held on every row since the
capture. Nothing reads it, so there is nothing to fix today; recorded because
the next person to find that column will find it half true, and a column that
agrees with its neighbour on 2,816 rows and disagrees on the 2,817th is worse
than one that never agreed.

Whether the legacy ever meant them to differ is the shop's to say, and is not
worth asking about until something reads it.

## 329. The certification charge looked like a rate the bill was ignoring, and is not

`certification_type` is filled on 2,801 of the 2,816 tags and named by no INSERT,
no UPDATE and no non-test Go at all. It holds `by_val` (2,683) or `per_ct` (118)
-- the same shape as `making_type`, which decides how a charge is computed. Since
defect 300 made certification a billing route rather than a label, a per-carat
RATE being billed as though it were an AMOUNT would be wrong on 118 tags and
wrong quietly.

**It is not, and the bill is right to read `certification_charge` alone.** The
stored figure is the computed amount, not the rate:

	per_ct tags with stones                          118
	  charge = rate x ALL the tag's carats           111
	  charge = rate x SOME of its stone rows           6
	  neither                                          1

The six are exact to the paisa against a subset of the tag's own stone rows --
one row on four of them, two rows on 70733986R1, three on 69492299R1 -- so the
charge is computed from real parcels, not typed in. **Which parcel was certified
is recorded nowhere**, and the excluded row is not the one you would guess: on
89558954 the 24 small stones totalling 0.420 ct were charged and the 1.250 ct
pair was not.

The last one, 70630587, is **90 paise** out: 9,252.90 stored against 9,252.00 for
its 10.280 ct row, and no subset of its rows gives 10.281 ct. One tag, under a
rupee, in the legacy's arithmetic.

### What was nearly claimed here

The first reading of this was from column averages -- `by_val` showed avg rate
31.02 and avg charge 31.02, and an average matching an average proves nothing
about any row. Checked properly: **2,683 of 2,683 by_val tags have rate equal to
charge, none differing.** The conclusion survived; the evidence for it did not,
and this is the fourteenth adjacent measurement caught before it was written
down rather than after.

### The gap that is real, and was not built

A certified tag raised in this system records a charge with no stated basis --
neither the type nor the rate has a box on the screen. Nothing reads either
column, so no bill and no report is affected today, and adding two fields with no
consumer would be building furniture. Recorded rather than built; it belongs
with defect 328's `making_sales`, which is the same shape -- a legacy column the
new screens quietly stop maintaining.

## 330. Building the fix made the decision list wrong, and the guard for that covers a quarter of it

Defect 328 put a department picker on the tag screen. A row on the shopkeeper's
decision list said, in bold, **"nothing in the app writes it"**. That sentence
was true when written and false by the time the tests passed, and nothing
complained.

`check_blocker_citations.py` exists for exactly this -- defect 310 wrote it after
B26 sat at the top of the decision list asking for something already built and
decided. It reads every row keyed to a **blocker** and fails if that blocker is
settled. The list is not mostly blockers:

	rows on the decision list          28
	  keyed to a blocker (checked)      7
	  keyed to a defect (unchecked)    13
	  no id at all (uncheckable)        8

**7 of 28.** The guard was written against the one row that had gone wrong and
sized to it.

### The obvious extension is wrong, and the data said so

Fail a defect-keyed row when the changelog calls that defect fixed. Run against
the thirteen, it fires exactly once -- on **defect 295**, which is marked
`(fixed)` because the report's `(no department recorded)` row was built, while
the question that defect raised (*which* department a new record should belong
to) is untouched and genuinely still open.

That is a false positive on the only row it catches, so it was not built. **A
defect's number and the question it raised have different lifecycles**, and
treating the first as a proxy for the second turns a decision list into a
nagging one -- which costs the shopkeeper the scarcest thing this project
spends, and is the failure defect 310 was trying to prevent, not repeat.

The row was corrected by hand instead. What can be checked mechanically is
already checked; what is left is a claim in prose about the state of the code,
and this one is recorded so the next person knows the list is only as fresh as
the last person to read it.

### A choice was made on the shop's behalf, and it is reversible

The question offered three answers: attach a department to each app user, put a
picker on the screen, or decide the column describes history only. **I built the
picker for tags without being asked**, because 328 needed something and a picker
is the least presumptuous of the three -- it does not preclude defaulting from
the user later, and blank remains allowed. Bills and orders still have nothing,
and the mechanism is still the shop's to choose. The row now says that rather
than claiming the app writes no department at all.

## 331. The menu was honest about what works and silent about what is missing

Every unbuilt screen was simply absent. `navigation.go` said so as a principle --
*"Nothing renders a link to a screen that has not been built ... never advertises
a 404"* -- and it kept the menu truthful about the 126 that work. It also meant a
person hunting for a screen they used every day could not tell **not built** from
**moved somewhere I have not found**, and the 67 missing ones existed only in a
document they will never read.

**All 193 legacy screens are now in the menu.** The 67 lead to a stand-in that
says what the screen would have shown and why it shows nothing, in the evidence's
own terms rather than as a category:

	Karigar Gold Issue                    MANUFACTURING > Issue Voucher
	Not built
	The capture holds no karigar master and no issue-or-receive table. The
	only manufacturing rows in the whole of it are karigar_gold_stock (2
	rows) and karigar_wip_bal (1) -- which is why this survey counted rows
	rather than reading table names.
	What would change it: A karigar master and the vouchers behind it.
	Whether this work is done on paper is Rahul's to say.

### The count had to survive it, and did not at first

A stand-in registers through a new `TODOFor` field, never `LegacyFile`, because
the coverage figure is counted by grepping non-test Go for `LegacyFile:`. I wrote
that reasoning into a comment, then named the field on my own `TODOScreen` struct
**`LegacyFile`** -- and the figure read **193 of 193**:

	Legacy menu screens rebuilt: STATUS.md says 126 of 193, taken as 193 of 193

Caught by `status_figures.py --check`, which is the whole reason that tool exists
(defects 75 and 102: every hand-kept figure here was wrong at some point). The
field is now `PHPFile`, and the comment above it records what it is not called
and why.

### A guard, because two lists that must agree will not

`check_todo_screens.py` fails if a screen is in both lists (built, and still
apologising for itself), in neither (invisible again), or stands in for something
the menu never listed. Proven by making a screen claim both:

	1 screen(s) built and still standing in:      colur_master.php
	1 screen(s) in the menu, neither built nor stood in for:   back_up.php

Now a step in `check_all.sh`. **Building a screen is now the act of deleting its
stand-in**, and forgetting is a failed check rather than a stale page.

### The menu had a rule about this and I broke it

`TestModule_NavigationIsDeclared` refuses a nav entry with no visibility policy,
because one shows to everybody -- including staff who could not open the real
screen. All 67 arrived with none, and the whole Go suite failed:

	nav entry for /mcj/todo/change-psw-php has no visibility policy
	-- it would show to users who cannot open it

Right rule. A stand-in appearing for people who would never have used the screen
is noise dressed as an explanation. Each now takes the permission its section's
BUILT screens predominantly use -- `VoucherRead` for RETAIL, where every unbuilt
screen is a sale or purchase voucher; `TagPrintRead` for INVENTORY, where the two
are barcode merge and split; `ReportRead` for the rest -- so a placeholder is
visible to exactly the people who would have used the thing it stands in for.

**The fallback would have hidden a bug.** An unmatched heading falls through to
`ReportRead`, which is a valid policy, so a broken split would still have passed
the test with every screen silently mis-gated. Checked separately:

	"RETAIL > Sales Voucher"          -> top="RETAIL"     found=true
	"INVENTORY > Barcode Management"  -> top="INVENTORY"  found=true
	"AUDIT"                           -> top="AUDIT"      found=false

### What the survey's own numbers turned out to be

Assigning a reason per screen does not reproduce defect 284's five buckets. Mine
splits out two the prose already discusses as checked exceptions -- estimates
(the Estimates report covers it) and ledger settings (the Ledger Master shows
every column it has) -- which 284 folded one into "no source table" and one into
"utility". Same 67, better shelved.

**One of 284's evidence lines is wrong in kind.** It says `sales_vou_appr`,
`purchase_approval` x4, `barcode_merge`, `barcode_split` and `discount_master`
hold **0 rows each**. None of those tables exists: the capture has 149 tables and
not one of them is any of these. The doc insists on that exact distinction two
paragraphs earlier -- *"loaded-and-unread is data the shop cannot see;
never-touched is a table that should not exist"* -- so the stand-ins say **"no
table for this exists among the 149 the capture contains. Not an empty table --
none at all."**

`item_merge` does exist, with 40 rows, and looked for a moment like the merge
table the survey had missed -- the `karigar_gold_stock` mistake all over again.
It is a 40-row fragment of the item master (item_id, short_code, grp, uom, rate),
not a barcode-merge transaction. Checked before it was written down.

### The landing page and the status doc have never agreed

While fixing the count I found they differ by one, and always have:

	the landing page   127 of 194
	STATUS.md          126 of 193

`statistics_report.php` sits under two top menus. `Progress()` counts screens per
heading, so it counts that one twice; `status_figures.py` counts distinct links.
Both are defensible and neither is wrong, but a person reading one and then the
other has no way to know that. Not caused by this change and not fixed by it --
recorded, because a figure on the front page of the application is the one people
quote.

## 332. Four of the six screens defect 117 flagged now write their detail rows, and the two that do not are the returns

STATUS.md has carried this caveat since defect 117: *"Six of the built screens
post accounting and not their detail rows -- the sale, credit note, debit note,
purchase, purchase against an order, and old gold purchase."* Checked one by one
against what each save path actually inserts:

	sale                        mcj_sales_invoices + mcj_sales_invoice_lines
	purchase                    mcj_purchase_invoices + mcj_purchase_contents
	purchase against an order   mcj_purchase_invoices + mcj_purchase_contents
	old gold purchase           mcj_old_gold_lines
	credit note (sale return)   voucher and stock movements only
	debit note (purchase ret.)  voucher only

**Four of the six were fixed and the caveat was never narrowed.** It is the
front-page qualifier on the coverage figure, and it has been overstating the gap
by two thirds. `WritesInvoice` is true for exactly the two purchase kinds, which
is what makes the remaining pair easy to state: **the gap is the returns.**

### What that costs, in the one place it is not recoverable

`reports/gstr.go` builds the sales return from `mcj_sales_invoices` alone. A
credit note writes no row there, so it appears in no GST return:

	SALE-RET vouchers                                   3
	output tax debited on them              61,899.33

That tax is reversed in the ledgers and absent from GSTR-1, so the return
over-declares output tax by 61,899.33 while the books are right.

**Checked against the legacy's own returns before it was written down**, because
a figure taken from voucher lines alone is the shape of mistake this file records
thirteen times:

	SR/2627/00001   20,04,854.00 + 60,145.62  =  20,65,000.00 voucher (0.38 round)
	SR/2627/00002      16,505.00 +    495.15  =     17,000.15 voucher (exact)
	SR/2627/00003      41,952.00 +  1,258.56  =     43,211.00 voucher (0.44 round)
	                                 61,899.33

### The legacy recorded the thing GST asks for, and this system has nowhere to put it

`sale_return_main` carries a `sale_bill` column, filled on all three rows:

	SR/2627/00001  ->  GST/2627/00004
	SR/2627/00002  ->  GST/2627/00099
	SR/2627/00003  ->  GST/2627/00173

Every return names the bill it reverses. That is precisely what GSTR-1's
credit-note table needs, and a credit note raised here records no such link,
because it stores no document of its own -- only a voucher. **The old system was
better at this than the new one.** Its three returns are also not loaded: no
loader mentions `sale_return`, and there is no `mcj` table for them.

### And the returned-bill banner cannot reach most bills

Defect 306 made a fully returned bill print GOODS RETURNED, driven by the
barcodes coming back. Counted against the bills it has to work on:

	bills                                        224
	  with no tagged line at all                  95   flag unreachable
	  tagged and untagged mixed                    4   flag overstates
	  tagged only                                125   works as intended

The 95 can never be flagged: the UPDATE requires a returned barcode to match a
line on the bill, and an untagged bill has none. **42% of the shop's bills cannot
be marked returned by any route.** The 4 mixed ones fail the other way -- the
"everything is back" test filters untagged lines out, so returning the tagged
half stamps the banner across a bill whose untagged half is still with the
customer, which is the overstatement 306's own comment set out to avoid.

**Not fixed here.** A returns document, the link to the bill it reverses, and a
credit-note section in GSTR-1 is a migration and a screen, not an edit, and
half-building it at the end of an evening is how the GST return acquires a second
wrong number instead of one. It is the next thing worth building.

## 333. A return is now a document, so it reaches the registers and the GST return

Defect 332 measured the gap and left it. Built:

	migration mcj-1787416000    mcj_credit_notes, one table for both directions
	creditnote.go               writeCreditNote, gated on a new IsReturn kind
	creditnote.templ            an "Against bill" box on the two return screens
	load_credit_notes.sh        the shop's own 6 returns, as documents
	gstr.go                     the credit notes, NEGATED, on the outward return
	check_invariants.py         a return agrees with its own voucher (rule 24)

**The GST return now nets.** Over the whole captured period the outward return
showed 6,98,933.87 of output tax; it now shows **6,37,034.54**, which is that
figure less the 61,899.33 the three credit notes reverse. The books had it right
all along and the return was over-declaring by exactly the tax on the notes.

Each note carries the invoice it reverses, which is what GSTR-1 asks for and what
this system had nowhere to put:

	SR/2627/00001  -20,04,854.00  -60,145.62   credit note against GST/2627/00004
	SR/2627/00002     -16,505.00     -495.15   credit note against GST/2627/00099
	SR/2627/00003     -41,952.00   -1,258.56   credit note against GST/2627/00173

SR/2627/00002 is Chandigarh against a West Bengal shop and prints IGST, taken
from the note's own recorded flag rather than re-derived -- defect 302's rule,
applied to the new table from the start.

**A debit note stays off the outward return.** It is a purchase return and
belongs on the inward side; putting it here would understate what the shop
supplied. There is a test that would catch it moving.

### Two mistakes worth keeping

**I compared the wrong two numbers and nearly filed a defect against the data.**
Checking each note against its voucher, two of six came out 15 and 32 paise
short, and both were notes with a NEGATIVE round-off. The vouchers were right:
a negative rounding sits on the opposite side of the voucher, so summing debits
alone misses it. The comparison is now against the PARTY LINE, which is the
note's face value whichever way the rounding fell -- and that is what rule 24
checks. Fifteenth adjacent measurement, caught before it was written down.

**My own loader reported success while losing every party link.** It joined
ledgers on `legacy_id` where every other loader in this directory joins on
`code`, and the two numberings are not the same -- one of the notes points at
ledger 12154 and the highest `legacy_id` in the table is 11919. Nought of six
resolved. It printed *"loaded 6 return document(s), every one tied to its
voucher"*, which was true and beside the point, because the guard checked the
voucher join and not the ledger one. **A loader that checks one of its two joins
reports success for half a load** -- defect 294 in a different costume. There is
now a second guard, and the message says both.

### What is still not done

The debit note has a document but no inward-return section reads it yet: the
purchase register and GSTR purchases still read `mcj_purchase_invoices` alone.
The exposure is 25,229.67 of input tax across 3 notes, and it is overstated
input rather than understated output -- the shop claiming back more than it
should, which is the same size of error pointing the other way. Next.

## 334. The inward return claimed back input tax on goods the shop had sent away

Defect 333 closed the outward half and named this one. A debit note reverses the
input tax claimed on goods returned to a supplier, and `gstrPurchasesQuery` read
`mcj_purchase_invoices` alone, so the shop's three debit notes counted for
nothing:

	input tax on the purchase bills          5,21,364.93
	less the three debit notes                  25,229.67
	the inward return now shows              4,96,135.26

**The same error as 332's, pointing the other way.** That one declared more
output tax than was due; this one claimed back more input tax than was owed. One
overpays the government and the other is the kind that gets noticed.

	PR/2627/00001  SHISH JEWELS LTD                 IGST   -5,45,749.83  -16,372.49
	PR/2627/00002  HASTMILAP PVT LTD                IGST   -1,60,219.39   -4,806.58
	PR/2627/00003  SWARN SHILP CHAINS AND JEWELLERS  CGST/SGST  -1,35,020.30

Each is labelled *debit note -- goods sent back* in the "Posted to" column, so a
negative line on a filed return says what it is rather than looking like a
mistyped bill.

**The two halves stay on their own sides**, and each has a test that fails if it
moves: a credit note on the inward return would understate recoverable input tax,
a debit note on the outward one would understate what was supplied. Both were
run against the un-fixed report first --

	the debit note moved input tax by 0.00, want 300.00
	the debit note row is posted to "", want it named as a debit note

-- because a test that passes before the change is not evidence of it.

### What defect 117's list is now

Both return screens write a document, and both documents are read by the return
that has to account for them. The list that defect 117 opened -- six screens
posting accounting and not their detail rows -- is empty, four of the six having
been quietly fixed long before anyone narrowed the sentence (defect 332).

## 335. The two registers disagreed about whether a return is trade

The purchase register has listed its own returns since it was written --
`v.type LIKE 'PURC%'`, with "Returned to a supplier" in its own filter. The sales
register asked for `v.type = 'SALE-GST'` and nothing else. Same shop, same kind
of document, two different answers.

**And the sales register disagreed with the GST return printed beside it**, by
exactly the tax on the notes that defect 333 had just made count:

	sales register        6,98,933.87 of tax
	GST outward return    6,37,034.54
	the difference           61,899.33   the three credit notes

### Listing a return and showing nothing for it is worse than leaving it out

The purchase register was not right either. It read
`SUM(l.debit) FILTER (WHERE lg.name LIKE 'INPUT %')` -- debits alone -- and a
return CREDITS the input tax it reverses, so all three appeared as rows of
nothing:

	03 Jun 2026  PURC-RET 1  PURCHASE_RETURN                0.00  0.00  0.00
	29 Jun 2026  PURC-RET 2  PURCHASE_RETURN, ROUNDED OFF   0.00  0.00  0.00
	01 Jul 2026  PURC-RET 3  PURCHASE_RETURN, ROUNDED OFF   0.00  0.00  0.00

**8,66,219.00 of returns, present and worth nothing.** A reader who sees the
return on the screen concludes it has been accounted for, which is the one thing
that cannot be concluded here. The "From" column names the ACCOUNT rather than
the supplier for the same reason: it asked for credited ledgers, and a return
debits the party.

Both are now debit-less-credit, and the party is taken from whichever side it
sits on:

	03 Jun 2026  PURC-RET 1  SHISH JEWELS LTD         -5,45,749.83  -16,372.49
	29 Jun 2026  PURC-RET 2  HASTMILAP PVT LTD        -1,60,219.39   -4,806.58
	01 Jul 2026  PURC-RET 3  SWARN SHILP CHAINS...    -1,35,020.30   -4,050.60

### The registers and the returns now agree to the rupee

	                       goods            tax            total
	sales register    2,20,03,143.00   6,37,034.54   2,26,40,175.00
	GST outward       2,20,03,143.00   6,37,034.54   2,26,40,175.00

	purchase register input tax   4,96,135.26
	GST inward        input tax   4,96,135.26

### A third thing the sign broke

The sales register decides the tax basis with `igstP > 0` and `localTaxP > 0`.
A return carries the same tax negated, so every one of them would have been
labelled "—", as though no tax had been charged on a document whose whole purpose
is to give tax back. Tested against nought instead. **The bug and its fix arrived
in the same change**, which is the only reason it is written down: nothing would
have failed, and the column would have quietly been wrong on every return the
shop ever raises.

## 336. Swept for the one-sided sum, and found two more — one of them in the total itself

Defects 334 and 335 were both the same mistake: reading one side of the ledger
for a figure a RETURN posts to the other. Two instances is a class, so the rest
of the reports were swept for it rather than waited for.

Most were already right -- the balances, the ratios and the carry-forward all
read `SUM(debit) - SUM(credit)`; the cash flow takes both sides separately and the
statistics one correctly-chosen side per figure. **Two were not.**

*(This paragraph originally named the day book among those checked. It had not
been opened, and the claim about it was wrong in both directions -- see defect
337, which corrects it and fixes what the correction found.)*

### The gross profit netted its sales returns and not its purchase returns

The screen has subtracted sale returns since it was written. Its purchases line
names `v.type IN ('PURC-GSC','PURC-GCO')` and stops, so goods the shop had sent
back still counted as bought:

	                              before          after
	Purchases                2,34,35,413.81  2,34,35,413.81
	Old gold bought in          50,71,370.00    50,71,370.00
	Less returned to suppliers          --       8,40,989.52
	Bought in total          2,85,06,783.81  2,76,65,794.29
	What is knowable           -65,03,640.81   -56,62,651.29

The corrected bought-in figure is **exactly** the purchase register's own goods
total after defect 335, which is how it should have been all along and was not:
one screen said the shop bought 2,85,06,783.81 and the other 2,76,65,794.29.

### And the HSN summary's caveat was adding itself to the total

Table 12 is gross, because a credit note carries no line detail and so no HSN to
subtract from. That is defensible; leaving a person to discover it by comparing
two screens is not, so the summary now says so. **The row that said it made the
total wrong.**

	total before the new row     2,40,66,454.00
	total with it                2,61,29,765.00
	the difference                  20,63,311.00   the returns, ADDED

A disclosure row carrying money in the taxable and tax columns is summed into the
footer like any other. **The line reading "this summary is SHORT by X" made the
total X too BIG** -- and that fault was already there, on the shortfall row this
report has carried since defect 156, waiting for a period with a detail-less
bill. Both rows now state their figures in the sentence and carry no columns.

`check_no_double_totals.py` did not catch it, and could not: it looks for a
footer that double-counts its own rows, and this footer added a row that was
never trade. The test that catches it is the one that now exists.

### The test encoded the bug

`TestHSNSummary_NamesTheBillsItCannotSee` asserted the shortfall row carried
`taxable` and `tax` as amounts -- the exact thing that inflated the total. It
passed for as long as the fault existed and would have failed the fix. Rewritten
to assert the opposite: the figures appear in the sentence, and the row carries
no money columns at all.

## 337. I described a report I had only skimmed, and the sentence was wrong

Defect 336 published this, about the sweep for one-sided sums:

	the cash flow, the day book and the statistics take both sides separately

Checked, one at a time, because a claim about code is worth exactly what was read
to make it:

	cash flow    money_in = SUM(credit), money_out = SUM(debit)      accurate
	statistics   one side per figure, the RIGHT one each time        loose
	day book     SUM(l.debit) alone, and deliberately                WRONG

The day book has a comment above that line saying so: *"The amount of a voucher
is the sum of ONE side, not of both. A balanced voucher's debits equal its
credits, so adding the two reports every entry at twice its value."* It is
correct, it is the opposite of what I wrote about it, and the sweep that produced
the sentence never opened it.

### The correction found a real one

If debits always equal credits, then BOTH sides carry the rounding, and one side
is either

	the transaction + a positive rounding   = the document's face value
	the transaction + |a negative rounding| = a rupee over it

So a voucher rounded DOWN reads high. Measured, and confirmed against a second
query:

	vouchers carrying a rounding CREDIT              129
	overstated in total                            35.30
	the largest single one                          1.00

Pennies, and the exact kind of difference that costs an afternoon when somebody
holds a day book against a cash book and cannot find the last rupee. The amount
is now the debit side less any rounding sitting on the credit side, which leaves
a positively-rounded voucher untouched and brings a negatively-rounded one back
to its face value.

### Why this is filed as a defect and not a typo

The sentence was in `docs/data-defects.md`, which is where the next person looks
to find out what has already been checked. **A wrong entry there is worse than a
missing one**: it retires a question that was never asked. The sweep it described
was real and its other findings stand -- but it covered two reports it named and
not the third.

## 338. The purchase register's Total was not the bill's total

Found by carrying defect 337's question -- *where else does the rounding fall on
the wrong side of a sum?* -- to the next report along. The register builds its
Total in Go as `g.Add(t)`, goods plus tax, and the rounding is neither, so it
never arrived:

	                  register       the supplier's bill    out by
	GDP/2627/00001   29,99,998.60         30,00,000.00       1.40
	GDP/2627/00013    1,46,361.41          1,46,380.00      18.59

	bills carrying a rounding      23 of 43
	out by in total                   25.47
	the worst single one              18.59

**A register whose Total is not the document's total is one nobody can tie to a
supplier statement.** It is small money and a whole afternoon: the figures agree
on every bill that happens to round to zero and disagree on the 23 that do not,
which is the pattern that makes a person check the arithmetic three times before
doubting the screen.

The rounding now goes into the Total and stays out of the goods and the tax,
which are its two parts. Checked against the books rather than only in a test:

	register footer, purchases from a supplier    1,80,38,003.00
	mcj_purchase_invoices, the same 24 bills      1,80,38,003.00

### The same question, asked of the rest

The sales register's Total was already right, and for a reason worth writing
down: it reads the PARTY line (`SUM(debit - credit)` over the non-tax, non-sales
groups) rather than adding its own parts up. **A total taken from the document
cannot drift from the document.** Where the register above assembles a figure out
of the pieces it happens to display, that one asks the voucher what the customer
owed -- and the rounding is already inside the answer.

That is the better shape, and it is why this defect exists in one register and
not the other.

## 339. The 8.8 crore the suppliers owe is an opening balance, not a debt this system watched build

`Why is 8.8 crore owed to the shop by its own suppliers?` has sat on the decision
list unchanged since defect 51. The figure is right -- it reproduces exactly --
but as asked it cannot be answered, because it does not say WHERE the money came
from. Split:

	17 supplier accounts in debit          8,80,84,874.22
	  from opening balances                8,80,38,622.00
	  from trade this system recorded             46,252.22

**The trade half is not a mystery and never was.** Six accounts, all of them
expense suppliers with a small prepayment:

	INTERGLOBE AVIATION (WB)   20,873.00     SBS LEGAL          10,000.00
	GROWTH IS LIFE FOUNDATION  11,330.00     BHARTI AIRTEL       2,976.04
	ARPITA MERCHANDISE            600.00     VODAFONE              473.18

Airline tickets, phone bills and a legal fee. Nobody needs to be asked about
those.

### What is actually being asked

One account carries three quarters of it:

	SHREE SAROJ JEWELSS   opening   6,98,45,346.00 debit
	                      13 postings  -19,07,775.00
	                      balance    6,79,37,571.00

and ten more carry 2,01,01,051.00 between them with **not one posting** -- their
balance is their opening figure and nothing else has touched it since.

The opening is the shop's own, carried in as it was found. Checked against the
legacy's own file rather than assumed:

	legacy.ldgr_open_balance   ldgrcd 9797   debit 69845346.00   acc_year 2026-2027
	mcj_ledgers                code   9797   opening_balance 69845346.00 debit

**So the question is not "why do your suppliers owe you 8.8 crore".** It is
"your books opened the year saying SHREE SAROJ JEWELSS owed you 6,98,45,346.00 --
is that real, and what is it?" That is answerable in a sentence by somebody who
knows the shop, and the old one was not. It also belongs beside **B19**, whose
opening trial balance is short 15.32 crore: both are questions about what the
year opened with, not about anything the new system did.

**Nothing is fixed here and nothing was wrong.** The report reproduces, the
loader is faithful, the arithmetic is standard. What changed is that the ask now
names one account and one figure.

## 340. B14 asks the shop for three ledgers its own vouchers already name

B14 has been open since screen 19: three of the six payroll components point at
ledger codes absent from the chart -- 2677 (P.TAX), 2657 (I.TAX), 3373 (D.A) --
and it asks whoever runs payroll which ledgers those should be. **Two of the
three are answered by the shop's own postings, and the third has no money in it.**

### First, a hypothesis tested and refused

The obvious explanation is that those numbers are legacy `id`s rather than
`ldgr_code`s and the loader matched the wrong column. Checked:

	3372  exists as a CODE (id 2372) = DIRECTORS REMUNERATION
	2677, 2657, 3373  exist as neither id nor code

So they are missing, exactly as B14 says. Recorded so nobody spends the same
half hour.

### P.TAX -- answered to the rupee

	ledger 3242 PROFESSIONAL TAX (group: Payable)
	  51 postings, 6,140.00 CREDITED
	salary sheets, April to July 2026
	  1,470 + 1,600 + 1,470 + 1,600 = 6,140.00

Credited, which is what a deduction withheld from staff should be. The choice is
not arbitrary: **PROFESSIONAL TAX (COMPANY) (3340) also exists**, with one
posting of 2,500 debited -- the employer's own PT, a different thing -- and the
shop's vouchers pick 3242 for the payroll deduction.

### D.A -- answered within 600

	ledger 4291 DEARNESS ALLOWANCE (group: Employee Benifit Expences)
	  47 postings, 3,22,800.00 debited, across three payment runs
	salary sheets for the same four months            3,22,200.00

	posted 2026-05   11 rows    77,200.00
	posted 2026-06   24 rows  1,61,400.00   <- two months in one run
	posted 2026-07   12 rows    84,200.00

Agreeing within **600.00**, and the 600 sits in the June run that covers two

No employee has ever had an I.TAX amount: no rows for it in

### What is left of B14, and what it turned up

	P.TAX   1,470-1,600 a month   the vouchers say 3242
	D.A       77,200-84,200 a month   the vouchers say 4291
	I.TAX                 nil        nothing to decide

**A different question came out of it.** The three components that DO resolve --
PF, ESI and HRA, together 7,39,428.00 over sixteen months of sheets -- point at
3372 DIRECTORS REMUNERATION. That account carries 12 postings totalling 14,40,000.00,
which is 1,20,000 a month and reads like one director's pay; and all twelve
people on the payroll sit in the chart's own **Staff** group, not a directors'
one. Whether staff PF, ESI and HRA belong in a directors' account is a smaller
question than B14 asked and a real one.

**Nothing changed here.** The mapping is the shop's chart of accounts and naming
