## 341. No coin in the capture was ever billed from the coin price list

Defect 54 asks which coin rate is right, the daily list or the item master, and
rests on a sentence: *"Coins are priced and sold as products from this list, not
by weight off the shelf."* **The shop's own bills say otherwise, and they say it
without a single exception.**

	coin lines billed                                    32
	  priced by WEIGHT (a rate and a weight)             23
	  flat-priced (rate 0, a figure typed in)             9
	  matching the coin list's per-piece price            0

Not one. And the 23 weight-priced lines track the day's METAL rate:

	within 5% of that day's rate for that purity         23 of 23
	within 1%                                            10
	exactly equal to it                                   8
	average, billed rate over metal rate               0.9826

Worked through on one line, because a ratio is not an explanation:

	SILVER COIN-5 GM, 21 July 2026, 40 pieces, 46,900.00
	  the day's SLV999 sale rate                232.50 per gram
	  the line's rate                           232.50 per gram
	  5 g x (232.50 + 2.00 making)            1,172.50 per piece
	  the coin list that day                  1,220.00 per piece

The bill used the metal rate to the paisa and the coin list not at all.

### So the question was the wrong one

**Nothing in this system prices a sale from either source.** `mcj_coin_rates` is
read by the coin-rate screen and its own report and by nothing else;
`mcj_items.rate` is read by nothing at all. Coins are sold from a tag (14 of the
32 lines) or as a typed untagged line (18). The item master's five-year-old rates
undercharge by 79% only if something prices from them, and nothing does.

That does not make the stale rates harmless -- a screen built tomorrow could
reach for `items.rate` and be 4.8x low -- but it is a trap, not a leak, and it
has never cost the shop a rupee.

### What is worth asking instead

The shop kept `coin_rate_master` **daily**: 5,966 rows, 52 items, 115 trading
days, every day it traded between 3 April and 19 August 2026. Somebody typed
those in. And no coin was billed from them.

**What is the daily coin list for?** It may be the counter display, or what the
shop pays to buy coins in, or a price it quotes and then discounts to the metal
rate at the till -- the average of 0.9826 is consistent with the last. This
measured SALES only, and cannot see the rest.

Defect 54 stays open, because the list being unused for billing is not the same
as the item master being right, and neither is a thing this repository can
decide. But it is no longer HIGH: there is no undercharging happening.

## 342. The shop was getting better at recording hallmarks every year, and this system could not record one at all

Defect 296 noted that nothing here can set the hallmark flag. What that costs was
not measured until now, and the measurement is the argument:

	gold jewellery tagged in    tags    hallmarked    %
	2024                         198        12       6.1
	2025                         570       159      27.9
	2026                         387       203      52.5

**Not an abandoned practice -- an adopted one.** The share has climbed nine-fold
in two years and stands at better than half. A tag raised in this system carried
`hallmarked = false` whatever the piece was, so the first one made here would
have started that climb again from nought.

**Fixed:** a Hallmarked box on the tag screen, written through to the column.
Confirmed on the running app, not in the markup. Two tests, and the first was run
against the un-fixed INSERT before being kept:

	--- FAIL: TestTag_RecordsAHallmark
	    tag_e2e_test.go:794: the box was ticked and the tag records no hallmark

Unticked means unticked, and the second test says so: a screen that assumed a
hallmark would put the doubt hanging over 739 old pieces into every new one too.

### Defect 50's table has a wrong column

Checking the population turned up an error in the entry this came from. Every
figure in defect 50 reproduces today to the paisa -- except one column:

	         no hallmark      value           "On the shelf"   really
	18kt         411     5,95,69,420.89          539            505
	22kt         217     4,20,34,082.23          352            319
	14kt         104     1,37,93,189.74          196            165
	9kt            7          67,169.00           38             34

The four "On the shelf" figures sum to **1,125**, and the sentence above them
says **1,023** -- which is the right number and the one today's shelf gives. The
column matches neither the tags in stock nor all tags ever made for those
purities (547/361/247/41).

It matters in the direction that flatters: 739 of 1,125 reads as **66%**
unrecorded, and 739 of 1,023 is **72%**. Corrected in place.

### What is still the shop's to say

Whether the 739 are unhallmarked or hallmarked-and-unrecorded is unchanged, and
no measurement here can settle it. But the ask is narrower now: the flag IS in
live use and rising, so "is hallmarking recorded in the ERP at all" has an
answer -- **yes, on 52.5% of this year's gold** -- and what is left is the older
stock and the paper trail behind it.

## 343. Eighty-three orders carried forward from earlier years all say they were placed on 1 April 2026

Found while checking whether defect 28's four-year-overdue order was real. It is,
and the thing that made it look wrong is a different defect.

**83 order lines promise delivery before the order was taken** -- the earliest
due 9 August 2022 against an order dated 2026. That reads as a broken delivery
date and it is not. The order NUMBERS carry the financial year:

	FY in order_no    orders    ordered_on
	2122                   2    all 2026-04-01
	2223                   5    all 2026-04-01
	2324                   6    all 2026-04-01
	2425                  14    all 2026-04-01
	2526                  56    all 2026-04-01
	2627                 201    2026-04-01 to 2026-08-19

**The delivery dates are right and the order dates are the artefact.** Eighty-
three orders still open at the year end were carried forward and stamped with the
first day of the new financial year. Exactly one order genuinely numbered in
2026-27 also falls on that date, so 84 orders share it.

Checked against the legacy before blaming the loader, which is faithful on both
sides:

	legacy.customer_order        284 orders, every date1 in 2026
	legacy.customer_order_main   delivery dates 2022:1 2023:2 2024:6 2025:39 2026:318
	mcj_customer_order_lines     the same distribution exactly

So the legacy did this, and the capture reproduces it.

### What it costs

Every screen that shows an order's date shows **01 Apr 2026** for 83 of the
shop's 284 orders -- 29% of them -- as though a third of a year's book was taken
in one morning. `statistics.go` goes further and FILTERS on it: a statistics run
covering April 2026 counts all 83 as orders taken that month, when the oldest of
them was taken four financial years earlier.

**Defect 28 is unaffected and was right.** It measures against `delivery_date`,
which is the sound column, and its headline -- `RP/2223/00194` due 9 August 2022,
1,474 days over -- is a real order from financial year 2022-23, not a typo.

### Not fixed, and why

The true order date is not in the capture. The financial year is recoverable from
the order number and nothing finer, so the honest repair is to show *"carried
forward from 2022-23"* rather than a date the shop never recorded -- and inventing
1 April 2022 to replace 1 April 2026 would be trading one wrong date for another
that merely looks better. Which of those the shop wants is a question, and it is
now on the list.

## 344. There is no making percentage over 6 g, and the shop's own shelf shows why

Defect 47 ends with three overlapping bands and no way to choose:

	6 - 100 g    12%
	6 - 250 g    15%
	6 - 300 g    14%

The question went on the list as *"what is the making percentage on a gold
ornament over 6 g?"* **The shelf answers it, and the answer is that there is no
such number.** Of the 186 gold jewellery tags over 6 g priced as a percentage of
the metal:

	12%   52 tags    1,71,22,284.58
	18%   44 tags      58,10,166.60
	10%   32 tags    1,06,88,365.48
	11%   31 tags      45,54,552.00
	15%   15 tags      21,50,634.63
	14%   10 tags      53,81,403.10
	20%    2 tags         91,968.00

Seven rates, not three -- and the two commonest, 12% and 18%, are one that IS in
the ladder and one that is not in it anywhere above 6 g.

### The ladder's PRINCIPLE holds, though, past where it stops

A heavier piece costs proportionally less to make, and the shelf keeps doing that
after the table runs out:

	band          tags   average   commonest   range
	6 - 10 g        41    15.24%      18%      10-20
	10 - 20 g       46    14.17%      18%      10-20
	20 - 50 g       81    12.07%      11%      10-18
	over 50 g       18    12.61%      12%      10-18

The average falls from 15.24% to 12.07% across the range, which is the ladder
carrying on. **The spread does not narrow with it** -- every band runs 10% to
18% or 20% -- so the rate is chosen piece by piece and the band only moves where
the middle sits. The rise at over-50 g is 18 tags and not worth reading.

### So the question dissolves and a smaller one is left

Nothing prices from the ladder: making comes from the tag, as defect 47 already
says. Nobody needs to pick between 12, 14 and 15 because nothing consults them.

What could be asked instead is a design question, not a data one: **should the
tag screen suggest a making percentage from the piece's weight**, given the shop
plainly has a habit -- about 15% just over 6 g easing to about 12% by 20 g -- and
given that whatever it suggested would be overridden a third of the time by the
look of that spread.

Recorded rather than built. A suggestion nobody asked for, on a screen that
prices real stock, is worth a conversation first.

## 345. Six of the tag prices that "differed" differ by the tax and nothing else

*Is a printed tag price a fixed price or a starting point?* went on the decision
list with **24 of 28 flat-priced sales differed from it; 9 were above**. The
figures reproduce. What they mean does not survive looking at the ratios:

	ratio of billed to tag price
	0.718 - 0.839    8 sales   all SILVER
	0.952            1 sale
	0.97087          6 sales   all COINS
	1.000            4 sales
	1.003 - 1.163    6 sales
	2.98769          2 sales   the same piece twice

**0.97087 is 1/1.03.** Every one of those six is a coin, and the ratio is exact
to five places on five of them. The tag price is GST-INCLUSIVE and the invoice
line's amount is the taxable value, so those pieces sold at their printed price
to the paisa -- 140,534.00 x 1.03 = 144,750.02 against a tag of 144,750.00.
Nothing was discounted.

	                            sales      amount
	tax, not a discount             6   15,966.00
	sold at the tag exactly         4          --
	genuinely below the tag         9    6,005.00
	sold above the tag              9    4,864.00

**93% of the 17,107.00 that looked given away is tax.** The real movement is
6,005.00 off on nine pieces against 4,864.00 on top on nine others -- **net
1,141.00 across 28 sales**, which is a shop haggling, not a shop leaking.

### So the answer is different for a coin and for silver

	coins   sold at the printed price, every time, 6 of 6
	silver  sold 16-28% under it on 8 of the 9 that moved at all

For a coin the tag is a price. For silver it is a starting point, and the
starting point is about a fifth above where the piece actually goes. Ten of the
28 honoured the tag, not four.

### The one that is not either

Two sales of SILVER EXCLUSIVE PCS billed **1,942.00 against a 650.00 tag** --
2.98769 times, identical on both. Three at the tag price would be 1,950.00, eight
rupees off, so a three-piece sale against a per-piece tag is the likely reading
and not a certain one. Worth a look at that tag rather than a rule.

## 346. The 4,000 a gram placeholder is on 360 tags, five purities, and 4,391 grams

Defect 36/58 put *"re-rate the tags carrying placeholder rates"* on the decision
list with **154 tags at exactly 4,000/g at 18kt**. Measured today the shelf holds
more than twice that, and the reason it is certainly a placeholder is not the
round number.

	purity   tags at exactly 4,000/g   tagged on
	18            307                  5 distinct days, 2024-04-01 to 2025-11-21
	22             39                  3 days
	14              8                  3 days
	95              5                  2 days
	9               1                  1 day
	              360 tags, 4,391.116 g net

**22kt and 9kt cannot share a metal rate.** They differ by more than double in
gold content, and here they carry the same figure to the paisa, on a handful of
batch-entry days. That is a default being written into a rate field, not a price
anybody set.

### It priced the tags, it did not merely sit beside them

The tell that matters is whether the figure was USED. For every one of the 307
at 18kt:

	amount = rate x net_weight + the tag's own stones      307 of 307, to the rupee

So the stock value on those tags was computed from 4,000 a gram. This was not
obvious: on 234 the amount is exactly rate x weight and on the other 73 it is not,
which reads as two different populations until the stones are added back -- and
then it is one.

### What it is worth

	the 360 tags, valued as tagged            1,75,64,464.00
	the same metal at today's rate per purity 5,69,65,495.93
	difference                                3,94,01,031.93

18kt alone is 2,50,96,717.57 of that. The shelf stands at 14,23,61,188.20, so
this is **28% of it** sitting on a number that was never a rate.

**The difference is not all error.** These were tagged between April 2024 and
November 2025 and gold has risen since, so some of the gap is the market. But
none of it can be *read* from the tag, because a single figure covering 9kt and
22kt cannot be a historical rate either.

### Not re-rated here

Re-rating stock is the shop's decision and not a repair -- it moves the value of
the shelf by 3.94 crore, and which basis to use (the rate the day it was tagged,
today's, or a stock-take) is exactly the sort of choice this project does not
make on its own. The ask on the list is now a number and a basis rather than a
count.

## 347. The opening stock that is not moving is not the old stock

*8.5 crore of opening stock has sold 1.7% in five months -- is that expected?*
went on the decision list beside **"251 pieces date from 2023 or earlier"**. Both
figures reproduce exactly:

	                  tags    still held    sold    turned
	opening stock    1,571        1,545      26     1.65%
	everything else  1,245        1,030     215    17.27%

Ten times faster, as stated, and the opening shelf stands at
**8,51,58,772.85**.

**The two halves of the sentence describe different stock.** The 251 pieces from
2023 or earlier are real and they are worth **14,00,024.17** -- 1.6% of the
figure in front of them:

	tagged        on the shelf         value     at the 4,000 placeholder
	2016                     2      3,910.00        --
	2021                   106    1,36,530.00       --
	2022                    45    1,52,639.38       --
	2023                    98   11,06,944.79       --
	2024                   196  1,64,44,212.40     129
	2025                   692  6,65,62,696.93     229
	2026                   406     7,51,839.35      --

**8,30,06,909.33 of the 8,51,58,772.85 was tagged in 2024 and 2025.** The stock
that is not moving is one to two years old, not ancient. The ancient stock is
1.6% of it and could be given away without changing the answer.

### And more than half of it is priced at the placeholder

Of the 360 tags carrying exactly 4,000 a gram (defect 346), **358 are opening
stock**, and they hold **4,69,17,081.28** -- **55% of the opening shelf value**.

So the question as asked cannot be answered from this data. "Is 1.7% expected for
8.5 crore of stock" assumes the 8.5 crore means something, and the majority of it
rests on a figure that spans 9kt and 22kt alike.

### What is worth asking

**Is 1.7% expected for stock tagged in 2024 and 2025?** -- which is what this
actually is. The 26 pieces that did sell went for 1,08,995.31 between them, so
what moved was the cheap end and what stayed is the value.

Turnover is counted by PIECES here, as the original figure was. By value it is
worse, and saying so precisely needs the re-rating in defect 346 first, which is
the shop's decision and not a measurement.

## 348. The shop does honour an order's locked rate, and its own bills show the rule

*Do you honour an order at the rate it was taken?* has sat on the decision list
with the exposure attached -- **60,14,200.75 to honour the live book**. Nobody
asked the 47 orders that have already been delivered and billed.

	order lines matched to their bill by barcode      47
	  billed at EXACTLY the locked rate               33
	  billed BELOW it                                 12
	  billed ABOVE it                                  2

**Seventy per cent to the paisa, and the exceptions have a shape.** All twelve
billed below the lock; between them the customers paid **21,855.52 less** than
the locked rate would have charged. Four were billed at exactly that day's rate
where the day's rate had fallen -- 18kt locked at 12,045 and billed at 11,075,
silver locked at 275.00 and billed at 231.50, both the market that morning.

So the working rule is not "the rate it was taken". It is **the better of the two
for the customer**, which is a more generous rule than the question assumes and
one the shop follows without being asked.

### Two went the other way

	barcode       purity   locked     billed    net wt   the customer paid
	38323709        22    13,610.00  14,618.00   2.100        2,116.80
	95831681R1      22    13,583.00  13,758.00   1.440          252.00

Both were billed at exactly that day's rate, which was higher than the lock. On
the reading above -- the customer gets the better of the two -- these are the two
where it did not happen, and together they are **2,368.80**.

Whether that is a mistake or a renegotiation the data cannot say. It is two bills
out of 47 and under two and a half thousand rupees, so it is worth a glance and
not an investigation.

### What this does to the question

The 60,14,200.75 still stands: it is what honouring every LIVE order would cost
if metal stays where it is. But the question behind it -- do you honour the lock
-- is answered by the shop's own counter, 33 times exactly and 12 times better.

What is left to ask is narrower: **the two that were charged the day's higher
rate.** And a design question that follows from it -- should the sale screen warn
when a tag reserved against an order is being billed above the rate that order
locked? Nothing does that today, and it is the only place these two would have
shown up before the customer paid.

## 349. The "second system" in defect 66 is called `test_bill` in the schema

Defect 66 is a BLOCKER and its arithmetic holds. What it never says is what the
second numbering IS, and the column name says it plainly:

	legacy.sale_bill_link (id, mcj_bill, TEST_BILL, rt_code, comp_code, ac_yr)

Everything else about the pair is consistent with a parallel system that raised
MORE documents than the real one over the same window:

	                     links   distinct   lowest   highest
	mcj_bill              135        132        1       220
	test_bill             135        134        1       338
	real bills on file    224                   1       224

**The gap widens monotonically and never reverses.** Not one link has the test
number BEHIND the shop's, and the offset grows from 0 at bill 1 to 119 by bill
220 -- the two series start together and the test one pulls away by about one bill
in two.

	bill 1-2      offset 0
	bill 4-6      offset 3
	bill 27-39    offset 21
	bill 99-113   offset 79
	bill 212-220  offset 118-119

That is what a practice or staging environment looks like beside a live one: the
same series, the same retail and company codes, and extra documents in the test
one that the shop never issued.

### It does not dissolve the blocker, it aims it

Defect 66's danger is exact and unchanged: **test number GST/2627/00007 is also a
real bill of the shop's**, belonging to ANITA ROY, 4 April 2026, 32,886.00 --
while the link says it stands for the shop's GST/2627/00004, which is MANISH
KUMAR SHARMA on 2 April for 20,65,000.00. If anybody ever took away an invoice
printed by the test side, the number on it names a different customer's sale in
the shop's own books.

**Whether that ever happened is the whole question, and it is one sentence long.**
The old ask -- *"which bill numbering is the shop's own, and do customers hold
invoices carrying the other one?"* -- has a first half the schema answers: the
shop's own is `mcj_bill`, and the other is labelled test. What is left is the
second half.

Nothing here proves no such invoice left the counter. A column name is evidence
and not a guarantee, and 83 collisions are 83 whatever the environment was called.

## 353. Two customers' stones are being held against orders the shop cancelled

*Return the 14.43 carats of customers' own stones* has sat on the decision list
as one lot. It is not one lot. Joining each receipt to the order it came in
against splits it cleanly:

	receipt         customer            carats  held   the order
	CG/2627/00003   RASHMI SARAF         2.750  58 d   CANCELLED
	CG/2627/00005   POOJA PRASAD         2.850  34 d   CANCELLED
	CG/2627/00005   POOJA PRASAD         1.300  34 d   CANCELLED
	CG/2627/00006   TAHA.M. TAMBAWALA    6.250  30 d   Urgent
	CG/2627/00007   PRABHA BHANSALI      0.930   7 d   Urgent
	CG/2627/00008   PRABHA BHANSALI      0.170   7 d   Process
	CG/2627/00009   P. K. MUNDRA         0.180   6 d   Urgent

**6.90 carats belong to two customers whose orders were cancelled.** RASHMI
SARAF's stone has been here 58 days and POOJA PRASAD's four have been here 34,
in both cases against work the shop is no longer doing. Nothing is owed to the
shop on either; there is no reason to still have them.

The other **7.53 carats across three customers are against live orders** --
Urgent or in Process -- and holding those is the job. They are not the same
question and should not be on the same line of a to-do list.

### The screen can do it

`partysample.go` writes `returned`, `returned_on` and `return_note`, so marking
these back is a counter action and not a build. Nothing is blocked.

### What is actually being asked

Not *"return 14.43 carats"* but:

**Two customers' stones are held against cancelled orders, 58 and 34 days on. Are
they being kept back deliberately, or did the cancellation just not reach the
counter?**

The second is likelier and neither is knowable from here. Cancelling an order
does not prompt anybody to hand back what came in with it -- there is no link
from the order's status to the goods receipt, and defect 335 found the same shape
on the sales side, where a status change left another record standing.

## 354. The vendor's login out-ranks the super admin, on the one right the super admin was denied

*Should the vendor's `rps` login keep all four override rights?* sat on the
decision list with the four named and nothing about who else has them. `users`
carries them as four flags -- `barcode_change`, `back_date_entry`,
`due_date_change`, `home_rate_change` -- and across 24 logins:

	can post to a closed period   9
	can change the gold rate      6
	can edit a tag                4
	can move a due date           4
	ALL FOUR                      2

The two are **`rps` (ADMIN)** and **`Shibananda` (SUB ADMIN)**.

### And the super admin is not one of them

	login        role          tag   back-date   due date   rate
	GKS          SUPER ADMIN    1        0          1        1
	Shibananda   SUB ADMIN      1        1          1        1
	rps          ADMIN          1        1          1        1

**`GKS`, the super admin, cannot post to a closed period. `rps` can.** Whoever
set these up withheld back-dating from the highest role in the shop and left it
with the vendor's login and the sub admin.

That is either deliberate -- the vendor needed it to fix data and the owner did
not want it -- or it is what happens when a support login is set up once and
never revisited. Nothing here can tell which.

### Why back-dating is the one that matters

The other three are visible in their own records: an edited tag, a moved due
date and a changed rate all leave the thing they changed. Back-dating does not
announce itself -- **a voucher posted into a closed period looks exactly like one
posted at the time**, and this rebuild has already found what a wrong date does
in defect 325, where a bill dated before the rate feed gave the gold away.

Nine logins can do it, so it is not a vendor question alone. But the vendor's
login is the one on the list, and the answer to *"should it keep all four"* now
has a shape: **it holds a right that the owner's own login does not.**

*Eight live orders are promised for a Thursday, when the shop is closed* went on
the decision list as something to reschedule. Both halves check out and the
conclusion does not.

**Thursday is the closing day, and the evidence is strong:**

	holidays recorded    109
	  on a Thursday      108     2016-01-07 to 2024-12-26
	  on a Monday          1     2017-05-01, May Day

**The eight are real.** They are also all in the past:

	live lines with a Thursday delivery date        8
	  falling after today                           0
	  earliest                             2024-02-15
	  latest                               2026-07-30

Nothing is coming up to be missed. These are past-due lines that happen to carry
a Thursday date, and they are already counted among defect 28's overdue work.

### The practice is sound

Across the 149 live lines that carry a delivery date at all:

	Friday      35        Monday      19
	Sunday      27        Tuesday     12
	Saturday    25        THURSDAY     8
	Wednesday   23

**Thursday is the least-used day of the week**, by a clear margin -- 5.4% of live
promises against Friday's 23%. The counter is already avoiding it. Eight over

### What is actually worth noting

	the holiday list was last written   2024-12-26

Twenty months dead, so **nothing in this system can tell anybody today whether a

That is the only part of this worth doing anything about, and it is small: a

## 356. Correcting a legacy tag's making rewrites its value on a different basis

Found by testing an invariant the code's own formula implies. `pricing.Calculate`
ends:

	Total: rupees.Sum(amount, making, l.OtherMaking)

so for anything this system prices, `total = amount + making + other`. Across the
shelf:

	tags                                     2,816
	  where total = amount + making + other  1,678
	  where it does not                      1,138

All 2,816 are legacy rows, and certification closes **none** of the 1,138. The
legacy simply did not compute `total` the way this system does. Worked through on
the largest:

	29522987  DIAMOND SET, on the shelf
	  rate 11,800.00 x net 64.138        =   7,56,828.40   metal
	  amount                                19,76,308.40   metal AND stones
	  making                                   64,138.00
	  total on the tag                       8,20,966.40   = metal + making

**The tag's `total` excludes its stones and its `amount` includes them.** The gap
is 12,19,480.00 and it is exactly the stone value.

### Why that is a defect and not a curiosity

`tagcorrect.go` reprices whatever it touches and writes the result:

	SET ... making = $6, total = $7

`total` there is `price.Total`, which is `amount + making + other` -- and the
repricing rebuilds `amount` from the tag, stones included. So **correcting the
making on 29522987 would move its value from 8,20,966.40 to 20,40,446.40**, a
silent 12,19,480.00 added to the shelf by a screen the user opened to fix a
making charge.

	tags on the shelf that would move            1,038
	  by more than 10,000.00                        62
	  by more than 1,00,000.00                       3
	worst single tag                       12,19,480.00
	the shelf if every one were corrected     -4,10,891.26

**The net is small and that is the trap.** Positives and negatives nearly cancel,
so a bulk revaluation would look almost free while individual pieces moved by
lakhs in both directions.

### Not fixed here, and the reason is which basis is right

The screen is not wrong to price the way the rest of the system prices. What is
wrong is that it changes a figure the user did not ask it to change and does not
say so. Three repairs are possible -- leave `total` alone unless the making
actually moved it, carry the legacy's own basis per tag, or re-state every tag on
this system's basis and accept the shift -- and the third is defect 346's
re-rating question again, which is the shop's.

**What can be said without deciding:** 1,038 tags on the shelf carry a total that
this system would compute differently, and nothing warns anybody.

## 357. The companion invariant holds on every row, which is what makes 356 measurable

Defect 356 rests on `amount` being trustworthy. If `amount` were computed on two
bases as well, there would be nothing solid to measure `total`'s drift against and
the finding would be two unknowns instead of one. So it was tested:

	tags                                                    2,816
	  where amount = rate x net weight + the tag's stones    2,816
	  where it is not                                            0

**No exceptions at all** -- across legacy and every purity, stone-bearing and
plain. `amount` means one thing.

Pinned as the 25th rule in `check_invariants.py`, so it stays that way. Proven
able to fail rather than assumed: tightening its tolerance from a rupee to a
millionth surfaces 172 rows, which is the rounding in a numeric(18,2) against a
product of two numerics and exactly why the tolerance is there.

	x  a tag's amount is its metal and its stones   172 tag(s) ... -- 172 more than the 0 allowed

### What the pair says together

	amount   metal + stones          2,816 of 2,816   one basis
	total    two bases               1,678 of 2,816   the other 1,138 exclude stones

The problem in 356 is not that the legacy data is arbitrary. It is that ONE field
carries two conventions and the field beside it does not, so nothing in the tag
itself says which convention any given row follows -- and a screen that reprices
has no way to tell.

## 358. The same two-basis problem is on the sold lines, and there it is harmless

Defect 356 found `total` carrying two conventions on the shelf. The sale side was
checked for the same thing, because the sale writes its line amount from the same
formula:

	amount = price.Total = rate x net weight + stones + making + other making

	sold lines                                        367
	  satisfying that                                 138
	  not                                             229

The same split, and largely explainable: of the 229, **122 carry a certification
charge** -- which `pricing.Calculate` deliberately leaves out (defect 47) and a
certified piece is billed at a price agreed across the counter (defect 300) --
**38 are flat-priced** with rate 0, and **68 are untagged** lines typed by hand.

### Why it does not matter here and does on the shelf

	writers that change a bill after it is raised:
	  creditnote.go:572   UPDATE mcj_sales_invoices ... SET is_returned = true

**That is the only one, and it sets a boolean.** Nothing in this system ever
recomputes a sold line's amount, so a line whose composition follows the legacy's
basis simply stays as the shop billed it. It is a record, not an input.

A tag is the opposite: `tagcorrect.go` reprices it and writes the answer back,
which is exactly why 356 is a defect and this is not.

### And the aggregate was already guarded

	bills                                     224
	  goods_amount equals the sum of its lines 224

Checked, clean, and it turns out this is already the first rule in
`check_invariants.py` -- *"every bill's lines add up to its goods"*, from defect
220. **Re-derived a guard that already existed**, which is a fair use of an hour:
the rule now has a second pair of eyes on it and the answer did not change.

## 359. Old gold was the one document type with no rule saying it agrees with its voucher

Listing the invariants out rather than adding to them found a gap in a family.
Three of the four documents this shop raises had a rule:

	a bill agrees with its own voucher        defect 308
	a purchase agrees with its own voucher    defect 309
	a return agrees with its own voucher      defect 332
	old gold                                  -- nothing

**That is the sort of gap that survives because nobody writes the family down.**
Each rule was added when its own defect was found, and old gold never had a
defect, so it never got a rule -- which is not the same as being checked.

Checked now:

	old gold documents                        25
	  whose lines sum to what the party was credited   25
	  that disagree                                     0

Exact on every one. The party is CREDITED here, unlike a sale: the shop buys
metal across the counter and owes for it.

### Proven able to fail, on the second attempt

The first falsification was no falsification. Removing the `ROUNDED OFF`
exclusion should have broken the arithmetic and did not -- **old gold vouchers
carry no rounding line at all**, so the clause it removed was doing nothing on
this data. The rule still passed and that proved nothing.

Flipping the comparison to the debit side did it:

	x  old gold agrees with its own voucher   25 ... -- 25 more than the 0 allowed

**A test that passes when you break it has not been run**, which is the same
lesson as defects 298 and 302 arriving by a different road: this time the break
itself was wrong rather than the assertion.

Twenty-six rules now, and the four document types are symmetric.

	purchases with no contents          0 of 43

	conversions with no pieces          0 of 859
	orders with no lines               13 of 284

	the order screen   refuses an empty order: "Say what the customer has asked for."

## 361. A rule that would have caught a bug I wrote, proven by writing it again

Continuing the family sweep: does every document name a party that exists?

	bills                 224   0 without one
	credit/debit notes      6   0
	orders                284   0
	old gold lines         25   0
	purchases              43   0
	customer goods          7   0

Clean everywhere. **Added anyway, because it would have caught defect 333's
loader bug** -- `load_credit_notes.sh` joined ledgers on `legacy_id` where every
other loader in that directory joins on `code`, nought of six notes resolved, and
the loader's own guard checked the VOUCHER join and not the ledger one. It printed
success. I found it by measuring afterwards, which is luck dressed as method.

### Proven by reproducing the bug

Rather than argue the rule would have caught it, the bug was written back in --
the wrong join restored, the guard removed -- and the loader run:

	loaded 6 return document(s, every one tied to its voucher and its party
	x  every document names a party that exists   3 document(s) naming no party

**The loader still says "and its party".** That sentence is now false and the
script cannot tell; the rule can.

### And the wrong join half worked

Three of six, not nought. Some ledgers' `legacy_id` happens to equal another
ledger's `code`, so the broken join resolves a few rows **to the wrong party**
rather than to none. That is worse than failing cleanly and it is why a spot
check of one row is not a test: pick the right row and the bug is invisible.

Loader and data restored; 28 of 28 rules hold.

## 362. No other loader has 333's bug, and the rule that catches it only catches half of it

Two questions came out of defect 361. Both answered.

### Is the wrong join anywhere else?

Every loader that reaches a ledger was read:

	load_bank_accounts   load_carry_forward   load_customer_goods   load_invoices
	load_estimates       load_oldgold         load_orders           load_schemes
	load_payroll         load_payroll_history load_purchase_invoices load_vouchers
	repair_opening_balances

**All of them join on `lg.code`.** The three that appear to join on an id --
`ON lg.id = l.ledger_id` -- are second-stage joins against a UUID this system
already resolved, which is correct. `load_credit_notes.sh` was the only one, and
it is fixed.

### How dangerous is the wrong key?

	ledgers                                              785
	  whose code equals their own legacy_id                0
	  whose legacy_id is ANOTHER ledger's code            43

The two keys never coincide by accident on the same row, so a wrong-key join
never quietly works. **But 43 times in 785 it resolves to a DIFFERENT ledger** --
5.5% -- which is why the reproduction in defect 361 attached 3 of 6 notes rather
than nought.

**A join on the wrong key does not fail. It picks somebody else.**

### And that is the half rule 361 cannot catch

`every document names a party that exists` finds a document with NO party. The
43-collision case gives the document a party -- the wrong one -- and the rule
passes it, because the ledger it names is perfectly real.

So the new rule caught 3 of the 6 broken notes and would have missed the other 3.
**Stated here rather than left implied**, because a guard that catches half a bug
is more dangerous than none if nobody knows which half.

The only thing that catches mis-attachment is a loader comparing its output to
its source, party by party -- which is what a loader's own guard is for, and what
`load_credit_notes.sh` now does on both its joins.

## 363. Seven loaders join a ledger without checking it resolved, and one of them has 272 that did not

Defect 362 ended by saying the loader's own guard is the load-bearing check.
So which loaders have one?

	guard their ledger join     carry_forward, credit_notes, customer_goods,
	                            estimates, vouchers
	do NOT                      bank_accounts, invoices, orders, payroll,
	                            payroll_history, purchase_invoices, schemes

**Seven join and do not check.** Six of those seven are clean anyway --
invoices, orders, purchase invoices, schemes and both payroll loaders resolve
every row, and rule 361 now watches four of them from the data side.

*(Wrong about one of them. `payroll_history` has 37 rows with no ledger -- found
in defect 364 by measuring each TABLE rather than reading each loader. The other
five are as stated, and the count of clean ones is five, not six.)*

**`load_bank_accounts.sh` is not.**

	mcj_bank_accounts rows        398
	  with a ledger               126
	  WITHOUT one                 272

### It is the shop's data, and the ledger load is complete

The obvious suspicion is 333's again -- a wrong key, or a partial ledger load.
Both were checked and both are innocent:

	legacy.ledger_master rows                785
	mcj_ledgers rows                         785      every one with a code and a name

	legacy.ledger_bank_details rows        1,071
	  whose party_ldgr exists in ledger_master   349
	  whose party_ldgr does NOT              722

**722 of the legacy's own 1,071 bank-detail rows name a ledger code that is not
in the legacy's own ledger master.** The bank details outlived the accounts they
belong to. Nothing was lost in the migration; the rubble is original.

That is the mechanism behind defect 284's warning -- *"398 rows sounds
operational and 272 name no ledger at all, so a screen over it would mostly be
built over rubble"* -- which said what and now has a why.

### What is worth doing

Not a guard on `load_bank_accounts.sh`: a guard that fails on 272 rows the shop
genuinely has would stop the load for a fact nobody can fix. **The other six
should have one**, because for them nought is the true number and a guard would
hold it there. That is a small change and it is not made here, because six
loaders' worth of new failure modes on the evening a rule was added is how a
green check becomes a habit of ignoring red ones.

## 364. A correction: one of the two payroll loaders does not resolve every row

Defect 363 said *"invoices, orders, purchase invoices, schemes and both payroll
loaders resolve every row"*. Five of those six are right. **`payroll_history` is
not**, and the way to find that out was to measure each rather than group them:

	sales invoices                  224     0 without a ledger
	customer orders                 284     0
	scheme enrolments               239     0
	purchases (supplier resolves)    43     0
	payroll history                 209    37

I had checked the loaders and not the tables. Four of the five were clean, and
"both payroll loaders" was a sentence written about a pair when only one had been
looked at.

### The 37 are the shop's data, checked the same way as the bank details

	rows with no ledger                   37
	distinct staff codes                   4      8827, 4023, 8855, 8828
	months covered            2025-04 to 2026-03
	components on those rows      4,39,640.00

	rows in legacy.staff_salary_sheet_payroll_detail naming a code
	that is NOT in legacy.ledger_master                 37

**Exactly the same 37.** The four codes return nothing from the legacy's own
ledger master, so this is not a join failure: the payroll history outlived the
staff ledgers, as the bank details outlived their accounts (defect 363).

Four people, a year of months each, and 4,39,640.00 of PF, ESI, professional tax,
HRA and dearness allowance recorded against ledgers the shop has since deleted.
Whether those staff left and their accounts were cleaned up is a question the data
cannot answer and the shop can in a sentence.

### What it means for the guard

`load_payroll_history.sh` cannot carry the guard 363 proposed either: nought is
not its true number, 37 is. It joins on the right key and gets the right answer,
and the answer includes 37 rows whose party no longer exists.

**Two of the seven unguarded loaders turn out to have a real non-zero**, which is
the reason the sweep was worth doing at all -- and the reason not to have added
six guards on the assumption they would all pass.

## 365. Four loaders now check their own ledger join, and the first version of one guard tested the wrong column

Defects 363 and 364 established which loaders could carry the guard: five of the
seven unguarded ones resolve every row, and two -- `bank_accounts` (272) and
`payroll_history` (37) -- have a real non-zero that is the shop's own data.
`load_payroll.sh` writes no ledger column at all, so four remained.

	load_invoices.sh            mcj_sales_invoices       ledger_id IS NULL
	load_orders.sh              mcj_customer_orders      ledger_id IS NULL
	load_schemes.sh             mcj_scheme_enrolments    ledger_id IS NULL
	load_purchase_invoices.sh   mcj_purchase_invoices    supplier_code resolves

All four pass on the real data. **Each was then broken on purpose**, its ledger
join switched from `code` to `legacy_id` -- 333's bug, exactly:

	load_invoices    ERROR: 219 row(s) in mcj_sales_invoices match no ledger
	load_orders      ERROR: 267 row(s) in mcj_customer_orders match no ledger
	load_schemes     ERROR: 227 row(s) in mcj_scheme_enrolments match no ledger

**And not one of them catches every row.** 219 of 224 bills, 267 of 284 orders,
227 of 239 schemes -- the remainder resolved through the wrong key to the WRONG
ledger, which is defect 362's 43 collisions doing exactly what was predicted.

### The fourth guard was decoration and the break proved it

`load_purchase_invoices.sh` passed with its join broken. The reason is that the
column the guard reads is not the column the join feeds:

	supplier_code   <- si.ldgr        straight from the legacy
	supplier_name   <- lg.name        through the join

So *"does supplier_code resolve to a ledger"* is a real check and a blind one: it
cannot notice the join failing, because its input never went through the join. A
second guard was added on the column that does:

	ERROR: 42 purchase(s) name a real ledger and carry no supplier name

**Both guards are kept.** The first catches a legacy code that is not in the
chart; the second catches the join that fetches its name breaking. They fail on
different things and the first one's blindness is why it looked sufficient.

### The test method failed once too, before any of this

The first attempt to break all three used `sed` with `\\|` alternation, which BSD
sed does not support, so nothing was substituted and all three "passed". Reported
as *"guard is decoration"* for a moment, when the truth was that the test had not
run. **Twice in three days a falsification has been the thing that was broken**
(defect 359 was the other), which is its own small lesson: when a break does not
break anything, suspect the break.

## 366. Re-running the purchase loader emptied the register hanging off it

Found by triggering it. After adding the ledger guards in defect 365 I re-ran the
four loaders, and the next full check came back with two failures that had
nothing to do with ledgers:

	x  a purchase says what it bought   43 purchase bill(s) with no contents
	x  report (no data)   /mcj/reports/mrp-purchases
	x  report (no data)   /mcj/reports/purchase-contents

`load_purchase_invoices.sh` DELETEs its 43 invoices and reloads them.
`mcj_purchase_contents` hangs off them with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, so every re-run
takes all 60 content rows with it -- and the loader printed
`OK mcj_purchase_invoices 43 rows, input tax ties at 521364.93` while it did.

**This is defect 294's shape and 294's own fix was never applied here.**
`load_invoices.sh`, `load_conversions.sh` and `load_orders.sh` each carry a guard
that PUTS THE ROWS BACK when they cascade something away. This one had none, so
the family was three of four -- the same gap that defect 359 found in the
invariants and 363 found in the loader guards.

**Fixed** the same way as its siblings: count the contents, reload them if they
are gone, and fail loudly if the reload does not take. Run three times in a row to
prove the repair is idempotent -- 43 invoices and 60 contents, every time.

### Two mistakes inside the fix

The repair called `"${HERE}/load_purchase_contents.sh"`, copied from
`load_invoices.sh` where `HERE` exists. **This loader does not define it** -- it
`cd`s to the repository root instead -- so the first run died with
`HERE: unbound variable` **after** it had already emptied the table. A guard that
crashes is worse than no guard: it leaves the damage and stops.

And the check that caught all this was `check_all.sh`, run out of habit at the
end of an unrelated piece of work. **The loaders' own output said OK.**

## 367. The cascade family, swept to the end: eleven of eleven now survive a re-run

Defect 366 was found by tripping over it. The obvious next question is how many
more are waiting, so the whole family was listed from the database rather than
from memory:

	SELECT ... FROM pg_constraint WHERE contype='f' AND confdeltype='c'

**Eleven cascading foreign keys between mcj tables.** Three of them --
`mcj_voucher_lines`, `mcj_sales_invoice_lines`, `mcj_customer_order_lines` --
are written by the same statement that writes their parent, so a re-run rebuilds
both and there is nothing to lose. The other eight split two ways:

	child written by ANOTHER script     parent repairs it?
	  mcj_ordered_stones                  yes  (defect 294)
	  mcj_sold_stones                     yes  (defect 294)
	  mcj_conversion_stones               yes
	  mcj_stock_conversion_pieces         yes
	  mcj_purchase_contents               yes  (defect 366, yesterday)

	child written by the SAME script    reloaded in the same run?
	  mcj_design_stones                   proven
	  mcj_estimate_lines                  proven
	  mcj_scheme_payments                 proven

### The three "same script" ones were proven, not assumed

Reading a script and concluding it reloads what it deleted is how defect 366
survived: `load_purchase_invoices.sh` looked fine too. So all three were run and
counted on both sides:

	                    before   after
	design_stones        3,416    3,416
	estimate_lines           2        2
	scheme_payments      2,144    2,144

Unchanged. Then the whole check: 9 of 9, after six loaders had been re-run in one
sitting.

**The family is closed.** Eleven cascades, eleven that survive a re-run, and the
one that did not was found by running the check out of habit rather than by
reading anything.

## 368. Every loader verifies its own output, and it took three wrong greps to establish it

The family after the cascades: does each loader check what it wrote? Swept by
grepping for the pattern the loaders I had written use --

	loaders                                39
	with SRC/DST comparison                26
	without                                13

-- and the thirteen looked like a real gap. They are not one.

**The second grep was wrong too.** Looking for `|| { echo "FAIL` found assertions
in all twelve real ones (`load_all.sh` is an orchestrator), between one and five
each, which suggested the opposite conclusion: verified, just differently.

**`load_masters.sh` looked worst and is the most strictly checked file here.** One
assertion by that grep, seventeen tables written -- and a `check()` function it
calls once per table with an EXACT expected count:

	check mcj_items 322        check mcj_metal_rates 2820
	check mcj_packets 205      check mcj_ledger_groups 96
	check mcj_states 36        check mcj_value_bands 43        ... 17 in all

A pinned absolute is stronger than a source-to-destination comparison, because it
survives the source changing underneath it.

`load_codelists.sh` looked like it wrote nothing -- it builds
`INSERT INTO ${target}` dynamically, so a literal grep cannot see the table names
-- and it compares src to dst per list, sets `fail=1`, and ends `[ "$fail" = "0" ]
|| exit 1`.

### What is actually true

**All 38 loaders verify their output.** No gap, nothing to fix, and the family is
closed like the four before it.

### The part worth keeping

Three greps, three wrong answers, and the truth only when the files were opened.
Each grep encoded *"a check looks like the checks I write"* -- SRC/DST, then
`|| { echo "FAIL`, and both missed a `check()` helper and a dynamic loop.

That is the same error as defect 359's inert falsification and 365's `sed` that
did not substitute: **the measurement passed and measured nothing.** Third time
this week, and the tell is the same every time -- a sweep that returns a
suspiciously tidy gap, in files nobody has read.

	last movement   tags        value

	NEW-BAR           33    29,89,769.63   defect 314's known 42, with

	SALE-RET           3    18,53,671.28   returned -- and still gone

	22157192        4,271.20   sold GST/2627/00013, returned SR/2627/00002

	legacy.barcode_main.stk_status
	  70630587, 36568032, 22157192      0    out of stock
	  the 2,575 on the shelf            1

Testing the complement of rule 13 -- it says a payment names a bill that exists,

	bills (not cancelled)                224
	  with no payment row at all          83     1,82,16,133.00
	  paid in full                       115
	  underpaid                           26
	  overpaid                             0

The 83 look alarming and are mostly not. Followed through:

	  the customer has a RECEIPT voucher            44

**38,77,608.00 on PURC-OG vouchers** -- the customer brought jewellery in and

## 372. A rule called "names a document" that 8,165 movements passed by containing a word

Third turn running, an allowance turned out to hide something. This time the
allowance was fine and the RULE was not.

	("a stock movement names a document", 470 allowed)
	    SELECT count(*) FROM mcj_stock_movements WHERE btrim(reference) = ''

It checks that a text field is not blank. Across the 9,031 movements:

	6,395   "New Create"                  a word
	1,770   "Opening"                     a word
	  470   nothing                       the allowance
	  396   a document number             SALE-GST 324, CST-ORD 44, SALE-RET 17,
	                                      ISS-HM 4, REC-HM 4, EST 2, PURC-IN 1

**Only 396 movements in 9,031 name a document, and that is correct.** A piece
being created or carried in has no document to name -- "New Create" and
"Opening" are honest labels for events that have none. Nothing here is wrong
with the data.

**The title was wrong.** It promised that every movement is traceable to a
document, and 8,165 of them satisfied it by containing a word. Anybody reading
the rule list -- which is the point of the rule list -- would have taken the
trail to be far more documented than it is.

Renamed to **"a movement's reference is filled in"**, which is what it does, with
the four-way split written above it so the next reader does not have to run the
query.

### And the 470 is two events missing their label

	278  OP-STK   should say "Opening"
	192  NEW-BAR  should say "New Create"

161 of those 192 barcodes are still on the shelf, worth **57,41,225.14** -- and
it does not matter, because the label they are missing carries no information
either. A tidiness allowance, not a hole, and now recorded as one.

### The pattern across three turns

	defect 370   an allowance held a diamond ring sold on a bill it is not on
	defect 371   an allowance made a report overstate its own coverage
	defect 372   an allowance was fine and the rule above it was misnamed

**A number that passes is not a fact that was checked.** Three different shapes
of the same lesson, from the same habit: reading what a green line claims rather
than what it measures.

## 374. The 31 uncleared-date vouchers are two different things, and neither can happen again

Fifth allowance opened. *Clearing a cheque sets both columns* permits 31 vouchers
marked `bank_cleared` with no `bank_cleared_on`.

	all 31    type PMNT, dated 13 May to 5 Aug 2026
	all 31    carry a legacy_v_id -- not one was raised here
	all 31    touch a Bank Account; none touches cash

	12   carry a cheque number, a cheque date and a bank name    3,30,462.00
	19   carry none of the three                                 8,37,549.97

**The 19 are not missing a cheque -- they are not cheques.** A bank transfer has
no number to record, so the only thing absent is the clearing date, and for a
transfer that is the same day as the payment.

**The 12 are cheques, and there the date is the whole point.** A cheque clears
days after it is written; without `bank_cleared_on` the lag cannot be measured,
which is what a reconciliation is for.

### It cannot grow

	reconcile.go
	  var clearedOn *time.Time
	  if want { clearedOn = &on }
	  UPDATE mcj_vouchers SET bank_cleared=$1, bank_cleared_on=$2 ...

The date is written in the same statement that sets the flag, so a clearance made
through this system always has one. The 31 are closed history and the allowance
should never move.

### Five allowances, five different answers

	470  two events missing a label that carries no information   (372)
	  8  payments naming bills that do not exist, and a report
	     that counted them as coverage                            (371)
	  9  one of them a diamond ring sold on a bill it is not on   (370)
	 57  53 documented on the tag, 4 with nothing anywhere        (373)
	 31  12 cheques with no clearing date, 19 that are not
	     cheques at all                                           (374)

Not one of the five was a single population, and not one of the numbers said so.

## 375. Eight of the eighteen duplicate movements are one bill, saved twice a day apart

Sixth and last sizeable allowance. *One voucher moves a tag once* permits 18
events recorded twice under one voucher number. Split by how far apart the two
rows sit:

	 6   within the hour     worst 21 minutes      a save made twice
	 3   same day            worst 4 hours
	 9   days apart          worst 28 days

**The nine are not nine accidents.** Eight of them are a single bill:

	GST/2627/00150
	  2026-07-03 09:25   9 pieces   BAPI
	  2026-07-04 14:06   8 pieces   BAPI      the same eight, again

A bill re-saved the next afternoon, by the same person, writing its stock
movements a second time instead of replacing them. Eight of the nine pieces moved
twice; one did not, which is what makes it a re-save of an edited bill rather
than a duplicate submission.

The ninth is `84188080R1` on **SR/2526/00005**, 28 days apart and from the
financial year before -- a different event entirely, and the only one of the
eighteen that is genuinely on its own.

### It cannot happen here

`sale.go` writes one movement per line inside the voucher's own transaction, and
nothing in this system re-posts a saved bill: there is no edit path that reaches
the movement writer twice. The 18 are legacy behaviour and the allowance is
closed history, like the 31 in defect 374.

### Six allowances, and the sweep is done

	470  (372)   two events missing a label that carries no information
	 57  (373)   53 documented on the tag, 4 with nothing anywhere
	 31  (374)   12 cheques with no clearing date, 19 that are not cheques
	 18  (375)   one bill saved twice, six double-saves, one from last year
	  9  (370)   one of them a diamond ring sold on a bill it is not on
	  8  (371)   payments naming bills that do not exist, counted as coverage

**Six numbers, none of which was one population.** Every rule now carries its
split in the comment above it, so the next reader gets the meaning without
running a query -- which is the whole difference between a check that passes and
a fact that is known.

## 376. The last two allowances are a paisa and a pair of malas

Finishing the sweep. Of the nine rules that allow anything, six were opened in
defects 370-375 and the coin one (14) was itemised when it was written. Two were
left, both of size one.

### Every voucher balances -- allowed 1

	JRNL 312, 16 May 2026
	  debits   509.15
	  credits  509.14
	  out by     0.01

**One paisa, in 1,848 vouchers.** A rounding remainder rather than a missing
line: nothing is absent, the two sides simply do not meet at the last decimal.
There is no adjustment worth making and none is proposed.

### A barcode names one tag -- allowed 1

	86065435, on TWO tags
	  both MALA, both 900.00, both karigar D603,
	  both created 2024-03-31, both still on the shelf

Scanning that barcode finds two pieces. The sale screen resolves it with

	ORDER BY s.in_stock DESC LIMIT 1

-- a piece still on the shelf, and one of them. **With two rows identical in
every visible respect the choice cannot be wrong**: 900.00 leaves the shelf and
one of the two malas is marked sold, whichever it is. That is only true because
the tie-break prefers a piece in stock; without it the screen could pick a tag
already sold and refuse a sale of something the shop is holding.

	  9  (370)   one of them a diamond ring sold on a bill it is not on
	  8  (371)   payments naming bills that do not exist, counted as coverage

**Nine allowances, 609 rows, all now described rather than counted.** Six needed

## 377. Fifteen reports are named by no test, and one of them is mine

A coverage family, prompted by defect 269 having once found seventeen of them:

	report specs                81
	named by no test            15

	BackDatedSubgroupStock  ConversionStones     DesignCatalogue
	ItemCatalogue           PacketStockSummary   Quarterly
	RatioAnalysis           RawStockTally        SchemeBook
	StockJournal            StockValuation       SubgroupStockTally
	SuspectRates            UntaggedItemStock    UserMaster

**`ConversionStones` is the one I built in defect 327**, and it went in without a
test while its own entry described reconciling 2,60,68,682.20 three ways. The
reconciling was real and it was done by hand, once, in a terminal that is gone.

### A render check is not a test, and this is the difference

`check_screens_render.py` fetches all 81 on every run and has always returned
green for this one. It proves the query runs and returns rows. **It cannot tell
2,60,68,682.20 from 26,06,868.20.**

Three tests written, and both of the report's real risks proven catchable:

	the summary equals the lines, and the lines are 3 not 6
	  broken by joining shapes on the tenant instead of the id --
	  x  the report lists 6 stone line(s), want 3

	a zero says whose it is
	  broken by giving the customer's stone the shop's wording --
	  x  the customer's stone is marked "no price recorded"

The first break is the exact fault the report was written to avoid: four lookups
per row, any one of which fanning out doubles the money with no other symptom.

### And the first run failed on the seed

The customer-stone tests failed before the report was touched, because the test
tenant has no item named CUSTOMER STONE and the join found nothing. **The seed
was wrong, not the screen** -- the fourth time this week a measurement failed
before the thing it measures, after defect 359's inert break, 365's `sed` and
368's three greps. It is worth noticing that all four were caught by the result
looking wrong rather than by any check.

Fourteen reports still carry no test. That is a list, not a claim that they are
broken.

## 378. The valuation screen revalues metal and not stones, and now something says so

Second from defect 377's list of fifteen. `StockValuation` is the screen that
answers what the shelf is worth at today's rate rather than the rate on each tag
-- which is the question defect 346 raised about the 4,000-a-gram placeholder,
and the one that would decide a 3.94 crore re-rating.

It had no test.

### The arithmetic it must not get wrong

**Only the metal revalues.** Stones and making were agreed when the piece was
tagged and do not move with the gold rate:

	SUM(s.total + (c.sale_rate - s.rate) * s.net_weight)

Three tags seeded -- two on the shelf, one sold -- 30 g at 6,000 rising to 7,000,
with 5,000 of stones on one of them:

	tags counted        2      the sold one absent
	net weight         30.000
	book value      1,85,000.00
	value today     2,15,000.00
	difference         30,000.00     30 g x 1,000, and nothing else

**Broken on purpose** by revaluing the whole tag total instead:

	x  value today 215833.33, want 215000.00 -- only the metal revalues
	x  difference   30833.33, want  30000.00

833.33 on a three-tag seed, from 5,000 of stones. The error scales with the
stones in the case, and this shop's shelf carries them in quantity.

**And the rate today is the LATEST**, not the first:

	x  rate today reads "6,000.00", want 7,000.00 -- the 1 August rate

Reversing one `ORDER BY` turns a revaluation into a restatement of what the tags
already say, and every difference to nought. Nothing else in the screen would
look wrong.

### Why this one mattered more than most

The 346 question -- on what basis is the shelf valued -- gets answered from this
screen. **An untested screen was the evidence for a 3,94,01,031.93 decision.**
It is right, and now it is checked.

Thirteen of the fifteen remain.

	1  "inconsistent types deduced for parameter $2"
	   the instalment date built as `$2::int * INTERVAL '1 month'`.
	   Cast it again -- no. Moved the arithmetic into Go -- no.

## 380. The ratio screen prints +Inf and NaN without its guard, and a group name is nearly a synonym

Fourth from defect 377's list. `RatioAnalysis` is mostly restraint: it refuses
gross margin, stock turnover and return on stock because all three need closing
stock inside the ledgers and blocker B19 is precisely that it is not there. What
it prints is liquidity and gearing, which need only balances.

Seeded a shop with 1,00,000 in the till, a customer owing 50,000, a 30,000
overdraft and 20,000 owed to suppliers:

	quick ratio            (1,00,000 + 50,000) / (30,000 + 20,000)   3.00
	cash to overdraft       1,00,000 / 30,000                        3.33
	receivable to payable      50,000 / 20,000                       2.50

Three tests, and each risk proven catchable.

**A division can be inverted and still look like a ratio:**

	x  Cash to overdraft reads "0.30", want 3.33

0.30 is a perfectly plausible number for a jeweller. Nothing about it says the
division went the wrong way round, which is why the numerator and denominator are
shown beside it and now checked.

**And the zero guard is load-bearing:**

	x  Quick ratio reads "+Inf" with a zero denominator, want a dash
	x  Receivable to payable reads "NaN"

A shop with no overdraft and no supplier debt is not an error; it is a shop
having a good month. Without `if b.IsZero()` this screen prints `+Inf` and `NaN`
at a reader.

### The seed was wrong in a way worth writing down

The first run gave a quick ratio of 5.00 against a hand-worked 3.00, and a
receivable-to-payable of "—". The cause was one word:

	seeded    'Sundry Creditors'
	counted   'Sundry Creditors Expenses'

The screen names three supplier groups explicitly and the shop's chart uses the
longer one. My seed's supplier existed, had a credit balance, and was counted as
nothing -- so payable was nought, and the quick ratio quietly divided by the
overdraft alone.

**A group name that is a near-synonym of a real one fails silently**, because
nothing joins to it: there is no foreign key to violate and no row to be missing.
The same shape as defect 371's coverage figure and 362's wrong key -- something
that resolves to nothing rather than to an error.

Eleven of the fifteen remain.

## 381. The screen that finds tags priced off the rate cannot see the 360 that are

Fifth from defect 377's list, and the one that found something.

`SuspectRates` exists to catch a tag carrying a figure that was never a rate. Its
two structural tests are exactly right for the job:

	a round hundred                 what somebody types meaning to come back
	a rate equal to the net weight  a transposition

**And a pre-filter runs before them:** `s.rate < c.sale_rate * 0.25`. Only tags
under a QUARTER of today's rate reach the structural tests at all.

	                today's rate   a quarter   tags at exactly 4,000   reaching the test
	18kt              12,398.00     3,099.50            307                    0
	22kt              15,153.00     3,788.25             39                    0
	14kt               9,643.00     2,410.75              8                    0
	95                 7,500.00     1,875.00              5                    0
	9kt                6,199.00     1,549.75              1                    0
	                                                    360                    0

**Not one of defect 346's 360 placeholder tags reaches the test that would catch
it** -- 3,94,01,031.93 of understatement, invisible to the screen built to find
it, because 4,000 is above a quarter of every rate in the shop. The 22kt case
misses by 212 rupees.

The screen currently flags **18 tags, 6,33,930.93**.

### The filter is not a mistake, which is what makes this hard

It was set deliberately (defect 36) after a first version that used the fraction
AS the finding and was 90% noise: 159 of 177 rows were silver tagged when silver
was genuinely a quarter of today's price. The captured rate history starts 1
April 2026, so a tag made before then cannot be checked against the rate of its
own day, and being far below today's is evidence of nothing.

Removing the filter entirely and letting the structural tests stand alone:

	831 tags flagged, of which
	  18kt 400 (2,83,69,578.84)  22kt 187 (3,25,63,979.47)   the signal
	  999  112 (39,855.45)       SLV  22 (39,544.67)         the noise

**134 tags of noise worth about 79,400 against 631 of signal worth 6.28 crore.**
That looks decisive and it is not mine to decide: it changes what a screen shows,
the threshold was chosen on evidence, and a jeweller may have reasons for pure
gold and silver that this reading does not see.

### What was done instead

Four tests, and one of them pins the exclusion:

	TestSuspectRates_TheQuarterFilterExcludesSomeRealOnes

It seeds a round-hundred tag at 40% of today's rate and asserts it does NOT
appear. If somebody changes the fraction the test fails and says why -- so the
change becomes a decision instead of a side effect.

Ten of the fifteen remain.

## 382. The stock journal is tested, including the label it must not print

Sixth from defect 377's list. `StockJournal` is the metal side of a conversion --
859 documents, 1,242 pieces -- and its companion `ConversionStones` got tests in
defect 377 while this one had none.

Four written. Two of the breaks are worth keeping.

**The summary must cover the selection, not the page.** The list stops at 500
rows and the summary counts separately, which is the guard defect 145 earned
after a screen presented a partial page as a total:

	x  the summary counts "2 piece(s)", want 3 piece(s)
	x  the summary says 0.00 and the lines say 1,14,500.00

**And the direction flag must stay a flag.** The screen shows 0 or 1 exactly as
the shop recorded it, because the capture does not settle which means stock in --
defect 323 is still on the decision list asking, and every measurement points one
way while the whole case for the other is an absence. Labelling it would answer
the question by assertion:

	x  the flags shown are map[in:true out:true], want both 0 and 1
	x  the flag reads "out" -- defect 323 has not been answered and this screen
	   must not answer it by labelling

**That is a test against a plausible improvement.** "in" and "out" read better
than "0" and "1", and somebody tidying this screen in a year would have every
reason to make that change. The test is there to tell them what it costs.

The other two cover a negative piece being flagged rather than hidden -- the
shop's own books carry two, the same silver bangle -- and the direction filter
