Nine of the fifteen remain.

## 383. The screen that warns against adding gold to silver was adding gold to silver

Seventh from defect 377's list, and the second of the fifteen to turn up a fault
rather than just a gap.

`RawStockTally` carries this comment, above the code that classifies each purity:

	// Gold and silver are kept apart. Adding them gives a number that is
	// neither, which is the mistake this record made four times before defect
	// 78 was corrected -- so the tally never prints a combined weight.

Thirty lines below it, the total row:

	"net": fmt.Sprintf("%.3f", goldWt+silverWt+otherWt),

**On the shop's own books that read 27,326.609** -- gold plus silver plus a
silver article -- in the Net wt column, one column to the left of a note
explaining that such a number is neither.

	before   10 line(s) | | | | 27,326.609 | Gold 12304.524 g, silver 15022.085 g. Kept apart...
	after    10 line(s) | | | |            | Gold 12304.524 g, silver 15022.085 g. Kept apart...

The eye goes to the figure in the column, not to the prose beside it. A reader
taking one number off this screen was taking the wrong one, and the screen was
telling them so in the next cell.

### Fixed and pinned

The total row now carries no weight at all. The split stays in the note, where it
is true, and anything that is neither gold nor silver is named there too --
conditionally, because a standing "other 0.000 g" would invent a third metal for
symmetry.

Three tests, and the break is the change somebody would make to tidy this:

	x  the total row carries a net weight of 350.000 -- gold and silver added
	   together is the number defect 78 corrected four times

### The same shape, a fourth time

	defect 372   a rule whose NAME promised more than it checked
	defect 371   a caveat that sized its own coverage wrongly
	defect 358   a comment describing four screens, right about two
	defect 383   a comment saying "never prints a combined weight", printing one

**Prose and code drift, and the prose is what gets believed.** Every one of these
was found by reading the two against each other rather than by anything failing.

## 384. Two live comments still said 39 bills have no line detail, four months after the last one was recovered

Defect 383 found a comment contradicting the code beneath it. That is four of
these now, all stumbled on, so this time the class was swept: code comments that
state a checkable figure, checked.

Most hold. `2,401 of the shop's 2,816 tags came in as opening stock` is exact
(`created_from = 'stk'`). `2,816 captured tags carry R001` is exact. **One did
not, in three places:**

	invoice.go            "39 of the shop's 224 bills carry no line detail at all,
	                       and for those this is the only place the tax exists"
	invoice_e2e_test.go   the same claim, opening the test
	hsn_e2e_test.go       "39 of the shop's 224 are like that in the capture itself"

**There are none.** 0 of 224, and invariant rule 2 has been asserting it on every
run. The figure came from blocker B21, which read `sales_vou_main` alone; the
loader also reads `sales_vou_detail`, and together they cover all 224. Defect 155
recovered them -- the lines went from 328 to 367.

### The docs had already corrected it

	data-defects.md:  "### B21 said 39 bills have no line detail. There are none"
	gstr.go:          "That was true when written. Defect 155 recovered those 39"

`gstr.go` rewrote its own paragraph to say so and kept the old text as a
correction. Two other files did not hear about it, and one of them is a comment
justifying a real design decision -- taking tax from the voucher -- on a fact
that stopped being true.

**The decision is right and did not need the 39.** Its comment now says so
without them, which makes it stronger: a reason resting on a number that moved is
a reason that expires.

### What the sweep says about the class

	383   a comment saying "never prints a combined weight", printing one
	384   a comment citing 39 bills, of which there are none

Both were true when written. **Neither was wrong in a way any test could catch**,
because a comment cannot fail. The only thing that finds these is reading the
prose against the data on purpose, which is now done twice and worth doing again.

## 385. The rest of the comment claims hold, and the two that looked wrong were my arithmetic

Finishing the sweep defect 384 started. Every code comment stating a checkable
figure, checked against the shop's data:

	2,401 tags came in as opening stock        exact   (created_from = 'stk')
	2,816 captured tags carry R001             exact
	2,797 tags name the document they came on  exact
	  699 tags are certified                   exact
	6,587 NEW-BAR movements, of 9,031          exact
	6,395 of those name a person               exact
	  366 order lines                          exact
	2,68,52,217 estimated across them          exact
	   50,71,370 of old gold bought in         exact
	   39 bills with no line detail            WRONG -- there are none (defect 384)

**Ten of eleven hold to the digit.** One was wrong and is fixed.

### Two of the ten looked wrong first, and were not

	certified tags     I counted certificate_no <> ''            678
	                   the comment says certificate_no <> '' OR
	                   certification_charge > 0                  699

	naming a person    I counted done_by across ALL movements  6,789
	                   the comment says of the NEW-BAR ones    6,395

Both comments state their own definition in the sentence before the number, and
both times I measured something adjacent and got ready to file a defect against
prose that was exactly right.

**That is the seventh measurement error this week** -- after 359's inert break,
365's `sed`, 368's three greps, 377's seed, 379's three seeds, 380's group name.
Every one had the same shape: a number that disagreed, and a check I had not read
closely enough to know what it was counting.

The lesson is not "be careful". It is that **the comment told me how to measure it
and I measured something else** -- so the fix is mechanical: when prose and data
disagree, re-read the prose for its definition before believing the disagreement.

### What the class is worth

Two real findings in eleven claims (383, 384), both invisible to every test,
both true when written. A comment cannot fail, and there is no guard to build
here -- only the habit of reading the two against each other, which has now paid
twice and cost seven false starts.

## 386. The back-dated shelf is tested, and it disagrees with in_stock on purpose

Eighth from defect 377's list. `BackDatedSubgroupStock` answers what was on the
shelf on a chosen day, which is the question anybody reconciling a physical count
a week later actually has. There is no snapshot, so it rolls the shelf back from
two facts:

	created on or before the date
	its LAST sale-or-return movement up to that date was not a sale

Three tests, seeded with four tags that each take one branch:

	KEPT      never sold                     held on 30 June
	SOLD      sold 10 May                    gone by 30 June
	RETURNED  sold 10 May, returned 20 May   held on 30 June
	LATER     created 1 July                 not yet made on 30 June

**The return is the case worth having a test for.** Read the FIRST movement
instead of the last and a piece that came back stays sold:

	x  on 25 May the shelf holds "1", want 2 -- the return brought one back

And dropping the created-date clause puts a piece on a shelf it was not made for
yet:

	x  on 30 June the shelf holds "3", want 2 -- LATER is not made yet

### It disagrees with the tag's own flag, and should

Defect 369 found three pieces whose last movement is a return while the tag still
reads out of stock. **This screen counts them as held and `in_stock` says gone.**
That is not a contradiction to fix: `in_stock` is a fact about now, maintained by
whatever last touched the tag, and this screen is a reconstruction from the trail
for a date in the past. Where they differ, the trail is the thing with dates in
it.

Worth stating because the natural instinct on finding two answers is to make them
agree, and here that would mean throwing away the only record that can be asked
about June.

Seven of the fifteen remain.

## 387. Twenty-nine silver articles the shop owns and no screen showed

Ninth from defect 377's list. `UntaggedItemStock` is the loose metal read by
item rather than by purity — how much GOLD ORNAMENTS is loose, not how much
18kt. Four tests to start, and they hold: one item held at two purities is ONE
row that names both (grouping by purity as well splits it: *shows "1" line(s),
want 2 … gross is "40.000", want 100.000*), a line whose item was never named
gets `(item not on file)` rather than an empty label (*an unnamed item is shown
under an empty label*), and the summary counts items and lines and no weight,
for the same reason the tally's does not.

Then the seed needed the shape of the real table, and the real table had
something in it.

### Nine rows are weighed. The tenth is counted.

The whole untagged holding is ten rows in `barcode_main_rawstone`:

	id 7   item 916 SILVER ARTICLE   purity ARTIC(PCS)   gw 0.000   nw 0.000
	                                 qty 29              nag 29

**Twenty-nine silver articles, counted in pieces, weighing nothing.** `qty` and
`nag` are kept in parallel by the legacy and both read 29 — the second reading
this figure was checked against. `mcj_raw_stock` had no column for either, the
loader took neither, and so on both raw-stock screens that line showed **0.000
g**: a row that looks like something somebody forgot to delete, and is stock the
shop owns.

Built: migration `mcj-1787417000` adds `pieces`, the loader carries
`GREATEST(qty, nag)` with a guard on the 29, and both screens grow a Pieces
column. **Blank, not nought, on the nine weighed rows** — a column of noughts
against nine lines held by weight says "none" where the truth is "not counted
that way", and that falsifies cleanly:

	x  SILVER ORNAMENT is held by weight and shows 0 piece(s)
	x  GOLD ORNAMENTS is held by weight and shows 0 piece(s)

The summary **does** total pieces, and still totals no weight. A piece is a piece
whatever metal it is made of; it is the one column on this screen that can be
added down.

### What this is not

The obvious guess on finding one dropped column is that its neighbours went too.
`rate`, `amount`, `making` and `total` sit right beside `qty` in that table — and
they are **0.00000 on all ten rows**. So defect 78's finding that the untagged
holding carries no rate and no value is a fact about the shop's books, not a
column this migration forgot. Checked before the column was added, because the
two cases want opposite responses and look identical from a distance.

Also corrected: the screen's own comment said *"Ten rows describe the whole of
it"*. Ten lines, five rows — it groups them.

Six of the fifteen remain.

## 388. gofmt rewrites doc comments, and one of them was a SQL predicate

Found while formatting after 387. `gofmt -l` flagged 13 files, and the diff on
one of them was not whitespace:

	- // `certificate_no <> '' OR certification_charge > 0`, and a certified piece is
	+ // `certificate_no <> ” OR certification_charge > 0`, and a certified piece is

**Two single quotes become one closing smart quote.** Go 1.19 taught gofmt to
reformat doc comments, and part of that is the old troff convention: `` `` ``
opens a quotation and `''` closes one. In prose that is a kindness. In an empty
string it is a rewrite from SQL into punctuation — true of the typography and
false of the code, and the reader who copies it out gets a syntax error.

Reproduced minimally to be sure it was gofmt and not something local:

	// F decides it with `certificate_no <> '' OR certification_charge > 0`
	→
	// F decides it with `certificate_no <> ” OR certification_charge > 0`

Exactly **one line** in this repository would have been corrupted, and it is the
certified-piece rule in `daystrade_e2e_test.go` — the same predicate defect 385
corrected one turn earlier, which would have been silently un-corrected by
anybody's editor on save.

Fixed by indenting the predicate. gofmt leaves an indented block in a doc comment
verbatim, so the rule now reads:

	//	certificate_no <> '' OR certification_charge > 0

The explanatory sentence beneath it had to be reworded too: my first draft said
what gofmt does to a bare `''` **by writing one**, and gofmt duly ate it. It now
says "the two single quotes of the empty string" in words.

The tree is now gofmt-clean, and `tools/check_gofmt.sh` keeps it so — check 11.
Not for tidiness: a formatted tree means that rewrite happens under a check
rather than unnoticed in an editor. `tag.go` carries the same predicate in an
ordinary comment inside a function body, which gofmt does not touch — only doc
comments are reformatted.

## 389. The tally's unweighed count was 218. It is 369, and the extra 151 are a different thing

Tenth from defect 377's list. `SubgroupStockTally` is the sheet somebody carries
around the shop with a pen: ordered by where the goods sit, leading with the
count and the weight, because those are the two figures a person can check
against a tray. Five tests, and the three rules that matter all falsify:

	x  MIXED says "counted by the piece, not weighed", want it to count the one unweighed tag
	x  WEIGHED holds "3" tag(s), want 2 -- TAL-WSOLD is sold
	x  the ungrouped tag is not on the sheet at all

### A count of zero and a weight of zero are different facts

The screen's own comment said *"218 imitation pieces carry no weight at all"*.
The real figure is **369 of the 2,575 tags**, and `gross_weight = 0` picks out
the identical 369 — two columns agreeing, which is the second reading:

	IMITATION JEWELLERY      218 of 218    counted by the piece
	SILVER ARTICLE (PCS)     128 of 129    counted by the piece
	22KT JEWELLERY            16 of 606    GOLD RAKHI
	SILVER JEWELLERY           5 of 736    SILVER BANGLE
	CUSTOMER GOODS             2 of 2      the customer's own

The 218 was true and was not the whole of it. The extra 151 divide into two
kinds, and the difference is the whole reason this screen has two different
notes.

### The 21 in weighed subgroups are all priced at exactly 2,000

A gold tag with no weight looks like a weighing somebody skipped. These are not
that. Sixteen GOLD RAKHI at one piece each and five SILVER BANGLE at two, and
**every one of the 21 is 2,000.00 exactly** — min and max both — so they are
goods sold at a flat price sitting in a subgroup that is otherwise weighed.

Worth stating plainly because the screen already handles it correctly: a subgroup
where NOTHING is weighed is described (*"counted by the piece, not weighed"*),
and a subgroup where SOME of it is has them counted (*"16 of these carry no
weight"*). Collapsing the two into one message is the break that fails above.

What a zero weight does cost: those 21 cannot be re-priced when the metal rate
moves, because there is no weight to multiply. That is correct for a flat-priced
rakhi and would be wrong for anything else, so it is worth knowing that the set
is exactly 21 and exactly two descriptions.

### One dead branch, and why it is not dead code

`'(no subgroup on the item)'` cannot be reached through an ungrouped item:
`mcj_items.group_id` is NOT NULL, so every item has a group. The only route is a
tag whose `item_id` is null — **and the shop has eight of those**, all out of
stock, so the row never appears today and appears the moment one of them comes
back. Seeded and tested at defect 390, which is what those eight turned out to
be.

Five of the fifteen remain.

## 390. Eight barcodes carried forward twice with nothing in them

Found through 389's dead branch. Eight tags have no `item_id` at all:

	19684380/SR    30223979/SR    30683902    45174064
	55380544       65910625/SR/SR/SR/SR       67141215    69375796

No item, no description, no purity, no weight, no value, `is_opening` true and
`in_stock` false. Each carries a `legacy_id` and **exactly two movements**, and
the two are the same on all eight:

	OP-STK  2024-04-01  0.000  from barcode_wise_all_transaction
	OP-STK  2025-04-01  0.000  from retail_all_stock

Two successive financial-year openings, from two different legacy tables, each
rolling an empty barcode forward.

**Not a migration loss.** The legacy row is empty too — checked before writing
any of the above, because a dropped column and an empty column look identical
from a distance and want opposite responses (defect 387, one entry earlier):

	tran_type Opening   item_id 0   qty 0   nw 0.000000   gw 0.000000
	rate 0.00000        purity ''   ac_yr 2025-2026       status N

`item_id 0` is why they arrive here as null. So the shop's own opening-stock
table carries these eight as barcodes with no payload, and has done for two
years running.

`65910625/SR/SR/SR/SR` is the one to look at: the legacy appends `/SR` to a
barcode each time the piece comes back, so that one was returned **four times**
before ending as an empty shell. Two of the other seven carry a single `/SR`.

### What it costs, and what it does not

Nothing on the shelf: all eight are out of stock and worth 0.00, so the
₹14,23,61,188.20 and the 2,575 are untouched. What they do sit inside is the
counts — 8 of the 2,816 tags ever created, and **16 of the 9,031 movements** are
openings of nothing. Any tally of movements by year picks up sixteen rows that
describe no goods.

Left in place, not cleaned. They are what the shop's books say, and a barcode
that was returned four times is a history somebody may want to ask about.

## 391. The packet stock summary counted stones that had left the shop

Eleventh from defect 377's list, and the first of these to be wrong rather than
merely untested.

A packet is one envelope of loose diamonds of a grade, drawn on as pieces are
made. `PacketStockSummary` says how much of each is in the building. Its title
says Stock, its doc comment said *"drawn on by anything on the shelf"*, and its
own empty-state line says *"No packet is drawn on by anything in stock."*

**The query never mentioned `in_stock`.** It joined packets to stones and
totalled the lot, so a diamond set into a ring sold last year still counted as
stock in the packet it came from.

	                stones   tags   stone value
	as it read        107     104   13,80,534.60
	on the shelf       85      82   11,91,170.00
	difference         22      22    1,89,364.60

Every one of the 22 is on a tag that exists and has been sold — no orphans, so
this is a filter that was never written rather than data that does not join.

### One packet carries almost all of it

	DMIX     96 stones drawn   76 held   6,15,580.00 → 4,28,290.00
	DRF1      1 stone          0 held      1,720.00 → nothing
	IPRD1     1 stone          0 held        354.60 → nothing

DMIX is the shop's working mixed packet and 20 of its stones have gone out set
into pieces. The other two are emptied entirely: the screen reported ten packets
"in use" when eight hold anything.

### Fixed, and the emptied packets keep their rows

The stone columns now count what is on the shelf. **A packet whose whole draw has
been sold keeps its row**, saying `all 1 sold`, because "which packets does this
shop draw on" and "what is left in them" are both real questions and dropping the
row answers the first one wrong. Partly-drawn packets say `20 more sold`, so the
gap between 96 and 76 is on the row rather than left for somebody to find.

Five tests, and both halves falsify:

	x  PKT-PART holds "3" stone(s), want 2 -- the third went out on a sold piece
	x  PKT-PART is worth 80000.00, want 40000.00
	x  PKT-GONE has vanished from the summary along with its stones

The summary now separates the two: totals for the shelf, and a line saying how
many stones went out and how many packets have nothing left. The 195 packets
nobody has drawn on stay off the screen, which was already right — a packet
master is a catalogue of grades the shop buys, and listing them would bury the
ten that matter.

Four of the fifteen remain.

## 392. "The edge of what was captured" was a guess the screen could not make

Twelfth from defect 377's list. `Quarterly` is trading by quarter read from the
vouchers, and it already refuses to call its bottom line a profit, because
closing stock sits outside the ledgers entirely (blocker B19).

Its per-row note did not have that discipline. Any quarter holding a single
voucher was labelled:

	one voucher only — the edge of what was captured

That is true of both of the shop's:

	2026 Q1      1 voucher    the 1,399.00 journal of 9 March
	2026 Q2   1,196
	2026 Q3     650
	2026 Q4      1 voucher    the post-dated cheque of 5 December

Both are first and last. So the sentence has never yet been wrong — and it is
not something the row can know. **A single-voucher quarter in the MIDDLE of the
range is a quiet quarter**, which is a fact about the shop's trade, and calling
it an edge of the capture explains away the very thing a reader should stop at.
The same blind spot as defect 381: a claim that happens to hold on today's data
and is stated as though it were derived from it.

Now only the first and last rows may say it. The middle says `one voucher only`
and leaves the reader to ask why. On today's data the screen reads exactly as
before; the change is what it will say the first time a quiet quarter appears.

	x  2026 Q3 says "one voucher only — the edge of what was captured"
	   -- it holds one voucher and it is not an edge

### Two rules that were already right, now held down

**A voucher is counted once however many lines it has.** The join to lines and
ledgers multiplies rows, so a count without DISTINCT counts postings and calls
them vouchers. Seeded a four-line voucher to prove it:

	x  2026 Q2 holds "6" voucher(s), want 2

**Income and expense take opposite natural sides** — income is credit less
debit, expense is debit less credit — so both read positive and the gap is one
subtraction. Taking expense on the income side does not merely flip a sign:

	x  2026 Q2 expense is -4000.00, want 4000.00
	x  2026 Q2 gap is 14000.00, want 6000.00

A 6,000 gap reported as 14,000. The error inflates the result, which is the
direction nobody queries.

Also seeded: a voucher touching neither income nor expense, which is the shop's
December cheque. It still counts, because counting it is how a reader learns
December has anything in it at all.

Three of the fifteen remain.

## 393. The item catalogue holds, and the one HSN worth watching is a watch

Thirteenth from defect 377's list, and the first in a while with nothing wrong
in it. Six tests, three falsifications, no fault.

Its headline claim checks out exactly: **221 of the 322 items have no stock at
all**, 101 do, and the stock those 101 carry sums to ₹14,23,61,188.20 — the
shelf baseline, arrived at from the item side rather than the tag side, which
makes it a second reading of a figure this project has quoted often.

The rules that hold:

- **A dormant row shows nothing, not a nought.** 221 noughts in a column of 322
  rows hide the 101 that are not. Printing them: *NEVER shows 0 in the tag
  column, want it left empty*.
- **A sold tag does not make an item look stocked** — defect 391's trap, one
  screen over, and this screen has the `in_stock` filter 391 was missing.
  Removing it: *SOLDOUT shows 1 tag(s) -- its only piece has been sold*, and
  the "only items with none" filter drops from 2 rows to 1.
- **The stocked filter cuts both ways**, because "show me what is dormant" and
  "show me what is working" are the two questions this screen is opened for.

### A filter that cannot quietly drop off

Breaking the group filter did not produce a wrong answer. It produced:

	item catalogue: expected 1 arguments, got 2

The clause and its parameter are appended together, so removing one without the
other is an arity error at the database rather than a full-table listing that
looks like a filter finding everything. Worth naming as a property: the failure
mode of a hand-built WHERE is usually silence, and here it is not.

### Four items carry no HSN, and the legacy says the same four

	ALLOYS       stone   gm    a making input
	Old Gold     raw     gm    metal taken in exchange
	Old Silver   raw     gm    metal taken in exchange
	WATCH        metal   pcs   a thing the shop sells

`legacy.item_master` records exactly 4 blank `hsn_no` against 318 set, so nothing
was dropped in loading. **None of the four has ever been on a bill** — 0 of the
367 sale lines carries an item without an HSN — so nothing is wrong today.

Three of them are inputs and would not normally go out on a sale line. WATCH
would. If one is ever sold, the invoice has no HSN to print, and the GST return
has nothing to group it under.

Not raised as a blocker: one unsold item code is a thing to notice, not a thing
to stop for. Named here so that when a watch is finally billed, the reason the
line looks wrong is already written down.

Two of the fifteen remain.

## 394. Three design numbers name two designs each, and a status flag nobody reads

Fourteenth from defect 377's list. `DesignCatalogue` is what the shop can make:
5,221 designs, their weights, their making charge and their stones. Six tests,
and defect 145's rule is the one they exist for.

### The cap and the summary, held apart

The list stops at 500 rows and the summary does not. Totalling the 500 dearest
and printing it under the column would give a number that answers nothing —
neither the page nor the catalogue. Seeded 504 designs and broke it properly:

	x  the summary counts "500 design(s)", want 504
	x  the summary making is 250000.00, want 252000.00
	x  the summary stone value is 3000.00, want 3800.00 -- DBNG0002 is off the
	   page and its stones are still the shop's

That last line is why the rule matters: the design pushed off the page by the
cap is a cheap one, so capping the summary loses the stones of the designs
**least** likely to be looked at, and the error is invisible from the page.

**My first attempt at that break was inert**, and it is worth writing down.
I added `LIMIT 500` to the summary query — which is `SELECT count(*), SUM(...)`
with no `GROUP BY`, so it returns exactly one row whatever the limit says. The
test passed and for a moment that looked like the test failing to bite. The real
break wraps the cap in a subquery and aggregates over that. Same shape as defect
359: a falsification that changes nothing proves nothing, and reads exactly like
one that proves the code right.

The other two rules bite first time: a design search matches a **family** prefix
(DBNG0103, DBNG0104 — a jeweller asks for the family), and every filter reaches
the summary as well as the list, which is defect 145 wearing a different hat.

### Three design numbers are ambiguous

	GBLI0001   1.500 g, making 400.00,   estimate 2,650.00   (legacy 395)
	GBLI0001   1.320 g, making 1,050.00, estimate 4,350.00   (legacy 4347)
	GBLI0002   3.250 g, making 585.00,   estimate 5,460.00   (legacy 865)
	GBLI0002   1.620 g, making 729.00,   estimate 4,779.00   (legacy 4462)
	GBLI0003   1.640 g, making 900.00,   estimate 3,360.00   (legacy 1516)
	GBLI0003   1.310 g, making 622.25,   estimate 3,897.25   (legacy 4463)

Not a double load: `design_transaction_main` has exactly **3** duplicated design
numbers of its own, and the six rows carry six distinct legacy ids. It is the
shop's own catalogue.

A design number is how somebody asks for a design. "Make me a GBLI0001" has two
answers, and on the dearest of the three they differ by 64% of the estimate.
Three out of 5,221 is small; the reason to write it down is that the catalogue
screen searches by that number and will show both without comment.

### 5,242 rows saying which designs are which, and nothing reads them

`legacy.design_no_status` is one of the 53 tables never opened, and it covers the
same design set exactly — every design here has a row there and every code there
has a design here, so it is not a stray:

	status 0    5,066 rows
	status 1      176 rows

The 176 are not a random slice. Their average estimate is **₹49,286.68** against
₹28,618.81 for the rest, and **68% of them carry stones** against 48%. Something
selected them.

What the flag means is not in the data — active, discontinued, featured,
photographed, sent to a karigar. **Added to the ask list**, because loading a
column whose meaning is guessed is worse than leaving it: a design shown as
discontinued when the flag meant "featured" is a wrong answer with a
confident face.

(The duplicate rows in that table — DWAT0016 appears five times — all carry the
same status, so they are repeats rather than disagreements.)

One of the fifteen remains.

## 395. Three people worked the books who were never in the user master

The last of defect 377's fifteen. `UserMaster` is who could sign in to the old
system and what each was trusted with — the question anybody setting up real
accounts has to start from.

Four tests. Two bite hard:

	x  POWERFUL is not shown as able to back-date a voucher: "things, things, things, things"
	x  POWERFUL has "1 screen(s) granted", want 2
	x  PLAIN has "no screens granted to this login", want 1
	x  UNGRANTED has "1 screen(s) granted" -- the row keyed '10' is a role, not a login

That second break is the bug this screen was born with, reproduced: grants live
in `mcj_legacy_access` keyed by **login name** in a column called `role_code`,
while the user master's own `role_code` is a number. Joining the two columns that
share a name matches almost nothing and shuffles the rest onto the wrong people —
note that it does not merely undercount, it hands UNGRANTED a screen it never
had.

The shop's 24 logins, as they stand:

	9 can back-date a voucher       6 can change a rate
	4 can edit a barcode            4 can move a due date
	11 of 24 can change something after the fact
	2,755 screen grants, and every login has some

`rps` and `Shibananda` hold **all four**. `rps` is the login defect 354 asks
about; this is what the old system says it could do.

### Two of the nine back-daters are desks, not people

	CASH      90 screen grants, can back-date
	COUNTER   18 screen grants, can back-date

A shared till login that can back-date a voucher means a back-dated voucher
cannot be attributed to anybody. Not a fault in this data — it is how the shop
ran — but it bounds what any audit of back-dating can conclude.

### And three names on the books are in no master at all

	ADMIN      68 vouchers entered, 1,837 movements
	RANAJIT                            438 movements
	AMIT                                39 movements

**2,314 of the 6,789 movements that name a doer — 34% — name somebody the user
master does not have.** (The other 2,242 movements name nobody at all.)

Not a loader filter losing them: `load_users.sh` skips rows with a blank name,
and `legacy.users` holds exactly **24 rows, none blank**. The master really is
24 people, and these three are not among them. ADMIN reads like a system account
the old application knew about without storing; RANAJIT and AMIT read like
people.

So the screen answers "who had which powers" for the 24 it has, and cannot answer
it for a third of the stock movements. Worth knowing before anybody uses this
screen as the basis for real accounts — which is the whole reason it exists.

### B15 is held by the schema, not by care

`mcj_legacy_users` has **no password or security-code column at all**. The
credentials were never loaded, so no query written later can leak one by
accident. There is now a test that fails if they are added back for
completeness — which is exactly how a protection like this gets undone.

**All fifteen of defect 377's untested reports are now tested.** Four of them
turned up real faults: 381, 383, 391, and 392.

## 396. Two of the five tables worth opening turned out to be empty of meaning

With defect 377's fifteen reports done, the next work is the 53 legacy tables no
loader has ever read — 21,436 rows. Five of them looked substantive enough to
open. Two are now closed, and neither should be loaded.

### `item_adjustment` — 922 rows, five of which say anything

Per-item making percentage, making rate per gram, and a gold plus-minus. Exactly
the parameters that would explain a price the pricing formula cannot reproduce,
which is why it was opened first.

	922 rows       460 distinct item ids
	  5 rows carry a making percentage
	  2 carry a rate per gram
	  3 carry a plus-minus

**917 of the 922 rows are entirely zero.** And the five that are not do not
agree with each other:

	1066  GOLD ORNAMENTS   8% making   250.00/g   10 plus-minus
	1066  GOLD ORNAMENTS  15% making        —      —
	1066  GOLD ORNAMENTS   8% making   250.00/g   10 plus-minus

The same item, twice at 8% and once at 15%. Two more rows (items 657 and 735)
name item ids the master does not have — and **150 of the 460 ids in this table
are in no item master at all**, with 67 ids appearing more than once.

Nor is it live: across 367 sale lines, `making = 250` appears **once** and
`making = 15` **once**. Whatever these values were meant to drive, the billing
did not use them.

A table that is 99.5% empty, whose non-empty rows contradict each other, and a
third of whose keys point at nothing, cannot be a source of truth about anything.
**Examined and deliberately not loaded**, on the same footing as `sales_quotes`
and `barcode_detail_rawstone`.

### `voucher_hsn` — 756 rows, every HSN zero

An HSN per voucher would be an independent check on the GST returns: what the
old system actually stamped, against what this one derives from the item. That
was the hope.

	756 rows over 608 vouchers, 1 April to 5 December 2026
	hsn_no: min 0, max 0, non-zero rows 0
	v_typ:  PMNT 592, RCPT 164 — and nothing else

Every row is zero, and the only voucher types present are **payments and
receipts** — the two kinds that move money rather than goods, and so the two
kinds an HSN could never apply to. Not one sale or purchase voucher appears.

So it is a table that was created and then filled by whatever code ran on
payments and receipts, recording a zero each time. The shop's real HSN data is
where it always was: 21 codes on the item master, which is what the returns
already use.

**Examined and deliberately not loaded.**

### What this leaves

Three of the five still stand: `barcode_history` (3,083 rows — per-tag bill and
date), `order_rate_master` (2,520 — the rate agreed per order), and
`design_no_status` (5,242 — the flag defect 394 put on the ask list).

Worth saying plainly: two of the five most promising unread tables held nothing.
That is a real result about how much is left, not a wasted hour — the estimate of
remaining work should come down by their row counts, and the 53 unopened tables
should be assumed emptier than they look until each is opened.

## 397. ₹9,26,698 was sold by barcode against tags that never existed

`barcode_history` was the third of defect 396's five tables to open. It is not
worth loading — and it pointed straight at something that is.

### The table itself adds nothing

3,083 rows, 2,824 barcodes, seven transaction types, 1 April 2024 to 19 August
2026. Every type it has, `mcj_stock_movements` already has more of:

	              history    ours
	NEW-BAR         2,533   6,587
	OP-STK            278   2,048
	SALE-GST          242     324
	CST-ORD            19      44
	SALE-RET            7      17

A partial log of the same events, from a system that already gave us the fuller
one. **Examined and deliberately not loaded**, like `item_adjustment` and
`voucher_hsn` before it.

### What it did do was name ten barcodes we hold no tag for

Ten of its 2,824 barcodes are not in `mcj_stock_items`, and eight of those ten
sit on one bill. Following that thread:

	499 distinct barcodes in mcj_stock_movements have no tag
	  0 of the 499 are in legacy.barcode_main

**The shop's own tag master never had them.** Not a loader gap — `barcode_main`
holds 2,816 rows and all 2,816 were loaded. Every one of the 499 arrives through
`barcode_wise_all_transaction`, the movement log, and 488 of them carry a
NEW-BAR movement: the old system recorded these barcodes being created and its
tag master does not know them.

### Twenty-four of them were sold

	24 sale lines across 14 bills          ₹9,26,698.00

The worst is **GST/2627/00150, 3 July 2026 — ₹7,11,438.00 over nine lines,
eight of them tagless**:

	66357120   GOLD SET           31.900 g  18kt   4,20,793.00
	69879664   DIAMOND LOCKET      2.774 g  18kt      88,922.00
	70729576   GOLD MANG TIKA      4.230 g  18kt      57,444.00
	53147276   GOLD RING           3.180 g  18kt      43,252.00
	19486670   DIAMOND RING        2.368 g  14kt      39,791.00
	30244386B  GOLD MANGAL SUTRA   2.700 g  18kt      36,887.00
	33455507   SILVER SET         50.730 g  SLV       16,500.00
	92255551   DIAMOND NOSEPIN     0.142 g  14kt       7,849.00

**The invoices are not damaged.** All 24 lines carry a description, a net weight,
a purity and an amount — none blank. What is missing is the piece's history:
where it came from, what it cost, when it was made. The bill is right and the
provenance is absent.

Ruled out before writing this: these are not tags under a slightly different
number. None of the 24 matches a tag with a trailing letter stripped
(`30244386B` → `30244386`) or as a prefix. They are absent, not renamed.

For scale, the three states a sale line can be in:

	232 lines   barcode resolves to a tag
	111 lines   no barcode at all — untagged goods sold by weight, expected
	 24 lines   a barcode, and no tag anywhere

**Added to the ask list.** The likeliest innocent explanation is goods bought in
and sold the same day without ever being tagged — which the shop would know and
the data cannot say. The reason to ask rather than assume: if that is what
happened, ₹9.27 lakh of purchases should appear somewhere, and if it is not, then
eight pieces left the shop on one bill with no record of how they arrived.

Three of defect 396's five tables are now closed. `order_rate_master` and
`design_no_status` remain.

## 398. The rate card is loaded now, reversing defect 59's decision — and the code already knew more than I did

`order_rate_master` was the fourth of defect 396's five tables. It is not a
discovery: defects 35 and 59 both read it, and **defect 59 ended with "recorded,
not loaded — the rates belong to a decision the shop has not made."**

That decision is reversed here, and the reason is defect 59's own correction.
Its headline figure moved from ₹42.85 lakh to **₹60,14,200.75** when the card was
opened by hand, because the earlier number had been computed without it. A second
reading that has to be re-derived by hand each time it is wanted is not a second
reading — it is a thing somebody remembers to do.

Loading the card does not act on the rates. Whether to honour them is still
defect 35 and still an ask.

### What it holds

	2,520 rows over exactly the shop's 284 orders
	0 orders unmatched in either direction, 0 rates zero

	22  284    18  284    995 284    14  284    95      284
	SLV 284    SLV999 280 999 268    9   266    ARTIC(WT) 2

Ten rows per order against the order's one line: the whole day's rate card was
frozen, not only the purity that was ordered. `mcj_order_rates` keeps it that
way, keyed by order and purity, because the purities nobody ordered are the
answer when a line is added later.

`DISTINCT ON` in the loader, lowest id first: the legacy repeats a purity for an
order in a few cases, and the rate struck first is the one the customer was told.

### The two readings agree 340 times and differ 21

The order line carries a `metal_rate` of its own. Where the two disagree, one is
wrong — and the Customer Order Book already computes "costs extra to honour" from
the line alone. So the card now appears on the row **only where it differs**,
under `Rate card says`. Silent on the 340 that agree, because a column filled on
every row is a column nobody reads.

Nineteen of the 21 differ by ₹13 to ₹866 a gram — the rate moving between when
the order was struck and when the line was priced.

### The near-miss worth writing down

The other two are the largest by far, and I had them wrong:

	CO/2627/00041   995   line 1,52,000   card 15,548    ratio exactly 10.000
	CO/2526/00402   SLV   line 24,600     card 242.50    ratio about 100

An exact ×10 with no making charge reads as a decimal slip, and that is what I
was about to write. **The comment already sitting in `orders.go` had worked it
out properly**: CO/2627/00041 is a **COIN-10 GM** order, and 1,52,000 is a rate
*per coin* — 15,200 a gram against the day's 15,482, and rate × pieces is exactly
the ₹3,04,000 estimate on the line. Not an error at all. The same comment already
records that the card is per gram for both, and that the unit is not consistent
even among coin orders, and that the shortfall is therefore deliberately not
computed for them.

I found the ratio, read it as a fault, and was saved by prose somebody had
written for exactly that reader. Recorded because the lesson is not "check the
comments" but that **a ratio is not a diagnosis** — ×10 fits a slipped decimal
and a ten-gram coin equally well, and only the unit tells you which.

Four of the five tables are closed. `design_no_status` remains, and it is on the
ask list at defect 394.

## 399. A return you cannot itemise is a return you cannot restock

The returns built at defect 333 are headers. They say **₹20,04,854.00 came back
from MANISH KUMAR SHARMA against GST/2627/00004** and not one word about what
came back. Four legacy tables held the answer and no loader had read any of
them:

	sale_return_main        3 rows   the metal line of each sale return
	sale_return_detail      4 rows   its stones, keyed by main_id
	purchase_return_main    3 rows   the metal line of each purchase return
	purchase_return_detail  2 rows   its stones

One line per return in both directions, and **every line total reconciles to its
header exactly** — 5,45,749.83 / 1,60,219.39 / 1,35,020.30 against the three
debit notes, 20,04,854.00 / 16,505.00 / 41,952.00 against the three credit notes.
That reconciliation is the loader's guard, not a remark: a line that does not sum
to the note it hangs off has found the wrong note.

**Built:** `mcj_credit_note_lines`, its loader, and a *What came back* column on
both return registers. The shop's six returns now read:

	SR/2627/00001  DIAMOND BRACELET  76.264 g 18, 10.630 ct  (70630587 → 70630587R1)
	SR/2627/00002  DIAMOND RING       0.928 g 14,  0.060 ct  (36568032 → 36568032R1)
	SR/2627/00003  GOLD CHAIN         2.790 g 22
	PR/2627/00001  DIAMOND ORNAMENTS 25.709 g 14,  7.150 ct
	PR/2627/00002  GOLD ORNAMENTS    22.481 g 9
	PR/2627/00003  GOLD ORNAMENTS    10.030 g 22

### The re-tag number is written on the stones

`sale_return_main.new_barcode` is blank on all three sale returns. The number the
piece was re-tagged under is on the **stone rows** instead. So the loader takes it
from whichever record carries it — the piece was re-tagged once, and which table
the clerk's cursor was in when he typed it is not a fact about the piece.

### And neither re-tag was ever made

	70630587R1   is a tag: no
	36568032R1   is a tag: no

Not here, and **not in `legacy.barcode_main` either**, so nothing was dropped in
loading. Meanwhile the original barcodes 70630587 and 36568032 both read out of
stock. A ₹20 lakh diamond bracelet came back on 15 April, the shop wrote down the
number it would wear, and no tag was ever created under it.

The convention itself is real and mostly works: `barcode_main` holds **263**
R-suffixed barcodes and all 263 were loaded. These two are where it broke. The
loader prints them every run, because the day one of them resolves is the day
those goods come back on the books.

For scale, of the 499 tagless barcodes defect 397 found, **30 carry an R-style
suffix**, and their conventions do not agree with each other:

	R1   R2   R4   /SR2   BR1   AR1   and 52013986r4R1

That last one has been returned twice under two different spellings of the same
idea.

### Two things that cost time, written down

`sql-migrate` parses `--` inside a **string literal** as the start of a comment,
so `'… never created anywhere -- defect 399.'` in a `COMMENT ON COLUMN` swallowed
the closing quote and the migration failed with *"The last statement must be
ended by a semicolon"*. It fails loudly, which is the good kind of trap.

And the same figure has different column names on the two sides: the metal line's
total is `amount` on a sale return and `value` on a purchase return, and the
stone line's total is `value` on both. Written into the loader rather than
remembered.

## 400. Eighty-three bill numbers mean two different sales, and now the bill says so

Defect 349 read `sale_bill_link` and worked out what defect 66's "second system"
is: the column is literally called `test_bill`, and the test series ran ahead of
the shop's, reaching **GST/2627/00338 while the book reached GST/2627/00224**.
That analysis was correct and it stayed on paper.

The consequence is not documentary. **83 of the shop's 224 bill numbers are
ambiguous** — each is a real bill belonging to one customer *and* the number a
test print carries for a different customer's sale:

	number on paper   our books say       a test print means   whose sale
	GST/2627/00007    ANITA ROY           GST/2627/00004       MANISH KUMAR SHARMA
	GST/2627/00008    SUMAN CHATURVEDI    GST/2627/00005       ASHIM MAJUMDER
	GST/2627/00009    NEETU JAISWAL       GST/2627/00006       SHIREEN AHMED
	GST/2627/00013    PRABHA BHANSALI     GST/2627/00008       SUMAN CHATURVEDI
	GST/2627/00014    PANKAJ GOYEL        GST/2627/00008       SUMAN CHATURVEDI

Thirty-seven percent of the book. A clerk typing a number off a customer's piece
of paper had no way to know which sale he had landed on, and the system said
nothing.

**Built:** `mcj_bill_number_links`, its loader, and a notice on the bill itself:

> This number is shared. A copy printed by the old test system and numbered
> GST/2627/00007 is in fact bill GST/2627/00004, sold to MANISH KUMAR SHARMA.
> Check which system produced the paper in front of you — see defect 66.

It appears on the invoice sheet, not beside it, because the person who needs it
is the one holding the paper. Silent on the other 141.

The loader guards the three figures that matter — 134 links, every mapped bill
one we actually hold, and **83 ambiguous numbers** — so a reload that quietly
changed the exposure would stop rather than print a different number.

### What this does and does not settle

It does not answer defect 66. Whether a test-printed invoice ever left the
counter is still a question only the shop can answer, and it is still on the ask
list.

What it does is remove the way that question hurts somebody who never reads the
ask list. The hazard was one sentence in a defect file; it is now a line on the
document.

Loaded as recorded, duplicates and all: `GST/2627/00207` appears twice against
the same test number and collapses, because a repeat of the same fact is not a
second fact. Three real bills map to two different test numbers each and keep
both rows, because that is two facts and one of them is surprising.

## 401. The shop set reorder levels and nothing has ever shown them

Four more of the unread tables, and one of them pointed at something that was
already loaded and invisible.

### Three closed, with their numbers

	ledger_ref_details                    1,071 rows   2 carry a reference name
	barcode_create_from_purchase_detail      21 rows   all 21 already have stones here
	item_merge                               40 rows   1 of the 40 is still an item

`ledger_ref_details` is `item_adjustment` again: a table with a thousand rows and
two facts in it. `barcode_create_from_purchase_detail` is stone lines for 21
tags, and every one of those tags already carries the same stones in
`mcj_stock_stones` — fully redundant. `item_merge` is a copy of the item master's
own shape for 40 items, **39 of which no longer exist in the master**; it
explains **none** of the 150 orphan item ids `item_adjustment` pointed at, which
was the reason to open it.

All three examined and deliberately not loaded.

### The fourth had a finer number than we hold

`item_wise_tagging` is 158 rows over **34 items** — a reorder level per item AND
CATEGORY, where the item master holds one per item. An item whose master level is
150 has 33 rows here summing to 456. Two different grains of the same idea, and
the finer one belongs to a screen this rebuild does not have.

Not loaded either, but it is what sent me to look at the coarser one.

### And the coarser one was already here, read by nothing

`mcj_items.minimum_quantity` is loaded. **31 items carry a level**, set by
somebody at the shop who decided how many GOLD RINGS a counter should never fall
below. Nothing in the old menu displayed it, and nothing here did either:

	GOLD RING           wants 200   has  38
	DORI                wants 100   has   0
	GOLD TOPS           wants 150   has  57
	GOLD MANGAL SUTRA   wants  25   has   0
	DIAMOND RING        wants 200   has 129

**26 of the 31 are below their level, 7 have nothing at all, and the shelf is 873
pieces short across all of them.** That is not a fault in the data. It is the
data doing its job the first time anybody asked it.

**Built:** a `Reorder Levels` report, under REPORTS › Stock Tally Report. Five
tests, and the two rules that matter falsify:

	x  FULL shows a shortfall of -1 while holding 3 against a level of 2
	x  EMPTY is priced at 0.00 off a shelf that holds nothing

A NOUGHT IN "SHORT BY" IS NOT A MEASUREMENT, and the break shows why the guard is
`short <= 0` and not `short == 0`: an item stocked ABOVE its level reads as minus
one short, which is worse than a nought. A fully stocked row says `stocked` in
words. And an item with nothing on the shelf cannot be priced from the shelf, so
it carries no money figure at all — a nought there would be a claim that filling
it is free.

The money column is the shortfall at the average of the pieces already there, and
the row says so. It is an indication and not a quotation: the pieces still to buy
are not those pieces.

### Two things this cost

A report needs a **navigation entry** as well as a registry entry — registering it
in `reports.go` alone gave `404 Not Found` from the render check. And a screen
with no `LegacyFile` needs `Top`, `Subgroup` and `Item`, because inventing a
plausible `.php` name would read as evidence about the old system.

Then it needed an **i18n key**: `MCJMenu.Item.reorder-levels` missing panicked
every page, not just this one. The same trap as defect 331, which is why the
render check catches it in eleven seconds and a person would not.

## 402. ₹43,88,746 of bank items the reconciliation cannot see, and looks right without

`brs1` is the old system's bank reconciliation working list. Twenty-six rows,
and **every one of them is uncleared** — no clearance date anywhere in the table
— and every one stamped **2025-2026**:

	24 payments    25,16,608.00
	 1 receipt     15,28,530.00
	 1 journal      3,43,608.00
	              ------------
	              43,88,746.00

**Not one of the 26 resolves to a voucher in this database**, and it could not:
`voucher_main` holds 1,840 vouchers for 2026-2027 and **none at all for
2025-2026**. The year those items belong to was never captured.

### Why it belongs on a screen and not only here

The Bank Reconciliation computes *balance as per bank statement* by adding back
the withdrawals it knows are unpresented and subtracting the deposits not yet
credited. That arithmetic is right and it is tested. What it cannot do is add
back items it has never seen — so a reconciliation covering a period these span
comes out **up to ₹43,88,746.00 away from the real statement and looks complete
while doing it**. A screen that is confidently wrong is worse than one that
refuses.

**Built:** `mcj_prior_uncleared`, its loader, and a line beneath the statement:

> This statement cannot see everything. 26 item(s) totalling 43,88,746.00 stood
> uncleared when 2025-2026 closed, and the vouchers behind them are not in this
> capture, so they cannot be ticked off here and are not in the figures above.
> Which bank account each belongs to was not recorded.

**Beneath the table, not inside it.** A line in the statement reads as a figure
that has been accounted for, and this is the opposite of that.

The figure is read from the table on every render rather than written into the
sentence, so it cannot drift away from the data it describes.

### Which bank is not recorded

`brs1` has no ledger column. So the caveat shows against **every** bank account,
including the two small ones, rather than being attributed to UNION BANK OF INDIA
on the grounds that it is the big one. That guess would probably be right and it
would still be a guess printed as a fact.

The loader carries only uncleared rows — there are none of the other kind today,
and the filter is there so a fuller dump does not quietly bring settled items in.
It also warns, without failing, if one of the 26 ever resolves to a voucher here:
that would mean the missing year had arrived, and this table would no longer be
the right answer.

### Three more tables closed while here

	currency_master              108 rows   countries and currency codes
	dept_user                    103 rows   which users are in which departments
	ledger_wise_document_upload  104 rows   scanned KYC images, paths only

The first is a reference list of the world's currencies in a shop that trades in
rupees. The third is 104 file paths under `../ledger_doc/` and the files were not
captured — the same shape as `barcode_image` and blocker B24. `dept_user` is real
and small, and belongs with defect 395's user picture rather than on its own.

## 403. Twelve hundred contacts attached to customers who do not exist, and a default bank ledger that is a customer

A sweep of what is left. Nothing loaded this time, and two of the findings are
worth as much as a table would have been.

### `address_book_sub_name` — 1,247 names, 107 of them attached to anybody

The second name on an account: the spouse who collects the order, the son who
pays for it. 1,247 rows across 1,039 ledger codes, with 399 mobile numbers and
84 email addresses on them.

	rows                                        1,247
	rows whose ledger code is a customer we hold  107
	codes present in legacy.address_book_master    90 of 1,039

**Not a loader gap.** `address_book_master` is clean — 40,519 rows, 40,519
distinct codes, not one blank name — and our copy of it matches row for row. The
107 that resolve here are the same 107 that resolve in the legacy. The other
1,140 rows name a customer number **the shop's own address book does not have**.

Examined and deliberately not loaded, for two reasons and the second matters
more. A contact list where 91% of the entries point at nobody is not a contact
list. And loading 1,140 personal names, 399 mobile numbers and 84 email addresses
that attach to **no account at all** would be adding personal data with no owner
and no purpose to a database blocker **B18** already says is holding more of it
than it should.

The 107 that do resolve are real and readable — KETAN CHOPRA against NIRAJ
KAYATHWAL's account, KALA TULSYAN against ASHOK TULSYAN's. If a second name on an
account is ever wanted, 107 of them are there to load and the rest are not.

One row, holding the ledgers the old system posted to by default:

	sale             1016   SALE       Sales Account       resolves
	purchase         1011   PURCHASE   Purchase Account    resolves
	cash             1422   CASH       Cash in Hand        resolves
	bank             2636   —          —                   NOT A LEDGER
	stock transfer   1438   —          —                   NOT A LEDGER

The first three are worth something on their own: this system hard-codes
`ledgerSale = "1016"`, and here is the shop's own configuration file saying the

constant.

**The other two resolve to nothing** — not here, and not in `legacy.ledger_master`

its default stock-transfer account named nothing at all.

Nothing depends on them here — this rebuild never read that file — but it is worth
knowing that two of the five defaults the old system was configured with were
already broken when the dump was taken.

Exactly the 3% the sale screen defaults to, split the way it splits it. The

Of those, **13 have now been examined and declined** across defects 396, 397, 401,
