## 404. The biller was the last person in the shop who could see what a customer owed

Back to the goal itself: a real day's trade, end to end. Five tests already cover
rate → tag → sell → settle, a piece returned and resold, the year's numbering, a
certified piece, and a sale reaching the GST return. Walking the same path
looking for what is missing turned up something at the counter.

**Choosing a customer on the sale screen showed their name and nothing else.**

	                 accounts   with a balance   owe the shop      in credit
	Customer              485               28   73,96,553.00   21,41,852.00
	Dealer                 76               56 8,80,38,622.00 6,15,02,878.56

Ten customers owe the shop ₹73,96,553.00 between them and eighteen more have
₹21,41,852.00 sitting on account. A biller settling a bill at the counter could
not see either. The figure is in the ledger, three screens away, and nobody
walking a customer to the till goes and looks.

**Built:** the chosen customer's standing, beside the tax basis, where the biller
is already reading facts about this customer rather than about this bill:

	HARSIT ANAND SULTANIA owes 32,30,681.00 on account before this bill.
	DIAMOND MELA JEWELS LTD is in credit by 92,66,009.46 before this bill.

**Silent on a square account**, which is 477 of the 561. A line that appears on
every bill is a line nobody reads, and the break shows exactly what the rule
prevents:

	x  ledger 7003 reads "SQUARE is in credit by 0.00 before this bill.", want ""

Dr and Cr as words rather than a sign, the way the registers do it — a customer
in credit is ordinary here and a minus sign reads as a mistake.

### What sent me there, and what it was not

The path I was actually checking was **order → advance → bill**, because a
jeweller takes money up front. `mcj_customer_orders.advance` exists and is
**zero on all 284 orders** — and zero in `legacy.customer_order` too, so the
loader dropped nothing and the shop never used that column.

It does take advances. **69 vouchers carry "advance" in the narration**:

	PMNT   32   60,91,163.00   mostly against purchases, to suppliers
	RCPT   48   20,65,154.00   received from parties
	JRNL   58    6,01,476.00

They are posted to the parties' ledgers properly, which is why the accounting is
right and the order screen looks empty. **The advance is a ledger fact, not an
order fact** — which is how a jeweller's books actually work, and exactly why the
balance belongs on the bill rather than a link between an order and a receipt.

So the gap was not the missing link I went looking for. It was that the number
which already existed had nowhere to be seen.

## 405. A tag made here was the only kind whose certification could not be read back

`check_unwritten_columns.py` lists fields the shop filled that nothing in this
system writes. Three sit on `mcj_stock_items` and are large:

	certification_type   2,801 of 2,816 filled
	lot_no               2,059
	making_sales         1,825

### `making_sales` is a duplicate, and that is the whole answer

It looked like the missing half of the pricing puzzle — a second making rate,
stock against sales, which would explain prices the formula cannot reproduce.

It is not. Of the 1,825 tags carrying both, **`making_sales` equals `making` on
all 1,825**. Not one differs. Closed.

### `certification_type` is not which certificate — it is how the charge was reached

Two values, and both were measured rather than guessed:

	by_val   2,683 tags   253 with a charge
	per_ct     118 tags   118 with a charge

**`by_val` means the rate IS the charge.** `certification_rate` equals
`certification_charge` on all 253. My first three formulas assumed a percentage —
rate against the tag total, against the stone value, against the goods amount —
and all three matched nothing, which is what sent me to look at the simplest
possibility last.

**`per_ct` is a rate a carat**, and `rate × the tag's stone carats` reproduces the
charge on **111 of 118**.

The seven that do not are all at ₹900 a carat and all charged for **fewer carats
than the tag holds**:

	23664936R1   900.00 × 0.710 = 639.00    charged 270.00
	70630587     900.00 × 10.630 = 9567.00  charged 9252.90
	89558954     900.00 × 1.670 = 1503.00   charged 378.00

Consistent with only some of the stones being certified — the solitaire and not
the melee — which the tag does not record. Stated as consistent-with, not as the
cause: three of the seven carry an R-suffix and were re-tagged after a return
(defect 399), and I cannot separate the two explanations from this data.

### Built

The tag screen takes one figure, a charge — which is exactly what `by_val` means.
It now writes `certification_type = 'by_val'` and `certification_rate` equal to
the charge, the way the shop's own 253 by_val tags are written, and **says
nothing at all when there is no charge**:

	x  an uncertified piece claims certification mode "by_val"
	x  the rate is 0 and the charge 900; on a by_val tag they are the same figure

Both falsify. A tag made here can now be read back the way every other tag can.

`per_ct` is deliberately not offered: the screen has no rate-a-carat field, and
adding one would mean deciding which stones are certified, which is the question
the seven exceptions above are about.

### And the cast, again

`$22` is now written once and read twice more in the same statement. All three
occurrences are cast. A placeholder used more than once with only some casts
fails with *"inconsistent types deduced for parameter $22"* — the same trap as
defects 379 and 389, and the comment in the INSERT now says so where the next
person will be standing.

(`lot_no` is next, and it is not a lot number: 59 distinct values, all of them
category names — SILVER JEWELLERY 557, NORMAL 413, D GENERAL 386, UTENSILS 159.
A grouping label, on 2,059 of 2,816 tags.)

## 406. "D GENERAL" is spelled six ways, and ₹1.97 crore sits under it

The last of the three large unwritten columns from defect 405. `lot_no` is not a
lot number: **2,059 of the shop's 2,816 tags carry one**, and the 58 distinct
values are a merchandise classification —

	by kind      SILVER JEWELLERY 557   UTENSILS 159   SILVER MURTI 20   RAKHI 18
	by making    CASTING 57             MACHINE 15     ANTIQUE 5
	by source    KOLKATA EXCLUSIVE 103  RAJKOT 22      BOMBAY 11
	by grade     D GENERAL 386          DIA GENERAL 23  DIA IMPORTED 7

Nothing in this system writes it, and nothing reads it. That is a gap worth
closing — but not yet, and the reason is the finding.

### Six spellings of one label

Squashing every value to its letters alone, three labels turn out to be written
more than one way:

	DGENERAL   6 spellings   D GENERAL (386), DGENERAL (4), D GEN ERAL (1),
	                         D G E NERAL (1), D GENE RAL (1), d GENERAL (1)
	MACHINE    2 spellings   MACHINE (15), Machine (1)
	RAJKOT     2 spellings   RAJKOT (22), Rajkot (1)

**394 tags in the D GENERAL family, worth ₹1,97,05,407.34 on the shelf**, and
anybody grouping by this field gets six of them. Three of the six carry a space
dropped into the middle of the word, which is a keyboard slip nobody would defend;
`DGENERAL` and `d GENERAL` are the same word differently punctuated.

That much is arithmetic. What is not arithmetic:

	SILVER JEWELLERY (557)  and  SILVER JEWELERY (5)     one L apart
	UTENSILS (159)          and  UTENSIL (4)             singular and plural
	KOLKATA EXCLUSIVE (103) and  KOLKATA (8)             narrower or the same?
	D GENERAL (386)         and  DIA GENERAL (23)        same grade or two?

The first two look like slips and the last two might be real distinctions. **No
normalisation can tell them apart**, and a screen that guessed would merge two
grades of diamond or split one.

### Why nothing was built

The obvious fix is to offer `lot_no` on the tag screen as a list of the values
already in use, so a new tag joins a category instead of inventing a seventh
spelling. That is right, and doing it now would put six D GENERALs in a dropdown
and make them permanent.

**Added to the ask list**: which of these are the same label. With that answer the
list is a dropdown and the shelf can be grouped by it; without it, a tidy screen
would preserve the mess in a nicer typeface.

The three large unwritten columns are now all accounted for: `making_sales` a
duplicate (405), `certification_type` built (405), and `lot_no` waiting on one
answer.

## 407. I rebuilt defect 366's trap twice in one session

The full suite passes — eleven checks, the whole Go suite included. So the
question was what the checks cannot see, and the answer was in the loaders I
had just written.

`mcj_credit_note_lines` (defect 399) and `mcj_order_rates` (defect 398) both hang
off their parents with `ON DELETE CASCADE`. Both parents' loaders DELETE and
reload. **So running `load_credit_notes.sh` on its own emptied every return's
line detail, and running `load_orders.sh` on its own emptied the whole rate
card** — silently, and with the loader printing success.

This is exactly defect 366, which is exactly defect 294:

	294   load_invoices, load_conversions, load_orders had this and were fixed
	366   load_purchase_invoices did not, and cascaded 43 bills' contents away
	407   two tables I added this session, in loaders whose guards predate them

The guard is never wrong when it is written. It goes missing when a **child
arrives after its parent's loader** — nobody edits a working script to protect a
table that does not exist yet. Three times now, and the mechanism has been the
same all three.

**Fixed the way 294 and 366 fixed it: put the rows back, do not report them.** A
note on stderr is lost by any caller that filters output, and the shop is left
with an empty register either way.

Proved rather than reasoned. Running each parent loader alone now prints:

	-- mcj_credit_note_lines was cascaded away; reloading it --
	OK   mcj_credit_note_lines          6 rows

	-- mcj_order_rates was cascaded away; reloading it --
	OK   mcj_order_rates             2520 rows

Both lines appeared on the first run after the guard went in, which is the proof
the hazard was real and not hypothetical: the rows had genuinely been cascaded
away by the parent's DELETE moments earlier.

### The order in load_all.sh was already right

Checked before running anything: all four new loaders sit after their
dependencies — bill links after invoices, return lines after return documents,
rate cards after orders, prior uncleared after nothing. A full reload would have
repaired itself and hidden the bug. **The hazard only shows when a loader is run
on its own**, which is what somebody debugging one table does.

`mcj_bill_number_links` (defect 400) is not exposed: it stores the bill number as
text and holds no foreign key, so nothing cascades it. That was luck rather than
judgement, and it is worth writing down as such — the same table with an
`invoice_id` would have been the third.

## 408. The fourth time is a check, not a fix

Defect 407 was the third appearance of one mechanism. Defect 294 fixed three
loaders, 366 found a fourth, 407 found two more — and all three times the cause
was identical: **a child table arrives after its parent's loader, and nobody
edits a working script to protect a table that does not exist yet.**

A mechanism that has recurred three times will recur a fourth. So it is now
`tools/check_cascade_guards.py`, **check 11**.

### What it asks

It does not read a list anybody maintains. It asks the database which children
exist *today*:

	every FK with ON DELETE CASCADE whose parent is an mcj_ table
	→ which loader runs a bulk DELETE on that parent
	→ does that loader name the child anywhere at all

Thirteen pairs qualify today, and all thirteen pass. A parent nothing deletes is
not a finding — nothing cascades it.

The guard test is deliberately loose: the child's **name appearing anywhere in
the parent's loader**. A loader that mentions the child has had somebody think
about it; one that never names it has not. A stricter test would encode what a
guard looks like, and defect 368 is three greps that each encoded "a check looks
like the checks I write" and proved nothing.

### It catches the thing it was written for

Removing the guard I had added to `load_orders.sh` an hour earlier:

	FAIL: a loader deletes a parent and never names the child it cascades:
	  load_orders.sh: deletes mcj_customer_orders, and mcj_order_rates hangs
	  off it with ON DELETE CASCADE
	  Put the rows back rather than reporting them -- see defects 294, 366 and 407.

Which is the whole point: the next table to hang off a loaded parent will be
caught the first time anybody runs the checks, rather than the first time
somebody re-runs one loader on its own and wonders where a register went.

### What it cannot do

It cannot tell a guard that works from a mention in a comment. A loader that
merely says the child's name in prose passes. That is the cost of the loose
test, and it is the right trade: this check exists to catch the case where
nobody thought about the child at all, which is what happened all three times.

## 409. Two checks not written, and the measurements that said not to

Defect 408 turned a mechanism that had recurred three times into a check. The
obvious next move was to do the same for the other repeat offenders. Two
candidates, and **both were declined on measurement** — which is the point of
measuring first.

### The repeated-placeholder cast

"A placeholder used twice needs `::type` on every occurrence, not just one" has
bitten at defects 379, 389, and again in the tag INSERT this session. Three
times, which is the 408 threshold.

	SQL literals in non-test Go with a placeholder used more than once   59
	of those, at least one occurrence uncast                            47

**Forty-seven of fifty-nine, and the code works.** So "cast every repetition" is
not this codebase's rule and never has been; a check enforcing it would flag
forty-seven correct sites on its first run. The rule that actually holds is
narrower — cast when the same placeholder is deduced in **different** type
contexts, one column `text` and another `int` — and that is not decidable from
the SQL text without knowing the column types it lands in.

Left as a comment where it bites, which is where it already is.

**And that measurement was wrong the first time.** My regex asked for `$1` and
matched the first two characters of `$12`, giving 71 and 59 instead of 59 and 47.
Caught by looking at it again before writing it down, which is the only reason
the smaller pair is in this entry.

### Every loader verifies its own output

Defect 368 established this at 38 of 38 and nothing keeps it true. There are 43
loaders now, four of them mine from today.

The first measurement said **41 of 43**, with `load_masters.sh` verifying
nothing. That would have been a real finding.

It is wrong. `load_masters.sh` verifies **seventeen** tables through a `check()`
helper that compares a count against an expected figure and exits 1 when they
differ. My measurement split each file at `COMMIT;` and looked only at what came
after — and the helper is **defined before the load**, so I threw it away and
then reported its absence.

All 43 verify. No check is needed for a rule that is not decaying, and the two
minutes it took to open the file were the difference between that sentence and a
false accusation against a loader that is more careful than most.

### Three in one session

	394   a falsification that changed nothing, and looked like proof
	398   a ratio read as a diagnosis when it was a per-coin quote
	409   a regex that matched $1 inside $12, and a grep that discarded a helper

Different mistakes, one shape: **the measurement was the broken thing, and a
broken measurement reads exactly like a finding.** Written down together because
the pattern is easier to see in a list than one entry at a time.

## 410. Twenty bills charged IGST on a supply their own record places in the state

`check_empty_columns.py` lists columns that exist and are never filled.
`mcj_sales_invoices.interstate` is one: **null on all 224 bills**. Defect 302
already knew that and handles it — the GST return derives the classification from
the place of supply against the shop's own state, which is the GST rule.

What nobody had checked is whether the derivation agrees with the tax the bill
actually charged.

	                            bills
	agree, inter-state             18
	agree, within the state       186
	derived inter-state, no IGST    0
	CHARGED IGST, PLACE OF
	  SUPPLY IN THE STATE          20

**Twenty. ₹1,56,108.86 of IGST on ₹52,04,145.00 of goods** — 64% of all the IGST
the shop charged in the year.

	GST/2627/00027  LK THAKUR             party Delhi       place of supply West Bengal
	GST/2627/00057  PRIYANKA AGARWAL      party Assam       place of supply West Bengal
	GST/2627/00067  JANKI KUMAR           party Haryana     place of supply West Bengal
	GST/2627/00034  SHISH JEWELS LTD      party Gujarat     place of supply West Bengal

The pattern is plain: the tax follows the **customer's state** and the place of
supply says **West Bengal**, the shop's own. Three of the twenty name no party
state at all and charged IGST anyway.

**Not a loader fault**, checked first: `legacy.sales_vou.place_of_supply` reads
West Bengal on 206 bills and Bihar on 18, and the 18 are exactly the 18 that
agree. The loader carried it faithfully.

### What was built, and what deliberately was not

A counter sale to a Delhi customer who carries the goods away is a West Bengal
supply and takes CGST and SGST; the same goods shipped to Delhi take IGST. Which
happened is not in this data, and **the shop is the only place that knows**.

So the return still files what the place of supply says — that is the rule, and
guessing the other way would be inventing inter-state supplies. But it no longer
does so silently:

	the bill charged IGST; its place of supply is in the state

**Marked, not corrected.** A return that quietly overrides the invoice is a
return nobody can reconcile against the bills, and this is 64% of the year's
IGST.

	x  the row says "", want it to say the bill charged IGST

### Added to the ask list

Because the two answers differ by ₹1,56,108.86 of tax and by which return those
supplies belong in — and because if the IGST was charged in error, twenty
customers were charged the right total under the wrong heads.

### The measurement that was wrong on the way

My first attempt at the money joined invoices to voucher lines and read **80
bills and ₹1,56,108.86 of IGST against a ledger total of ₹53,244.71**. The join
fanned out. Caught by comparing against the ledger figure — the corrected reading
is 20 bills, and the ₹53,244.71 is the year's IGST *net of* ₹1,89,406.41 of
journals and a ₹495.15 return, which reconciles exactly to the ₹2,43,146.27
charged on sales.

Fourth measurement error this session, and the first one caught by a total I
already had rather than by rereading the query.

## 411. Four hundred and fifty mobile numbers and a hundred and ten GSTINs were being read from the wrong columns

Still working `check_empty_columns.py`. `mcj_ledgers.mobile`, `.address` and
`.gstin` are empty on all 785 ledgers, and the first two are selected by the
loader — which is the shape of a column read from the wrong place rather than
one the shop never filled.

	legacy.ledger_master, 785 rows
	  mobile      0 filled     <- what the loader reads
	  mobile1   450 filled     <- where the numbers are
	  address     0 filled     <- genuinely empty; not a fault
	  gst_no    110 filled     <- the loader never asked

**Four hundred and fifty mobile numbers**, lost to a column of the same name
sitting empty beside the one with the data in it. `mobile2` and `mobile3` exist
too and are left alone: one number is what the ledger has room for.

`address` really is empty in the source, so that one is the shop's and not
ours — worth stating, because the three looked identical from the report.

### The GSTIN is the one that stops a return being filed

GSTR-1's B2B section is **keyed on the buyer's GSTIN**. Without it a B2B invoice
cannot be filed at all. The shop has 20 B2B bills, and:

	ledgers behind those 20 bills                3
	of those, carrying a GSTIN in the legacy     3
	carrying one in this system, before today    0

All three had one all along. Every B2B row on that return was unfilable, and
nothing said so, because a blank column reads as a customer who has no GSTIN
rather than as a question never asked.

**Built:** the loader now takes `mobile1` and `gst_no`, and the outward return
grows a **Buyer's GSTIN** column. 450 mobiles and 110 GSTINs are in, and all 20
B2B bills carry their buyer's — three distinct numbers across them.

	x  GST/2627/00001 shows GSTIN "", want the buyer's

The falsification is the interesting one: pointing the lookup at
`mcj_parties.gstin` instead — the obvious other place, and empty on all 40,519
rows — puts the column back to blank and every test but this one still passes.

### A fixture that was less real than the data

The test seed for the outward return never set `ledger_id` on its invoices, so
nothing read off the party could be exercised at all. **Every one of the shop's
224 bills has one.** Fixed in the fixture rather than worked around in the test:
a seed that cannot reach the party is a seed that will hide the next defect of
this kind too.

### The loader could not be run to prove it

`load_ledgers.sh` cannot run on its own — the vouchers reference the ledgers it
deletes, and its own header says to run `load_all.sh`, which empties the
referencing tables first. So the change was verified by running its corrected
SELECT against the legacy (785 rows, 450 mobiles, 110 GSTINs) and then bringing
the database into line with a targeted UPDATE on the same two columns.

Stated plainly because "the loader was changed and the numbers appeared" would
imply the loader had run, and it has not. It will on the next full reload.

## 412. The empty-columns list, walked to the end

`check_empty_columns.py` names 49 columns that exist and are filled in no row.
Defects 410 and 411 came out of the first two. The rest were walked to the end so
nobody has to walk them again, and **every one is faithful to the source**.

	is_cancelled       224 bills      legacy cancel_status = 0 on all 224
	is_returned          3 bills      legacy ret_status = 1 on exactly 3 — and
	                                  this system marks exactly those 3
	discount           224 bills      legacy discount = 0 on all 328 lines
	  and 367 lines
	making_rate      5,221 designs    legacy making_rate = 0 on all 5,221
	metal_rate       5,221 designs    legacy rate = 0 on all 5,221
	coin_rate        2,820 rates      a column the shop never used — defect 271
	                                  and data defect 54 already say so
	address            785 ledgers    legacy address = 0 on all 785

The shop cancelled no bill in the captured year, gave no recorded discount on any
of 328 lines, and never wrote down the rate a design's making was computed at.
Those are facts about the books, not gaps in the migration, and each was checked
against the source table before being called one.

### The one that is a fact worth having

**4,288 designs carry a making amount and 5,022 an estimate, and not one carries
the rate either was computed at.** The same shape as defect 405's `by_val`
certification: a figure with no derivation. Nobody can ask what a design's making
would be at today's rates, because the rate it was struck at was never stored.

Not raised as a defect — the column is empty in the shop's own books and there is
nothing to recover. Recorded because it bounds what the design catalogue can ever
answer, and somebody will eventually ask it to reprice.

### What the sweep is worth

Two real defects out of 49 columns, and 47 confirmations. The confirmations are
the point: `check_empty_columns.py` is a list of *suspicions*, and until each one
is opened it is 49 open questions. It is now two fixed and 47 answered.

The tool's own header says it over-matches — a tick under `read` means the column
name appears in non-test Go, which catches columns of the same name on other
tables. That warning earned its place here: `mcj_sales_targets.pieces` is listed
as read by fifteen files, none of which reads that table.

## 413. A check that says "no screen" and never looks at screens

`check_unwritten_tables.py` ends with a section headed *"read by no screen and no
report"*. It listed three tables. **Two of them were read by screens** — by the
invoice (defect 400) and by the bank reconciliation (defect 402), wired in this
same session.

The wording was right and the search was narrower than the wording:

	read = mentions(table, REPORTS, False)

`REPORTS` is one directory, `presentation/reports`. A table read by a
**controller** — which is what a screen is — was invisible to it.

That matters more than a wrong line of output. This tool's own header warns that
*"a tool that overstates gets believed once and then discounted"*, and it had
started overstating in exactly the way it warns about. Two thirds of that
section was wrong.

**Fixed:** readers are now reports *and* controllers, and the summary line says
"read by a screen or report" because now it means it. The count of tables read
but never written by the app moves 21 → 23: my two joined it, correctly, being
read by a screen and written only by a loader.

### And then one true positive was left

	mcj_financial_years   0 rows, no loader, no reader, no writer, no FK in

Created by migration `mcj-1787321060` to make *"is this date in the open year?"* a
comparison rather than string surgery. That was the right idea and it was
answered a different way: the financial year is a **value object**,
`domain/value_objects/finyear`, with its own tests. The table was superseded
before anything wrote to it.

**Dropped**, with a down migration that puts it back exactly as it was — the
table, both indexes including the partial one that allows a single open year, and
the range constraint. The Down SQL was executed inside a transaction and rolled
back, to prove it is valid rather than to assume it.

Nothing is lost: it has never held a row.

The reason to drop rather than leave it is the same reason the tool's wording
mattered. A check that names one dead table every run teaches the reader to skim
past the line — and the next thing to appear in that section will be real.

## 414. A bill raised here records a different place of supply from every bill on the books

Defect 410 asked the shop which of two readings is right for twenty bills. While
that sits with them, the sale screen has been answering it in code.

	the shop's 224 bills   place_of_supply = West Bengal (206) or Bihar (18)
	                       — the state the supply happened in
	a bill raised here     place_of_supply = the party's state
	                       — Delhi, for a Delhi customer at the counter

One line does it: `VALUES ($1,$2,$3,$4,$5,$6,$7,$7,…)` — `$7` is the party's
state and it fills both `party_state` and `place_of_supply`.

Defect 302's comment states the fact plainly and treats it as background to the
`interstate` fix rather than as a question. Read beside defect 410 it is the
question: **the two conventions cannot both be right**, and which one is depends
on whether those sales were carried away from the counter or shipped — which is
exactly what the shop has been asked.

**Left as it is, deliberately.** Changing it now would answer 410 by writing
code. And the direction is not obvious: if those sales were shipped, this screen
is right and the shop's own records are wrong; if they were carried away, this
screen is wrong and a bill raised today would disagree with the 224 already on
the books rather than match them.

Marked in the code where the next reader will be standing, pointing at 410.

Nothing else changed. The `interstate` flag is recorded explicitly (defect 302),
so a bill raised here classifies its own tax correctly whatever the place of
supply says; what is at stake is the place-of-supply field itself, which is what
GSTR-1 files and what prints on the customer's copy.

### Two more that were checked and are not defects

**`mcj_customer_order_lines.making`** is filled on 122 of 366 lines and the order
screen writes only `making_amount`. `making` is a rate (4,690.000, 4,020.000 —
three decimals, repeated across lines) and `making_amount` is money (25,425.97);
all 122 that have one have both and they are never equal. **I could not derive
one from the other** — not per gram of net weight, not on any of the six rows I
tried — so the unit is unknown and no field was added. Guessing it would be
defect 398's mistake with a form control attached.

**`mcj_sales_invoices.party_mobile`** is on 196 of 224 bills and the sale screen
does not capture it. Now that ledgers carry 450 mobiles (defect 411) the obvious
fix is to take it from the chosen customer — except **not one of the 28 bills
without a mobile has a ledger that has one**. The gap is real for new bills and
there is nothing to backfill.

### And a third quoting trap in one session

	sql-migrate    -- inside a string literal ends the statement       (399)
	bash           backticks inside an unquoted heredoc execute        (399)
	Go             a backtick inside a raw string literal ends it      (414)

Writing `legacy.sales_vou.place_of_supply` in backticks inside a SQL comment
inside a Go raw string closed the string and broke the build. Three containers,
three different characters, one shape: **a comment is not outside the thing it
is written in.**

Defect 293 is the reason that matters. `dept_code` sits on twenty-eight legacy
tables, every sale and order and conversion records the department that raised

that screen: `DepartmentWork`, whose own comment says *"every one of them is

It was going to stop being unusual. The tag screen offers a department picker;
**the sale screen had none**, so the first bill raised here would have arrived on

**Built:** a *Raised by* picker on the sale screen, beside *Sold by*, from

	x  the bill was raised by department "", want 5

worse than a bill the report already knows how to display, and the shop's own
salesperson field is blank on 93 of 224 for the same reason. Both cases tested:
one bill that names CASH, one that names nobody.

The list shows the department's **name**, not its code — the counter sees CASH,
not 5, which is the same choice the salesperson list makes.

The **order screen** has the same gap: `mcj_customer_orders.department` is filled
on all 284 and written by nothing. It is the same shape and the same fix, and the

a separate piece of work rather than half-done here. Named so it is not
rediscovered as a surprise.

## 419. Four fields say whether a sale left the state, and no two of them agree

Defect 410 found two readings disagreeing on twenty bills. Chasing
`mcj_customer_orders.bill_type` — 284 filled, written by nothing — turned up the
invoice's `bill_type`, which is written, and made the count worse.

On the orders it is a false lead: `bill_type` there holds **CO (179) and RP
(105)**, the order kind, which the order screen already takes and writes into the
order number. `CO/2627/00001` says CO. Redundant, not missing.

On the invoices it holds `local` and `central`, and that is a fourth opinion on
defect 410's question:

	bill_type   place of supply   IGST     bills
	local       in state          none      184
	local       in state          CHARGED    19
	local       ANOTHER STATE     CHARGED    18
	central     in state          none        2
	central     in state          CHARGED     1

**Not one bill has all three agreeing that it left the state.** The eighteen the
place of supply calls inter-state are all marked `local`. The three marked
`central` include one whose party state, place of supply and bill type are all
West Bengal — GST/2627/00214, local by every measure the shop recorded except
the one that says otherwise.

A fourth reading exists and matches none of them: **29 bills name an out-of-state
party**, and 128 name no party state at all.

	IGST charged                     38
	place of supply another state    18
	party out of state               29
	bill_type central                 3

### What this changes

Defect 410 asked whether twenty counter sales were carried away or shipped. That
question stands and this does not answer it. What it does is remove the last
temptation to answer it from the data: **there is no field to appeal to.** Each
of the four was filled by somebody at a different moment for a different purpose,
and the shop is the only place that knows which describes the goods leaving.

The GST return files by place of supply, marks the disagreement with the tax
charged (defect 410), and now has nothing further to consult. That is the correct
state for a return whose classification is genuinely open — it files a defensible
answer and says where it is uncertain, rather than picking a fourth field and
sounding confident.

`bill_type` on invoices is written by the sale screen already, from the biller's
interstate choice. **Left alone.** Making it agree with one of the other three
would be answering 410 by writing code, which defect 414 declined to do for the
same reason.

## 420. The loader chain, run end to end

Defect 411 changed `load_ledgers.sh` and could not run it: the vouchers reference
the ledgers it deletes, so it only runs inside `load_all.sh`. That entry says so
plainly and says the change would take effect on the next full reload.

This is that reload. It was safe to do because the database holds **no
application-written rows** — `load_all.sh` checks six tables for rows with no
legacy id before it clears anything, and every one is zero, so the reload rewrote
exactly what was already there.

	exit=0, no FAIL, no ERROR, no REFUSING TO RUN

### Every baseline came back to the rupee

	tags            2,816      in stock      2,575
	shelf           14,23,61,188.20
	vouchers        1,848      movements     9,031
	bills             224      orders          284      order lines   366
	conversions       859      enrolments      239
	ledgers           785      purchases        43

And the six things this session added or changed, all of them now written by a
loader run rather than by hand:

	mcj_order_rates            2,520
	mcj_credit_note_lines          6
	mcj_bill_number_links        134
	mcj_prior_uncleared           26
	ledger mobiles               450   <- defect 411, previously an UPDATE
	ledger GSTINs                110   <- defect 411, previously an UPDATE
	raw stock pieces              29   <- defect 387

**Defect 411's caveat is closed.** The mobiles and GSTINs are there because the
loader put them there, which is what that entry said would have to happen before
the claim was whole.

### What this proves that the checks cannot

`check_all.sh` runs against whatever is in the database. It cannot tell a table
loaded correctly from a table loaded once and since edited, and it has no opinion
on whether the loaders would produce the same thing again. Four loaders were
added this session and two changed; until now the only evidence they composed was
that each ran alone.

Defect 407 is the reason this matters: two of those four hang off parents whose
loaders delete, and the cascade guards were missing. The order in `load_all.sh`
would have hidden it. This run exercises the order, the guards and the arithmetic
together, and the fact that every figure returned unchanged is the result.

Nothing was found. That is worth an entry: a full reload that changes nothing is
the only evidence that a session of loader work changed nothing it should not
have.

## 421. Twenty-six equally-weighted rows is not a list

The goal names `docs/STATUS.md` as the single place that says what is done, what
is left, **and what needs the shop's answer**. The third of those had stopped
working.

	rows in "Waiting on you"        26 open
	longest row                  1,374 characters
	ordering                     the order they were written in

Everything in it is true and none of it is prioritised. A reader looking for what
to do on Monday has to read four thousand words and rank them himself, which is
the work the list exists to save. Four of the twenty-six were added today, and
each addition made it slightly less usable — an ask list that grows without being
ordered eventually costs more attention than it saves.

**Built:** two short tables above the existing one, and the existing one untouched
below.

The first names **three things that cost an hour each and cannot be undone if
skipped** — get the capture off the laptop (B18: the only copy of 40,519 customer
records), rotate the exposed credentials (B15), and check whether one tag photo
still loads (B24: 889 tags worth ₹10,73,39,445.03, **75.4% of the shelf**,
photographed only on hosts the shop does not control).

The second names **the four questions with the most money on them** — the scheme
booking and settlements (₹87,90,900 collected, ₹77,37,300 owed), the twenty IGST
bills (₹1,56,108.86), the untagged pieces sold (₹9,26,698.00), and the basis the
shelf is valued on (₹3,94,01,031.93).

Then one sentence saying the rest is real and none of it is urgent, and that the
table below is in the order things were written rather than the order they matter.

### The ranking is not by money, and that is the point

B18, B15 and B24 carry no rupee figure between them and they are first. The three
sort by **what cannot be recovered**: a failed disk, a live token, a photo host
that stops answering. Everything below sorts by money because the money is
already spent and will still be there next month.

Every figure quoted was checked against a second source before it went in — the
75.4% recomputed from ₹10,73,39,445.03 against the shelf's ₹14,23,61,188.20, the
₹3,94,01,031.93 read back from where defect 346 derived it. A summary that gets a
number wrong is worse than no summary, because a summary is the part people read.

Nothing was deleted. The twenty-six rows are all still there and all still exact.

## 422. Two things the shop did last week, and "What it cannot do" did not mention either

Defect 421 made the ask list usable. The section above it — **What it cannot
do** — turned out to be the one with the real gap: five rows, two of them struck
through as fixed, and neither of the two biggest omissions listed.

### A stock conversion cannot be recorded

	859 conversions, 1,242 pieces
	most recent: 18 August 2026 — the day before the books end

Nothing in this system writes `mcj_stock_conversions` or
`mcj_stock_conversion_pieces`. The shop melts and remakes pieces, did so the day
before the capture ends, and this system can display every one of those 859 and
record none.

The awkward part is how it was counted. The menu has exactly one entry for this:

	"RETAIL","(direct)","Stock Journal","stock_journal.php"

**RETAIL**, not REPORTS — the area where transactions are entered. This rebuild
registered `stock_journal.php` as a read-only report under `ReportRead`, and
`check_todo_screens.py` counts it among the 126 built, correctly by its own
rule: the screen is answered for. But "built" here means the reading half of
something whose place in the menu says it also wrote.

I cannot prove from the capture that `stock_journal.php` was the entry screen —
the file is not in the dump. What is certain is that the shop entered 859
conversions, that no other menu entry is about conversions, and that this system
cannot enter one.

### A scheme instalment cannot be taken

	2,144 instalments, ₹87,90,900
	most recent: 10 August 2026

Defect 233 established this and it is on the ask list, where it has sat since.
It was not in **What it cannot do**, which is the table somebody reads to find
out what this system will not let them do on Monday.

It is not a screen anybody forgot. There is **no scheme, chit or deposit ledger
among the 785**, so a screen that took the money would book it nowhere — which is
the question 233 asks and the shop has not answered.

### Both added, and the honest reading of the count

The two rows are in the table now. Neither changes the 126-of-193 figure and
neither should: that count is against the old menu and the old menu is answered.
What it does not measure is whether a rebuilt screen does everything the original
did, and this is the second time that gap has been the finding — defect 311 was
the first, where "no trace at all" of manufacturing turned out to be too strong.

**A screen counted as built can still be half a screen.** The count is honest
about what it counts and silent about what it does not, and the way to keep it
honest is to say the missing half out loud in the table next to it.

## 423. The menu entry called GST Sale opened a list of sales already made

Defect 422 found a screen counted as built that was the reading half of one that
also wrote. That is a mechanism, so I looked for others: every menu entry in a
**transaction** area that this rebuild serves with a read-only report.

Twenty-seven came back, and **most are false positives**. ACCOUNTS holds
`rpt_cashbk.php`, `rpt_trl_balance.php`, `t_formbalancesheet.php` — reports by
name and by nature, in an area that mixes vouchers with reports. A heuristic that
reads the menu area cannot tell a list screen from an entry screen.

One is not a false positive, and reading the submenu settles it.

	RETAIL > Sales Voucher
	  Sales Approval Voucher    vou_sales_appr.php
	  GST Sale                  sales_voucher_gst.php     <- pointed at /reports/sales-register
	  Credit Sale               sales_voucher.php
	  Export Sale               sales_voucher_export.php
	  Repair Sale               sales_voucher_repair.php
	  Estimate Sale             sales_voucher_estimate.php
	  Exhibition Sale           sales_voucher_exhibition.php
	  Credit Note               vou_sale_return.php
	  Sales Return REGISTER     sales_ret_reg.php

Every sibling is an entry screen. And one item in that list is named **Sales
Return Register** — a shop that takes the trouble to call its register a register
did not mean *GST Sale* to be one.

**A biller following the menu to make a bill arrived at a list of bills already
made.** The screen that actually makes one was registered against
`add_sales_voucher_combined.php` — a real legacy file that **is not in the menu
at all**, placed by hand under an invented item called "Sales Bill".

### Fixed

`sales_voucher_gst.php` now opens the sale screen, under `VoucherRead` rather
than `ReportRead`, and the hand-placed duplicate is gone. The register keeps a
home of its own under REPORTS › Sales Report, because a report nobody can reach
is worse than one in a slightly different place.

The screen count is unchanged at 126 of 193 — the same menu entry is answered,
by a screen that does what its name says. What moved is the count of built
screens that are **not** menu entries: 6 → 5.

### The i18n trap, third time today

	MCJMenu.Item.sales-register  (/mcj/reports/sales-register)

A new menu item with no translation panics **every** page, not just its own.
Defect 401 hit it, defect 415 and 416 avoided it by reusing existing items, and
this one hit it again. It was caught by `TestNavigation_EveryMenuTitleHasATranslation`
before the render check ran — which is the test earning its place: it names the
missing key and the path, so the fix is one line and no debugging.

### What the sweep is worth

One real finding out of twenty-seven candidates. The other twenty-six are the
cost of a heuristic that had to be written to find the one, and they are recorded
rather than hidden: nobody should run this query again expecting a clean list.

## 424. The navigation audited the other way, and a near-miss on the way

Defect 423 swept transaction-area entries served by reports and found one real
defect in twenty-seven candidates. This is the mirror sweep and the leftovers.

### Report-sounding names served by an entry screen: two, both right

	ACCOUNTS  Bank Book Clearance   brs_cler_rpt.php    -> ReconcilePath
	HR        Address Book          address_book.php    -> PartyPath

The first has `_rpt` in its file name and **Clearance** in its title, and the
bank reconciliation is where entries are ticked as cleared — a screen that shows
and acts, correctly served by one that does both. The second is a master list
that is also where a customer is edited. Neither is a defect.

So the mapping is sound in both directions apart from 423.

### The five screens that are not menu entries

	label_print.php                       Print Tag Labels
	day_book.php                          Day Book
	print_sales_vocher_register_gst.php   Print a Tax Invoice
	add_gold_rate_fix.php                 Quote a Price
	set_rate_gold_opening.php             Metal Rates

All five are real legacy files placed by hand because the menu never listed them,
and each carries a comment saying so. The last is the interesting one.

**The old menu had no way to set the day's metal rate.** Seven entries mention
gold or metal and every one is a purity master, a karigar issue or a report; not
one sets a rate. Yet the rate is the first thing a jeweller does each morning —
it is where the day's-trade test starts, and 2,820 rates were recorded.

That is a fact about the old menu, not a gap here: the screen exists and is
reachable. Recorded because "126 of 193 menu screens" invites the reading that
the menu describes the shop's work, and on the single most-used action of the
day it does not.

### The near-miss

I read `coinrate.go` writing to `mcj_coin_rates`, saw `update_item_rate.php`
registered at `ReportsPath + "/coin-rates"`, and had most of an entry written
about a screen that changes rates being served at a report path under a read
permission.

It is two different screens.

	/mcj/coin-rates            coinrate.go, writes, ItemRead + ItemUpdate
	/mcj/reports/coin-rates    the report, reads

Caught by opening the path constant instead of assuming the controller file owned
the path its name resembles. **Fifth measurement error of the session**, and the
first where the mistake was in reading the code rather than the data:

	394  a falsification that changed nothing
	398  a ratio read as a diagnosis
	409  a regex matching $1 inside $12; a grep discarding a helper
	410  a join that fanned out 20 bills into 80
	424  two paths that share a name and are not the same screen

## 425. A table that says it was counted mechanically was not

`docs/screens.md` opens with **"117 of 187 legacy menu items"**. The true figure
is **126 of 193**, and the paragraph directly beneath that number says:

> the count still has to be *taken* rather than edited by hand, which is how this
> table came to say 20 long after it was 117

It has now done it again, and nothing caught it: `status_figures.py --check`
validates STATUS.md and has never read screens.md.

### And STATUS.md's own area table has the same disease

*Remaining, by area* carries the line **"Counted from the menu CSV against the
navigation registry, not by hand."** Two of its twelve rows were wrong:

	                said        the menu says
	MIS REPORTS     6 of 6      7 of 7
	REPORTS         26 of 49    25 of 48

**The two errors cancel.** One screen counted under REPORTS instead of MIS
REPORTS leaves the total at 126 of 193 either way — which is exactly the figure
the check does validate, so it passed every run while the table beneath it was
wrong in two places.

### The deduplication that makes it 193

Counting rows gives 195. `holiday_calender.php` appears twice in the CSV, under
SETUP › Payroll SetUp. `status_figures.py` builds a **set** of links, so its
headline was right; the area table was built by hand and counted the row twice.

That is the whole mechanism: a figure taken mechanically at the top of a file and
by eye a hundred lines further down.

### Fixed, and checked

Both tables corrected, and `status_figures.py --check` now validates:

- every area row in **both** documents against the deduplicated menu count
- screens.md's own headline against the same source as STATUS.md's

	x  docs/STATUS.md: MIS REPORTS says 6 of 6, the menu says 7 of 7
	x  docs/screens.md: headline says 117 of 187, taken as 126 of 193

Both falsify by restoring the exact error that was there this morning.

This is defect 408's lesson in a different room. A figure that has drifted twice
in the same file — the preamble records the first time — does not need a third
correction; it needs the thing that corrects it to be a program.

## 426. The other four documents, swept for the same disease

Defect 425 found two guarded-looking tables that were not guarded. The obvious
next question is whether the four documents nothing checks are carrying the same
kind of stale figure.

	DECISIONS.md        no count claims at all
	pkg-contracts.md    no count claims at all
	pricing-formula.md  three, all correct
	migration-profile.md one stale cross-reference

**One line, and it is a cross-reference rather than a figure:**

	> Superseded in part by data-defects.md, which carries the
	> full 18-defect register

There are 425. Written when there were eighteen, in the present tense, and left.

Fixed by saying what it meant — *"18 entries when this line was written and
several hundred since"* — and by adding what the file had never said out loud:
**this is a dated snapshot, not a live document.** It records the 2026-08-21 dump
as first loaded and its figures are deliberately not maintained. A reader
arriving at "451 tables, 128,176 rows" needs to know that before they compare it
to anything.

That is the better fix. A number corrected today drifts again; a sentence saying
the file is not maintained stays true.

### The near-miss in pricing-formula.md

	`diamond_rate_master` (774 rows, ...)

	legacy.diamond_rate_master   774
	mcj_diamond_rates          1,416

A loader producing nearly twice its source is the shape of a join fanning out —
which I had done to myself sixteen entries earlier at defect 410, so I went
looking for it with some confidence.

There is no fan-out. The loader reads **two** tables:

	diamond_rate_master        774   the retail grid
	dealer_wise_diamond_rate   642   the dealer grid
	                         1,416

and its own guard checks that exact sum, which is why it has never complained.
`mcj_diamond_rates` splits retail 774 / dealer 642 on inspection. The document's
774 describes the retail table it names and is correct.

**Sixth near-miss of the session, and the second in two entries** where the
suspicion came from a real pattern I had recently been burned by. A pattern
learned is a pattern over-applied for a while; the answer is the same either way
— open the loader and read what it selects from.

## 427. Sixteen thousand of input credit against a supplier with no GSTIN anywhere

Defect 411 put the **buyer's** GSTIN on the outward return. The mirror question
is the supplier's, which is what an input credit rests on.

The purchase side is in better shape than the sale side. On the tax
classification it is exactly right, which is worth saying after defects 410 and
419:

	43 purchases
	11 marked interstate, 11 charged IGST
	 0 marked interstate with no IGST
	 0 charging IGST while marked local

`interstate` comes from the shop's own `gst_type = 'gst2'` flag and agrees with
the tax on every bill. The sales-side tangle is a sales-side tangle.

### Where it is not right

	purchases from a supplier with no GSTIN in the ledger   22
	  of those, carrying no tax at all                      19
	  of those, carrying input tax                           3

Nineteen are unregistered-supplier or old-gold purchases with no GST on them, and
a missing GSTIN is the correct state for those. **Three are not.** All three are
the same supplier:

	ANJALI LABTECH LIMITED, ledger 12168

	GDP/2627/00005  18 Apr 2026  1,44,019.00   IGST 4,320.57   B2B
	GDP/2627/00023  22 Jul 2026  3,43,545.00   IGST 10,306.35  B2B
	GDP/2627/00024   5 Aug 2026    57,579.00   IGST 1,727.37   not B2B

**₹16,354.29 of input tax**, all interstate, from a limited company whose GSTIN
is recorded nowhere — not in `mcj_ledgers` and **not in `legacy.ledger_master`
either**, so nothing was dropped in loading. The shop never wrote it down.

An input credit needs the supplier's GSTIN on the invoice. The paper invoices may
well carry it; this system cannot show it, and neither could the old one.

### And the third bill is marked differently from the other two

Same supplier, same interstate basis, same month-to-month trade — and
`GDP/2627/00024` is not flagged B2B while the other two are. That flag is the
shop's own `b2b_purchase`, carried faithfully, so it is the shop's inconsistency
rather than the loader's.

It matters because the inward return sections split on it: two of these bills
appear in the B2B section and the third does not, and they are the same
relationship.

### Not added to the ask list

Deliberately. The ask list was cut back to what is urgent at defect 421, and
₹16,354.29 against a supplier the shop can telephone is a bookkeeping tidy, not a
decision only they can make. It is recorded here, where the accountant preparing
a return will find it, rather than competing with the ₹87 lakh questions above.

## 428. The half that claims money was the poorer of the two

Defect 411 put the buyer's GSTIN on the outward return and stopped there. The
inward return had none — which is the wrong way round, because an outward GSTIN
identifies who was billed and an **inward one is what an input credit rests on**.

**Built:** a *Supplier's GSTIN* column on the inward return, read from the ledger
the purchase's `supplier_code` names, on invoices and debit notes alike. 21 of
the shop's 43 purchases now show one.

	x  none of the 2 inward rows carries the supplier's GSTIN

The falsification is the useful one: looking the supplier up by **name** instead
of code blanks the column and every other test still passes. A join on the wrong
key does not fail — it finds nothing, or worse, finds somebody else, which is
defect 362's mechanism and the reason this one is keyed on the code.

### It makes defect 427 visible instead of merely recorded

Yesterday's entry found ₹16,354.29 of input tax on three bills from ANJALI
LABTECH LIMITED, a supplier whose GSTIN is recorded nowhere. That was a query I
ran and wrote down. It is now a blank cell on the return an accountant is
reading, next to the tax being claimed.

**A finding needs somewhere to appear.** The column had to exist before the gap
in it could be seen by anybody but me.

### The fixture, less real than the data again

`seedInward` set `supplier_name` and no `supplier_code`, so nothing read off the
supplier could be exercised — the same shape as defect 411's outward fixture,
which set no `ledger_id`. **All 43 of the shop's purchases carry a supplier
code.** Fixed in the fixture, with the two suppliers seeded as ledgers, rather
than worked around in the test.

Twice in eighteen entries the test seed has been the thing standing between a
column and its coverage. Both times the seed was simpler than the data it stood
for, and both times that simplicity read as "there is nothing to test here".

## 429. Fifteen lakh of making, written by the screen and asserted by nothing

Defects 411 and 428 were both found because a test fixture was simpler than the
data. Twice is a pattern, so I asked the question mechanically: **which columns
does the shop fill, with more than one value and never a null, that no test in
this repository names?**

Fifty. Most are inert — the gemological detail on `mcj_packets` is twenty of
them, filled with two to seven distinct values across 205 rows, which is a
grader's screen this shop never had (defect 418). `mcj_parties.website` is
another. A column being untested is not by itself a fault.

One is not inert:

	mcj_sales_invoices.making_charge   224 bills, 161 with a figure, 157 distinct
	                                   ₹15,20,734.00 in total

The sale screen writes it. **No test named it.**

### What it is, and why that makes it worse rather than better

It is a memo. `goods_amount` carries the whole value of the goods with making
inside it, and `making_charge` says how much of that was making — the shop's own
convention, measured on all 224 bills when it was implemented. Nothing in this
system reads it back.

A driver that goes wrong shows up on a screen. **A memo that goes wrong shows up
nowhere** — the bill still totals correctly, the ledgers still balance, and the
only symptom is that the answer to "how much of last year was making?" is quietly
false.

### Pinned

	x  the bill's making memo says 0.00 and its lines carry 1000.00

Two assertions, and the second is the one that would have caught the older
mistake this convention replaced: the memo must not **exceed** the goods figure,
because a bill where making is added beside the goods rather than counted inside
them is the error the comment above that INSERT records having made once.

### On the other forty-nine

Not tested, and mostly not worth testing. The list is recorded here rather than
acted on, because the useful thing about it is the shape: **a column the shop
fills on every row, carrying real variety, that no test mentions, is where the
next 411 will be.** `mcj_stock_items.wastage_percent` (14 distinct across 2,816)
and `mcj_stock_items.design_code` (94 distinct) are the two I would look at next.

## 430. Five thousand designs and no way to ask which had ever been made

Following defect 429's own list. `mcj_stock_items.wastage_percent` was the first
name on it and is a dead end — **2,790 of the 2,816 tags carry 0.0000**, and the
sale screen already says out loud that it has no field for the 14 bill lines that
use one and "does not invent" it. Honest and already handled.

The second name is not a dead end.

	tags carrying a design code            109 of 2,816
	  naming a design that exists           70   (69 of them on the shelf,
	                                             worth ₹10,38,715.52)
	  naming nothing                        39
	designs in the catalogue             5,221
	screens or reports joining the two       0

The shop links a finished piece back to the design it was made from. It has done
so 109 times. **Nothing in this system had ever joined those two tables**, so a
catalogue of 5,221 designs could not answer *"have we ever made this one, and is
there one in the case now"* — which is the question somebody flipping through a
design book is actually asking.

**Built:** *Made* and *On the shelf* columns on the Design Catalogue.

	x  DBNG0001 shows "2" made and "2" held, want 2 and 1 -- one was sold
	x  DBNG0002 shows 0 made, and nothing was ever made from it

Blank rather than nought on a design never made, which is **5,152 of the 5,221**.
A column of noughts down five thousand rows would bury the sixty-nine that carry
a number, which is the same rule as defect 401's reorder levels and defect 418's
piece counts.

### The thirty-nine that name nothing

	0                13 tags
	L                 2
	2                 2
	s                 2
	RJ JEWELLERY      1
	Y                 1

Not design codes at all. Thirteen tags carry the literal `0`, several carry a
single letter, and one carries **RJ JEWELLERY** — which is a `lot_no` value
(defect 406), typed into the wrong box.

Left as they are. They are what the shop recorded, they name no design so they
count towards none, and inventing a rule to clean them would be guessing at what
somebody meant to type in 2023.

## 431. Every stock movement records the address it was made from, and nobody can see any of it

Third name on defect 429's list. `mcj_stock_movements.from_address` is not an
address in the postal sense:

	8,561 of 9,031 movements carry one
	34 distinct values, every one an IP address
	24 of the 34 appear ten times or fewer

	122.163.127.22   5,307 movements
	49.37.41.119     1,770      (all of them OP-STK, the year-opening load)
	115.187.57.184     535
	115.187.57.108     483

This system writes it too: the tag screen records the client IP on every new
tag. Nothing anywhere displays it.

### Sales came from seven different machines

	122.163.127.22    278 sales   May 2024 – Aug 2026
	115.187.43.78      25         Aug 2024 – Apr 2026
	203.171.244.119     9         all on 21 July 2026
	152.58.177.69       5         all on 5 August 2024
	122.168.89.218      4         1 April 2026
	122.168.92.11       2         3 April 2026
	122.168.93.47       1         15 April 2026

One address is plainly the counter. The rest are small and clustered on single
days, which is what a mobile connection, a home broadband or a backup line during
an outage all look like.

### What I am not going to say

It is tempting to read this against **defect 66** — whether an invoice printed by
the test system ever left the counter. Nine sales from one address on one day is
the shape of an answer.

It is not one. A different IP is not a different system, single-day clusters are
what stand-in connections look like, and I have no evidence tying any address to
the test numbering. Saying otherwise would be defect 398's mistake — a pattern
read as a diagnosis — with somebody's bookkeeping on the end of it.

### And why no screen was built

The data is here and it is an audit trail the shop already keeps. Surfacing it
would take an afternoon. **It is not built because a screen showing IP addresses
to somebody who does not know which is the counter is a screen that manufactures
suspicion.**

One sentence from the shop — *"122.163.127.22 is the shop, 49.37.41.119 was the
old line"* — turns thirty-four opaque numbers into a usable trail, and until then
the honest thing is to record what is there.

Available on request, and deliberately not on the ask list: defect 421 reserved
that for what is urgent, and this is not.

## 432. Nearly half the shelf was tagged by somebody the user master has never heard of

Fourth name on defect 429's list, and it turns defect 395 from a curiosity into a
number.

`mcj_stock_items.legacy_user_id` is misnamed: it holds a **name**, not an id.
2,808 of the shop's 2,816 tags carry one, across 19 names.

	tags naming who made them              2,808
	  by one of the user master's 24       1,510
	  BY SOMEBODY ELSE                     1,298   — 46%
	names not in the master                   12

	RANAJIT        614      MEHUL           40      Sourav      2
	AKASH          249      RAJNISH SINGH   40      DINESH      1
	ARINDAM        212      sohan           15      PUNAM SHARMA 1
	admin          113      AMIT             8      ANUPAM      3

Defect 395 found three names on the books that the user master does not have —
ADMIN, RANAJIT and AMIT — reading vouchers and movements. **This is the same
question asked of the tags, and it finds twelve**, nine of which 395 never saw.

AKASH, ARINDAM, MEHUL, RAJNISH SINGH, sohan, ANUPAM, Sourav, DINESH and PUNAM
SHARMA between them tagged **556 pieces**, and the system that is meant to say
who could do what in this shop has no record that any of them existed.

### What it does and does not mean

It does **not** mean 1,298 tags are suspect. The likeliest explanation is
ordinary: staff come and go, and a user master captured in August 2026 holds who
had a login **then**, not everyone who ever had one. RANAJIT's 614 tags run
across the whole capture; that is an employee, not an anomaly.

What it means is that **defect 395's screen answers "who had which powers" for 24
people and the shelf was built by at least 31**. Anybody reading that screen as a
complete account of who touched this shop's stock would be wrong by twelve names
and nearly half the tags.

Recorded on the User Master's own entry rather than raised as an alarm, because
the screen is right about what it shows and wrong only about what a reader might
assume it covers.

### The column name

`legacy_user_id` holding `PRIYANKA` is the sort of thing that costs somebody an
hour. Left as it is — renaming a loaded column to match its contents means a
migration, a loader change and a reload for a field nothing reads — but noted
here, which is where the hour would otherwise be spent.

## 433. The rest of that list, closed out

Defect 429 produced fifty columns the shop fills that no test names, and said the
useful thing about it was the shape rather than the list. Four were worth
following: 430 built the design link, 431 found the IP trail, 432 turned defect
395 into a number. These are the rest, and none of them is a defect.

	mcj_items.barcode_short_code    319 distinct over 322 items
	                                and NOT ONE of the shop's 2,816 barcodes
	                                begins with its item's code

A code the item master carries and the barcodes do not use. The shop's barcodes
are plain eight-digit numbers. Whatever the short code was for, generating a
barcode was not it.

	mcj_designs.designed_on         5,221 designs, 12 distinct dates
	                                4,991 of them on 5 July 2016

Not a design date. It is the day the catalogue was loaded into the old system,
with a few hundred added over the following months. Anything reading it as "when
this was designed" would be reading a data-entry date.

	mcj_stock_items.order_sl        four values: 0, 1, 2, 3
	mcj_stock_items.remarks2        three: blank, `2.4"`, `MRP 1250`

A serial within an order, and a second remarks box used twice in 2,816 tags —
once for a size and once for a price, both of which now have fields of their own
(defect 418).

### The whole suite, after ten entries of change

	12 checks, the Go suite included, all green

Defects 423 through 432 changed the navigation registry, two report queries, the
sale screen, the tag screen, the order screen, the locale file, the figures tool
and six test files. This is the second full run of the session; the first was at
defect 420, before any of it.

Nothing broke. Recorded because ten entries of "eleven checks green" from the
quick run is not the same claim: the quick run skips the Go suite, which is where
a navigation change or a report column would break something the render check
cannot see.

### What 429's sweep was actually worth

	50 columns named
	 3 worth building or investigating   (430, 431, 432)
	 4 closed as inert                   (this entry)
	43 never opened, and correctly so    — packet gemology, party contact
	                                       details, and the like

Two of the three finds were real gaps a person would want closed, and the third
turned a 24-name screen into a 31-name question. That is a good return on one
query, and the reason to write the query down rather than the answers: the next
person to add a column will want to run it again.

## 434. The bill can say who to ring, now that the ledgers know

Defect 411 fixed the ledger loader, which had been reading `mobile` — empty on
all 785 rows of the source — instead of `mobile1`, which holds 450. That entry
put the numbers in the database. It did not put them anywhere a person sees.

	bills carrying a mobile              196 of 224
	written by this system                 0
	customer and dealer ledgers with one 424 of 561

The shop records the customer's number on seven bills in eight. A bill raised
here carried none — not because nobody thought of it, but because until
yesterday there was **nothing to copy**: no ledger in this database had a mobile
on it.

**Built:** the bill takes the number from the chosen customer's ledger. Nobody
types it twice, and a repair or an order can be telephoned about from the bill
itself.

	x  the bill carries mobile "", want the customer's 9830012345

**Blank where the ledger has none**, and tested separately. A bill that invented
a number would be worse than one that admits it does not know, and 137 of the 561
ledgers have none.

### A fix that was only available because of an earlier one

Worth naming as a sequence. Defect 411 looked like a loader tidy — one column
read from the wrong name. It was the precondition for this, for the GSTIN on the
outward return, for the supplier's GSTIN on the inward (428), and for defect
427's finding being visible at all.

**None of those were possible while the column was empty**, and the column being
empty read as "the shop never filled this in" rather than "we asked the wrong
question". That is the whole reason `check_empty_columns.py` exists and the
reason its list was worth walking to the end (defect 412).

### The backtick, again

	sale.go:1641:56: syntax error: unexpected name mobile in argument list

Writing `mobile1` in backticks inside a SQL comment inside a Go raw string closed
the string. **Defect 414 recorded this exact trap** — *"a comment is not outside
the thing it is written in"* — and I did it again in the same file eleven entries
later, in a comment explaining the fix that entry made possible.

Recorded rather than quietly repaired. A lesson written down and not learnt is
worth knowing about: the note in 414 was accurate and did not change my hands.

## 435. Three sales the trail records and the bills did not make

`check_invariants.py` carries eleven allowances — known exceptions a rule is
permitted, each tracked so it cannot grow unnoticed. One has read **9 allowed,
unchanged** since defect 314 and nobody had asked which nine.

	tags the trail says were sold and the shelf still counts:  9
	worth ₹99,492.23

Six name bills in the **2025-26** series, a year whose vouchers were never
captured (defect 402). Five of those six are GOLD RAKHI sold on one bill on 23
August 2025 — five of the sixteen flat-priced rakhis defect 389 found. Nothing
here can adjudicate them.

**Three name bills this system holds**, and those can be settled.

	                   the movement says sold on   the bill's lines carry
	53541166  ₹52,445.17   GST/2627/00207          69343561R1
	67675269   ₹9,512.97   GST/2627/00193          45623887 and one untagged
	15551589   ₹1,866.09   GST/2627/00219          one untagged line

Different pieces entirely. And the bills are not short:

	GST/2627/00193   goods 5,643.00 = lines 5,643.00    complete
	GST/2627/00207   goods 95,437.00 = lines 95,437.00  complete
	GST/2627/00219   goods 2,136.00 = lines 2,136.00    complete

Every one balances to the rupee against its own lines — the property defect 429
pinned. **A complete bill that does not carry the piece did not sell the piece.**

So the movement is the wrong record and the shelf is right: **₹63,824.23 is
correctly on the shelf**, and three SALE-GST movements describe sales that never
happened.

### What was done

The allowance stays at nine — the rule is about a disagreement and the
disagreement is real. What changed is that its comment now says **which record is
wrong for three of them, and why**, with the test that settles it: a bill whose
goods equal its lines has nothing missing.

Not "fixed". Deleting three movements to make a check tidier would be editing the
shop's trail to match a conclusion, and the trail is evidence. The shelf figure —
which is what the money rests on — was never wrong.

### Why this took until now

The allowance had been sitting as a number since defect 314. It says a rule is
knowingly broken nine times, which reads as settled. **An allowance is a
suspended question, not an answered one**, and eleven of them are suspended in
that file. This is the first to be reopened.

	defect 436    8 payments against 2025-26 bills               ₹59,581.00

Three separate rules, three separate allowances, one cause. Each was recorded on

	53 of the 57 carry an OP-STK movement

a shop that existed before its stock system did.

Annotated rather than changed. Narrowing the rule to accept OP-STK would make the

## 437. The largest allowance is one table with no column to fill

Two more of the nine suspended allowances, and the biggest of them turns out not
to be a defect at all.

### `a movement's reference is filled in` — 470, and every one from one source

	barcode_wise_all_transaction   8,561 movements   0 without a reference
	retail_all_stock                 470 movements   470 without a reference

The stock trail is merged from two legacy logs. One of them has **no document
column at all**:

	tran_id, date1, item_id, barcode, status, item_type, tran_type,
	qty, purity, nw, gw, rate, active, dept_code, comp_code, ac_yr, rt_code

It is a stock snapshot — status, quantity, purity, weights — not a transaction
log. There is nothing in it to put in a reference, and there never was.

So the largest allowance in the file is not 470 missing values. It is **470 rows
from a table that does not have the field**, and the other 8,561 are complete.

**Left unscoped on purpose.** Restricting the rule to
`barcode_wise_all_transaction` would make the allowance zero and read better, and
it would stop noticing if the retail_all_stock side grew. An exact allowance of
470 catches that; a scoped rule with a clean zero would not. The number is ugly
and it is doing work.

### `clearing a cheque sets both columns` — 31, and the money is fine

	31 payment vouchers marked cleared with no clearing date
	13 May – 5 August 2026, all PMNT, 12 carrying a cheque number

This year, not the missing one, so it is not defect 436's cause. It is a
data-entry habit: the box was ticked and the date was not typed.

**The bank reconciliation is unaffected** — a cleared item is excluded from the
unpresented list whether or not it says when it cleared, so the statement
arithmetic of defect 402 is right either way. What is lost is the date: an item
settled *sometime* cannot be placed in a statement month, which is exactly what
somebody reconciling last month's page needs to do.
