## 439. Two rules for the failure this shop has already had

Defect 438 ended on a question it did not ask: GST/2627/00150 was saved twice and
wrote its stock movements twice. **Did it double anything else?**

	duplicate invoice lines   (same bill, same barcode, same amount)      0
	duplicate voucher lines   (same voucher, same ledger, same figures)   0
	bills whose goods equal the sum of their own lines                224 of 224

No. The double-save reached the stock trail and stopped there. **The money was
never doubled** — not on that bill and not anywhere in the shop's books.

That was a query I ran once. It is now two rules.

	no bill counts a piece twice      0 allowed
	no voucher posts a line twice     0 allowed

	31 of 31 rules hold

### Why they are not redundant

Forcing a real duplicate in — inserting one, running the checks, removing it —
fires **three** rules at once:

	x  every bill's lines add up to its goods
	x  the line detail sees every taxable rupee
	x  no bill counts a piece twice

which looks like the new rule adding nothing. The cases it exists for are the
ones that move no total:

- a doubled line of **zero amount** — some lines are, and they carry a piece
- a doubled **debit and credit pair** in a voucher, which leaves the voucher
  balancing perfectly, every ledger correct, and every total unchanged

Both of those pass every other rule in this file. A bill that re-saves is exactly
the mechanism that would produce them, and this shop has one on record.

### Falsified for real, and put back

The duplicate was inserted into the live table rather than a transaction that
rolls back, because a rule that only fails against a rolled-back row has not been
shown to work. Three rules fired, the row was removed, and the table is back to
its 367 lines with 31 of 31 holding.

Defect 359's lesson applied deliberately: a falsification that changes nothing
proves nothing, and the safest way to prove a check works is to break the thing
it checks and watch it complain.

## 440. A bill that names the wrong customer would balance perfectly

Defect 439 added two rules for failures that move no total. That framing is worth
following: **what else could go wrong in this shop's books without a single
figure changing?**

A bill that names one customer while its voucher charges another.

	bills whose ledger matches their voucher's debtor      224 of 224
	purchases whose supplier matches their voucher's        43 of 43
	rules checking it                                        0

Everything about such a bill is arithmetically perfect. The voucher balances, the
sales register totals, the GST return files, the trial balance ties. The only
thing wrong is **who owes the money** — and no total anywhere would move.

### It matters more since yesterday

Defect 404 put the customer's standing on the sale screen: *"HARSIT ANAND
SULTANIA owes 32,30,681.00 on account before this bill."* That figure is read off
the **ledger**. The name on the bill comes from the **invoice**.

They are the same today on all 224. If they ever came apart, the biller would be
shown one customer's debt beside another customer's name — and would have no way
to tell, because both numbers are individually correct.

**Built:** two rules, 0 allowed, one for each direction of trade.

	a bill names the party its voucher charges
	a purchase names the party its voucher pays

	33 of 33 rules hold

### Falsified against the live table

Pointing GST/2627/00001 at a different customer and running the checks:

	x  a bill names the party its voucher charges
	   1 bill(s) naming a different party from their voucher
	32 of 33 rules hold

Then restored from the voucher itself — the voucher is the record that decides,
which is the whole premise of the rule — and back to 33 of 33.

Live table again rather than a rolled-back transaction, for defect 439's reason:
a check that has only ever failed against a row that was never really there has
not been shown to work.

## 441. Ten thousand rupees a customer is recorded as having paid twice

Two more in defect 440's class — failures that move no total — and one of them is
a real figure with a customer's name behind it.

### `a sold line is the purity the tag says` — 232 of 232, and nothing checked

The bill line carries its own `purity_code` and the tag carries a `purity_id`.
The money comes from the line, so a line reading 22 against an 18kt tag **bills
correctly and describes the wrong metal**. It also feeds the fine-weight figure —
net weight at the purity's fineness — so the customer's copy would state a fine
weight the piece does not contain.

All 232 lines with a resolvable tag agree. Now a rule at 0 allowed, falsified
against the live table and restored from the tag, which is the record that
decides.

### `one instalment number, one payment` — 1, and it is worth ₹10,000

	party 9588
	contracted   10 instalments × 10,000.00 = 1,00,000.00
	recorded     11 payments = 1,10,000.00, across 10 distinct numbers
	the twin     instalment 2, recorded twice on 20 November 2022

**The books say this customer paid a whole instalment more than the scheme is
worth.**

Same day, same amount, same instalment number is the signature of a double entry.
It could also be an eleventh payment misnumbered — a customer who paid ahead.
Only the shop's receipt book for 20 November 2022 can say which.

It matters at maturity. A scheme settled on "paid ₹1,10,000" either pays out on
₹10,000 that never arrived, or short-changes a customer who really did pay it.

Not added to the ask list as its own row — the scheme questions are already there
(defect 233, blocker B23) and ₹10,000 does not outrank the ₹87,90,900 sitting
above it. Recorded in the invariant itself, allowed at one **so that a second one
fails**, which is the part that protects the shop going forward.

### The 34 enrolments with gaps are not a finding

	34 enrolments skip 41 instalment numbers between them, worst 3

A chit customer who misses March and pays in April leaves a hole in the
numbering. That is what a savings scheme looks like, not a defect, and it is the
reason the rule counts repeats rather than gaps.

	35 of 35 rules hold

## 442. The third document type, and a rule for what this system writes next

Defect 440 built the party-agreement rule for sales and purchases. There are
**three** document types that carry both a party and a voucher, and it left the
third out.

	credit notes whose ledger matches their voucher's party   6 of 6

Now covered. A return crediting the wrong customer is the same silent failure as
a bill charging one: perfect arithmetic, wrong person.

### A weight rule for 2.7% of the trail, and all of the future

	movements carrying a weight        246 of 9,031
	  NEW-BAR                          185
	  OP-STK                            61
	  sales, orders, returns             0
	movements whose weight differs from their tag's   0

The legacy trail mostly does not record weights, so a rule over it covers almost
nothing today. It is worth having for what comes next: **`tag.go` writes the net
weight on every NEW-BAR movement it creates**, so every piece tagged in this
system from now on lands in the 2.7% this rule covers.

It guards the path this system uses, measured against the path the legacy left —
and 246 of 246 agreeing to the milligram is what makes it safe to assert at zero.

	37 of 37 rules hold

### Six rules in three entries, and what they have in common

	439  no bill counts a piece twice           the money doubled
	439  no voucher posts a line twice          the money doubled
	440  a bill names the party its voucher charges     the wrong person owes
	440  a purchase names the party its voucher pays    the wrong person is owed
	441  a sold line is the purity the tag says         the wrong metal described
	441  one instalment number, one payment             a customer credited twice
	442  a return names the party its voucher credits   the wrong person refunded
	442  a movement states the tag's weight             the trail contradicts the shelf

Every one is a failure where **each figure is individually correct and the
relationship between them is wrong**. None would be caught by a total, a balance
or a reconciliation, because nothing is out by a rupee.

That is the shape worth looking for, and this session found eight of them by
asking one question repeatedly: *what could be wrong here that no arithmetic
would show?*

### The data is untouched

Both falsifications ran against the live table and both were restored from the
record that decides — the tag for the weight, the voucher for the party. Verified
after: 9,031 movements, 367 sale lines, 224 bills, shelf ₹14,23,61,188.20.

## 443. A barcode is not a piece — it is a number the shop lends out

Chasing defect 442's question along a new axis: **chronology**. Can a piece move
before it exists?

	movements whose tag records a created_date          7,725
	dated BEFORE that date                              3,326   — 43%

Forty-three percent looked like a serious finding for about ten minutes. It is
not one, and what it actually is matters more.

	NEW-BAR   2,114 of 5,488 predate their tag, by 131 days on average
	OP-STK    1,176, by 597 days
	SALE-GST     25, by 493 days

A tag's own *creation* movement dated before the tag was created is a
contradiction on its face. The worst are `46225943C`, `46225943D`, `86883721D`,
`11157159` — and one barcode, `74472468`, carries two NEW-BAR movements thirteen
days apart.

### The shop re-issues barcodes, and the trail remembers every life

	barcodes with more than one NEW-BAR movement    2,062
	  of those, on DIFFERENT days                   2,060
	  same day (the doubling of defect 375)             2
	distinct barcodes in the trail                  3,314
	tags                                            2,816

**Two thirds of the barcodes in the trail have been tagged more than once**, on
different days, over years. A barcode is retired and re-issued; the movement log
is keyed by that number and accumulates every piece that ever wore it.

So `created_date` preceding a movement is not an error — it is the current tag's
date sitting above an older piece's history. The 3,326 are explained, and the
rule I was about to write would have been wrong.

### What it costs, and where

Any report that joins movements to tags by barcode reads one number's whole
history as one piece's. **BackDatedSubgroupStock** (defect 386) does exactly that:
it rolls the shelf back by finding each tag's last sale-or-return movement up to
a chosen date.

	sale or return movements predating their tag's created_date   28
	barcodes involved                                             27
	all of them on tags still in stock                            27

Twenty-seven of 2,575 tags could be put on the wrong side of a past date. That is
the whole exposure, and it is now written into that report's header rather than
left for somebody to discover.

**Not corrected, because it cannot be from this data.** Nothing distinguishes
*"sold in 2024 while a different piece wore this number"* from *"sold in 2024"*.
A report that guessed would be worse than one that says what it cannot see.

### And one clean result

	sale lines whose bill predates the tag's creation   0 of 232

Not one piece was billed before it was tagged. The chronology that would actually
be alarming holds perfectly.

## 444. The same exposure, in the screen most likely to be trusted with it

Defect 443 measured barcode re-use and wrote the limit into one report. The
obvious next question is which others carry it.

	joins the movement trail to a tag by barcode
	  backdatestock.go    annotated at defect 443
	  movements.go        StockHistory — NOT annotated

	joins a document line to a tag by barcode
	  mrpsales.go         sale lines
	  ordertobarcode.go   order lines

### StockHistory is the one that matters

Its own header calls it **"the only multi-year history that survived"** — 1 April
2024 to 19 August 2026, against vouchers covering a single year. It is the screen
somebody opens to trace one barcode through time, which is exactly the thing a
re-issued number cannot support.

It labels each movement with the piece wearing that barcode **now**, through a
lateral join. So:

	movements shown with a description belonging to a later piece   3,326

A 2024 movement carrying a 2026 piece's name, on a screen headed *"what happened
to a tag"*. The report already flags `tag_gone` when no tag holds the barcode at
all — it knows the two can come apart — and had nothing to say when they come
apart the other way.

Now annotated: **this is the history of a NUMBER, and a number can have been worn
by more than one piece.** Nothing can say which piece a past movement belonged
to, because the trail does not record it.

### The two document joins are clean, and measured rather than assumed

	sale lines whose bill predates the tag's creation      0 of 232
	order lines whose tag was created after the order     31 of 55

Zero on sales, which defect 443 established: a piece is billed after it is
tagged, always.

Thirty-one on orders, and **that is the correct answer, not an exposure**. A
customer orders a piece, the shop makes it, the tag is created weeks later and
its barcode written back onto the order line. `ordertobarcode.go` exists to show
exactly that pairing. Twenty-three were made after the due date as well, which is
lateness, not a data fault.

The difference between the two cases is worth stating: a movement's barcode is a
number the trail happened to see, while a document line's barcode was written
down when the piece was in somebody's hand. Only the first can drift.

### Where this leaves the pair

	443   BackDatedSubgroupStock   27 of 2,575 tags could sit on the wrong side of a date
	444   StockHistory             3,326 movements labelled with a later piece

Both stated in the code, neither corrected, because the data does not contain the
answer. Two reports that were quietly confident are now explicitly bounded.

## 445. Barcode re-use is not a fault to fix — and the tag table keeps only the last life

Defects 443 and 444 described what barcode re-use costs two reports and
deliberately did not correct it. That leaves a design question open: **should the
system stop allowing it?**

	barcodes last re-tagged in 2024      9
	                        in 2025  1,029
	                        in 2026  1,022

**About a thousand a year.** This is not legacy residue; it is how the shop
works. A number is retired when its piece is sold and issued again to the next
one. Blocking it would break a daily practice to protect a report.

And the system already draws the line in the right place:

	barcodeInUse: SELECT count(*) FROM mcj_stock_items
	              WHERE btrim(barcode) = btrim($2) AND in_stock

A barcode **on the shelf** cannot be issued again; one whose piece has gone can
be. That is exactly the shop's own rule, and
`TestTag_RefusesABarcodeAlreadyOnTheShelf` already holds it down.

So the answer is no. 443 and 444 chose correctly: describe the consequence,
do not prevent the practice.

### Why the history can never be disambiguated

	tag rows                        2,816
	distinct barcodes among them    2,815   (the one repeat is blocker B8)
	distinct barcodes in the trail  3,314

**The tag table keeps one row per barcode — the current life.** When a number is
re-issued the previous tag's row is not retained beside it; there is one row and
it describes whatever wears that number now.

That is what makes defect 444's 3,326 mislabelled movements permanent rather than
merely unfixed. The trail knows 3,314 numbers and the tag table can describe
2,815 pieces, and the 499 difference (defect 397) plus every retired life are
gone. **There is no record to join to**, so no report could do better however it
was written.

	the one barcode on two tag rows   B8, known and open

### What was measured and not built

No guard, no migration, no screen. Three questions asked and answered:

	is re-use current?              yes, ~1,000 a year
	does the system limit it right? yes, and it is tested
	can the history be recovered?   no, the previous life is not kept

An entry that builds nothing is worth writing when the alternative was building
the wrong thing — and "stop the shop re-using barcodes" would have been exactly
that.

## 446. Four hundred and forty-five entries, two hundred and ninety-nine of them cited

This register is now large enough to be a reference rather than a diary. Sixty
entries were added today and they lean on each other heavily — 443 leads to 444
leads to 445; 439 through 442 are one argument in four parts.

A citation is only worth anything if it lands.

	defect entries on file            445
	distinct numbers cited elsewhere  299
	citations pointing at nothing       0

Checked across every `.go`, `.templ`, `.py`, `.sh` and `.sql` in the tree plus
all four documents. Not one comment, loader or entry sends a reader to a defect
nobody wrote.

`check_blocker_citations.py` has asked this question of blockers since defect
318 — whether live text cites a blocker that has been closed. It has never asked
it of the register, which is twenty times the size.

**Built:** the same question, of defects, in the same tool.

	x  docs/screens.md cites defect <a number nobody wrote>, which is not
	   in the register

(The message is quoted with the number removed on purpose. Writing a real
example of a dangling citation *into* the register makes it a dangling citation:
the check flagged this entry the moment it carried one, which is the honest
limitation — **it cannot tell a quoted example from a real reference.**)

### It caught the comment that introduced it

The check's first run reported **one** dangling citation before I had broken
anything on purpose: the docstring of the function itself, which says *"Defect
446"* — this entry, not yet written.

That is the correct answer. A comment referring forward to an entry that does not
exist yet is exactly the state the check exists to catch, and it caught its own
author within a minute of being written.

### And a bug in the check, caught by falsifying it

The first version appended its findings to the list the blocker half already
uses. That list holds four-part tuples and mine were strings, so the reporting
loop would have crashed — **on the first real finding, and never before it.** It
passed cleanly while there was nothing to report.

	findings += dangling_defect_citations()   # crashes when it finds something

Defect 359's lesson, met again from the other side: a check that has only ever
been run against a clean tree has not been shown to work. This one now has a
list of its own, its own reporting, and a falsification that ran end to end —
insert a bad citation, watch it exit 1, remove it, watch it pass.

## 447. I emptied a document with a one-line idiom, and got it back by luck

While falsifying defect 446's new check I appended a line to `docs/screens.md`,
then removed it with:

	open(p, 'w').write(open(p).read().replace(marker, ''))

**Python opens the left-hand file before it evaluates the argument.** `open(p,
'w')` truncates on open, so `open(p).read()` then read an empty file and wrote it
back. A 1,998-line document, 105 KB, gone in one statement that looks like a
substitution.

It was caught within the minute — not by noticing, but by `status_figures.py`:

	Screens written up in `screens.md`: STATUS.md says 69, taken as 0

The figures check compares STATUS.md against the filesystem, and a document with
no `## Screens N` headings left in it reads as zero written up. **The check that
defect 425 extended to guard against drift caught a deletion instead**, which is
not what it was for and is the second time today a check has earned its keep on a
failure nobody designed it for.

### Correction, made at defect 448: it was not only luck

This IS a git repository — the environment banner says otherwise and it is wrong.
`docs/screens.md` is tracked, and `git checkout` would have recovered it.

It would have recovered the version committed on **22 August**, three days stale:
without defect 425's headline correction, without its area-table fix, without
anything else that has touched the file since. A safety net that returns the
wrong version is better than nothing and is not the same as a backup.

The scratchpad copy was two hours old and correct. That part was still luck.

### Recovered from a backup made for something else

	scratchpad/sc.bak   105,584 bytes, taken at 08:33

I had copied `screens.md` two hours earlier to falsify defect 425 — break the
headline, watch the check fail, restore. That copy was made to prove a check
worked, not to protect the file, and it happened to be the corrected version
rather than a stale one.

Restored and verified identical, 1,998 lines, 41 screen headings, the 126-of-193
headline and the area table intact. `status_figures.py` passes, which is a
stronger statement than "the file is back": it says the file agrees with the menu
CSV and the navigation registry, so it is the right version and not merely a
version.

**The recovery was luck.** Nothing in this session's method would have saved that
file if the falsification at 425 had happened to use a different document.

### What changes

That idiom is never safe and I have used it repeatedly today — every
`python3 - <<'PY'` block that rewrites a file in place has the same shape, and
they only worked because they read into a variable first:

	s = open(p).read()      # read completes
	...
	open(p, 'w').write(s)   # then truncate and write

That is the safe form and it is what the rest of this session used. The one-liner
collapses the two steps and inverts their order.

Written down rather than quietly corrected because the failure mode is invisible:
the statement is shorter, reads naturally, and destroys the file every time.

Defect 448 established there is a git baseline from 22 August. That makes

accounting for every file in it.**

104 tracked files are modified. One of them should not be:

	modules/mcj/presentation/navigation/legacy_menu.csv   196 +, 190 -

That file is the capture of the legacy menu. It is the source of the 193-screen
count, of `check_todo_screens.py`, and of the area tables defect 425 corrected.

changed.

### It is two changes, and neither is a loss

	rows removed since the commit    0
	rows added                       6
	committed file carriage returns  0
	working copy carriage returns  196

**Every line differs because the line endings do.** The working copy is CRLF and
the committed version is LF, so a whole-file diff reports 386 changed lines and
means six.

The six are all REPORTS entries:

	Karigar Repair Report  Issue From User
	Karigar Repair Report  Karigar Issue/Receive Register
	Karigar Repair Report  Shape Wise Issue Receive Repair

### What the audit was worth

One file out of 104 looked wrong, and looking took ten minutes to answer
completely. The answer is reassuring, and the reason to write it down is that the
next person to read this diff will stop at the same line — a 386-line change to
the file that defines what "built 126 of 193" means is exactly where a reader
should stop.

The line-ending difference is left alone. Normalising it would produce a second
whole-file diff on top of the first and make the six real rows harder to find,
not easier.

## 451. The commit defect 448 asks for would have swept in 26 MB of binaries

Defect 450 audited the 104 modified files and concluded nothing in the diff was
unaccounted for. That claim was true and incomplete: **`git add -A` commits the
untracked files too, and there were 270 of them.**

	go     166
	sql     45
	sh      30
	py      11
	other    3

The three are not source.

	reconcile    13,114,658 bytes   Mach-O 64-bit arm64 executable
	seed-admin   13,249,506 bytes   Mach-O 64-bit arm64 executable
	tools/__pycache__/              Python bytecode

**Twenty-six megabytes of compiled binaries**, left in the working directory by
`go build` naming its output after the package. And `.gitignore` was four lines
long:

	.env
	.env.local
	*.log
	/tmp/

Nothing covering build output. So the thirty-second commit at the top of the ask
list would have put two Mach-O executables into the history permanently — a
binary cannot be removed from git without rewriting every commit after it, which
is a far worse afternoon than this was a minute.

**Fixed** by extending `.gitignore`, which commits nothing and prevents the
mistake:

	/seed-admin  /reconcile  /wingold  /wingold-cli  /specgen  /legacy-extract
	__pycache__/  *.pyc

	untracked files: 270 -> 267, and all 267 are source

Named individually rather than by a pattern. A bare `reconcile` in a `.gitignore`
matches a *directory* of that name too, and `reconcile.go`, `reconcile.templ` and
`reconcile_templ.go` all exist already — a pattern that swallowed a future
`reconcile/` package would be a subtler bug than the one being fixed. The leading
slash pins each to the repository root.

Checked afterwards that no tracked file became ignored: `git ls-files -i -c
--exclude-standard` returns nothing.

### The shape of this one

449 audited what changed. 450 audited who changed it. Neither asked what would
happen when the change is *committed*, which is the only step that makes any of
it permanent.

Three entries to audit one commit that has not happened. That is the right ratio
when the commit is three days of work and the alternative to checking is finding
out afterwards.

## 452. A check that was right about the code and wrong about its own reach

`check_failed_saves.py` guards a class that has bitten three times — defects 206,
319 and 320 — where a handler renders the reason for a failed save without
setting a status, `atomic` sees a 2xx, and whatever the save had already written
is committed.

It passes. It has always passed. **It was watching four branches out of thirteen.**

	SAVE = if err := c.(save|apply|record|reserve|cancel|post)…(

Six of those six verbs are guesses about naming; two are used. The controllers
hold seven more calls whose failure leaves a write possibly done:

	writeSaleDetail        sale.go        — edited today, defects 415 and 434
	settle                 sale.go
	writeCreditNote        creditnote.go
	writePurchaseInvoice   creditnote.go
	writeOldGoldLines      oldgold.go
	addRawStock            rawstock.go
	removeRawStock         rawstock.go

**None of them is rendering a failure on a 200.** The check was right about the
code. It was wrong about how much of the code it was looking at, and that is the
worse of the two errors: a passing check reads as coverage.

	branches watched   4 -> 13

### Falsified by breaking one of the newly-covered paths

Making `writeSaleDetail`'s failure branch render without a status:

	renders: templ.Handler(voucherpage.Sale(props)).ServeHTTP
	atomic commits on 2xx, so whatever that save wrote is kept
	1 screen(s) tell the wrapper a failed save succeeded

Before the widening that would have passed silently — the exact shape of defects
206, 319 and 320, on a function I had edited twice today.

Restored, and the tree builds.

### The pattern this belongs to

	408   a rule three times repaired became a check
	413   a check that said "no screen" and never looked at screens
	446   a check that asked its question of blockers and not of the register
	452   a check that watched four of the thirteen places its class can occur

Four checks written to catch a recurring fault, each one narrower than the
sentence describing it. **A check is a claim, and its reach is part of the
claim** — "no screen renders a failed save on a 200" is a different statement
from "no screen whose save is spelled `save` or `apply` does".

The docstring said so honestly: *"what it cannot see: a save spelled some other
way."* Nobody had measured how many other ways there were.

## 453. Auditing my own check, written today, for the fault I had just named

Defect 452 named a class: **a check whose claim is broader than its search.**
Four instances, one of them mine. So I audited the rest of the eleven, and the
first one I looked at was also mine, written this morning at defect 388.

	check_gofmt.sh:  gofmt -l modules/ tools/ pkg/ cmd/
	its message:     "every Go file is gofmt-clean"

Four directories named by hand. Two are not in the list:

	e2e/smoke_test.go       NOT gofmt-clean
	internal/assets/assets.go   clean, and also unwatched

**The check has been passing all day while a Go file in this repository was not
formatted.** Not a serious file and not a serious difference — one import line —
but the check's sentence was false and its output was green, which is the
combination 452 was written about.

### Fixed by searching rather than listing

	DIRTY=$(find . -name '*.go' -not -path './.git/*' -print0 | xargs -0 gofmt -l)

A directory list goes stale the day somebody adds a directory. `find` cannot.

Formatted the one file — checking the diff first, because defect 388's whole
point is that **gofmt rewrites doc comments** and can turn `''` into a smart
quote. The diff was one import line and no quote changes, so it was safe.

	FAIL: gofmt would rewrite these files:
	  ./e2e/smoke_test.go

Falsified afterwards by appending a badly formatted function, which it caught —
in the directory it could not see an hour ago.

### Five now, and the shape is consistent

	408   a rule three times repaired became a check
	413   a check that said "no screen" and never looked at screens
	446   a check that asked its question of blockers, not the register
	452   a check watching four of the thirteen places its class occurs
	453   a check saying "every Go file" while naming four directories

Every one was written carefully by somebody who then described it in a sentence
slightly larger than the code. **The sentence is what the next reader believes.**

Two of the five are mine and both were written today. That is not carelessness
accumulating — it is what happens when a check is written to catch a specific
thing that just happened and then summarised in general terms.

## 454. Two reports that net credit notes were outside the check that guards footers

Continuing defect 453's audit of the eleven checks for reach. Four remained.
Three are clean, and each derives its targets rather than listing them:

	check_screens_render   discovers 39 Path constants; 35 navigation entries
	                       resolve to a path and 0 are missed
	check_empty_columns    `table_name LIKE 'mcj\_%'` over information_schema,
	                       which is all 83 mcj_ tables
	check_todo_screens     states its own covering: 126 built + 67 stood in = 193

The fourth is not.

	check_report_footers   scans for  Key: "..."     found 82
	report specs that exist                          84

	missed: sales-returns, purchase-returns

### Why those two and no others

`ReturnRegisters()` builds both from a struct:

	key: "sales-returns",    title: "Sales Returns"
	key: "purchase-returns", title: "Purchase Returns"
	...
	Key:          k.key,

The literal is spelled with a lower-case `key:` a few lines above the spec, and
the spec's own `Key:` is a variable. A scan for `Key:\s*"` cannot see either.

**They are the two reports where a doubled footer would matter most.** Defects
332 and 334 rebuilt them to net credit notes against sales and debit notes
against purchases — the halves that carry negated figures. A footer that added a
summary row on top of negated rows is precisely defect 143's fault in the place
it would be hardest to notice.

Neither is doubling. The check was right about the code and blind to two of the
places its sentence covers.

**Fixed:** both spellings, 82 -> 84.

### The check that caught me writing this

Adding the comment above made `check_blocker_citations.py` fail:

	docs/... cites defect 454, which is not in the register

Defect 446 built that. It has now caught a forward reference twice — once to the
entry introducing it, and once here, to the entry recording the fix it was
guarding. A check that fires on its own author twice in one session is a check
that works.

### The audit is finished

	eleven checks
	  narrower than their claim, now widened   4   (413, 446, 452, 453, 454 — five fixes across four tools)
	  reach measured and correct               6
	  deliberately loose and documented        1   (cascade guards, defect 408)

Two of the fixes were checks I wrote today. The lesson from 453 stands and is now
measured: **a check written to catch one incident describes itself in general
terms, and the general terms are what everybody afterwards believes.**

## 455. The two reports nobody had ever fetched

Defect 454 fixed a blind spot in `check_report_footers` and I did not think to
ask whether the same pattern appeared anywhere else. The full suite answered it
without being asked:

	39 screen(s) and 82 report(s) render ...

Eighty-two, against the eighty-four specs 454 had just counted.

`check_screens_render.declared_reports()` uses the identical regex:

	re.finditer(r'Key:\s*"([^"]+)"', src)

So `sales-returns` and `purchase-returns` — built from a struct, their spec
reading `Key: k.key` — **have never been fetched by the check that proves a
screen works at all.**

This is worse than 454's version. A footer check that misses two reports fails to
notice one class of arithmetic error. **A render check that misses two reports
would not notice them returning 500 for a year.** Its sentence is *every screen
and every report*, and it had been fetching all but two since it was written.

### They were fine

	39 screen(s) and 84 report(s) render, including over a range that
	matches nothing, and 84 of them show real data

Both render, both over an empty date range, both with real data. Nothing was
broken. **The exposure was that nobody could have known.**

### Two tools, one regex, two entries

	454   check_report_footers    82 of 84   fixed
	455   check_screens_render    82 of 84   fixed

Same pattern copied into two tools, and finding it in the first did not make me
look in the second — the full suite did, by printing a number I could compare
against one I had measured an hour earlier.

That is the argument for a check printing **counts** rather than a verdict. "No
report doubles a total" tells you nothing about how many it looked at; "82
report(s) render" is a number that can disagree with another number. Defect 279
made that change to the footer check for its own reasons, and it is the reason
this was catchable at all.

### The citation check, a third time

	docs/... cites defect 455, which is not in the register

Defect 446's work has now fired on its own author three times in one session,
each time on a comment written to explain a fix. It is the most consistently
useful thing built today.

	tools that derive a list       7

Six fixes across four tools, and two of the four were tools written today. Not

Both true, and side by side they invite a subtraction that means nothing.
