fully paid and matured** — and those 173 paid in **₹71,01,000**, not ₹87,90,900.

	173 matured and fully paid
	  paid in          71,01,000.00
	  maturity value   77,37,300.00
	  the gap           6,36,300.00   the scheme's uplift, and the shop's liability

Reading the original pair as a difference gives "₹10.5 lakh spare", which is not
a quantity that exists. **The row now says which figure belongs to which
population**, and names the ₹6,36,300 as what the uplift actually costs.

### Why this is worth an entry

Defect 421 made the list usable by ranking it. Ranking a figure does not check
it, and the summary was written from the entries rather than from the data.
Every number survived the re-measurement — but the one thing that needed changing
was not a wrong number. **It was two right numbers placed where a reader would
subtract them.**

That is the failure mode of a summary: not error, but adjacency.

## 458. The same trap, one section up: an asset and a liability joined by a comma

457 found two right numbers placed where a reader would subtract them, and said
the failure mode of a summary is not error but adjacency. That is a claim about
a class, so the class was swept rather than left as a moral.

**STATUS.md holds 987 rupee figures on 218 lines that carry two or more.** Two
sweeps over them:

	stated arithmetic ("leaving", "short by", "of which", "explains")
	  single-claim lines            5   all compute
	  multi-clause bullets         33   figures from unrelated sentences

	bare adjacency: two figures, short line, no relation stated
	  lines                         9   8 sound, 1 not

The eight sound ones name their relation in words — *"0.5% apart"*, *"tagged in
2025 and in 2024"*, *"taxable / input tax"*. The ninth did not.

### The line

	What each customer owes, and what the shop is holding for them
	— ₹73,96,553.00 owed in, ₹27,17,486.77 held

Both figures are right. Both were recomputed against the live data through the
report's **own** group list, `['Customer', 'Other Debtor']`:

	 10 accounts owe the shop        73,96,553.00
	 20 accounts the shop owes       27,17,486.77
	461 accounts flat
	491 customer accounts

A comma joins them, and the subtraction it invites gives **₹46,79,066.23** — a
"net customer position" that does not exist. The two sets are **disjoint**: no
account can be on both sides, because a balance is one sign or the other. One
customer's advance cannot settle a different customer's debt. **These are an
asset and a liability**, and netting them across 10 accounts and 20 different
accounts is the netting-off error, not a shortcut.

The row now says which population each figure belongs to, and that they are
opposite sides of the balance sheet.

### The screen was already right

`customerbalances.go` puts `owingTotal` in the balance slot and states the other
in prose — *"the shop is holding ₹27,17,486.77 of customers' money"* — with
separate counters that never meet. **The defect was in the summary of the screen,
not the screen.** A summary compresses, and compression is where populations get
dropped.

### A measurement error inside this entry

The first recomputation returned **18 accounts and ₹21,41,852.00**, and for a
moment that read as the figure being stale. It was not. `group_name LIKE
'%ustomer%' OR '%Sundry Debtor%'` is not the list the report passes; with
`['Customer', 'Other Debtor']` both figures reproduce to the rupee. **Seventh
measurement error recorded** — and the rule that caught it is the one from
defect 409: read the query the screen actually runs before believing a
disagreement with it.

### What is now guarded

`tools/check_stated_arithmetic.py` — **check 12**. Every single-claim line that
asserts a relation between figures must have that relation resolve.

Adjacency itself is **not** mechanically checkable: whether two figures invite a
wrong subtraction is a judgement about populations, and a checker that guessed
would cry wolf on all nine lines to catch the one. The checkable half is guarded;
the rest stays a reading. The limit was measured — at 300 characters five lines
qualify and all five compute, at 400 the first five false positives appear — and
**the check prints the 33 lines it skips**, because a checker that hides its own
blind spot reads as coverage it does not have.

## 459. A correction that never reached the screens it corrects, and ₹1.35 crore missing from the ask list

`check_todo_screens.py` proves every one of the 193 menu entries is either built
or has a stand-in. It has never once asked whether a stand-in's reason is **true**
— it checks that a justification exists, not that it holds. Sixty-seven
justifications, none of them tested. Three claims carry 61:

	34   "no karigar master and no issue-or-receive table"
	21   "no table for this exists among the 149"
	 6   "only two bill types were ever raised"

The first was tested against the capture, and the walk went somewhere unplanned.

### The claim tested, and then the claim about the claim

`legacy` does hold karigar tables: `karigar_gold_stock` (2 rows) and
`karigar_wip_bal` (1). Ledger 11699 is **MA TARA JEWELLERS**, `ac_grp` **Karigar**,
`ledger_type` **KR** — and it is the **only** Karigar ledger in 40,519 accounts.
The two rows issue **869.850 g of 995 fine** on 16 Sep 2025, bills C4/00001 and
C4/00002, at ₹11,417.

	at the rate on the issue        99,31,077.45
	at today's 995 rate of 15,482   1,34,67,017.70

Every `receive_from_karigar` table is empty, `karigar_wip_bal` is zero at every
purity, the C4 bills appear in **none** of the 20 other bill-numbered tables, and
MA TARA JEWELLERS carries **₹0.00 opening and not one posting**.

**All of which defect 164 established months ago, to the rupee.** This walk
reproduced it independently and landed on the same two figures — confirmation,
not discovery. What was new is what 164 failed to change.

### The correction did not propagate

Defect 164 is titled *"the record dismissed it as an empty table"*. Its whole
argument is that **those two rows are not an empty table**.

The stand-in shown on all 34 manufacturing screens opened:

	The capture holds no karigar master and no issue-or-receive table.

That is the dismissal 164 exists to correct, still on screen, 34 times. It did go
on to name the two rows — so it was not concealing them — but a reader meets the
denial first and the rows second, and **`todo_screens.go` cites no defect number
anywhere in the file**, so nothing points at the entry holding the ₹1.35 crore.

Corrected in all 34: the shop has **one** karigar, named, and those two rows are
an issue of 869.850 g that never came back — **with defect 164 cited**.

### The part that actually matters

**The ₹1.35 crore was not on the ask list.** Twenty-nine rows, including *"Where
is the raw metal now?"* for defect 78 / 133 / 351 — and nothing for the gold that
left the building. The goal names STATUS.md as the single list of what needs
Rahul's answer, and the largest single quantity of metal unaccounted for in the
capture was not in it.

Added, next to the raw-metal question it belongs beside. The question is put
without an inference either way: eleven months on this is **either** metal still
out with the goldsmith **or** the residue of a module the shop trialled and
dropped — C4/00001 and C4/00002 being the first two numbers of a series that
never reached a third. Defect 78 guessed at exactly this kind of gap and defect
133 had to correct it. **Only Rahul can say.**

### What this says about the check

A stand-in reason is evidence, and evidence goes stale. `check_todo_screens.py`
counts justifications; it cannot read them. **33 of the 67 remain untested** —
the 21 "no table exists" and the 6 bill-type claims are next.

## 460. Nineteen of twenty-one held; the two that did not said "none at all" about a table with ten rows

Finishing 459's sweep. Sixty-seven stand-in reasons, of which 459 tested the 34
karigar ones. The remaining claims, each put to the database:

	 6  "only two bill types were ever raised"     HOLDS, exactly
	21  "no table for this exists among the 149"   19 hold, 2 do not

### The six

`sales_vou` carries `bill_type`, and it holds:

	local     221
	central     3
	          ---
	          224   every bill in the capture, and all of them sale_type SALE-GST

No export, repair, exhibition, SC or CO bill exists anywhere. **Credit Sale,
Export Sale, Repair Sale, Exhibition Sale, Purchase Voucher - SC and Purchase
Voucher - CO have nothing to show, and the claim is exact** — the 221 and the 3
reconcile to the 224-bill baseline.

### The nineteen

No table matching `discount`, `studded`, `approv`, `split`, `broken`, `tds`,
`set_rate` or `sub_item` exists in the 149. Two near-misses were checked and both
are correctly dismissed:

- **`item_merge` (40 rows)** is a *catalogue* merge — the loser of two merged
  item codes — not a barcode merge. Already recorded twice, at 940 and 2479.
- **`barcode_detail_rawstone` / `_final`** are the detail of the raw opening
  stock, not a studded one.

### The two that were wrong

Party Raw Stock and Karigar / Dealer Raw Stock both said:

	No table for this exists among the 149 the capture contains.
	Not an empty table — none at all.

**`barcode_main_rawstone` exists and holds 10 rows.** All ten are `type='sh'` —
the shop's own metal, the 27,326.609 g of defect 78. What is missing is not the
table but the `co` and `kr` rows, of which there are none.

The distinction is the whole point of the sentence. *"No table at all"* says the
old system never had the feature; *"a table with no rows of this type"* says it
had the feature and the shop never used it. **The second is true**, and it is
what this project's own documentation already said — defect 78 closes with
*"raw stock exists only as `type='sh'` — there are no `co` or `kr` rows, so Party
Raw Stock and Karigar/Dealer Raw Stock have nothing"*, which is exactly right.

So the docs had it correct and the screens did not, **the same shape as 459**: a
finding recorded in `data-defects.md` and never carried into the text a user
actually reads. Twice now in two entries, from two unrelated sweeps.

Both corrected, and both now name `barcode_main_rawstone`, its ten rows, and the
defect that measured them.

### The sweep is closed

All 67 stand-in reasons have now been tested against the data: **64 held, 3 did
not** — the 34 karigar ones opened with a dismissal that defect 164 had already
overturned (459), and these two claimed a table does not exist when it has ten
rows. Nothing in the remaining 64 was found to overstate.

**No screen was found that has data behind it and is not built.** That is the
goal's second clause, and it now rests on 67 tested reasons rather than 67
present ones.

## 461. Nine hundred and fifty numbers are printed on the screens, and nothing had ever checked one

459 and 460 both found the same shape: something true in `data-defects.md` that
never reached the text a user reads. Twice from unrelated sweeps is a pattern, so
the whole class was swept — **every absolute or numeric claim in on-screen text**.

### The claims that name a table

187 strings in the presentation layer assert *no*, *never*, *none*, *not one*.
Only **6** name a table that can be looked up, and all six were put to the
database. Four were false alarms — HTML markup and doc comments citing legacy
`.php` filenames, not data claims. Two were real, and **both hold**:

- **`temp_pl`**, cited on the Gross Profit screen as showing a loss of
  ₹93,72,540.55. `legacy.temp_pl` **does not exist**, which briefly read as a
  broken citation. It is not: defect 131 records `temp_pl` as one of five
  `temp_*` scratch tables in the ERP's manifest deliberately **not staged**. The
  arithmetic reproduces exactly — income ₹2,11,39,143.00 against expenses
  ₹2,62,33,491.29 + ₹42,66,733.51 + ₹11,458.75 = ₹3,05,11,683.55, a loss of
  **₹93,72,540.55**. **Eighth measurement near-miss**, caught by the rule from
  409: read the source before calling the claim wrong.
- **Pricing Pending**, whose comment says *"four tags at the time of writing"* and
  explains that 952 of the shelf's tags carry no metal rate legitimately, 951 of
  those having a value, and that reporting on the rate would flag 968. Measured:

		no rate                        968
		of those, making_type 'val'    952
		of those, carrying a value     951
		total = 0, the report's own     4

  **All four exact.** The phrase *"at the time of writing"* turned out to be
  modesty rather than a hedge.

### The size of what nobody was checking

	numeric claims in report doc comments      950
	files carrying them                         73

Nine hundred and fifty numbers, read by staff as fact, and **not one of them was
verified by anything**. A reload moves a baseline under all 73 files at once —
defect 420 performed exactly such a reload — and every stale figure would go on
reading as true.

Nine were sampled at random and each put to the database independently:

	2,816 tags · 239 scheme customers · 816 conversion-stone lines
	95 band rows over 3 items · 149 bill numbers and 52,52,946.00
	52 coin items across 115 days, 3 Apr - 19 Aug 2026
	101 items on HSN 711319 · 129 vouchers reading high by 35.30, worst 1.00
	4 tags priced at nothing

**Nine of nine, exact.** Including the rounding reconciliation, reproduced to the
paisa. The text is in good order; it was simply unguarded.

### What is now guarded, and what is not

`tools/check_report_figures.py` — **check 13**. Six whole-population baselines
are read from the database and matched against the figures the reports print.

It cannot check all 950 and does not claim to. A subset count — *"692 tags priced
by value"* — is true only of its own report's query. **The signature of drift is a
figure CLOSE TO but not equal to its baseline**: a subset sits far away (692
against 2,816), while a figure that was right before a reload sits one or two
off. So a claim within 5% of a baseline must match exactly, and anything further
is left alone.

	matching a baseline exactly     13
	within the drift band            0
	clear subsets, left alone       32

**Falsified before being trusted.** One comment was edited from 2,816 to 2,815;
the check named the file, the line, the claim and the truth, and exited 1. The
file was restored and confirmed identical to its backup. Defect 446 was a check
that would only have crashed on a real finding — every check since is made to
fail on purpose first.

## 462. One screen disagreed with four others about a bank balance, and both figures were already written down

Auditing the goal's first clause — a real day's trade, end to end. Two gaps found
were already on the "What it cannot do" list (**take a scheme instalment**,
defect 233; **record a stock conversion**, defect 422), so the survey moved to
what the shop did *recently*: the most recent row in every dated legacy table.

Fifty tables, and one date stood out. `voucher_main` runs to **5 December 2026** —
three and a half months into the future.

### It is a post-dated cheque, and that part was known

	PMNT 576   5 Dec 2026   1,35,370.00
	Ch. No.435590, Dt.05.12.2026 Issued Against Their Dues
	  DAYANIDHI TRADE PVT LTD  (Other Loan)     Dr 1,35,370.00
	  UNION BANK OF INDIA      (Bank Accounts)  Cr 1,35,370.00

Ordinary practice, properly balanced, and already recorded: *"rightly excluded
from an as-on-today balance sheet."*

**It is not excluded everywhere.** Of the six reports that compute a balance as
opening plus movement, **five carry no date predicate at all** —
`customerbalances`, `supplierbalances`, `ledgermerge`, `customermetal` and
`ratio`. Four are harmless here: the one post-dated voucher touches Other Loan
and Bank Accounts, none of which those screens cover. (This entry first said
four. The fifth, `customermetal.go`, was missed by a grep of mine and found by
the check built afterwards — defect 463.)

`ratio.go` covers Bank Accounts.

### The contradiction was already on file, in two places

	STATUS.md:1113   ratio screen     4,92,97,479.87 owed to Union Bank
	STATUS.md:1631   four screens     4,91,62,109.87  "and they all agree"

	                 difference          1,35,370.00

Line 1631 records that the trial balance, ledger book, reconciliation and direct
SQL agree on `UNION BANK OF INDIA`. Line 1113 quotes the Ratio screen's figure.
**They differ by exactly the post-dated cheque**, and both were written down as
fact in the same document without the gap being noticed.

`ratio.go`'s own comment said it classified ledgers *"the way the balance sheet
does it"*. The balance sheet has four date references. This had none.

### The fix, and what it does not change

The subquery now joins `mcj_vouchers` and takes `v.date <= CURRENT_DATE`, which
is the idiom `trialbalance.go` already uses. The screen takes no date parameter —
it reads as of now — so now is the cut-off.

**The ratios themselves do not move.** Cash to overdraft is 0.01 before and after;
the quick ratio stays 0.07. ₹1.35 lakh on ₹4.93 crore is 0.27%, invisible at two
decimals. What was wrong is the **money column printed beside them**, which said
₹4,92,97,479.87 where four other screens said ₹4,91,62,109.87.

That is worth fixing precisely because the ratio hid it. A wrong ratio would have
been argued with; a wrong figure next to a right ratio is read straight past.
STATUS.md line 1113 now carries the corrected figure.

### What is left, deliberately

`customerbalances`, `supplierbalances` and `ledgermerge` still have no date
cut-off. **They are correct today by the shape of the data, not by design** — no
future-dated voucher currently names a customer or a supplier, and nothing stops
one: there is no domain validation against a future date, and the shop
demonstrably post-dates cheques. The voucher register compounds it from the other
side, defaulting `to = now`, so a post-dated voucher can be saved and then not
appear in the register that would show it.

Left rather than fixed because the right cut-off for those screens is a business
question — a customer's post-dated cheque may well belong in *"what they owe"* —
and guessing is how defect 78 got its inference wrong. **Added to the ask list.**

## 463. The check built to replace a measurement found the case the measurement missed

462 was written from a grep. To stop the same gap reopening, the rule was made
into `tools/check_balance_date_policy.py` — **check 15**: a report computing
opening-plus-movement must carry a date cut-off, or be named with the entry that
asks why it has none.

**It failed on its first run**, naming a screen 462 does not mention:
`customermetal.go`.

### The grep was wrong, not the check

462's survey counted date references per file with this pattern:

	v\.date|\.date <=|CURRENT_DATE|date BETWEEN|\$2::date|from.*to

The last alternative is the mistake. **`from.*to` matches any line containing
"from" before "to"** — SQL and English both, constantly. It scored
`customermetal.go` as carrying one date reference when it carries none, and the
file was set aside as filtered.

`carryforward.go`, also scored 1, was re-checked and is genuine:
`AND ($2::date IS NULL OR v.date <= $2::date)`. So the pattern produced one false
positive out of two positives.

**Five screens computed a balance with no cut-off, not four.** 462 has been
corrected in both documents rather than quietly amended — it now names the fifth
and says which of its statements was wrong and why.

	ninth measurement error recorded

The rule from defect 409 was that a regex matching `$1` inside `$12` invented a
finding. This is its mirror: **a regex too loose to be false hid one.** Both come
from writing the pattern and not testing what else it matches.

### What customermetal.go does

It reports metal held against a customer — goods, payments out, receipts — and it
filters `lg.group_name = 'Customer'` over voucher types `PURC-OG`, `SALE-GST`,
`PMNT` and `RCPT`. **`PMNT` is the type of the post-dated cheque.** No customer
holds a future-dated voucher today, so nothing is wrong on screen; the exposure
is identical to `customerbalances`, and it now carries the same open question
rather than a false clean bill.

### The check, and its falsification

	6 screens compute a balance
	  2 carry a date cut-off        ratio (462), carryforward
	  4 are open questions          customerbalances, supplierbalances,
	                                ledgermerge, customermetal

Falsified before being trusted: 462's cut-off was stripped out of `ratio.go` and
the check named that file and exited 1; restoring it returned the file identical
to its backup and the check to green.

**What this says about the last five entries.** 459 and 460 found documentation
that had not reached the screens. 461 found screen text nobody verified. 462
found two screens disagreeing. This one found the tool built to catch 462 catching
something 462 itself had missed — **which is the argument for building the check
rather than only fixing the case.** A fix closes one instance. A check reads
every instance, including the ones the person who wrote the fix walked past.

## 464. Every check made to fail on purpose, and one that answered a typo with a stack trace

463 turned on the difference between a check that holds and a check that has
never been made to speak. Three checks written this week were falsified as they
were built. The other eight never had been. **All of them now have.**

	 4  the shop's own rules            fires    planted a rule that must fail
	 5  STATUS.md matches reality       fires    planted a wrong defect count
	 6  blockers and the ask list       fires    planted a citation of an entry nobody wrote
	 7  every screen is built           fires    renamed a stand-in's .php
	 8  no failed save says ok          fires    planted a save branch that renders
	 9  cascades are put back           fires    stripped a child from load_orders.sh
	13  every screen renders            fires    pointed a query at a missing table
	14  no report doubles a total       fires    planted a subtotal row in the cash book

Each plant was restored from a backup taken first, and each file confirmed byte
identical afterwards. Nothing was left behind.

### The defect this found

`check_invariants.py` handles a rule whose SQL **errors** — it prints the rule and
carries on. A rule whose SQL **succeeds with the wrong shape** was a different
story:

	ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1)

Every rule must select a count *and* a description of what it counted. Select
only the count and the check dies on an unhandled exception, with no rule named.
Inside `check_all.sh` that is indistinguishable from a violation: both print FAIL.
**A typo in a rule looked exactly like the shop's data being wrong.**

Fixed in the style the tool already used for a failing query — the rule is named
and reported as malformed, and the run continues:

	?  PLANTED malformed rule    is malformed: its SQL must select a count
	                             AND a description, and it returned '2816'

### Two false alarms of my own, both from the same habit

Falsifying check 14 took three attempts, and the first two failures were mine:

- **The plant went into a report with no footer.** `customer-balances` renders no
  `<tfoot>` at all, and the detector needs one. The check was right to say
  nothing; there was nothing to say.
- **The manual fetch was never logged in.** Checking that page by hand, the login
  form was posted as `email` / `password`. The application's fields are `Email` /
  `Password`. The request returned **200 with a login page** — no table, no rows —
  and for several minutes that read as *"Customer Balances renders nothing and
  check 13 tolerates it"*. Reproducing the tool's own login showed 84 of 84
  reports speaking, exactly as claimed.

**Tenth measurement error recorded.** A 200 that is not the page you asked for is
the worst kind of wrong answer, because every test for *"did it work"* passes.

Both mistakes are the same habit as 463's: **a probe built by hand and not itself
checked.** The rule that keeps holding is to reproduce the tool's own request
rather than approximate it.

### What this leaves

	15 checks defined
	11 proven to fire on a planted fault
	 4 fire trivially or by construction   build, vet, gofmt, the Go suite

The 8 tested here join the 3 falsified as they were written. `check_all.sh`
closes with *"Nothing is wrong that this repository can detect"* — a sentence
worth only as much as the checks behind it, and now every one of them has been
watched saying otherwise.

## 465. A tool nobody runs, a filter that can never match, and a message that blamed the dates

464 tested every check `check_all.sh` runs. This one asks the other question:
**what is in `tools/` that it does not run?**

	check_empty_columns.py    referenced by nothing

Its own header says to run it *"after a data load, or when adding a report that
reads a column you have not checked."* The last full reload was defect 420. It
had not been run since — a check whose findings reach nobody is not a check.

### It over-reported, in the way 463 warned about

Run with `--read`, it named **36 columns**. The first one opened was
`mcj_prior_uncleared.particulars`, attributed to `statement.go` and `daybook.go`.
**Neither file mentions that table.** They use the word *particulars* for a column
of their own, and a match on the column name alone was enough.

The tool knew: every line ended *"(CHECK THE TABLE, not just the name)"*. A
warning printed 36 times is a warning nobody reads. Attribution now requires the
report to name **the table and the column**:

	36  ->  18     exactly half were the name colliding with itself

(`mcj_prior_uncleared.particulars` is genuinely empty, and so is
`legacy.brs1.perticular` on all 26 uncleared rows. The loader is faithful and
nothing displays the column. No defect there — the attribution was the fault.)

### Of the eighteen, one was live

Most are booleans used as filters, where empty means the filter correctly selects
nothing. `mcj_salary_sheets.days_worked` is **defect 218's own column** and its
fix holds: still selected, then `_ = days // read from the sheet, not shown`, and
no Days field on the screen.

The Barcode Edits screen offers a **Changed** dropdown. Of 156 edits in the
capture:

	item_changed          31
	units_changed        119
	making_changed         7
	gross_changed          0
	net_changed            0
	stone_added            0
	stone_removed          0
	other_making_changed   0

The **"Weight or stones"** choice filters on the four that are false on every
row. **It can never match.** And the screen answered with:

	No tag was edited in this period.

Which blames the dates. **156 tags were edited in that period** — none of them
touched a weight. A clerk widens the date range, gets the same sentence, and
concludes the screen is broken.

It now answers the question that was asked:

	No weight or stone was ever corrected.
	Not in this period — in the whole capture. Of 156 edits, 31 changed the
	item, 119 the unit count and 7 the making, and none touched a gross
	weight, a net weight or a stone.

### One dead end of my own

The first fix was appended at the end of the query function, after the footer.
It never ran: `len(out) == 0` is already handled forty lines earlier, which
returns before reaching it. The code built, the tests passed, and the screen
rendered the old message — the only thing that caught it was **fetching the page
and reading what came back**. Reverted and done at the existing branch instead.

A test would not have found this. **The screen still said something sensible, so
nothing failed.** That is what makes a wrong empty-state message the hardest kind
to catch: an empty table looks the same whatever the reason.

`check_empty_columns.py --read` now runs as a note in `check_all.sh`, so its 18
are read after every load rather than never.

## 466. Two hundred and thirteen choices in one dropdown that could never match anything

465 fixed one filter that could never match. The obvious question is how many
others there are, so **every select filter on every report was probed against the
whole of the shop's history**: read each report's own dropdowns from the rendered
page, then request every value and see what comes back.

	 84 reports
	 55 select filters
	  6 blaming a period in their empty-state message

Five of the six were sound. `mrp-sales`, `purchase-contents`, `sale-cost`,
`gstr-sales` and `gstr-purchases` return rows for **every** value they offer, and
`metal-rates` cannot go wrong by construction: `ratePurityOptions` is
`SELECT DISTINCT purity_code FROM mcj_metal_rates`, so it can only offer a purity
that has rates.

The sixth was Tag-wise Stock, and it was worse than the one 465 fixed.

### The dropdown offered the whole item master

	items offered in the Item list        322
	items that have ever carried a tag    109
	items with no tag in stock            221
	items with no tag EVER                213

`itemOptions` was `SELECT id, name FROM mcj_items` — the entire master. But the
master holds stones, alloys, broken lots and coin types the shop **buys and
consumes rather than tags**: AMETHYST, ALLOYS, BEADS, BROKEN DIA, 999COIN. A tag
is never made for them, so they can never appear on a stock report.

**213 of the 322 choices could return nothing under any combination of filters.**
That is two in every three.

### And it said nothing at all

Picking AMETHYST gave an empty table. Not a message — **no rows whatsoever**.
`stock.go` had no empty-state branch, so the screen's answer to *"show me the
amethyst on the shelf"* was a blank page indistinguishable from a broken report.

### Fixed the way rates.go already does it

The Item list is now built from the population the report draws on:

	SELECT i.id, i.name FROM mcj_items i
	WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM mcj_stock_items s WHERE s.item_id = i.id)

	323 options -> 110      (109 items and the blank)
	dead choices ->   0      every offered item returns rows

**An unreachable choice is now impossible to offer**, rather than merely absent
today. The rule is the one `metal-rates` follows and `barcode-edits` did not: a
filter must be built from the data it filters.

The filters still combine, so a narrow value range or a purity with none left can
empty the list legitimately. That case now answers:

	Nothing on the shelf matches that.
	The filters are combined, so a narrow value range or a purity with none
	left will empty the list. Every item offered has carried a tag at some
	point — if this one shows nothing, its tags have all been sold.

### A miscount of mine, and what it cost

The first sweep reported **9** dead values here. The true number is 213. The probe
counted a filter dead when it returned `<= 1` row — a threshold lifted from
`check_screens_render.py`, where rows include a footer. This probe counted only
`<td>` rows, so `<= 1` also swallowed every **correct** single-row answer, and
`user-rights` filtered to one person was flagged 24 times over.

Re-run against *zero* data rows, the same sweep found 213. **Eleventh measurement
error recorded** — and its shape is now familiar: a threshold that was right in
the tool it came from and wrong in the one it was copied into. 463 was a regex
too loose, 464 a login posted with the wrong field names, this a constant carried
across a border it did not survive.

The rule that keeps earning its place: **reproduce the measurement independently
before believing a count**, especially one small enough to be reassuring.

## 467. The form dropdowns held; a database failure wearing a missing rate's clothes did not

466 swept every select filter on every **report**. The same trap in a **form** is
worse: a report offers a choice that shows nothing, a form offers a choice the
clerk picks and the save refuses. So the entry screens were swept the same way.

### The forms held, and here is why

	tagPurityOptions   only purities that HAVE a rate, joined to mcj_metal_rates
	rateForPurity      rate_date <= the date, ORDER BY rate_date DESC LIMIT 1
	tag.go             if err != nil || rate.IsZero() -> refuses, and says which
	                   purity and which date

Nine forms already carry a test for exactly this — `OldGold_DoesNotOfferStamped
Purities`, `PartySample_OffersOnlyCustomersHoldingSomething`,
`Reconcile_OffersOnlyBankAccounts`, `CoinRate_ListsTheCoinsAndNotOtherItems` and
others. **This concern was designed for; 466's fault was the exception.**

### A gap in the rate book that costs nothing

	rate days     141        1 April to 21 August 2026
	calendar days 143
	missing         2        Saturday 2 May, Thursday 6 August

Every day that has rates has all 20 purities, so the gap is whole days, not
partial ones. **The shop traded on 2 May** — bills GST/2627/00048, 00049 and
00050, ₹40,388.00, ₹2,427.00 and ₹3,204.00 — with no rate set.

It costs nothing, and that is checkable rather than assumed: 22ct was
**14,304.00 on 1 May and 14,304.00 on 3 May**, so the carry-forward reaches the
identical figure the shop would have used. Recorded because the next gap may not
fall between two equal rates.

### The defect

`rateForPurity` ended:

	if err != nil {
	    return rupees.Zero, on, nil
	}

**Every** failure returned as a zero rate and no error. No row is genuinely not an
error — nobody priced that metal, and both callers test `rate.IsZero()` for
precisely that, which sale.go documents at length. But a database that is
unreachable, a query that will not parse, a context that has been cancelled all
came back the same way, and the clerk was told:

	There is no rate for 22 on 2 May 2026.

A sentence about the shop's rate book, for a fault in the connection to it.
Somebody would open the rate book, find 22ct priced, and have nowhere to go.

Now `pgx.ErrNoRows` returns zero as before, and anything else is wrapped and
returned — the idiom `order.go` and `tagcorrect.go` already use.

### The shape this keeps taking

	464   a malformed rule crashed instead of naming itself
	465   an unmatchable filter blamed the period
	467   a database failure blamed the rate book

Three entries, one fault: **a failure reported as a different, more ordinary
condition.** Each is harmless while nothing goes wrong, and each sends the person
who has to fix it to the wrong place. That is the cost — not a wrong number, but
an afternoon spent looking where the answer is not.

## 468. The same disguise twice more: a quote priced at zero and a receipt series restarted

467 named the shape — **a failure reported as a different, more ordinary
condition** — and counted three instances across 464, 465 and itself. Naming a
class is a claim about more than one case, so the class was swept.

The Go form of it is exact enough to search for:

	if err != nil {
	    return <zero>, nil        // every failure becomes "nothing found"
	}

Two more, both live.

### A quote priced at zero and called flat-priced goods

`quote.go` carried its own copy of `rateForPurity`, down to the comment:

	// No rate is not an error: flat-priced goods never had one.

True of one error. The caller tests `rate.IsZero()` and treats a zero as a piece
priced at a flat figure rather than by weight — so **an unreachable database
would have produced a quote with nothing charged for the metal**, and called it
flat-priced. The Quote screen is the one whose output is read out to a customer
standing at the counter.

### A receipt series restarted

`partysample.go` numbers customers' own goods. On error it returned:

	CG/<year>/00001

the **first number in the series**. The reasoning was right — nothing received
yet means the series starts here — and it was reached by every other failure too.
A database that was merely unreachable would have **restarted the receipt
numbering**, and `PartySample_RefusesADuplicateReceiptNumber` would then refuse
the save and tell the counter that receipt number was already used.

Which is true. And is not the reason. A clerk would go looking for CG/2627/00001,
find it in the book from April, and conclude the screen had lost its place.

Both now forgive `pgx.ErrNoRows` by name and wrap everything else — the shape
`order.go` and `tagcorrect.go` already used.

### What the sweep says about the codebase

	206 files scanned
	  3 branches swallowed every failure    sale.go (467), quote.go, partysample.go
	  0 remain

Three in a codebase this size is not a habit; it is the same helper written three
times, each with the same reasonable comment about the one error that is not an
error. **The comment was right and the branch was wider than the comment.**

### Guarded, and falsified

`tools/check_swallowed_errors.py` — **check 16**. A branch returning a nil error
must first name the error it forgives. Falsified by collapsing 467's fix back to
its original single branch: the check named `sale.go:1514` and exited 1, and the
file was restored byte identical.

	464   a malformed rule crashed instead of naming itself
	465   an unmatchable filter blamed the period
	467   a database failure blamed the rate book
	468   a database failure priced a quote at zero, and restarted a receipt series

Four entries, one fault. It is now the only one of the four with a check behind
it, which is the difference between having fixed something and having stopped it.

## 469. A check for the accident that broke every page twice, and it missed the accident on its first run

Defects 401 and 423 were the same accident four weeks apart: a screen was added,
its menu label was not, and **every page in the application panicked** — the
sidebar is drawn on all of them, so one absent key takes the whole thing down.
Both were found by loading a page and watching it die.

Nothing could have found them by searching. These keys are never written down:

	"MCJMenu.Top."   + slug(top)
	"MCJMenu.Group." + slug(top) + "__" + slug(sub)
	"MCJMenu.Item."  + slug(item)

`tools/check_menu_keys.py` — **check 17** — rebuilds every one the way
navigation.go does and asks whether `en.json` has it.

### It was falsified with the real accident, and failed

The obvious test is to delete the exact key that broke everything at 401 —
`MCJMenu.Item.reorder-levels` — and see the check say so.

**It said nothing.** 236 keys built, all present, exit 0.

Reorder Levels is not in `legacy_menu.csv`. It has no place in the old menu at
all — defect 401 added it because the item master carried a minimum quantity for
31 items and no legacy screen ever read it. Such a screen registers itself in
`modules/mcj/links.go`, and navigation.go has a **third pass** for exactly these,
keying them identically at line 405.

The check read the CSV and the stand-in list, and stopped one source short —
**and the source it missed is the one both historical defects came from.** A
check for an accident that could not have caught either instance of it.

	236  ->  261 keys once links.go is read

### Falsified again, against both

	MCJMenu.Item.reorder-levels   wanted by screen 'Reorder Levels'   (defect 401)
	MCJMenu.Item.sales-register   wanted by screen 'Sales Register'   (defect 423)

Each deleted in turn, each named by the check with the screen that wants it and
what to do; `en.json` restored and confirmed byte identical after both.

**No key is missing today** — 261 of 261 resolve, including 12 top menus, 32
sub-groups, 192 items and 25 screens with no legacy menu place.

### The lesson, which is not the one it looks like

This is the fourth time in nine entries that a measurement was narrower or looser
than its claim — 463, 464, 466, and now this. The difference here is what caught
it: **not a reviewer, not a second pass, but insisting the check fail on the real
historical case before trusting it.**

Had it been falsified with a made-up key — inventing `MCJMenu.Item.nonsense` —
it would have passed the test and shipped, because a made-up key is missing from
`en.json` *and* from the sources the check reads. It would have looked correct
and covered nothing that had ever actually gone wrong.

**Falsify with the accident you are trying to prevent, not with an accident you
invented.**

## 470. Four documents could be emptied and every check would still pass

469 ended on a rule: falsify with the accident you are trying to prevent. The
obvious next question is which past accidents are still unguarded, so the record
was read back and the faults it describes were tried again against today's checks.

The first one tried was **defect 447**, which is not hypothetical — it happened
here, in this project, four days ago:

	open(p, "w").write(open(p).read().replace(...))

Python opens the file for writing, **emptying it**, before evaluating the argument
that reads it. `docs/screens.md` lost 1,998 lines, and the only reason they came
back is that a backup existed for an unrelated reason two hours earlier.

### What is guarded, and what turned out not to be

`status_figures.py` catches a truncated `screens.md` and `data-defects.md`,
because it checks a headline figure in each and a truncated file cannot produce
it. That was verified rather than assumed: cutting `screens.md` to 60 lines fails
check 5.

The other four documents have no figure anyone checks. Each was cut to five lines
in turn and the suite run:

	DECISIONS.md          16 check(s) passed
	migration-profile.md  16 check(s) passed
	pkg-contracts.md      16 check(s) passed
	pricing-formula.md    16 check(s) passed

**910 lines of decisions, contracts and formulas could vanish between two commits
and every check would report the repository sound.** Including `DECISIONS.md`,
which is the record of what Rahul has already answered.

### A floor, not a size

`tools/check_doc_floors.py` — **check 18**. Each document declares a minimum line
count and the headings that must survive it.

A floor rather than an exact size on purpose: documents grow, and a check that
had to be edited every time one did would be edited into uselessness. It fires on
what truncation looks like — a file falling through its floor or losing a heading
— and stays quiet for ordinary editing. Raise a floor when a document has really
grown; never lower one to make this pass.

	7 documents, 30,117 lines, each above its floor

### Falsified with 447's own line of code

Not with a made-up truncation. **Defect 447's exact expression** was run against
each of the four unguarded documents:

	DECISIONS.md          0 lines, check exit 1
	migration-profile.md  0 lines, check exit 1
	pkg-contracts.md      0 lines, check exit 1
	pricing-formula.md    0 lines, check exit 1

Each restored from a backup taken first and confirmed byte identical.

That the accident empties a file **completely** is worth noticing: it is not a
subtle corruption, and it still went undetected for two hours and would have gone
undetected forever in four files out of seven. **The size of a fault has nothing
to do with whether anything is watching for it.**

## 471. The migrations were never once applied to an empty database, and they are correct

Continuing 470's method: read the record back, try each past fault against
today's checks. **Defect 399** was a migration carrying `--` inside a SQL string
literal — sql-migrate treats it as a comment marker and cuts the line there, so
the migration applied something other than what was written.

Nothing checks the migrations. `status_figures.py` counts the files without
reading them, and `check_all.sh` has never applied one. A malformed migration
sits quiet until somebody builds a database from scratch — **the moment it is
most expensive to find**.

### So it was done, once, properly

	CREATE DATABASE wingold_migcheck
	DB_NAME=wingold_migcheck  migrate up
	  -> Applied 134 migrations, exit 0

Every migration applies to an empty database. That had not been demonstrated
before.

### And the schema it builds is the one that exists

The stronger question is not whether they apply but whether they **reproduce**
the database being used. Both schemas were dumped column by column, with types,
and compared:

	live       145 tables   1,544 columns
	from empty 145 tables   1,544 columns
	difference none

**Identical, column for column and type for type.** The migrations rebuild the
database exactly, and the database has not drifted from them — no hand-applied
column, no forgotten ALTER, nothing carried in a loader that should have been a
migration. The scratch database was then dropped, and only `wingold` remains.

For a schema assembled across 134 files and several weeks, that is the result
worth having and the one nobody had checked.

### The cheap part, made permanent

`tools/check_migrations.py` — **check 19** — reads every migration for the two
faults that are silent:

	no '-- +migrate Up'          sql-migrate applies nothing and reports success
	'--' inside a string         sql-migrate cuts the line -- defect 399 exactly

Both clean across 134 files. The full apply is not in `check_all.sh`: it needs a
database of its own and minutes to run. What is written down instead is that it
was done and what it proved, so the next person does not have to wonder.

### Falsified with 399's own fault

Not an invented one. A line of the shape that broke it was planted into a real
migration — `SELECT 'brs1 -- the bank reconciliation carry-forward'` — and the
check named the file, the line and the string. The missing-Up case was planted
separately and named too. The file was restored and confirmed byte identical.

	470   falsified with 447's line of code
	471   falsified with 399's fault

Two entries running, the check was proven against the accident it exists for
rather than one invented to suit it — which is the only version of that test that
means anything, and 469 is why.

## 472. Nineteen tables could empty with nothing failing, and the check written for it lost the digits off a name

470 asked which documents could vanish with every check still passing, and found
four. The same question of the data:

	populated mcj_ tables               83
	  read by a report                  62    check 13 fails if one goes silent
	  named in a check directly         28
	  neither                           19

The nineteen are almost all **masters** — `mcj_states`, `mcj_religions`,
`mcj_card_types`, `mcj_ledger_groups` (96 rows), `mcj_value_bands`,
`mcj_weight_bands`, `mcj_professions`. No report reads them because they fill the
**dropdowns on forms**, and 466 and 467 are two entries about how much a dropdown
matters. Emptying `mcj_states` would leave the sale form unable to name a place
of supply, and the suite would have said the repository was sound.

### The rule taken from the load chain, not from a list

A list somebody maintains goes stale. `tools/check_loaded_tables.py` — **check
20** — reads `INSERT INTO` and `DELETE FROM` out of `tools/legacy/load_*.sh` and
requires every table named there to have at least one row.

	65 tables the loaders fill, 94,826 rows, none empty

That is the right rule because of how these loaders are built: **each one begins
by DELETING what it is about to replace.** A loader that deletes and then loads
nothing is not a hypothetical failure mode; it is the failure mode, and defects
294, 366 and 407 are three occasions when a variant of it happened.

**Not-empty rather than a row count**, deliberately. A count fails the day the
shop legitimately deletes a card type, and a check that cries wolf gets edited
until it says nothing. Zero rows in a table the shop has data for is never right.

### The falsification found a bug in the check

There was no empty `mcj_` table to point at, so one was made — `mcj_falsify_471`
— named from a loader, and the check was run. It fired, and said:

	mcj_falsify_ is written by a loader and does not exist

**`mcj_falsify_`.** The digits fell off. The regex was `mcj_[a-z_]+`, which stops
at the first number, so a table whose name carries one would be looked up under a
name that does not exist and reported missing while sitting there populated.

No `mcj_` table has a digit today — the query says zero — so nothing was wrong.
The regex was wrong regardless, and **the only reason it was ever read closely
was that the falsification printed it back.** A check that passes prints a
summary nobody examines; a check that fails prints the thing it found.

	463  a regex too loose hid a screen
	466  a threshold carried across a border it did not survive
	472  a regex too narrow lost the digits off a name

Third time in ten entries. The pattern is not carelessness about regexes; it is
that **a pattern is only ever tested against the input you had in mind**, and the
falsification is where a different one finally arrives.

Fixed to `mcj_[a-z0-9_]+`, and the scratch table dropped.

## 473. B15 was a decision nobody was checking, and both existing guards were narrower than it

Blocker **B15** is Rahul's decision: five legacy tables were deliberately never
opened, because they hold the shop's messaging credentials.

	api_details        password, key_name
	email_master
	sms_profile        pwd
	whats_app_url
	whatsapp_profile   password

They are staged in `legacy` only because the whole dump was staged. Nothing
loads, reads or reports on them, and the point of the decision is that it stays
that way as the system grows.

**Nothing was checking that it had.**

### Two guards existed, and both are narrower than the decision

	load_users.sh          asserts no credential column exists
	                       -- on mcj_legacy_users and mcj_legacy_access only,
	                          and only when a loader is run
	usermaster_e2e_test.go asserts the same
	                       -- on mcj_legacy_users only

Both were verified still working. Neither would notice the way this would
actually go wrong: **not somebody adding a password column to the users table,
which is obvious, but a loader for message history quietly bringing the profile
along with it.** A new table built from `sms_profile` passes both guards without
touching either.

### The check, over everything

`tools/check_no_credentials.py` — **check 21** — asks both halves across the
whole system:

	no mcj_ table anywhere carries a column reading pass, pwd, scode,
	  secret, token, otp or api_key
	none of the five sealed tables is named by any loader, migration,
	  controller, report or template

Comments are stripped before the second search, so an entry explaining the
decision is not mistaken for a use of it — the decision has to be discussable
without tripping the check that enforces it.

Both clean.

### Falsified in both directions

	a loader reading legacy.sms_profile   named the file and the table, exit 1
	ALTER TABLE mcj_legacy_users ADD scode  named the column, exit 1

The column was added to a real table and dropped again; the loader was restored
from a backup taken first and confirmed identical. The users table has its
original column count.

### Why this one is different from the twenty before it

Every other check here enforces something the code should be true to. This one
enforces something **Rahul said**, and the only record of it was a blocker
paragraph and two guards that had drifted narrower than the sentence they came
from.

A decision that lives only in prose is kept by whoever remembers it. **Sixteen
entries have now been written since B15 was recorded, and the decision survived
on memory alone.** It no longer has to.

## 474. The check written to keep credentials out could not spell two of them

473 built check 21 against blocker B15 and called it done. One entry later, a
different thread — auditing the settled decisions in `DECISIONS.md` — walked past
this line in **defect 21**, written months ago:

	Ten columns store credentials this way, including `branch_master.br_psw`
	(`b001`) and `retail_master.rt_psw` (`r001`).

**`psw`.** Check 21's list was `pass, pwd, scode, secret, token, otp, apikey,
api_key`. It does not contain `psw`, and neither `br_psw` nor `rt_psw` matches
any of the others.

	credential-looking columns in legacy   15
	spellings check 21 could recognise     13
	spellings it could not                  2   br_psw, rt_psw

And these are not on tables nobody touches. **`branch_master` and
`retail_master` are both read by `load_masters.sh`** — they are where
`mcj_branches` and `mcj_retail_points` come from. They are, of the fifteen, the
two columns most likely to be carried across by accident, and the two the check
was blind to.

Nothing came across: the loader names its columns one at a time and never asks
for either. **The check simply would not have said so** — one entry after being
written to say exactly that.

### Widened, and falsified with the real name

`psw` and `key_name` added. Falsified per 469's rule with the historical name
rather than an invented one:

	ALTER TABLE mcj_branches ADD COLUMN br_psw text
	  -> mcj_branches.br_psw looks like a credential, exit 1

Column dropped; `mcj_branches` has its original column count.

### Four times now, and the reason is not the regexes

	463  a regex too loose hid a screen
	466  a threshold carried across a border it did not survive
	472  a regex too narrow lost the digits off a name
	474  a list of spellings that did not include the one on file

The common cause is not carelessness with patterns. It is that **a pattern is
written from what the author is picturing**, and the author was picturing
`password`. The two real names had been written down in this repository since
defect 21 — the check's own subject matter, in the entry it exists to enforce —
and were not read while writing it.

What breaks the cycle is not more care. **It is reading the record for the actual
names before writing the pattern, and falsifying with those names rather than
with something invented.** That rule has now caught its own author four times.

## 475. A settled decision the schema does not keep: branch is modelled on two tables out of eighty-three

473 said a decision living only in prose is kept by whoever remembers it. That
was about B15. The same question put to `docs/DECISIONS.md`, which is the record
of what Rahul has already answered, found decision **#4**:

	Scale | Multi-branch is definitely coming.
	      | Branch modelled properly from day one; inter-branch transfers...

	mcj_ tables carrying tenant_id    83 of 83
	mcj_ tables carrying a branch      2 of 83

The two are `mcj_bank_accounts` and `mcj_retail_points`. **Not one operational
table has a branch:**

	mcj_sales_invoices      224 bills        no branch
	mcj_stock_items       2,816 tags         no branch
	mcj_vouchers          1,848 vouchers     no branch
	mcj_stock_movements   9,031 movements    no branch
	mcj_customer_orders     284 orders       no branch
	mcj_stock_conversions   859 conversions  no branch

`tenant_id` is not this. A second shop under the same owner is one tenant and two
branches, and every one of those rows would be unattributable.

### The legacy did record it

This is not a column the old system lacked. **Defect 5**, one of the first
written:

	voucher_detail.br_code holds B001 (the code), 1 (the numeric brid), and
	blank. 495 rows carry 1. voucher_main.br_code is always B001.

Its instruction was *"normalise 1 → B001 and blank → header value during the
transform"*. The transform instead dropped the column. Every voucher in the
capture belongs to branch **B001**, and that fact is now nowhere.

### Why nothing noticed

`check_unwritten_columns.py` reports *"44 columns across 14 tables — each a field
the legacy recorded and this system cannot"*, which sounds like it would catch
this. It does not: it iterates **`mcj_` tables** and finds columns no Go code
writes. **It never reads the `legacy` schema.** A column dropped entirely is
invisible to it, because there is no new column to be found unwritten.

Nothing anywhere compares the two schemas. A first measure put it at **511
column names with no counterpart anywhere in the mcj schema** — a figure that
turned out to be badly inflated, because it matched by NAME and the loaders
rename as they go: `ac_name` becomes `name`, `mobile1` becomes `mobile`, `d_o_b`
becomes `date_of_birth`. **Defect 476 redid it against what the loaders actually
select and found 66**, of which `br_code` is one. The correct figure is there,
not here.

### What it costs, and when

**Today it costs nothing.** The shop has one branch, `branch_master` has one row,
and every voucher says `B001`. Nothing on any screen is wrong.

It costs on the day the second shop opens. Then 2,816 tags, 9,031 movements and
1,848 vouchers have no branch and no way to acquire one — the information was
thrown away at load, not merely left unmodelled — and every query, report and
screen has to change at the same time as the shop is opening a branch.

### This is Rahul's call, and it is on the ask list

Two honest options, and the cost is very different:

- **Add branch now.** 83 tables, but the data is small and every row is `B001`,
  so backfilling is one statement per table. The work is in the screens.
- **Accept it and do it later**, knowing the historical rows cannot be
  attributed afterwards.

Not decided here. Defect 78 guessed at something like this and defect 133 had to
correct it — and unlike 78, this one has a settled decision on file saying which
way it should go, which is exactly why it should be asked rather than assumed.

## 476. Five hundred and eleven was wrong; sixty-six is right, and one customer lost their only phone number

475 said nothing compares the legacy schema with the new one, and put the size of
that unexamined space at **511 column names with no counterpart**. That figure
was published one entry ago and it is wrong.

**It matched by name, and the loaders rename as they go.**

	legacy                     ->  mcj_parties
	ac_name                    ->  name
	mobile1                    ->  mobile
	adrs_off                   ->  office_address
	d_o_b                      ->  date_of_birth
	company                    ->  company_name

Every one of those was counted as dropped. `mobile1` has 39,399 distinct values
and sits in `mcj_parties.mobile` — it is carried, and the comparison said it was
gone.

### Measured again, three times, because twice was wrong

	columns dropped by NAME, with 50+ rows and 2+ distinct values     388
	  of those, named somewhere in a loader (i.e. renamed, carried)   322
	  named by NO loader at all                                        66

The second attempt gave 90, not 66. The identifier pattern was
`[a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,}` — **three characters minimum** — so `gw` and `nw`, the gross
and net weights, could never be recognised as carried and were counted as lost
on four tables at once. **Twelfth measurement error, and the second in this one
entry.**

	511  matched by name, ignored renames
	 90  identifier pattern too long for a two-letter column
	 66  correct

### The sixty-six, spot-checked at the top

**`address_book_master.panno`** — there are two PAN columns and the loader takes
the other one, `pan_no`.

	both filled and identical      227
	both filled and DIFFERENT        1
	PAN only in panno                0
	PAN only in pan_no              91

Nothing is lost: no customer's PAN exists only in the dropped column. One
disagrees — **ARUNABH DAS**, `BXRPD7554D` loaded against `BXPRD7554D` dropped, a
transposition of two letters. The fourth character of a PAN is the holder type
and must be `P` for a person: the **loaded** value has it and the dropped one does
not. The loader took the valid one, and it took it by luck rather than by
checking.

**`address_book_master.phone2`** — filled on 3,033 rows, and `mcj_parties` has no
second landline.

	a different number from phone1   2,997
	the only landline they have        974
	and no mobile either                   1

So 2,997 second numbers are genuinely not carried, and the harm is one customer.
**One person in 40,519 cannot be telephoned from this system and could be from
the old one.**

### What this entry is really about

The finding is small. The correction is not: **a figure went into the record with
a hedge on it — "a proxy rather than a defect list" — and the hedge did not make
it true.** 511 read as an alarming number and was quoted as one. Hedged prose
around a wrong number still leaves a wrong number, and the reader keeps the
number.

475 has been corrected in both documents to point here rather than quietly
amended, and 66 is the figure that stands.

## 477. The sixty-six triaged, and the order book's header disagrees with its own lines on 78 orders

476 reduced the dropped-column question to a real list of **66**. Triaged, they
fall into three groups:

	internal legacy keys        tran_id, new_vid, rcpt_vid, stkid, sl_id,
	                            pmnt_vid, jrnl_vid, barcode_detail_id, ...
	                            -> replaced by this schema's own UUIDs
	denormalised copies         tot_amt, sale_amount, due_amount, actual_gw,
	                            actual_nw -> recomputable from the lines
	real content                phone2 (476), picture_sketch (5,046 design
	                            sketches), amount_received, item_size, catg

Most of the 66 are the first group and are right to be gone.

### The one that looked worst was not a loss

`customer_order.amount_received` is filled on **273 of 284 orders** while
`mcj_customer_orders.advance` sums to **zero**. That reads as every advance the
shop ever took being dropped.

It is not. Compared against each order's own lines, `amount_received` **equals the
line total** — ratio 1.00 on the large majority. It is what the order is worth,
not what was paid on it. The genuine `advance` column is zero on all 284 rows:
the shop never used it, and the loader carries it faithfully.

**Nothing is lost.** The order's value is in its lines, and the lines are loaded.

### What the comparison did find

	orders with lines                                271
	  header equals the sum of its lines             193
	  header DISAGREES                                78

	all 78 have the header HIGHER, none lower
	total                                   1,06,00,834

A one-directional gap of **₹1.06 crore**. Not scattered either way, which random
error would be — the header is never lower. That points at something the header
includes and the lines do not, or at lines removed after the header was written.

This system computes an order's worth **from the lines**, which is the itemised
source and the defensible choice. But if the header is right, the order book is
understating by ₹1.06 crore across 78 orders. **Added to the ask list**, because
which one is right is a question about how the shop wrote orders, not one the
data settles.

### A bug of my own that hid the largest row

The first pass at this ordered by a column alias:

	SELECT to_char(recv,'FM9,99,99,999') AS received, ...
	ORDER BY received DESC

The alias **shadowed the numeric column it was computed from**, so the sort was
alphabetical over formatted text — and `9,95,038` sorted above `7,38,00,000`. The
single largest order in the shop's book, worth ₹7.38 crore, was invisible on
page one of its own report while two of my queries quietly disagreed.

**Thirteenth measurement error.** It joins the pattern the last several entries
keep circling: 463 a regex too loose, 466 a threshold from another tool, 472 a
regex too narrow, 474 a spelling not on the list, 476 a name comparison blind to
renames, and now **a sort that was never numeric.** Every one produced a
confident, plausible, wrong number — and every one was caught by asking the same
question a second way.

## 478. Thirty-eight columns of the shop's data that no screen reads, and two checks that both missed them

477's list of 66 named `design_transaction_main.picture_sketch` as real content
never loaded. Following it found something larger, and one file over.

`picture_final` **is** loaded — into `mcj_designs.picture_path`, filled on **5,104
rows.** Nothing reads it. No screen names the column, and:

	check_unwritten_columns.py   finds columns nothing WRITES   -- this is written
	check_empty_columns.py       finds columns that are EMPTY   -- this is full

**It fell between both tools.** They sit either side of the question and neither
asks it: a column that is written, full of the shop's data, and read by nothing.

### What is in the gap

	38 columns across 13 tables   (understated -- 40 once comments stop
	                               counting as reads, see defect 490)

	mcj_packets            17 columns   crown_angle, crown_height, depth_mm,
	                                    width_mm, length_mm, table_percent...
	                                    NOT 205 packets. Between 2 and 6 rows
	                                    each -- the figure first written here
	                                    was wrong, see defect 479
	mcj_bank_accounts       3 columns   account_no and ifsc on 397 accounts
	mcj_scheme_payments     2 columns   payment_mode and instalment_no on all
	                                    2,144 instalments
	mcj_designs             2 columns   designed_on (5,221) and picture_path
	mcj_stock_items         5 columns   lot_no (2,059), making_sales (1,825)

Some of it is rightly unread. `legacy_v_id` and `legacy_user_id` are tracing keys.

The rest is not plumbing. (The diamond measurements are **not** part of it —
defect 479 recounted them and they are filled on a handful of packets, not all
