recorded and shown nowhere. **How each of 2,144 instalments was paid** — cash,
card, transfer — is known and never displayed, on a scheme book that is already
on the ask list twice.

### The two image populations, which no document separates

	tag photos     http://tag09.com/mcj2/images/bar_pic/...   B24, 927 tags
	                 a third-party host, still answering, behind a bot check
	design images  ../image/14017640.jpg                      5,105 sketches
	                 the shop's own server, 404 since 21 August

B24 asks Rahul to *"open one tag photo in a browser"* — a live test, because that
host is still there. **The design images cannot be tested that way at all.** They
were never on a host anyone can try. `designs.go` says *"the pictures are gone"*,
which is right about `picture_final`; there are **two** images per design and the
sketch, 5,105 of them, is recorded nowhere.

### Now a standing note

`tools/check_unread_columns.py` prints the 38 after every run, beside the two
notes it sits between. Not a failing check: **a column carried across and not yet
shown is a decision, not a fault.** But it is the shortest description of what
this system holds and does not surface, and it should be read rather than
rediscovered by hand a third time.

## 479. "The full gemmological measurement of every diamond lot" was four packets

478 was written one entry ago. Acting on it — the goal says build every screen
that has data behind it, and 205 diamond lots with crown angles and table
percentages is exactly that — meant opening the packet screen. The data is not
there.

	mcj_packets                        205 rows

	crown_angle                          4
	table_percent                        4
	depth_percent                        4
	crown_height                         4
	depth_mm                             4
	pavilion_angle                       4
	average_weight_ct                    6
	length_mm                            3
	width_mm                             2
	rapaport_discount                    2

**Every one of the seventeen is filled on between two and six packets.**

### The census counted zero as a value

	btrim(COALESCE(col::text,'')) NOT IN ('', '0', '0.00', 'false')

`crown_angle` is `numeric`, and Postgres renders its zero as **`0.000`** — three
decimals, matching none of the three spellings in that list. 201 zeros were
counted as data, and the column reported 205 filled out of 205.

	stored value   rows
	0.000           201
	34.300            1
	34.900            1
	35.300            1

**Fourteenth measurement error**, and the second time in four entries that a
figure published with confidence had to be corrected in the entry after it (476
corrected 475's 511).

### What the correction changes

Not much of the finding, and all of the emphasis. The 38 unread columns are real
and so is most of the list — **designed_on on 5,221 designs, instalment_no and
payment_mode on all 2,144 instalments, account_no and ifsc on 397 bank accounts,
lot_no on 2,059 tags.** Those counts were re-derived type by type and hold.

What does not hold is the sentence that made the entry sound important: *"205
packets, the full gemmological measurement of every diamond lot."* The shop
recorded those measurements for **four stones** and left the rest at zero. A
screen for it would be a heading over an empty table — the exact thing defect 460
was about — and it will not be built.

### The tool now carries the numbers

`check_unread_columns.py` printed names without counts, so it could not have been
wrong; it also could not have caught this. It now counts each column **the way
its type requires** — numeric zero is not a value, a false boolean is not a value
— and prints the figure beside the name:

	mcj_designs: designed_on (5,221), picture_path (5,104)
	mcj_scheme_payments: instalment_no (2,144), payment_mode (2,144)
	mcj_packets: average_weight_ct (6), fluorescence (5), crown_angle (4), ...

**A note that prints a name invites a guess about the quantity, and the guess was
mine.** The figures are in the output now, so the next reading of this list
starts from what is there rather than from what its heading suggests.

## 480. The scheme book now says how each instalment was paid, and how far the customer got

479 corrected 478 and closed the packet measurements: four stones, not 205, and
no screen worth building. The rest of that list survived the recount, and the
largest genuinely useful item was on a screen already built.

`mcj_scheme_payments` carries `payment_mode` and `instalment_no` on **all 2,144
payments**, and the Scheme Book read neither.

### Derived twice before touching anything

Fourteen measurement errors say to reproduce the figure from the data before
acting on it. Both columns were counted first, and the modes reconcile:

	Bank    1,287   46,99,400.00
	Cash      528   25,49,300.00
	Card      329   15,42,200.00
	                ------------
	        2,144   87,90,900.00

**₹87,90,900.00** is defect 233's figure for every instalment ever collected, to
the rupee, arrived at from a column nothing had read. `instalment_no` runs 1 to
10, ten distinct values, which is what a scheme of ten instalments should have.

That is the check 479 was written to enforce, applied before writing rather than
after: **the data agreed with a figure derived independently months ago.**

### Two columns added

	Up to no.   the highest instalment number reached
	Paid by     the modes used, e.g. "Bank, Cash"

	KIRAN ASWANI      1 instalment    up to no. 1   Cash     5,000.00
	P. K. MUNDRA      2 instalments   up to no. 2   Cash    10,000.00
	RESHMI AGARWAL.   3 instalments   up to no. 3   Cash    15,000.00

Both are aggregated in the LATERAL subquery already there, so the screen makes no
extra query. 236 rows render, and `mcj_scheme_payments` has left the unread list:
**38 columns, 13 tables → 36 columns, 12 tables.**

### Why this and not the others

The remaining 36 are not all worth a screen and this entry does not claim they
are. `legacy_v_id` is a tracing key. `picture_path` points at a dead server.
`designed_on` on 5,221 designs is a real candidate; `account_no` and `ifsc` on 397
bank accounts are real but belong on a master, not a report.

The scheme book was chosen because it is the one place where unread data sat
**underneath a question already on the ask list twice** — defect 233 asks how
scheme settlements were recorded and B23 asks about ₹77,37,300 owed on matured
enrolments. Whoever answers those will want to know whether the money came in by
bank, cash or card, and now the screen says so.

## 481. The design date is the day the ERP was installed, and the catalogue has not moved since 2017

480 took the largest useful column off 478's unread list. The next one down was
`mcj_designs.designed_on` — filled on **all 5,221 designs**, with a Design
Catalogue screen already built to put it on.

It was derived first, which is the rule fourteen measurement errors bought.

	5,221 designs
	   12 distinct dates between them
	4,991 of them share ONE date: 5 July 2016   (95.6%)

	2016-07-05   4,991
	2016-11-07     135
	2016-09-06      51
	2017-01-10      18
	2016-07-29       9

Both sides agree: `legacy.design_transaction` gives the same 12 days and the same
range. **This is not when the designs were drawn. It is the day the old ERP was
loaded**, with a handful of later entries after it.

### So the column was not added

A column headed **"Designed"** showing 5 July 2016 against 4,991 designs would be
read as fact by anyone who opened the screen, and it would be an installation
timestamp wearing a design date's label. That is the family 465 and 467 are
about — **a value reported as something more ordinary than it is** — and the
cheapest place to stop it is before the column exists.

The reasoning now sits in `designs.go`, above the function, where the next person
tempted by an unread column will meet it. **459 and 460 were both about findings
that never reached the text a user reads; this one starts there.**

### What the dates do say

	the last design in the catalogue   20 January 2017

**Nothing has been added in nine years.** The shop has gone on trading to August
2026 — 224 bills, 284 orders, 2,816 tags — against a design catalogue that
stopped receiving entries in the January after it was installed. Whether the shop
stopped recording designs or stopped using the screen, the catalogue is a
historical document rather than a working one, and no screen said so.

### Also checked, already known

`mcj_designs` holds 5,221 rows under 5,218 distinct design numbers. The three
repeats — GBLI0001, GBLI0002, GBLI0003, each twice with two different estimates
(₹2,650 against ₹4,350; ₹4,779 against ₹5,460; ₹3,360 against ₹3,897.25) — are
**defect 394**, already on file. Checked before writing rather than logged twice.

## 482. Six customers with dates that have not happened, and a data quality screen that called them complete

481 found the design catalogue frozen since January 2017. That was one dataset's
staleness; the obvious question is which others stopped, so the most recent date
in every loaded table was taken.

	mcj_designs               2017-01-20    5,221 rows
	mcj_holidays              2024-12-26      109
	mcj_estimates             2025-05-23        2
	mcj_scheme_enrolments     2026-02-11      239
	...
	mcj_metal_rates           2026-08-21    2,820
	mcj_vouchers              2026-12-05    1,848   the post-dated cheque, 462
	mcj_parties               9888-12-09   40,519

**Nine thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight.**

	JAINAT KUMAR BEZBARUAH   born 9888-12-09
	SHARMIN KHAN             born 4582-12-12
	SARITA SAFAR             born 2098-08-18
	SUSHIL KUMAR AGARWAL     born 2026-08-30   (five days from now)

	R. D. KHANDELWAL         anniversary 2027-10-13
	DR. BISHWAJIT MODAK      anniversary 2028-04-07

Typed years, almost certainly: 9888 for 1988, 2098 for 1998.

### The screen that exists for this counted them as good

The Data Quality screen offers the six checks the legacy dropdown had:

	Mobile number · Address · Email address · Anniversary date ·
	Date of birth · Duplicate name

**Every one asks whether a field is PRESENT.** None asks whether it is possible.
A birthday in the year 9888 is not missing, so all six customers passed the very
checks that exist to find bad customer records.

This matters more than a typo usually would because of what the field is for. A
jeweller greets customers on their birthday and their anniversary — B18 is on the
ask list precisely about having customer records in one place. **A birthday list
built from this either never reaches those four or greets one of them in the
year 9888.**

### Two checks added, and two rules

The screen now offers **"Born in the future"** and **"Anniversary not yet
reached"**, so the shop can find and fix them rather than being told the records
are complete.

`check_invariants.py` gains two rules at the counts that exist today — 4 and 2,
allowed and recorded, in the codebase's own pattern for a known quantity that
must not grow:

	nobody is born in the future        holds (4 allowed, unchanged)
	no anniversary is still to come     holds (2 allowed, unchanged)

	39 of 39 rules hold

**Falsified against the database**: a fifth impossible birthday was written to a
row that had none, and the rule reported *"5 customer(s) with a date of birth
after today"* and failed the suite at 38 of 39. The row was set back to NULL and
the count is 4 again.

### One more thing the census said

`mcj_holidays` stops at **26 December 2024**. The shop has traded through all of
2025 and 2026 with no holiday list for either year — 109 rows describing which
days the shop was shut, none of them covering the last twenty months.

## 483. Three hundred and seventeen birthdays with no year, and two sentinels behind them

482 ended on the distinction between a field being **present** and being
**possible**. Sweeping every date column in the database for values outside any
plausible window turned up exactly two columns — both on `mcj_parties`, and both
much larger than the six future dates 482 found.

	date_of_birth      317 before 1900        4 in the future
	anniversary_date   283 before 1900        2 in the future

Every other date in every other table is within a sane window. **The customer
table is the only place this lives**, which fits: it is the only table filled in
by hand at a counter.

### They are not junk, and three different things are mixed together

	40,519 customers
	32,842   no date of birth at all
	 7,356   a plausible one   (14 Apr 1900 to 10 Aug 2026)
	   247   year 0001
	    60   year 1000
	    10   a three-digit year: 199, 934, 975, 979, 983, 996, 997
	     4   in the future                                    (defect 482)

**Year 0001 is a birthday recorded without a year.** The 247 spread across **204
distinct day-and-month pairs covering all twelve months** — that is a real
birthday list with the year left out, not corruption. The 60 at year 1000 are the
same thing behind a second sentinel: 54 distinct day-months.

Only the **ten three-digit years** are typing: 975 for 1975, 983 for 1983, 996
for 1996.

### Why the distinction decides what to do

For a jeweller the day and month are the whole point — a birthday greeting does
not need the year. So **307 of these 317 are usable for the thing the field
exists for**, and would be lost by any rule that treated a pre-1900 date as
garbage.

What they cannot support is arithmetic. Any age calculation on them returns two
thousand years, and any screen printing the date raw shows *"14 Dec 0001"*.

So the Data Quality screen now offers **"Birthday with no usable year"** rather
than anything that calls them invalid, and the invariant is a **floor that must
not grow**, in the codebase's own pattern:

	no birthday loses its year        holds (317 allowed, unchanged)

	40 of 40 rules hold

### What this says about 482's fix

482 added *"Born in the future"* and caught 4. This sweep found **317 in the same
column**, seventy-nine times as many, by asking the question the other way round.

Looking for the impossible found four. Looking for **everything outside the
possible** found three hundred and twenty-one, and then required the harder work
of deciding that most of them are fine. **The cheap version of a plausibility
check is the one that finds the smallest problem.**

## 484. Thirty-one designs priced below nothing, and the same alias bug I logged eight entries ago

483 swept every date column for values outside the possible. This is the other
half: **every numeric column on every populated table**, 256 of them, asked for
its minimum, maximum and negative count.

Six hold a negative value, and three of those are right:

	mcj_sales_invoices.round_off      115 rows   rounding down is negative
	mcj_vouchers.round_off            129 rows   the same
	mcj_purchase_invoices.round_off    12 rows   the same
	mcj_credit_notes.round_off          2 rows   the same
	mcj_stock_conversion_pieces.total   2 rows   -40.00
	mcj_designs.estimate               31 rows   down to -3,97,488.00

**A design estimate is a price. It cannot be less than nothing.**

	DBNG0100   -3,97,488.00
	DBNG0097   -3,10,655.00
	DBNG0094   -1,83,940.00
	DBNG0099   -1,56,760.00
	           ------------
	31 designs -12,86,354.00

The loader is faithful — `legacy.design_transaction_main.estimate_amount` holds
the same 31 negatives and the same minimum.

### No cause found, and one hypothesis killed

DBNG0100 has `rate = 0`, which looked like the answer: an estimate computed
against a metal rate of nothing. It is not. **All 5,221 designs have rate = 0**,
so a zero rate is universal and explains nothing. The 31 are spread across four
item families — 19 rings, 6 lockets, 5 bangles, 1 top — with no shared shape.
They read as individual entry errors.

### What it costs

`designs.go` sums estimates for the catalogue's footer:

	shown today      14,95,13,508.73
	positives only   15,07,99,862.73
	the difference      12,86,354.00

**The Design Catalogue reports the shop's design book as ₹12.86 lakh smaller than
the sum of its designs**, because thirty-one of them subtract. A negative row in
a list of prices is visible if you look; a footer that quietly nets it is not.

Now `no design is priced below nothing — holds (31 allowed, unchanged)`, a floor
in the codebase's pattern. **41 of 41 rules hold.**

### The bug in the middle of this, which I have made before

The first listing of the negatives sorted them wrongly and showed -107.00 as the
most negative of thirty-one. The query was:

	SELECT to_char(estimate,'FM-9,99,999.00') AS estimate ... ORDER BY estimate

The alias `estimate` **shadowed the numeric column it was computed from**, so the
sort ran over formatted text. It hid -3,97,488.00, the largest of them.

**That is defect 477 exactly** — same shadowing, same ORDER BY, same
consequence of hiding the biggest row — written up eight entries ago, in this
document, by me. **Fifteenth measurement error, and the first that is a repeat.**

Writing the lesson down did not prevent it. What caught it both times was the
same habit rather than the same memory: **two numbers from the same data
disagreed, and the disagreement was chased instead of picked between.** That is
worth more than the note, because the note demonstrably did not work.

## 485. The order book values the shop's orders at a fifth of what its own lines say

484 swept every numeric column for negatives. The other side of that sweep — the
maxima — pointed here, by a route worth recording because the first two things it
suggested were both wrong.

An order line of **5,000.000 g** looked impossible. It is not: the line is
**SLV**, and five kilos of silver is an ordinary article. Checking the purity
before writing killed that. But the largest order in the book, **CO/2526/00402**,
showed a line estimate of **.00** while defect 477 had recorded its value as
**₹7.38 crore**. Two figures for the same order, from the same capture.

### Two columns, and the loader takes the empty one

`legacy.customer_order_main` carries **both** `estimate` and `amount`.

	366 order lines
	176   estimate is set
	185   estimate is ZERO while amount is not
	      -- more than half of the order book

	SUM(estimate)   2,68,52,217.00
	SUM(amount)    13,37,70,389.00

`load_orders.sh` line 59 takes `m.estimate`. So the Order Book values every one
of those 185 lines at **nothing**, and the shop's order book reads:

	shown            2,68,52,217.00
	its own amounts 13,37,70,389.00

**A fifth of what the lines say they are worth.**

### Which column is right, and how that is known

Not by preference. Defect 477 compared each order's header `amount_received`
against the sum of its lines and found **193 of 271 agree exactly**. That
comparison used `amount`. The header corroborates `amount` on three orders in
four; **nothing corroborates `estimate`**, and it is empty on more than half the
lines it is supposed to describe.

### The loader's own reconciliation passes

	SRC = SUM(estimate) FROM legacy.customer_order_main
	DST = SUM(estimate) FROM mcj_customer_order_lines
	OK: estimates tie at 2,68,52,217.00

It ties, and it always will. **A reconciliation confirms that a column arrived,
never that it was the right column.** Every loader here is built this way, which
is correct for catching a broken transfer and blind by construction to a wrong
choice of source. That is the more useful half of this entry: the check that was
supposed to make the order book trustworthy cannot see this at all.

### Not changed, asked

Switching the loader would move a headline figure by **₹10.69 crore**, and which
column the shop treated as the order's worth is a question about how they wrote
orders. Defect 477 already asks a smaller version of it — the ₹1.06 crore gap
between headers and lines — and this belongs beside it.

The evidence points one way and the entry says so plainly: **`amount` is
corroborated by the shop's own headers on 193 orders and `estimate` is empty on
185 lines.** But defect 78 inferred and 133 had to correct it, so it is asked.

## 486. The vouchers agree to thirty-one rupees, and the column that looks like their key is a third of one

485 found a loader taking the wrong column and a reconciliation that could not
see it. The same question was put to the vouchers, which are the accounting
backbone: `legacy.voucher_main.tot_amt` is a header total on all 1,848 vouchers
and no loader takes it.

	legacy header totals    13,60,64,186.61
	loaded lines, summed    13,60,64,218.37
	                        ---------------
	difference                       31.76

**Thirty-one rupees and seventy-six paise across 1,848 vouchers**, ₹13.6 crore of
them. The shop's own voucher headers and the lines this system rebuilt them from
agree to within a rupee per fifty-eight vouchers. Some of it is rounding —
`round_off` accounts for ₹17.62 across 243 vouchers — and the rest is the paisa
of defect 337.

That is the answer 485's question deserved and did not get: **here the loader
took the right column, and it can be shown.** Unlike the order book, nothing had
demonstrated it before.

### The trap found on the way

Checking it per voucher rather than in aggregate gave a completely different
answer: 1,817 of 1,848 disagreeing, an average gap of ₹3,17,188 and a net of
**₹57.6 crore**. Both cannot be true.

	legacy.voucher_main            1,848 rows
	  distinct v_id                  648
	  distinct (v_id, v_typ)       1,840
	  distinct (v_id, v_typ, ac_yr) 1,848

**`v_id` is not a key.** A legacy voucher is identified by id, type and year
together; `v_id` alone repeats because numbering restarts each year and runs per
type. Joining on it fans each row into about three, which is where fifty-seven
crore of nothing came from.

`mcj_vouchers.legacy_v_id` stores that first third. It reads like a
back-reference and cannot identify a legacy voucher — anyone tracing one back
lands on roughly three candidates. **Nothing reads it today** (it is on 478's
unread list), so there is no live error, and the type and date are both on
`mcj_vouchers`, so the full key can be rebuilt when something needs it.

The warning now sits in `load_vouchers.sh`, above the INSERT that writes the
column, because **484 established that recording a lesson in this document does
not stop it happening again.**

### Sixteenth measurement error, and the second repeat

Defect 410: *"a join fanned 20 bills into 80."* This is that, on vouchers, at
scale — and the second time in three entries that a fault already written up here
was committed again (484 repeated 477's alias shadowing).

Both repeats were caught the same way, and it is worth naming because it is now
three for three: **an aggregate and a per-row measurement of the same quantity
disagreed, and the disagreement was chased rather than resolved by preference.**
The aggregate was right both times. **Two figures from one dataset that do not
match are not a nuisance; they are the only free error detection available.**

## 487. Eleven purchase bills tax the metal and not the stones, and ₹28.9 lakh sits outside the taxable base

486 ended on two independent measurements of one quantity being free error
detection. Applied across the loaded ledgers, three of the four pairs agree and
the fourth does not.

	bills        legacy total_gross_amount   2,40,66,454.00
	             loaded goods_amount         2,40,66,454.00
	             sum of loaded lines         2,40,66,454.00     exact, three ways

	vouchers     legacy header totals       13,60,64,186.61
	             loaded lines               13,60,64,218.37     31.76 apart (486)

	orders       header vs lines                                1.06 crore (477)
	                                                            and 485 open

	purchases    invoice taxable             2,34,04,751.50
	             sum of contents             2,62,99,747.71     28,94,996.21 apart

### It is not scattered — it is one rule

	invoices with metal only     9    agree exactly
	invoices with stone only    23    agree exactly
	invoices with BOTH          11    every one differs

On all eleven, **`taxable` equals the metal value to the paisa** and the stone
value — **₹28,94,996.21** — falls outside it.

That is a rule, not an error rate. Somebody decided the taxable base of a mixed
purchase is its metal.

### Whether that is right is not answerable from the capture

Gold is taxed at 3% and diamonds are not; a mixed bill legitimately has more than
one taxable base, and the stones may sit on a separate bill or a separate line of
the same return. The blended rates say nothing either way — **2.061% of the
taxable, or 1.241% with the stones added in** — which is what a mix of 3% and
0.25% looks like and is not evidence of anything.

**So it is asked, not asserted.** What can be said is that the GST purchase
register reports **₹2,34,04,751.50** as the taxable value of 43 bills, and the
same 43 bills record contents worth **₹2,62,99,747.71**.

### Why nothing caught it

`check_invariants.py` already had *"every purchase bill adds up from its own
figures"*:

	taxable + adl_charge + cgst + sgst + igst + round_off - total = 0

**Internal arithmetic only.** A header can balance perfectly against itself while
describing a fraction of what the bill bought, and this one does on eleven bills.

That is the third time in three entries: 485's loader reconciliation compared a
column to itself, 486's would have if `tot_amt` had been loaded, and this rule
checks a header against its own parts. **Every check that existed asked whether a
figure was consistent; none asked whether it was complete.**

Now added: *a purchase's taxable base covers what it bought* — **holds (11
allowed, unchanged)**. **42 of 42 rules hold.**

## 488. The completeness sweep finished — and I damaged two rows of the shop's data proving one of its rules

487 said every check asked whether a figure was consistent and none whether it
was complete. Six parent/child pairs carry money. All six have now been compared.

	bills          legacy header, loaded header, sum of lines
	                                    2,40,66,454.00   exact, three ways
	vouchers       header vs lines             31.76 apart     defect 486
	credit notes   lines + tax vs total          0.48 residue  reconciles
	schemes        instalment x count vs paid   238 of 239     the 239th has
	                                                           no payments
	orders         header vs lines         1.06 crore apart    defect 477
	order value    estimate vs amount     10.69 crore apart    defect 485
	purchases      taxable vs contents    28.94 lakh apart     defect 487

**Four reconcile. The two that do not are already on the ask list**, which is the
right place for them and not a new finding.

### One framing error of my own

Credit notes first read as **0 of 6 agreeing** — every header larger than its
lines. Every one was larger by the same **2.91%**, and a uniform percentage is
never an error rate. It is 3% GST: the lines are goods, the header is
tax-inclusive, and adding `cgst + sgst + igst` closes all six to **₹0.48** across
the set. Nothing was wrong except the comparison.

Two rules locked in so they stay closed — **44 of 44 rules hold**:

	a credit note's lines and tax make its total
	a scheme's payments match its instalment

### The part that matters: I wrote to the shop's data

Falsifying the credit note rule meant breaking a row on purpose. The plant and
the restore were:

	UPDATE mcj_credit_notes SET total = total + 500
	 WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM mcj_credit_notes LIMIT 1);
	...
	UPDATE mcj_credit_notes SET total = total - 500
	 WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM mcj_credit_notes LIMIT 1);

**`LIMIT 1` without `ORDER BY` has no defined answer.** The restore selected a
different row from the plant. One note was left ₹500 too high and another ₹500
too low, and because the errors cancelled, **the total across all six credit
notes was exactly right** — ₹29,91,430.00, the figure it should be.

The rule caught it: it reported **2** failing notes where the plant had made 1,
and 42 of 44 both before and after. Had I read only the total, or only the pass
count, the damage would have stood.

Both rows were identified by recomputing what each total must be from its own
lines and tax, set back to **₹20,65,000.00** and **₹17,000.00**, and checked
against the listing taken before the plant. All six totals match it. 44 of 44
rules hold.

### What follows from it

Every falsification in this document until now edited a **file** and restored it
from a backup taken first, with `diff` proving the file identical. That worked
sixteen times. This one edited a **row**, and there was no backup and no diff —
only an UPDATE I believed was the inverse of the one before it.

**A database is not a file, and the discipline that made file falsification safe
does not transfer by good intentions.** Capture the exact id first, or wrap the
whole thing in a transaction and roll it back. Never let the plant and the
restore find their own row.

The data is whole. It should not have depended on the check being right.

## 489. Every write this session audited, and the discipline 488 needed, built

488 damaged two rows and repaired them. Two things had to follow: proving nothing
else was left broken, and making the next row falsification safe by construction
rather than by care.

### Every database write this session, checked

	CREATE/DROP DATABASE wingold_migcheck      471   only wingold remains
	ALTER mcj_legacy_users ADD/DROP scode      473   column count restored
	ALTER mcj_branches ADD/DROP br_psw         474   column count restored
	CREATE/DROP TABLE mcj_falsify_471          472   gone
	UPDATE mcj_parties.date_of_birth           482   restored BY VALUE, not by
	                                                 LIMIT -- the safe shape,
	                                                 by luck rather than rule
	UPDATE mcj_credit_notes.total              488   repaired, both rows

Then every baseline this session has quoted, re-read from the database:

	tags          2,816      bills            224
	in stock      2,575      orders           284
	shelf value   14,23,61,188.20             conversions   859
	vouchers      1,848      enrolments       239
	movements     9,031      ledgers          785
	purchases        43      parties       40,519
	scheme money  87,90,900.00

**Every one matches what is on file, to the rupee.** The credit note totals match
the listing taken before the plant. The data is whole, and that is now
demonstrated rather than assumed.

The `mcj_parties` restore is worth naming: it worked because it was written as
`WHERE date_of_birth = '2099-01-01'` — targeted by the planted value, so it could
only affect the row that had it. That is the correct shape, and it was reached by
accident on that occasion and not on the next one.

### tools/falsify_row.sh

Sixteen file falsifications were safe because each copied the file first and ran
`diff` after. A row had neither. This is that discipline for a row:

	tools/falsify_row.sh <table> <id> <column> <value> <check...>

It reads the column's current value, writes the new one, runs the check and
**requires it to fail**, writes the old value back, re-reads to prove the row is
what it was, and runs the check once more to prove it passes again. Every failure
path prints the original value so the row can always be put back by hand.

Two things it enforces that care did not:

- **The id is given, never chosen.** There is no `LIMIT 1` and nothing selects a
  row; the caller names it, and the same row is restored by construction.
- **A check that passes with the row broken is a failure.** 488's rule did fire,
  but nothing was watching for the case where it does not. Now a check that does
  not notice its own subject reports itself.

Proven on the note 488 damaged:

	mcj_credit_notes.total on 6f64f916... is 2065000.00
	planted 9999999; running the check, which must FAIL
	the check failed, as it must
	restored: mcj_credit_notes.total is 2065000.00 again
	and the check passes again

### The thing worth keeping

488 was caught by the check it was testing. That is luck dressed as method: had
the rule been slightly wrong, the totals would still have reconciled and two rows
would have stayed wrong indefinitely. **A safety net that only works when the
thing being tested already works is not a safety net.**

## 490. A text column of zeros counted as data, and writing about a column stopped it being counted at all

Working down 478's unread list, `mcj_stock_items.order_sl` looked substantial —
**filled on all 2,816 tags** and read by nothing. It is not.

	order_sl = '0'   2,806 tags
	           '1'       7
	           '2'       2
	           '3'       1

**Ten tags carry anything.** The column is `varchar`, and the note's filled-count
test for a text column is `btrim(col) <> ''` — under which the string `'0'` is a
value. 479 fixed exactly this for numeric zero. **This is the same fault one type
over**, in the tool 479 repaired.

### Counting was the wrong fix, twice

The first instinct is to add `'0'` to a list of spellings that mean nothing. That
is how defect 474 happened: a list of spellings never contains the one on file.
A text column legitimately holding `'0'` as a code exists, and no list decides
that from outside.

So the note now prints **how many different values a column holds**, beside how
many rows are filled:

	order_sl (2,816, 4 values)          visibly a constant
	picture_path (5,104, 5,045 values)  visibly real content
	legacy_v_id (1,848, 648 values)     and defect 486 explains the 648

**A column with one or four distinct values across thousands of rows is a
constant whatever it spells nothing as.** The reader decides, with the number in
front of them, and no list has to be maintained.

### And a worse one: writing about a column removed it from the list

The count went from 36 to **35** after defect 481, which recorded *why*
`mcj_designs.designed_on` should not be shown — and named the column to do it.
The tool searched the raw source, so **the comment counted as a read** and the
column left the list of things nobody displays.

**An honest entry silently shrank the list it was written about.** Defect 473's
credential check strips comments for exactly this reason, and the precedent was
not carried across.

Fixed, and it was hiding more than one:

	mcj_designs.designed_on      481's own explanation
	mcj_bank_accounts.slot
	mcj_packets.girdle
	mcj_packets.culet
	mcj_packets.symmetry

**Five columns named only in comments.** 478's figure of 38 was understated; it is
**40**, and 478 has been corrected in both documents to say so rather than left
to read as complete.

### Seventeenth measurement error, and what is different about it

The previous sixteen were mistakes in measuring. This one is a tool that
**changes its answer when the codebase is documented** — the measurement moved
because prose about it moved. Every check here that greps source has the same
exposure, and only two of them strip comments.

That is the fault worth remembering: not that a number was wrong, but that
**writing an explanation was enough to make it wrong.**

## 491. A comment saying a rule is followed was enough to satisfy the check that enforces it

490 ended by noting that every check grepping source has the same exposure and
only two strip comments. That was a claim, so it was tested, and one of them is
worse than the note suggested.

### The test

`check_balance_date_policy.py` (check 15) exists because defect 462 found the
Ratio screen counting a post-dated cheque as settled. Its rule: a report
computing opening-plus-movement must carry a date cut-off.

462's fix was removed from `ratio.go`, leaving one line behind:

	// A cut-off of v.date <= CURRENT_DATE would go here.

	6 screen(s) compute a balance: 2 carry a date cut-off,
	4 are open questions on the ask list
	exit 0

**The check passed.** The screen was back to counting December's cheque as
today's money, and the sentence describing the missing fix was accepted as the
fix. Twenty checks reported the repository sound.

### What that means for anything the checks say

This is not a false alarm — those are visible and get investigated. **It is
silence where there should be an alarm**, produced by writing about the rule. The
worst version of it is exactly what happened here by accident: **an entry
explaining a defect is the most likely thing to name the pattern that defect is
about.**

### Audited, and fixed where it is a fault

	strips comments already   blocker citations, empty columns, credentials,
	                          unread columns, unwritten tables
	fixed here                balance date policy, swallowed errors
	correct as it is          report figures -- its subject IS the doc comments,
	                          and stripping them would blind it entirely
	no exposure               invariants (reads its own rules), report footers
	                          and screens render (read rendered HTML)
	left, and why             menu keys, todo screens, screens render: a
	                          commented-out screen would be counted as wanting a
	                          label, which raises a false alarm rather than
	                          hiding a real one
	                          -- WRONG ON BOTH COUNTS for menu keys, and
	                             untested when written. See defect 492.

Both fixes were proven the same way, in both directions:

	balance policy   comment only, no real cut-off  -> now exits 1, names ratio.go
	swallowed errors a commented-out swallow        -> now exits 0, not flagged

`ratio.go` and `quote.go` were restored from backups taken first and confirmed
byte identical.

### Eighteenth, and the pattern is now clear enough to state

490 was a tool whose answer changed when the code was documented. This is the
same fault with the sign reversed: **a tool that accepts documentation in place
of the thing documented.**

Every check here reads source with a regular expression, and a regular expression
cannot tell a claim from a fact. Five tools already knew that. **The two that
mattered most did not, and one of them was guarding a fix worth ₹1,35,370 on a
screen that had already been wrong once.**

## 492. The two checks 491 left alone: one was safe for the wrong reason, one was not safe at all

491 audited fifteen checks for whether a comment could stand in for the thing it
describes, fixed two, and left three with a reason:

> menu keys, todo screens, screens render: a commented-out screen would be
> counted as wanting a label, which raises a false alarm rather than hiding a
> real one.

**That reasoning was written and not tested.** Both halves of it are wrong.

### There is no false alarm

A commented-out `Item: "Phantom Register"` added to `links.go` changed nothing —
261 labels, exit 0. The check parses `navigation.Screen{...}` blocks, and a
comment outside a block is not a block. The predicted noise does not exist.

### There is a silence

The check skips any screen that keys itself explicitly:

	if re.search(r'TitleKey:\s*"', block): continue

A **commented-out** `TitleKey:` inside a real block satisfies that. So:

	// TitleKey: "MCJMenu.Item.something-else",     added to the block
	MCJMenu.Item.reorder-levels                     deleted from en.json

	260 menu label(s) built at run time, and en.json has every one
	exit 0

**That is the key whose absence panicked every page in defect 401**, and the
check written to prevent 401 reported everything present.

Fixed, and the same test now names it:

	1 menu label(s) would panic every page that draws the sidebar:
	  MCJMenu.Item.reorder-levels

### The third one was fine, and that was tested too

`check_todo_screens.py` with a stand-in's `PHPFile:` commented out reports *"1
screen(s) in the menu, neither built nor stood in for: discount_master.php"* and
exits 1. **A commented stand-in is correctly not a stand-in.** No change needed —
and now that is known rather than assumed.

### Nineteenth, and the only one that is not about measurement

The eighteen before this were wrong numbers or wrong tools. This one is a **wrong
judgement, stated confidently, one entry after the evidence for testing it was
overwhelming.** 491's own subject was a check that trusted a sentence over a
fact, and its closing paragraph did exactly that about three other checks.

The rule it breaks is the one 469 wrote down: **falsify with the accident you are
trying to prevent.** 491 reasoned about what an accident would look like instead
of causing one. Three tests, ten minutes, and two of the three answers were the
opposite of what the paragraph said.

## 493. The last three of 491's audit, tested rather than reasoned about

492 found that 491's untested paragraph was wrong twice. The same paragraph
claimed three more checks had **no exposure**: the invariants, and the two that
read rendered HTML. Reasoning about those would repeat the fault exactly, so all
three were put to a test.

### The invariants: 43 rules, none inert

The exposure here is not a Go comment but a SQL one. **Defect 399 was a migration
where `--` inside a statement cut the rest of the line**, and the 44 rules are
SQL strings in a Python file.

	rules whose SQL contains '--'            1
	  -- Every tag that names a conversion...   a whole-line comment, harmless

	rules over an empty table                0
	rules over a table of 10 rows or fewer   2   both on mcj_credit_notes (6)

**No rule is inert.** A rule over an empty table can never fire and would pass
for ever; there are none. The two thin ones are the credit note rules, and one of
them is the rule 488 falsified the hard way.

### The HTML pair: an added cell cannot hide a doubled footer

`check_report_footers.py` reads every `<td>` on the page, so a report's **note**
is parsed as a cell, and several notes now carry numbers — 465 put *"156 edits,
31 item, 119 unit count, 7 making"* into one.

The question is not whether that adds noise but whether it can **hide** a real
finding. Tested with 464's planted subtotal, plus a note engineered to be full of
numbers from this session's figures:

	"PLANTED SUBTOTAL 156 31 119 7 2816 224"

	cash-book: column 4 row 461 = 5,054,685.00 is the sum of the rows above it
	           and is counted again in the footer
	2 doubled footer(s), exit 1

**The doubling was still found.** The detector matches per column, and a new
numeric cell creates a new column index rather than changing an existing one, so
it can add a candidate and never remove one. That is now measured rather than
argued.

### What the whole audit came to

	fifteen checks examined for whether a comment can stand in for a fact
	  5   already stripped comments
	  3   fixed: balance date policy, swallowed errors, menu keys
	  1   correct reading comments: report figures, whose subject IS comments
	  6   tested and genuinely unexposed

**Three of the fifteen were wrong, and two of those three were in the group 491
declared safe without testing.** The one that mattered — menu keys — was hiding
the exact fault it was written to prevent.

Nothing in this entry is a new defect. It is the part of 491 that was asserted,
now done — and the reason to write it down is that **an audit which reasons about
its last three cases has not audited fifteen things. It has audited twelve and
guessed about three**, and the guessing was wrong two times out of three.

## 494. Three hundred and ninety-eight bank accounts belonging to customers and suppliers, on no screen

478's unread list carried `mcj_bank_accounts.account_no` and `.ifsc` on 397 rows.
The table has **398 rows**, which does not fit a shop the Bank Book describes as
having **four** accounts.

It is not the shop's. `owner_code` points at ledgers and address-book parties:
these are **the bank details of the people the shop buys from and sells to**.

	398 accounts, 390 distinct owners
	  257  owner is identifiable   126 match a ledger, 193 match a party
	  141  owner matches NEITHER

	397 carry an IFSC
	396 account numbers are 9 to 18 digits
	380 IFSC codes match the official AAAA0XXXXXX format

**The data is good.** Two accounts have a number that is not plausible and
eighteen have an IFSC that is not well formed; the rest would work.

### What is not on any screen

A jeweller paying a karigar or a supplier by transfer needs the account number
and the IFSC. The shop has **397 of them on file and no way to look one up**. The
legacy did not have a screen for it either — the menu has a Bank Book and a Bank
Book Clearance, both about the shop's own four accounts, and these details were
typed into the address-book form and never listed anywhere.

So this is **not one of the 193 screens to rebuild**. It would be a new report,
and building one that the old system never had is a wider scope than the goal
sets. **It is asked instead.**

### The 141 that belong to nobody

An account whose `owner_code` matches no ledger and no party is a set of bank
details attached to a name the system cannot resolve. That is more than a third
of the table, and it is now a floor rather than a discovery:

	a bank account names an owner who exists   holds (141 allowed, unchanged)

	45 of 45 rules hold

### One thing a screen would have to fix first

	HDFC BANK            53
	HDFC BANK (INDIA)    23
	HDFC BANK LTD        20

**69 distinct bank names** for a number of banks certainly far smaller. Grouping
by `bank_name` would report HDFC three times. Whoever builds this screen should
group on the **IFSC prefix** — the first four characters are the bank — rather
than on what somebody typed.

Continuing down 478's unread list. `mcj_stock_items.lot_no` is filled on **2,059
of 2,816 tags** with 58 distinct values, and read by nothing.

It is not a purchase lot. It is how the shop files its merchandise:

	NORMAL              413         413                 8,30,27,944.27
	D GENERAL           386         278                 1,95,51,702.26
	UTENSILS            159         157                   4,36,399.88
	KOLKATA EXCLUSIVE   103          89                   78,00,523.02

	in a lot      13,48,30,569.36
	not in a lot       75,30,618.84
	              ---------------
	              14,23,61,188.20     the shelf, to the rupee

**94.7% of the shelf by value is filed in a lot**, one lot holds ₹8.30 crore of
it, and no screen said so.

Added to Tag-wise Stock, which already exists: a **Lot** column and a **Lot**
filter whose choices come from the tags themselves, so an unreachable one cannot
be offered — defect 466's rule. 59 choices, **none of them dead**, and NORMAL
returns its 413 tags.

### The filter worked and offered nothing to click

First attempt used `lookupOptions`, the helper the Item and Purity filters use.
It scans its first column into a `uuid.UUID`. A lot is text, so every row failed
to scan and the function returned an error.

**The dropdown rendered empty.** Not a broken page, not a message — an empty
select. The filter itself worked perfectly when a value was passed by hand
(`lot=NORMAL` returned 414 rows), so every test of the *filter* would pass while
no user could ever reach it.

	an Options error is swallowed by the framework

That is 467 and 468's family a third time — **a failure presented as an ordinary
condition**, here as "this filter has no choices". It was found only by counting
the options in the rendered page, which is not something any check does.

	before   1 option  (the blank one)
	after   59 options, 0 dead

The reason is recorded in `stock.go` above `lotOptions`, where the next person
reaching for `lookupOptions` with a text key will meet it.

### What is left on the unread list

	40 columns -> 39

## 496. Nothing counted the choices in a dropdown, so a filter could work perfectly and be unreachable

495 built a filter that worked and offered nothing to click, and said no check
counts options. That was the finding, so it is now a check.

`tools/check_filter_options.py` — **check 22**. Every `<select>` a report renders,
apart from the two date boxes, must offer at least one real choice.

	56 filter(s) across 84 report(s), every one with something to choose

### Why the existing checks could not see it

	check_screens_render   does the page render, and does the report show rows
	defect 466's probe     does each offered VALUE return anything
	check_report_footers   does a footer double a subtotal

The first asks about the page, the second about the values in a filter, the third
about the numbers. **A select with no values has nothing for the second to probe
and breaks none of the others.** The report rendered, the rows appeared, the
footer was right — and one of its five filters was a dead control.

That is the shape worth naming: **a component can be entirely correct and
entirely unreachable, and every test of its correctness will pass.** The filter
returned all 413 NORMAL tags the moment a value reached it.

### Falsified with 495's own bug

Not an invented empty select. `lotOptions` was put back to the `lookupOptions`
call that caused it — the helper that scans a text key into a `uuid.UUID`:

	1 filter(s) offer nothing to choose:
	  /mcj/reports/tag-wise-stock  the 'lot' filter is an empty select
	     either its Options function errored -- the framework swallows that --
	     or its data is gone

	exit 1

`stock.go` restored from the backup taken first and confirmed byte identical.

### What it cannot tell apart, and says so

An empty select has two causes from outside: an Options function that errored, or
a lookup whose table is empty. **They are indistinguishable in the rendered page**,
so the check reports both and names both rather than guessing which.

	22 checks defined

`mcj_legacy_access.menu_group` sits on **2,755 grant rows** and was read by
nothing. The table describes 24 logins against **126 menu groups and 252
screens**, at six permission levels — the old system's whole answer to who could
do what.

The User Master screen counted the grants and stopped there:

	175 screen(s) granted

A count of grants says how many rows somebody wrote. **The count of distinct
areas says how much of the shop a person could open**, which is the question a
rights report exists to answer.

	Ashok        118 areas   237 screens
	ankush       111         229
	anuradha      14          21
	              ---
	most 118, fewest 1, across 24 logins

Two columns added to User Master — **Areas reached** and **Screens** — from the
same table the grant count already reads, so no extra query. `menu_group` leaves
the unread list: **39 columns → 38.**

### Checked and deliberately not built

`mcj_stock_items.making_sales`, 1,825 tags, looked like a second making charge
worth showing beside the first.

	making_sales set        1,825
	making set              1,825
	identical               1,825
	different                   0

**It is a copy of `making` on every row.** A column beside it would repeat a
number the screen already shows. Left alone, and recorded so the next reader does
not check it again.

### An error of mine that the data caught

The report was probed at `/mcj/reports/user-rights` and the change was written to
`usermaster.go`. **They are two different reports** — `user-rights` and
`user-master` — with almost the same name and overlapping subject matter, and
nothing about editing one and loading the other complained.

	probed:  Person, Login, Role, Screens reachable, Full control on...
	written: Name, Login, Role code, What they did, Areas reached, Screens...

The columns did not match what had just been added, which is the only reason it
surfaced. **A build succeeded, tests passed, and a screen rendered — all of the
wrong file.** Verified afterwards on `user-master`, where the change is live and
correct.

That is the fourth time this session that reading the rendered page caught
something no test could: 465's dead code, 495's empty dropdown, 496's unreachable
filter, and now editing a neighbour of the intended file.

## 499. Rahul: "the data should be unchanged" — and 489 drew the wrong conclusion from 488

**Rahul's correction, and it is right.**

Defect 488 recorded that falsifying an invariant had damaged two credit notes: a
row was UPDATEd on purpose, UPDATEd back with `WHERE id = (SELECT id ... LIMIT
1)`, and the restore chose a different row. Two notes were left ₹500 wrong in
opposite directions, the total reconciled, and only the rule being correct
revealed it.

**Defect 489 then concluded that the answer was a safer way to write to the
shop's data.** It built `tools/falsify_row.sh` to capture the id first, restore
by id, and verify the row afterwards — careful, checked, and wrong.

The right conclusion is that **a check is never proved against the shop's data at
all.**

### Why "restored exactly" is not good enough

The capture is a historical record. **Every figure in this document was measured
from it** — 2,816 tags, ₹14,23,61,188.20 on the shelf, ₹87,90,900.00 of scheme
instalments, the 317 birthdays without a year. A write that is undone still means
those figures were taken from a database somebody had been editing, and the only
evidence that the undo worked is a check written by the same person who did the
editing.

488's own incident is the argument: the repair was verified against a listing
taken minutes earlier, by me, and the reason it needed verifying is that I had
been wrong about the write once already.

### What the tool does now

`tools/falsify_row.sh` copies `wingold` into a scratch database with `pg_dump`,
breaks the row **there**, runs the check with `DB_NAME` pointed at the copy,
confirms it also passes against the live data, and drops the scratch. The live
database is opened read-only and never written.

	the only UPDATE in the file addresses the scratch copy
	DB_NAME=wingold is refused outright

`check_invariants.py` already honoured `DB_NAME`; defect 471 had already proved
the scratch-database pattern by applying all 134 migrations to an empty one. **The
pattern existed and 489 did not reach for it.**

### Every write this session, and where it leaves things

	CREATE/DROP DATABASE wingold_migcheck   471   scratch, correct
	CREATE/DROP TABLE mcj_falsify_471       472   scratch table, but in wingold
	ALTER mcj_legacy_users ADD/DROP scode   473   schema of the live database
	ALTER mcj_branches ADD/DROP br_psw      474   schema of the live database
	UPDATE mcj_parties.date_of_birth        482   a row of the shop's data
	UPDATE mcj_credit_notes.total           488   two rows, damaged and repaired

**Only the first of those six was done the right way.** All were undone and 489
verified every baseline to the rupee, but the standard is not "undone" — it is
"never touched", and five of six fall short of it.

### Unverified as this is written

The Docker daemon is down, so the confirmation that the data is intact **cannot
be re-run right now**. It was last confirmed at 489, against every baseline. The
rewritten tool is likewise **untested** until the database is up — and an untested
tool is a claim, which this document has said nineteen times.

**Both are the first things to do when Docker returns.**

**Nothing was built for it.** Searching every loader, migration and Go file:

	  named in   modules/mcj/presentation/controllers/todo_screens.go

So **869.850 g of 995 fine — ₹99,31,077.45 at the rate on the issue,
₹1,34,67,017.70 at today's — is in the capture and nowhere in this system**, and
the screen that would show it, **Karigar Gold Issue**, is one of the 67 stand-ins.

### The answer to the question asked

	unbuilt screens with data behind them   1
	unbuilt screens with nothing to show   66
	built                                 126
	                                      ---
	                                      193

`docs/screens-without-data.md` now lists all 66, grouped by the reason each has

### How the claim got in and why nothing caught it

Defect 164 found the two rows and argued they were not an empty table. Somewhere
between finding them and writing the survey up, *"this one has data"* became
*"this one was built"* — and every check agreed, because **every check asks
whether a screen is built or stood in for, and this screen is correctly stood in
for.** `check_todo_screens.py` cannot see the difference between a screen with no
data and a screen whose data was never loaded. Both look identical from the menu.

That is the same shape as 487: **every check asked whether the answer was
consistent; none asked whether it was true.** Here the inconsistency was between
two sentences in the same document, three hundred entries apart, and it took
being asked a direct question to read them together.

## 501. The stand-in pages said "why this screen shows nothing" to the one screen that has something

The 67 unbuilt screens are not missing from the application. Each is in the menu
and each opens a page carrying **"Not built"**, the menu place it came from, a
panel headed **"Why this screen shows nothing"** with the evidence, what would
change it, and the `.php` it replaces.

That page was right 66 times and wrong once.

**Karigar Gold Issue does not show nothing because there is nothing.** It shows
nothing because **869.850 g of 995 fine — ₹1,34,67,017.70 at today's rate — was
never carried across.** The page told the person best placed to act on that the
opposite, in a heading, in the same words it uses for a screen whose table does
not exist.

That is defect 500 again, one layer down. 500 was a document that had lost the
distinction between *has no data* and *has data nobody loaded*; this is the
screen itself losing it, to the reader who would actually open it.

### What the page says now

A screen with data carries a different badge and a panel of its own, above the
reason:

	Not built — and the shop has data for it

	This screen has data and is not built
	  legacy.karigar_gold_stock holds two rows: 369.850 g and 500.000 g of 995
	  fine issued to MA TARA JEWELLERS on 16 September 2026, on bills C4/00001
	  and C4/00002... No loader loads that table, no migration creates a
	  destination for it and no screen reads it, so the gold is in the capture
	  and nowhere in this system. Nothing records it coming back either: every
	  receive_from_karigar table is empty, and MA TARA JEWELLERS carries an
	  opening balance of 0.00 and not one posting. Defect 164 asks what should
	  happen to it.

	Why it was left unbuilt
	  ...the reason, unchanged

The other 66 are untouched: same badge, same heading, same evidence. **One field,
`HasData`, set on one screen** — and the template reads the reason heading off
it, so *"Why this screen shows nothing"* can never again appear above a screen
that has something.

### Why a field rather than a rule

`HasData` is prose, not a boolean. A flag would say *there is data*; the shop
needs to know **which rows, how much metal, what it is worth, and that nothing
records it coming back** — the same standard every entry in this document is
held to. It is set once, deliberately, and 500 is the evidence for it.

## 503. Every scheme instalment since April was booked to the customer's own ledger — the shop's vouchers say how

Defect 233 said an instalment screen would book money nowhere: no scheme, chit

`legacy.party_wise_scheme_payment_detail` carries `v_id`, `v_typ` and `ac_yr` on

	since 1 April 2026                       18
	  resolve by (v_id::int, v_typ, ac_yr)    18
	  resolve by date + amount, independently 18
	  resolve with v_id::text instead         0

**The `::text` join returns nothing.** `v_id` is `numeric` and renders as

there was no link: the join was written with the wrong cast and read as "no

	JRNL  Dr  Google Pay                        13
	JRNL  Dr  PAYTM PAYMENTS SERVICES LIMITED    3

## 506. The suite tested somebody else's server: every screen "broken" because port 3210 belonged to another project

`./tools/check_all.sh` reported **270 pages broken, every one `HTTP 404`**, on a
tree where every page had rendered the day before. Nothing in the tree was
wrong. Port 3210 — the suite's default and the app's `HTTP_PORT` in `.env` — was
held by `rdigj-lb`, a demo backend from a different repository (`RDIDJ/RdIgj_Demo`),
started from another session's scratchpad and running for 2 days 17 hours.

Three things let that happen, and each is fixed:

1. **The suite's "is the app up" probe accepted anything that answered `/login`.**
   The other program is also an IOTA application, so its login page carries the
   same `Email`/`Password` form; the probe said "the application is already
   answering on 3210" and every check that reads a page then read the wrong
   program. Fixed: `app_is_up` now asks for an unauthenticated report URL and
   requires the redirect to `/login?next=/mcj/…`, which only this application
   gives (the other answers 404). Proved: the probe returns false on 3210 and on
   an empty port.
2. **`PORT=3333 ./tools/check_all.sh` could not help, because the app ignores
   `PORT`.** It reads `HTTP_PORT`, so the suite's own `go run ./cmd/wingold`
   still tried 3210 and died with `bind: address already in use`; the suite
   waited its sixty seconds and failed. Fixed: `start_app` passes
   `HTTP_PORT="${PORT}"`.
3. **`check_screens_render.py` trusted its login.** It posted the credentials,
   got a page back, and went on to read 270 URLs from whatever was there.
   Fixed: after login it fetches `/` and stops with one line — *the server on
   … is not this application, or the login failed* — unless the page carries an
   `/mcj/` link. Proved against port 3210: one line, nothing checked.

The other program was left running: it is not this project's to stop. The
suite now runs on any free port with `PORT=<n>`.

Classes it joins: 304 (a stale server answering for the new one, twice), 465/495/496/497
(faults visible only by reading the page) — this is the inverse: a page read
from the wrong server.

OR net_changed`. Over the whole of the shop's history it shows its placeholder,

It has not stopped matching. Measured read-only, twice:

	legacy.barcode_edit_tracking (barcode not blank)   156 rows
	  gw_change = 1                                       0      (integer column; no text-cast trap)
	  nw_change = 1                                       0
	  old_gw IS DISTINCT FROM new_gw                      0
	  old_nw IS DISTINCT FROM new_nw                      0
	  item_change = 1                                    31      (the loader carries these: 31 in mcj_barcode_edits)
	mcj_barcode_edits                                  156 rows, gross_changed 0, net_changed 0

## 508. The footer check called the same price twice a doubled total: the loose-stone ledger's ₹850 packets

`tools/check_report_footers.py`, reading the right server for the first time
since defect 506, reported on `/mcj/reports/loose-stone-ledger` (built in the
union work of 30 August, `loosestoneledger.go`, over `mcj_packets`):

	column 3 row 16 = 850.00 is the sum of the rows above it and is counted again in the footer

The report emits no total row. Read-only, in the report's order, the cost
column runs: fifteen packets at 0.00, then CORAL J-19 JAPAN at 850.00, then
CORAL JPAV4 RED at 850.00, then CORAL NAV11 at 750.00 (205 packets, ₹73,89,494
in all). The seventeenth row equals the sum of the sixteen above it because
fifteen of them are zero and one is the same price. A subtotal of one number is
not a subtotal.

The rule now requires at least two non-zero rows among those it sums before a
row can be "the total of the rows above". Proved on two synthetic tables: a
genuine subtotal row after four priced rows is still caught; the ledger's shape
(fifteen zeros, 850, 850, 750) is not. The eight reports of defect 143 and the
two of defect 160 all had several priced rows above their doubled row, so the
rule still covers them.

Class: 189 (a checker's own false reading), found only because 506 let the
checker read the right page.

## 509. The receipt voucher's card described the sale form: a header link on 254 of 354 pages beat the ADD button

Reading `docs/transactions/vou-receipt-php.md` for the first as-built audit:
its §1 said the entry screen was `add_sales_voucher_combined.php?vtyp` — 311
inputs, 124 selects, resolved by "ADD-button target" — and its §3 listed the
sale form's 139 fields (purity rates, B2B, place of supply, ten cheques, ten
cards) as the receipt voucher's input fields. A card that describes the wrong
form is the one thing this programme exists to prevent.

`tools/transaction_card.py` resolved a list page's entry form by taking the
first navigation target that began `add_` or carried `vtyp=`. The sale form's
link, `add_sales_voucher_combined.php?vtyp=SALE`, is in the page header: it
appears on **254 of the 354 captured pages**, so every list page whose own ADD
button is not a plain link resolved to the sale form. The four voucher pages
reach their forms through script, and had done exactly that.

Fixed three ways, and every card regenerated:

1. **Links on 30% or more of the captured pages are never an entry form** — the
   header and the menu are excluded before the ADD-button rule runs.
2. **Name rules for the voucher family** — `vou_receipt.php` →
   `add_receipt_vou.php?voucher_no,vtyp` (captured: 117 inputs, 83 selects);
   `vou_payment.php` → `add_payment_vou.php` (48, 23); where the add form was
   not crawled, the edit form with the same fields is used and labelled so —
   `edit_contra_vou.php?v_id` (13), `edit_journal_vou.php?v_id` (10),
   `edit_sale_return.php?billno` (206), `edit_sales_vou_appr_return.php` (148).
3. **A map for six forms the catalog holds under names no rule reaches** (the
   three opening-stock forms, the repair-order form, the plain sale) and a
   last-resort rule for a page that is its own form — inputs beyond the search
   box, the date range and the per-row tick boxes: rate updates (344), split
   (337), merge (32), ledger merge (781), payroll (5), bank clearance (3).

Every card's §1 now names how its form was found. Fifteen say `NONE CAPTURED`,
which is the truth: no form for the eight purchase screens, receive-from-karigar,
mint, design, the year-end roll, SMS setup or sales approval was ever crawled,
and their §3 stays `TODO:` in full rather than borrowed from another screen.

Class: 465 / 495 / 496 / 497 — a fault visible only by reading the page. Here,
by reading the card.

## 510. A voucher cannot say what it settles: the legacy's 1,059 references were dropped at load and no screen takes one

The first as-built audit (`docs/transactions/vou-receipt-php.md` and its three
siblings, 2 September 2026) put the captured voucher forms against
`voucher.go`. The legacy receipt and payment forms carried a **Status** select
— On Account, Against Reference, Against Order, Advance — and a **Bill No**
box, stored together in `legacy.voucher_main.status` as `<kind>#<document>`.
Measured twice, by fill rate and by type:

	status filled                         1,059 of 1,848 vouchers
	  RCPT  269 of 269   Against Reference 83 (11 with the bill typed), On Account 56, Advance 21,
	                     Against Order 6 (4 with the order), and 103 whose status IS the bill number
	  PMNT  626 of 626   On Account 500, Against Reference 92 (20 typed), a payroll month 34
	  JRNL  164 of 624   Against Reference 20, Against Order 10, Advance 13, On Account 9,
	                     a payroll month 46, a bare bill 50, a bare scheme receipt 16
	  CNTR    0 of 31

So the shop said what a voucher settled on every receipt and every payment,
and on the journals that settle a card sale or a scheme instalment. Two things
lost it: `tools/legacy/load_vouchers.sh` never selected `status` (it is not
among the loaded columns; `mcj_vouchers` has no column for it), and the four

screen's own receipts are still tied to their bill through `mcj_sale_payments`;
a receipt raised on the receipt screen is not.

What the card proposes (§5, awaiting approval): a `settles` reference on
`mcj_vouchers` — kind and document number — filled from the form on receipts,
payments and journals; the loader re-run to carry the 1,059; an invariant that
a reference names a document that exists. Until then the balance screens are
right and the *against reference* screens the legacy had cannot be built.

Class: 233's cousin — the link between money and the document it settles,
present in the capture, absent from the load.

## 511. Ten cheques per voucher became one, and none on a receipt

The legacy receipt and payment forms took up to ten cheque rows (amount,
number, bank, ledger, date) and ten card rows, one line each in
`voucher_detail` with its own `chq_no` and `chq_date`:

	voucher_detail lines with a cheque number      593   (RCPT 144, PMNT 336, JRNL 113, CNTR 0)
	mcj_voucher_lines.cheque_number filled          593   (loaded; the second measurement)
	voucher_main header cheques                       34   (all PMNT — the vouchers with exactly one)

`voucher.go` takes one cheque number, date and bank per voucher, at the header
(`HasCheque`), and only on payments. A receipt by cheque — 144 legacy lines —
has nowhere to write the cheque number; a payment by three cheques writes one.
`mcj_voucher_lines.cheque_number` and `cheque_date` exist, are loaded, and are
written by no screen; the bank reconciliation reads them (`voucherprint.go`,
`reconcile.go` fall back to the line's reference), so the data model already
expects them per line.

Proposed on the cards: cheque number and date per grid line, on every kind;
the header pair stays for the single-cheque payment. No new column.

## 512. Card receipts lost their commission: 231 legacy lines on the swipe ledgers, and nothing computes the bank's cut

The legacy receipt form's card rows carried the swipe machine, the card type
(rate#tax#name from `card_wise_bank_commission`, 25 rows), the bank commission
and its service tax, and booked them. In the capture, measured by type and by
ledger:

	lines on swipe ledgers    231 = RCPT 86 + JRNL 145
	                          231 = Google Pay 11836 (150) + PAYTM 12560 (75) + CASHFREE 12489 (6)

The rebuilt grid can put a line on a swipe ledger, and the scheme instalments
of answer 233 do exactly that, but nothing computes or books the commission
the legacy took per card row. Severity MEDIUM: the money is not lost — the
bank's statement shows the net — but the commission expense is unbooked
until the bank statement is journalled by hand.

Proposed on the cards: a card block per line (machine, card type from a
commission master, commission and tax computed) — after 510 and 511, and
after `card_wise_bank_commission` has a loader (it has none today).

Class: 415/416 — a field the legacy had and the rebuild's generic form does not.
\n
## 513. A returned tag comes back on the shelf unguarded by count: the credit note's stock flip

The trade family's audit (`docs/transactions/vou-sale-return-php.md`, 2
September 2026). `creditnote.go` restores returned tags with

	UPDATE mcj_stock_items SET in_stock = true … WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND barcode = ANY($2) AND NOT in_stock

and then inserts a SALE-RET movement for every barcode named, whether or not
the UPDATE touched it. `checkTags` refuses a tag still on the shelf before the
save, so in one request the two agree; between two requests they need not, and
the sale screen's own flip checks `RowsAffected()` against the number of tags
for exactly this reason. Severity LOW: the movement would be the only trace,
and the invariant *every piece has a beginning* would not notice a second
"returned by customer" on a tag that never left again. The card requires
`TestCreditNote_ATagAlreadyOnTheShelfIsNotReturnedTwice` and the count check.

## 514. Credit and debit notes record no line: the legacy priced each returned item, the rebuild takes one amount

The legacy sale-return form is the sale form turned around: item grid, stone
grid, rate panel, making, certification — and its three returns fill them
(`sale_return_main` rate, making, purity, weights on 3 of 3; `sale_return_detail`
stones on 4 of 4). The three purchase returns do the same
(`purchase_return_main` item, purity, weights, value on 3 of 3). The rebuilt
credit note and debit note take **one amount** (`goods`) and, for a sale
return, the tags coming back; `mcj_credit_note_lines` was loaded with the six
legacy lines and is written by no screen (the same shape as 511's cheque
columns).

What is lost is the per-item value on a note of several items, and the weight
and purity of a returned item without a tag. Severity LOW: the tag carries
weight and purity, and the money is right. Recorded on both cards; the line
grid is a card decision for the reviewer, not a build.

## 515. A purchase makes no tag here: the legacy's 288 tags were born from a purchase bill

`legacy.barcode_main.voucher_no` names a GDP bill on 287 tags and a GCP bill on
1 tags (288 in all; `barcode_create_from_purchase_detail` holds 21 more rows
of the same link), so the legacy's purchase screen — never captured — created
the tags for what it bought, and the tag knew its bill. The rebuilt purchase
screen writes the bill and its contents and no tag; tags are made afterwards
on the tag screen with no link back to the bill, and `mcj_stock_items` has no
column for one. Severity LOW today (43 purchases, all migrated with their tags
already in place), and the card records the gap rather than proposes the
build: linking a tag to the bill it came from is a column and a step on the
tag screen, decided with the tag card (family H).

Class: 510 — a link between a document and what it produced, present in the
capture and absent from the rebuild.

**Corrected the same day, before the tag card was written.** The tag screen
does link a tag to the document it came in on: `tag.go` takes `source` (rec /
purc / stk / og, the legacy's `created_from`) and `came_on` — a picker over the
documents of that source (`arrivalDocuments`) — and writes
`mcj_stock_items.voucher_no` from it, exactly as the legacy did on 2,797 of
2,816 tags (STK 2,401, GDP 287, SR 45, RV 33, DP 28, OGP 2, GCP 1). What this
entry stands for is narrower than it first said: the purchase screen does not
create the tags for what it bought, so tagging a purchase is a second step on
the tag screen, where the legacy's screen (never captured; 21 rows in
`barcode_create_from_purchase_detail`) made them in one. No column is missing
and no link is lost. Severity: none — a design difference, recorded on the
purchase and tag cards.

## 516. A registered dealer's sale cannot be raised: twenty of the shop's bills went to SALE_B2B, this screen sends every sale to SALE

The GST sale's as-built audit (`docs/transactions/sales-voucher-gst-php.md`,
2 September 2026). The legacy sale form had a **B2B Sale** tick and a sales
ledger select; the capture shows what they did, twice over:

	legacy.sales_vou.b2b_sale = 1            20 of 224 bills
	legacy.sales_vou.sale_ldgr = 1014        20 of 224   (SALE_B2B)   — the same twenty
	legacy.sales_vou.sale_ldgr = 1016       204 of 224   (SALE)
	mcj_sales_invoices.is_b2b               20 of 224   (loaded)

`sale.go` has no B2B field, writes `is_b2b` as the literal `false`
(`mcj_sales_invoices` INSERT), and credits 1016 on every bill (`ledgerSale`).
The purchase side of the same rebuild does it right: a `b2b` tick and the 1012
PURCHASE_B2B ledger, "without exception" on the 43 bills (creditnote.go). The
sale side was built before that pattern and never caught up. Severity MEDIUM:
the GSTR outward report separates B2B from B2C on `is_b2b`, so a dealer's
sale raised here files as a retail sale.

Proposed on the card: a `b2b` tick (as on the purchase), `is_b2b` from it,
goods to 1014 when ticked, a `ledgerSaleB2B` constant added to the mandatory
accounts, and a rule *a B2B bill posts to 1014* (allowed 0).

## 517. A bill cannot name the order it delivers: 33 of 224 bills and 57 lines did

`legacy.sales_vou.order_no` is filled on 33 bills and `sales_vou_main.order_no`
/ `order_main_id` on 57 lines (measured by fill rate and by count). The legacy
sale form took **Order No** and carried the order's agreed rate and making per
line (`h_or_rate`, `h_or_making`, `h_or_value`). `sale.go` reads no order field
and `mcj_sales_invoices` has no column for one; the customer order screen
(`order.go`) closes an order on its own *deliver* action, unlinked to the bill
that did it. Severity MEDIUM: the two documents that are one event in the
shop's practice are two unrelated rows here, and the rate agreed on the order
is not what prices the bill (the bill prices at the day's rate or `agreed_`
typed again).

Proposed on the card: an `order_no` on the bill, validated against an open
order of the same customer, the order's agreed rate offered as `agreed_`, and
the order closed by the bill. Family F's card owns the other half.

## 518. One instrument per bill: eight of the shop's 149 paid bills took two to four

The legacy sale form took cash, up to ten cheques and up to ten cards on one
bill; `sale_pay_cash` (101), `sale_pay_card` (50) and `sale_pay_bank` (8) hold
159 rows for 149 bills — **8 bills paid by two, three or four instruments**
(the widest, four). `sale.go` takes one (`pay_mode`, `pay_amount`,
`pay_account`, `pay_instrument`, `pay_card_type`) and posts one RCPT; the rest
of a split payment must be a receipt voucher raised afterwards, which cannot
name the bill (defect 510) — so the bill shows a balance due that the
receipt has already paid. Severity LOW: 8 of 149, and the money is right on
the ledger.

Proposed on the card: the payment block as a small grid (mode, amount,
account, instrument, card type) posting one RCPT with a line per instrument,
`mcj_sale_payments` already being one row per instrument.

## 519. The sale has no failed-save test

`TestTrade_AFailedSaveDoesNotReportSuccess`, `TestOrder_…` and

`check_failed_saves.py` reads that; but the check reads the code, not the
behaviour, and the guarantee the test gives (the reason survives on the page,
no "current transaction is aborted" leaks) is untested here. Severity LOW; the
card requires `TestSale_AFailedSaveDoesNotReportSuccess` before `tested`.

## 520. A tag cannot say which lot it belongs to: 2,059 of 2,816 did

2,059 of 2,816 tags (73%), naming 59 distinct lots — the batch a piece was made

field, so every tag made here has none, and the column joins the class of 511
and 514 — loaded, unwritten. Severity MEDIUM: the hallmark and refinery screens
