## 521. A customer's goods are held by carats alone: their weight and purity were dropped

The party-sample audit (`customer-own-goods-php.md`). The legacy receipt took,
per line, pieces, carats, gross weight, metal purity and diamond purity, and
its seven lines fill all five (`customer_own_goods_receive_detail`: pcs, ct,
gw, metal_purity, diamond_purity 7 of 7; rate, value, shape, colour, loss,
wastage, fine weight, packet 0 of 7). `mcj_customer_goods` has `pieces` and
`carats`; `partysample.go` takes those two. A customer's gold piece left for
setting is therefore recorded with a carat weight and no gram weight and no
purity — the two things a dispute about it would turn on. Severity MEDIUM.

Proposed on the card: `gross_weight`, `metal_purity` and `stone_purity` on
`mcj_customer_goods`, the loader re-run for the seven, the receive grid
taking them; `TestPartySample_RecordsTheWeightAndPurity`.

**Corrected on review, the same day.** Read again with the seven rows in
front of me: `metal_purity` and `diamond_purity` are **0 on all seven lines**,
and `gw` equals `ct × 0.2` on all seven — the carat weight restated in grams,
not a second measurement. The seven lines are stones, and the rebuild's
pieces-and-carats record holds everything the legacy held for them. Nothing
was dropped. What remains true is narrower: the legacy form could also take a
gold piece with a gram weight and a purity, and the rebuilt screen cannot —
a limit to record on the card, not a loss in the data. Severity: none for the
seven; LOW for the day a customer leaves a gold piece.

## 522. A diamond's clarity was dropped at load and cannot be tagged: 416 of 819 stone lines carried one

`legacy.barcode_details.diamond_purity` — the clarity grade (IF, VVS, VS, SI …)

The register shell renders one parameter bar for every report: the parameters,
then Run, then the export link. 73 of the 134 registered reports declare no
parameters at all, so what those screens drew was a bordered box holding a
single button, and pressing it submitted an empty GET and re-fetched the

	  declaring at least one parameter                     61
	  declaring none — Run could not act                   73

the way to get the numbers, and on more than half of them it did nothing.

	links.go, gst_output_register_new.php  -> /mcj/reports/gst-register

## 528. Print a Tax Invoice and Voucher Print asked for a query string to be typed by hand

Both are reached from the menu with no query string, and both answered with the

	/mcj/voucher-print  "Give a voucher, for example ?type=RCPT&number=3&year=2026-2027"

That asks the shop to know a bill number — or a voucher type, number *and*

A sweep of all 253 registered navigation screens for entries sharing a URL, run

Also checked in the same sweep and clean: every one of the 133 report

## 533. Every image the application asks for answered 404, so the sidebar drew a broken icon where the logo belongs

Reported from the running app: the logo slot showed the browser's
broken-image glyph. Measured against the live server, signed in:

	/assets/css/*        200   (5 stylesheets)
	/assets/fonts/*      200   (3 faces)
	/assets/js/*         200
	/assets/images/logo-<hash>.webp          404
	/assets/images/logo-compact-<hash>.webp  404
	/assets/images/favicon.ico               404

Every other asset class serves. Only `images/` is missing, and for the reason
`internal/assets` already exists: the SDK's `modules/core/presentation/assets`
is a build output, gitignored upstream, so it is absent from the published Go
module. The stylesheet was lost this way once before — that is why
`internal/assets` and `TestLoginPageStylesheetsResolve` exist — and the images
were the other half of the same hole, never noticed because every page still
returned 200.

**Vendoring the files alone does not fix it.** `hashfs.FS.open` strips the hash
from a request only when it matches *its own* hash of that file:

	base, hash := fsys.ParseName(name)
	if hash != "" && fsys.HashName(base) == name { name = base }

The SDK hashes `images/logo.webp` from its own embed; a copy of a different file
in our embed hashes differently, so the SDK's URL still misses. The application
therefore provides the logo component itself — `assets.Logo()`, naming the files
by our hash — through an after-middleware on `constants.LogoKey`, which runs
later than the SDK's `Provide(LogoKey, DefaultLogo())` and earlier than
`middleware.ProvideDynamicLogo`, so a tenant that uploads its own logo still
wins. The favicon needed no component: the SDK asks for it unhashed.

The files are Nimbus Systems' own mark rather than a placeholder, built from
`Logo1.jpg` in the repository root: the white surround flood-filled away from
the four corners so the white strokes inside the mark survive, then fitted to
the boxes the SDK asks for — 96×96 for the collapsed sidebar, 300×100 for the
expanded one, where the square mark is centred on a 3:1 canvas because the img
carries `width="150" height="50"` as attributes and would otherwise be
stretched to them. The mark alone, with no wordmark, is what lets one image
serve both themes: the sidebar's surface tokens flip with the theme, and the
mark's green and blue both hold on white and on near-black.

`TestSidebarImagesResolve` in the smoke suite now fetches every image the
sidebar draws, the favicon included, and fails on a 404 or an empty body.

## 534. The captured menu's own note, "(direct)", was read as a subgroup and became 52 sidebar entries

Reported from the running app: the sidebar carried a group called *(direct)*.

`legacy_menu.csv` writes `(direct)` in the subgroup column for an item that
hangs straight off its top-level group — a note about the capture, not a name.
`loadLegacyMenu` took the column verbatim, and every `if e.Subgroup != ""` in
the tree builder then treated it as a real subgroup:

	legacy_menu.csv rows carrying "(direct)"          32
	links.go screens copying it into their Subgroup    3
	occurrences on one rendered page                  52

Fifty-two because the SDK repeats a group's name in its label, its tooltip and
its `aria-label`, so a screen reader announced "(direct)" as well. Seven groups
had one — Manufacturing, MIS Reports, Retail, Audit, GST Reports, DSS Report,
Imp Reports — and under each, screens that belong one level up sat one level
down inside a folder named after a note.

**Why no check caught it.** `check_menu_keys.py` asks whether every menu label
has an i18n entry. Each of the seven did:

	"manufacturing__direct": "(direct)"
	"mis-reports__direct":   "(direct)"
	...

The key existed, so the check passed; nothing looked at the value. The seven
entries are deleted with the groups they named.

`ownSubgroup` now maps the sentinel to "" at both boundaries — the CSV parse and
`Register`, so a screen placed by hand cannot reintroduce it either — and two
tests in the navigation package hold it there, one for a legacy screen
(MIS Reports › User Right Report) and one for a placed screen.

## 535. The sidebar gave a top-level menu the same rhythm as another menu's children, so nothing said where one ended

Reported from the running app: the menu has no clear division between one entry
and the next.

Read off the rendered page, the sidebar is:

	nav#sidebar-navigation > div > ul        the top-level menus
	  > div | > li                             one menu each
	      > details.group > ul.ml-4            that menu's children

Both lists carry the same `flex flex-col gap-2`, both rows the same
`btn btn-sidebar btn-md`, and the children are indented one rem and marked in no
other way. With Administration open, its seven children ran into Retail's header
at the same spacing as everything else, so Users and Roles read as peers of Setup
and Retail rather than as theirs.

Two rules in `internal/assets/css/mcj.css`, the application's own stylesheet,
loaded after the SDK's:

- a rule between one top-level menu and the next, suppressed when the sidebar is
  collapsed to a column of icons (Alpine puts `px-2` on the list in that state),
  where a line straight across reads as a divider between sections that are not
  there;
- a rail down the left of a group's children, at every depth the menu nests to —
  it nests three deep in places.

Nothing about what is in the menu, or the order it comes in, changes.

Getting the stylesheet loaded needed the same move as the logo in defect 533:
the SDK builds its whole head in one component with no slot to add to, so
`assets.Head()` renders `layouts.DefaultHead()` and follows it with the one
link, installed on `constants.HeadKey` by an after-middleware that runs later
than the SDK's own Provide.

The selectors are anchored to the nav rather than written against the classes,
because a child list carries the same classes as the top-level one; both were
checked against the live page's DOM before being written — 28 top-level entries
under the first list, 76 nested lists under `details.group`.

## 536. The landing page said 144 of 194 screens where the menu holds 193, and STATUS.md said 143 of 193

Reported from the running app: why does it show 144?

`statistics_report.php` is listed twice in the captured menu — MIS REPORTS ›
Statistics Report, and REPORTS › Sales Report › Statistics Report. One screen,
reachable from two places. `navigation.Progress()` counted a link once per
SECTION and then added the sections up, so that screen was two in the headline:

	menu rows carrying a link          195
	distinct links                     193
	  rebuilt                          143
	Progress() said                    144 of 194
	STATUS.md said                     143 of 193

The landing page was contradicting the status document in public, and nothing
compared them.

**The opposite error was hiding behind it.** `status_figures.py`'s `by_area`
deduplicated globally, so it credited Statistics Report to whichever section
came first in the file and not the other — REPORTS read **36 of 48** for a menu
that offers 49. One tool double-counted and the other under-counted, and the two
faults were in different figures so neither check saw the other.

The two counts now have their own rule, because they answer different questions:

- a SECTION counts what that section offers, so a screen two menus offer is
  counted by both — REPORTS is 37 of 49, corrected in `STATUS.md` and
  `screens.md`;
- the HEADLINE counts screens, so it is 143 of 193.

They therefore differ by one, and the page says so outright rather than leaving
a reader who adds the cards up to decide which figure to distrust:

	143 of 193 screens rebuilt from the previous system.
	One screen is counted in both the menus that offer it, so the cards add to 194.

`TestProgressCountsScreensNotMenuRows` counts the distinct links straight from
the CSV rather than through Progress, because a check that reuses the
arithmetic under test agrees with it however wrong it is.

## 537. There was no search on the page at all below 1024px, and never one in the sidebar

The SDK has a search — the spotlight — and it indexes the `Keywords` every
screen registers, which is what somebody hunting for "karigar" or "hallmark"
needs across 193 screens. It sits in the top bar inside `hidden lg:block`, so
below 1024px the page carried no search at all, and the sidebar — where a person
looks for one, and where all 193 screens are listed — never had it.

`internal/assets/js/mcj.js` adds a Search button as the first entry of the
sidebar list. It opens the SDK's own panel rather than being a second search:
the spotlight's Alpine component listens for ctrl/cmd-K on the WINDOW
(`@keydown.window="handleShortcut($event)"`), so dispatching that reaches it
wherever it is and whether or not the top-bar trigger is hidden.

Checked in a browser against the real script: the button is inserted, it is
first in the list, clicking it reaches a window keydown listener, and running
the installer again after an htmx swap leaves one button rather than two.

## 538. Eleven stand-ins said "not built" and did not say the data was on screen under another name

Of the fifty screens the old menu has and this system had not rebuilt, eleven
are covered by a screen that IS built — the register exists and only the entry
form is missing, or the same list is built under a newer legacy file name. Each
one's own `WouldChangeIt` said so:

	Nothing to view here -- see the screen named above.

but the page a visitor reached said only *not built*, and sent them away from
the screen that would have answered them.

**Five where BOTH the viewing and the entry are covered** are claimed against
that screen, the way `gst_input_register_new.php` is claimed against the GST
register: ledger_setting.php → Ledger Master, sales_voucher.php → GST Sale,
purchase_vou_sc_new.php and purchase_vou_co_new.php → the trade vouchers built
for PURC-GSC and PURC-GCO, karigar_full_ledger_detail.php → the karigar ledger
built under its `_new.php` name.

**Three of the five were then reverted, by this repository's own gate.**
`check_transaction_cards.py` refuses a screen built against a card marked
`decision: not built` whose `approved_by` is empty:

	sales-voucher-php.md:        decision: not built, approved_by: (blank)
	purchase-vou-sc-new-php.md:  decision: not built, approved_by: (blank)
	purchase-vou-co-new-php.md:  decision: not built, approved_by: (blank)

The gate is the point — a screen becomes built against an APPROVED card, and
approval is the shop's, not the builder's. Ledger Setting and the old Karigar
Ledger slot have no card and landed; the other three wait on three signatures.
Coverage 143 → **145 of 193**, and RETAIL stays 15 of 26 until they are signed.

**The remaining six** keep their stand-in and carry a new `SeeInstead` link —
*This is on screen elsewhere*, with a button straight to the built register.
Five of those six are the karigar and mint entry vouchers, which additionally
wait on questions 3.11–3.14; the sixth, Opening Stock Rate, waits on nothing but
a rate-master screen over `mcj_diamond_rates`.

Two of the five claims made a second menu entry share a URL, which
`TestNavigation_NoTwoEntriesOpenTheSameURL` (defect 532) caught on the next run.
Both are declared in its allow-list with the reason, alongside user-rights:
`/mcj/ledgers` and `/mcj/reports/karigar-ledger-detail` each answer two of the
old menu's names in full.

`mcj_problems.md` in the repository root lists all 48 remaining in plain
language, generated from `todo_screens.go` so the document cannot drift from the
list the application serves.


## 539. Nine legacy registers had no table and so had no screen, when what they were for was recoverable and their shape was not the missing part

Defect 538 left 48 screens standing in, each showing a page that said it was not
built and why. That is honest and it is nearly useless: a reader learns that the
screen is absent and nothing about what it was for, what it would have shown, or
whether they need it. Sixteen of the 48 stood in for the same reason — *no table
for this exists among the 149 the capture contains* — and that reason was taken
to settle the matter.

It does not. **A register's columns and filters are most of what a register
tells you**, and for nine of the sixteen both survive.

**What was measured.** Every table the capture's own reconstruction proposes for
these screens was searched for among all 149 recovered tables:

	purchase_approval                  absent
	purchase_approval_return           absent
	container_receive_detail           absent
	temp_purchase_register             absent
	temp_work_order_wise_stone_report  absent

Not empty — **absent**. So the reason the stand-ins gave was correct, and it was
also not the whole story: the parameter bars are in the captured HTML, which is
server-rendered, so the from/to pair each of these offered is **evidence, not
inference**. Only the columns are reconstructed, because the legacy filled these
tables by AJAX and the JavaScript did not survive.

**Built as shells** under decision 13: real columns, real filters, real export,
no rows, and a sentence on the page saying there is no table behind it *and that
the columns are a reconstruction*. Purchase Approval Register, Sales Approval
Register, Approval Pending Report, Purchase During Receive, Broken Stone Ledger,
TDS On Job Charge Register, Work Order Report, Work Order Wise Stone Report,
Work Order Wise Stone Balance. **148 → 157 of 193**; REPORTS 38 → 46 of 49 and
IMP REPORTS 2 → 3 of 3, which completes that area.

**The seven not built** are the ones where the capture does not say what the
columns were: the two barcode screens, the four studded and sample opening-stock
screens, and Discount Scheme Master. A screen that looked authoritative about a
system nobody can confirm is worse than the gap.

**Two things this got wrong on the way, both caught by the repository's own
checks rather than by me:**

**One — I recorded in the plan that empty shells were safe with the render
check.** They are not. `check_screens_render.py` fails a report that shows no
data over the whole of the shop's history, on the reasoning that *a report that
has stopped matching looks like one with nothing to say* — and all nine failed
it on the first run. The mechanism for this already existed and I had not read
far enough to find it: `KNOWN_EMPTY` takes a report key, **the placeholder the
page must show**, and the evidence. All nine are declared there. That is
stricter than an exemption would have been: a shell that stopped *saying* it has
no table now fails, and any of them that ever shows a row must come off the list.

**Two — `mcj_problems.md` claimed to be generated from `todo_screens.go` and was
written by hand.** It drifted the moment a screen landed. It is now genuinely
generated (`tools/gen_mcj_problems.py`, checked by `check_all.sh`), and the
first honest run of the generator **dropped two screens** — `karigar_gold_issue`
and `set_rate_sub_item` — because their fields are written as concatenated Go
strings across a dozen lines and the parser read line by line. The screen it
silently lost is **the one with ₹1.35 crore of gold behind it**. Reconciling the
generator's count against `check_todo_screens.py` is what caught it; the
generator alone would have printed a confident 34 and been wrong.

## 540. The screen called Backup returned the whole database to anyone who opened it, and this project's own copy of the data is that page's output

`back_up.php` sat under AUDIT and stood in here as *"a utility rather than a
screen with data behind it"*. That was true of the stand-in. It was not true of
the original.

**What opening that URL returned.** The entire database as SQL, in the HTTP
response body:

	1,28,628  INSERT statements
	37,389,767  bytes
	149  tables, including the five credential tables blocker B15 is about
	40,519  customer records

**It is not an inference, and the evidence is uncomfortable: this project's own
`gopiji/mcj_full_backup_2026-08-21.sql` IS that page's output.** The two files
have the same md5 over their first 200 bytes, end on the same bytes, and differ
in length by **121 bytes** — 37,389,767 against 37,389,646. The dump every
figure in this repository is measured from was obtained by fetching a web page.

That is the finding twice over. **For the legacy:** any account that could reach
one URL could take the whole shop — the customer list, the ledgers, and the SMS
and WhatsApp credentials — with no export permission, no audit record, and
nothing on any screen that would show it had happened. **For this rebuild:** a
faithful port of that screen would put it straight back, and "faithful to the
legacy" is the argument that would have carried it.

**Built instead** as the half worth having. The screen reports the row count of
every `mcj_` table — scoped to the tenant where the table carries one, whole
where it does not, in one query rather than a round trip each — and says plainly
at the top that it does not send the database to a browser, and why. **Checking
a backup is the real need**: a restore that brings back 83 tables where the shop
has 102 is a bad backup, and nothing else on any screen would have said so.
Taking the backup stays a server operation, where the file can be written to a
disk that is not the database's.

AUDIT is now **4 of 4**, complete.

## 541. There was no way for anybody in the shop to change a password

`change_psw.php`, SETUP › Retail Management, stood in for the same reason as
Backup and with the same mistake in it. It is not a utility. It was the only way
anybody in the shop could change a password without somebody opening the
database — and **blocker B15 is a list of passwords that need changing**.

The SDK does not provide one: its account controller covers the profile and the
session list and stops there, while `CheckPassword` and `SetPassword` sit on the
user aggregate unused by any screen.

**Built**, with the security decisions written down rather than assumed:

  * **It changes only the password of whoever is signed in.** An administrator
    resetting somebody's forgotten password is a different screen against a
    different permission. A screen that can change any password is worth
    attacking; this one is worth nothing to an attacker already signed in as you.
  * **It is the one screen here with no permission gate**, on purpose. Every
    other screen asks whether this user may see this data; this one only ever
    acts on the requester, so a permission could only take away somebody's
    ability to change their *own* password.
  * **The current password is checked first and alone.** Validating the new one
    first would let somebody at an unattended counter tell a correct password
    from a wrong one by which complaint came back.
  * **Nothing typed in is echoed back into the page.** A password in the HTML is
    in the page source, the browser's back cache and any proxy log between the
    counter and the server, which is the whole of what the screen protects.

**Tested five ways, and the harness had to be corrected to do it.** `itf.User`
builds a user with **no password at all**, and `CheckPassword` on an empty
password is false for every input — so the "a wrong password is refused" test
would have passed against a screen that refused nothing. The suite now signs in
a user whose password is known and asserts the user recognises it before
proceeding. `itf` also never writes the user to the database, so the save failed
on a foreign key that had nothing to do with the screen; the test seeds the
signed-in user. Falsified by making the screen save the OLD password: the test
reports *the OLD password still works after the change*.

## 542. Twenty-five screens were "not built" for four different reasons, and only one of them was a reason not to build

Asked to complete the thirty screens that still needed a transaction card, the
first useful thing was to stop treating them as one list. Every one carried a
`decision: not built` card, and the cards' own §12 sections divide them sharply:

	16 of 30   nothing open — buildable now
	13 of 30   blocked by 3.9 / defect 164 alone
	 1 of 30   blocked by 3.14 (does the shop use a mint at all)

**The thirteen are one question, not thirteen.** Defect 164 asks whether MA TARA
JEWELLERS still holds 869.850 g of 995 fine — ₹1.35 crore at today's rate — and
its third answer, *an abandoned trial*, makes every karigar screen
`decision: not built`. It is one of the five money questions decision 15
excludes from assumption, so building those thirteen would have meant asserting
that the gold is outstanding. **One answer unblocks fourteen screens** (the
thirteen plus Karigar / Dealer Studded Stock, which is karigar entry under
another name).

**Of the sixteen, eleven were built and five were not, for reasons worth
separating:**

**Three were aliases nobody had noticed.** A studded piece *is* a tag with
stones, and the built Tag Opening Stock screen writes `mcj_stock_stones` — all
819 stone lines the shop holds were entered that way. A party's studded stock
*is* the party's own stones held by the shop, which is `mcj_customer_goods`,
233 pieces and 14.43 carats. Neither needed building; both needed noticing.

**Two were a filter.** `raw_opening_stock.php` appears three times in the old
menu and is one screen over one table, separated by `holder`. Two were
stand-ins — and **the read was unfiltered**, so Own Raw Stock would have shown a
party's metal the day any existed. Correct today because all ten rows are `sh`;
wrong the moment the screens it was missing were used.

**Six were genuinely new** — Opening Stock Rate, the four approval vouchers,
and barcode split/merge — and each is recorded with what is measured and what
is borrowed. Three of the six take their shape from SRI GANESH because MCJ has
never performed the workflow, and every one of those cards says so in an
`assumption:` line rather than leaving it to be discovered.

**Five could not honestly be built, and the reasons differ:**

  * **SEND WHATSAPP and SMS ORDER SETUP** — this repository's own
    `check_no_credentials.py` forbids any `mcj_` column whose name reads like a
    secret, which is blocker B15 enforced in code. A credential settings screen
    cannot store credentials, so it is not a screen; it is deployment work.
  * **Export Sale and Exhibition Sale** — no such sale type exists in either
    capture, and an export sale's GST treatment (zero-rated under LUT, or IGST
    paid and refunded) is a tax decision. Now asked rather than assumed.
  * **Discount Scheme Master** — its captured page holds **no discount fields at
    all**, only the shared chrome: the export widget, the logout field and the
    state selector. The form was drawn by JavaScript that did not survive. Its
    columns are unrecoverable, and inventing them is what the sixteen
    no-table screens were spared for the same reason.

**Two findings inside the work:**

**A screen that was already built had an unfiltered read.** Own Raw Stock read
every row of `mcj_raw_stock` whatever its `holder`. Nothing was wrong with the
output because every row is the shop's own — the fault was invisible precisely
because the two screens that would expose it did not exist. Both the read and
the **delete** are scoped now: three screens sharing a table need the filter
that separates them on the way in to separate them on the way out, or the party
screen could remove the shop's own metal by being handed its line id.

**Adding a permission needs `seed-admin` re-run, and nothing said so.** The
Opening Stock Rate screen answered **403 to an administrator holding every
permission**, because a permission declared in the binary is not a permission
anybody holds. It is not a visible failure — the menu entry is simply absent —
so it is easy to deploy and believe the screen was never built. Now in
`deploy/README.md`.

**Three failures the quick suite could not have caught, found by the full one.**
`tools/check_all.sh --quick` skips the Go suite, so eleven screens were built
and committed against 23 green checks that never ran a Go test. The full suite
found three:

  * **`reports/approval.go` cast `$3` and `$4` on one use and not the other.**
    That is the rule this project has already written down twice —
    `TestSQL_ARepeatedParameterIsCastConsistently` exists because of defect 486
    — and it was reintroduced anyway. Postgres deduces a parameter's type from
    the uncast use and then fails at run time; the register would have worked
    empty and broken on its first row.
  * **Change Password's POST is not behind a permission**, and
    **its menu entry has no visibility policy.** Both were deliberate and
    neither was declared, which is the same thing as an accident to a checker.
    They are declared now, in the tests themselves, with the reasoning: the
    screen acts only on the user making the request, so a permission could only
    take away somebody's ability to change their own password, and a visibility
    policy could only hide the one screen every signed-in user may open. Any
    other ungated POST or policy-less entry still fails.

**A fourth, on the next run, and it was mine twice over.** Moving the three
approval registers onto a real table left my own phase-2 test still asserting
they say *there is no table behind this screen*. The test was right to fail: the
registers had changed what they claim and the test had not been told. It is
split now — six shells assert the no-table wording, three approval registers
assert the merely-unused wording, and **each asserts the OTHER wording is
absent**, so the two can never quietly converge on one message.

**What this says about the checks:** the 23 that pass in two minutes are worth
having and they are not the suite. A phase that ends green on `--quick` has not
been tested — it has been linted. The Go suite belongs at the end of every phase
that adds a controller, not at the end of the day's work. **Four real failures
accumulated behind that gap in a single day's work**, and three of them were in
code I had just written and believed verified.
